docs.title: About
docs.text:
LinkedIn | GitHub | Podcast | Email

Andrea Dainese works alongside organizations as a cybersecurity advisor with over 20 years of experience protecting critical infrastructure and industrial control systems (ICS/OT). He helps organizations define a concrete and effective security strategy, aligned with international standards, leveraging automation to scale compliance, defenses, and optimize operational processes.

Known in the technical community as the father of UNetLab (now EVE-NG), he is an author, podcast host, and active mentor for professionals looking to grow into CISO-level roles.

He also brings digital security awareness into schools, educating students and adults on how to recognize and defend against cyber threats.

For Andrea, hacking means understanding something deeply and making it better, and that includes oneself. After years of growing more sensitive to the cold, he decided to stop avoiding it and train for it instead. Cold-water immersion and daily cold showers became a practice in consistency and self-discipline, and a reminder that discomfort fades if you stay with it. He brings the same mindset to his work: understand the system, respect the process, and keep going.

docs.title: Series
docs.text:
Each series is a self-contained path. If you are new, start with the fundamentals and then pick the topic you need.

  • Ansible automation series

    This series is about Ansible, a tool that automates a wide range of IT tasks, from configuration management to application deployment, and simplifies the orchestration of complex infrastructures.

  • Cisco automation series

    This series explores how to automate Cisco infrastructures with APIs, SDKs, Terraform, Catalyst Center and plain Python. We start from the fundamentals and move to hands-on examples, covering network management, configuration compliance and device provisioning.

  • EVE-NG

    Ready to build your network automation lab? In this path, we’ll show you how to set up EVE-NG, the powerful network emulator, to create an effective testing environment. Ideal for all skill levels.

  • Fundamentals of network automation series

    This series covers the core principles of network automation, the essential tools and the practical techniques that streamline network operations. Whether you are new to the field or want to sharpen your skills, the posts provide the foundational knowledge you need. You can follow the series and support the work on Patreon.

  • ISA/IEC 62443, step by step

    This series collects what I learned in the ISA IC32 course on IEC 62443, the standard series for the cybersecurity of industrial automation and control systems. It has three goals: to give a big picture of the standard, to turn it into a strategy that we can implement step by step, and to help prepare for the exam.

  • Nautobot automation series

    Nautobot is an open-source Network Source of Truth and Network Automation Platform. It centralizes the data of a network infrastructure and lets us automate repetitive tasks, manage the network more efficiently and reduce human error.

  • OT/ICS series

    Securing and understanding Operational Technology (OT) and Industrial Control Systems (ICS) is more important than ever. This series explores hands-on lab setups, security best practices and key learning resources to help you build, test and protect critical infrastructure.

  • Palo Alto Networks automation series

    This series covers the automation of Palo Alto Networks products: Cortex XSOAR, firewalls and Strata Cloud Manager. Each post includes working examples that we can reproduce in a lab.

  • Threat Intelligence automation series

    Tracking and responding to cybersecurity threats manually is no longer enough. Automating threat intelligence streamlines detection, analysis and response. This series introduces MISP, an open-source threat intelligence platform, and shows how to install it, integrate it and use its indicators of compromise in a firewall.

  • UNetLab v3 development series

    UNetLab (Unified Networking Labs) is a comprehensive network emulation tool that allows users to build complex network topologies in a virtualized environment. It has been widely used by network engineers, IT professionals, and students to simulate real-world network scenarios without the need for physical hardware.

docs.title: Introduction to network automation with Ansible
Introduction to network automation with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

This series is about network automation with Ansible. It is designed to help you streamline operations, standardize workflows and manage multiple devices in significantly less time. Network automation is no longer just the domain of network engineers: it is expanding to include Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) teams.

Among the many automation frameworks, Ansible is an excellent choice: it does not require programming skills and has a relatively easy learning curve.

The Ansible Workbook for DevNetOps is the guide for the students of my network automation courses. It provides practical "recipes" to help you develop your own automations with Ansible. By the end of this series, you will be able to design and write Ansible playbooks that automate tasks across many network devices.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Become familiar with Ansible terminology.
  • Learn how to approach an automation project with Ansible.
  • Understand the pros and cons of Ansible.
  • Develop the skills to write Ansible playbooks and roles.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Some prerequisites are covered in other courses:

  • Automation fundamentals: Approaching automation projects.
  • DevOps fundamentals: Understanding the DevOps methodology and tools.
  • Infrastructure as Code: Managing infrastructure with coding practices.
  • Automation frameworks: We will focus on Ansible, but also discuss its pros and cons compared to other frameworks. The choice of framework should result from the needs of the project, not be a prerequisite.
  • Modeling: Abstracting infrastructure into data structures for automation.
  • Golden configurations: Approaches, pros and cons.
  • Templating: Tools for writing parameterized templates.
  • Text scraping: Converting human-readable text into data structures.
  • Parsers: Writing and modifying parsers for text scraping.

docs.title: Required Tools
docs.text:
You will need the following tools, described in a specific course:

  • A development server (Ubuntu Linux 22.04).
  • A programming language (Python 3.10).
  • A distributed version control system (Git).
  • A testing environment (EVE-NG).
  • An IDE (Visual Studio Code).

docs.title: Required Skill Sets
docs.text:
• Linux: Ability to install and configure.
  • Python: Ability to read and write simple scripts.
  • Git: Ability to manage repositories.
  • Vi/Vim: Ability to edit and exit.
  • RegEx: Ability to read and write simple regular expressions.
  • Jinja2: Ability to write simple templates.
  • Parsers: Ability to write and modify templates.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
Keep these essential points in mind:

  • Network automation engineers must often find documentation through research (e.g., searching the web or reverse engineering).
  • Network automation engineers need to write code and prototypes (sometimes called "spaghetti code").
  • Developers can turn prototypes into robust software, but that is not the job of network automation engineers.
  • Developers are better at writing code, but they often lack the networking skills and vendor knowledge needed to write network automation software.

docs.title: Preparing your Ansible environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Ansible is built on Python and can be installed easily with the package manager pip. The available functionality obviously depends on the Ansible version, which is closely tied to the Python version in use. The examples that follow assume Ansible core 2.15.10 and Python 3.10.

To set up your own development lab, refer to EVE-NG for DevNetOps, which describes it in detail. In particular, we will use the GitHub repository for the DevNetOps courses, available in /opt.

Let's prepare a dedicated Python environment and install Ansible:

python3.10 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r /opt/courses/requirements.txt

We can verify the installed version by running:

$ ansible --version
ansible [core 2.15.10]
  config file = None
  configured module search path = ['/home/dev/.ansible/plugins/modules', '/usr/share/ansible/plugins/modules']
  ansible python module location = /home/dev/venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/ansible
  ansible collection location = /home/dev/.ansible/collections:/usr/share/ansible/collections
  executable location = /home/dev/venv/bin/ansible
  python version = 3.10.13 (main, Oct 29 2023, 09:51:31) [GCC 9.4.0] (/home/dev/venv/bin/python3.10)
  jinja version = 3.1.3
  libyaml = True

docs.title: Introduction to Ansible Automation
docs.text: 01 August 2024

docs.title: Introduction to Ansible Automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Ansible is often described as an agentless automation framework. However, it relies on Python, which must be installed, together with certain modules, on the managed hosts. In this sense, Python acts as the necessary "agent" on the remote system.

Originally designed to automate Linux hosts, Ansible has expanded to support various systems, including Windows, network devices and security appliances.

In this series, we focus on automating network devices. In this case, Ansible really is agentless.

docs.title: Declarative vs. Procedural
docs.text:
There are two main approaches to automation: declarative and procedural.

  • Declarative approach: You define the desired state of a system. The automation system works out the steps needed to move from the current state to the desired one. Terraform is a popular example of this approach.
  • Procedural approach: You specify the exact steps the automation system must take to reach the desired state. This method is generally more intuitive, because it follows the way humans break a task into smaller sub-tasks. Troubleshooting is also simpler, because there is no underlying "magic." Ansible is a prime example of this approach.

Ansible is often considered a hybrid system, because some modules let you declare a desired state, which Ansible then translates into multiple sub-tasks. For instance, the community.vmware.vmware_guest module can create a virtual machine in a single task (declarative), but the VM depends on a vSwitch that must already exist (procedural).

A third concept is immutability: instances cannot be modified, and any change requires redefining the instance from scratch. It is common in container management and can be applied to network automation through golden configurations.

docs.title: Pros and Cons of Ansible
docs.text:
Knowing the strengths and weaknesses of Ansible helps you decide whether it is the right framework for your project.

Pros:

  • No Programming Skills Required: Playbooks are written in YAML, which is human-readable and requires no complex programming knowledge. This lowers the entry barrier: network engineers and administrators can automate tasks without learning a programming language.
  • Idempotency: Running a playbook multiple times leads to the same state on the managed hosts. This reduces the risk of errors and ensures consistency across deployments, which makes Ansible reliable in continuous integration and delivery pipelines.
  • Procedural Approach: Playbooks follow a step-by-step approach, which matches the way people naturally think about task execution. This makes them easier to write, understand and debug, and keeps the automation workflow clear and organized.
  • Integrated Documentation: Tasks can include names and comments, which serve as in-line documentation: the purpose of each task is clear without separate documentation files.
  • Compliance Checks: Playbooks can verify whether network devices or systems comply with predefined configurations, ensuring that they adhere to company policies and standards. This improves security and governance.
  • Standardization: Playbooks provide a standard way to execute tasks and manage configurations. This promotes consistency across environments and reduces the variability and errors of manual processes.
  • Reusable Code: Roles and collections can be reused across multiple playbooks. This encourages modular design, reduces duplicated code and saves time when maintaining the automation.
  • Sensitive Data Protection: Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive data such as passwords and API keys, so that they are not exposed in plain text in playbooks.
  • Troubleshooting: Individual steps can be isolated and run on their own to find and fix errors, so you can focus on the tasks that cause the problem.
  • Multiple Connection Methods: Ansible can connect to managed nodes via SSH, local connections, WinRM and network connections. This flexibility lets it manage a wide range of devices and platforms in diverse environments.
  • User Interfaces: Tools such as AWX and the automation controller (formerly Ansible Tower) provide graphical interfaces that simplify the execution and monitoring of playbooks, making large-scale automation easier to manage.

Cons:

  • Performance: Ansible can be slower than other automation tools, especially in large environments. Optimizing playbooks for speed requires specific strategies.
  • Complexity in Statements: Complex logic, such as conditionals (if-then-else) and loops, is not intuitive to write in a playbook. It makes playbooks harder to read and maintain, and it requires a deeper understanding of the syntax and capabilities of Ansible.
  • Troubleshooting: Debugging playbooks can be complex and time-consuming. Errors can be hard to trace, especially in large playbooks or complex workflows, and effective troubleshooting requires experience with Ansible.
  • Limited Callback Plugins: The options for customizing output and logging via callback plugins are limited. Ansible tends to operate as a stand-alone system, which makes it harder to integrate with some external monitoring and logging tools.
  • Breaking Changes: Major Ansible versions can introduce changes that break existing playbooks. Playbooks must be updated and tested continuously to ensure compatibility, which adds maintenance overhead.
  • Module Limitations: Ansible supports a wide range of platforms, but not equally well. Some platforms lack comprehensive module support, which requires custom modules or workarounds.

With these pros and cons in mind, you can decide whether Ansible is the right tool for your projects.

docs.title: Ansible Components
docs.text:
These are the core components of Ansible:

  • Data Format: YAML. YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) is a human-readable data serialization format used by Ansible to define playbooks and variable files. Its readability makes playbooks easy to write and understand without extensive programming knowledge, and its simple structure reduces the likelihood of syntax errors.
  • Templating: Jinja. Jinja is a templating engine for Python, which Ansible uses to render dynamic content in playbooks. With Jinja, you can use variables, control structures (such as loops and conditionals) and filters to generate configuration files or scripts dynamically, based on the needs of each host.
  • Parsers: TextFSM, NTC Templates, pyATS and TTP. Parsers are tools that Ansible uses to convert raw text into structured data.
  • Plugins: Python. Plugins extend the core functionality of Ansible: they are small pieces of Python code that add new capabilities.

Several interfaces can simplify playbook execution, such as:

  • Ansible Navigator: A command-line tool that improves the experience of running and troubleshooting playbooks.
  • Automation controller (formerly Ansible Tower): A web-based interface with enterprise features such as role-based access control, job scheduling and logging.
  • Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform: A complete enterprise framework for automating across IT operations, including security, network and infrastructure.
  • AWX: The open-source upstream project of the automation controller (formerly Ansible Tower), with a web-based interface and an API to manage playbooks.
  • ARA Records Ansible: A tool that records Ansible playbook runs and provides reporting and analysis.
  • eNMS: An open-source network management system that integrates with Ansible to provide automation and orchestration capabilities.

docs.title: Learning Approach
docs.text: We follow a learn-by-doing approach: we start with simple cases and expand them gradually. Documenting your work and keeping your set of recipes up to date will be invaluable for implementing specific scenarios in the future.

docs.title: Ansible inventory
docs.text: 02 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible inventory
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

The inventory is the source of truth for the information Ansible uses to connect to devices. It also allows defining variables at the host or group level. In advanced scenarios, variables can define all the infrastructure parameters, such as interfaces, IP addresses and router IDs.

Ansible supports both static and dynamic inventories. A static inventory is a file in INI or YAML format, while a dynamic inventory is an executable that prints JSON to standard output.

We must also select the correct protocol to communicate with the remote devices and the correct platform for each device. In the examples that follow, we connect to Cisco IOS devices, which require running commands over an SSH connection. We therefore need to set:

  • ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli, indicating that we use the CLI over an SSH channel;
  • ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios, indicating that we use the module written for Cisco IOS devices.

Initially, we assume that we can log in with a privileged user. We will address how to manage non-privileged users later.

docs.title: Static Inventory in INI Format
docs.text:
The static inventory in INI format has the following structure:

[all]
r1.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.21

[routers]
r[1:9].example.com

[routers:vars]
ansible_user=admin
ansible_ssh_pass=cisco
ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios

All devices belong to the group all and can then be added to other groups. We can also define variables at the host or group level.

We can verify the correctness of our inventory with the following command:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --list

docs.title: Static Inventory in YAML Format
docs.text:
The static inventory in YAML format has the following structure:

all:
  hosts:
    r1.example.com:
      ansible_host: 169.254.1.21

routers:
  hosts:
    r[1:9].example.com:
  vars:
    ansible_user: admin
    ansible_ssh_pass: cisco
    ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
    ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios

We can verify the correctness of our inventory with the following command:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list

docs.title: Dynamic Inventory in JSON Format
docs.text:
As described earlier, a dynamic inventory must write the inventory to standard output, in JSON format, with the following structure:

{
    "_meta": {
        "hostvars": {
            "r1.example.com": {
                "ansible_host": "169.254.1.21"
            }
        }
    },
    "routers": {
        "hosts": [
            "r1.example.com"
        ],
        "vars": {
            "ansible_connection": "ansible.netcommon.network_cli",
            "ansible_network_os": "cisco.ios.ios",
            "ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco",
            "ansible_user": "admin"
        }
    }
}

Now suppose that our inventory is stored in the following CSV file:

FQDN;IP Address;Groups
r1.example.com;169.254.1.21;routers
r2.example.com;169.254.1.22;routers
sw1.example.com;169.254.1.101;switches,core
sw2.example.com;169.254.1.102;switches,core
sw3.example.com;169.254.1.103;switches,access
sw4.example.com;169.254.1.104;switches,access
sw5.example.com;169.254.1.105;switches,access
sw6.example.com;169.254.1.106;switches,access

We can write a simple Python script that creates the inventory dynamically. First, let's create the inventory structure:

inventory = {
    "_meta": {
        "hostvars": {},
        "vars": {
            "ansible_connection": "ansible.netcommon.network_cli",
            "ansible_network_os": "cisco.ios.ios",
        },
    },
    "routers": {
        "hosts": [],
        "vars": {"ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco", "ansible_user": "admin"},
    },
    "switches": {
        "hosts": [],
        "vars": {"ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco", "ansible_user": "admin"},
    },
    "core": {
        "hosts": [],
    },
    "access": {
        "hosts": [],
    },
}

For now we do not worry about security: handling passwords is deferred to a later lesson.

Next, we read the CSV file line by line:

with open(INVENTORY_CSV, "r") as fh:
    csv_reader = csv.reader(fh, delimiter=";", dialect="excel")
    next(csv_reader, None)  # skip first row (header)

    for row in csv_reader:
        # Parse each row

For each row, we populate the structure described earlier:

fqdn = row[0]
ip_address = row[1]
groups = row[2].split(",")

# Add device to group "all"
inventory["_meta"]["hostvars"][fqdn] = {"ansible_host": ip_address}

for group in groups:
    # Add device to group
    inventory[group]["hosts"].append(fqdn)

Finally, we print the inventory in a readable format to standard output:

# Print inventory
print(json.dumps(inventory, sort_keys=True, indent=2))

We can verify the correctness of our inventory with the following command:

python3 inventory.py
ansible-inventory -i inventory.py --list

This provides a flexible and scalable way to manage inventories for network automation with Ansible.

The inventories used in this article can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: Ansible configuration
docs.text: 05 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible configuration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Ansible typically works out of the box, without additional configuration. Advanced usage, however, may require some customization. Ansible can be configured through files or variables.

For example, the DEFAULT_HOST_LIST parameter defines the inventory file. The official documentation specifies:

  • Default: The default value when not specified otherwise (/etc/ansible/hosts).
  • INI: How to specify the parameter in an INI configuration file (in this case, the section is [defaults] and the parameter is inventory).
  • Environment: The environment variable used to specify the parameter (ANSIBLE_INVENTORY).

If you configure Ansible through INI files, there are four options:

  • Use the file at /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg.
  • Use the file ~/.ansible.cfg in the home directory.
  • Use the file ./ansible.cfg in the current directory.
  • Use the file defined by the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable.

The DEFAULT_HOST_LIST parameter can also be specified on the command line with -i. Additionally, some parameters can be defined within a playbook.

Ansible applies a precedence to decide which value to use when a parameter is specified more than once. The order is:

  • Configuration settings.
  • Command-line options.
  • Playbook keywords.
  • Variables.

Lower items in the list override higher ones.

There are handy utilities to get general and specific information about your environment:

  • ansible-config list: Lists all possible variables and how to configure them.
  • ansible-config dump: Prints the current value of each variable.
  • ansible-config init > ansible.cfg: Creates a sample configuration file (comprehensive but complex).
  • ansible-config view: Verifies and prints the current configuration.
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST:
  default: /etc/ansible/hosts
  description: Comma separated list of Ansible inventory sources
  env:
  - name: ANSIBLE_INVENTORY
  expand_relative_paths: true
  ini:
  - key: inventory
    section: defaults
  name: Inventory Source
  type: pathlist
  yaml:
    key: defaults.inventory

Let's check the current configuration of the DEFAULT_HOST_LIST variable:

$ ansible-config dump | grep DEFAULT_HOST_LIST
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST(default) = ['/etc/ansible/hosts']

Now let's change it with an environment variable and verify the result:

$ export ANSIBLE_INVENTORY=inventory.yml
$ ansible-config dump | grep DEFAULT_HOST_LIST
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST(env: ANSIBLE_INVENTORY) = ['/Users/dainese/inventory.yml']

As we will see later, ansible-navigator is a useful tool: it shows the configuration and highlights the variables that change the default behavior:

docs.title: Configuring SSH
docs.text:
One case needs careful handling: automating obsolete devices via SSH. Two parameters matter here:

  • ANSIBLE_HOST_KEY_CHECKING: Set it to False to skip the host key checking performed by the underlying tools Ansible uses to connect to the host. In other words, it disables host verification. It can be configured in both the [defaults] and [paramiko_connection] sections.
  • PARAMIKO_LOOK_FOR_KEYS: Set it to False to disable the search for private key files. In other words, it disables private key authentication. It can be configured in the [paramiko_connection] section.

Ansible can use either Paramiko or LibSSH to connect to remote devices via SSH. By default, LibSSH is used if available; otherwise Paramiko is used.

To force Paramiko, use the following configuration:

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = paramiko

[paramiko_connection]
host_key_checking = true
look_for_keys = true

To increase performance or to meet specific constraints, you can force LibSSH:

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = libssh

[libssh_connection]
host_key_checking = False
look_for_keys = False

docs.title: SSH Access to Obsolete Devices
docs.text:
When accessing very old devices, such as those in a lab, you might encounter the following error:

Unable to negotiate with 169.254.1.21 port 22: no matching key exchange method found. Their offer: diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

This occurs because the device supports only weak key exchange algorithms, which the system you are connecting from no longer accepts. Edit the ~/.ssh/config file to re-enable them, knowing that this weakens the security of your environment:

KexAlgorithms +diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

On macOS, the + symbol is not recognized, so you must specify the entire list of algorithms:

KexAlgorithms diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1,diffie-hellman-group1-sha1

docs.title: pylibssh on macOS
docs.text:
The pylibssh library is generally installed with the following command:

pip install ansible-pylibssh

On macOS, you might encounter the following error:

Failed to import the required Python library (ansible-pylibssh)

This happens because ansible-pylibssh, although it appears to be installed correctly (pip freeze | grep pylibssh), does not work. You need to install it from source:

sudo xcode-select --install
brew install libssh libssh2
export CFLAGS="-I $(brew --prefix)/include -I ext -L $(brew --prefix)/lib -lssh"
git clone https://github.com/ansible/pylibssh.git ~/src/pylibssh
pip install ~/src/pylibssh/

docs.title: Ansible ad hoc commands
docs.text: 03 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible ad hoc commands
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Ansible can execute single commands without building a playbook. This mode is called ad hoc and is useful for one-time commands in very specific scenarios.

Let's open the Simple Network Lab and start R1. Make sure the router is up and reachable:

$ ping -c3 169.254.1.21
PING 169.254.1.21 (169.254.1.21) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 169.254.1.21: icmp_seq=1 ttl=255 time=0.515 ms
64 bytes from 169.254.1.21: icmp_seq=2 ttl=255 time=0.539 ms
64 bytes from 169.254.1.21: icmp_seq=3 ttl=255 time=0.522 ms

--- 169.254.1.21 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss, time 2051ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.515/0.525/0.539/0.010 ms

If it is not, connect to the console and check that it is powered on, configured and has the correct IP address.

Now let's run ping in ad hoc mode:

$ ansible all -m ping
r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}
r2.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}

We immediately notice that R2 appears to be active even though it is not powered on. This happens because the command we used is not a real ping, but a connectivity test performed via SSH, which checks the access and the presence of a usable Python interpreter on the remote host. This is the classic mode used to manage Linux systems, but as we have seen, we are working with network devices, and here the behavior changes significantly. In particular, Ansible uses a local Python interpreter, and for this reason the ping module does not work as expected.

The correct module is net_ping, which requires the destination IP address. In our case, it is the IP address of the node itself, defined in the ansible_host variable:

$ ansible all -m net_ping -a "dest='{{ ansible_host }}'"
r2.example.com | FAILED! => {
    "changed": false,
    "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: Failed to resolve hostname r2.example.com (Name or service not known)"
}
r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "commands": "ping ip 169.254.1.21",
    "packet_loss": "0%",
    "packets_rx": 5,
    "packets_tx": 5,
    "rtt": {
        "avg": 1,
        "max": 1,
        "min": 1
    }
}

In the example, dest is set to the value of ansible_host using Jinja syntax. We also see that an IOS command was executed, not a Linux one. We are not pinging R1 from the Ansible host: we are running a ping command on R1 itself, which pings its own interface.

There is no simple fix, and the reason is that we are asking the wrong thing of Ansible: it is not a monitoring system, but a task execution system. Tasks fail if the system is unreachable, and that is enough for our needs.

In the last example, we run the show version command:

$ ansible r1.example.com -m ios_command -a "commands='show version'"
r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "stdout": [
        "Cisco IOS Software, Linux Software (I86BI_LINUX-ADVENTERPRISEK9-M), Version 15.7(3)M2, DEVELOPMENT TEST SOFTWARE\nTechnical Support: http://www.cisco.com/techsupport\nCopyright (c) 1986-2018 by Cisco Systems, Inc.\nCompiled Wed 28-Mar-18 11:18 by prod_rel_team\n\nROM: Bootstrap program is Linux\n\nR1 uptime is 5 minutes\nSystem returned to ROM by reload at 0\nSystem image file is \"unix:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/i86bi_LinuxL3-AdvEnterpriseK9-M2_15\"\nLast reload reason: Unknown reason\n\n\n\nThis product contains cryptographic features and is subject to United\nStates and local country laws governing import, export, transfer and\nuse. Delivery of Cisco cryptographic products does not imply\nthird-party authority to import, export, distribute or use encryption.\nImporters, exporters, distributors and users are responsible for\ncompliance with U.S. and local country laws. By using this product you\nagree to comply with applicable laws and regulations. If you are unable\nto comply with U.S. and local laws, return this product immediately.\n\nA summary of U.S. laws governing Cisco cryptographic products may be found at:\nhttp://www.cisco.com/wwl/export/crypto/tool/stqrg.html\n\nIf you require further assistance please contact us by sending email to\nexport@cisco.com.\n\nLinux Unix (Intel-x86) processor with 863257K bytes of memory.\nProcessor board ID 73402369\n4 Ethernet interfaces\n1024K bytes of NVRAM.\n\n\n\nConfiguration register is 0x0"
    ],
    "stdout_lines": [
        [
            "Cisco IOS Software, Linux Software (I86BI_LINUX-ADVENTERPRISEK9-M), Version 1
[...]

The output shows the result of the command for R1.

docs.title: Ansible Playbooks and variables
docs.text: 15 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible Playbooks and variables
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

A playbook is a YAML file that lists, in sequence, the operations to perform on a device or a group of devices. Each playbook is made of one or more plays, which can include pre_tasks, tasks, and post_tasks.

Variables play a crucial role when planning and writing playbooks. They can be defined at different levels: configuration, playbook, inventory, environment, files or facts. It is helpful to have a way to print the value of all the defined variables.

Let's start by opening the Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology lab and making sure that all devices are active and reachable.

docs.title: Printing All Variables
docs.text:
As we know, a playbook is a YAML file containing a list of plays. Each play defines the operations to perform and where to run them:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: PRINT DEBUG VARIABLES
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: true
  pre_tasks:
    - ...
  tasks:
    - ...
  post_tasks:
    - ...

The example above defines a play with the general lists pre_tasks, tasks, and post_tasks. The play runs on all the inventory objects (all) and collects facts before running any task. Gathering facts can slow down the play, but it is essential for our purpose.

The first line, known as the "shebang", lets you run the playbook file directly, without specifying the ansible-playbook interpreter manually. As the names suggest, pre_tasks and post_tasks group the tasks that must run before all the others and just before the end of the play, respectively. In this example, we focus only on the tasks.

The targets of the playbook are defined by the hosts key, which can select all the hosts in the inventory (all), specific groups or individual hosts. Some examples:

  • all: selects all hosts in the inventory;
  • r1.example.com: selects only R1;
  • routers,switches: selects hosts in the routers or switches groups;
  • routers,!switches: selects hosts in the routers group but not in the switches group.

Now let's write a playbook that prints all the variables. The variables we want to print are grouped into:

  • Module variables (vars).
  • Environment variables (environment).
  • Group names variables (group_names).
  • Groups variables (groups).
  • Host variables (hostvars).

We define five tasks to print these variables:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: PRINT DEBUG VARIABLES
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: true
  tasks:
    - name: PRINT MODULE VARIABLES (vars)
      tags: modules
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ vars }}"
    - name: PRINT ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES (environment)
      tags: environment
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ environment }}"
    - name: PRINT GROUP NAMES VARIABLES (group_names)
      tags: group_names
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ group_names }}"
    - name: PRINT GROUPS VARIABLES (groups)
      tags: groups
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ groups }}"
    - name: PRINT HOST VARIABLES (hostvars)
      tags: hosts
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ hostvars }}"

Each task uses the ansible.builtin.debug module to print the msg parameter, set to the content of vars, environment, group_names, groups and hostvars.

If Ansible is correctly configured and the playbook is executable, running it is straightforward:

$ ./playbook-print_all_vars.yml
TASK [PRINT HOST VARIABLES (hostvars)] *****************************************
ok: [sw1.example.com] => {
    "msg": {
        "r1.example.com": {
            "ansible_check_mode": false,
            "ansible_config_file": "/home/dev/courses/Ansible/07. Playbooks/ansible.cfg",
            "ansible_connection": "ansible.netcommon.network_cli",
            "ansible_diff_mode": false,
            "ansible_facts": {},
            "ansible_forks": 5,
            "ansible_host": "169.254.1.21",
            "ansible_inventory_sources": [
                "/home/dev/courses/Ansible/07. Playbooks/inventory.ini"
            ],
            "ansible_network_os": "cisco.ios.ios",
            "ansible_playbook_python": "/home/dev/venv/bin/python3.10",
            "ansible_run_tags": [
                "all"
            ],
            "ansible_skip_tags": [],
            "ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco",
            "ansible_user": "admin",
            "ansible_verbosity": 0,
            "ansible_version": {
                "full": "2.15.10",

The output shows many available variables but, for example, none containing the domain of the devices (example.com).

The facts include, for instance:

            "ansible_net_hostname": "SW6",
            "ansible_net_image": "unix:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/i86bi_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.SS",
            "ansible_net_iostype": "IOS",
            "ansible_net_operatingmode": "autonomous",
            "ansible_net_python_version": "3.10.13",
            "ansible_net_serialnum": "73412614",
            "ansible_net_system": "ios",
            "ansible_net_version": "15.2(CML_NIGHTLY_20190423)FLO_DSGS7",

As we saw earlier, Ansible works differently when managing network devices (network_cli). Here the facts are gathered with the cisco.ios.ios_facts module, which depends on the ansible_network_os in use. If we switch to another device and module, the behavior might differ.

docs.title: Limiting Execution
docs.text:
During development, and in general use, it helps to limit the execution to specific hosts or groups, and to particular parts of the playbook. Some examples:

./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --limit sw1.example.com
./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --limit switches
./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --limit 'switches,!sw1.example.com'

The three examples above run the playbook only on:

  • The host sw1.example.com.
  • Hosts in the switches group.
  • Hosts in the switches group, except sw1.example.com.

To limit the execution to parts of the playbook, we use tags. Tasks and roles can be associated with tags: if we assign a specific tag to each task, we can limit the execution to a single task:

./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --tags groups

There are also special tags:

  • always: tasks with this tag are always executed unless the --skip-tags always parameter is specified.
  • never: tasks with this tag are never executed unless the tag is explicitly specified (--tags never).

docs.title: Configuring NTP with ios_ntp_global
docs.text:
Now that we have seen how to create a playbook, let's take it further and create our first role. A role is a reusable set of tasks that can be shared across playbooks. It has a specific structure and is typically stored in the roles directory. Roles are executed after pre_tasks but before tasks.

Let's create the skeleton for our first role, which will configure NTP on Cisco IOS devices:

ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_ntp

The structure includes several directories that we will explore in later lessons. For now, we only need the tasks directory, which contains the list of operations to perform.

In this role we use ios_ntp_global and, before starting, we always read the official documentation. The examples show that the module configuration can become quite complex: we keep it simple and only configure two NTP peers.

Before developing the role, we need to decide how to model the variables used to configure the NTP peers. For simplicity, let's assume two variables holding the IP addresses of the two NTP peers: ntp_server_1 and ntp_server_2.

- name: CONFIGURE NTP PEERS
  cisco.ios.ios_ntp_global:
    config:
      peers:
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_1 }}"
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_2 }}"
    state: replaced

Next, we create a playbook that calls the role we just wrote:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10
  roles:
    - role: cisco_ios_ntp

We run the playbook and check that the idempotence property is satisfied:

  • The first run should configure (status changed) the two IP addresses (verify with show running-config | include ntp);
  • The second run should confirm what was done (status ok);
  • If we change an IP address, the run should add the missing IP address and remove the one that is no longer needed (verify with show running-config | include ntp).

The third point is not met. This happens because the module uses the merged state, which combines the current and the intended configuration. What we want requires the replaced or overridden state.

After modifying the role and testing again, it behaves as expected.

docs.title: Saving the Configuration
docs.text:
By default, the Ansible modules for Cisco IOS do not save the configuration. Let's see how to save it easily and only when necessary. We again refer to the ios_config module and its official documentation: the save_when option can be used even without making any configuration change. We can either create a dedicated role or use post_tasks. We choose the latter, because saving the configuration is a task that ideally runs at the end of the play.

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10
  roles:
    - role: cisco_ios_ntp
  post_tasks:
    - name: SAVING CONFIG
      tags: always
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: modified

We also added the always tag, because we want the configuration to be saved every time.

Repeating the tests, everything now works as expected.

docs.title: Ansible Galaxy and Collections
docs.text:
You might need modules that are provided by external collections, which can be managed with ansible-galaxy. For example, to list all the installed collections:

ansible-galaxy collection list

To update a specific collection:

ansible-galaxy collection install -U cisco.ios

It is good practice to track the collections you use, and their versions, in a collections/requirements.yml file:

collections:
  - name: cisco.ios
    version: 8.0.0
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com

You can install all the collections specified in the file with a single command:

ansible-galaxy collection install -U -r collections/requirements.yml

Later, we will see how to create and publish your own collection on Ansible Galaxy.

The playbooks used in this article can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: Defining and using variables in Ansible
docs.text: 01 September 2024

docs.title: Defining and using variables in Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Variables in Ansible can be defined in various ways, which gives you flexibility in managing configuration and customizing playbooks.

Defining Variables in the Playbook: one simple and direct way is to include the variables in the playbook itself:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  vars:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

In this example, the variables ntp_server_1 and ntp_server_2 are defined within the playbook.

Defining Variables in a Configuration File: to keep playbooks cleaner and manage the configuration separately, variables can be defined in an external file:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  vars_files:
    - config.yml

The config.yml file contains the variable definitions:

ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

Defining Variables in the Inventory: variables can also be defined directly in the inventory, and applied to all hosts or to specific groups:

[all:vars]
ntp_server_1=194.239.208.213
ntp_server_2=130.60.204.10

This option is useful when you want to apply the same configuration to multiple hosts.

Defining Variables at the Role Level: variables can also be defined within roles, which makes them available only when the role is used:

# roles/cisco_ios_ntp/vars/main.yml
ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

Defining Variables at the Host or Group Level: you can define variables specific to a single host or to a group of hosts with host_vars and group_vars files, respectively:

  • host_vars/sw1.example.com
  • group_vars/all.yml

Using the set_fact Module: variables can also be created dynamically while a playbook runs, with the set_fact module:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

docs.title: Accessing Variables from Other Hosts
docs.text:
In some cases, you need to access the variables of another host while a playbook runs. You can do it with the hostvars syntax:

hostvars['sw2.example.com']['ansible_host']

docs.title: Storing the Output of a Task
docs.text:
To store the output of a task in a variable, you do not use set_fact: you use the register parameter in the task whose output you want to capture:

- name: GETTING NTP CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "show running-config | include ntp peer"
  register: show_run_ntp_peer

docs.title: Ansible statements
docs.text: 16 September 2024

docs.title: Ansible statements
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible jinja2

If you have some experience with programming languages, you might find the constructs of Ansible a bit clunky. Let's break them down with practical examples.

docs.title: Conditionals (if, then, else)
docs.text:
In Ansible, the if-then-else construct is simplified to a single word: when.

- ansible.builtin.command: /sbin/shutdown -t now
  when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == "Debian"

Unlike traditional languages, there is no else or elif: you handle those cases with separate when statements and the right expressions.

If several conditions must all be true at the same time (logical AND), list them:

- ansible.builtin.command: /sbin/shutdown -t now
  when:
    - ansible_facts['distribution'] == "CentOS"
    - ansible_facts['distribution_major_version'] == "6"

Each variable in Ansible can be one of the following types:

  • List.
  • Dictionary.
  • Boolean (True/true/yes/on or False/false/no/off).
  • Integer.
  • Float.
  • String (if wrapped in quotes, or if it does not fit the other types).

Ansible relies heavily on Jinja, which adds some complexity. Any variable created with Jinja is treated as a string, and you often need to convert it before use. Sometimes, however, Ansible does it for you: for example, it automatically converts a string containing JSON into a list or a dictionary when it is used in a loop.

In short:

  • Variables can be either defined or undefined.
  • A defined variable can be empty (None) or hold data.
  • The type of a variable depends on the data it holds (Ansible uses weak typing).
  • Jinja often produces strings, which may need to be converted.
  • Ansible automatically converts strings into lists or dictionaries when needed.
  • Before mathematical operations, convert variables explicitly with Jinja filters such as | int or | float.

The best approach is to always check how Ansible handles each case. You can use debug tools to inspect the type and the value of your variables:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "Type of var is {{ var | type_debug }}"
- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "Content of var is {{ var }}"

For more details and examples, see the official Ansible documentation.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
A block is a group of tasks. Blocks can be used to:

  • Group tasks that share the same when condition.
  • Handle errors with the rescue and always directives.
- block:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ value | int }}"
  rescue:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Value is not defined"

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
A loop can be applied to lists or dictionaries to iterate over their elements and perform an action on each of them. There are two important considerations:

  • Using loops directly impacts performance.
  • A loop can only be applied to a single action, not to a group of actions.

For simplicity, let's look at three common approaches and leave deeper insights to the official documentation.

With with_items, you iterate over a list of elements. In each iteration, by default, the item variable takes the value of the current list element:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ item }}"
  with_items:
    - red
    - green
    - blue

With with_dict, you iterate over a dictionary. In each iteration, item.key and item.value hold the key and the value of the current key-value pair:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ item.value }} is {{ item.key }}"
  with_dict:
    red: tomato
    green: grass
    blue: sky

Ansible later standardized loops with the loop construct. Out of habit, I still tend to use with_items and with_dict, which feel more straightforward to me, but loop can be more useful in complex scenarios.

docs.title: Nested Loops
docs.text:
We have already seen how to implement loops in Ansible. Sometimes, however, you need loops within loops (nested loops) or loops over groups of tasks. In both cases the solution is similar and uses external files:

- ansible.builtin.include_tasks: sub_task1.yml
  with_items:
    - macos
    - windows
    - linux
  loop_control:
    loop_var: os_item

In this example, we iterate over a list and call an external task file, sub_task1.yml. All the tasks in this file can use the variable os_item, which takes each value of the list.

When I call an external task file, I always prefer to specify the variable name explicitly. This avoids confusion and prevents the variable from being overwritten by loops inside the external file.

docs.title: Until
docs.text:
Finally, let's look at how to execute a task until the desired result is achieved:

- ansible.builtin.shell: /usr/bin/foo
  register: result
  until: result.stdout.find("ready") != -1
  retries: 5
  delay: 10

In this example, we run a (fictional) command until the output contains the word ready. The execution stops with an error after 5 failed attempts, with 10 seconds between attempts.

docs.title: Configuring NTP with ios_config
docs.text:
Let's see how to configure NTP peers with the ios_config module. Before writing the playbook, we review the official documentation and think about how we would configure NTP peers manually. The typical process is:

  • Configure the NTP servers.
  • Verify the NTP servers configured on the device.
  • Remove any NTP servers configured on the device that are not in the desired NTP server list.

We now write a role that performs these three steps exactly as described.

First, following the official documentation, we add the missing NTP peers:

- cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - "ntp peer {{ ntp_server_1 }}"
      - "ntp peer {{ ntp_server_2 }}"

Next, we need to remove any unnecessary NTP peers. When working manually, we would retrieve the running-config to check for unknown addresses. In Ansible, we do something similar:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "show running-config | include ntp peer"
  register: show_run_ntp_peer

The register option saves the output into a variable that we define. If we print this variable with debug, we can analyze its structure.

The output is in JSON format and contains the raw output (stdout) and the output split into lines (stdout_lines). Both are arrays because multiple commands can return output at the same time.

For convenience, we extract only the NTP peer IP addresses into specific variables:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    current_ntp_peers: "{{ show_run_ntp_peer['stdout'][0] | regex_findall('^ntp peer .*$', multiline=True) | regex_replace('ntp peer ', '') }}"
    expected_ntp_peers:
      - "{{ ntp_server_1 }}"
      - "{{ ntp_server_2 }}"

The current_ntp_peers variable stores all the lines starting with ntp peer. Before saving, the prefix ntp peer is removed, which leaves a list of only the NTP peer IP addresses.

Note: if any of our IP addresses is configured as preferred, the configuration becomes more complex.

At this point, we need to compare the current configuration with the expected one and remove any unnecessary peers. Specifically, we compare each element of the configuration, and if it is not in the expected NTP peer list, we remove it:

- name: REMOVING NTP PEERS
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - "no ntp peer {{ item }}"
  with_items: "{{ current_ntp_peers }}"
  when: item not in expected_ntp_peers

The code above loops (with_items) through the current_ntp_peers list, and each item is compared with the expected_ntp_peers list. If (when) the address is not found, it is removed with the ios_config module.

This playbook could be optimized, but I designed it to be readable and easy to understand.

docs.title: Strategies for troubleshooting Ansible errors
docs.text: 02 October 2024

docs.title: Strategies for troubleshooting Ansible errors
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate troubleshooting

One of the biggest challenges when using Ansible, especially at the beginning, is troubleshooting. You often run into errors that are unclear, poorly described or misleading.

Let's look at some strategies to resolve otherwise incomprehensible errors.

dos2unix: In rare cases, issues arise from how different operating systems handle text files (line endings). When working in Linux environments, make sure your files use Unix line endings.

yamllint and yamlfmt: Ansible playbooks are written in YAML. Before troubleshooting further, make sure your files are valid, correctly formatted YAML.

ansible-lint: Ansible playbooks follow a specific structure, which can be validated with the ansible-lint linter.

Verbosity: You can make the execution of playbooks more verbose by adding one or more -v flags. Usually, -vvv is enough to reveal hidden errors.

Simplify: If the cause of the error is still unclear, simplify the playbook until you isolate the task that causes the issue.

ansible.builtin.debug: The debug feature lets you print the content of variables, which helps to identify anomalies.

type_debug: In addition to checking the content of a variable, make sure its type is correct, especially if you are performing mathematical operations.

fail...when: Using fail-when lets you check whether conditional tests return the expected result.

Facts: Before using facts, always check that they are available and have the correct values. The to_nice_json filter prints them in a readable format.

Debugger: Once you have identified the task that causes the issue, you can enable the debugger:

- ansible.builtin.command: "false"
  debugger: on_failed

Timeout: If tasks take too long, you can increase the timeout for SSH connections:

- ansible.builtin.command: "false"
  debugger: on_failed

Async: For long-running tasks, it is good practice to configure them as asynchronous:

- ansible.builtin.command: /bin/sleep 15
  async: 45
  poll: 5

SSH no match: If you need to manage outdated devices, you might run into issues where a common set of encryption ciphers cannot be established between the Ansible host and the device:

fatal: [pe.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: kex error : no match for method encryption client->server: server [aes128-cbc,3des-cbc,aes192-cbc,aes256-cbc], client [aes192-ctr,aes256-ctr]"}

This example shows a failed connection because there is no matching encryption cipher. If you use libssh, the ~/.ssh/config file is loaded by default. You can specify a different configuration file in ansible.cfg:

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = libssh

[libssh_connection]
config_file = ansible_ssh.conf

docs.title: Handling errors in Ansible playbooks
docs.text: 09 October 2024

docs.title: Handling errors in Ansible playbooks
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

When developing playbooks, it is often necessary to change the default behavior of Ansible in case of errors.

Here are three common scenarios:

  • When a task should only run in a specific mode.
  • When a task should never report changes.
  • When a task should fail under certain conditions.

We will also see three scenarios that are useful to know but rarely needed in practice.

docs.title: Running Tasks in a Specific Mode
docs.text:
You can make a task run only in a specific mode. For instance, the following task runs only in check mode (-C):

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "show running-config | include ntp peer"
  when: ansible_check_mode

However, this does not change the behavior of the task, only when it is executed. In check mode, commands that can alter the system are not executed. Each module handles check mode differently.

For example, in check mode the ios_command module only runs commands that start with show: a command like dir is not executed.

You can force the ios_command module to behave normally, even in check mode:

- name: Forced in check mode
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "dir"
  check_mode: false

docs.title: Forcing Changed and Failed Status
docs.text:
Task execution returns the changed and failed status, to indicate whether something in the system has changed and whether the task completed successfully.

You can force the behavior as follows:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  register: output
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: '"I86BI_LINUX" in output.stdout[0]'

docs.title: Custom Failure Messages
docs.text:
To print a more informative error message when forcing a failed state, split the task into two parts, as shown:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  register: output
- ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: "Router is IOL"
  when: '"I86BI_LINUX" in output.stdout[0]'

docs.title: Try-Catch with Blocks
docs.text:
In Ansible, you can implement a try-catch block to handle errors across multiple tasks:

- block:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ value | int }}"
  rescue:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Value is not defined"

docs.title: Running Playbooks on Failed Hosts
docs.text:
Ansible can keep track of the hosts where a playbook has failed. To enable it, set the retry_files_enabled parameter in the configuration:

[defaults]
retry_files_enabled: True

Then you can rerun the playbook, limiting it to the failed hosts only:

./playbook.yml -i inventory.ini --limit @playbook.retry

docs.title: Ignoring Unreachable Hosts
docs.text:
A task can be configured so that an unreachable host does not interrupt the playbook:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  ignore_unreachable: true

If a host is unreachable at this task, the playbook continues with the following tasks.

docs.title: Using Ansible handlers for optimized task execution
docs.text: 16 October 2024

docs.title: Using Ansible handlers for optimized task execution
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Handlers let you associate actions with tasks that change devices. Their key feature is that they are executed once, right before the end of the playbook.

A good example is saving a configuration. Throughout a playbook, the configuration may be modified multiple times, but it only needs to be saved once, at the end.

Here is a task that configures NTP servers:

- cisco.ios.ios_ntp_global:
    config:
      peers:
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_1 }}"
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_2 }}"
    state: replaced
  notify: SAVE CONFIG

The task calls (notify) the SAVE CONFIG handler. At the end of the playbook, the handler is triggered once, even if it is notified by multiple tasks.

- name: SAVE CONFIG
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    save_when: always

The handler is simply a task stored in the handlers directory. The only thing to keep in mind is to give it a name, which is used to invoke it.

However, handlers have a significant drawback. Let's look at an example:

  • A series of tasks modify the configuration of a device, and the execution of the handler is deferred.
  • Due to an error, the playbook stops before the handler is executed.
  • The next time the playbook is run, no changes are made to the device configuration, so no handler is triggered.

In this scenario, we end up in an undesirable state: the device has been reconfigured, but the changes have not been saved.

For this reason, I tend to avoid using handlers.

docs.title: Ansible parsers and filters
docs.text: 06 November 2024

docs.title: Ansible parsers and filters
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible ntc-templates textfsm

The method we are using with Ansible is called "screen scraping": the interaction with the device does not go through APIs but through the CLI, emulating human activity. Typing the commands may be straightforward, but reading the output can be particularly challenging.

Consider the following output:

R1#show ip int brie
Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up
Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

The output above is readable by humans but requires some work to be usable in a program. For instance, to read the IP address of the Ethernet0/0 interface, we would need to find the line where the interface name appears and then move a certain number of characters until we reach the IP address. Moreover, this is the format used by the Cisco IOS device in this example: if we change vendor or, in some cases, version, the format of the table might change.

Parsers in Ansible handle this task: they read a text and convert it into a data structure. Parsers, which are essential unless you work with APIs, are available for various types of text.

Here we look at four of them:

  • TextFSM.
  • NTC Templates.
  • pyATS / Genie.
  • TTP.

For our tests, we use the Simple Network Lab environment, with R1 already running and reachable.

docs.title: TextFSM
docs.text:
TextFSM, explored in a module of the basic course, is a module that reads a text and transforms it into a list of dictionaries. For example, the following text:

R1#show ip int brie
Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up
Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

Can be transformed into:

[
    {
        "interface": "Ethernet0/0",
        "ip_address": "169.254.1.118",
        "proto": "up",
        "status": "up"
    },
    {
        "interface": "Ethernet0/1",
        "ip_address": "unassigned",
        "proto": "down",
        "status": "administratively down"
    }
]

Writing a TextFSM template may not look simple at first glance, but once you understand it, it is not that complex. In this course, we limit ourselves to using existing templates, and in particular we refer to the NTC Templates repository. Let's retrieve the template for the show ip interface brief command on Cisco IOS devices.

Now we write a short playbook that connects to the device, issues the show ip interface brief command and saves the output in a variable. The task is as follows:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show ip interface brief
  register: output

We now transform the output with the TextFSM parser and its corresponding template:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.utils.textfsm
      template_path: templates/cisco_ios_show_ip_interface_brief.textfsm
    set_fact: output_parsed

If we print the content of output_parsed with debug, we see that it is structured in JSON format.

docs.title: NTC Templates
docs.text:
NTC Templates, as mentioned, is a public repository maintained by network.toCode(), containing TextFSM templates for various vendors and devices. Anyone can contribute to the repository by publishing their own templates.

NTC Templates is also available as a Python module, which is simpler than the previous method but offers less flexibility. The Python module is not released frequently, so if you need updated templates, the previous method is preferable.

Once the ntc_templates module is installed, we can use the repository in our playbook:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    command: "show ip interface brief"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.ntc_templates
      os: "cisco_ios"
    set_fact: output_parsed

This parser requires the device type (cisco_ios) and the command. If we print the content of output_parsed with debug, we see that it is structured in JSON format and differs slightly from the previous one, although the template is the same.

In the task above, the module executes the command directly on the device, retrieves the output and applies the parser. For performance reasons, which we will see later, it is possible to use the output stored in a variable. In this case, the syntax is slightly different:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.ntc_templates
      os: "cisco_ios"
      command: "show ip interface brief"
    set_fact: output_parsed

docs.title: TTP
docs.text:
TTP, or Template Text Parser, is more elaborate than TextFSM but, on the flip side, the ttp_templates repository has very few templates, and the effort to create new ones is often not worth it. TTP, however, can be used to parse entire configurations, and this is its main strength compared to TextFSM. Like TextFSM, TTP is also covered in the basic module.

Once the ttp_templates module is installed, let's download, for example, the template for the show ip arp command on Cisco IOS devices into the templates directory, with a .ttp extension.

We can now use the repository in our playbook:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    command: show ip arp
    parser:
      name: ansible.utils.ttp
      os: "cisco_ios"
    set_fact: output_parsed

Here too, the output can be passed as a variable:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.utils.ttp
      os: "cisco_ios"
      command: "show ip arp"
    set_fact: output_parsed

docs.title: pyATS / Genie
docs.text:
Alongside TextFSM and TTP, there is the pyATS / Genie suite developed by Cisco. It is an open solution, but clearly designed for Cisco devices and therefore generally limited to them.

The list of parsers confirms that there is a parser for show ip interface brief.

Once the pyats and genie modules are installed, we can write a task that uses this parser in our playbook:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    command: "show ip interface brief"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.pyats
    set_fact: output_parsed

Note a few things:

  • Unlike the previous parsers, we did not have to specify the type of device. The parser reads this information automatically from the ansible_network_os variable.
  • The output is not a list but a dictionary, with the interface name as the key. This can be very useful to select the desired line more easily.

Here too, the output can be passed as a variable:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.pyats
      command: show ip interface brief
    set_fact: output_parsed

docs.title: Custom Filters
docs.text:
Ansible provides several filters that alter the content of a variable. For example:

  • var | int converts the variable to an integer;
  • var | to_nice_json formats JSON in a human-readable way;
  • var | upper converts a string to uppercase.

If the parsers we have seen are insufficient, or if no filter meets our needs, we can easily add a custom filter by writing Python code.

We can divide filters into two groups: those that do not accept additional parameters, meaning that their only input is the variable they are applied to, and those that do. Let's see two examples.

In the first example (without additional parameters), the filter:

  • takes as input the output of show ip interface brief, processed with the NTC Templates parser;
  • removes inactive interfaces.

The first consideration concerns typing. Python is dynamically typed, and Ansible is even murkier. Later, we will look at the type_debug filter, which can help us when in doubt.

Custom filters must be saved in the same file, filter_plugins/filters.py. Filters are, in fact, functions of the FilterModule class. The reserved function filters maps the names used to call the filters to the functions that define them.

Let's see an example:

class FilterModule(object):
    """Ansible filter."""

    def drop_down_interfaces(self, interfaces: list) -> list:
        """Return a list of active interfaces."""
        result = []
        for interface in interfaces:
            if interface["status"] == "up":
                result.append(interface)
        return result

    def filters(self):
        """Invoked function. Keys define how filters are called."""
        return {
            "drop_down_interfaces": self.drop_down_interfaces,
        }

In the example class:

  • The drop_down_interfaces function takes a list of interfaces as input and returns a list of interfaces. The output includes only the interfaces in the up state.
  • The filters function associates the name drop_down_interfaces with the corresponding function.

In a playbook, the filter can be used as follows:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ output_parsed | drop_down_interfaces }}"

Now let's add a second filter to our class, which transforms a list of dictionaries into a dictionary of dictionaries. The key to use is read as an additional parameter. Let's add this function to the class we saw earlier:

class FilterModule(object):
    """Ansible filter."""

    def get_to_dict(self, items: list, key: str = None) -> dict:
        """Convert a list of dict into a dict of dict."""
        return {item[key]: item for item in items}

    def filters(self):
        """Invoked function. Keys define how filters are called."""
        return {
            "to_dict": self.get_to_dict,
        }

The to_dict function transforms the list of dictionaries items into a dictionary of dictionaries, using the value of the specified key as the key.

We can use this second filter as follows:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ output_parsed | to_dict(key='interface') }}"

All the scripts and playbooks described in this post are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Password Management with Ansible
docs.text: 25 December 2024

docs.title: Password Management with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate passwords

Password management is one of the topics that should be analyzed during the design phase, i.e., before starting to write code. For learning purposes, however, I prefer to postpone it until you have some basic knowledge.

In general, I discourage any approach that stores credentials in plain text in files or playbooks. Where possible, I recommend named credentials, entered manually during playbook execution.

Orchestrators such as Ansible Tower (now the automation controller) or AWX might make it preferable to choose a particular vault, i.e., an encrypted password database accessible via API. In my opinion, using a vault when playbooks are executed manually makes little sense, because it simply shifts the problem: the credentials are in the vault, but the token that gives the playbook access to the vault must be saved somewhere.

Finally, as we saw earlier, dynamic inventories might make it preferable to keep the credentials in the inventory itself, which, being generated dynamically, leaves no trace except in RAM. Once again, however, we are shifting the problem: the script that generates the inventory must somehow authenticate itself.

Let's see two examples, knowing that each environment requires specific considerations about the security and confidentiality of credentials. Let's open the Simple Network Lab and start R1.

docs.title: Named Credentials
docs.text:
The simplest and safest way to manage credentials is to provide them on the command line at each execution:

./playbook-auth.yml -u admin -k

Before the execution, we are asked for the password of the admin user. If the user needs to perform privilege escalation, we can use the -K parameter, which prompts us for the enable password.

docs.title: Ansible Vault
docs.text:
Especially when we use an orchestrator, it is difficult to use named credentials to access devices. In this scenario, it is easier to keep one or more service accounts in the vault.

Let's see how to create a native Ansible vault:

ansible-vault create secrets.vault

The file is nothing but an encrypted key-value dictionary, protected by the password requested during creation. For example, we can save the password of the admin user:

ansible_ssh_pass: cisco

If necessary, the vault can be edited:

ansible-vault edit secrets.vault

As we said, we are shifting the problem: the playbook must know the vault password to read it and access the device. There are several options:

  • enter the vault password on the command line (--ask-vault-pass);
  • read the password from a specific file or script (--vault-password-file);
  • read the password from an environment variable through a script (see the previous point).

As mentioned, vaults should be preferred when the playbooks are managed by an orchestrator. In this case, the best choice depends on the orchestrator itself. Whatever system we choose, the vault file is loaded as a variable file and then used:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: ANSIBLE VAULT
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars_files:
    - secrets.vault

This is why we used the key ansible_ssh_pass in the vault.

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
As we have seen, the integrated vault of Ansible is quite simple. In corporate environments, more advanced vaults are generally present, and I very often come across HashiCorp Vault. Let's refer to the official documentation and see how to use it.

Let's install the hvac library and assume that HashiCorp Vault is configured with two keys, to be used as username and password:

$ vault read -tls-skip-verify kv/ansible
Key Value
--- -----
refresh_interval 768h
password cisco
username admin

We set environment variables for the vault access parameters:

export VAULT_TOKEN=hvs.R3R5z2SmlSFGi9aR1VJlBZJH
export VAULT_ADDR=https://localhost:8200

In particular, we use the lookup feature, which allows us to define variables dynamically:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: HASHICORP VAULT
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    ansible_user: "{{ lookup('hashi_vault', 'secret=kv/ansible:username validate_certs=no') }}"
    ansible_ssh_pass: "{{ lookup('hashi_vault', 'secret=kv/ansible:password validate_certs=no') }}"

By defining the variables at the play level, we can still use gather_facts.

All the sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Enhancing Ansible output
docs.text: 01 January 2025

docs.title: Enhancing Ansible output
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

By default, the output of Ansible lists the tasks executed on each device, with a brief summary at the end of what has been done. The color indicates the outcome of each task: green if no changes were made, yellow if the configuration was modified, red in case of an error, and blue if the task was skipped.

The output can be customized with callbacks, in the ansible.cfg configuration file:

  • stdout_callback sets the main plugin that generates the output (by default ansible.builtin.default);
  • callbacks_enabled specifies which plugins are enabled (by default the list is empty).

The official documentation lists numerous plugins, which you can also list with:

ansible-doc -t callback -l

Let's see the ones I find most interesting.

docs.title: ansible.builtin.default
docs.text:
We already know the default plugin: it is explanatory enough, and you can increase the detail with -v.

PLAY [TEST OUTPUT] *************************************************************

TASK [READING OUTPUT] **********************************************************
ok: [r1.example.com]

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
r1.example.com             : ok=1    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0
   rescued=0    ignored=0

The default plugin is the best choice for normal operation.

docs.title: ansible.builtin.minimal
docs.text:
The minimal plugin provides a minimal output: only the result of each task, for each host:

r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "stdout": [
        "Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol\nEthernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      \nEthernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    \nEthernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    \nEthernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"
    ],
    "stdout_lines": [
        [
            "Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol",
            "Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      ",
            "Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ",
            "Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ",
            "Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"
        ]
    ]
}

The minimal plugin can be helpful on very complex playbooks.

docs.title: ansible.posix.json
docs.text:
The JSON plugin returns the execution information in JSON format.

{
    "custom_stats": {},
    "global_custom_stats": {},
    "plays": [
        {
            "play": {
                "duration": {
                    "end": "2024-10-26T06:58:57.910802Z",
                    "start": "2024-10-26T06:58:54.813940Z"
                },
                "id": "72edea89-cc55-4261-0c41-000000000002",
                "name": "TEST OUTPUT",
                "path": "/Users/dainese/src/courses/Ansible/15. Output/playbook-output.yml:2"
            },
            "tasks": [
                {
                    "hosts": {
                        "r1.example.com": {
                            "_ansible_no_log": false,
                            "action": "cisco.ios.ios_command",
                            "changed": false,

The JSON plugin is particularly useful when the output of the playbook must feed other processes.

docs.title: community.general.log_plays
docs.text:
The log_plays plugin saves a log file for each device. The plugin must be configured by specifying the directory where the logs are saved:

[callback_log_plays]
log_folder = /var/log/ansible/hosts

The plugin is designed to be used together with a plugin that handles the screen output.

Oct 26 2024 09:00:03 - ./playbook-output.yml - READING OUTPUT - cisco.ios.ios_command - OK - {"module_args": {"commands": ["show ip interface brief"], "match": "all", "retries": 9, "interval": 1, "wait_for": null}} => {"changed": false, "stdout": ["Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      
Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    
Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down
