Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"], "stdout_lines": [["Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol", "Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      ", "Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ", "Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ", "Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"]], "_ansible_no_log": false}

All the sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Boosting Ansible performance
docs.text: 13 November 2024

docs.title: Boosting Ansible performance
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible troubleshooting

Ansible is an ideal choice in terms of accessibility, but it is certainly not the best choice for those seeking performance.

Let's look at a few configurations that improve performance in a simple way.

docs.title: Parallelism (fork)
docs.text:
The first setting is the number of forks, the parallel processes that interact with the devices. In general, it should be proportional to the number of processors, but note that much of the playbook time is spent waiting for the device to execute a command. The optimal number of forks could therefore be double the number of available processors, or even more. Obviously, forks improve performance only if the playbook runs in parallel on multiple nodes; otherwise they have no effect.

[defaults]
forks = 8

docs.title: Dependency (strategy)
docs.text:
The second setting is the execution strategy (strategy). There are two types of strategies: linear and free.

With the linear strategy, a task starts only when the previous one has completed on all nodes: in the output, the results of a task appear grouped together. With the free strategy, each node runs its own tasks without waiting for the others. The free strategy can, and should, be used if each task depends only on the previous tasks of the same node. In other words, free can be used if the execution of a play on R2 never depends in any way on the execution of the same play on R1. Again, the strategy improves performance only if the playbook runs in parallel on multiple nodes; otherwise it has no effect.

[defaults]
strategy = free

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text:
The next step to improve the performance of a playbook is to profile it, that is, to understand where time is spent: globally, by role and by task.

Three callbacks add time-related information to the standard output.

[defaults]
stdout_callback = ansible.builtin.default
callbacks_enabled = ansible.posix.profile_roles,ansible.posix.profile_tasks,ansible.posix.timer

These three plugins are essential to understand which tasks take more time and, following the Pareto Principle, where to focus.

docs.title: Reduce "show running-config"
docs.text:
In screen-scraping mode, the show running-config command is used a lot. When specific modules cannot be optimized, ios_config can read the configuration from a variable populated earlier:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    command: show running-config
  register: output
- cisco.ios.ios_config:
    running_config: output.stdout_lines[0]

docs.title: Disable "gather_facts"
docs.text:
As we have seen, Ansible can read some information from the nodes (facts) before running tasks. If this information is not needed, disabling gather_facts can significantly improve performance.

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- hosts: all
  gather_facts: false

docs.title: Save the Configuration Only Once
docs.text:
We have already chosen to save the configuration only once, at the end of the play, with post_tasks. Saving the configuration can take a long time, depending on the platform, so doing it only once significantly reduces the execution time.

We therefore confirm the choice we have already made:

post_tasks:
  - cisco.ios.ios_config:
      save_when: modified

docs.title: Eliminate Loops
docs.text:
Loops significantly impact the performance of Ansible. Where possible, avoid them or convert them. Let's see an example.

Suppose we have a list of NTP peers:

ntp_servers:
  - 194.239.208.213
  - 130.60.204.10

We can create a list to use with the ios_ntp_global module:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_peers_config_list: "{{ ntp_peers_config_list|default([]) + [{'peer': item}] }}"
  with_items: "{{ ntp_servers }}"

This approach, however, is rather slow. We can move the loop into a Jinja template:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_peers_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for host in ntp_servers %}
          {"peer": "{{ host }}"},
        {% endfor %}
      ]

Since Ansible is not strongly typed, the result is the same, but much faster.

docs.title: Running Ansible playbooks through a Bastion host
docs.text: 20 November 2024

docs.title: Running Ansible playbooks through a Bastion host
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

In many environments, a particularly secure host, the bastion host, handles all the management operations that operators perform on production systems. It is usually subject to audits and continuous verification.

Ansible can work through a bastion host, but the configuration depends on the protocol used. Here we limit ourselves to SSH.

In our lab, our computer (Linux or macOS) is the Ansible controller, and the EVE-NG server is the bastion host: the devices are reachable only from the EVE-NG server.

Note that the local Python environment is used, not that of the bastion host, so any library or module errors refer to the local system. The bastion host is only a bridge: it needs no special configuration, except public key authentication.

docs.title: SSH via Bastion Host
docs.text:
As the diagram above shows, we must be able to connect via SSH to the EVE-NG server using public key authentication. We therefore exchange the keys, manually or with a dedicated command, so that we can connect automatically to the bastion host as the user dev:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub dev@172.25.82.110

At this point, we use the ansible_ssh_common_args parameter to force the connections through the bastion host.

We can set the ansible_ssh_common_args variable at the playbook level:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ansible_ssh_common_args: >-
      -o ProxyCommand="ssh
      -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa
      -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no
      -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
      -W %h:%p
      -q dev@172.25.82.110"

The >- syntax lets us write the content of a variable on multiple lines, without end-of-line characters in the value.

We can set it as an environment variable, which is probably the most convenient choice in a mixed development environment:

export ANSIBLE_SSH_COMMON_ARGS='-o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110"'

Or we can set it on the command line:

./playbook-ntp-via-bastion.yml -i inventory.ini --ssh-common-args '-o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110"'

If we run into problems, let's try to connect to R1 through the bastion host:

ssh -o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110" admin@169.254.1.21

Then we analyze any errors.

docs.title: Ansible orchestrators and integration tools
docs.text: 13 January 2025

docs.title: Ansible orchestrators and integration tools
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

In this course, we ran Ansible manually. To take the next step, we need an orchestrator that organizes playbooks, manages their execution and generates reports.

There are several solutions: in this post, we describe the most popular ones.

docs.title: Ansible Navigator
docs.text:
Ansible Navigator is a command-line tool and a text-based user interface (TUI) for creating, reviewing, running and troubleshooting Ansible content, including inventories, playbooks, collections, documentation and container images (execution environments).

Ansible Navigator is designed to run from within containers. Personally, I prefer to disable this behavior:

ansible-navigator --ee=false run playbook-output.yml

As we have seen, Ansible Navigator is not exactly an orchestrator: it is a utility to run playbooks, analyze configurations, inventories and collections, and perform linting.

docs.title: ARA Records Ansible
docs.text:
ARA provides Ansible reporting by recording ansible and ansible-playbook commands, regardless of how and where they run.

The recorded results are available via an included CLI, a REST API and a self-hosted, local-first web interface.

ARA is not an orchestrator, but it provides a simple dashboard that displays the progress of playbook executions. The playbooks, however, must be run manually or from an external system.

docs.title: Automation Controller (Formerly Ansible Tower)
docs.text:
Ansible Tower, now called the automation controller, is the commercial web-based user interface and REST API of the Ansible ecosystem. It makes it easier to manage Ansible projects, inventories and schedules.

It is the official Red Hat orchestrator for Ansible, designed to centralize the Ansible ecosystem and give users a single pane of glass to manage automation tasks.

docs.title: Ansible AWX
docs.text:
AWX provides a web-based user interface, a REST API and a task engine built on top of Ansible. It is one of the upstream projects of the Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform.

AWX is the open-source upstream of the automation controller (formerly Ansible Tower), and it is often subject to significant changes, including major refactoring.

docs.title: Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform
docs.text:
The Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform includes the automation controller (formerly Ansible Tower) as one of its components and adds further tools, integrations and features.

The Ansible Automation Platform also includes Event-Driven Ansible (EDA), which automates the response to events or triggers in your infrastructure: EDA recognizes the specified event, matches it with the appropriate action and executes it automatically. Actions can be existing playbooks, templates or modules, so you extend the value of automation you already trust.

docs.title: eNMS
docs.text:
eNMS is a vendor-agnostic Network Management System (NMS) designed for building workflow-based network automation solutions.

An Ansible Playbook service runs a playbook on a set of target devices and returns a JSON-formatted result. The output can be validated with a command/pattern mechanism, like the Data Validation Service.

eNMS centralizes the Ansible ecosystem and gives users a single pane of glass.

docs.title: Other Orchestrators and Tools
docs.text:
Ansible can be integrated with numerous other tools, for example:

  • Spacelift: a sophisticated CI/CD platform for OpenTofu, Terraform, Terragrunt, CloudFormation, Pulumi, Kubernetes and Ansible.
  • NetBox / Nautobot: the network Source of Truth.
  • Semaphore UI: a modern UI for Ansible.
  • Uyuni: the open-source configuration and infrastructure management solution for software-defined infrastructure.
  • Infrahub: unifies and syncs your infrastructure data foundation while preserving its context and intent, so teams can store and manage their automation blueprints in one place and integrate natively with the deployment tools they already use.

docs.title: Key takeaways from the Ansible course
docs.text: 18 December 2024

docs.title: Key takeaways from the Ansible course
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

We have seen that Ansible is an excellent tool for improving operations by automating tasks and orchestrating processes. Its procedural structure makes it easy to transform manual tasks into automated ones: if we can describe a task, we can build a playbook to implement it.

When properly structured, a playbook not only becomes the official way of operating, but also documents the process itself.

However, Ansible is not the only framework available, and it is important to understand its strengths and limitations.

Ansible is well suited to those without a programming background, which is why it is often my first choice when I approach automation projects.

Organizations rarely have the capacity to develop and maintain new modules, so in that sense the scope of Ansible is limited to the existing modules.

From a performance perspective, there are more efficient frameworks than Ansible. Initially this is rarely a concern, but as projects grow, different needs may emerge.

docs.title: Comprehensive Ansible Lab
docs.text: 11 December 2024

docs.title: Comprehensive Ansible Lab
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible lab

In the final exercise, we put together what we have learned to configure and manage a legacy fabric (based on STP).

Let's open the Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology lab, start all the devices and make sure they are reachable.

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
Before even thinking about writing playbooks, we need to create a model of our environment, which means creating a data structure that can represent our fabric and serve as a working tool. There are many possibilities:

  • NetBox / Nautobot: I have seen an integration between these applications, Ansible and the devices. A change to a device interface in NetBox / Nautobot triggers an Ansible playbook that modifies the configuration of the physical device.
  • GitLab / GitHub: This approach leans more towards Infrastructure as Code. An operator changes the data structure, typically based on CSV / YAML / JSON, and the CI / CD pipeline runs various tests. If everything works, it adjusts the configuration of the devices in production.
  • CSV / XLS / YAML: This is the simplest case: a plain file contains the parameters of the structure, and the manual execution of a playbook adjusts the configuration of the devices. Any tests are done manually by the operator.

For simplicity, let's choose the third approach. The first two would require significant development, beyond the scope of this course.

We choose a YAML file for its readability and flexibility. It should contain all the parameters that define our fabric. We definitely need to include information about:

  • DNS.
  • Hostname and domain.
  • NTP.
  • SNMP.

Operationally, we also need to:

  • Harden the devices.
  • Configure the interfaces.

We can imagine that the interfaces have a template based on their function. We definitely need templates for:

  • Inter-switch-link (ISL) interfaces.
  • Interfaces to endpoints.

Furthermore, the interfaces to endpoints have a profile based on the connected device, for example:

  • Virtualization server.
  • Firewall.
  • Client access with VoIP phone.
  • Management access.
  • Office devices access.

We made this analysis based on our experience, but in a real case the analysis must be done on the environment we want to automate. We must understand how that environment is structured and how people work. Our goal is to formalize a structure (modeling) and standardize the way of working. Only then can we start developing the working tools, which in our case are based on Ansible.

Practically speaking, we can create a first draft of a data structure that defines our environment:

dns_domain: example.com
dns_lookup: false
dns_servers:
  - 8.8.4.4
  - 8.8.8.8
ntp_servers:
  - 195.201.19.162
  - 141.98.136.83
snmp_community: 494174af4b08f87467a138584f4edb33

We also need to define the VLANs that must be configured in the fabric:

vlans:
  - id: 50
    name: SERVER
  - id: 51
    name: DMZ
  - id: 52
    name: MGMT
  - id: 53
    name: OFFICE
  - id: 54
    name: VOIP
  - id: 55
    name: INTERNET
  - id: 999
    name: NATIVE

Finally, we need to define the profile associated with each interface:

interfaces:
  Ethernet0/1:
    profile: unused
  Ethernet0/2:
    description: to Hypervisor
    profile: hypervisor
  Ethernet0/3:
    description: to Firewall
    profile: firewall
  Ethernet1/0:
    description: to SW3
    profile: isl
  Ethernet1/1:
    description: to SW4
    profile: isl
  Ethernet1/2:
    description: to SW5
    profile: isl
  Ethernet1/3:
    description: to SW6
    profile: isl

The decision on how to formalize the interface-profile association is crucial, because it has a huge impact on the way of operating while having to protect the integrity of the infrastructure. The format in the example above looks cumbersome, but it guarantees that an interface cannot be associated with multiple profiles.

Let's see a second example:

profiles:
  isl:
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/0
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/1
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/2
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/3
  firewall:
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet0/3
  unused:
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet0/1
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet0/2

If we had chosen the second format, apparently more convenient, the operator would have had to make sure that an interface is not associated with multiple profiles.

We therefore use the first format, where the interface is defined as a unique key within the file.

docs.title: Define the Inventory
docs.text:
Next, let's define the inventory file, which for convenience we implement as an INI file:

[all]
sw1.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.101
sw2.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.102
sw3.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.103
sw4.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.104
sw5.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.105
sw6.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.106

[access]
sw[3:6].example.com

[core]
sw[1:2].example.com

[cisco_ios]
sw[1:6].example.com

[cisco_ios:vars]
ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios

We place the variables associated with hosts and groups in the host_vars and group_vars directories, respectively. In particular:

  • host_vars/sw1.example.com.yml: contains the interface-profile association for SW1;
  • host_vars/sw2.example.com.yml: contains the interface-profile association for SW2;
  • host_vars/sw3.example.com.yml: contains the interface-profile association for SW3;
  • host_vars/sw4.example.com.yml: contains the interface-profile association for SW4;
  • host_vars/sw5.example.com.yml: contains the interface-profile association for SW5;
  • host_vars/sw6.example.com.yml: contains the interface-profile association for SW6;
  • group_vars/all.yml: contains all the fabric variables.

docs.title: Credential Management
docs.text:
In planning our automation, we need to consider how credentials are managed. This choice is tied to the use of any orchestrators and directly impacts the security of our environment.

In general, two choices are possible:

  • The playbook is invoked manually by an operator: in this case, the best choice is for the operator to enter the credentials interactively.
  • The playbook is invoked by an orchestrator: in this case, the credentials will probably be passed as environment variables. The use of a vault is strongly recommended.

For simplicity, we choose the first option: the credentials are entered interactively during playbook execution.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Given the purpose we have set, we can easily identify five roles:

  • system, which handles the configuration of the hostname, domain and DNS servers;
  • ntp, which handles the configuration of the NTP servers;
  • snmpv2, which handles the configuration of the SNMPv2 community;
  • interface_profile, which handles the configuration of the interfaces, applying the correct profile;
  • vlan, which handles the creation of the necessary VLANs.

Let's create the skeleton for the five roles:

ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_ntp
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_interface_profile
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_snmpv2
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_system
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_vlan

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_system
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_system role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_system/tasks/main.yml file, which contains the tasks that configure the hostname, domain, DNS lookup and DNS servers.

We split the task into two parts, because it is more convenient for compliance to know which configuration needs to be changed. In the first part, we configure the hostname and domain. In particular, as a standard, we want the hostname in uppercase and the domain in lowercase:

# Set and normalize hostname and domain
- name: SETTING FACTS
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    device_hostname: "{{ inventory_hostname_short | upper }}"
    device_domain: "{{ inventory_hostname.split('.', 1)[1] | lower }}"
# Configure hostname
- name: CONFIGURING HOSTNAME AND DOMAIN NAME
  cisco.ios.ios_system:
    hostname: "{{ device_hostname }}"
    domain_name: "{{ device_domain }}"

In the second part, we configure the DNS servers:

# Configure DNS lookup
- name: CONFIGURING DNS LOOKUP
  cisco.ios.ios_system:
    lookup_enabled: "{{ dns_lookup }}"
    name_servers: "{{ dns_servers }}"

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_ntp
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_ntp role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_ntp/tasks/main.yml file, which contains the tasks that configure the NTP peers.

Before configuring the NTP peers, we need to transform the list of IP addresses into the data structure required by the module:

# Convert a list of IP into a list of peers
- name: SETTING NTP PEER LIST
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_peers_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for peer in ntp_servers %}
          {"peer": "{{ peer }}"},
        {% endfor %}
      ]

Now we can apply the configuration:

# Configure NTP peers
- name: CONFIGURING NTP PEERS
  cisco.ios.ios_ntp_global:
    config:
      logging: true
      peers: "{{ ntp_peers_config_list }}"
    state: replaced

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_snmpv2
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_snmpv2 role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_snmpv2/tasks/main.yml file, which contains the task that configures a single SNMPv2 read-only community.

# Configure the SNMPv2 read-only community
- name: CONFIGURING SNMPv2 COMMUNITY
  cisco.ios.ios_snmp_server:
    config:
      communities:
        - name: "{{ snmp_community }}"
          ro: true
    state: replaced

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_vlan
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_vlan role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_vlan/tasks/main.yml file, which contains the tasks that configure the VLANs.

Before configuring the VLANs, we need to transform the list defined in the design phase into the data structure required by the module:

# Convert a list of VLAN to be used with ios_vlans module
- name: SETTING VLAN LIST
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    vlans_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for vlan in vlans %}
          {
            "vlan_id": "{{ vlan.id }}",
            "name": "{{ vlan.name }}",
            "mtu": 1500,
            "state": "active",
            "shutdown": "disabled",
          },
        {% endfor %}
      ]

Now we can apply the configuration:

# Configuring VLANs
- name: ADDING VLANS
  cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
    config: "{{ vlans_config_list }}"
    state: replaced

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
In the initial phase, we identified seven types of interfaces:

  • isl: used for interfaces connecting to other switches (inter-switch-link);
  • hypervisor: used for hypervisor interfaces, configured as trunks with all VLANs passing;
  • firewall: used for firewall interfaces, configured as trunks with all VLANs passing;
  • client: used for user computer interfaces, configured in access mode with the VoIP VLAN passing;
  • management: used for device management interfaces, configured in access mode;
  • office: used for office devices such as printers and fax machines, configured in access mode;
  • unused: used for unused interfaces.

We have two options for developing the profiles:

  • We can parameterize the profiles, creating a single set of tasks that configures the interfaces;
  • We can create multiple sets of tasks, one per profile.

The first choice would be more correct from a software design perspective, but the second is simpler, more readable and more maintainable for the network automation we are creating. Once again, there is no correct choice, but a balance between different possibilities that determines the best choice in the specific context.

For each device, the cisco_ios_interface_profile role reads the interface definitions and applies the correct profile. It requires the roles/cisco_ios_interface_profile/tasks/main.yml file and a file for each profile, placed in the same directory.

To optimize performance, the main file reads the configuration once, and it is then used while configuring the individual interfaces. Then the task file for the associated profile is invoked:

# Get running-config
- name: GETTING RUNNING CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - show running-config
  register: show_running_config
# Attach profile to interface
- name: ATTACHING PROFILE TO INTERFACE
  ansible.builtin.include_tasks: "profile_{{ interface.value.profile }}.yml"
  with_dict: "{{ interfaces }}"
  loop_control:
    loop_var: interface

The main file also handles the interface state and description. First, however, we need to create a data structure usable with the ios_interfaces module:

# Generate interface status/description data to be used with ios_interface
- name: SETTING INTERFACE LIST
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    interface_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for interface, interface_data in interfaces.items() %}
          {
            "name": "{{ interface }}",
            {% if interface_data.profile == 'unused' %}
              "enabled": false,
            {% else %}
              "description": "{{ interface_data.description }} ({{ interface_data.profile }})",
              "enabled": true,
            {% endif %}
          },
        {% endfor %}
      ]
# Set description and activate interface if used
- name: "SETTING INTERFACE STATUS"
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config: "{{ interface_config_list }}"

Finally, let's implement the files that define the profiles. The ios_interfaces module allows various configurations, but it does not give us enough freedom of action. We therefore use the ios_config module to configure the interfaces as we want.

# Configure profile isl
- name: "APPLYING PROFILE ISL TO INTERFACE {{ interface.key }}"
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    config: "{{ show_running_config.stdout.0 }}"
    lines:
      - switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
      - switchport mode trunk
      - switchport nonegotiate
      - udld port aggressive
    parents: "interface {{ interface.key }}"
    before: "default interface {{ interface.key }}"

The code above shows the configuration of the isl profile in detail. In particular, if the module detects any difference, it first deletes the interface configuration (default interface) and then configures it again. This is why we decided to separate the description.

docs.title: Playbook
docs.text:
All that is left is to put together what we have created, writing the playbook that calls the roles in order and saves the configuration:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: CONFIGURE FABRIC
  hosts: core,access
  gather_facts: false
  roles:
    - role: cisco_ios_system
      tags: dns,hostname
    - role: cisco_ios_ntp
      tags: ntp
    - role: cisco_ios_snmpv2
      tags: snmp
    - role: cisco_ios_vlan
      tags: vlan
    - role: cisco_ios_interface_profile
      tags: interface
  post_tasks:
    - name: SAVING CONFIG
      tags: always
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: modified

We are aware that we have omitted some important configurations, such as those related to spanning tree and logging.

docs.title: Ansible Configuration
docs.text:
Before running the playbook, let's configure Ansible through the ansible.cfg file and optimize performance by adjusting the forks and strategy parameters:

[defaults]
inventory = inventory.ini
stdout_callback = ansible.builtin.default
strategy = free
forks = 8

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = libssh

[libssh_connection]
host_key_checking = false
look_for_keys = false

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Now let's move on to the testing phase. For each role, we need to verify:

  • That the configuration performed by the role is as expected;
  • That a new execution confirms the state of the devices without further changes (idempotence);
  • That a change in the configuration is correctly reflected on the devices.

We execute the playbook and wait for it to finish without errors:

./playbook-fabric-setup.yml -i inventorydev.ini -u admin -k

Now we need to check on the devices that the configuration is as expected.

Then we run the playbook again to verify that there are no further changes.

Now we need to change the configuration, for example:

  • By replacing a DNS server;
  • By replacing an NTP peer;
  • By changing the SNMP community;
  • By changing the profiles of two interfaces.

We run the playbook again and, when it completes, we verify the configuration on the devices.

We run the playbook one last time and verify that there are no further changes.

All the sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Managing CLI prompts with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Some commands ask the operator for confirmation before they run. Ansible has a basic capability to handle these situations thanks to the cli_command and ios_command modules. The first one is generic, the second one is specific to Cisco IOS systems, but both essentially perform the same function, with some peculiarities and limitations. In general, vendor-specific modules should handle syntax errors correctly but, as we will see, this is not always true.

Let's see some examples based on the Simple Network Lab lab.

docs.title: Resetting Interface Counters
docs.text:
The first example is resetting the interface counters. The command requires a simple confirmation:

R1#clear counters
Clear "show interface" counters on all interfaces [confirm]

We can use cli_command to execute the command and answer the confirmation. We refer to the official documentation:

- name: CLEARING INTERFACE COUNTERS WITH cli_command
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: clear counters
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Clear "show interface" counters on all interfaces
    answer:
      - y

Technically, the check_all parameter should check all the listed prompts. However, if we change the command to show interfaces, we can verify that the task does not generate any errors. In other words, it is not always possible to tell whether the operation was successful.

Alternatively, we can use ios_command. We refer to the official documentation:

- name: CLEARING INTERFACE COUNTERS WITH ios_command
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - command: clear counters
        prompt: Clear "show interface" counters on all interfaces
        answer: y

We can verify that this option has the same problem.

docs.title: Saving Configuration
docs.text:
The second example is saving the configuration. Previously, we used write memory, which does not require any confirmation. Now let's implement a task that handles the following command:

R1#copy running-config startup-config
Destination filename [startup-config]?
Building configuration...

  [OK]

The implementation with cli_command is similar to the previous one:

- name: SAVING CONFIGURATION WITH cli_command
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: copy running-config startup-config
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Destination filename
    answer:
      - startup-config

Here is the implementation with ios_command:

- name: SAVING CONFIGURATION WITH ios_command
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - command: copy running-config startup-config
        prompt: Destination filename
        answer: startup-config

docs.title: Multiple Prompts
docs.text:
Some commands require handling multiple prompts, for example:

R1#ping
Protocol [ip]: ip
Target IP address: 8.8.8.8
Repeat count [5]: 3
Datagram size [100]: 40
Timeout in seconds [2]: 1
Extended commands [n]: n
Sweep range of sizes [n]: n
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 3, 40-byte ICMP Echos to 8.8.8.8, timeout is 1 seconds:
!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 13/13/13 ms

We can handle multiple prompts with cli_command as follows:

- name: PING WITH cli_command
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: ping
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Protocol
      - Target IP address
      - Repeat count
      - Datagram size
      - Timeout in seconds
      - Extended commands
      - Sweep range of sizes
    answer:
      - ip
      - 8.8.8.8
      - 3
      - 40
      - 1
      - n
      - n

All the sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Reboot a device with Ansible and wait for it to come online
Reboot a device with Ansible and wait for it to come online
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

Rebooting a device and waiting for it to be available again is a more complex interactive task than those seen so far. Ansible is not designed specifically for this purpose, but it can be useful, for example, in a procedure that updates the firmware of a device.

Let's analyze the manual procedure:

  • The device must obviously be reachable.
  • The configuration register should be set to 0x2101.
  • The configuration must be saved.

At this point, the reload command can be issued, and we wait for the device to be reachable again before issuing further commands.

The preliminary tasks, which we have already analyzed, can be implemented very simply:

- name: READING SHOW VERSION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  register: output
- name: CHECKING CONFIGURATION REGISTER
  ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: The configuration register must be 0x2101
  when: "'0x2101' not in output['stdout'][0]"
- name: SAVING CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    save_when: modified

The check of the register could have been done with a single task, but with significantly lower usability:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  failed_when: "'Configuration register is 0x2101' not in output['stdout'][0]"

In case of error, the output would have been as follows:

fatal: [r1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "failed_when_result": true, "stdout": "Cisco IOS Software, Linux Software (I86BI_LINUX-ADVENTERPRISEK9-M), Version 15.7(3)M2, DEVELOPMENT TEST SOFTWARE\nTechnical Support: [http://www.cisco.com/techsupport\nCopyright (c) 1986-2018 by Cisco Systems, Inc.\nCompiled Wed 28-Mar-18 11:18 by prod_rel_team\n\nROM: Bootstrap program is Linux\n\nR1 uptime is 10 minutes\nSystem returned to ROM by reload at 0\nSystem restarted at 10:01:15 UTC Sun Apr 7 2024\nSystem image file is \"unix:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/i86bi_LinuxL3-AdvEnterpriseK9-M2_15\"\nLast reload reason: Unknown reason\n\n\n\nThis product contains cryptographic features and is subject to United\nStates and local country laws governing import, export, transfer and\nuse...

Using fail instead of failed_when lets us specify the error message, which is much more usable:

fatal: [r1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "The configuration register must be 0x2101"}

The task to reboot the device is similar to what we have seen before:

- name: RELOADING DEVICE
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: reload
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Proceed with reload
    answer:
      - y
  async: 1
  poll: 0

The difference from the previous examples is the async and poll parameters. The reboot will surely close the SSH connection. The async mode lets us disconnect from the SSH connection and move on to the next task immediately (poll: 0).

The version with ios_command is very similar:

- name: RELOADING DEVICE
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - command: reload
        prompt: Proceed with reload
        answer: "y"
  async: 1
  poll: 0

Finally, we need to wait for the device to be available again. Technically, we are waiting for port 22 (SSH) to be listening again. This is done locally by the Ansible controller (connection: local):

- name: WAITING FOR REBOOT
  ansible.builtin.wait_for:
    delay: 30
    connect_timeout: 3
    sleep: 10
    port: 22
    host: "{{ ansible_host }}"
    timeout: 600
  connection: local

The wait_for module waits for an event, such as a particular line in a log file or, as in our case, the availability of a port:

  • port: specifies the TCP port number to check.
  • host: specifies the IP address of the device on which to check the port.
  • delay: specifies the time to wait before starting the test.
  • connect_timeout: specifies the time to wait before declaring the port inactive.
  • sleep: specifies the time between two tests.
  • timeout: specifies the maximum waiting time (task duration).

This method cannot be used with bastion hosts, because it requires direct connectivity between the Ansible controller and the device.

After this task, all the post-reboot verification operations can be performed.

All the sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Event-Driven Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

Event-Driven Ansible (EDA) triggers the execution of an Ansible playbook when a specific event occurs.

This capability greatly expands the potential of Ansible, turning it into a tool that automates processes based on events: troubleshooting, threat intelligence, IoCs, data collection and general analysis. These activities can be partially or fully automated.

Many security vendors have released specific modules. For instance, Palo Alto Networks has developed a plugin that analyzes firewall logs and triggers initial automated diagnostics in case of SSL decryption errors.

docs.title: Rulebook
docs.text:
An Ansible Rulebook is a set of rules that EDA uses to execute specific actions. A rulebook can:

  • Monitor one or more sources.
  • Contain one or more rules.
  • Trigger one or more actions.

The first part of a rulebook defines one or more event sources to monitor. EDA uses Event Source Plugins to monitor these sources.

docs.title: Event Source Plugins
docs.text:
Event Source Plugins fall into three types:

  • Event Bus Plugins: listen to a stream of events from a source, where the connection is established by the plugin itself (e.g., the Kafka and AWS SQS Queue plugins).
  • Scraper Plugins: connect to a source and scrape data from it, usually at predefined intervals (e.g., the URL Check and Watchdog plugins).
  • Callback Plugins: provide a callback endpoint that the event source calls when data is available (e.g., the Webhook and Alertmanager plugins). Callback plugins are the least reliable, because they depend on the event source calling the endpoint and are highly susceptible to data loss.

When an Event Source Plugin detects an event, EDA uses rules to decide which action to take. If an event matches a rule, EDA executes the specified actions. Actions can include:

  • run_playbook: executes an existing Ansible playbook.
  • run_job_template: runs a job template through the Ansible Automation Platform.
  • run_module: runs a specific Ansible module, without running an entire playbook.
  • post_event: posts an event to a running ruleset, so that the results of actions feed back into EDA.
  • set_fact: stores specific event data to be reused within EDA.
  • debug: outputs debug information, similar to the debug module in Ansible playbooks.

docs.title: Installing Event-Driven Ansible
docs.text:
First, we need a JRE. We use OpenJDK 21.0.1:

tar xzvf openjdk-21.0.1_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz
export PATH=~/jdk-21.0.1/bin:$PATH
which java

Then we install EDA:

pip install ansible ansible-rulebook ansible-runner
ansible-galaxy collection install ansible.eda

docs.title: Example: Monitoring Router Configuration Changes
docs.text: In this example, we configure a Cisco router to send syslog messages and set up EDA to read those logs and trigger a playbook when the router configuration is modified. The playbook exports the router configuration to a local directory.

docs.title: Action Playbook
docs.text:
First, we create a simple playbook to handle the backup action:

- hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: "BACKUP RUNNING CONFIG"
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        backup: true
        backup_options:
          filename: "/tmp/{{ ansible_host }}-backup.cfg"
          dir_path: backup

The playbook uses the cisco.ios.ios_config module to back up the configuration to a local directory, using the ansible_host variable as the base for the file name.

docs.title: Rulebook Example
docs.text:
Now we define a rulebook that triggers the playbook when a relevant syslog message is received:

- name: "LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG"
  hosts: all
  sources:
    - dainok.courses.syslog:
        host: 0.0.0.0
        port: 1514
  rules:
    - name: "RUN PLAYBOOK WHEN ROUTER IS CONFIGURED"
      condition: event.message is match("Configured from.*", ignorecase=true)
      actions:
        - run_playbook:
            name: playbook-backup.yml
        - print_event:
            pretty: true

The rulebook monitors all hosts and uses the dainok.courses.syslog plugin as the event source. It contains a single rule: if event.message contains Configured from, it runs the backup playbook and logs the event.

docs.title: Syslog Callback Plugin
docs.text:
The most complex part is handled by the dainok.courses.syslog plugin. It receives the syslog messages from the devices, formats them and makes them available to the rulebook.

async def main(queue: asyncio.Queue, args: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Receive events via syslog."""
    # Load or set default variables
    host = args.get("host") or "0.0.0.0"
    port = args.get("port") or 1514

    # Listening
    transport, protocol = await asyncio.get_running_loop().create_datagram_endpoint(
        lambda: SyslogUDPProtocol(queue), local_addr=((host, port))
    )

    # Listening
    logging.info(f"Starting daemon on {host}:{port}")
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(300)
    finally:
        transport.close()

The main function starts the syslog server on the specified host and port. The SyslogUDPProtocol class receives the messages, formats them and returns them to the rulebook:

output = {
    "prival": prival,
    "version": version,
    "host": host,
    "seq": seq,
    "timestamp": timestamp,
    "facility": facility,
    "severity": severity,
    "mnemonic": mnemonic,
    "message": message,
    "raw": raw,
}
if host:
    # Limit the inventory for the action
    output["meta"] = {"hosts": host}

# Send data to Ansible
logging.info(f"Sending to EDA {output}")
queue = self.edaQueue
await queue.put(output)

The hosts key must be present to restrict the execution of the playbook to the host that generated the event. The router sends this information via syslog.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
We can now activate our rulebook:

ansible-rulebook -r playbook-rulebook.yml -i inventory.ini -v

The output tells us that the rulebook has started and that the syslog server is ready to receive events.

2025-03-09 17:28:38,987 - ansible_rulebook.engine - INFO - Waiting for all ruleset tasks to end
2025-03-09 17:28:38,987 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - Waiting for actions on events from LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG
2025-03-09 17:28:38,987 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - Waiting for events, ruleset: LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG
2025-03-09 17:28:38 987 [drools-async-evaluator-thread] INFO org.drools.ansible.rulebook.integration.api.io.RuleExecutorChannel - Async channel connected

To make sure that the syslog parser formats the events correctly, we configure the devices with the following commands:

service timestamps debug datetime msec localtime year
service timestamps log datetime msec localtime year
service sequence-numbers
logging host 169.254.1.1 transport udp port 1514
logging origin-id hostname

If we configure a router, as soon as we return to exec mode the router sends a message to the syslog server, which processes it:

2025-03-09 17:32:18,965 - root - INFO - Received Syslog message: <189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)
2025-03-09 17:32:18,967 - root - INFO - Sending to EDA {'prival': 189, 'version': 85, 'host': 'sw1.example.com', 'seq': 97, 'timestamp': 'Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933', 'facility': 'SYS', 'severity': '5', 'mnemonic': 'CONFIG_I', 'message': 'Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'raw': '<189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'meta': {'hosts': 'sw1.example.com'}}
2025-03-09 17:32:19 006 [main] INFO org.drools.ansible.rulebook.integration.api.rulesengine.RegisterOnlyAgendaFilter - Activation of effective rule "RUN PLAYBOOK WHEN ROUTER IS CONFIGURED" with facts: {m={prival=189, version=85, host=sw1.example.com, seq=97, timestamp=Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933, facility=SYS, severity=5, mnemonic=CONFIG_I, message=Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1), raw=<189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1), meta={hosts=sw1.example.com, source={name=dainok.courses.syslog, type=dainok.courses.syslog}, received_at=2025-03-09T16:32:18.967429Z, uuid=978910b9-6589-47e5-bdf1-b6784eb39b39}}}

The playbook is then executed only on the host that generated the event:

2025-03-09 17:32:19,015 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - call_action run_playbook
2025-03-09 17:32:19,015 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - substitute_variables [{'name': 'playbook-backup.yml'}] [{'event': {'prival': 189, 'version': 85, 'host': 'sw1.example.com', 'seq': 97, 'timestamp': 'Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933', 'facility': 'SYS', 'severity': '5', 'mnemonic': 'CONFIG_I', 'message': 'Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'raw': '<189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'meta': {'hosts': 'sw1.example.com', 'source': {'name': 'dainok.courses.syslog', 'type': 'dainok.courses.syslog'}, 'received_at': '2025-03-09T16:32:18.967429Z', 'uuid': '978910b9-6589-47e5-bdf1-b6784eb39b39'}}}]
2025-03-09 17:32:19,015 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - action args: {'name': 'playbook-backup.yml'}

If needed, EDA passes the event data to the playbook through the ansible_eda variable.

TASK [debug] *******************************************************************
ok: [sw1.example.com] => {
    "msg": {
        "event": {
            "facility": "SYS",
            "host": "sw1.example.com",
            "message": "Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)",
            "meta": {
                "hosts": "sw1.example.com",
                "received_at": "2025-03-09T16:35:14.521860Z",
                "source": {
                    "name": "dainok.courses.syslog",
                    "type": "dainok.courses.syslog"
                },
                "uuid": "4a1a9a8c-e386-4f48-b666-0c80be4cc558"
            },
            "mnemonic": "CONFIG_I",
            "prival": 189,
            "raw": "<189>86: SW1: 000098: Mar  9 2025 17:35:13.514: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)",
            "seq": 98,
            "severity": "5",
            "timestamp": "Mar  9 2025 17:35:13.514",
            "version": 86
        },
        "rule": "RUN PLAYBOOK WHEN ROUTER IS CONFIGURED",
        "ruleset": "LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG"
    }
}

Using EDA:

  • Requires authentication to be automatic (non-interactive).
  • Requires the use of collections. In theory, local plugins can be used, but I could not find the correct syntax in practice.

The collection that contains the plugin is available in the Ansible GitHub repository and can be installed via Galaxy. The playbook is available in the GitHub repository of the course.

docs.title: Ansible reporting with ARA
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

ARA Records Ansible provides a simple dashboard to visualize the execution of Ansible playbooks. It is not an orchestration tool but a reporting tool that makes visualization and troubleshooting easier.

ARA works with any Ansible playbook, regardless of how it is executed, so it can be integrated with other tools. However, the information stored by ARA can be enriched by integrating specific parameters into the playbooks.

To better understand ARA, we can explore the demo.

When ARA is configured as a callback, the results of the playbook executions are stored in a database:

docs.title: Installing and Configuring ARA
docs.text:
ARA is installed as a Python module:

pip install ara[server]

We then need to configure ARA as a callback. To do this, we run the following command:

python -m ara.setup.ansible

We add the output of the command above to the ansible.cfg file:

[defaults]
inventory = inventory.ini
stdout_callback = ansible.builtin.default
callback_plugins = ../../venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ara/plugins/callback
action_plugins = ../../venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ara/plugins/action
lookup_plugins = ../../venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ara/plugins/lookup
strategy = free
forks = 8

ARA can be customized with specific parameters configured in the ansible.cfg file. Initially, the default parameters are fine.

We start the ARA server with the following command:

ara-manage runserver

docs.title: Executing a Playbook
docs.text:
ARA does not require any change to the way Ansible playbooks are executed. For example, we can run a playbook we created earlier to configure a small sample fabric.

On the first execution, ARA creates default settings and an SQLite database:

[ara] No setting found for SECRET_KEY. Generating a random key...
[ara] Creating data & configuration directory: /Users/dainese/.ara/server
[ara] Writing default settings to /Users/dainese/.ara/server/settings.yaml
Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, api, auth, contenttypes, db, sessions
Running migrations:
  Applying contenttypes.0001_initial... OK
  Applying auth.0001_initial... OK
  Applying admin.0001_initial... OK
  Applying admin.0002_logentry_remove_auto_add... OK
  Applying admin.0003_logentry_add_action_flag_choices... OK
  Applying api.0001_initial... OK
  Applying api.0002_remove_host_alias... OK
  Applying api.0003_add_missing_result_properties... OK
  Applying api.0004_duration_in_database... OK

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
After the first execution, we can connect to the ARA server and verify that the playbook execution has been recorded correctly:

In the hosts tab, we can analyze the duration of the playbook on each host:

We can view the details of the tasks executed on a specific host:

Finally, we can review the execution details of each task:

docs.title: Recording Additional Values
docs.text:
ARA can be configured to record additional parameters. This requires adding specific tasks:

- name: "ARA: INTERFACE CONFIG"
  delegate_to: localhost
  throttle: 1
  ara_record:
    key: interface_config
    value: "{{ interface_config_list }}"

There are some important caveats:

  • Adding ara_record tasks breaks compatibility with normal execution.
  • Running ARA with ara_record tasks often results in errors:
An exception occurred during task execution. To see the full traceback, use -vvv. The error was: requests.exceptions.ConnectionError: HTTPConnectionPool(host='localhost', port=60417): Read timed out.
An exception occurred during task execution. To see the full traceback, use -vvv. The error was: requests.exceptions.ConnectionError: ('Connection aborted.', BadStatusLine('Date: Sun, 09 Mar 2025 10:18:10 GMT\r\n'))

These errors can be mitigated with the delegate_to and throttle parameters; however, my tests showed that ARA becomes unusable.

When it works, the output is similar to the following:

The playbook is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Orchestrating playbooks with Ansible AWX
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible awx docker

Ansible AWX is the open-source project that the automation controller (formerly Ansible Tower) is derived from. Both are orchestrators for Ansible playbooks: they manage playbooks in the form of projects, credentials, schedules and reports.

The installation of AWX is particularly complex and has changed several times over the years. Currently, it requires a Kubernetes environment, which we install on an Ubuntu Linux Server system.

We need a system with the following specifications:

  • Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04.
  • 8 cores.
  • 8 GB of RAM.
  • 50 GB of disk space.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
First, we install Docker by following the official documentation.

Remove any packages related to previous versions:

apt-get purge docker.io docker-doc docker-compose docker-compose-v2 podman-docker containerd runc

Add the official Docker repository:

wget -qO- https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | apt-key add -
add-apt-repository "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture)] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable"

Finally, install Docker:

apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

docs.title: Minikube
docs.text:
Minikube gives us a complete Kubernetes instance inside a single virtual machine.

Let's install Minikube:

curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube && rm minikube-linux-amd64

Then, with an unprivileged user that belongs to the docker group, we create the Kubernetes instance:

minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=6g --addons=ingress
minikube kubectl -- get nodes

For simplicity, let's add an alias that lets us use the kubectl command:

alias kubectl="minikube kubectl --"

docs.title: Installing AWX
docs.text:
Check the AWX Operator repository to see which tag we can use (2.16.1) and create the files needed to set up the environment:

# awx/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: awx
images:
  - name: quay.io/ansible/awx-operator
    newTag: 2.16.1
resources:
  - github.com/ansible/awx-operator/config/default?ref=2.16.1

Then apply the changes:

kubectl apply -k awx/

Monitor the creation of the pods with the following command and wait for it to finish:

kubectl get pods -n awx -w

Then create the resource file:

# awx/awx.yaml
apiVersion: awx.ansible.com/v1beta1
kind: AWX
metadata:
  name: awx
spec:
  service_type: nodeport

And associate it with the file created earlier:

# awx/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: awx
images:
  - name: quay.io/ansible/awx-operator
    newTag: 2.16.1
resources:
  - github.com/ansible/awx-operator/config/default?ref=2.16.1
  - awx.yaml

Then apply the changes again:

kubectl apply -k awx/

And monitor the logs related to the creation of the AWX service:

kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-operator-controller-manager -c awx-manager

We can also monitor the status of the pods:

kubectl get pods -A

At the end of the process, the AWX service should be available:

minikube service awx-service --url -n awx

Now we need to make the AWX service reachable from the outside:

kubectl port-forward svc/awx-service -n awx --address 0.0.0.0 8080:80 &> /dev/null &

The AWX web interface should now be available on port 8080. We can log in with the user admin; the password can be retrieved with the following command:

kubectl get secret awx-admin-password -n awx -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 --decode; echo

In case of issues, we check the status of the entire environment with the following commands:

minikube status
minikube service list
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl get services -n awx
kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-operator-controller-manager
kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-task
kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-web

In extreme cases, we can get a shell inside the various containers:

kubectl exec --stdin --tty --namespace awx awx-task-5f88767b44-87m9p -- /bin/bash

docs.title: ansible-pylibssh
docs.text:
If we need the ansible-pylibssh library, we have to make an additional change. By default, AWX, like Ansible, uses the paramiko library. The playbook is executed by a container created at runtime from the awx-ee image:

minikube ssh docker images

If we run a playbook using the default environment, we get the following error:

[WARNING]: ansible-pylibssh not installed, falling back to paramiko
fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "No existing session"}

We can force the use of pylibssh by setting the following variable:

ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: libssh

In this case, we get a more explicit error:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "Failed to import the required Python library (ansible-pylibssh) on automation-job-11-m85n8's Python /usr/bin/python3. Please read the module documentation and install it in the appropriate location. If the required library is installed, but Ansible is using the wrong Python interpreter, please consult the documentation on ansible_python_interpreter"}

There is a third-party EE image (Execution Environment) that contains ansible-pylibssh, but it is a year old and comes with no guarantee.

The GitHub repository contains the structure used to create the dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh image. In particular, there are four files:

  • dependencies/bindep.txt: contains the list of RPM packages to install in the image.
  • dependencies/requirements.txt: contains the list of Python packages to install in the image.
  • dependencies/requirements.yml: contains the Ansible Galaxy collections to install in the image.
  • execution-environment.yml: defines how to create the image from a specific version of awx-ee, based on the dependencies defined above.

Let's create the environment to build the image:

cd "/opt/courses/Ansible/A5. AWX"
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install ansible==9.5.1 ansible-builder==3.0.1
ansible-builder build --tag dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1 --container-runtime docker --verbosity 3

Once the build is complete, we can publish the image on Docker Hub:

docker login
docker tag dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1 dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:latest
docker push dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1
docker push dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:latest

docs.title: Bastion Host
docs.text:
We described the architecture of the bastion host in a previous lesson, and here we use the same architecture.

First, we copy the content of the id_rsa.pub file into the authorized_keys file of the bastion host. Then we make the private key id_rsa available to AWX:

kubectl create secret generic bastion-host-key -n awx --from-file=ssh-privatekey=.ssh/id_rsa

In AWX, go to Instance Groups → default → Edit → Customize pod specification. The content should be similar to the following:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: awx
spec:
  serviceAccountName: default
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - image: quay.io/ansible/awx-ee:latest
      name: worker
      args:
        - ansible-runner
        - worker
        - '--private-data-dir=/runner'
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 250m
          memory: 100Mi

Customize the configuration so that the key stored as a Secret is available as a local file:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: awx
spec:
  serviceAccountName: default
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - image: quay.io/ansible/awx-ee:latest
      name: worker
      args:
        - ansible-runner
        - worker
        - '--private-data-dir=/runner'
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 250m
          memory: 100Mi
      # Custom config starts here
      volumeMounts:
        - name: ssh-keys
          mountPath: /opt/bastionhost_id_rsa
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: ssh-keys
      secret:
        secretName: bastion-host-key
        defaultMode: 0400
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000 # The AWX user
    fsGroup: 1000 # The AWX user

Finally, in the inventory (Resources → Inventories → Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology), add the variables that force the use of the bastion host:

ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios
ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: paramiko
ansible_ssh_common_args: -o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=/opt/bastionhost_id_rsa/ssh-privatekey -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110"

Now all the playbooks associated with the Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology inventory are executed via the bastion host.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
The playbook repositories we use in AWX must list the Ansible Galaxy collections they need in the collections/requirements.yml file:

collections:
- name: cisco.ios
  version: 8.0.0
  source: https://galaxy.ansible.com

The same file can be used to install the dependencies in the local environment:

ansible-galaxy collection install -r src/courses/collections/requirements.yml

docs.title: Configuring AWX
docs.text:
First, let's create the execution environment (EE) using the Docker image we built earlier. In Administration → Execution Environments, add a new image:

  • Name: awx-ee-pylibssh.
  • Image: dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1.
  • Pull: Only pull the image if not present before running.

Now go to Resources → Projects and add a project that uses the GitHub repository of the course:

  • Name: Courses.
  • Execution Environment: awx-ee-pylibssh.
  • Source Control Type: Git.
  • Source Control URL: https://github.com/dainok/courses.

Next, go to Resources → Inventories and create a new inventory of type inventory:

  • Name: Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology.

The inventory has the following variables, defined in YAML format:

ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios
ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: libssh

Then create the two groups used in the playbooks: core and access.

Add the credentials by going to Resources → Credentials:

  • Name: Cisco Lab.
  • Credential Type: Machine.
  • Username: admin.
  • Password: cisco.

Finally, add the six devices, associating each with the correct group:

  • sw1.example.com: core group, with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.101.
  • sw2.example.com: core group, with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.102.
  • sw3.example.com: access group, with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.103.
  • sw4.example.com: access group, with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.104.
  • sw5.example.com: access group, with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.105.
  • sw6.example.com: access group, with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.106.

Finally, create the template to run the playbook. Go to Resources → Templates and add a new template:

  • Name: Fabric provisioning.
  • Job Type: Run.
  • Inventory: Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology.
  • Project: Courses.
  • Playbook: Ansible/21. Final lab/playbook-fabric-setup.yml.
  • Credentials: Cisco Lab.

Save the template and run it. Under Jobs, you can see the result of the job and its logs.

The first execution may take longer, because AWX has to create the container used to run the playbook:

$ kubectl get pods -A
NAMESPACE   NAME                                               READY   STATUS              RESTARTS        AGE
awx         automation-job-5-plmtj                             0/1     ContainerCreating   0               6m56s
awx         awx-migration-24.3.1-qmncx                         0/1     Completed           0               42h
awx         awx-operator-controller-manager-5b795f7bb-597fv    2/2     Running             17 (22h ago)    42h
awx         awx-postgres-15-0                                  1/1     Running             0               42h
awx         awx-task-77b9bcbc8d-txjl8                          4/4     Running             0               42h
awx         awx-web-7569c8f4f9-dxmvk                           3/3     Running             0               42h

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
There are many moving parts that can fail. Let's summarize the errors we may encounter.

The execution of the job should trigger the download of the Docker image we created. Let's verify it with:

$ minikube ssh docker images
REPOSITORY                  TAG   IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh      1     f2bee65d1f1c   18 hours ago   3.36GB

If the creation of the container takes longer than expected, and in particular if it stops at ContainerCreating, we can analyze the problem with:

kubectl describe pods -n awx automation-job-12-gqzxr

If the image is not downloaded correctly, we check the URL, including the tag. The error associated with the failure to retrieve the image is:

Receptor detail:
Error creating pod: container failed to start, ImagePullBackOff

If the logs report a timeout when connecting to the devices, the configuration of the bastion host may be incorrect:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: Timeout connecting to 169.254.1.111"}

A similar error probably indicates that the bastion host, if used, is not reachable:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: Socket error: Connection reset by peer"}

In this case, we should see similar logs on the bastion host:

May 11 06:14:50 eve-ng sshd[1885336]: Failed password for dev from 172.25.82.1 port 49826 ssh2

If we get errors related to the pylibssh library, we must make sure that we are using the correct EE image, referenced at the inventory and/or template level. For instance, if we receive a warning that ansible-pylibssh is not installed, followed by a failure message about a missing session, we see the following:

[WARNING]: ansible-pylibssh not installed, falling back to paramiko
ok: [sw1.example.com]
TASK [cisco_ios_system : CONFIGURING HOSTNAME AND DOMAIN NAME] *****************
fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "No existing session"}

To avoid ambiguity, if we are not using a bastion host, we make sure that the use of pylibssh is enforced by the configuration; otherwise, we may get an error similar to this:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "Failed to import the required Python library (ansible-pylibssh) on automation-job-11-m85n8's Python /usr/bin/python3. Please read the module documentation and install it in the appropriate location. If the required library is installed, but Ansible is using the wrong Python interpreter, please consult the documentation on ansible_python_interpreter"}

If we have connection problems with outdated devices, we may see an error like this:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: kex error : no match for method kex algos: server [diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1,diffie-hellman-group1-sha1], client [curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256,diffie-hellman-group14-sha256,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18-sha512]"}

In this case, we may need to use paramiko instead of ansible-pylibssh by setting the following variable:

ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: paramiko

Finally, if we receive an error related to the credentials or the credential type, we may see a message like this:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: Failed to authenticate public key: Access denied for 'none'. Authentication that can continue: publickey,keyboard-interactive,password"}

docs.title: Ansible Galaxy
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Ansible provides Galaxy, which manages packages containing roles and collections. Roles and collections can be referenced directly by Ansible playbooks. Galaxy allows you to use packages published on the public portal, but it also lets you manage private repositories.

In this post, we focus on the official Galaxy portal. The portal is fully integrated with GitHub, where the repositories available as collections in Galaxy are stored.

The structure of a collection is quite rigid, so to create one it is best to rely on ansible-creator, which we can install with pip:

pip install ansible-creator

We then create a collection using the format github_nickname.collection_name. In my case, I used dainok.courses:

ansible-creator init collection dainok.courses

This command creates a complete but rather complex structure:

Let's examine the essential parts.

docs.title: galaxy.yml
docs.text:
The galaxy.yml file contains the metadata of the collection and the instructions to build it. For further details, refer to the official documentation and the example repository.

namespace: "dainok"
name: "common"
version: 1.0.0
readme: README.md
authors:
  - your name <example@domain.com>
description: your collection description
license_file: LICENSE
tags: ["linux", "tools"]
dependencies:
  "ansible.utils": "*"
repository: http://example.com/repository
documentation: http://docs.example.com
homepage: http://example.com
issues: http://example.com/issue/tracker
build_ignore:
  - .gitignore
  - changelogs/.plugin-cache.yaml

docs.title: Extensions, Plugins, Roles, and Playbooks
docs.text:
Extensions, plugins, roles and playbooks must be stored in their respective directories. Each role must be described by a README.md file and the meta/main.yml file.

galaxy_info:
  author: foo
  description: Dainok.Common Run Role
  company: Dainok
  license: GPL-2.0-or-later
  min_ansible_version: "2.14"
  galaxy_tags:
    []
dependencies:
  []

Note that some information is duplicated: for example, the description is present in both the meta file and the README, and dependencies exist at both the role level and the collection level.

Filters are stored in the plugins directory and are described in Python files:

DOCUMENTATION = """
    name: hello_world
    author: Your Name
    version_added: "1.0.0"
    short_description: A custom filter plugin for Ansible.
    description:
      - This is a demo filter plugin designed to return Hello message.
    options:
      name:
        description: Value specified here is appended to the Hello message.
        type: str
"""

EXAMPLES = """
# hello_world filter example

- name: Display a hello message
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ 'ansible-creator' | hello_world }}"
"""

docs.title: Ansible Galaxy Token
docs.text:
Before proceeding, we need to register on the Galaxy portal and obtain a token. Since Galaxy is integrated with GitHub, we need a valid GitHub account and we must authenticate on Galaxy via GitHub:

A token can be obtained by navigating to Collections → API token.

docs.title: Building and Publishing
docs.text:
Once the repository is ready, we can create the package and publish it as a collection:

ansible-galaxy collection build
ansible-galaxy collection publish --token <token> dainok-courses-0.0.17.tar.gz

The courses collection is available under the dainok namespace. We can manage our collections on the Galaxy portal by navigating to Collections → Namespaces → My namespaces.

We can also view the logs related to the publication of the collection:

docs.title: Using a Collection
docs.text:
The simplest way to install a collection is via the command line:

ansible-galaxy collection install --force dainok.courses

It is more practical, however, as we do with Python, to define a collections/requirements.yml file that describes the dependencies:

collections:
  - name: cisco.ios
    version: 8.0.0
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com
  - name: paloaltonetworks.panos
    version: 2.20.0
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com
  - name: networktocode.nautobot
    version: 5.2.1
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com
  - name: dainok.courses
    version: 0.0.17
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com

We can install the collections defined as dependencies:

ansible-galaxy collection install -r collections/requirements.yml

Finally, we can list the installed collections:

ansible-galaxy collection list

The sample collection is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Delegate Ansible tasks to a different host
Delegate Ansible tasks to a different host
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

By default, each task runs on the host that is being configured. In various scenarios, however, tasks need to be executed across multiple hosts in a specific sequence. A common example is a web server that must be taken offline from the load balancer before being modified. A typical playbook for this scenario would:

  • Reconfigure the load balancer to take the web server offline.
  • Reconfigure the web server.
  • Reconfigure the load balancer to bring the web server back online.

In our network fabric, we can adapt this approach:

We can write a playbook that configures the access switches while enabling the corresponding core switch interfaces step by step.

In other words, once an access switch is configured, a specific task connects to the core switches to configure the interfaces associated with that switch.

To do this, we use the delegate_to functionality.

docs.title: Using delegate_to in Ansible
docs.text:
The syntax is straightforward: in a task, we specify which host is delegated to execute it. In many cases, we can use localhost to run a task locally. In our scenario, we delegate the configuration tasks to the core switches:

- name: "CONFIGURING UPSTREAM SW1"
  delegate_to: sw1.example.com
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
      - switchport mode trunk
      - switchport nonegotiate
      - udld port aggressive
    parents: "interface {{ upstream_interface }}"
    before: "default interface {{ upstream_interface }}"
- name: "ENABLING UPSTREAM SW1 INTERFACE"
  delegate_to: sw1.example.com
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config:
      - name: "{{ upstream_interface }}"
        enabled: true
        description: "to {{ inventory_hostname }}"

docs.title: Key Considerations
docs.text:
There are some important points to keep in mind when using delegate_to:

  • delegate_to cannot be used with loops (with_items). We can work around this limitation by including a separate task, as shown above.
  • delegate_to does not work correctly with a bastion host. If misconfigured, we might get the following error:
fatal: [sw6.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "unable to connect to socket /Users/dainese/.ansible/pc/ff42547828. See the socket path issue category in Network Debug and Troubleshooting Guide"}

The official documentation provides a detailed explanation of this functionality, including specific cases related to variable handling.

When we run the playbook, the output of Ansible indicates that a task for a specific switch has been delegated to another host, such as sw1.example.com:

TASK [cisco_ios_uplink_interface : CONFIGURING UPSTREAM SW1] *******************
ok: [sw3.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]
ok: [sw5.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]
ok: [sw6.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]
ok: [sw4.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]

The playbook is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Network Provisioning with ServiceNow and Ansible
Automating Network Provisioning with ServiceNow and Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

ServiceNow is a cloud-based SaaS platform that digitalizes, automates and optimizes enterprise workflows.

One of its core capabilities is the definition of the services offered to users through a service catalog, together with the full lifecycle management of the requests. The goal here is to extend that catalog to all the relevant IT services, automating their provisioning end to end.

We walk through a practical example: a network provisioning entry in the service catalog, which end users can parameterize and order.

A Python script handles the incoming requests automatically and applies the changes in the production environment.

The architecture supports two integration modes:

  • Pull: the script polls ServiceNow periodically to retrieve the unfulfilled requests.
  • Push: a webhook notifies the script of new requests in real time.

Polling is generally discouraged, but many organizations apply infrastructure changes only within specific maintenance windows. In that context, it is natural to pull all the pending requests at the start of each window and process them one after the other until it closes.

This experiment requires a ServiceNow instance. I used a personal developer instance, available free of charge through the ServiceNow Developer Program.

docs.title: ServiceNow Catalog Configuration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

In this post, we extend the ServiceNow service catalog with a new item to create networks. The example is intentionally simple, but in real environments a thorough analysis of the architecture, the services offered and the existing processes must come first. Automation improves processes: if the processes do not exist yet, that is where the work needs to start.

Open ServiceNow and navigate to All → Service Catalog → Catalog → Catalog Definitions → Maintain Catalogs, then go to Technical Catalog → Catalog Items → New.

After filling in the details of the item as shown, confirm with Submit and reopen the object to add the associated variables.

We need to define three variables:

  • name: What is the network name?
  • vlan: What is the network ID (VLAN)?
  • ip_address: What is the gateway IP address (if required)?

At this point, the new Network Provisioning item should appear in the catalog. Users can select it and order a new network by entering the desired parameters.

Once the order is submitted, ServiceNow creates a Request (REQ) that contains the corresponding Requested Item (RITM).

docs.title: Ansible playbook for Network provisioning
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

On the infrastructure side, we can configure the network devices in three ways: a custom script, Ansible or Terraform.

The tasks here are atomic and there is no infrastructure state to maintain, so Ansible is the most appropriate tool for this type of operation.

The playbook is intentionally minimal: it configures the VLAN and brings up an SVI only if a gateway IP address has been specified.

- name: ServiceNow Network Provisioning
  tasks:
    - name: VLAN Provisioning
      cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
        config:
          - name: "{{ network_name }}"
            vlan_id: "{{ network_vlan }}"
            state: active
            shutdown: disabled
        state: merged
    - name: SVI Provisioning
      cisco.ios.ios_l3_interfaces:
        config:
          - name: "Vlan{{ network_vlan }}"
            ipv4:
              - address: "{{ network_ip_address }}"
        state: merged
      when: network_ip_address is defined and network_ip_address != ""
    - name: Interface Provisioning
      cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
        config:
          - name: "Vlan{{ network_vlan }}"
            description: "{{ network_vlan }}"
            enabled: true
        state: merged
      when: network_ip_address is defined and network_ip_address != ""
  post_tasks:
