    - name: SAVING CONFIG
      tags: always
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: modified

We can test the playbook manually to validate its behavior:

./playbook-snow_network.yml -e network_name="Network-97" -e network_vlan="97" -e network_ip_address="10.0.97.1/24"

PLAY [ServiceNow Network Provisioning] *****************************************

TASK [VLAN Provisioning] *******************************************************
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.netcommon does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.utils does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
changed: [sw1.example.com]

TASK [SVI Provisioning] ********************************************************
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.netcommon does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.utils does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
changed: [sw1.example.com]

TASK [Interface Provisioning] **************************************************
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.netcommon does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.utils does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
changed: [sw1.example.com]

TASK [SAVING CONFIG] ***********************************************************
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.netcommon does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
[WARNING]: Collection ansible.utils does not support Ansible version 2.15.13
changed: [sw1.example.com]

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
sw1.example.com            : ok=4    changed=4    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0

The full playbook is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: ServiceNow Poll-Based Request Processing
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

In this post, we process ServiceNow requests in pull mode, through periodic polling.

The first step is to retrieve all the RITMs that are still in the open state, that is, not yet taken over.

def get_ritms(category=None):
    """Get active RITMs for a specific category."""
    url = f"{SN_INSTANCE}/api/now/table/sc_req_item"
    params = {
        "sysparm_query": f"state={STATE_MAP.get('open')}",
        "sysparm_fields": "sys_id,state,number,variables,cat_item,sc_item_option"
    }
    if category:
        params["sysparm_query"] += f"^cat_item={CATALOG_MAP[category]}"

    r = requests.get(url, auth=AUTH, params=params)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["result"]

The field values in ServiceNow are not plain strings but integers that reference entries in lookup tables. To handle this cleanly, we define a set of maps for the states of the items and for the catalog entries.

STATE_MAP = {
    "open": 1,
    "work_in_progress": 2,
    "closed_complete": 3,
    "closed_incomplete": 4,
}

CATALOG_MAP = {
    "network_request": "8ea0b64593908710be22fd245d03d61b",
    "whitelist_request": "e91336da4fff0200086eeed18110c7a3",
}

More dynamic solutions exist, but for this experiment static maps are more than adequate.

For each RITM, we retrieve the associated variables in two steps: first we fetch the IDs of the variables used in the request, then we resolve them to their actual values.

def get_ritm_variables(ritm_sys_id):
    url = f"{SN_INSTANCE}/api/now/table/sc_item_option_mtom"
    params = {
        "sysparm_query": f"request_item={ritm_sys_id}",
        "sysparm_fields": "sc_item_option",
        "sysparm_limit": 100,
    }
    r = requests.get(url, auth=AUTH, params=params)
    r.raise_for_status()
    option_ids = [
        item["sc_item_option"]["value"]
        for item in r.json()["result"]
    ]

    # Get all RITM variables
    variables = {}
    ids_query = "^ORsys_id=".join(option_ids)
    url = f"{SN_INSTANCE}/api/now/table/sc_item_option"
    params = {
        "sysparm_query": f"sys_id={ids_query}",
        "sysparm_fields": "item_option_new.name,item_option_new.question_text,value",
        "sysparm_display_value": "all",
        "sysparm_limit": 100,
    }
    r = requests.get(url, auth=AUTH, params=params)
    r.raise_for_status()
    for item in r.json()["result"]:
        name  = item.get("item_option_new.name", {}).get("value", "")
        value = item.get("value", {}).get("display_value", "")
        if name:
            variables[name] = value

    return variables

Once we have the RITM and its variables, we mark the item as Work in Progress.

def update_ritm(ritm_sys_id, state, output=None):
    """Update RITM."""
    url = f"{SN_INSTANCE}/api/now/table/sc_req_item/{ritm_sys_id}"
    payload = {
        "state": STATE_MAP[state],
    }
    if output:
        payload["work_notes"] = output

    requests.patch(url, json=payload, auth=AUTH)

    # Close REQ if all RITMs are closed
    req_sys_id = get_req_from_ritm(ritm_sys_id)
    ritm_list = get_all_ritm_from_req(req_sys_id)
    if all_ritm_closed(ritm_list):
        close_req(req_sys_id)

We then pass the variables to the Ansible playbook for execution.

# Run Ansible
result = run_ansible_network(**variables)
rc = result.rc
stdout = result.stdout.read()
stderr = result.stderr.read()
if rc == 0:
    update_ritm(sys_id, "closed_complete", stdout)
else:
    update_ritm(sys_id, "closed_incomplete", stdout + "\n" * 3 + stderr)

Finally, we update the ticket based on the outcome of the playbook run. Whether it succeeds or fails, the Ansible output is attached to the ticket as a work note.

The full script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automated VM Provisioning from a ServiceNow Ticket
Automated VM Provisioning from a ServiceNow Ticket
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

This is the second practical example in our series on automating managed service operations. Here we see how to provision a virtual machine automatically, starting from a ticket opened in ServiceNow.

docs.title: Workflow Analysis
docs.text:
This example is intentionally simplified, but real implementations require a thorough analysis of the provisioning workflow. Details that look trivial at first glance can introduce complex edge cases and exception handling if they are left unaddressed.

Provisioning a VM with a remotely accessible operating system involves:

  • Identifying the target vCenter, datacenter, cluster and datastore.
  • Providing either an unattended installation ISO or a template that regenerates the host identifiers on first boot.
  • Defining the hostname, domain and fully qualified domain name (FQDN).
  • Allocating a free IP address, the default gateway and the network name as defined in vCenter.
  • Configuring DNS and NTP servers.
  • Registering the FQDN-to-IP mapping in DNS.
  • Storing the access credentials securely in a password manager.

The result is a VM that is remotely accessible, with the connection details delivered to the end user.

If we also want a service catalog that lets users select additional software at provisioning time, it is worth defining a controlled set of options upfront. To minimize variability and complexity, I recommend mapping each option to a dedicated Ansible playbook that configures the freshly installed system. For example, we can define a role variable that accepts the following values:

  • undefined: no post-installation customization.
  • tomcat: installs Apache + Tomcat.
  • www: installs Apache + PHP and pulls the website codebase from a Git repository.

docs.title: ServiceNow Service Catalog
docs.text:
On the development instance, a Technical Catalog should already be present under Service Catalog → Catalog Definitions → Maintain Catalogs, and within it a catalog item named VM Provisioning.

The catalog item exposes three input variables to the end user.

docs.title: Serving Tickets
docs.text:
We reuse the Python polling script introduced in the previous article (available in the GitHub repository). Following the same pattern, the script retrieves the values of the RITM, normalizes them and passes them as parameters to the Ansible playbook.

# Mark ticket as WIP
update_ritm(sys_id, "work_in_progress")

# Run Ansible
print(variables)
storage=variables.get("storage")
storage=storage.replace(" GB", "")
storage=storage.replace(" TB", "000")
storage=int(storage)
result = run_ansible_vm(cpu=variables.get("cpu"), ram=variables.get("ram"), storage=storage)
rc = result.rc
stdout = result.stdout.read()
stderr = result.stderr.read()
if rc == 0:
    update_ritm(sys_id, "closed_complete", stdout)
else:
    update_ritm(sys_id, "closed_incomplete", stdout + "\n" * 3 + stderr)

The playbook is then executed with the sanitized and normalized input parameters. In this simplified example, the hostname is set only at the VM level, using a UUID to guarantee a unique name.

def run_ansible_vm(cpu, ram, storage):
    """Run Ansible."""
    extravars = {
        'vm_name': f'vm-snow-portal-{str(uuid.uuid4())}',
        'vm_ram': int(ram) * 1024,
        'vm_cpu': int(cpu),
        'vm_storage': storage,
    }
    print("Running Ansible playbook with", extravars)
    run = ansible_runner.run(
        private_data_dir='.',
        playbook=f'playbook-snow_vm.yml',
        extravars=extravars,
        envvars={
            "ANSIBLE_FORCE_COLOR": "false",
            "NO_COLOR": "1",
        }
    )
    return run

docs.title: Building an Unattended Installation Image
docs.text:
This example focuses on Ubuntu Linux, but the same approach applies to any operating system we choose to support.

Ubuntu uses cloud-init to standardize and reproduce system installations. Let's prepare a fully unattended Ubuntu ISO.

First, download the base ISO:

wget https://releases.ubuntu.com/26.04/ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso

Extract its contents into a working directory:

xorriso -osirrox on -indev ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso -extract / iso_extracted/

Next, create the cloud-init configuration directory and files:

  • iso_extracted/nocloud/meta-data: leave empty.
  • iso_extracted/nocloud/vendor-data: leave empty.
  • iso_extracted/nocloud/user-data: contains the cloud-init parameters.
#cloud-config
autoinstall:
  version: 1
  identity:
    hostname: myserver
    username: ubuntu
    # echo password | mkpasswd -m sha-512 -s
    password: "$6$Lyb2/s0n8bZA1Orw$2v/JLCxyoX4uTvkbBFPzijfaLTJ1J6q56VPFoFsZHH2sD48.6TZRqyyePTTZz3NMjzlg5qxrHlTqV7cL9Vzge/"
  storage:
    layout:
      name: direct
  late-commands:
    - shutdown -r now

The user-data file contains the cloud-init configuration. In this example, it:

  • Sets a temporary hostname.
  • Creates an initial user account with a password.
  • Triggers a reboot when the installation completes.

Update the GRUB configuration (iso_extracted/boot/grub/grub.cfg) so that it points to the cloud-init files. Be sure to escape the ; character where required.

menuentry "Try or Install Ubuntu Server" {
    set gfxpayload=keep
    linux  /casper/vmlinuz autoinstall ds=nocloud\;s=/cdrom/nocloud/
    initrd /casper/initrd
}

Finally, repackage the directory into a new bootable ISO:

xorriso -as mkisofs -r -V 'Ubuntu-Server 26.04 amd64' --grub2-mbr --interval:local_fs:0s-15s:zero_mbrpt,zero_gpt:'ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso' --protective-msdos-label -partition_cyl_align off -partition_offset 16 --mbr-force-bootable -append_partition 2 28732ac11ff8d211ba4b00a0c93ec93b --interval:local_fs:5689428d-5699723d::'ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso' -appended_part_as_gpt -iso_mbr_part_type a2a0d0ebe5b9334487c068b6b72699c7 -c '/boot.catalog' -b '/boot/grub/i386-pc/eltorito.img' -no-emul-boot -boot-load-size 4 -boot-info-table --grub2-boot-info -eltorito-alt-boot -e '--interval:appended_partition_2_start_1422357s_size_10296d:all::' -no-emul-boot -boot-load-size 10296 -o ubuntu-26.04-server-amd64-autoinstall.iso iso_extracted/

All the configuration files are available in the GitHub repository.

Note on VM templates: if we prefer to clone from a template instead of booting from an ISO, we must make sure that the provisioning process regenerates all the unique identifiers, in particular the SSH host keys and the machine ID, before the VM is handed over.

docs.title: Ansible Playbook and Configuration
docs.text:
Start by adding the vCenter to the Ansible inventory.

[vcenter]
vcenter.example.com

[vcenter:vars]
vm_datacenter="Datacenter"
vm_cluster="Cluster"
vm_datastore="172.25.10.11-SSD"
vm_network="LAB_EVENG"
ansible_user="administrator@vsphere.local"
ansible_password="password"
ansible_connection="local"
ansible_python_interpreter="venv/bin/python3"

The playbook performs three main tasks:

  1. Create the VM, using a module of the official vmware.vmware collection.
  2. Power on the VM and boot from the ISO, using the same collection.
  3. Wait for the installation to complete, using a module of the community.vmware collection that can run commands through VMware Tools.
tasks:
  - name: VM Provisioning
    vmware.vmware.vm:
      <<: *vcenter_auth
      name: "{{ vm_name }}"
      datacenter: "{{ vm_datacenter }}"
      cluster: "{{ vm_cluster }}"
      datastore: "{{ vm_datastore }}"
      guest_id: amazonlinux3_64Guest
      cpu: …
      memory: …
      disks: …
      scsi_controllers: …
      sata_controllers: …
      cdroms: …
      network_adapters: …
    register: vm
  - name: Power on VM
    vmware.vmware.vm_powerstate:
      <<: *vcenter_auth
      moid: "{{ vm.vm.moid }}"
      datacenter: DC01
      state: powered-on

For the third step, the playbook:

  • Polls for the file /var/lib/cloud/instance/boot-finished, which cloud-init creates once the installation is complete.
  • Retrieves the assigned IP addresses and prints them to stdout, so that they can be attached to the originating ServiceNow ticket.
tasks:
  - name: Power on VM
    vmware.vmware.vm_powerstate:
      <<: *vcenter_auth
      moid: "{{ vm.vm.moid }}"
      datacenter: DC01
      state: powered-on
  - name: Wait for cloud-init completion
    community.vmware.vmware_vm_shell:
      <<: *vcenter_auth
      datacenter: "{{ vm_datacenter }}"
      vm_id: "{{ vm_name }}"
      vm_username: "ubuntu"
      vm_password: "password"
      vm_shell: /usr/bin/test
      vm_shell_args: "-f /var/lib/cloud/instance/boot-finished"
      wait_for_process: true
    register: cloud_init_result
    until: cloud_init_result.exit_code is defined and cloud_init_result.exit_code == 0
    retries: 60
    delay: 15
    changed_when: false
  - name: Get VM info
    community.vmware.vmware_guest_info:
      <<: *vcenter_auth
      datacenter: "{{ vm_datacenter }}"
      moid: "{{ vm.vm.moid }}"
    register: vm_info
  - name: Print VM IP address
    debug:
      msg: "{{ vm_info.instance.hw_eth0.ipaddresses }}"

docs.title: End-to-End Execution Example
docs.text:
The user submits a VM request by filling out the service catalog form with the required parameters.

The polling script automatically picks up the open ticket and triggers the execution. When the Ansible playbook completes, the result, including the IP address of the VM, is posted back to the user as a comment on the ServiceNow ticket.

In vCenter, the new VM appears in the inventory, powered on and ready.

The full script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automatic CIS controls check with Ansible
Automatic CIS controls check with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible cis compliance intermediate

Security assessments are part of my daily job, and automation is part of my mindset. The CIS Controls are a set of standard controls that should be checked on... anything. CIS also provides benchmarks (a sort of step-by-step guide) for many environments. Moreover, Lockdown Enterprise delivers a set of Ansible playbooks ready to be used.

In this post, we see how to check the CIS controls on Ubuntu 20.04 servers and remediate them.

docs.title: Audit Phase
docs.text:
Ansible playbooks are good at remediation, but their reporting is often poor. Lockdown Enterprise uses goss to provide good audit reports.

Let's install goss and clone the Git repository on an Ubuntu Linux 20.04 system:

sudo curl -fsSL https://goss.rocks/install | sh
git clone https://github.com/ansible-lockdown/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit
cd /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit

We can audit the entire system using the provided script:

$ sudo ./run_audit.sh

## Pre-Checks Start

OK Audit binary /usr/local/bin/goss is available
OK /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit/goss.yml is available

## Pre-checks Successful

#############
Audit Started
#############


    "summary": {
        "failed-count": 154,
        "summary-line": "Count: 372, Failed: 154, Duration: 91.345s",
        "test-count": 372,
        "total-duration": 91344507858
    }
}

Completed file can be found at /var/tmp/audit_linux-station_1657459563.json
###############
Audit Completed
###############

We can also run goss manually on a subset of controls:

sudo goss --vars /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit/vars/CIS.yml -g /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit/section_1/cis_1.1/cis_1.1.1.1_7.yml validate
sudo goss --vars /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit/vars/CIS.yml -g /var/tmp/UBUNTU20-CIS-Audit/section_1/cis_1.1/cis_1.1.1.1_7.yml validate -f documentation

By default, the server profile is used. To audit with the workstation profile, we use:

sudo ./run_audit.sh -w

docs.title: Remediation Phase
docs.text:
Once the audit is complete, we can analyze the non-compliant items, evaluate the risk and decide whether to remediate them.

From our Ansible server, we clone the Ansible repository:

git clone https://github.com/ansible-lockdown/UBUNTU20-CIS
cd UBUNTU20-CIS

The following Ansible commands may vary depending on your Ansible infrastructure. We can remediate all the controls with:

ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini -u andrea -b -k -K site.yml

Remediating all the controls makes sense just after the OS installation. For production environments, we probably want to remediate single controls with:

ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini -u andrea -b -k -K --tags rule_1.1.1.1 site.yml

Always use the -C flag (check mode) on the first run, to see what would change before changing it.

docs.title: A CMDB for IT infrastructures
docs.text: 22 November 2017

docs.title: A CMDB for IT infrastructures
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog cmdb governance ssot

Can we use a CMDB for the whole IT management? In this post, we see what a CMDB should be and how to import existing network devices into a CMDB using NAPALM. Finally, we see how to operate on network devices from a CMDB and how to push configurations. This post is a compendium to my speech in Milan at the AutomateIT² event.

Suppose an IT manager asks his staff for the total number of active VMs:

  • Alice consults an Excel file and reports 1984 running systems. (What should be.)
  • Bob consults AWS, Azure, Google Compute Engine and the internal vCenter, and reports 2010 running systems. (What is.)
  • Carol remembers that 5 internal VMs are running 33 Docker containers, and asks whether to include them or not. (Exception.)

What happened?

The number of running VMs reported by an Excel file does not match the real world. The real world is reported by vCenter, AWS, Azure and Google Compute Engine. We can call them the Source of Truth.

Source of Truth (SOT) The source of truth is a trusted data source that gives a complete picture of the data object as a whole. (What is.)

The Excel file reports what should be. We can call it the Source of Record and, because it should be unique, the Single Source of Record:

System of Record (SOR) A system of record is the authoritative data source for a given data element or piece of information. (What should be.)

I know that these definitions differ from what others use, but I guess you agree that vCenter is a Source of Truth, not an Excel file. Let me give you an example.

Suppose you have a fantastic system that synchronizes vCenter with an Excel file. Are you sure that a manually created VM is added to the Excel file? Are you sure that a powered-off, orphaned VM is added to the Excel file? Are you sure that Excel reports the real number of VMs at any moment?

That is why I am convinced that the definition "Single Source of Truth" is wrong, and why I changed it to "Single System of Record".

Suppose now that we want to store all the IT data in a single place: Excel is obviously not the right place. We should use a different and more flexible data structure, depending on our needs: we could use CMDBuild, iTop, or simply Git/CVS, depending on the requirements.

In this example, we suppose that we want to store every single IT item (device, service, database schema...) in a single place. In this case, we need a CMDB:

A configuration management database (CMDB) is a repository that acts as a data warehouse for information technology (IT) installations. It holds data relating to a collection of IT assets (commonly referred to as configuration items (CI)), as well as to descriptive relationships between such assets.

Let's now focus on CMDBuild as a CMDB.

docs.title: CMDBuild Installation on Ubuntu 16.04
docs.text:
Before starting, we download the following three packages:

  1. The latest JRE.
  2. The latest Tomcat.
  3. The latest CMDBuild.

We make sure the locale is set to en_US.UTF-8. If not, we reconfigure it:

dpkg-reconfigure locales

We install PostgreSQL and set the admin password:

$ sudo dpkg-reconfigure locales
$ sudo apt-get -y install postgresql
$ sudo -u postgres psql
\password postgres
\q

We unpack Java and set it as the default for the system:

$ tar -xzf jre-8u141-linux-x64.tar.gz -C /opt
$ update-alternatives --install /usr/bin/java java /opt/jre1.8.0_141/bin/java 1
$ echo 1 | update-alternatives --config java
$ java -version
java version "1.8.0_141"
Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 1.8.0_141-b15)
Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.141-b15, mixed mode)

We unpack Tomcat, add the CMDBuild app to it and start the container:

$ tar -xzf apache-tomcat-8.5.16.tar.gz -C /opt
$ unzip cmdbuild-2.4.3.zip
$ cp cmdbuild-2.4.3/cmdbuild-2.4.3.war /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16/webapps
$ cp cmdbuild-2.4.3/extras/tomcat-libs/6.0\ or\ higher/postgresql-9.4.1207.jar /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16/lib
$ /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16/bin/startup.sh
Using CATALINA_BASE:   /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16
Using CATALINA_HOME:   /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16
Using CATALINA_TMPDIR: /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16/temp
Using JRE_HOME:        /usr
Using CLASSPATH:       /opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16/bin/bootstrap.jar:/opt/apache-tomcat-8.5.16/bin/tomcat-juli.jar
Tomcat started.

Now CMDBuild is available at http://cmdb.example.com:8080/cmdbuild-2.4.3/. We connect to the CMDBuild web app and do the first configuration:

  • Type: Empty.
  • Name: cmdbuild.
  • Host: localhost.
  • Port: 5432.
  • Super user: postgres.
  • Password: <the password configured before>.
  • User type: Super user.

We make sure the cmdbuild database does not exist. If it does (or if we want to start from the beginning), we delete it with:

psql -h localhost -U postgres -W -c "drop database cmdbuild"

If we encounter errors, we also check /var/log/postgresql for logs.

docs.title: Minimal Configuration of CMDBuild
docs.text:
The configuration of CMDBuild is out of scope, but a brief introduction is needed for this post.

CMDBuild presents two views:

  • The data management module, the default after login, which lets us manage data.
  • The administration module, which lets us manage structures.

The first step is to build the structures for our asset data. We open the administration module, go to classes and add the following classes:

  • Name: asset
  • Description: Asset
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Class
  • Superclass: yes
  • Name: infrastructure
  • Description: Infrastructure
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Asset
  • Superclass: yes
  • Name: networkdevices
  • Description: Network Devices
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Infrastructure
  • Superclass: no
  • Name: networks
  • Description: Networks
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Asset
  • Superclass: yes
  • Name: ipv4addresses
  • Description: IPv4 Addresses
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Networks
  • Superclass: no
  • Name: ipv4networks
  • Description: IPv4 Networks
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Networks
  • Superclass: no
  • Name: interfaces
  • Description: Interfaces
  • Type: Standard
  • Inherits from: Networks
  • Superclass: no

The second step is to build the relationships for the classes above. The idea is the following:

  • A network device (a router, for example) contains many interfaces.
  • Each interface can have VLANs, one VRF, IPv4 addresses and one OSPF area.
  • Each IPv4 address is part of an IPv4 network.

We go to domains and add the following domains:

  • Name: networkdevice2interfaces
  • Description: Network Device to Interfaces
  • Origin: Network Devices
  • Destination: Interfaces
  • Direct description: Interface
  • Inverse description: Device
  • Cardinality: 1:N
  • Name: interface2ipv4addresses
  • Description: Interface to IPv4 Addresses
  • Origin: Interfaces
  • Destination: IPv4 Addresses
  • Direct description: IPV4 Address
  • Inverse description: Interface
  • Cardinality: 1:N
  • Name: ipv4addresstoipv4network
  • Description: IPv4 Address to IPv4 Network
  • Origin: IPv4 Addresses
  • Destination: IPv4 Networks
  • Direct description: IPv4 Network
  • Inverse description: IPV4 Address
  • Cardinality: N:1
  • Name: interface2interface
  • Description: Interface to Interface
  • Origin: Interfaces
  • Destination: Interfaces
  • Direct description: Connected to
  • Inverse description: Connected to
  • Cardinality: 1:1

Finally, we configure the attributes of each class:

  • Network Devices:
  • Code: Serial (Unique, Mandatory, STRING(100))
  • Description: Hostname (Unique, Mandatory, STRING(250))
  • Vendor: Vendor (Unique, Mandatory, STRING(256))
  • Version: Version (Mandatory, STRING(256))
  • Interfaces:
  • Code: MAC Address (Mandatory, STRING(100))
  • Description: Interface Name (Unique, Mandatory, STRING(250))
  • IPv4 Addresses:
  • Description: IPV4Address (Unique, Mandatory, STRING(100))
  • FQDN: FQDN (STRING(250))
  • IPv4 Networks:
  • Description: IPv4 Network (Unique, Mandatory, STRING(100))

Now a basic structure of the CMDB is ready.

docs.title: Discovering a Network Device
docs.text:
Nowadays there are many ways to discover a network device. The classic one is based on the widely supported SNMP protocol. Suppose we have a Cisco router, and we configure it with an SNMPv3 user:

snmp-server view ISO iso included
snmp-server group MONITORING v3 auth read ISO
snmp-server user snmpmonitor MONITORING v3 auth sha snmppassword

Now we can get some useful information via SNMPv3:

apt-get -y install snmp snmp-mibs-downloader
snmpwalk -mALL -v3 -l authNoPriv -a SHA -u snmpmonitor -A snmppassword -On 192.168.6.201 sysName
snmpwalk -mALL -v3 -l authNoPriv -a SHA -u snmpmonitor -A snmppassword -On 192.168.6.201 ifName
snmpwalk -mALL -v3 -l authNoPriv -a SHA -u snmpmonitor -A snmppassword -On 192.168.6.201 ipAddrTable

Finding all the information via SNMP can be hard, because the data structures (MIBs) are not easy to find and understand. Another way to get information from network devices is NAPALM:

apt-get -y install python3-pip
pip3 install napalm

Before using NAPALM with a classic Cisco IOS device (via SSH), we must configure the device:

hostname R1
ip domain name infra.example.com
username admin privilege 15 password cisco
crypto key generate rsa
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

Remember that we need a key of at least 768 bits and, of course, a reachable IP address.

Now we can discover the devices using the first script:

./1-scan.py 192.168.6.201
./1-scan.py 192.168.6.202

After the execution, CMDBuild is populated with some information gathered from the discovered devices. The script:

  • Collects the hostname, interfaces, MAC addresses and IP addresses.
  • Adds all the collected data to CMDBuild and creates the relationships between the objects.

docs.title: Managing the Infrastructure from a CMDB
docs.text:
Every network change should start from a CMDB. Let's see, for example, how to configure a new interface. In Asset → Networks → IPv4 Networks, we add a card: 10.1.2.0/24. Then we go to Asset → Networks → IPv4 Addresses and add two IP addresses: 10.1.2.1 and 10.1.2.2. We make sure that we link each IP address to the parent network (10.1.2.0/24), creating the proper relationship. Then we go to Asset → Networks → Interfaces and create two relationships, each between an interface and an IP address.

The configuration is complete, so we push it to the devices:

./2-push.py R1
./2-push.py R2

Now R1 can ping R2:

$ ./3-test.py 192.168.6.201 10.1.2.2 | python -m json.tool
{
    "success": {
        "packet_loss": 0,
        "probes_sent": 5,
        "results": [

docs.title: Useful CMDBuild APIs
docs.text: I found the official documentation by Tecnoteca not very exhaustive. Here are the APIs I used.

docs.title: Authentication and Sessions
docs.text:
The first request must authenticate against CMDBuild and get a session token:

$ curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary '{"username": "admin", "password": "admin"}' "http://localhost:8080/cmdbuild-2.4.3/services/rest/v1/sessions" | python3 -m json.tool
{
    "data": {
        "username": "admin",
        "role": "SuperUser",
        "availableRoles": [

        ],

    }
}

docs.title: Filter the Output (Cards)
docs.text:
We prepare a filter like the following:

{
    "attribute": {
        "simple": {
            "attribute": "Description",
            "operator": "equal",
            "value": [
                "R1"
            ]
        }
    }
}

The operators can be contain, equal, notequal, like (using %), isnull, isnotnull, greater and lower.

We can combine filters with and or or:

{
    "attribute": {
        "or": [{
            "simple": {
                "attribute": "Description",
                "operator": "equal",
                "value": ["R1"]
            }
        }, {
            "simple": {
                "attribute": "Description",
                "operator": "equal",
                "value": ["R2"]
            }
        }]
    }
}

We apply the URL-encoded filter using a GET request:

$ curl -s -X GET -H "CMDBuild-Authorization: hb90u9d3l4jqunf8ni6s7jisli" --data-urlencode 'filter={"attribute":{"simple":{"attribute":"Description","operator":"equal","value":["R1"]}}}' -G "http://localhost:8080/cmdbuild-2.4.3/services/rest/v2/classes/networkdevices/cards" | python3 -m json.tool
{
    "data": [
        {
            "Description": "R1",

docs.title: A local HashiCorp Vault server in ten minutes
docs.text: 21 November 2026

docs.title: A local HashiCorp Vault server in ten minutes
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese blog intermediate passwords security vault

Secrets in .bashrc, in Git, in a text file on the desktop: we all know where this ends. In this post, we will start a local HashiCorp Vault server from scratch, initialize it, and store the first secret.

This is a lab setup: a self-signed certificate, file storage and a single node. It is enough to understand how Vault works before using it for real.

docs.title: Certificate and configuration
docs.text:
Vault listens on TLS only, so we need a certificate first. A self-signed one is fine for a lab:

# Create the private key and the signing request
openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout cert.key -out cert.csr
# Sign the certificate with our own key (valid 10 years)
openssl x509 -req -days 3650 -in cert.csr -signkey cert.key -out cert.crt

Then the configuration file, vault.json:

{
    "backend": {
      "file": {
        "path": "/vault/file"
      }
    },
    "listener": {
      "tcp":{
        "address": "127.0.0.1:8200",
        "tls_cert_file": "cert.crt",
        "tls_key_file": "cert.key"
      }
    },
    "ui": true
}

The data lives in /vault/file; the listener is bound to localhost only; the web UI is enabled. Start the server:

vault server -config vault.json

docs.title: Initialize and unseal
docs.text:
From another terminal, check the status. Since the certificate is self-signed, we need -tls-skip-verify on every command:

vault status -tls-skip-verify

The output says Initialized false and Sealed true. A new Vault is like a safe that has just been delivered: it exists, but nobody has set the combination yet.

We split the master key in 3 shares, and we require 2 of them to unseal:

vault operator init -tls-skip-verify -key-shares=3 -key-threshold=2

The output contains the unseal keys and the initial root token. This is the only time Vault shows them: copy them somewhere safe right now. Then unseal, running the command twice and pasting a different key each time:

vault operator unseal -tls-skip-verify

After the second key, vault status reports Sealed false.

docs.title: First secret
docs.text:
Authenticate with the root token and list the secrets engines:

export VAULT_TOKEN="<initial root token>"
vault secrets list -tls-skip-verify

Only the system engines (cubbyhole/, identity/, sys/) are there. Let's enable the Key-Value engine and write a secret:

vault secrets enable -tls-skip-verify kv
vault write -tls-skip-verify kv/infra value=mypassword

Mind the last command: the password ends up in the shell history. Put a space in front of the command (with HISTCONTROL=ignorespace), or use the file/stdin forms that Vault provides.

docs.title: Lesson learned
docs.text:
• Unseal keys and root token: shown once, never stored on the same server.
  • Root token: for the first setup only; day-to-day work needs policies and dedicated tokens.
  • Self-signed certificate: acceptable in a lab; in production use a certificate your clients trust, and drop -tls-skip-verify.

I believe a secrets manager is the first thing to put in place, before the automation that needs it.

docs.title: APT proxy with APT-Cacher NG
docs.text: 13 August 2020

docs.title: APT proxy with APT-Cacher NG
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese blog intermediate linux proxy

On large Debian installations, I usually configure an APT proxy to optimize upgrades. I configure APT-Cacher NG in the following way, in the /etc/apt-cacher-ng/acng.conf file:

CacheDir: /proxydata/cache/apt-cacher-ng
LogDir: /var/log/apt-cacher-ng
SupportDir: /usr/lib/apt-cacher-ng
Port:3142
Remap-debrep: file:deb_mirror*.gz /debian ; file:backends_debian # Debian Archives
Remap-uburep: file:ubuntu_mirrors /ubuntu ; file:backends_ubuntu # Ubuntu Archives
Remap-secdeb: security.debian.org ; security.debian.org deb.debian.org/debian-security
Remap-elastic: http://artifacts.elastic.co ; https://artifacts.elastic.co
Remap-docker: http://download.docker.com ; https://download.docker.com
ReportPage: acng-report.html
ExThreshold: 4
LocalDirs: acng-doc /usr/share/doc/apt-cacher-ng
VfileUseRangeOps: -1

Clients access the repositories via HTTP, and the APT-Cacher NG daemon maps them to HTTPS when necessary.

docs.title: Auditing Active Directory passwords against HaveIBeenPwned
docs.text: 08 February 2022

docs.title: Auditing Active Directory passwords against HaveIBeenPwned
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog governance passwords security

Any password policy, even with strict rules, can be bypassed easily with simple tricks: Passw0rd!, Passw0rd$ and Password!1 can all be valid passwords for length and complexity.

In this common scenario, it is useful to audit the Active Directory passwords regularly against password dictionaries (like RockYou) and/or HaveIBeenPwned.

Let's see how to audit Active Directory passwords with the Directory Services Internals PowerShell Module and Framework.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
We open PowerShell with administrative privileges and check the PowerShell version:

PS C:\Windows\system32> $PSVersionTable

$PSVersionTable must report version 5.1 at least.

We install DSInternals:

PS C:\Windows\system32> Install-Module DSInternals -Force

If we get the error PackageManagement\Install-PackageProvider : No match was found for the specified search criteria for the provider 'NuGet'. The package provider requires 'PackageManagement' and 'Provider' tags, we modify the security protocols (the default is Ssl3 and Tls) and reinstall:

PS C:\Windows\system32> [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
PS C:\Windows\system32> $PSVersionTable

We list the available cmdlets:

PS C:\Windows\system32> Get-Command -Module DSInternals*

docs.title: Find Weak Passwords on a Domain Controller
docs.text:
Before we start the audit, we need at least one dictionary file. We download any wordlist.

We set the environment:

$DictFile = "C:\Users\Administrator\Downloads\rockyou.txt"
$DC = "dc01"
$Domain = "DC=example,DC=com"

We start the audit:

Get-ADReplAccount -All -Server $DC -NamingContext $Domain | Test-PasswordQuality -WeakPasswordsFile $DictFile -IncludeDisabledAccounts

We can also build a report in CSV format:

PS C:\Users\Administrator> $Accounts = Get-ADReplAccount -All -Server $DC -NamingContext $Domain
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $Results = $Accounts | Test-PasswordQuality -WeakPasswordsFile $DictFile
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $RiskyAccounts = $Accounts | where {$Results.WeakPassword -match $_.SamAccountName}
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $RiskyAccounts | select SamAccountName,DisplayName,DistinguishedName | Export-Csv output.csv

Note that there are no built-in tools to set the list of bad passwords for Active Directory Domain Services.

docs.title: Export Data for a Remote Audit
docs.text:
At the moment, DSInternals cannot serialize accounts. See the associated issue.

Once it is fixed, the procedure should be as follows:

PS C:\Users\andrea> $Password = Read-Host "Enter password (16 chars)" -AsSecureString
PS C:\Users\andrea> $Accounts = Get-ADReplAccount -All -Server $DC -NamingContext $Domain
PS C:\Users\andrea> $SerialAccounts = [System.Management.Automation.PSSerializer]::Serialize($Accounts)
PS C:\Users\andrea> $SerialAccounts | ConvertTo-SecureString -AsPlainText -Force | ConvertFrom-SecureString -SecureKey $Password | Set-Content -Path credentials.txt

We move the file to an external station with PowerShell 7 and get the data back:

PS C:\Users\andrea> $Password = Read-Host "Enter password (16 chars)" -AsSecureString
PS C:\Users\andrea> $SerialAccounts = Get-Content -Path credentials.txt | ConvertTo-SecureString -SecureKey $Password | ConvertFrom-SecureString -AsPlainText
PS C:\Users\andrea> $Accounts = [System.Management.Automation.PSSerializer]::DeSerialize($SerialAccounts)

We analyze the data as before:

$DictFile = "C:\Users\andrea\Downloads\rockyou.txt"
$DC = "dc01"
$Domain = "DC=example,DC=com"
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $Results = $Accounts | Test-PasswordQuality -WeakPasswordsFile $DictFile
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $RiskyAccounts = $Accounts | where {$Results.WeakPassword -match $_.SamAccountName}
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $RiskyAccounts | select SamAccountName,DisplayName,DistinguishedName | Export-Csv output.csv

docs.title: Check for Breached Credentials (HaveIBeenPwned)
docs.text:
I usually test whether users use leaked passwords. To do so, we download the password list from HaveIBeenPwned and use the NTLM file ordered by hash.

We analyze the weak passwords with the downloaded file:

PS C:\Users\Administrator\Downloads> $Accounts | Test-PasswordQuality -WeakPasswordHashesSortedFile .\pwned-passwords-ntlm-ordered-by-hash-v8.txt
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $RiskyAccounts = $Accounts | where {$Results.WeakPassword -match $_.SamAccountName}
PS C:\Users\Administrator> $RiskyAccounts | select SamAccountName,DisplayName,DistinguishedName | Export-Csv output.csv

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: We should force each account with a weak password to change it at the next login, and notify the user via email. Depending on the policies of the organization, this could count as a security incident.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Directory Services Internals PowerShell Module and Framework
  • Auditing Weak Passwords in Active Directory
  • Test-PasswordQuality
  • Active Directory Password Audit – Using Pwned Passwords
  • SecLists
  • Downloading the Pwned Passwords list

docs.title: Automatic network discovery and documentation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese blog intermediate netdoc

NetBrain is a well-known software for network discovery and management. Let's focus on network discovery and documentation: we want to discover network devices automatically, learn how they are connected, and store everything in a version control repository (Git/CVS).

So we want to:

  • Discover all the network devices.
  • Map how they are connected.
  • Track changes automatically.
  • Store everything in a version control repository (Git/CVS).
  • Visualize any updated map with a simple browser.

This is how we can solve the problem:

  • We assume all devices are Cisco, so we can use CDP.
  • We can get the CDP data via SNMPv3.
  • We can build a (source, destination) topology.
  • We can store the topology in a revision control repository (Git/CVS).
  • We can use jsPlumb to render the (source, destination) topology into a web page.

docs.title: NetDoc
docs.text:
NetDoc is the small experiment I wrote to solve the problem. It contains two Python scripts:

  • netdiscover.py: discovers network devices via SNMPv3 and generates two .ini files:
  • discovered_nodes.ini: contains all the network devices with some additional information.
  • discovered_connections.ini: contains all the network connections with some additional information.
  • netplot.py: plots a web page from the .ini files above.

The .ini files can be stored in a revision control repository.

docs.title: Running NetDoc
docs.text:
NetDoc is currently a proof-of-concept script, so it may or may not work on your infrastructure. To start it, run:

./netdiscover.py -u snmpv3user -p snmpv3password -h 10.1.1.4 -h 10.1.1.5 -h 10.1.1.6

The discovered_nodes.ini file contains all the devices discovered via CDP in the following form:

[AccessServer]
id = AccessServer
image = router.svg
disabled = false
platform = cisco 2610

The title is the CDP neighbor ID (usually the hostname). The other attributes are:

  • id: the CDP neighbor ID (usually the hostname).
  • image: an image used to display the node in the web page.
  • disabled: true if the node was missing during the last scan.
  • platform: the CDP neighbor platform.

The discovered_connections.ini file contains all the connections discovered via CDP in the following form:

[AccessServer:e0/0-switch.example.com:gi2/0/46]
source = AccessServer
source_if = e0/0
destination = switch.example.com
destination_if = gi2/0/46
disabled = false

The title is the source and destination CDP neighbor IDs with the interface names. The other attributes are:

  • source: the source CDP neighbor ID.
  • source_if: the source interface name.
  • destination: the destination CDP neighbor ID.
  • destination_if: the destination interface name.
  • disabled: true if the connection was missing during the last scan.

After a successful scan, we can create the HTML page:

./netplot.py > netdoc.html

And here we go, a draggable web page:

docs.title: Automating Google searches
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner blog osint

I usually do not write about OSINT techniques, because I think we should talk about ethics and respect before approaching OSINT. Some OSINT automation techniques are harmless, though: if you do not know what to search for, you will not get anything, whether you automate or not.

docs.title: Google Dorks
docs.text:
We probably know Google Dorks already: in short, they are parameters that reduce the results. There are a lot of them, but I usually use:

  • intitle: limits the search to pages that contain a specific pattern in the title (HTML tag).
  • inurl: limits the search to URLs that contain a specific pattern.
  • site: limits the search to a specific domain or TLD.
  • filetype: limits the search to a specific file type.

For example, site:adainese.it filetype:pdf displays all the PDF files included in my website.

Be aware that you should also check my robots.txt.

docs.title: Manual Google Searches
docs.text:
If you run many Google searches in a short timeframe, you will see that Google tries to interrupt you, especially if you are not authenticated.

During an OSINT analysis, however, you probably have a set of requests that you want to run on each target.

Finally, the standard Google output is probably not the most usable data format in the world.

docs.title: SerpApi
docs.text:
We use SerpApi, which executes each request, solving CAPTCHAs when possible, and parses (web scraping) the Google result into JSON. SerpApi supports Google Search, Maps, Jobs, Product, PlayStore, YouTube... and also DuckDuckGo, Yandex, eBay, Yahoo...

We need to create an account, which includes 100 free requests per month.

docs.title: Automating Google Searches
docs.text:
Let's try to automate the search mentioned before: site:adainese.it filetype:pdf.

We can approach the problem with the REST API directly or with the Python module. Let's see both:

wget -q -O- "https://serpapi.com/search.json?engine=google&q=site%3Aadainese.it+filetype%3Apdf&api_key=<SERPAPI_API_KEY>" | jq

    "created_at": "2022-07-11 12:53:19 UTC",
    "processed_at": "2022-07-11 12:53:19 UTC",
    "google_url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=site%3Aadainese.it+filetype%3Apdf&oq=site%3Aadainese.it+filetype%3Apdf&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8",

  "search_parameters": {
    "engine": "google",
    "q": "site:adainese.it filetype:pdf",
    "google_domain": "google.com",
    "device": "desktop"
  },
  "search_information": {
    "organic_results_state": "Results for exact spelling",
    "query_displayed": "site:adainese.it filetype:pdf",
    "total_results": 8,
    "time_taken_displayed": 0.22
  },
  "organic_results": [
    {
      "position": 1,
      "title": "PoC Cyber Range Platform - Andrea Dainese",
      "link": "https://www.adainese.it/files/slides/20200922-cyberrange.pdf",
      "displayed_link": "https://www.adainese.it › 20200922-cyberrange",
      "date": "Sep 22, 2020",
      "snippet": "Rosario is a Cybersecurity professional with around 20 years of experience. Rosario is the. South Europe Cyberbit Sales Engineer and.",
      "about_this_result": {
        "source": {
          "description": "adainese.it was first indexed by Google in January 2021"
        },
        "languages": [
          "English"
        ],
        "regions": [
          "the United States"
        ]
      },
      "about_page_link": "https://www.google.com/search?q=About+https://www.adainese.it/files/slides/20200922-cyberrange.pdf&tbm=ilp&ilps=ADNMCi11pvVrwLJY0LqGhLcTwhibCc9pIw",
      "cached_page_link": "https://webcache.googleusercontent.com/search?q=cache:EhJFMGqqonQJ:https://www.adainese.it/files/slides/20200922-cyberrange.pdf+&cd=1&hl=en&ct=clnk&gl=us"
    },
[...]

That is good, but we can do better with a script. Maybe we want to download all the PDF files included in the result. First, we install the Python module:

pip3 install google-search-results

Finally, we customize the following script:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import json
import requests
from serpapi import GoogleSearch

params = {
    'engine': 'google',
    'q': 'site:adainese.it filetype:pdf',
    'api_key': '<SERPAPI_API_KEY>'
}

search = GoogleSearch(params)
result = search.get_json()

with open('search_result.json', 'w') as outfile:
    json.dump(result, outfile)

for organic_result in result['organic_results']:
    link = organic_result['link']
    filename = os.path.basename(link)
    r = requests.get(link, allow_redirects=True)
    open(filename, 'wb').write(r.content)

We get the JSON (for future reference) and all the PDF files downloaded in the current directory.

You probably know that acting this way is pretty noisy. You should evaluate countermeasures to stay hidden.

docs.title: Back up only your own data with Time Machine
docs.text: 24 November 2026

docs.title: Back up only your own data with Time Machine
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese backup beginner blog digital-self-defence macos

A backup is one of the most important actions to keep control of our data, and it is one of the basic habits of Personal digital protection. It matters even more to me, since I am using fewer and fewer cloud services. In this post, we will tune Time Machine so that it backs up only what I care about.

docs.title: Why Not Back Up Everything
docs.text:
For years I have chosen Apple systems, and on the Mac I rely on Time Machine. It is a good tool; there are better ones, but it is embedded in the system, so it is immediately available to less technical people too.

Time Machine has one big problem: it backs up everything. In my case this is useless and harmful:

  • Useless: if the Mac breaks, is lost or is replaced, I want to restart from a clean point zero, not from a copy of the old system;
  • Harmful: backing up everything is slow, and it needs more and more space.

It is like moving to a new house: I take my belongings, not the walls. My belongings are all in my home directory, /Users/dainese. This is where I want Time Machine to focus.

docs.title: Exclusions in Settings
docs.text:
Time Machine lets us define exclusions in Settings → General → Time Machine → Options:

We can read the same list from the command line:

$ defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.apple.TimeMachine SkipPaths
(
    "/Users/dainese/Applications",
    "/Users/dainese/Library/Caches",
    "/System",
    "/Users/dainese/.local",
    "/opt",
    "/Users/dainese/.ollama",
    "/Users/dainese/.cache",
    "/Library",
    "/Users/dainese/.Trash",
    "/Applications",
    "/Users/dainese/Library/CloudStorage",
    "/cores",
    "/Users/dainese/Library/Containers",
    "/private",
    "/Users/dainese/Library/iTunes"
)

SkipPaths contains only the fixed-path exclusions added by the user. Other exclusions exist in other forms, and they are not in this list.

docs.title: Four Kinds of Exclusion
docs.text:
Time Machine has three kinds of exclusion that we can configure, and a fourth one that Apple configures for us:

  • Sticky: the default of tmutil addexclusion. It is an extended attribute (com.apple.metadata:com_apple_backup_excludeItem) attached to the item itself, so it follows the item when we move or copy it. It does not need root, and it does not appear in Settings;
  • Fixed-path: tied to a path, not to the item (option -p). It needs root. It is the kind that Settings writes, and the one that SkipPaths lists. It works even if nothing exists at that path yet, and it applies again as soon as something is moved there;
  • Volume: tied to the volume UUID (option -v), so it survives a rename or a different mount point. If we erase the volume, the exclusion is gone;
  • Standard: the built-in list of items that Time Machine skips by itself. We do not configure it, and it does not appear in Settings.

The consequence is simple: a folder can be excluded and not appear in any list. For this reason, "what is in the list?" is the wrong question. The right one is "is this path excluded?", and we will ask it in a moment.

docs.title: A More Practical Way
docs.text:
The Settings route often did not behave as I expected. Recently I found an alternative, more practical way to exclude directories: one command, with all the paths:

sudo tmutil addexclusion -p /Applications /Library /System /cores /opt /private /Users/$(whoami)/.cache /Users/$(whoami)/.local /Users/$(whoami)/.ollama /Users/$(whoami)/.Trash /Users/$(whoami)/Applications /Users/$(whoami)/Library/Caches /Users/$(whoami)/Library/CloudStorage /Users/$(whoami)/Library/Containers /Users/$(whoami)/Library/iTunes

The command adds a fixed-path exclusion for each path, the same kind that Settings creates. sudo is required by -p. $(whoami) is replaced by the current user, so the command works on any account without editing.

docs.title: Check What Is Included
docs.text:
We can verify which folders are included or excluded, including the ones that matter to me:

$ tmutil isexcluded /Applications /Library /System /cores /opt /private /Users/$(whoami)/.cache /Users/$(whoami)/.local /Users/$(whoami)/.Trash /Users/$(whoami)/Applications /Users/dainese/Library/Application\ Support/MobileSync /Users/dainese/Library/Caches /Users/$(whoami)/Desktop /Users/$(whoami)/Documents /Users/$(whoami)/Music /Users/$(whoami)/Pictures /Users/$(whoami)/src
[Excluded]  /Applications
[Excluded]  /Library
[Excluded]  /System
[Excluded]  /cores
[Excluded]  /opt
[Excluded]  /private
[Excluded]  /Users/dainese/.cache
[Excluded]  /Users/dainese/.local
[Excluded]  /Users/dainese/.Trash
[Excluded]  /Users/dainese/Applications
[Included]  /Users/dainese/Library/Application Support/MobileSync
[Excluded]  /Users/dainese/Library/Caches
[Included]  /Users/dainese/Desktop
[Included]  /Users/dainese/Documents
[Included]  /Users/dainese/Music
[Included]  /Users/dainese/Pictures
[Included]  /Users/dainese/src

For each path, the command prints [Excluded] or [Included]. I expect system, applications and caches to be excluded, and Desktop, Documents, Music, Pictures and src to be included. As far as I know, tmutil has no verb that lists all the exclusions, so this check is the only way to be sure.

docs.title: Lesson Learned
docs.text:
The result is a much faster and lighter backup, adapted to what I need.

  • Know where your data lives: for me it is one directory; everything else can be reinstalled;
  • Ask the path, not the list: sticky and standard exclusions are invisible in Settings, so use tmutil isexcluded;
  • Choose the right kind: sticky for an item that may move, fixed-path for a location that must stay excluded.

I believe a backup should follow what we value, not what the system decides to copy.

docs.title: Building an IoT testing lab
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog digital-self-defence iot lab security

As private individuals, we use many consumer IoT devices: almost any standard piece of home equipment can now be controlled remotely with a specific application installed on a smartphone.

The question is: how much can we trust those IoT devices? How do they affect our digital security and privacy?

To answer these questions, we build a small and cheap IoT testing lab.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
The design is simple: we want a flexible device (Linux-based) that intercepts any Ethernet/IP traffic emitted by the IoT device.

The Linux device provides an Internet connection to the IoT device, dumps all the traffic data and metadata, and also intercepts the encrypted traffic.

docs.title: Bill of Materials (BOM)
docs.text:
For our testing lab, we use:

  • Raspberry Pi 4 8 GB RAM.
  • Raspberry Pi 4 case and accessories.
  • microSD Samsung Evo plus 128 GB.
  • Ethernet 10/100/1000 USB 3.0 adapter.
  • D-Link DWL-G730AP.
  • Logitech K360 Wireless keyboard.
  • Kali Linux for ARM.
  • NextDNS account.

We can write the Kali Linux ARM image to the microSD with the Raspberry Pi Imager.

I use an old portable wireless access point that I bought years ago. This one should work too in "Access Point" mode.

docs.title: First Boot
docs.text:
After the first boot, we can start configuring the Raspberry Pi. SSH is enabled by default on Kali Linux:

sudo systemctl start ssh
sudo systemctl enable ssh

We install some packages required by the next steps:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get dist-upgrade
sudo apt-get autoremove
sudo apt-get install iptables-persistent dnsmasq
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/analysis/zeek/

If needed, we adjust the keyboard and the timezone:

sudo dpkg-reconfigure keyboard-configuration
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Rome

We disable the embedded Bluetooth and wireless adapters:

sudo echo "dtoverlay=disable-bt" >> /boot/config.txt
sudo echo "dtoverlay=disable-wifi" >> /boot/config.txt

We reboot to apply all the configurations above.

docs.title: Network Configuration
docs.text:
The Pi acts as a router, so we need to configure two network interfaces. The first one is configured with DHCP by default, and we must configure the second one:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/network/interfaces.d/eth0
auto eth0
    allow-hotplug eth0
    iface eth0 inet dhcp
EOF

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/network/interfaces.d/eth1
auto eth1
allow-hotplug eth1
iface eth1 inet static
    address 192.168.0.1
    netmask 255.255.255.0
EOF

To let the Pi act as a router, we enable IPv4 forwarding. We edit /etc/sysctl.conf and set:

net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

At the end, we reload the sysctl settings:

sysctl -p

To make the Internet reachable from the devices attached to eth1, we need to enable NAT. We also add some tricks to force DNS traffic and log the requests that come from eth1:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/iptables/rules.v4
*nat
:PREROUTING ACCEPT [0:0]
:INPUT ACCEPT [0:0]
:OUTPUT ACCEPT [0:0]
:POSTROUTING ACCEPT [0:0]
-A PREROUTING ! -d 192.168.0.1/32 -p udp -m udp --dport 53 -j MARK --set-xmark 0x1/0xffffffff
-A PREROUTING -m mark --mark 0x1 -j LOG --log-prefix "iptables: direct_dns "
-A PREROUTING -m mark --mark 0x1 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.0.1
-A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
COMMIT
*filter
:INPUT DROP [0:0]
:FORWARD ACCEPT [0:0]
:OUTPUT ACCEPT [0:0]
:Services - [0:0]
-A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -i eth1 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -m state --state NEW -j Services
-A FORWARD -i eth1 -m state --state NEW -j MARK --set-xmark 0x2/0xffffffff
-A FORWARD -m mark --mark 0x2 -j LOG --log-prefix "iptables: new_conn "
-A Services -p tcp -m tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
-A Services -p tcp -m tcp --dport 9090 -j ACCEPT
COMMIT
EOF

We can reload the firewall with:

sudo iptables-restore /etc/iptables/rules.v4

Finally, we make iptables log to a dedicated file:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/rsyslog.d/iptables.conf
:msg, regex, "iptables: " -/var/log/analysis/iptables.log
EOF

We restart rsyslog:

sudo systemctl restart rsyslog

docs.title: DNS and DHCP Server
docs.text:
To intercept and track the DNS requests, we use DNSMasq, which can act as a DNS and DHCP server. We make sure that DNSMasq loads the external configuration files by editing /etc/dnsmasq.conf:

conf-dir=/etc/dnsmasq.d/,*.conf

We configure DHCP as follows:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/dnsmasq.d/network.conf
interface=eth1
dhcp-range=192.168.0.50,192.168.0.150,24h
EOF

We forward the DNS requests to NextDNS. We must use our CPE ID, otherwise we do not see the DNS requests on the NextDNS dashboard:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/dnsmasq.d/nextdns.conf
port=53
no-resolv
no-hosts
bogus-priv
strict-order
server=45.90.30.0
server=45.90.28.0
add-cpe-id=aaaaaa
EOF

We want DNSMasq to log all the requests to a specific file:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/dnsmasq.d/logging.conf
# Log each DNS query
log-queries

# Log lots of extra information about DHCP
log-dhcp

# Log into a dedicated files
log-facility=/var/log/analysis/dnsmasq.log
EOF

Finally, we restart DNSMasq:

sudo systemctl enable dnsmasq
sudo systemctl restart dnsmasq

docs.title: Full Traffic Capture
docs.text:
The captured packets are not easy to analyze, but it is still useful to have them, so that we can analyze specific conversations. We configure a small service that captures all the packets entering from eth1:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/systemd/system/tcpdump.service
[Unit]
After=network.target

[Service]
Restart=always
RestartSec=30
Environment="TCPDUMP_FORMAT=%%Y%%m%%d-%%H:%%M:%%S"
ExecStartPre=/bin/mkdir -p /var/log/analysis
ExecStart=/usr/bin/tcpdump -G 3600 -i eth1 -w "/var/log/analysis/tcpdump-eth1-${TCPDUMP_FORMAT}.pcap"
ExecStop=/bin/kill -s SIGINT $MAINPID

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

We enable and start the new service:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable tcpdump
sudo systemctl start tcpdump

docs.title: Light Traffic Capture (Metadata)
docs.text:
We need a faster way to understand what the device under test is doing.

Zeek captures traffic metadata in a human-readable format. Zeek is not available on Kali Linux for Raspberry Pi, so we need to compile it. The process takes a few hours:

sudo apt-get install cmake flex bison libpcap-dev libssl-dev python3 python3-dev swig zlib1g-dev
sudo apt-get install python3-git python3-semantic-version exim4
git clone --recursive https://github.com/zeek/zeek
cd zeek
./configure
make
sudo make install

We also install the auxiliary programs of Zeek:

cd auxil/zeek-aux
./configure
make
sudo make install

We can include the Zeek binary directory in the path:

export PATH=/usr/local/zeek/bin:${PATH}

To configure Zeek, we edit /usr/local/zeek/etc/node.cfg:

[zeek]
type=standalone
host=localhost
interface=eth1

We also want Zeek to log in the same directory we used before. We edit /usr/local/zeek/etc/zeekctl.cfg and set:

LogDir = /var/log/analysis/zeek

Finally, we update the Zeek installation and configuration:

sudo zeekctl install

We can start Zeek manually or configure a systemd service:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/systemd/system/zeek.service
[Unit]
Description=zeek network analysis engine

[Service]
Type=forking
PIDFIle=/var/run/zeek.pid
ExecStart=/usr/local/zeek/bin/zeekctl start
ExecStop=/usr/local/zeek/bin/zeekctl stop

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

And we enable it at boot:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable zeek
sudo systemctl start zeek

docs.title: MITM Proxy
docs.text:
We use MITM Proxy to analyze the encrypted HTTP connections. We install it with:

sudo apt-get install mitmproxy

We configure MITM Proxy as a system service:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/systemd/system/mitmproxy.service
[Unit]
Description=MITMProxy

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/bin/mitmweb --mode transparent --web-port 9090 --web-host 0.0.0.0 --no-web-open-browser
StandardOutput=file:/var/log/analysis/mitmproxy.log
StandardError=file:/var/log/analysis/mitmproxy.log

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

And we start it at boot:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start mitmproxy
sudo systemctl enable mitmproxy

To intercept the traffic, we NAT (REDIRECT) the HTTP and HTTPS connections to the port used by MITM Proxy (the default is 8080):

sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth1 -p tcp --dport 80 -m comment --comment "mitmproxy" -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080
sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth1 -p tcp --dport 443 -m comment --comment "mitmproxy" -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080

Because we need to activate and deactivate the MITM Proxy traffic inspection, we can use a simple script:

#!/bin/bash

function disable() {
    iptables -t nat -S | grep mitmproxy | cut -d" " -f2- | xargs -rL1 iptables -t nat -D
}

function  enable() {
    disable
    iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -m comment --comment "mitmproxy" -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080
    iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 -m comment --comment "mitmproxy" -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080
}

case $1 in
    enable)
        enable
        ;;
    disable)
        disable
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Use $0 enable|disable"
        exit 1
        ;;
esac

We activate and deactivate the traffic interception with:

sudo /root/mitmproxy.sh enable
sudo /root/mitmproxy.sh disable

The MITM Proxy web interface is available on port 9090 by default.

docs.title: Traffic Interception
docs.text:
Once the traffic interception is activated, the HTTPS connections are split into two parts:

The first diagram shows non-intercepted HTTPS connections: in this case, the client gets a valid signed certificate.

The second diagram shows HTTPS connections intercepted by MITM Proxy: the client gets an invalid certificate, self-signed by the MITM Proxy server.

We have three different scenarios:

  1. The application does not validate certificates, and MITM Proxy can intercept the traffic.
  2. The application validates certificates, and certificate pinning is not configured in the application.
  3. The application validates certificates, and certificate pinning is configured in the application.

In the second scenario, we can enable the traffic interception by installing the MITM Proxy certificate in the device and trusting it. From the device, we open http://mitm.it and install the self-signed certificate.

In the third scenario, the application validates a specific certificate, so even if the MITM Proxy certificate is trusted, the application recognizes a MITM attack:

192.168.0.126:34170: Client TLS handshake failed. The client may not trust the proxy's certificate for www.google.com (OpenSSL Error([('SSL routines', 'ssl3_read_bytes', 'sslv3 alert certificate unknown')]))

To bypass certificate pinning, see the post about Frida.

docs.title: Log Rotation
docs.text:
To keep the system clean, we rotate the logs:

sudo cat << EOF > /etc/logrotate.d/analysis
/var/log/analysis/iptables.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    nocompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    dateext
}
/var/log/analysis/dnsmasq.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    nocompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    dateext
}
/var/log/analysis/tcpdump {
    daily
    rotate 0
    ifempty
    lastaction
        /usr/bin/find /var/log/analysis/ -name "tcpdump-*" -mtime +7 -delete
    endscript
}
EOF

The next logrotate executions clean the obsolete files.

docs.title: Clean Logs
docs.text:
Before and after testing an IoT device and its related apps, we probably want to purge the old log files. A short script automates this task:

sudo cat << EOF > /root/clean.sh
#!/bin/bash

NEXT_DNS_PROFILE=aaaaaa
NEXT_DNS_APIKEY=<NEXTDNS_API_KEY>

find /var/log/analysis -type f -exec rm -f {} \;
rm -rf /var/log/analysis/zeek/2*
systemctl restart tcpdump
systemctl restart dnsmasq
systemctl restart rsyslog
systemctl restart mitmproxy

curl -X "DELETE" --header "X-Api-Key: ${NEXT_DNS_APIKEY}" https://api.nextdns.io/profiles/${NEXT_DNS_PROFILE}/logs
EOF

We replace the two parameters with our own data and run the script:

sudo chmod 755 /root/clean.sh
sudo /root/clean.sh

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
We built a small and cheap lab to test consumer IoT devices. The same tools can be used in a threat hunting scenario or during network analysis (performance, troubleshooting, etc.). Learning Linux means having an invaluable toolkit ready for complex analysis.

We learn how to use this setup in dedicated posts.

docs.title: CCIE #38620 - My story
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog cisco

On March 19th I passed the R&S CCIE lab and became CCIE #38620. While I was studying for the exam, I loved reading the success stories of other CCIEs, so here is the story of my journey, with my tips.

In 2012 I had to renew a lot of Cisco Specialist certifications, and I chose to pass a single CCIE written exam rather than many Specialist exams. So I bought the CCIE Routing and Switching Certification Guide and I really loved it. It was better than the CCNP books: everything was explained clearly. During my journey I realized that the book was just a very small part of the entire CCIE ® Routing and Switching Written Exam Topics (Blueprint) v4.0.

After the written exam, I asked myself whether I would be able to prepare for the lab exam. I could not afford a bootcamp, so I had to prepare by myself. I found a mate, a good guy who was preparing for the same exam. I knew that a good mate could make the difference, and it did.

ifconfig.it is the best CCIE mate I could have found: similar skills, but a different approach. When he booked the lab, I realized I could pass it too. I booked as well, paying myself, and spending 1500 € turned out to be the best incentive ever.

Every weekend and two or three nights each week were dedicated to the CCIE. My job helped a lot: I work every day on networks, QoS, routing and switching.

In the meantime I met Paolo, who helped me prepare my mind for the exam. Time after time I stopped being scared and, in the end, I was sure about my success. And I succeeded, as did my friend Gian Paolo.

docs.title: Location
docs.text: My exam location was the Brussels Cisco Office. You can find a lot of good hotels near the location (NH Hotel, Holiday Inn...), but I needed the cheapest one, so I chose the Hotel ibis budget Brussels Airport.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
What you need, in order:

  • Enjoy your path, or you will never pass.
  • Find a mate who shares your path: it makes everything easier.
  • Learn to breathe and not to panic.
  • Buy an American layout keyboard: do not think you can pass without it.
  • Tell yourself you can do it, and believe it.
  • Plan your time, and during the lab reserve time to check your entire work.
  • Buy at least four switches: you can emulate routers, but you need real switches for L2 topics.
  • Prepare for the written exam at your best, and the lab will be easier.
  • Discuss each single blueprint topic and command you encounter in your preparation: you must understand the underlying technologies.
  • Learn and use the Product/Technology Support pages, and remember how to reach the Master Index (Products → Cisco IOS and NX-OS Software → Cisco IOS → Cisco IOS Software Release 12.4 Family → Cisco IOS Software Releases 12.4 T → Master Index).
  • Know the lab environment.

docs.title: Tricks
docs.text:
IOS can help you during the exam. The most time-consuming task is testing IP address reachability from routers and switches. Open a PuTTY terminal, connect to a router and type:

#show ip alias
Address Type             IP Address      Port
Interface                192.168.10.254
Interface                192.168.11.1

Now press and hold the right Alt key and draw a square to select the IP addresses only. Paste the selected IP addresses into a file (Notepad) and repeat for each device. At the end, create a Tcl script:

foreach i {
192.168.10.254
192.168.11.1
} { ping $i repeat 3 source Lo0 }

We can use this script to test IP address reachability from all routers with a tclsh shell.

For switches we need a different method: we create a macro and execute it:

conf t
Enter configuration commands, one per line.  End with CNTL/Z.
switch(config)#macro name ping
Enter macro commands one per line. End with the character '@'.
do ping 192.168.10.254 repeat 3 source Lo0
do ping 192.168.11.1 repeat 3 source Lo0
@

We can run the macro by typing:

switch(config)#macro global apply ping

Remember to delete it before the end of the lab.

A way to display the TCP/UDP port mapping is:

#show ip port-map
Default mapping:  snmp                 udp port 161                        system defined
Default mapping:  echo                 tcp port 7                          system defined
[...]

Sometimes you need to decrypt a Cisco Type-7 password:

key chain decrypt
 key 1
   key-string 7 060506324F41

#show key chain decrypt
Key-chain decrypt:
    key 1 -- text "cisco"
        accept lifetime (always valid) - (always valid) [valid now]
        send lifetime (always valid) - (always valid) [valid now]

Again, remember to delete the key chain before the end of the lab.

docs.title: Connecting an IPv6 only site to an IPv4 only world
docs.text: 17 February 2014

docs.title: Connecting an IPv6 only site to an IPv4 only world
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog ipv6 linux

Many Internet providers cannot offer a native IPv6 Internet connection. There are many ways to send IPv6 packets over an IPv4 network. This post shows how an IPv6-only site can be interconnected to IPv4-only networks. For example, we want to configure a small home or branch office using IPv6 only, avoiding a slow 6to4 tunnel.

docs.title: DNS64 and NAT64
docs.text:
An IPv6-only host can communicate with an IPv4-only host using NAT64. A NAT64 server translates IPv6 addresses into IPv4 addresses and vice versa. A virtual subnet is deployed to map all the IPv4 addresses.

We must also deploy an appropriate DNS server: IPv6-only hosts ask for AAAA DNS records, but IPv4-only hosts have A records only. DNS64 is a mechanism that translates AAAA DNS requests into A requests.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
We deploy the following scenario:

Requirements:

  • A Linux box implements the NAT64 and DNS64 services. The newest Cisco routers can act as NAT64 and DNS64 servers too, but in this case we use a Raspberry Pi. Two connections are needed:
  • eth0 connects the Linux box to the Internet, using a public IPv4 address.
  • eth0.2 (802.1Q) connects the IPv6-only network.
  • IPv6 addresses are not routed to the Internet, so we use ULAs (Unique Local Addresses). ULAs are like private IPv4 addresses and cannot be routed on the Internet. We should register a ULA IPv6 range with the SixXS registry. Two networks are required:
  • fd9f:590a:b158::/64 is assigned to the IPv6-only hosts.
  • fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff::/96 maps IPv6 and IPv4 addresses: because IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, a 96-bit prefix is needed (although a 64-bit prefix should be allocated).
  • An additional IPv4 network is needed for the TAYGA daemon, which implements the NAT64 service.

docs.title: Configuring the Raspberry Pi (IPv6 and 802.1Q)
docs.text:
In this scenario, we use a Raspberry Pi with an 802.1Q link. We must load the following modules:

$ cat /etc/modules
snd-bcm2835
8021q
ipv6

The eth0.2 interface interconnects the IPv6 hosts:

$ cat /etc/network/interfaces
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback

auto eth0
iface eth0 inet dhcp

auto eth0.2
iface eth0.2 inet6 static
    address fd9f:590a:b158::1
    netmask 64
    vlan-raw-device eth0

We install and configure the radvd daemon so that IPv6 hosts can autoconfigure:

$ cat /etc/radvd.conf
interface eth0.2 {
        AdvSendAdvert on;
        MinRtrAdvInterval 3;
        MaxRtrAdvInterval 10;
        prefix fd9f:590a:b158::/64 {
                AdvOnLink on;
                AdvAutonomous on;
        };
};

Finally, we configure the Raspberry Pi as a router (IP forwarding must be enabled):

$ cat /etc/sysctl.conf
[...]
net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1
[...]

docs.title: Configuring the DNS64 Daemon
docs.text:
We can use the well-known DNS server BIND (a.k.a. named) as a DNS64 server. IPv4 hosts use A records:

$ dig +short @::1 www.routereflector.com A
94.141.22.22

IPv6 hosts look for AAAA records, so we configure BIND to translate A records into AAAA ones:

$ cat /etc/bind/named.conf.options
options {
[...]
        dns64 fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff::/96 {
                recursive-only no;
                exclude {
                        ::/0;
                };
                clients {
                        ::1;
                        fd9f:590a:b158::/64;
                };
        };
};

At this point, if an AAAA record is requested, an A record is retrieved and mapped to an IPv6 address:

$ dig +short @::1 www.routereflector.com AAAA
fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:5e8d:1616

We add the exclude entry because this network has no IPv6 reachability. DNS64 translates only the domains that do not have AAAA records. Without exclusions, DNS64 answers with the real AAAA record:

$ dig +short @::1 www.google.com AAAA
2a00:1450:4002:802::1010

With the exclusion configured, DNS64 answers with mapped AAAA records, one for each A record:

$ dig +short @::1 www.google.com A
173.194.35.50
173.194.35.51
173.194.35.52
173.194.35.48
173.194.35.49
$ dig +short @::1 www.google.com AAAA
fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:adc2:2333
fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:adc2:2334
fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:adc2:2330
fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:adc2:2331
fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:adc2:2332

docs.title: Configuring the NAT64 Service
docs.text:
We can use the TAYGA daemon to convert IPv6 addresses into IPv4 addresses. We must use the same IPv6 prefix configured above:

$ cat /etc/tayga.conf
tun-device nat64
ipv4-addr 192.168.255.1
prefix fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff::/96
dynamic-pool 192.168.255.0/24
data-dir /var/spool/tayga

$ cat /etc/default/tayga
RUN="yes"
CONFIGURE_IFACE="yes"
CONFIGURE_NAT44="no"
DAEMON_OPTS=""

We disable NAT44 because we want to configure it manually. NAT44 is required to translate the private IP addresses in the 192.168.255.0/24 network to the public IP address currently assigned to the eth0 interface:

iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Finally, IPv4 sites are reachable from IPv6 hosts:

$ ping6 -c1 fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:5e8d:1616
PING fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:5e8d:1616(fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:5e8d:1616) 56 data bytes
64 bytes from fd9f:590a:b158:ffff:ffff:ffff:5e8d:1616: icmp_seq=1 ttl=52 time=61.7 ms

They are reachable through DNS too (note that /etc/resolv.conf must be configured properly):

$ ping6 -c1 www.routereflector.com
PING www.routereflector.com(srv-hp9.netsons.net) 56 data bytes
64 bytes from srv-hp9.netsons.net: icmp_seq=1 ttl=52 time=60.0 ms

Some protocols that embed L3 addresses into L4 datagrams (like FTP or SIP) can behave unexpectedly. DNSSEC also cannot be used, because of the DNS record manipulation.
