docs.title: Data center topology with Cisco Nexus, HP Virtual Connect and VMware
Data center topology with Cisco Nexus, HP Virtual Connect and VMware
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog cisco design ucs vmware

Integrating devices made by different vendors is a delicate task, because each component can behave differently from what we expect. In this post, we discuss a data center core network built with Cisco, HP, NetApp and VMware equipment and software:

The diagram above does not show the best data center implementation: it shows an implementation chosen to discuss limits, risks and solutions.

docs.title: Switching Within the Physical Core-Edge Network
docs.text:
The physical network is built with Cisco equipment:

  • 2 Cisco Catalyst 6500 (no VSS) implement the Core level.
  • 2 Cisco Nexus 5K implement the Distribution level.
  • 2 (or more) Cisco Nexus 2000 (Fabric Extender) implement the Access level (HP Virtual Connects implement an additional Access level, discussed later).

docs.title: Spanning Tree
docs.text:
STP is required to avoid loops in layer 2 networks. During a topology change, a VLAN can be frozen for up to 50 seconds. Rapid STP (802.1w) can shorten the STP topology change to about 30 seconds, not less. In this scenario, a lot of virtual machines run on an NFS datastore: each VM boots from a virtual disk, which is formally a file stored in the NFS datastore. Each virtual disk emulates a SCSI disk, so the virtual OS can send SCSI commands to it. A SCSI command needs a lossless medium: it cannot be delayed and it cannot be lost (the error recovery process takes too long). A topology change therefore stops all the SCSI commands of hundreds of VMs, and the operating systems crash or become unusable (Windows crashes with a blue screen, and Linux remounts all the filesystems read-only). There are fixes at the virtual machine level to avoid this behavior, discussed later.

We could eliminate STP almost completely by configuring VSS between the two Catalyst switches, but this discussion is not about VSS. We must therefore minimize the effect of an STP convergence.

Each Catalyst has a vPC link to both Nexus 5K. CoreA is the STP root for the NFS network, and CoreB is the root for the other VLANs. The N5K should not be the root because they present themselves with two different Bridge IDs: if the one with the lowest BID reboots, all the VLANs need to converge. Both Catalyst switches have two supervisors, so each root is more stable.

Both Catalyst switches act as gateways for the routed VLANs (management and production). A firewall (not shown in the diagram) routes the DMZ VLAN. The vMotion and NFS VLANs are isolated. A first-hop redundancy protocol (HSRP) can be configured between the two Catalyst switches: the primary gateway should follow the STP root.

docs.title: Switching Path
docs.text:
Each server has a teaming (Windows) or bonding (Linux) mechanism to survive a single path failure. One path is active and the other remains standby. Depending on the driver, an active path can be configured as preferred. In this scenario we assume no preferred path, so we analyze the worst case. Each NetApp storage can be configured with an active-standby path mechanism or with a LACP port-channel.

We analyze the path between each pair of hosts:

  • From ServerA to ServerC: the active path of both servers is attached to the same Fabric Extender (Nexus 2000), which is not a switching device. All the frames must be forwarded to the EdgeA switch and then back to the destination. The uplink path of the Fabric Extender can be a bottleneck.
  • From ServerA to ServerB: the active paths of the servers are attached to different Fabric Extenders, which forward frames to the upper Edge switch. Analyzing the STP topology, the link between the edge switches should be in the Alternate state (rapid-pvst is used), so frames should flow to the root Catalyst switch and then back to the destination Nexus 5K. Because vPC peer links are always non-blocking (a vPC domain uses another mechanism to ensure a loop-free topology), frames flow through the vPC peer link using the shortest path. The vPC peer link can be a bottleneck too.
  • Between NetApp storages: the traffic depends on the interface configuration (active-standby or active-active with LACP). As discussed in the previous point, the shortest path is used. Because storage traffic can impact the network heavily, NetApp should be attached directly to the Nexus 5K switches rather than to the Fabric Extenders. Otherwise, the N2K-N5K links are overused (the N2K are non-switching devices).
  • From a server to a NetApp storage: an active-standby NetApp configuration follows the ServerA-ServerB example. A LACP NetApp configuration behaves differently: the storage presents its MAC address to both N5K switches. ServerA uses the active path and finds the destination storage within the nearest N5K switch. The NetApp LACP configuration lets the server reach it always through the shortest path. On the other hand, an active-standby configuration lets us move cables to other switches without a Takeover/Giveback action.

N2K devices are not switches: they are extensions (Fabric Extender) of the N5K/N7K switches, with important features and limitations:

  • They are non-switching devices.
  • They provide end-host connectivity only.

We cannot attach a switch to an N2K device: each N2K has an implicit BPDU guard. If a BPDU is received, the port is immediately placed in the error-disabled state, which keeps the link down.

docs.title: The Additional Access Layer: HP Virtual Connects
docs.text:
HP Virtual Connects (VCs) are hybrid devices and can be compared to Cisco UCS 61xx devices: VCs virtualize server information as UCS does. This is not a discussion of VC vs. UCS 61xx. The comparison only points out what kind of devices VCs are.

Each HP blade is attached (VC downlinks) to both VCs located in the same chassis: each VC defines the WWNs and MAC addresses of the servers using profiles. Each profile can be moved or cloned to other servers. A bunch of trunk links from the upper Nexus layer brings all the VLANs to the VCs (VC uplinks). Each chassis must include a pair of VCs, which communicate through internal cross-connect 10GbE links. VCs on different chassis are connected with external fibers and form one VC domain. Each HP blade is connected to both VCs located in the same chassis, with internal hardware connections.

Within the same VC domain, traffic is forwarded internally. In other words, traffic between blade servers is switched:

  • Within a VC, if both blades use the links to the same VC.
  • Within the VC domain, using the loop connection, if the blades use links to different VCs.

A "Shared uplink set" is a group of VC uplinks. In "Auto" mode, the Shared uplink set negotiates a LACP port-channel. Each blade can use one or more Shared uplink sets to transmit and receive data. From the OS perspective, a single Shared uplink set is a network interface.

A LACP port-channel can be configured within the same VC only.

docs.title: Smart Link
docs.text:
With the Smart Link feature, each Shared uplink set brings the blade network connections down if there are no more active VC uplinks in the same Shared uplink set. See the following example:

In the leftmost diagram, the blade servers are configured with a bonding/teaming device that holds two Shared uplink sets. Each Shared uplink set has only one VC uplink, which connects to the external networks. The black arrow indicates the active path of the bonding/teaming.

In the center diagram, a VC uplink is broken and a Shared uplink set becomes unusable. The blade servers still use the same path because it is in the up/up state: the data path is broken and the blade servers are unreachable.

In the rightmost diagram, the Smart Link feature is enabled and shuts down the unusable links. The blade servers recognize the broken link, and the active paths now use the other Shared uplink set (thanks to the bonding/teaming feature).

Now consider the following, more complex example:

In the configuration above, each Virtual Connect has one Shared uplink set with a single VC uplink inside it. The rightmost blade servers use a remote Shared uplink set as the active path. If the uplink of Virtual Connect B goes down, Smart Link notifies the directly connected blade servers, but it does not notify the other Virtual Connects about the broken link. The right blade server therefore keeps using the same link and becomes unreachable.

A Shared uplink set can contain interfaces from different Virtual Connects, but this is outside the scope of this post.

docs.title: BPDU Guard
docs.text:
A VC behaves as an edge device on the network and does not transmit BPDUs: it does not participate in the spanning tree process. A BPDU guard is configured by default, and when a VC receives a BPDU from a blade server, it shuts down the internal link of that blade server. There is no BPDU filter feature.

This is a good thing: if a BPDU were forwarded to the N2K, the implicit BPDU guard on the N2K would shut down the entire VC uplink.

docs.title: VMware
docs.text:
VMware software provides the end-host network access. Physically, VMware vSphere is software installed on servers, and inside it there is a complex system that emulates an entire data center.

A VMware virtual network (vNet) does not run STP and does not participate in any spanning tree process. Let's see the following example:

The red VM is transmitting BPDUs:

  • The first BPDU is forwarded through the blade server where the VM is active. When the BPDU reaches Virtual Connect A, the link is shut down because of the BPDU guard.
  • The VMware ESXi server links the red VM to the other active link (through Virtual Connect B).
  • Another BPDU causes the shutdown of the second link. Now the first VMware ESXi server is unreachable.
  • The VMware HA feature restarts all the VMs on another server.
  • The red VM is active again and can transmit another BPDU.
  • The process continues until all the servers are unreachable.

A VM can transmit a BPDU if:

  • Two vmnics are configured and bridged together: in this case, if a BPDU (originated by the N5K) is received from one vmnic, it is forwarded through the other vmnic.
  • An STP instance runs within the VM.

We can avoid the first case by configuring each vmnet to reject Forged Transmits:

We cannot avoid the second case with VMware ESXi 4.1. The solution is to install the Cisco Nexus 1000v or upgrade to VMware ESXi 5.1, which has a BPDU filter feature.

As discussed before, another potential issue is caused by STP convergence: because each virtual machine uses the SCSI protocol, packet loss or delay can be dangerous. To avoid crashes during an STP convergence, we must increase the SCSI and NFS timeouts.

On Windows (persistent):

[HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Disk]
"TimeoutValue"=dword:000000be

On Linux (not persistent):

echo 180 > /sys/block/sdc/device/timeout

On Linux systems, VMware Tools also set the proper timeout (persistent across reboots).

We must also configure the ESXi servers with proper NFS settings. The easiest way is to install the NetApp Virtual Storage Console and check the NetApp tab from the vSphere Client:

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Building a data center requires deep knowledge. This example showed that:

  • The Cisco Fabric Extender (Nexus 2K) is a non-switching device with an implicit BPDU guard.
  • A Cisco Nexus 5K vPC acts as a single switch for a port-channel, but originates two different Bridge IDs.
  • HP Virtual Connects have a BPDU guard by default and a Smart Link feature to notify blade servers about link problems. Smart Link is not forwarded to other Virtual Connects (local significance only).
  • A VMware virtual machine can originate BPDUs that are forwarded to other network devices.
  • NFS datastores transport SCSI frames over an unreliable medium (STP can delay frames).

docs.title: Designing a cloud provider with both VMware NSX and Cisco ACI
docs.text: 19 September 2018

docs.title: Designing a cloud provider with both VMware NSX and Cisco ACI
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog cisco design firewall vmware

A few months ago I had a chat with a customer about IaaS. The customer wanted to change its business model from an internal-only ICT to an IaaS-style ICT, for both internal and external users.

The customer's prerequisites were:

  • Infrastructure distributed across two data centers, 30 km apart.
  • Ability to move workloads transparently between the two data centers.
  • Users able to do everything through a self-service portal.

These prerequisites are not enough, of course: customers often do not know what they want. After an additional chat, we agreed on:

  • High Availability Zones: each data center must be designed to be completely independent. The data centers are interconnected with redundant 100GbE links.
  • Mobility: workloads can be moved transparently from one data center to the other. Tenants usually run in one data center only, except when moving. Latency is accepted because moving is a temporary and planned event. The idea is that users get space in a data center, but they can be moved to the other one. Users cannot buy space in both data centers to deliver distributed applications.
  • Physical devices: physical devices can be added to specific tenants, for example ISP routers, Oracle Exadata, IBM AS/400 and HSMs.
  • Connectivity: each tenant can be reached from outside via remote access VPN and site-to-site VPN. External connectivity such as MPLS/VPLS can be used too. Each tenant can rent some public IP addresses or just use the assigned ones. Tenants can be interconnected if they have non-overlapping IP addresses.
  • Storage: Fibre Channel storage is not stretched between the data centers.
  • Self-Service Portal: users cannot do "everything", only a set of defined actions.
  • Backup and Disaster Recovery: users can buy backup (BaaS) and/or disaster recovery (DRaaS) features on a per-VM basis.

docs.title: The Very High-Level Design (HLD)
docs.text:
We should not discuss the choice of technology at this level, but every technology has its own prerequisites, features, limitations and peculiarities, so we cannot go far without making assumptions.

The "mobility" prerequisite is one of the most stringent: moving workloads without disruption (vMotion) means that LANs must be stretched. To stretch LANs, we can use one of the following:

  • Standard VXLAN.
  • Cisco ACI.
  • VMware NSX.

This post focuses on VMware NSX and Cisco ACI, so I do not discuss standard VXLAN. The step between standard VLANs and Cisco ACI or VMware NSX is short, though.

Let's start by designing a big picture:

Each data center is connected to the Internet through one or more ISPs, announcing the same prefixes via BGP from the border routers. The border routers are connected to the inside routers and then to a distributed router.

A firewall connected to the distributed router isolates each tenant.

The diagram is inspired by VMware NSX, so let's discuss it in detail.

docs.title: VMware NSX
docs.text:
Let's look at the diagram again:

Each border router is connected to one or more ISP routers. Both border routers announce the same prefixes with the same AS. In other words, from the Internet both data centers look like a single data center with two independent exits.

The border routers also announce the prefixes of the users directly. Because of NSX limitations (discussed below), BGP peering between tenants and border routers is not permitted.

Both border routers also run OSPF, each peering with an edge router. An edge router (in the NSX world) is a clustered VM that acts as a router with some additional features such as NAT, firewall, load balancer and IPsec concentrator.

In this design, both edge routers are just routers, nothing more.

Both edge routers peer (OSPF) with a distributed logical router (DLR). A DLR is a router stretched across one or more physical servers running ESXi. On the other side, the DLR is connected to a stretched network.

Each tenant has its own gateway, implemented by a non-VMware firewall.

Let's discuss some VMware NSX limits and the design choices above. Note that the limits may have changed in the meantime, so feel free to add your opinion in the comments.

  • The edge routers cannot be moved (vMotion) automatically between data centers: a workload cannot be moved from DC1 to DC2 without manual intervention. We can still destroy a cluster of edge routers and recreate it in the other DC using the old configuration, but this is obviously a disruptive approach. Using non-VMware clustered firewalls lets us move one node at a time. Edge firewalls can also offer remote access VPNs, site-to-site IPsec VPNs and so on. Because the firewall can be moved to the other data center without changing any IP address, the "outside" network must be stretched between data centers.
  • The DLR cannot run OSPF facing the firewalls, so static routing is the only option. Each firewall uses the DLR as its default gateway, and the DLR forwards the packets destined to the public IP address assigned to each tenant. The DLR also cannot peer with the border routers directly. That is why edge routers are used between the DLR and the border routers.
  • The smallest network that we can announce to the Internet is a /24, so we can assume that several tenants share the same /24 network. In this case, we should try to run all those tenants in the same DC. The nearest border router announces a more specific network, so all the traffic enters from the right link.

docs.title: Distributed Firewall with VMware NSX
docs.text:
VMware NSX provides a distributed firewall to implement micro-segmentation. It sounds great, but the distributed firewall policy is a single one, shared by all tenants. In a multi-tenant environment, a single policy is not a great idea: every user has specific needs, and the policy cannot grow forever.

The distributed firewall was not in the feature list, but I think it is still a nice-to-have feature. How can we adapt a single-policy firewall to a multi-tenant environment?

We could use tags. Each VM can be tagged and get specific firewall rules.

Assume, for example, the following tags:

  • server_HTTP.
  • server_HTTP_Proxy.
  • client_HTTP_Proxy.
  • allow_any.

We can write a policy like the following:

  • VMs tagged with allow_any receive any traffic.
  • VMs tagged with server_HTTP receive HTTP connections.
  • VMs tagged with server_HTTP_Proxy receive connections from client_HTTP_Proxy VMs only.

In this scenario, which refers to the distributed firewall only, not to the edge firewall, each user knows what the policies are, and tagging the VMs lets them honor or bypass the firewall.

docs.title: Availability Zones with VMware NSX
docs.text:
One of the prerequisites is the independence of the data centers, so we must design the infrastructure to stay alive even if an entire data center is lost.

Remember that users can run VMs in one data center at a time. Letting users run VMs in both data centers is not so difficult, but it is not part of the prerequisites.

In the VMware NSX world we have:

  • NSX Manager: the management plane of the network. Each NSX Manager is bound to a single vCenter.
  • NSX Controllers: the control plane of the network. Three controllers must exist, and two must be alive. If only one controller or none is alive, all VMs "should" run fine as long as nothing changes (no vMotion, no power-on...).
  • vCenter.
  • PSC.
  • Active Directory.
  • vCloud Director / vRealize Automation.
  • ...

Because we need two independent data centers, we need one NSX Manager and three NSX Controllers per data center. In this configuration, we must be sure that we can move (vMotion) VMs between data centers. In other words, we must be able to move VMs between:

  • vCenters (that is fine).
  • vCloud Director / vRealize Automation instances (probably not possible: the best option is a disruptive export and import).

Moreover, we have to define the virtual networks as universal. In previous vCloud Director and vRealize Automation versions, users cannot create a universal virtual network: an administrator must create it manually.

If we relax the prerequisite, we can have a single stretched infrastructure with one NSX Manager, three NSX Controllers and one vCenter. In this case, VMs can be moved without issues, but we must consider how to recover from the loss of a data center containing unique infrastructure VMs (NSX Manager, NSX Controllers, vCenter...).

To be more specific, one data center runs two NSX Controllers and the other runs just one. If the first data center is lost, the NSX Controllers cluster loses quorum. At that point, we must redeploy one NSX Controller manually in the surviving data center.

docs.title: Backup and Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
Backing up VMs and mirroring them to the remote data center is not too difficult. The hardest part is restoring a backup or activating the VM in the remote data center.

As mentioned before, a VM can be imported into vCloud Director / vRealize Automation, but we must run deep tests to check whether everything works. I refer especially to tags, networks and service portal accounting.

docs.title: Onboarding
docs.text:
The onboarding service is usually omitted from many designs. As an architect, I can say that this is the most critical part for many users: how do we migrate a physical, legacy data center to a cloud provider with minimal disruption? Many enterprises do not know what is running in their data centers, and they often do not have the skills to plan a move. This can be a business opportunity and an enabler for the IaaS service.

For VMware, there is a lot of good software such as Veeam and Zerto. All of them have different costs, features and compatibility lists.

docs.title: Physical Devices Attached to VMware NSX
docs.text:
Last but not least, VMware NSX allows extending L2 networks to a physical domain. We must test high availability and convergence timers to be sure that they are compatible with the SLA.

Even if this works fine, it seems to me that such connections are not easy to maintain if their number increases a lot. Moreover, they probably must be configured manually, because they are not part of the default vCloud Director / vRealize Automation scripts.

docs.title: Conclusions for the VMware Design
docs.text:
I hope you now understand why this design is closely tied to the technological choice. Running the infrastructure can be more or less vendor-independent, but when we add a service portal, backup, disaster recovery and onboarding, we must evaluate a lot of software and check whether and how it can work together.

Deep customization can also be an issue: if we develop scripts for every single action we give to users, how can we make sure that all the scripts work after a release upgrade?

docs.title: Cisco ACI
docs.text:
Cisco ACI completely separates the fabric configuration from the tenant configuration. Once the fabric is deployed, each tenant can get its own contracts, policies and so on.

VMware has an edge gateway included (not used here), whereas Cisco ACI has no way to NAT addresses.

Because of the VMware NSX limitations (see above) and the Cisco ACI limitations, the design is pretty similar:

With Cisco ACI, the border routers can also peer with tenants, so users can announce their prefixes themselves.

The edge routers are not needed anymore, because ACI can peer with the external routers directly. With this design, customers can announce their prefixes directly, but the border routers must be configured as transit AS for the traffic sourced from or destined to the users.

Because Cisco ACI cannot NAT IP addresses, each tenant needs a gateway. We can use virtual or physical firewalls, as discussed in the VMware NSX section.

The infrastructure is relatively easy to design. The most critical part is once again the software: what should we use to virtualize the VMs and implement a service portal?

Once again, the VMware suite is a good choice, but we can also use OpenStack, OpenNebula or CloudStack.

A 100% VMware suite can mostly work out of the box, but we probably will not see a CloudStack + Cisco ACI service portal ready to use.

docs.title: Distributed Firewall with Cisco ACI
docs.text: The VMware NSX distributed firewall has a single policy. With Cisco ACI, each tenant gets its own separate rules.

docs.title: Availability Zones with Cisco ACI
docs.text:
To satisfy the prerequisites fully, we must deploy a multi-site fabric with three APIC controllers per site.

On top, we can deploy a Cisco ACI Multi-Site policy manager to manage the policies of both data centers from a single location. Of course, we must recover the policy manager if one site goes completely offline.

If we relax the prerequisite, we can deploy a multi-pod fabric. Because each fabric must have at least two running controllers (I do not discuss here how a five-controller fabric works), once again one data center gets only one controller.

With Cisco ACI, however, the controller is the management plane: the fabric can work fine even without controllers. We can also add a fourth APIC with the standby role (I guess turning it from standby to active is still a manual procedure).

If only one controller exists, the management can be read-only.

docs.title: Backup, Disaster Recovery and Onboarding
docs.text: We already discussed these topics in the VMware part. The considerations above are more or less still valid with Cisco ACI, but because Cisco does not provide a full suite, more development is probably required. That is not necessarily a bad thing.

docs.title: Physical Devices Attached to Cisco ACI
docs.text: Interconnecting physical devices to a VMware NSX environment is an "exception" to the virtual world. In Cisco ACI, physical devices are entirely part of the game: their number can increase a lot without any issue.

docs.title: Conclusions for the Cisco ACI Design
docs.text:
VMware offers a more complete suite to cover this design case, while Cisco ACI offers a more flexible infrastructure without any additional software.

Both solutions have strong limits, and both require a lot of integration development.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
I wrote this post to share the ideas and experiences of the last few years. It cannot be complete, and it is probably already outdated. It should still give you some details on where to start.

Today there are no out-of-the-box solutions for this case, so some prerequisites should be relaxed. My opinion is that in a 100% virtual world, VMware is probably the best solution today. With an important part of physical servers or devices, Cisco ACI is more flexible.

docs.title: Disable Android Certificate Pinning with Frida
Disable Android Certificate Pinning with Frida
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced android blog digital-self-defence frida

During security assessments of smart home applications, I usually need to analyze encrypted HTTPS communications. Applications usually check for valid certificates, but they also check that the certificates are signed by a specific issuer. This is called "Certificate Pinning". It is not recommended, but it is widely used:

Caution: Certificate Pinning is not recommended for Android applications due to the high risk of future server configuration changes, such as changing to another Certificate Authority, rendering the application unable to connect to the server without receiving a client software update.

To decrypt an HTTPS connection protected with Certificate Pinning, we need a different approach: Frida, a dynamic instrumentation toolkit for developers, reverse engineers and security researchers.

docs.title: Installing Frida on Kali Linux
docs.text:
Let's prepare our Kali Linux:

sudo apt install android-tools-adb android-tools-fastboot

We install an old Python version from sources:

sudo apt install libssl-dev libsqlite3-dev liblzma-dev libffi-dev zlib1g-dev
wget https://www.python.org/ftp/python/3.7.12/Python-3.7.12.tgz
tar xzvf Python-3.7.12.tgz -o -C /opt
cd /opt/Python-3.7.12
./configure --enable-optimizations
make

Finally, we build a virtual environment:

./python -m venv ~/.venv-frida

With the Python interpreter and the virtual environment above, we can install Frida:

source ~/.venv-frida/bin/activate
pip install frida-tools objection

docs.title: Installing Frida Server on the Android Device
docs.text:
On a rooted Android device, we enable USB Debugging. We go to Settings → About Phone → Software Information and click 7 times on Build Number, then we go to Settings → Developer Options → Enable → USB Debugging and enable it.

We connect the phone to the computer with a USB cable and restart ADB:

adb kill-server
adb devices
- daemon not running; starting now at tcp:5037
- daemon started successfully
List of devices attached
520011a1a0123143        device

We download the proper Frida version and frida-android-unpinning:

wget https://github.com/frida/frida/releases/download/15.2.2/frida-server-15.2.2-android-arm64.xz
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/httptoolkit/frida-android-unpinning/main/frida-script.js

We upload Frida Server to the Android device:

unxz frida-server-15.1.12-android-arm.xz
mv frida-server-15.1.12-android-arm frida-server
adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp/

Finally, we start Frida Server on the Android device:

adb shell
su
/data/local/tmp/frida-server

We open another shell on Kali Linux, using the Python virtual environment built for Frida, and check the network connection between the client (Kali Linux) and the server (Android):

frida-ps -U

The last command should return the list of the processes running on the Android device.

docs.title: Running an Application Without Certificate Pinning
docs.text:
We are now ready to run an application with certificate pinning disabled. All the following commands run on Kali Linux.

We identify the package name of the application we want to run:

adb shell pm list packages --user 0 -u | grep -i appname

We make sure that the application is not running on the Android device:

frida-ps -U | grep -i AppName

We start the application:

frida --no-pause -U -l ./frida-script.js -f com.appname.start

The app starts on the smartphone and pops up on the screen. All HTTPS connections have certificate pinning disabled and can be intercepted by MITM Proxy.

Andrea Dainese advanced blog cisco design ucs

This post covers disjoint L2 domains on Cisco UCS-B, and why and when to implement them.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Multi-Tenant Infrastructure
docs.text:

Now suppose you need to share the UCS-B infrastructure with multiple, physically L2-separated tenants:

docs.title: Scenario 2: Physically Separated Security Zones
docs.text:
Suppose your current UCS-B infrastructure is configured to support a single L2 uplink:

Now suppose you need some virtual machines in a different, physically L2-isolated security zone:

docs.title: Requirements for Working Disjoint L2 Domains
docs.text:
The configuration is pretty simple, but you must be 100% sure about the following points:

  1. All the ports related to the new port-channel must be in the shutdown state. Otherwise, after you add the new port-channels on the Fabric Interconnects, UCS-B uses them to carry the old VLANs too, and it becomes a mess because the new port-channels do not carry the old VLANs.
  2. VLANs must be unique: you cannot configure the same VLAN on more than one uplink/domain. Otherwise, UCS-B does not know which uplink/domain owns which VLAN.
  3. Each server must have a vNIC dedicated to a single uplink/domain: you cannot use a single vNIC to carry VLANs from multiple uplinks/domains. Otherwise, UCS-B does not know which uplink to pin the vNIC to.

docs.title: Configure Disjoint L2 Domains with a Zero-Downtime Approach
docs.text:
1. On the Nexus switches, configure all the ports dedicated to the new port-channels in the shutdown state.
  2. On UCS Manager (Equipment → Chassis → Fabric Interconnect A|B → Physical Ports → Ethernet Ports), configure all the ports dedicated to the new port-channels as "Uplink Port" and disable them:
  3. On UCS Manager (LAN → LAN Cloud → Fabric A|B → Port Channels), add a new port-channel, assign the ports dedicated to it, and disable the port-channel:
  4. On UCS Manager (LAN → LAN Cloud → VLANs), add all the VLANs assigned to the new port-channel:
  5. On UCS Manager (LAN → right click → LAN Uplinks Manager → VLANs → VLAN Manager → Fabric A|B), assign all the VLANs (both old and new) to a port-channel. This is the most critical phase, so make sure you assign each VLAN to a single uplink/port-channel on both Fabric Interconnects:
  6. On UCS Manager, enable the port-channels.
  7. On the Cisco Nexus switches, configure and enable the virtual port-channels.

docs.title: Evaluating security of RFID/NFC implementations
docs.text: 12 January 2018

docs.title: Evaluating security of RFID/NFC implementations
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced blog rfid security

Many companies rely on RFID (Radio-frequency identification) tags for many aspects. Employer badges are often RFID-based and allow for unique identification, authorization, and account for each employer.

Other companies use simple RFID tags or the more evolved NFC smartcards to identify and bill for services. Many home alarm systems use RFID tags to manage arm/disarm operations. Moreover, RFID tags are used to identify goods within stores or buildings in general. In a utopian world, everything would be fine, but in the real world, we should ask how we can trust users, and technology and we must evaluate the risks caused by a tampered NFC smartcard or RFID in general.

What about if an employer badge is duplicated? What about if a home alarm NFC smartcard is duplicated? What about if a laundry machine smartcard has been tampered? What about if an RFID tag is substituted/deactivated?

This won't be an exhaustive post about RFID technology, we'll focus on how they are used in the real world. The most common RFID devices we found, are:

  • 125kHz RFID tags (EM410x)
  • 13.56MHZ NFC smartcards (MIFARE Classic)

Both of them are old and very insecure for many reasons.

docs.title: The Red Team perspective
docs.text:
The cheapest and most flexible tool we found is ProxMark3 (PM3) Easy, it can be found on eBay at about 60€. It's a USB device with two antennas, for 125kHz and 15.56MHz tags. The bundle includes some blank tags.

We're using the PM3 attached to a VM running the latest Kali Linux on VMware Fusion. The PM3 can be mapped to the VM and it works fine.

docs.title: Upgrading the PM3
docs.text:

docs.text:
PM3 is now ready to read tags. To scan an unknown tag we need to type two commands, one for each antenna:

proxmark3> hf search
proxmark3> lf search

If the scanned tag is supported, one of the above commands should answer with the details of the tag.

docs.text:

docs.title: Analyzing a MiFare Classic NFC smartcard
docs.text:
The following is an access card for a restricted area:

proxmark3> hf search

ATQA : 00 04

Prng detection: WEAK

Valid ISO14443A Tag Found - Quiting Search

MiFare Classic smartcards are not secure:

We can recover the full 48-bit key of the MiFare algorithm in 200 seconds on a PC, given 1 known IV (from one single encryption). The security of this cipher is therefore close to zero.

Courtois, Nicolas T.; Karsten Nohl; Sean O'Neil (2008-04-14). "Algebraic Attacks on the Crypto-1 Stream Cipher in MiFare Classic and Oyster Cards". Cryptology ePrint Archive.

By the way, in many cases, we don't even need to crack a card because:

  • UID is enough
  • data are not encrypted or encrypted with a default key

Let's start with the easier and common scenario, and let's clone the UID only to another smartcard:

proxmark3> hf mf csetuid 11111111

Other implementations, like public laundry machines or public transport, save additional data, that can be possibly encrypted:

The above card is using the default key: ffffffffffff. If data are partially encrypted with a non-default key, we can try a nested attack, using one of the default keys:

proxmark3> hf mf nested 1 0 A ffffffffffff d

Or we can test other attacks:

proxmark3> hf mf mifare

Once we have all keys (dumped into dumpkeys.bin file), we can dump the card into the dumpdata.bin file:

proxmark3> hf mf dump 1

And we can copy the content to a new card:

proxmark3> hf mf restore 1

And it worked.

We discovered that even if additional (but weak) security layers are available, they are rarely used.

docs.title: The Blue Team perspective
docs.text:
Each component included, installed, and used in any enterprise (or any house) should be evaluated especially if it can lead to a security breach. Referring to a company, if the evaluation cannot be provided by an internal team, use one (or more) trusted external service. Don't trust vendors without testing them. Don't buy or implement solutions without knowing them in the detail.

Secure smartcard solutions currently exist, but the question is: for how long they will remain secure? The question is very important, because if a big worldwide enterprise decides to implement an access solution based on the latest and most secure smartcard for 30000 employers, what it should do if (better say when) that smartcard will no more secure? How much does cost the migration to another access control system? Should it use something upgradeable (like an app on a smartphone), or should it maintain a weak access control?

It depends, as always... on risk and cost analysis.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: We discovered a large number of weak implementations, provided also by respectable vendors but implemented poorly. Day after day we realized that no vendor can be blinded trusted, no matter how respectable it is. If enterprises can usually afford the cost of a third opinion, end users rarely can. The more IoT, smart homes we see, the more I tend to get a simple "smart less" building. This is still not the era of the "apartment thieves", but it will come soon.

docs.title: MITM on wired 802.1x with a Raspberry PI
MITM on wired 802.1x with a Raspberry PI
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese 802-1x advanced blog design security

In recent years, Network Access Control (NAC) solutions based on the 802.1x protocol have gained significant traction. Like any security solution, they must be evaluated carefully before we integrate them into a proper cybersecurity strategy.

I understand that this evaluation requires very specific technical knowledge, and those who assess these solutions often rely on what the datasheets say. This post has three purposes:

  • To raise awareness that assessing a security solution incorrectly exposes organizations to threats.
  • To describe the steps a threat actor can follow to exploit the weaknesses of NAC solutions.
  • To be informative, and understandable even to non-technical readers.

docs.title: Introduction: NAC Solutions
docs.text:
First, we need an overview of NAC (Network Access Control) solutions. They are based on the 802.1x protocol to authenticate and authorize connected devices. Some solutions, through additional components, also assess the behavior of the devices to identify anomalies.

These solutions address the problem of unauthorized devices accessing Ethernet ports. Specifically, they protect the ports that people can reach easily, particularly in offices and public areas.

Over time, these solutions have evolved: they authenticate, authorize and profile the connected devices. In other words, we can configure Ethernet ports dynamically based on the connected devices. This greatly helps to improve and automate the management of large and dynamic campus networks.

Device authentication is based on the 802.1x protocol: the switch requests authentication from the device, and external servers validate the authentication. Authentication can use a username and password or certificates. Once the device is authenticated, the channel stays active until the session expires and must be renewed.

Solutions have also evolved to support multiple connected devices, such as:

  • A phone with a computer cascaded behind it.
  • A computer with virtual machines.
  • ...

In the real world, however, many devices do not implement the 802.1x protocol. NAC solutions have "evolved" further (it would be more correct to say "devolved"), authenticating devices based on their MAC address: this functionality is called MAB, or MAC Address Bypass. The term "bypass" cannot be associated with a security feature, and we should remember that NAC solutions are also used for automation.

The most important consideration concerns how an authenticated session is established. 802.1x authenticates the channel, not the individual packets. The switch associates the authenticated session with the MAC address of the device. An attacker can therefore insert a malicious device between the authenticated device and the switch, and exploit the authenticated channel.

The final consideration concerns what I call "silent" devices. For NAC solutions to work, the connected devices must support 802.1x or transmit at least one packet, so that the switch learns their MAC address. Some devices are designed to receive data but not to transmit it, which makes it impossible to use any NAC solution.

docs.title: Switch Configuration
docs.text:
We should evaluate the switch configuration carefully to minimize the risks, which, as we will see later, are still present.

Each Ethernet port can be configured in different modes, depending on the vendor. On Cisco switches, the modes are:

  • Multi-Host: once the connected device authenticates the port, any other device can use the channel (for example, virtual machines).
  • Multi-Domain: each connected device, belonging to a specific VLAN, must authenticate (for example, a phone and a computer cascaded).
  • Multi-Auth: each MAC address that appears on the Ethernet port must authenticate.
  • MAB: no real authentication is performed, only a check that the MAC address is enabled.

Where possible, the preference should be, in order, Multi-Auth, Multi-Domain, Multi-Host and MAB (the definitions depend on the vendor: the important thing is to understand the concept).

docs.title: MITM on 802.1x
docs.text:
From the attacker's perspective, in the worst-case scenario, inserting a device between an authenticated device and a switch means being transparent. Specifically, the attacker must, in order:

  1. Forward any data to and from the switch without applying any filters to the local frames.
  2. Wait for the channel to be authenticated.
  3. Emit data using only the MAC address and the IP address of the authenticated device.

There are two ways to implement this:

  1. Build a software switch running in user space, which probably results in lower performance.
  2. Use the components offered by Linux, working in kernel space with better performance, albeit with some limitations.

With the second approach, the three steps translate operationally into:

  1. Compiling a custom kernel so that Linux Bridge forwards all the frames.
  2. Reading the MAC address of the connected device.
  3. Analyzing the passing data until we obtain the IP address of the connected device and the MAC address of the gateway.
  4. Configuring a Linux Bridge, iptables and ebtables so that we can communicate with the outside using the MAC address and the IP address of the connected device.
  5. Activating a covert channel that allows us to exploit the malicious device remotely.

The result is a practically invisible, remotely manageable device.

docs.title: Defense Strategies
docs.text:
Programming a device to exploit an authenticated 802.1x session transparently is not simple, but it is not overly complex either. We must therefore consider the risk that ports with promiscuous access are compromised as described above.

For several years, my approach has been to treat networks with promiscuous access like DMZ networks: high-risk areas that require high visibility and very restrictive policies. We cannot make any assumption about the security of the connected devices.

A first approach is to increase visibility by adding behavioral analysis of the devices: if a printer starts communicating with an unknown remote site and uploads a more or less significant amount of data, a red flag should go up somewhere.

A second approach is to apply zero trust, creating policies that allow only what is strictly necessary and limiting the scope of action of any malicious device. In this regard, Private VLANs can further reduce the attack surface. We must always keep in mind how a device is authenticated: for example, if a computer is authenticated based on the user using it, and the firewalls evaluate the policies based on the IP address of that user, we cannot consider this mechanism secure. The malicious device described above uses the same IP address assigned to the user.

A third approach, less common but extremely effective, is to add a layer based on IPsec or similar protocols. I like this approach a lot: it treats promiscuous networks as public networks, so users who authenticate on them must use VPN systems to reach the internal company networks.

One more approach, partially applicable, is to encrypt the channel between the device and the switch to make it unusable for MITM attacks. MACsec (802.1AE) is the standard that implements this functionality, but endpoint devices do not implement it natively at the moment. Third-party agents, such as Cisco AnyConnect, can be installed on the client operating systems.

docs.title: Malicious email analysis
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese blog digital-self-defence intermediate phishing security

These days I am receiving more requests for help than ever. Most of them concern suspicious emails, maybe because people are more aware, maybe because the current geopolitical situation is evolving fast.

I want to present a couple of cases I received recently, to help:

  • IT managers set up a proper notification and response process.
  • End users evaluate suspicious emails.

docs.title: GDPR Recap
docs.text:
European firms should already have a data breach notification process defined and communicated to employees. Just in case, let's review the relevant GDPR articles:

  • Art. 4.12 - Definitions: personal data breach means a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data transmitted, stored or otherwise processed.
  • Art. 33.1 - Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority: in the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall, without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Where the notification to the supervisory authority is not made within 72 hours, it shall be accompanied by reasons for the delay.
  • Art. 33.5 - Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority: the controller shall document any personal data breaches, comprising the facts relating to the personal data breach, its effects and the remedial action taken. That documentation shall enable the supervisory authority to verify compliance with this Article.

In practice, firms must have procedures to:

  • Communicate data breaches within the firm (notification).
  • Evaluate the risk associated with data breaches (response).
  • Register data breaches and the related analysis (tracking).

Given the GDPR definition of a data breach, most security incidents are data breaches. Following ITIL, an incident is:

ITIL defines an incident as an unplanned interruption to or quality reduction of an IT service.

An unplanned event will affect personal data one way or another, so any incident affecting personal data is a data breach. We can therefore have a single set of procedures that describe the incident management process.

docs.title: Notification
docs.text:
We will discuss incident management procedures in a later article. For now, just make sure a notification process is in place inside the organization. For this post, the notification is the request of a user about a suspicious email. Users are required to forward any suspicious email as an attachment, or to use any integration that does the same automatically.

I also use the same procedure to evaluate how many users detect phishing emails and alert the SOC.

docs.title: Email Analysis
docs.text:
In most cases, I receive an email in msg format (from Microsoft Outlook). I convert it into eml format with:

msgconvert *.msg

Below you can see the headers and bodies of both emails. From a user perspective:

  • The emails are written in correct Italian.
  • There is no valid reason why a government department would write via standard email (in Italy we have a special email system called PEC).
  • Both emails are unsolicited.
  • Both emails have image trackers.
  • Both emails have attachments (ZIP files).

Because the emails are unsolicited and carry ZIP attachments, users should report them to the internal department for further analysis. To be honest, I would not blame users who click on them, because they are very well formatted.

The questions we need to answer are:

  • Are the emails malicious?
  • Why were the emails delivered to users instead of being filtered by the anti-spam?
  • Did anyone open and execute the attachments?
