docs.title: Filtering Cisco API Output
docs.text: 11 January 2026

docs.title: Filtering Cisco API Output
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci api cisco intermediate

Previously, we created a simple script that prints a table of the CDP neighbors of all the interfaces in the fabric. While writing it, we realized that it could be optimized.

To optimize the script, we need to change the way we retrieve the data.

The class used to get the fabric nodes is fabricNode. Let's open Visore and run a query with role == leaf:

In the address bar, we can see that parameters have been added to filter the query. To get the same effect with the APIs, we call this URL:

https://172.25.82.1/api/class/fabricNode.json?query-target-filter=and(eq(fabricNode.role,"leaf"))

We queried the objects of the fabricNode class, filtering the nodes where role == leaf.

We can build our filters with different functions. The most common are:

  • eq(attr, val) → equals.
  • ne(attr, val) → not equal.
  • like(attr, "pattern") → pattern matching.

These functions can be combined with:

  • and(...).
  • or(...).

Now we can improve our script that shows the CDP neighbors by querying just two classes: fabricNode and cdpAdjEp. We can then combine the two results as follows:

# Print output

for neighbor in neighbor_list:
    m = re.search(r"topology/pod-(\d+)/node-(\d+)/.*?/if-\[([^\]]+)\]", neighbor["dn"])
    pod_id, leaf_id, interface_id = m.groups()
    leaf_id = int(leaf_id)
    leaf_name = None
    for leaf in leaf_list:
        if leaf["id"] == leaf_id:
            leaf_name = leaf["name"]

    data.append([
        pod_id, # PodID
        leaf_id, # LeafID
        leaf_name, # LeafName
        interface_id, # Interface
        neighbor["devId"], # RemoteName
        neighbor["portId"], # RemoteInterface
    ])

print(tabulate(data, headers=headers))

The second version of the script is 13× faster.

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Pagination with Cisco ACI
docs.text: 18 January 2026

docs.title: Pagination with Cisco ACI
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci cisco intermediate

When we deal with a large number of records, we need pagination. By default, Cisco ACI pagination lets us retrieve up to 500 objects. A maximum value is not explicitly documented, but going beyond this limit is not recommended, to avoid overloading the APIC.

Pagination is controlled with the following parameters:

  • page-size: defines the size of each page.
  • page: defines which page to retrieve, starting from 0.

The response includes the totalCount attribute, which indicates the total number of objects available for the specific query.

To use pagination correctly, each page should be requested only when it is actually needed. We can do this with yield, which returns one object at a time and suspends the iteration until the next request.

def fetch_objects(class_name, page_size=10):
    page = 0
    while True:
        url = f"https://{apic_address}/api/class/{class_name}.json?page-size={page_size}&page={page}"
        res = session.get(url, verify=False)
        res.raise_for_status()
        items = res.json().get("imdata", [])
        if not items:
            # No more data
            break
        for item in items:
            # Return one object
            yield item
        # Next page
        page += 1

We can retrieve the list of interfaces with:

interface_list = fetch_objects("l1PhysIf")

No API call is made, however, until we actually start using interface_list. The API calls are performed progressively while we iterate over the list, so we spread them out and execute them only when necessary.

Keep in mind that interface_list can be used only once. If we want to reuse it several times, we must convert the generator into a list:

leaf_list = list(fetch_objects("fabricNode"))

We can now use what we built to write a simple script that prints all the interfaces:

# Get leaves

leaf_list = list(fetch_objects("fabricNode"))

# Get interfaces

interface_list = fetch_objects("l1PhysIf")

for interface in interface_list:
    interface_attrs = interface["l1PhysIf"]["attributes"]
    m = re.search(r"topology/pod-(\d+)/node-(\d+)/.*?/.*", interface_attrs["dn"])
    pod_id, leaf_id = m.groups()
    leaf_name = None
    for leaf in leaf_list:
        leaf_attribute = leaf["fabricNode"]["attributes"]
        if leaf_id == leaf_attribute["id"]:
            leaf_name = leaf_attribute["name"]
    data.append([
        pod_id, # PodID
        leaf_id, # LeafID
        leaf_name, # LeafName
        interface_attrs["id"], # Interface
        interface_attrs["adminSt"], # Admin
        interface_attrs["autoNeg"], # AutoNeg
        interface_attrs["descr"], # Description
    ])

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: From Single-Site to Multi-Site with NDO
docs.text: 24 September 2025

docs.title: From Single-Site to Multi-Site with NDO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cisco ndo

As infrastructures expand across different geographic locations and distances grow, moving from a single-site setup to a multi-site architecture becomes a natural step.

In an ideal world, each site of a multi-site deployment operates independently. In practice, applications often have specific requirements that call for stretched L2 networks between sites. Since this is driven by the applications themselves, my advice is to design self-sufficient and independent silos that keep running even if another site goes down.

When the real need is to connect applications across multiple sites in a native and consistent way, the tool of choice is Cisco Nexus Dashboard Orchestrator (NDO).

NDO is a powerful platform, but also a complex one with some limitations. Like any automation project, it requires the involvement of multiple roles and skill sets. Here we focus only on the aspects that matter most for our use case, without going too deep into the overall design and configuration architecture of NDO.

docs.title: Object Structure
docs.text:
NDO organizes its configuration using schemas and templates, which are then applied to tenants and sites:

  • Schemas: collections of templates that share a common use case.
  • Templates: define the objects that are deployed to one or more sites. These objects can include Application Profiles, EPGs, Contracts, VRFs, Bridge Domains, Filters, External EPGs and L3Outs. At the template level, we choose the sites where the objects are applied.
  • Tenants: logical containers for objects, mapped one-to-one to the tenants defined in the APIC.

docs.title: Key Considerations
docs.text:
There are a few important points to keep in mind when working with NDO:

  • NDO does not cover everything. We cannot configure the entire fabric exclusively through NDO: some operations still need to be performed directly on the APIC.
  • Avoid circular dependencies. Objects defined in different templates must not create circular relationships between each other (we dive deeper into this later).

docs.title: Circular Dependencies with NDO
docs.text: 01 October 2025

docs.title: Circular Dependencies with NDO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese cisco intermediate ndo

We have already highlighted how critical the design phase is in any automation project. This is even more true with NDO, because a design mistake can easily compromise the entire project.

When we design templates, we must plan the deployment order carefully, so that no circular dependency is created. NDO checks the dependencies at the template level, not at the level of the individual objects inside the templates. Let's look at an example:

In this example (courtesy of Mario Rosi), we have a single schema that contains six templates. Each template includes the objects listed below:

  • The first two templates are site-specific and contain objects that are meaningful only within their site. These objects do not need to communicate with objects in other sites.
  • The third template is shared across all the sites and includes objects that must communicate with those in other sites.
  • The remaining templates contain reusable objects that are also shared across all the sites.
  • The arrows in the diagram represent dependencies: they start from the dependent object and point to the object it relies on. For example, a Bridge Domain requires a VRF to be created first.

In this case, the deployment order of the templates is:

  1. Template #6: Contracts and Filters.
  2. Template #4: VRFs.
  3. Templates #1, #2, #3: objects specific to each site or shared across all the sites (no dependencies between them).
  4. Template #5: External EPGs.

A circular dependency occurs when an object in one template depends on an object in another template, and the reverse is also true. For instance, if we put both External EPGs and VRFs in the same template, that template would have to be deployed both before and after others, because:

  • External EPGs depend on L3Outs.
  • Bridge Domains depend on VRFs.

docs.title: Key Factors for Approaching Automation
docs.text:
From an automation perspective, there are several important consequences:

  • NDO has limitations, and using NaC (Network as Code) on NDO adds more. We must always validate how our specific use case is handled.
  • Some objects are configured through NDO while others are managed directly on the APIC, so it is essential to validate the final outcome.
  • With Cisco NaC, the deployment sequence of the templates should not exceed three steps.

In the example above, we need to reduce the deployment sequence from four steps to three. The template with Contracts and Filters and the template with VRFs are independent from each other, so they can either be merged or deployed simultaneously.

From the customer's perspective, there is often an additional requirement: stretching networks across multiple sites without service disruption. We must factor this expectation into both the design and the automation workflow.

docs.title: Frameworks for Projects with Cisco ACI and NDO
docs.text: 12 October 2025

docs.title: Frameworks for Projects with Cisco ACI and NDO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci beginner cisco ndo terraform

When we develop an automation system for Cisco ACI and NDO, we can choose among several frameworks:

  • APIs: maximum flexibility, but they require significant effort and strong programming skills.
  • APIC: API-first approach, with the documentation available directly through the Web UI.
  • NDO: APIs are available, but beware of potential breaking changes. The documentation is online (via OpenAPI/Swagger), along with a changelog of breaking changes.
  • Ansible: a simplified framework that does not require programming experience.
  • APIC: a fairly complete Ansible collection is available.
  • NDO: a fairly complete Ansible collection is also available.
  • Terraform: more complex and requiring prior expertise; best suited for greenfield environments.
  • APIC: a fairly complete Terraform provider is available.
  • NDO: a Terraform provider exists, but with several limitations.
  • NaC (Network as Code): a framework that abstracts the complexity of Terraform.
  • APIC: a specific module is available, with some limitations.
  • NDO: a specific module exists, but with more significant limitations.

For NDO specifically, I recommend using NaC whenever possible, because it greatly simplifies automation. Objects in NDO must be created and deleted in a specific sequence. Terraform (and therefore NaC) implements the correct sequence out of the box, which lets projects move much faster.

We dive deeper into NaC in a dedicated article.

And no, we are not even considering the Web UI: managing this level of complexity manually is simply not practical.

docs.title: Managing Limitations
docs.text:
Unless we work directly with the APIs on both APIC and NDO, we inevitably run into the limitations of the frameworks. And even then, we know that NDO has inherent restrictions compared to the APIC.

A practical example is IGMP Snooping. Some products implement multicast in a somewhat "loose" way, so I often need to disable IGMP Snooping.

If we manage Cisco ACI fabrics through NDO, we must always check how (and if) this can be done. Here are some examples:

From this, we can conclude:

  • We almost always need a hybrid approach, working on both NDO and APIC.
  • APIs provide maximum flexibility, but they are also the most complex and expensive to implement.
  • NaC covers most scenarios, but sometimes it must be complemented with a custom Terraform module.

Hundreds of customers use NaC heavily to manage entire ACI infrastructures. In theory, we could find something that Terraform supports and NaC does not, but the probability is very low. As an example, we configure a vPC Explicit Protection Group outside of NaC.

We should apply this mindset to every configuration in our environment. As we said before, planning is the most important phase of any automation project.

docs.title: Managing Cisco NDO Limitations from the APIC
docs.text: 26 October 2025

docs.title: Managing Cisco NDO Limitations from the APIC
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco ndo netascode

We have seen that NDO currently has some important limitations that we must keep in mind:

  • The NDO frameworks have limitations, particularly NaC.
  • NDO itself has limitations.
  • Certain configurations must necessarily be managed directly on the APIC.

This is far from a trivial consideration, and to understand it fully we need to analyze how NDO creates objects on the APIC.

docs.title: Objects Created by APIC vs. NDO
docs.text:
When I create an object manually on the APIC, the annotation field is empty. If I create it through Terraform or Ansible, the field is populated with the name of the framework used.

When NDO creates the object, we get:

annotation: orchestrator:msc-shadow:no
children -> fvSiteAssociated -> children -> fvRemoteId

See the files BD-MANUAL-ON-APIC.json and BD-94-FROM-NDO.json in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Modifying an Object Created by NDO
docs.text:
Let's look at a practical example: we need to add the IGMP Snooping policy, because NDO does not support it with NaC. The Bridge Domain has unicastRoute disabled.

We modify the Bridge Domain with Terraform/NaC. The final result shows the following differences:

annotation: orchestrator:terraform
unicastRoute: no -> yes

See the files BD-94-SHADOW-FROM-NDO.json and BD-94-FROM-NDO-MODIFIED.json in the GitHub repository.

If I redeploy from NDO, I get:

annotation: orchestrator:terraform -> orchestrator:msc-shadow:no
unicastRoute: yes -> no
children -> fvSiteAssociated -> name: -> msc-local

This happens even if I manually modify, on the APIC, an object that was originally created by NDO.

See the files BD-94-FROM-NDO-REDEPLOYED.json and BD-94-FROM-NDO-MODIFIED.json in the GitHub repository.

We can therefore conclude that, if we modify on the APIC an object created by NDO:

  • NDO then interprets it as locally managed (msc-local).
  • If we use a framework, the annotation field is overwritten.
  • If we use a framework, the parameters are reset to their defaults.

We must therefore remember to:

  • Use the ndo_managed parameter to preserve the annotation field.
  • When we use a framework, specify the same parameters used to create the object in NDO.

docs.title: Shadow Objects
docs.text:
When we use NDO, even if the templates are tied to different sites, NDO creates all the objects on all the APICs. This is why identical objects that belong to different templates must have different names.

Objects on an APIC that belong to a different fabric are marked as shadow objects, and this information is always stored in the annotation field:

annotation: orchestrator:msc-shadow:yes
annotation: orchestrator:msc-shadow:no

See the files BD-94-FROM-NDO.json and BD-94-SHADOW-FROM-NDO.json in the GitHub repository.

From the Web UI, we can make shadow objects visible by navigating to Manage my profile → Settings → Show Hidden Policies:

At this point, the shadow objects become visible:

docs.title: Stretching a Stretched Network
docs.text:
A critical point of the design phase is how to extend networks without causing service disruption.

We have seen that, during the design, we configure our networks (Bridge Domains) in a template, which can be either local to a site or shared across multiple sites. As a consequence, if we need to extend a network that was previously configured in a site-local template, we must move it to the appropriate shared template.

NDO provides a dedicated function for this:

Our Infrastructure as Code approach, however, does not rely on the Web UI.

It is also likely that the names of the objects depend on the associated template: changing the template means changing the name, and changing the name means deleting the object on the APIC and recreating it from scratch, with all its dependencies.

My approach is therefore to define networks as shared, unless we are certain that they will always remain strictly local. Of course, we must consider the architectural limits, to make sure we do not exceed the allowed number of objects per type.

docs.title: Safeguarding the Critical Tenant
docs.text:
Each ACI fabric includes an infrastructure tenant, which defines its basic functionality and connectivity. The production workload tenants are added on top of it.

In my view, we must consider managing the infrastructure tenant separately from the production tenants: both can be handled through Infrastructure as Code, but they have different characteristics and requirements.

The Infra tenant is prepared at the beginning and changes very rarely. An error on the Infra tenant can compromise the entire fabric.

The production tenants are modified constantly. An error affects only the specific tenant.

My approach is therefore to separate the two implementations, minimizing the changes and limiting access to the Infra tenant.

With NDO, dividing the management into multiple workspaces also improves the performance of the automation system (especially with Terraform and NaC).

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case modelling
docs.text: 02 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case modelling
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo terraform

This example covers the deployment of a multi-site fabric managed through NDO. The current setup, based on a legacy environment, must be migrated to a newly implemented multi-site environment. This is not a greenfield project, but we can treat it as one, because the entire configuration is generated from scratch.

The requirements of the automation project are to:

  • Distribute the production workload across all the sites.
  • Ensure fast deployment.
  • Provide simple tools for the operations team.

In the current infrastructure, most of the L3 routing is handled by firewalls. Some basic L3 routing scenarios inside the fabric may be implemented in the future.

Unfortunately, there is no single "correct" approach that guarantees results. Moreover, what works today may require changes tomorrow, because NDO, the Terraform NDO provider and NaC are constantly evolving.

In this case, I chose to:

  • Focus on the production tenant, managing the fabric setup and the inter-site communication manually.
  • Prefer the tools in this order: NaC, Terraform, Python.
  • Store the automation code and the data structures in Git.
  • Manage the configuration on NDO, and configure only the unsupported features directly on the APIC.
  • Use NaC data structures for objects that rarely require modification.
  • Use a simple CSV-based structure for operations that require frequent updates (networks, L3Outs).
  • Create a parser that converts the CSV files into NaC and Terraform data structures.

docs.title: NDO
docs.text:
NDO manages all the logical configuration, i.e., everything related to templates, with a few exceptions described later. The physical configuration, instead, is managed directly on the APIC, for two reasons:

  • There is currently no complete NaC or Terraform module to manage the physical layer.
  • The Terraform provider for NDO has poor performance, so it is more efficient to perform non-critical tasks directly on the APIC.

NDO therefore contains:

  • The production tenant, applied across all the sites.
  • A schema.

The schema contains six tenant templates:

  • One template per site, containing BDs, subnets, Application Profiles and EPGs (deploy order 2).
  • One shared template for all the sites, containing BDs, Application Profiles and EPGs (deploy order 2).
  • One shared template for all the sites, containing VRFs (deploy order 1).
  • One shared template for all the sites, containing Contracts (deploy order 1).
  • One shared template for all the sites, containing External EPGs (deploy order 3).

Operational activity is typically limited to the templates that contain BDs, Application Profiles and EPGs. The others remain mostly static.

The Terraform provider for NDO does not support tenant-level policies (e.g., IGMP snooping policies). If such policies are required, we must configure them directly on the APIC.

docs.title: APIC
docs.text:
All the configuration not managed by NDO, in particular the physical configuration, is managed directly on the APIC. Specifically, the APIC manages:

  • Access policies (AAEPs, interface policies, leaf interface policy groups, physical domains, VLAN pools).
  • Physical topology (interfaces, vPCs).
  • Physical association with EPGs.

Each site also has its own dedicated Terraform environment, which ensures visibility into the changes and their impact on the infrastructure.

docs.title: NaC and Terraform
docs.text:
In this project, NaC manages nearly the entire configuration. The only exception is the vPC explicit protection groups, which are handled via Terraform.

Terraform may look complex at first, but it offers significant advantages with Cisco ACI: objects are created and deleted safely and automatically.

docs.title: Modelling
docs.text:
The infrastructure is built at multiple levels: NDO, APIC, NaC and Terraform. In practice, this requires building a relatively complex data structure that includes some duplicated information.

For example, when we create an EPG, we must associate it with both a BD and the relevant physical interfaces. On NDO, we define BDs, Application Profiles and EPGs; on the APIC, we associate the EPG with the physical interfaces.

Validating the data structure to prevent human errors can be challenging.

The modelling must never be influenced by the technical solution: it must be defined according to the architecture and the operational requirements.

In this case, I chose to work with:

  • CSV files containing networks and interfaces.
  • YAML files for NaC containing static, non-duplicated information.

I developed a parser that:

  • Validates the CSV data structure.
  • Performs integrity checks (e.g., the use of a VLAN depends on the definition of its associated network).
  • Generates the NaC and Terraform structures for NDO and APIC safely.

Adding or removing objects only requires editing the CSV files, which are designed to be human-readable. Terraform handles the rest safely.

docs.title: Parser
docs.text:
The core of the automation is a custom parser that converts CSV-based data structures into NaC and Terraform formats.

The parser provides a user interface that transforms the input files (CSV) into the structures required by NaC and Terraform.

It also validates and normalizes the CSV input, performing multiple integrity checks.

The parser can be integrated easily into a CI/CD pipeline: the user only needs to update a CSV file. After the commit, the deployment of the configuration is managed automatically during a maintenance window.

This approach also lets us modify the parser safely: if the generated data structure remains unchanged, no errors were introduced. Similarly, the CSV structure can evolve, for example by integrating with an IPAM.

docs.title: CSV
docs.text:
In this scenario, the input data is managed with two main CSV files.

Network CSV:

IT teams are typically used to thinking of networks in terms of VLANs. VLAN tags are also critical when connecting ACI with environments that do not natively support VXLAN. Moreover, all objects must have unique names, to avoid overlaps with the shadow objects created on other sites.

Each network can include a subnet and may be L2 stretched. If the VRF is not defined, a default one is used. The name of the Application Profile is derived from the site and the VRF name, because this migration project follows a network-centric model from legacy to ACI.

This CSV file generates:

  • VRFs (e.g., replica_VRF or default_VRF).
  • Application Profiles (e.g., MI-storage_replica_App or MI-default_App).
  • Bridge Domains (e.g., MI-0011-INFRA-DMZ_BD).
  • EPGs (e.g., MI-0011-INFRA-DMZ_EPG).

The objects (VRF, Application Profile, Bridge Domain, Subnets, Endpoint Groups) are created on NDO. They are deployed on the shared template if SITE=SHARED, or on the site-specific template otherwise.

With this model, we immediately identify a critical issue: if a site-local network (not L2 stretched) later needs to become L2 stretched, we must set SITE=SHARED. In practice, this destroys and recreates the object with a new name and requires all the associated interfaces to be bound again, which has a significant impact on the infrastructure.

The client requirement, however, is to make a network L2 stretched without disruption. To achieve this, only objects that will never need to be stretched should be defined as site-local. All the others, which may potentially be stretched, should be defined with SITE=SHARED.

Interface CSV:

Each interface group specifies the site, the corresponding leaf, the policy group, the configured interfaces, the tagged VLANs and the native VLAN.

We must define a unique GROUP_NAME: it is used to build the related objects and cannot be changed later. PORT_DESCRIPTION can be modified freely and defaults to the same value as GROUP_NAME.

For individual interfaces, POLICY_GROUP references one of the predefined policy groups, created via a dedicated NaC file.

This CSV file generates:

  • Selectors (e.g., MI-SERVER-1A_Sel) associated with the leaf interface profiles (e.g., TrustedPort_PolGrp).
  • Port blocks (e.g., Block3) associated with the selectors and their descriptions (e.g., to Server 1).

For vPC interfaces, POLICY_GROUP references a policy template used when the vPC policy group is created.

For vPCs, this CSV file generates:

  • vPC-type policy groups (e.g., MI-BLADE-1_PolGrp).
  • Selectors (e.g., MI-BLADE-1_Sel) associated with the policy groups and the leaf interface profiles.
  • Port blocks (e.g., Block1) linked to the selectors, with descriptions (e.g., vPC to Blade Servers Chassis 1).

Finally, the file creates the static EPG-to-port/vPC associations for each VLAN.

The CSV files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case additional configuration
docs.text: 09 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case additional configuration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo netascode

In the previous article, we built the data structure that defines our infrastructure and most of its operational logic. Some elements, however, require a different approach.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
I usually work with two main files to store the required variables: config.yaml and secrets.yaml.

The config.yaml file includes:

  • The access references for APIC and NDO:
apics:
  mi:
    name: MI-FABRIC
    url: https://192.168.1.1
    url_insecure: true
  rm:
    name: RM-FABRIC
    url: https://192.168.2.1
    url_insecure: true
ndo:
  url: https://192.168.0.1
  url_insecure: true
  • The names and the deployment order of the templates:
ndo:
  templates:
    contracts:
      name: Template-Contracts
      deploy_order: 1
    stretched_extepg:
      name: Template-Stretched-ExtEPG
      deploy_order: 3
    stretched_vrf:
      name: Template-Stretched-VRF
      deploy_order: 1
    site_mi:
      name: Template-MI
      deploy_order: 2
    site_rm:
      name: Template-RM
      deploy_order: 2
  • The parameters of the optional filters:
ndo:
  templates:
    site_stretched:
      filters:
        - name: ANY_Filter
          entries:
            - name: Any
              ethertype: unspecified
  • The name of the physical domain.

The secrets.yaml file, instead, stores the credentials required to access NDO and APIC:

ndo:
  username: admin
  password: "password"
mi:
  username: admin
  password: "password"
rm:
  username: admin
  password: "password"

Both files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: NaC Static Files
docs.text:
Some NaC-related configurations are rarely modified. Before changing them, it is essential to evaluate their potential impact on the fabric, because they are the foundational building blocks of the entire infrastructure.

My approach is to use the NaC data structure for the components that are defined statically, do not interact with other systems (e.g., NDO, APIC) and seldom require modification. These configurations are defined in the file custom-apic-fabric.nac.yaml.

In particular, I chose to define statically the fabric access policies for:

  • AAEPs:
apic:
  access_policies:
    aaeps:
      - name: Phy_AAEP
        routed_domains:
          - PhyL3Out_RoutedDomain
        physical_domains:
          - Phy_Domain
  • Interface policies (e.g., CDP, LLDP, port channel):
apic:
  access_policies:
    interface_policies:
      cdp_policies:
        - name: ENABLE_CDP_IntPol
          admin_state: true
        - name: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
          admin_state: true
      lldp_policies:
        - name: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
          admin_rx_state: true
          admin_tx_state: true
        - name: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
          admin_rx_state: false
          admin_tx_state: false
      port_channel_policies:
        - name: ENABLE_LACP_PO_IntPol
          mode: active
          suspend_individual: true
          graceful_convergence: true
        - name: ENABLE_STATIC_PO_IntPol
          mode: off
          suspend_individual: true
          graceful_convergence: true
  • Leaf interface policy groups (e.g., TrustedPort_PolGrp, UntrustedPort_PolGrp):
apic:
  access_policies:
    leaf_interface_policy_groups:
      - name: TrustedPort_PolGrp
        type: access
        cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
        lldp_policy: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
        aaep: Phy_AAEP
      - name: UntrustedPort_PolGrp
        type: access
        cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
        lldp_policy: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
        aaep: Phy_AAEP
  • Physical and routed domains:
apic:
  access_policies:
    vlan_pools:
      - name: Phy_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 1
            to: 1001
            role: external
          - from: 1006
            to: 3499
            role: external
      - name: PhyL3Out_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 3500
            to: 3999
            role: external
  • VLAN pools:
apic:
  access_policies:
    vlan_pools:
      - name: Phy_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 1
            to: 1001
            role: external
          - from: 1006
            to: 3499
            role: external
      - name: PhyL3Out_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 3500
            to: 3999
            role: external

These files are also available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Single Ports and vPC Profiles
docs.text:
We have seen that, when we define a static port, we can associate a policy group that acts as a template:

In our CSV file, port 3 of leaf 101 is associated with the TrustedPort policy group. The port is therefore configured with LLDP enabled and CDP disabled. As mentioned, the TrustedPort policy group is defined statically in custom-apic-fabric.nac.yaml.

When we configure a vPC, however, we cannot use the same approach, because each vPC requires a unique policy group: an abstraction layer is missing.

During the modelling phase, we decided to configure vPCs with a template-based approach, similar to the one we use for single interfaces.

The templates are defined in config.yaml:

fabric:
  port_channel_policies:
    TrustedLACPVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: ENABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_LACP_PO_IntPol
    TrustedStaticVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: ENABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_STATIC_PO_IntPol
    UntrustedLACPVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_LACP_PO_IntPol
    UntrustedStaticVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_STATIC_PO_IntPol

Each template contains the configuration applied when the policy group associated with each vPC is created.

For example, if a vPC is defined as TrustedLACPVPC in the fabric-interfaces.csv file, the automation creates a policy group by copying the configuration of the corresponding template.

This lets us manage both single interfaces and vPCs with a unified, centralized approach to defining configuration profiles.

The files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case data validation
docs.text: 16 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case data validation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo netascode

As we have seen, the CSV files are used to generate the NaC configuration. We need validation tests, however, to ensure correctness.

Let's start with the CSV file that defines the networks:

  • VLAN_ID must contain an integer within a defined VLAN pool.
  • VLAN_NAME must contain an alphanumeric string without spaces (hyphens and underscores are allowed). Uppercase or lowercase can be enforced if needed.
  • SITE must contain one of the following values: RM, MI or SHARED. This field defines the name of the object and the associated tenant template in NDO.

The fields VLAN_ID, VLAN_NAME and SITE together define the name of the object, e.g., MI-0011-INFRA-DMZ.

  • L2_STRETCHED specifies whether the network is stretched between MI and RM. Only networks in the SHARED template can be L2 stretched.
  • ANYCAST_ADDRESS defines the subnet associated with the Bridge Domain. If a network has an Anycast address and is associated with the SHARED template, it must be L2 stretched.
  • VRF defines the name of the associated VRF. If empty, a default VRF is created.
  • ADVERTISED specifies whether the subnet is advertised via dynamic routing protocols.

An additional check, not implemented yet, could verify whether a VLAN is already in use in the fabric-interfaces.csv file.

Now let's move on to the CSV file that defines the interfaces:

  • SITE must contain RM or MI.
  • LEAF_ID contains the ID of a single leaf or of a pair of leaves. Each ID must be present in fabric-leaves.csv.
  • POLICY_GROUP contains the associated policy group. If LEAF_ID is a single value, the policy group must exist in custom-apic-fabric.nac.yaml. If it is a pair, it must exist in config.yaml.
  • INTERFACES lists the interfaces to configure, separated by commas. Each interface can be used only once per leaf.
  • TAGGED_VLANS can include a VLAN range; each VLAN must exist in l2-networks.csv.
  • NATIVE_VLAN can include a VLAN defined in l2-networks.csv.
  • GROUP_NAME defines the names of the objects on the APIC (selectors, policy groups): these values must remain unchanged.
  • PORT_DESCRIPTION defines the description of the interface. If empty, the value of GROUP_NAME is used.

The CSV files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case building the parser
docs.text: 23 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case building the parser
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo netascode

The parser is a custom script that converts the user input (CSV files) into NaC configuration. It also performs the data validation described in the previous post. If it succeeds, the parser generates the NaC files in the nac-data directory, which Terraform then consumes to configure NDO and APIC.

The parser consists of two main files:

  • infra.py: reads the CSV files, validates the data and builds the NaC data structure.
  • build-nac-data.py: uses infra.py to generate the Terraform files, organized by environment (NDO, APIC) and site (MI, RM, SHARED).

It is nearly impossible to describe both Python files in full detail here, so we give a high-level overview.

docs.title: infra.py
docs.text:
The infra.py file defines the object classes for APIC, VRF, Leaf, Network and InterfaceGroup. The objects are defined with Pydantic, which provides data normalization and first-level validation.

The VRF class:

class VRF(BaseModel):
    name: str

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

    @field_validator("name", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def parse_name(cls, raw=str | None):
        if raw:
            return raw.strip()
        return "default"

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def validate_rules(self):
        if not self.name.replace("_", "").replace("-", "").isalnum():
            raise ValueError(f"With VRF {self.name}, name is not valid")

        return self

The class defines a name attribute (string type). A before validator assigns name=default if the field is empty, while an after validator ensures that the name is alphanumeric (allowing - and _).

The Infra class loads all the files that define the infrastructure (l2-networks.csv, fabric-interfaces.csv, fabric-leaves.csv, config.yaml, secrets.yaml) and builds a complete data structure:

class Infra:
    def __init__(self):
        # Reading config file
        with open(self._config_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)

        # Reading secret file
        with open(self._secrets_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.secrets = yaml.safe_load(f)

        # Read APIC customization
        with open(self._apic_customization_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.apic_customization = yaml.safe_load(f)

        # Reading input data
        self.__load_apics__()
        self.__load_l2_networks__()
        self.__load_fabric_leaves__()
        self.__load_fabric_interfaces__()

Each __load function performs global validation. For example, __load_l2_networks__ makes sure that VLANs are unique and belong to a defined VLAN pool.

Getter functions let us read the data structure and apply optional filters. For example, we can retrieve the interface groups based on site, leaf ID and interface:

# ***************************************************************************
# Getters: Interface
# ***************************************************************************

def get_interface_group_by_interface_leaf_site(
    self, leaf: Leaf, site: Site, iface: int
) -> InterfaceGroup | None:
    for item in self.interface_groups:
        if (
            item.leaf.name == leaf.name
            and item.site.name == site.name
            and iface in item.ifaces
        ):
            return item
    return None

This helps us determine whether an interface is already in use.

The NaC getters generate the NaC-formatted data structures:

# ***************************************************************************
# NaC getters: Fabric
# ***************************************************************************

def get_fabric_access_leaf_interface_vpc_policy_groups(
    self, site: Site, apic: bool = False
) -> List[dict]:
    """Return Fabric -> Access Policies -> Interfaces -> Leaf Interfaces -> Policy Groups."""
    if not apic:
        raise ValueError(
            "With get_fabric_access_leaf_interface_vpc_policy_groups, apic=False is not supported"
        )

    policy_groups_data = []
    for interface_group in self.get_interfaces_group_by_site(site=site):
        # Building vPC policy groups
        if "-" not in interface_group.leaf.name:
            # Skip non vPC
            continue

        policy_group_data = dict(
            self.config["fabric"]["port_channel_policies"][interface_group.profile]
        )
        policy_group_data["name"] = f"{interface_group.selector}_PolGrp"
        policy_groups_data.append(policy_group_data)

    return policy_groups_data

For example, build-nac-data.py uses get_fabric_access_leaf_interface_vpc_policy_groups to create the file nac-data/apic-fabric-mi.nac.yaml.

The NaC getters are particularly important when the data requires customization or is shared between NDO and APIC.

For instance, the subnets defined at the Bridge Domain level are managed in NDO. If a subnet is site-specific, however, it must be configured at the site level, not at the template level:

# NDO specific attributes
if site.name == "SHARED":
    bridge_domain["subnets"] = subnets
else:
    bridge_domain["sites"] = [
        {
            "name": self.get_apic_name_by_site(Site(site.name)),
            "subnets": subnets,
        }
    ]

Another example involves EPGs: they are configured in NDO, but their interface associations are applied at the APIC level. Since Terraform executed on the APIC overrides the configuration managed by NDO, the get_tenant_application_profiles function sets the ndo_managed flag, which keeps the object definitions consistent across both domains.

docs.title: build-nac-data.py
docs.text:
The build-nac-data.py script uses infra.py to process the input data and generate the Terraform configuration files.

Files created for NDO:

  • ndo.nac.yaml: defines sites, schema and templates.
  • ndo-*.nac.yaml: defines Bridge Domains, Subnets, Application Profiles and EPGs per site.

Files created for APIC:

  • apic-fabric-*.nac.yaml: defines the access policies (Leaf Interface Policy Groups, Leaf Interface Profiles and Leaf Switch Profiles) per site, mapping physical interfaces to policy groups.
  • apic-*.terraform.yaml: defines the switch access policies per site.
  • apic-tenant-*.nac.yaml: redefines Application Profiles and EPGs per site, mapping interfaces and VLANs to each EPG.

Terraform files generated from Jinja2 templates:

  • site-*/main.tf: defines the parameters for the NaC integration.
  • site-*/versions.tf: defines the module versions.
  • site-*/terraform.tfvars: includes the credentials to access NDO and APIC.
  • site-*/providers.tf: defines the Terraform provider.
  • site-*/variables.tf: defines the variables referenced in terraform.tfvars.
  • site-*/custom.tf: includes the Terraform module that configures the resources not supported by NaC.

The parser files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case config deploy
docs.text: 30 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case config deploy
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci beginner cisco ndo

At this stage, we can build the configuration:

./build-nac-data.py

If everything runs successfully, the script completes silently ("no news is good news") and creates or updates the files under the nac-data and site-* directories.

We can now apply the configuration to NDO with Terraform:

cd site-shared
terraform apply -parallelism=1

Then we proceed with the APIC configurations:

cd site-mi
terraform apply
cd ../site-rm
terraform apply

During testing, this workflow has consistently worked, except in one specific case: when we rename or reuse an object (e.g., when we reassign an interface).

In such cases, it is best to delete the old entry from the CSV, run Terraform to remove the previous object and then recreate it. Otherwise, resource conflicts may occur if the same object is recreated before the previous one has been fully deleted.

For example, creating approximately 600 networks on NDO (Bridge Domains, Application Profiles and EPGs, for a total of about 1,100 objects) took roughly 35 minutes.
