docs.title: Managing a brownfield Cisco ACI fabric with NaC and Terraform
Managing a brownfield Cisco ACI fabric with NaC and Terraform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco iac netascode terraform

After using NaC in recent projects, I started wondering whether it would be possible to manage an existing (brownfield) infrastructure with NaC. Within the NaC suite, this capability is provided directly by Cisco.

In theory, it is possible to import the objects of an existing infrastructure into the Terraform state file. Likewise, it should be possible to analyze a Cisco ACI fabric and describe (model) it with the language provided by NaC.

If everything works as expected, we can operate safely on a brownfield infrastructure with NaC and Terraform. Let's walk through the process step by step.

This is an educational post: nobody should run this process in a production environment, because it is highly likely to cause a service disruption.

docs.title: Analysis of a Cisco ACI Fabric
docs.text:
The first step is relatively straightforward: we read from a Cisco ACI infrastructure the objects that NaC models. In this example, we limit the scope to Tenants, VRFs and Bridge Domains (BDs).

The most direct approach is to use the APIs, which we have already discussed. This time I chose Cobra, the Python SDK that can be downloaded from any APIC at https://172.25.82.1/cobra/_downloads/.

Once we have downloaded the *.whl files, we can install them with:

pip install *.whl

Cobra is a powerful tool, but its documentation is very limited. Understanding how to use the SDK properly can therefore be challenging, and more than once I had to inspect the source code of the library to find out how to use it correctly.

Let's start by retrieving all the tenants:

# Get Tenants
fvTenant_objs = moDir.lookupByClass("fvTenant")
for tenant in fvTenant_objs:
    if tenant.name in IGNORED_TENANTS:
        # Ignore tenant
        continue
    nac_tenant_data = {}
    nac_tenant_data["name"] = tenant.name
    if tenant.descr:
        nac_tenant_data["description"] = tenant.descr

For each tenant, we must retrieve the associated VRFs:

    # Get VRFs
    fvCtx_objs = moDir.lookupByClass('fvCtx', parentDn=tenant.dn)
    if fvCtx_objs:
        nac_tenant_data["vrfs"] = []
    for vrf in fvCtx_objs:
        nac_vrf_data = {}
        nac_vrf_data["name"] = vrf.name
        nac_vrf_data["enforcement_preference"] = vrf.pcEnfPref
        if vrf.descr:
            nac_vrf_data["description"] = vrf.descr
        nac_tenant_data["vrfs"].append(nac_vrf_data)

And finally, the Bridge Domains:

    # Get BrideDomains
    fvBD_objs = moDir.lookupByClass('fvBD', parentDn=tenant.dn, subtree="children")
    if fvBD_objs:
        nac_tenant_data["bridge_domains"] = []
    for bd in fvBD_objs:
        nac_bd_data = {}
        nac_bd_data["name"] = bd.name
        nac_bd_data["multicast_arp_drop"] = parse_boolean(bd.mcastARPDrop)
        nac_bd_data["ip_dataplane_learning"] = parse_boolean(bd.ipLearning)
        nac_bd_data["unknown_unicast"] = bd.unkMacUcastAct
        if bd.descr:
            nac_bd_data["description"] = bd.descr
        nac_tenant_data["bridge_domains"].append(nac_bd_data)

        # Find VRF
        for child in bd.children:
            if child.meta.moClassName == "fvRsCtx":
                vrf = moDir.lookupByDn(child.tDn)
                nac_bd_data["vrf"] = vrf.name
                break

As the code shows, while we retrieve the objects we progressively build the NaC-formatted data structure that describes Tenants, VRFs and BDs.

Since NaC lets us organize the information freely, we generate one file per tenant:

    # Dump data
    with open(f"data/tenant-{tenant.name}.nac.yaml", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        nac_data = {"apic": {"tenants": [nac_tenant_data]}}
        yaml.dump(nac_data, fh, default_flow_style=False, sort_keys=False, allow_unicode=True)

The result is a set of NaC files that describe our infrastructure:

apic:
  tenants:
  - name: NTS_TRAINING
    vrfs:
    - name: PROD
      enforcement_preference: unenforced
    bridge_domains:
    - name: FW_OUTSIDE
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: false
      unknown_unicast: flood
      vrf: PROD
    - name: APP
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: true
      unknown_unicast: flood
      vrf: PROD
    - name: WEB
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: true
      unknown_unicast: proxy
      vrf: PROD
    - name: DMZ
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: true
      unknown_unicast: flood
      vrf: PROD

This is the simplest part. The next step is to import the objects from Cisco ACI into Terraform using the NaC data model.

The script used in this example is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Importing NaC objects from Cisco ACI into Terraform
Importing NaC objects from Cisco ACI into Terraform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci beginner cisco iac netascode terraform

In the previous post, we analyzed a Cisco ACI infrastructure and described it with the NaC data model. This is a simplification: NaC is a very comprehensive framework, but it does not support 100% of the configuration options available in Cisco ACI.

This is an educational post: nobody should run this process in a production environment, because it is highly likely to cause a service disruption.

Terraform can only manage the objects it knows about. We now need to create the Terraform representation of the objects (Tenants, VRFs, BDs) using the NaC data model.

Let's clarify this further.

If I try to import the tenant NTS_TRAINING, I get the following error:

$ terraform import aci_tenant.nts_training uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING
Error: resource address "aci_tenant.nts_training" does not exist in the configuration.

Before importing this resource, please create its configuration in the root module. For example:

resource "aci_tenant" "nts_training" {
  # (resource arguments)
}

The error states that Terraform cannot find any reference to aci_tenant.nts_training. This happens because no .tf file defines that object. This is expected: one of the key advantages of NaC is that it abstracts away the complexity of Terraform.

We must therefore import the tenant NTS_TRAINING following the naming convention used by NaC. We can obtain this information from the Terraform plan.

For example, the plan to create the tenant NTS_TRAINING shows:

# module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant will be created
+ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvTenant" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    + class_name  = "fvTenant"
    + content     = {
        + "descr"     = null
        + "name"      = "NTS_TRAINING"
        + "nameAlias" = null
      }
    + dn          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING"
    + escape_html = true
    + id          = (known after apply)
  }

The name of the module is composed, among other elements, of the tenant name and the class:

module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant

The correct import command is therefore:

$ terraform import 'module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant' uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING
module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant: Importing from ID "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING"...
module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant: Import prepared!
  Prepared aci_rest_managed for import
module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant: Refreshing state... [id=uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING]

Import successful!

The resources that were imported are shown above. These resources are now in
your Terraform state and will henceforth be managed by Terraform.

We can verify the result by running terraform plan again: the tenant object exists, but some attributes require modification:

# module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvTenant" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "ownerKey" = null
        - "ownerTag" = null
        - "userdom"  = "all" -> null
        # (3 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

This is the most critical point of the entire approach: we must make sure that the attribute values configured in Cisco ACI (and detected by Terraform) exactly match those defined through NaC for all the relevant parameters:

# module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "OptimizeWanBandwidth"     = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteBumTrafficAllow" = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteL2Stretch"       = "no" -> null
        - "ipv6McastAllow"           = "no" -> null
        - "llAddr"                   = "::" -> null
        - "ownerKey"                 = null
        - "ownerTag"                 = null
        - "userdom"                  = "all" -> null
        # (19 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

To complete the process, we must apply the Terraform plan. This may lead to unpredictable situations if we do not fully understand the purpose of each attribute and value.

We must now import the VRFs, the BDs and all the derived objects.

In general, the Terraform plan tells us how many objects must be created. The data structure is already defined in the NaC files, so we only need to run the correct import commands.

For reference, these are the commands to import Tenants, VRFs, BDs and related objects:

terraform import module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsBgpCtxPol uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsbgpCtxPol
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtxToExtRouteTagPol uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsctxToExtRouteTagPol
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsOspfCtxPol uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsospfCtxPol
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.vzAny uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/any
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/FW_OUTSIDE"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-FW_OUTSIDE
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/FW_OUTSIDE"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-FW_OUTSIDE/rsctx
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/APP"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-APP
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/APP"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-APP/rsctx
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB/rsctx
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/DMZ"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-DMZ
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/DMZ"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-DMZ/rsctx

When the process is complete, a new Terraform plan should show that some objects would be modified, but none should be created or destroyed.

The script used in this example is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Reconciling attribute drift Between NaC and Terraform
Reconciling attribute drift Between NaC and Terraform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco iac netascode terraform

In the previous post, we saw how to import an infrastructure defined through NaC into Terraform. We stopped when terraform plan reported differences in some attribute values:

# module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "OptimizeWanBandwidth"     = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteBumTrafficAllow" = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteL2Stretch"       = "no" -> null
        - "ipv6McastAllow"           = "no" -> null
        - "llAddr"                   = "::" -> null
        - "ownerKey"                 = null
        - "ownerTag"                 = null
        - "userdom"                  = "all" -> null
        # (19 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

I identified three possible scenarios:

  • The attribute is cosmetic or not relevant (e.g., annotation).
  • The attribute is not handled by our import script (ACI to NaC).
  • The attribute is not managed by NaC.

Let's examine the three cases in detail.

This is an educational post: nobody should run this process in a production environment, because it is highly likely to cause a service disruption.

docs.title: Cosmetic or Non-Relevant Attributes
docs.text:
Some attributes are purely cosmetic and have no real impact on the operation of a Cisco ACI fabric.

For example, annotation may contain a reference to who created and manages the object. By default, Ansible and Terraform set this parameter, and so does NDO. If NDO is used in the infrastructure, this parameter must be set correctly.

# module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtxToExtRouteTagPol will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvRsCtxToExtRouteTagPol" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "userdom" = "all" -> null
        # (1 unchanged element hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsctxToExtRouteTagPol"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

The escape_html attribute is internal to Terraform and not relevant. Other parameters (such as userdom) may affect the visibility of the object to other Cisco ACI users or groups.

docs.title: Attributes Not Imported
docs.text:
We need much more attention when an attribute is supported by NaC but was not imported from the fabric:

# module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/APP"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "OptimizeWanBandwidth"     = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteBumTrafficAllow" = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteL2Stretch"       = "no" -> null
        - "ipv6McastAllow"           = "no" -> null
        - "llAddr"                   = "::" -> null
        ~ "mcastARPDrop"             = "no" -> null
        - "ownerKey"                 = null
        - "ownerTag"                 = null
        - "userdom"                  = "all" -> null
        # (18 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-APP"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

In this case, we see the mcastARPDrop attribute of a BD. If we inspect the module source code, we can confirm that the attribute is supported:

resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
  dn         = "uni/tn-${var.tenant}/BD-${var.name}"
  class_name = "fvBD"
  annotation = var.annotation
  content = {
    name                  = var.name
    nameAlias             = var.alias
    descr                 = var.description
    arpFlood              = var.arp_flooding == true ? "yes" : "no"
    hostBasedRouting      = var.advertise_host_routes == true ? "yes" : "no"
    ipLearning            = var.ip_dataplane_learning == true ? "yes" : "no"
    limitIpLearnToSubnets = var.limit_ip_learn_to_subnets == true ? "yes" : "no"
    mac                   = var.mac
    epMoveDetectMode      = var.ep_move_detection == true ? "garp" : ""
    vmac                  = var.virtual_mac
    mcastAllow            = var.l3_multicast == true ? "yes" : "no"
    multiDstPktAct        = var.multi_destination_flooding
    type                  = "regular"
    unicastRoute          = var.unicast_routing == true ? "yes" : "no"
    unkMacUcastAct        = var.unknown_unicast
    unkMcastAct           = var.unknown_ipv4_multicast
    v6unkMcastAct         = var.unknown_ipv6_multicast
    epClear               = var.clear_remote_mac_entries == true ? "yes" : "no"
    mcastARPDrop          = var.multicast_arp_drop != null ? (var.multicast_arp_drop == true ? "yes" : "no") : null
  }
}

We must therefore read the mcastARPDrop attribute from the fabric and set the multicast_arp_drop variable in the NaC data file.

The source code of the module effectively shows all the attributes that we must read for each fabric object.

docs.title: Attributes Not Managed by NaC
docs.text:
The final case involves attributes that are available in Cisco ACI but not managed by NaC. NaC is a very comprehensive framework, but many attributes are not covered. We must determine whether they are not relevant (and therefore fall into the first case), whether they have no operational impact (for example, a changed default value) or whether they are critical.

# module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvCtx will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvCtx" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "bdEnforcedEnable" = "no" -> null
        - "knwMcastAct"      = "permit" -> null
        - "ownerKey"         = null
        - "ownerTag"         = null
        - "userdom"          = "all" -> null
        - "vrfIndex"         = "0" -> null
        # (6 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

In the example, the PROD VRF includes three attributes that certainly require attention: bdEnforcedEnable, knwMcastAct and vrfIndex.

By downloading and inspecting the source code of the module, we can quickly verify whether these attributes are supported. With fgrep or egrep, we find that these three attributes are not managed.

There are therefore two possibilities:

  • The change of value is not relevant, because it does not affect the operation of the fabric.
  • The change of value affects the fabric, and we must extend the Terraform module to support it.

At this point, the value of professional services in importing a Cisco ACI fabric into NaC becomes clear.

The script used in this example is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating configuration compliance verification for Cisco Switches
docs.text: 22 January 2025

docs.title: Automating configuration compliance verification for Cisco Switches
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced catalyst-center cisco compliance

This article stems from a colleague's request to automate the configuration compliance checks of hundreds of switches spread across the globe.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Ensuring configuration compliance is essential for:

  • Verifying that the devices meet the expected configurations.
  • Detecting unauthorized changes (out-of-process modifications).
  • Measuring the compliance level.

In this guide, we outline an integration that uses templates to check the configuration of the devices and generates reports with:

  • A list of the reviewed ports, showing their compliance status.
  • A summary of the number of compliant and non-compliant ports per device.

We focus on readability rather than on advanced code optimization.

docs.title: Using Catalyst Center
docs.text:
Our scenario assumes that all the devices are managed via Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly Cisco DNA Center). If you do not have a local instance, you can use the sandbox environment available at sandboxdnac2.cisco.com with these credentials:

  • User: devnetuser.
  • Password: Cisco123!.

If we navigate to Provision → Inventory, we get a list of the managed devices:

Clicking on a device opens a small popup that gives access to its detail page:

By going to Interfaces → Ethernet Ports → GigabitEthernet1/0/4, we can view the details of the interface:

The window displays some information, but it is rather limited.

Next, let's navigate to Configuration to check the configuration of the interface:

From this, we can draw some initial conclusions:

  • Catalyst Center contains the configurations (running-config) of all our devices.
  • Catalyst Center provides high-level information about the configuration of the interfaces, but the details (e.g., STP, Port Security, QoS) are accessible only by examining the running-config.

This situation arises because we still rely heavily on the CLI to manage switches. These devices are CLI-first: orchestrators like Catalyst Center tend to provide a limited view and leave the CLI as the primary tool to access detailed information.

With this in mind, we can refine our approach: we read the running-config of each switch and verify that each interface is configured correctly.

We could use show commands, but I advise against it because:

  • There is no guarantee that show commands exist to display clearly whether a specific configuration is present.
  • Our goal is to verify the configuration, not the operational state of the interfaces.
  • By working with the running-config, we can verify all the interface configurations with a single, unified method.

docs.title: Choosing an Approach: SSH, APIs or SDK
docs.text:
When we work via CLI, we have several options:

  • Connect to each device using SSH.
  • Retrieve the running-config via the Catalyst Center APIs.
  • Retrieve the running-config via the Catalyst Center SDK.

SSH requires downloading the running-config and storing it locally. We can do this, for example, with Netmiko or Ansible. We have already covered this approach in previous articles, so we do not discuss it here. If you choose this path, make sure you obtain the running-config of all the devices locally.

The Catalyst Center APIs are well documented. There is also a Python SDK, though its documentation is somewhat sparse.

When an SDK is available, I prefer to try it first and see whether it suits my needs. The advantage of an SDK is that it should handle challenges such as rate limiting (HTTP 429 errors) and pagination. However, I found that this SDK has some limitations that matter to me, such as the inability to work through a proxy server.

Whatever approach we choose, we need to obtain:

  • A list of devices with details such as hostname, site and operating system.
  • The running-config of each device.
  • A list of the interfaces of each device.

docs.title: Trial and Error
docs.text:
It is rare for documentation to be so thorough that it clearly identifies which APIs or methods are needed to achieve a specific goal. At this stage, we need to explore which APIs or methods can help us retrieve the required data.

Let's start with the SDK and connect to Catalyst Center:

from dnacentersdk import api

api_version = "2.3.7.6"
dnac = api.DNACenterAPI(
    base_url=config["dnac_url"],
    username=config["dnac_username"],
    password=config["dnac_password"],
    verify=config["verify_cert"],
    version=api_version,
)

We store the configuration parameters in the config.yml file.

With the dir function, we can search for potentially useful functions. For example, dir(dnac) shows that devices exists, and dir(dnac.devices) reveals the functions dnac.devices.devices(), dnac.devices.get_device_by_id() and dnac.devices.get_device_config_by_id().

The dnac.devices.devices() function provides a list of all the devices, including:

  • Device ID.
  • Device family.

A careful reading of the output shows that it also contains information about the health of the device.

The dnac.devices.get_device_by_id() function returns the following for a specific device:

  • OS type.
  • OS version.
  • Serial number.

Finally, the dnac.devices.get_device_config_by_id() function retrieves the running-config of a specific device.

Let's now see how to work directly with the APIs. First, we log in and retrieve the token required for the subsequent requests:

import requests

url = f"{config['dnac_url']}/dna/system/api/v1/auth/token"
response = requests.post(
    url,
    auth=(config['dnac_username'], config['dnac_password']),
    verify=config['verify_cert']
)
token = response.json()["Token"]

As before, we can now search for the necessary APIs. We find a direct correspondence between the SDK and the APIs:

  • dnac.devices.devices() → /dna/intent/api/v1/device-health.
  • dnac.devices.device_list() → /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device.
  • dnac.devices.get_device_by_id() → /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device/{id}.
  • dnac.devices.get_device_config_by_id() → /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device/{id}/config.

Our procedure now involves the following steps:

  • Retrieve the list of all the devices (device list).
  • For each device, fetch its running-config.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
At this stage, we have a data structure containing a list of devices with some details and their running-config. The next step is to transform the running-config into a structured list of interfaces and attributes.

As we have seen, several parsers are available, but the best suited for this task is TTP (Template Text Parser). TTP is an ideal tool to parse a running-config and convert it into structured data.

<group name="interfaces" default="default_values">
interface {{ interface }}
 description {{ description | re(".*") }}
 switchport mode {{ swport_mode }}
 switchport access vlan {{ access_vlan | to_int}}
 switchport voice vlan {{ voice_vlan | to_int}}
 switchport nonegotiate {{ swport_negotiate | set(False) }}
 device-tracking attach-policy {{ tracking_policy }}
 load-interval {{ load_interval | to_int }}
 spanning-tree portfast {{ stp_portfast | set(True) }}
 spanning-tree guard root {{ stp_guardroot | set(True) }}
 shutdown {{ disabled | set(True) }}
! {{ _end_ }}
</group>

This template lets us:

  • Parse text by identifying interface blocks.
  • Extract the configuration details within each block, assigning values to the corresponding parameters.
  • Ignore any configuration not explicitly defined in the template.

In the example, some parameters take their values directly from the configuration (e.g., access_vlan), while others are set to True or False depending on the presence of specific configurations (e.g., swport_negotiate and shutdown).

To make sure parameters are always initialized, even when a configuration is missing, we define a default value for each parameter:

<vars>
default_values = {
    "description": None,
    "swport_mode": None,
    "access_vlan": None,
    "voice_vlan": None,
    "swport_negotiate": True,
    "tracking_policy": None,
    "load_interval": None,
    "stp_portfast": False,
    "stp_guardroot": False,
    "disabled": False
}
</vars>

The following code applies the TTP template to each interface and saves the resulting structured data:

with open("interface.ttp", "r") as fh:
    ttp_template = fh.read()
for hostname, details in device_details.items():
    parser = ttp(
        data=device_details[hostname]["running_config"],
        template=ttp_template
    )
    parser.parse()
    device_details[hostname]["interface_config"] = parser.result()[0][0]["interfaces"]

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Our task is to verify each interface against a defined profile. We can represent the profile either as a data structure or as an example configuration.

Since network engineers will use this compliance verification system, I opted to reduce complexity by representing the profiles as if they were interface configurations.

ignore_value:
  - description
profiles:
  - name: ProfileAccess
    interface_regex: .*:.*Ethernet.*
    interface_template: |2
      interface GigabitEthernet0/1
       description Access Interface
       device-tracking attach-policy IPDT_MAX_10
  - name: ProfileUplink
    interface_regex: .*:.*Ethernet.*
    interface_template: |2
      interface GigabitEthernet0/1
       description Trunk Interface
       switchport trunk allowed vlan 101
       switchport mode trunk

The example above shows two profiles. Each profile includes a name, a regular expression that specifies which interfaces the profile applies to, and a configuration template.

Our program must use TTP on both the profile and the interfaces to check, and compare their values.

In some cases, certain parameters must be specified but their actual value is not important (e.g., the interface description). The ignore_value list lets us specify the parameters with this characteristic.

The following code applies the same TTP template used earlier to each profile and saves the resulting structured data:

# Getting templates
for profile in config["profiles"]:
    # Get template config (use template against interface profile)
    template_parser = ttp(data=profile["interface_template"], template=ttp_template)
    template_parser.parse()
    template_config = template_parser.result()[0][0]["interfaces"]

    # Save template
    profiles[profile["name"]] = template_config

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Now we iterate over all the interfaces, apply the first matching profile and verify compliance. Since each interface might have multiple associated profiles, we choose to:

  • Use, in order, the first profile whose regular expression matches the hostname:interface combination.
  • In any case, stop the verification at the first matching profile.

The following code searches for the corresponding profile for each interface. Once the profile is found, the compare_interface function verifies it. In all cases, the result of the compliance check is recorded and we move on to the next interface.

for hostname, details in device_details.items():
    # For each device
    for interface in details["interface_config"]:
        # For each interface
        full_interface_name = f"{hostname}:{interface['interface']}"

        # Find template
        profile_name = None
        is_compliant = False
        for profile in config["profiles"]:
            if re.match(f"^{profile['interface_regex']}$", full_interface_name):
                # Profile match, update counter
                total_interfaces = total_interfaces + 1

                # Test interface compliance
                is_compliant = compare_interface(
                    profiles[profile["name"]], interface, ignore_value=config["ignore_value"]
                )
                if is_compliant:
                    # Interface is compliant, update counter
                    compliant_interfaces = compliant_interfaces + 1

                # Profile checked, proceed with next interface
                break

The function that compares two interfaces simply checks the existence of the parameters and their values, ignoring any parameter that does not require a detailed verification:

def compare_interface(template, interface, ignore_value=None):
    if not ignore_value:
        # Set default
        ignore_value = []

    for key, value in template.items():
        if key not in interface:
            # template config does not exist in interface
            return False
        if key in ignore_value and interface[key] is not None:
            # template config value exists, value is ignored
            continue
        if interface[key] is False and value is not False:
            # template requires False
            return False
        if interface[key] is True and value is not True:
            # template requires True
            return False
        if interface[key] != value:
            # template config value differs from interface
            return False
    return True

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
The final step is to create a report. In a real case, this phase depends on the process we want to build. For example, we could create a non-compliance ticket for each interface or, as in this case, a report in XLSX format.

The interfaces array in our script contains all the verified interfaces. The first four fields represent:

  • The device.
  • The interface.
  • The associated profile.
  • The result of the compliance check.

We then use the openpyxl library to create an XLSX file that contains the already structured data:

wb = openpyxl.Workbook()
summary_ws = wb.active
summary_ws.title = "Summary"
interface_ws = wb.create_sheet("Interfaces")
profile_ws = wb.create_sheet("Profiles")

# Add headers
interface_ws.append(xlsx_headers)
profile_ws.append(xlsx_headers)
summary_ws.append(summary_headers)

# Add data
for line in summary:
    summary_ws.append(line)
for interface in interfaces:
    interface_ws.append(interface)
for name, profile in profiles.items():
    profile["profile"] = name
    profile_ws.append(
        profile.get(key) for key in xlsx_headers
    )

# Add filters
interface_ws.auto_filter.ref = interface_ws.dimensions
profile_ws.auto_filter.ref = profile_ws.dimensions
summary_ws.auto_filter.ref = summary_ws.dimensions

# Auto size
for ws in [summary_ws, interface_ws, profile_ws]:
    for column_cells in ws.columns:
        length = max(len(str(cell.value)) for cell in column_cells)
        ws.column_dimensions[column_cells[0].column_letter].width = length

# Save XLSX
wb.save("export.xlsx")

We add a summary sheet at the beginning, which shows the compliance level per device and the total. Both values are calculated from the interface list.

for interface in interfaces:
    device = interface[0]
    if not current_device:
        # Initial set
        current_device = device
    has_profile = True if interface[2] else False
    is_compliant = interface[3]

    if current_device and device != current_device:
        # Add to summary and reset counters
        summary.append([
            "device",
            current_device,
            int(device_compliant_interfaces / device_total_interfaces * 100) if device_total_interfaces > 0 else "NA",
            device_compliant_interfaces,
            device_total_interfaces,
        ])
        current_device = device
        device_total_interfaces = 0
        device_compliant_interfaces = 0

    if has_profile:
        overall_total_interfaces = overall_total_interfaces + 1
        device_total_interfaces = device_total_interfaces + 1

        if is_compliant:
            overall_compliant_interfaces = overall_compliant_interfaces + 1
            device_compliant_interfaces = device_compliant_interfaces + 1

The scripts are available in my GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automatic Cisco XR provisioning with ZTP
docs.text: 18 October 2023

docs.title: Automatic Cisco XR provisioning with ZTP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco ztp

This article explores how to optimize the provisioning of a hundred Cisco XR devices, so that they are configured with minimal human intervention. Depending on the context, the devices may be shipped directly from the factory and configured automatically on site or, more likely, configured automatically in a lab, verified and then shipped for installation. We rely on ZTP (Zero Touch Provisioning), which lets us configure a factory-delivered device without any human intervention. ZTP is vendor-specific, and on Cisco XR it requires:

  • A DHCP server that assigns an IP address to the devices.
  • A web server that generates a configuration for each device.
  • The devices powered on, so they can acquire an IP address via DHCP and reach the web server.

In the scenario we envision, we set up a lab where the devices are unboxed, configured automatically, packaged and shipped to the final destination. There, non-technical personnel install the devices, connect the network cables and power them on. We assume no technical skills at the remote sites and no possibility of sending technical personnel.

Let's go into the details.

docs.title: Lab Network Configuration
docs.text:
We set up the lab with a Linux system that has two network interfaces: pnet0 connects the system to the corporate network, and pnet9 connects it to a dedicated, isolated network. The devices to configure are connected to a dedicated physical switch, whose gateway is the pnet9 interface of the Linux system.

On the Linux system, we use Dnsmasq configured as follows:

port=0
interface=pnet9
dhcp-range=169.254.1.0,169.254.1.253,30d
dhcp-option=67,http://169.254.1.1:8080/ztp
log-dhcp

Dnsmasq serves the 169.254.1.0/24 network, assigns free IP addresses to the clients and keeps each assignment for 30 days. The DHCP replies include the URL for the ZTP auto-configuration. The DHCP requests are logged via syslog, typically saved in /var/log/syslog.

docs.title: Configuration Setup
docs.text:
The web server, reachable at the address configured in the previous section, must:

  • Make a Bash script available to all the devices.
  • Generate a specific configuration for each device.
  • Make the correct configuration available to each device.

We use Flask to create a small web application that generates the configuration of each device dynamically. The application responds to two URLs:

  • /ztp (GET), which makes the Bash script available to Cisco XR devices.
  • /config (POST), which makes the specific configuration available to each device that sends its serial number.

Once ready, we can run the Flask application with:

flask --app ztp run -p 8080 -h 169.254.1.1

We make sure that the application listens on the correct interface and that both URLs respond correctly:

wget -q -O- http://169.254.1.1:8080/ztp
wget -q -O- --post-data="serial=1234" http://169.254.1.1:8080/config

The /ztp URL returns text similar to the following, identical for all the devices:

#!/bin/bash

export CONFIG_FILE="/tmp/config.txt"
source /pkg/bin/ztp_helper.sh

SN=$(dmidecode | grep -m 1 "Serial Number:" | awk '{print $NF}')
PN=$(xrcmd "show inventory location 0/RP" | grep -m1 "PID" | awk '{print $2}')
RESULT=$(wget -O- --post-data="serial=${SN}&model=${PN}" {{ url }} > $CONFIG_FILE)

xrapply_with_reason "Initial ZTP configuration" $CONFIG_FILE

After acquiring an IP address via DHCP, the device retrieves this script. The script gets the serial number (via dmidecode) and the model (via show inventory). With these parameters, the device requests the second URL to obtain its initial configuration.

Based on the parameters passed in the POST, the /config URL returns the minimal configuration that makes the device accessible via SSH:

username cisco
 group root-lr
 password 0 cisco
!
hostname device01
!
domain name example.com
!
vrf OOB address-family ipv4 unicast
!
router static vrf OOB address-family ipv4 unicast
    0.0.0.0/0 169.254.1.1
!
interface MgmtEth0/0/CPU0/0
 vrf OOB
 ipv4 address 169.254.1.11 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
!
ssh server v2
ssh server vrf OOB
!
line default
 transport input ssh

docs.title: Power On and ZTP Process Verification
docs.text:
We have reached the final and most critical step: powering on the device and verifying that the ZTP process works correctly. When we start a factory-new Cisco XR device, the ZTP process should start immediately after the legal notice about the cryptographic features:

This product contains cryptographic features and is subject to United
States and local country laws governing import, export, transfer and
use. Delivery of Cisco cryptographic products does not imply third-party
authority to import, export, distribute or use encryption. Importers,
exporters, distributors and users are responsible for compliance with
U.S. and local country laws. By using this product you agree to comply
with applicable laws and regulations. If you are unable to comply with
U.S. and local laws, return this product immediately.

A summary of U.S. laws governing Cisco cryptographic products may be
found at:
http://www.cisco.com/wwl/export/crypto/tool/stqrg.html

If you require further assistance please contact us by sending email to
export@cisco.com.
