docs.title: Development and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The ZTP process described may look simple and straightforward, but it required several hours of testing to understand where and how it stalled. Let's see which tools we have for troubleshooting.

We can see the ZTP status with the show ztp status command:

State             : Terminated
Current Fetcher   : No active fetcher

The ZTP process runs only if the router has factory settings; otherwise, it is skipped. If our router is not factory-new, we have two options, both useful.

We can force the ZTP process from the command line:

ztp initiate

Or we can delete the configuration and reset ZTP, again from the command line:

ztp clean
configure terminal
commit replace
reload

The ZTP logs are stored on the device and we can view them with show ztp logging. Relying only on these logs is inconvenient, though, because each boot takes several minutes. The best solution I found was to use the Bash shell available on Cisco XR devices and invoke the script manually:

wget -O- http://169.254.1.1:8080/ztp | bash -x

Typed from the console, these commands open a Bash instance and execute the script served by our application. When the script completes, the device should be configured as expected.

docs.title: Attempted fraud via SMS and fake voice
docs.text: 29 September 2024

docs.title: Attempted fraud via SMS and fake voice
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced digital-self-defence phishing social-engineering

This post recounts an attempted fraud via SMS and a voice call with a fake voice, targeting an elderly person. This type of fraud is not new, but the way it was executed deserves a closer look. The article aims to be informative and understandable, to raise awareness among non-professionals.

I thank the friend who allowed me to experience and analyze this type of attack.

docs.title: The Facts
docs.text:
The mother (M) of a friend (her son, F) receives an SMS at 12:32 that looks like a simple scam:

Hi Mom, I lost my phone. This is my new number. +393791234567 Please send me a message on WhatsApp. I can be reached there! (Attachment 1)

We should be trained not to believe this type of SMS. Here, however, the sender provides the full name of F, a detail that makes the message more credible.

Anomalies:

  • Why does the new phone number already appear in M's address book?
  • Why does M have to use WhatsApp instead of a text message or a simpler and more convenient phone call?

Understandably, a few minutes later M replies to the SMS with a confirmation. Almost instantly, M receives a call from the attacker (A). The sender's number is still +393791234567, but the phone displays it with F's name. The voice on the phone is F's: it says that he lost his cellphone, dictates the new number and hangs up.

Anomaly:

  • Why is the phone call just a monologue from F?

Fortunately, shortly afterwards F goes to M's house, understands the situation and calls me for advice. The attack is stopped, and the people involved are informed and secured.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
The attack drew my attention to two facts that make it extremely credible and effective:

  • The use of F's voice.
  • The cellphone number displayed with F's full name.

By analyzing the evidence A left behind, I noticed that M's address book contained two entries for F: the correct one, saved on the cellphone, and a fake one, saved on Gmail. Since the cellphone is an Android, M's address book displays a combination of local and Google entries, and without specific checks the two look identical. Looking closer at the fake entry, I noticed that it was created moments before the first SMS.

Accessing Gmail lets us see the latest security events (Attachment 2):

We see that:

  • The first two entries are my own logins.
  • The one labeled "Mobile devices" was made near the time of the attack (unfortunately, the details did not let me understand exactly when).
  • The next two (Authorized request) relate to applications requesting authorization (via OAuth2) to access part of the Google data. I assume these are applications, websites or apps installed on the phone, that need Google data. Examples are applications that manage contacts and calendars, but also WhatsApp itself, which wants to make a backup.

In the Google account management, we can check which sessions are active and, in particular, which devices are connected (Attachment 3):

We see that:

  • The Firefox session on Mac is mine.
  • The first cellphone (Oppo) is M's.
  • The cellphone SM-G991B belongs to F's sister (S). In particular, S performed an activity on the Google account on the day of the attack, via Chrome Webview.

From there, unfortunately, the Google data was not helpful enough. I checked M's cellphone remotely and found nothing abnormal, while I find the activity on S's cellphone on the day of the attack a very interesting coincidence.

docs.title: Securing
docs.text:
The analysis tells us that:

  • M's account was violated, since a fake entry was added to the address book. We can assume that all the data associated with Google has been compromised: in this case contacts, Google Drive and email.
  • The attack probably originated from S's cellphone, so the same applies to her Google account.

Securing requires:

  • Making sure that everyone involved (M, F, S) knows what happened and can recognize even more realistic attacks, which will be possible with the data stolen from the two Google accounts.
  • Changing the passwords of the two Google accounts.
  • Enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA).
  • Deleting all active sessions.
  • Removing all connected applications.
  • Securing every account that shares a password with the Google accounts, is connected to them, or is used within potentially compromised devices.

In this case, the cellphones were mainly used as phones. I breathed a sigh of relief when I realized that there were no banking applications.

docs.title: The Attack
docs.text:
It is now clear how the attack was structured:

  • Through a compromise of the Google account (via an application, a vulnerability or credential theft), the attacker creates a fake entry in the target's address book.
  • The attacker creates an audio file impersonating the voice of a relative of the target.
  • The attacker sends a series of bait SMS messages, trying to move the conversation to WhatsApp.
  • When the target replies via SMS (and presumably via WhatsApp too), the attacker calls and plays the previously created audio.
  • The attacker tries to convince the target that there is an emergency and that money is needed, to be sent via bank transfer.

This attack was thwarted, but a brief investigation showed me that it is currently widespread and that, unfortunately, some elderly parents have fallen into the trap, losing several thousand euros.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
Current deep learning technologies that can create audio files with other people's voices are extremely dangerous. Outdated phones and insecure applications give attackers the tools to create false identities very easily and effectively.

We should expect even more complex attacks, where phone calls are no longer simple monologues but real conversations.

We must be able to identify anomalies and run control tests to understand whether the person communicating with us digitally is who they claim to be, or someone impersonating them with information easily available on the Internet.

Digital life blends with physical life, so it requires the same level of attention. Driving on the road requires a license and attention, and "driving" a cellphone that gives access to a bank account requires the same awareness. Keeping and using outdated cellphones, not updating them, or installing anything that appears on the screen out of curiosity is not a good idea and can have serious consequences.

In this case it turned out well, but in others I have seen, the attack succeeded and the bank account was emptied.

docs.title: Breaking the facial recognition
docs.text: 04 February 2021

docs.title: Breaking the facial recognition
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese digital-self-defence intermediate privacy

I drafted this article about a year ago, but I never published it. Revisiting it now has allowed me to follow up and confirm my initial concerns.

We know that nearly every photo we take likely passes through facial recognition software. Apple includes one in its Photos app, and both Google and Facebook have their own versions. Images are associated with people and objects, and can later be retrieved with text-based searches. If you have never tried it, take a picture of a car license plate with an iPhone and then search for the word "plate".

For corporations (Google, Apple, etc.), associating descriptive attributes with each photo, including the names of the people involved and the geolocation, provides immense value for behavioral analysis.

For government agencies, as we have seen, being able to link a photo (perhaps from a surveillance camera) with a name and surname is extremely valuable.

It is no surprise, therefore, that facial recognition is a subject of significant interest.

docs.title: Defeating Facial Recognition
docs.text:
Facial recognition relies on algorithms that learn, from a set of images, how to identify a person across different contexts. The more photos are available, the better the algorithm becomes.

About a year ago, Face Shield publicized an application designed to alter photos so that current facial recognition algorithms would fail to detect the people depicted.

These algorithms continuously improve, however, so such a strategy is effective only temporarily: the more popular the app becomes, the faster the countermeasures are developed to adapt the recognition systems.

docs.title: The Spread of Personal Photos
docs.text:
We have already discussed the risks of sharing personal data. Many services have a business model based on collecting massive datasets of personal, profiled information and reselling them. ClearView AI is a prime example.

The safest recommendation remains: publish online only content that you consciously decide to share, always considering the worst-case scenario if it ends up in the wrong hands.

docs.title: Face Shield
docs.text:
Face Shield provided a cloud-based app that altered photos to prevent facial recognition algorithms from identifying the people depicted. The tool offered three levels of obfuscation.

Original image:

Subtle effect: nearly identical to the original but able to deceive some recognition software (source: Face Shield website).

Medium effect: visually different from the original, and able to fool several recognition systems.

Intense effect: unrecognizable to both humans and recognition software.

docs.title: Key Questions
docs.text:
Before using any service, we should start asking the right questions. Face Shield is a perfect example.

Where is the company based?

It was headquartered in Canada, outside the EU and therefore beyond the reach of the GDPR.

Is there a privacy policy?

No. A privacy policy does not guarantee compliance (as discussed here), but its absence suggests a lack of consideration for the rights of users.

What is the business model?

Every company needs a sustainable business model. In this case, the application was free and had no revenue stream. The only plausible model was data collection and the eventual sale of the company.

Is the service useful?

Does it make sense to render the people in photos unrecognizable, which degrades the images, only to share those altered photos on social media?

Is the service effective?

In an ongoing arms race, will adding noise to photos plausibly keep them unrecognizable to facial recognition algorithms? In the short term, maybe. In the long term, certainly not.

If tools such as Depix can recover censored (pixelated) passwords, it is not difficult to imagine similar countermeasures being developed against Face Shield.

docs.title: What Happened Next
docs.text:
As mentioned, I wrote this article in April 2020 but never published it. Revisiting it now, I found that Face Shield no longer exists.

Its author announced on Twitter:

PhD Candidate @rllabmcgill/@Mila_Quebec Deep Learning SwissArmy Knife: CV, NLP, Graphs, Gen. Models. http://FaceShield.ai(acquired), Ex-@UberAILabs,@BorealisAI,@UofT

We do not know who acquired Face Shield, but it is safe to assume that the buyer obtained its software, its algorithms and potentially personal data. Under European law, such data belongs to the users. Under U.S. law, it typically belongs to the company that collected it, which is largely free to use it as it pleases.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Face Shield is a perfect case study to reflect on the lifecycle of many startups, their business models and the degree of caution we should exercise before entrusting them with our personal data.

The key takeaway: before joining any service, we should always ask ourselves:

  • Who operates it, where are they based and what is their business model (follow the money)?
  • Does it truly solve a problem, or does it create one?
  • Is the proposed solution effective?
  • What alternatives exist once the service disappears?

docs.title: Facebook data breach: a danger for state officers
Facebook data breach: a danger for state officers
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner digital-self-defence

A few days ago the news broke about a Facebook data breach: 553 million user records exposed in 2019 are now circulating freely online. The story caused an uproar because the dataset, which used to be sold for money, is now accessible to anyone for free.

Over 36 million of the records belong to Italian users and include phone numbers, Facebook IDs, dates of birth, employment details... The dataset contains executives, MPs, senators, military personnel, law enforcement officers...

The breach dates back to 2019, but the fact that it is now public changes the threat: a new category of threat actor has effectively been added.

docs.title: Threats to Individuals
docs.text: Regular readers will understand why such a data leak is dangerous for people. Possessing or using the dataset is obviously illegal, but saying so does not stop attackers, stalkers, scammers, unscrupulous call centers or criminal organizations: they now have a convenient phone directory for a large portion of the Italian population.

docs.title: Threats to the State
docs.text:
The existence of such a dataset is not new, but it is worth reflecting on how it could be used to threaten the State. The database contains a huge number of people who perform, directly or indirectly, critical functions for the State and who have potential physical access to highly sensitive areas.

Most of these people are not remotely prepared to recognize and handle a digital attack. In a somewhat paranoid but realistic scenario that experts in my field consider, we can imagine a massive, coordinated attack targeting these key figures. Because it would be massive, such an attack could be unprecedented and likely highly effective.

docs.title: Countermeasures
docs.text:
As with any data breach, once the data is out there, the containment options are limited. Changing your phone number (the most sensitive exposed field here) is possible, but some data, like the date of birth, cannot be changed.

We must also accept that this type of criminal (misleadingly called a "hacker") is often a professional seeking to monetize skills, and sometimes even backed by intelligence services. With that in mind, we need to reassess seriously what personal data we publish online: once a piece of data is online, it can become public, and we must plan accordingly.

There are strategies to reduce our exposure substantially. For example, instead of giving our mobile number to every service (often touted as a way to "improve security"), we should evaluate whether the trade-off is worthwhile given the real risks. This incident shows that it may not be.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: This story is far from over. In my view, the original impact was underestimated when the breach occurred, and it is still being underestimated now. It is hard to know how those who bought the data used it over the past year. It is far easier, and far more concerning, to imagine how it will be used now that it is public.

docs.title: Home phone call firewall
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced digital-self-defence firewall

I have a "landline" VoIP number that my parents use to reach me when my phone is turned off. Landline numbers are apparently preferred by spammers, so I wrote a simple zero-trust firewall configuration for my FRITZ!Box.

The firewall permits all the numbers included in the address book.

Let's see how to configure it:

  1. Add all the trusted numbers to the phone book (Telephony → Telephone Book).
  2. Optionally, configure an answering machine (Telephony → Answering Machine).
  3. Configure the firewall (Telephony → Call Handling → Call Diversion) as follows:

In my case:

  • All trusted incoming calls are routed to a telephone connected to port FON1.
  • The answering machine on the FRITZ!Box is disabled.
  • I use the answering machine provided by the VoIP provider.

docs.title: Monetizing personal data: the new form of prostitution
docs.text: 28 January 2021

docs.title: Monetizing personal data: the new form of prostitution
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese digital-self-defence intermediate privacy

I open this article with a quote from the Italian Data Protection Authority, which is also the title of a video:

Data protection is a fundamental right of freedom.

Let's reflect on the concept of personal data. Personal means something that belongs to us and whose ownership cannot be transferred. Under the GDPR, we can grant third parties the right to use our personal data, but at any time we retain the right to request its deletion from those to whom we granted that usage.

It is often said that:

The vast amount of personal data that users pour onto the Internet every day is the new oil. {Andrew Keen}

Some services even suggest that we could profit directly from our personal data, instead of leaving all the gains to multinational corporations.

Let's analyze why "renting" out our personal data does not work, why it must not work, and why we should be more cautious.

docs.title: Why It Does Not Work
docs.text:
Consider Facebook, not to single it out, but simply to make the example concrete.

Facebook's revenue in 2019 was $16,886,000,000:

This is an enormous figure, clearly driven by the monetization of user data. The idea that users should share in this profit is appealing. There is a problem, though: the active user base of Facebook is enormous too.

Dividing the revenue by the number of active users shows that the value of each individual user is less than \$10 per year. Certainly not life-changing.

We might assume that providing higher-quality data would increase this value. For example, we could give Facebook our geolocation and smartwatch data, link all our accounts, export our browsing history and take part in every survey. Perhaps we would earn slightly more.

It still would not change our lives.

And, truthfully, Facebook would not be affected if we deleted our account or updated our profile. We are just a drop in an ocean of 2 billion monthly active users.

docs.title: Why It Must Not Work
docs.text:
Facebook states that it profiles users to improve their experience by:

  • Showing news more aligned with their interests.
  • Promoting products more relevant to their needs.

In reality, Facebook monetizes the ability to target audiences precisely with news and advertisements.

Now suppose users began to share more in the profits of Facebook. To pay us more, Facebook would need to generate greater value by offering new services. For example, if I were an influencer, I might promote a fashion brand suggested to me by Facebook, and Facebook could then sell this influence to major fashion companies.

The more unconsciously I adopt the suggestions of Facebook, the more effective they are. The more people I manage to influence, the more profitable I become. In short, Facebook could begin shaping my behavior, and that of my network, and resell this capacity as a new form of advertising. The more complete and higher-quality my data, the more powerful this influence becomes.

To increase user payouts, platforms must also increase their own revenue. They could not pay all users equally. They would instead trigger a competition in which users are incentivized to provide higher-quality data than others. This would let platforms reward a small subset of loyal users while gaining greater power to manipulate the majority.

docs.title: "I Can Quit Anytime"
docs.text:
Joining a social network is like smoking: many smokers claim they can quit anytime, yet they rarely do. And smoking leaves lasting traces in the body, which may resurface years later.

For many people, social media use is the same: a release valve into a parallel reality, curated with tailored content. We believe we are in control, exercising free will, yet day by day we are subjected to increasingly powerful manipulation.

True free will can be exercised only when we can resist the emotions triggered by posts selected specifically to distort our perception.

Science fiction? Hardly. Facebook has been known to manipulate, or assist in manipulating, public opinion by:

  • Conducting social experiments that influenced the emotions of nearly 700,000 users (Facebook apologises for psychological experiments on users).
  • Interfering in political processes such as Brexit and the 2016 U.S. election (The Great Hack).

Years later, little has been done.

Even if we delete our accounts, Facebook erases our data, posts and activities, but it never erases the models derived from that data. The GDPR protects personal data, but not the derived insights. The behavioral models, built on our preferences and actions, remain.

Moreover, research has shown (NYT report) that even a few simple attributes can re-identify individuals with 99.98% accuracy.

docs.title: Why All This Is Allowed
docs.text:
As stated earlier, data is the new oil. The reason should now be clear, but there is another dimension: large platforms are potential instruments of social control. Governments, particularly the U.S. government (most platforms are based there), are eager to exploit such powerful tools under the pretext of ensuring security.

Clearview.ai is a company that scraped billions of photos from social networks to build a massive database. When we submit a photo to Clearview, the system, through facial recognition, returns all the matching photos of that person along with their sources.

Unsurprisingly, the first clients of Clearview include U.S. government agencies such as the FBI and DHS.

When it comes to privacy, many people casually claim to "have nothing to hide." Yet no one would be comfortable being part of a massive global mugshot database.

Let's be clear: Clearview.ai is illegal because it stole user photos entrusted to social networks. In Europe, it also violates multiple GDPR provisions.

Yet Clearview.ai remains operational and serves government entities worldwide, including in Europe. Remember the strict filters used to censor websites with copyrighted content? Clearly, there is no interest in blocking the services of Clearview.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Renting out our personal data for money is equivalent to prostitution: we sell far more than just "data", and we receive only a few coins in return. We must approach the use of any digital tool or service with full awareness of the mechanisms at play:

We must treat personal digital data with the same care and respect as weapons-grade plutonium. It is dangerous, long-lasting, and once leaked, it can never be recovered. {Cory Doctorow}

docs.title: Opt-out from Web Archive
docs.text: 29 September 2024

docs.title: Opt-out from Web Archive
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese digital-self-defence intermediate

Web Archive is a non-profit online service that has long been recording websites and archiving them in a virtually permanent manner, so that anyone can analyze the history and changes of a specific website.

I am an advocate of oblivion and, above all, of being in control of one's own data. I also use the Web Archive often for my work, so I know well the drawbacks of this type of service. The underlying idea is interesting, but I do not like that the service goes to great lengths to make opting out difficult.

A convenient system to instruct search engines (crawlers) on how to treat a specific website already exists: the robots.txt file lets each website define what may be recorded and what may not. Web Archive disregards it.

Let's see how, as of today, we can be partially ignored by Web Archive. I say partially because the engine seems to keep visiting pages that are not searchable.

First, we configure the robots.txt file to instruct Web Archive to ignore the website, even though this should not be necessary:

User-agent: archive.org_bot
Disallow: /

Next, we add a verify.txt file to the root of the website with the following content:

please remove from archive.org

Finally, we send an email to info@archive.org requesting the deletion of the domain and the associated data from the Web Archive:

I am NAME SURNAME owner of EXAMPLE.COM. I'm officially requesting the immediate removal of my site from all archive.org products. The "User-agent: archive.org_bot Disallow: /" code present in our robots.txt file is not being honored. It can be seen at:

https://www.example.com/robots.txt

I am requesting removal of EXAMPLE.COM from all stored dates, including today, and all days going forward. I have been the sole owner of this domain since inception. I have sent this message from my private address, but you can reply to any address hosted at the domain which should be removed. I have also placed a confirmation message at the following link:

https://www.example.com/verify.txt

Thank you for your prompt attention.

DMCA Notice:

I am the site owner and sole copyright holder for each of the domains cited above. This letter is official notification under Section 512(c) of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act ("DMCA"), and I seek the removal of the aforementioned infringing material from your servers. Archive.org does not have any right or permission to reproduce, sell or display my websites in any way, shape or form. I am providing this notice in good faith and with the reasonable belief that rights I own are being infringed. Under penalty of perjury I certify that the information contained in the notification is both true and accurate, and I am the copyright owner and therefore have the authority to act on behalf of the owner of the copyright(s) involved. Thank you for your prompt assistance with this matter.

NAME SURNAME
EXAMPLE.COM

You should receive a confirmation of the deletion shortly.

To be clear, the world will not be better or safer after this action, but it remains an action to consider. More and more services today crawl any public data, even for commercial purposes. Generative AIs, search engines, surveillance services (ClearView AI) and cybercrime come to mind.

docs.title: Personal digital protection
docs.text: 04 January 2021

docs.title: Personal digital protection
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner digital-self-defence

As human beings, because of our evolutionary background, we struggle to perceive the dangers of the digital world. We have always assessed risk based on our physical environment, evaluating the context (location, people, etc.). Walking through a dark, deserted alley at night, for example, we would likely feel heightened alertness combined with anxiety. These emotions are essential to trigger a flight response in case of a threat.

This sense of vigilance is generally absent when we use computers and smartphones. Often this is because we use such devices in safe places, such as our homes, offices or crowded waiting rooms. Nobody would use a social network in a situation that is perceived as dangerous.

We fail to grasp fully, however, that if the Internet connects us to the world, the world is also connected to us, with all its consequences. This causes a misperception of danger when we use digital tools.

docs.title: Personal Digital Protection
docs.text:
We are used to thinking that certain individuals (politicians, industrial leaders) require physical protection through armed guards and armored vehicles. We rarely consider the need to protect these individuals from a digital perspective. This is not merely a matter of understanding a specific technology, but of adopting a security-oriented mindset.

Consider two well-known cases: Boris Johnson (former British Prime Minister) and Ank Bijleveld (former Dutch Minister of Defense). Both inadvertently exposed access credentials to confidential meetings. Many colleagues commented harshly on these incidents, but the problem is more complex than it seems: we need to educate people to understand a world that, until recently, posed no significant threats. We must build awareness to mitigate the potential damage. I say "mitigate" because the damage has already occurred and, even if we start today, many more incidents will happen before enough informed people can minimize these risks.

We must focus on:

  • C-level executives, politicians and key personnel in national and corporate environments, who are potential targets for attacks against critical infrastructure.
  • Adults, both as individuals and as employees, who are susceptible to digital attacks, scams and phishing and can become entry points for corporate breaches.
  • Children and teenagers, who are often given technological tools without adequate education on digital threats and self-protection.

docs.title: A Case Study
docs.text:
Several months ago, I came across a job listing from an international company (which I keep anonymous) looking for a CISO. The position was interesting, and before considering it seriously I wanted to assess the security awareness of the company. I conducted an OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) analysis to identify potential vulnerabilities.

For those unfamiliar with OSINT, it is the practice of gathering publicly available data, comparable to research in a public library.

I performed no hacking or intrusion, yet because of the careless handling of information, I made some surprising discoveries. Specifically, I found personal details of the CEO, including their private email, personal phone number and home address.

These details were accessible via the website of the company, embedded in corporate documents from previous years, probably submitted for certification purposes and never removed. Search engines then indexed this information, making it publicly searchable, just like a library catalog.

docs.title: Threat Modeling
docs.text:
Threat modeling means hypothesizing the threats to which I am exposed, or expose myself, by performing or not performing a specific action. For example, if I give my personal mobile phone number to someone who asks for it during a conference, I know that this number can potentially be disseminated without limit. As a result, I might receive WhatsApp messages from unknown people, and I will need to assess any interaction with this awareness.

In the scenario above, making one's private contact details public exposes the individual to digital attacks (via email and phone number) and physical attacks (via home address), potentially opening the door to stalkers. Since the individual holds a highly significant role in the company, they could also become the ideal target to access sensitive corporate information such as bank accounts, commercial data and patents.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
This article may seem alarmist, but denying reality does not make it disappear. The issue is real and widespread across all sectors (corporate, personal and youth). We must first acknowledge that we all face digital security challenges and learn to manage them effectively.

The tools exist: we need to learn how to use them correctly. The best way is to apply time-tested principles: we must train ourselves to recognize and mitigate digital threats, as we did with traditional security threats before the Internet became widely accessible.

The parents of today's middle-aged adults often advised against talking to strangers. We need to translate that mindset into the digital world, where we are all constantly exposed to strangers.

docs.title: Post-mortem account security
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced digital-self-defence

In the last few years, I started working (pro bono) on a different topic: personal digital security. In this post, I want to discuss post-mortem security: how to minimize the threats to the family after death.

My concern is email security. What can a malicious actor do if they gain access to my mailbox? Through password recovery, they could access multiple attached accounts (social networks, e-commerce, utilities...), and many of those accounts could affect the security of my family.

The obvious solution is to plan for death: give instructions and passwords to relatives, so they can manage the accounts properly. It is not that simple, though:

  • Relatives may not have the skills to handle the accounts properly.
  • Accounts could be closed without notice.

This post summarizes some thoughts I had while listening to The Privacy, Security, and OSINT Show Podcast by Michael Bazzell, especially episode 259.

docs.title: Post-Mortem Risks
docs.text:
When an email account is dismissed, a malicious actor can impersonate the original owner.

The post above is a good example of what a malicious actor can do, and no particular skill is required. Just find interesting domains and pick some. Reactivate the domain, register a catch-all address and impersonate the original owner. Try to recover the associated accounts, and present yourself as the original owner...

This is scary, at least to me.

docs.title: Domain, Service and Account Retirement
docs.text:
Death is not the only event we should care about. A service can be retired, and an account can be suspended, closed or migrated to other users:

CTemplar is closing and the last day of operation for this email service will be on May 26 of 2022.

In some cases, we could also lose an Internet domain:

(EU) Domain names that are not reinstated will remain suspended until 30 June 2021. They will then be withdrawn as from 1 July 2021. On 1 January 2022, all the withdrawn domain names will be revoked. They will then start to be made available for registration by other entities.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text: I have not found a good solution yet. I am currently evaluating two scenarios.

docs.title: Robust Third-Party Email Account
docs.text:
In this scenario, I use an account from a large email provider (e.g., Google). I assume that:

  • The domain (e.g., gmail.com) will not be closed for years.
  • The account will not be reused (it may be closed or suspended, but not reused).

In this scenario, after my death, nobody can access my email account for years, except the people who have specific instructions to do so (username, password, token).

This solution does not cover unexpected account suspension or closure. In that case, I need to migrate all the associated accounts to another email address. It is doable, even if boring.

docs.title: Personal Domain with Email Sub-Addressing
docs.text:
In this scenario, I use an account on a personal domain (e.g., adainese.it). I assume that:

  • I register a domain with the TLD of the country I live in (let's avoid another .EU-style scenario).
  • I use sub-addressing (see below).

We know that sooner or (hopefully) later the domain will not be renewed and will become available to anyone. We also know that sooner or later our domain will be part of a data breach and associated with our physical identity.

We can use sub-addressing to minimize the risk associated with password recovery. Sub-addressing lets us use the + symbol to create multiple aliases, so we can use yourname+randomstring@example.com as the email address.

Is this enough? Not really, because sooner or later a service provider will send an unsolicited email that reveals the email address used to log in.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: In my view, there is no final solution yet. Both solutions can be used: each minimizes different risks and leaves others open.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Sieve Email Filtering: Subaddress Extension.
  • Registering and renewing .eu domain names in the UK.
  • CTemplar is shutting down.
  • Expired domain threat scenario.
  • The Privacy, Security, and OSINT Show.

docs.title: Privacy policy and non existent free will
docs.text: 13 January 2021

docs.title: Privacy policy and non existent free will
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner digital-self-defence privacy

Disclaimer: this article replaces the one I originally planned, because I noticed something important that caught my attention. Despite the title, this is not about privacy. If you landed here attracted by the title, at least read the conclusions at the end.

As you probably know, WhatsApp recently updated its privacy policy. The news triggered a massive exodus of users towards alternative messaging apps. Bad idea, really bad.

docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text:
A privacy policy is supposed to explain how a service processes personal data, especially in Europe, where the GDPR applies. I say "supposed to" because the reality is often more complex.

To me, the privacy policy is a litmus test of how much a company cares about data protection. Medium and large companies that offer multiple services should update their policies often: laws change, technologies evolve, partnerships shift and services (hopefully) become safer and more user-friendly over time.

WhatsApp has updated its privacy policy several times: in 2016, 2019, 2020 and again in 2021. For European users, nothing dramatically new has changed. To dive deeper into the legal side, I suggest Altroconsumo, Cybersecurity360 and Agenda Digitale.

One crucial point: WhatsApp falls under U.S. surveillance laws and therefore must grant access to personal data, even of non-U.S. citizens, regardless of where that data is stored. This has always been true. Nothing has changed.

Finally, in my experience, privacy policies never fully reflect reality. Processes are often undocumented, details are omitted and mistakes are left in. The bigger the company, the bigger the gap. That is why I call them litmus tests: if a company cares about data, its processes and technologies evolve, and so should its privacy policies.

docs.title: Manipulation of People
docs.text:
Here is the real issue.

As I said, little has changed. WhatsApp was subject to U.S. surveillance law before, and it still is. If that was a problem today, it was already a problem last month.

And yet a huge number of people uninstalled WhatsApp and moved to Signal or Telegram, not based on facts, but on an emotional wave of fear, amplified by media noise and viral social posts. This is THE PROBLEM.

I personally received messages full of false claims, with no references or sources, crafted solely to spread fear. Classic fake news. Fake news has a dual purpose: it manipulates emotions, and it censors dialogue (by shutting down critical thinking).

This fear-driven messaging convinced millions of people to take action without asking themselves whether it made sense. That is manipulation, not choice.

As Pavel Durov shared, Telegram gained 25 million users in just 72 hours. 27% were Europeans: 6.7 million people switching platforms in three days, not out of rational analysis, but because of emotional contagion.

docs.title: Free Will
docs.text:
A wise teacher once said that, given an event, free will lies in choosing the emotion with which we respond to it. The obvious consequence is that if I can manipulate your emotions around an event, you believe you are choosing freely, while in reality you act exactly as I designed.

If we binge-watch a fearmongering video and let emotions drive our decisions, free will disappears.

docs.title: Threat Modeling
docs.text:
This is the real threat we should worry about: the manipulation of our perception.

Before rushing into a new messaging app, we need to ask ourselves: who am I entrusting my information to, and what kind of data are they really collecting?

If you have never done such an exercise, try it now:

  • List the threats of using WhatsApp.
  • Rank them by severity.
  • Then decide whether switching makes sense, and to what.

Only then should you look at resources like this messaging comparison table.

docs.title: Privacy Protection
docs.text: If your concern is broader, the constant surveillance by almost any online service, brace yourself. It is a long, steep road. And no, deleting a single app will not solve it. We will have the chance to discuss that another time.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
For European users, nothing substantial has changed with the WhatsApp privacy policy. If privacy is the issue, it was already there. If trust is the issue, it was already broken.

But that is not the point.

I deliberately used current news, a sensitive topic and a catchy title to grab your attention, just like the manipulation I described. The difference is that my goal was to make you aware of the mechanism.

Two kinds of readers may have landed here:

  • Regular followers (thank you): I hope you still found a fresh perspective.
  • Worried WhatsApp users: I hope this helped you see how easily fear can drive actions, and why structured thinking, like threat modeling, is the real defense.

Greater awareness and critical thinking do not just make individuals safer: they also strengthen companies and digital ecosystems.

docs.title: Sanitize personal Android devices
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced android digital-self-defence

Following an idea of Michael Bazzell, I decided to write a short procedure to remove unwanted software from Android smartphones. It is not only about cleaning the phone, it is about privacy. My old approach required a rootable phone. This one does not, and it does not affect the warranty.

The uninstalled packages stay in the ROM, but they are removed from the running OS.

Be aware that we should not remove software just because we suspect it: we can easily make the phone unusable, and only a hard reset fixes it.

docs.title: Connect the Phone
docs.text:
We install the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) on our platform. The following command works on Raspberry Pi OS:

sudo apt install android-tools-adb

Now we enable USB debugging. We go to Settings → About Phone → Software Information and tap Build Number 7 times. Then we go to Settings → Developer Options and enable USB Debugging.

We connect the phone to the computer with a USB cable and restart ADB:

$ adb kill-server
$ adb devices
- daemon not running; starting now at tcp:5037
- daemon started successfully
List of devices attached
520011a1a0123143        device

Let's get the ID of the current user (usually 0):

$ adb shell pm list users
Users:
        UserInfo{0:+39 333 000 1234:13} running

Now we can:

  • List the installed and uninstalled packages (list packages).
  • Uninstall a package (uninstall).
  • Disable a package (pm disable-user).
  • Reinstall a package (install-existing).
  • Enable a package (enable).

docs.title: Android Sanitization
docs.text:
Let's find some unwanted packages. For example, let's assume we want to remove some social network apps:

$ adb shell pm list packages --user 0 | egrep -i "linkedin|microsoft" | cut -d ":" -f2 | sort
com.facebook.appmanager
com.facebook.katana
com.facebook.services
com.facebook.system
com.linkedin.android

Then we uninstall them one by one:

adb shell pm uninstall -k --user 0 com.linkedin.android

Or we can script the task:

PKGS_TO_UNINSTALL=$(adb shell pm list packages --user 0 | egrep -i "linkedin|microsoft" | cut -d ":" -f2)
for P in $PKGS_TO_UNINSTALL; do adb shell pm uninstall -k --user 0 $P; done

Disabling an app marks it as unavailable (which we can easily revert), while uninstalling physically removes the app and all its data from the device. The -k flag keeps the data and cache directories after the package removal.

docs.title: Restoring a Critical App
docs.text:
In my tests, I removed some critical apps. We can restore them without issues:

adb shell cmd package install-existing com.linkedin.android
adb shell pm enable com.linkedin.android

docs.title: Finding App Information
docs.text:
For some well-known apps, we know what a package is. For most of them, we have to find additional information. I automated this long task with a simple Python script:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import requests
from lxml.html import fromstring

with open('package_list.txt') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

print("Package,Name,Author,Category")
for line in lines:
    package_name = line.strip()
    package_title = 'N/A'
    package_author = 'N/A'
    package_category = 'N/A'
    url = f'https://apkcombo.com/en/visionprovider/{package_name}/'

    r = requests.get(url)
    if r.status_code == 200:
        tree = fromstring(r.content)
        information_table = tree.xpath("//div[@class='information-table']").pop()
        package_title = tree.findtext('.//title').split(' APK ')[0]
        try:
            package_author = information_table.xpath("//a[contains(@href,'developer')]")[0].text
        except:
            pass
        try:
            package_category = information_table.xpath("//a[contains(@href,'category')]")[3].text
        except:
            pass

    print(f'{package_name},{package_title},{package_author},{package_category}')

We can now look up the details of each installed app:

sudo apt install python3-pip
pip3 install lxml -U
adb shell pm list packages -u | cut -d":" -f2 > package_list.txt
./app_resolver.py > package_list.csv

docs.title: Finding the Uninstalled Apps
docs.text:
Finally, we want to save the list of the uninstalled apps. If we used the commands and flags above, we can list the installed packages, list the installed and uninstalled packages, and compare them:

adb shell pm list packages > a
adb shell pm list packages -u > b
diff a b | grep "^>" | cut -d":" -f2 | sort

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
I honestly hate bloatware: it affects my privacy by tracking users and collecting their data. I think this is a good method to disable unwanted software. It is not perfect, because we never know exactly what is installed on our phones, but it is easy and affordable for many people.

docs.title: The dangers of losing a domain
docs.text: 24 February 2021

docs.title: The dangers of losing a domain
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner digital-self-defence

The exit of the UK from the European Union is an opportunity to reflect on our dependency on digital "assets" that we do not actually own but often take for granted. Examples include IP addresses, domain names and accounts with third-party services (Amazon, eBay, etc.).

The following reflections raise questions about how we should assess the risks associated with these assets. Today, there are no definitive answers to these questions.

docs.title: Intangible Assets on Loan
docs.text:
Companies depend on numerous critical entities tied to their business. It may seem obvious that an eBay account is not truly owned by the user who registers it, but it is less intuitive that we cannot actually buy domain names and IP addresses outright.

This realization should trigger serious discussions about how to manage potential losses. In practice, very few organizations address this proactively, except those that have already been forced to face the problem the hard way.

docs.title: Losing a Domain
docs.text:
Brexit had an interesting consequence: .eu domains registered by UK-based companies had to be revoked. Since the EU–UK agreement did not account for this, many businesses were forced to rethink their online presence.

The issue goes deeper, though. Losing a domain can lead to several risks:

  • Whoever acquires the expired domain also acquires part of its reputation (linked to the website content previously hosted there).
  • They also gain access to all the associated email flows, both outbound (impersonating the former owner) and inbound (intercepting the messages intended for the previous owner).
  • Among these emails, password reset requests are particularly dangerous: they could grant access to critical accounts tied to the old domain.

docs.title: Account Suspension or Termination
docs.text:
Another misunderstood "asset" is the account with a third-party service provider.

Several companies that recently expanded into online retail through well-known platforms have faced sudden account suspensions. These actions often come without explanation and with no avenue for appeal. For a business that depends on such a channel, a unilateral suspension like this can be devastating.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Today, it is impossible to build a digital identity, personal or corporate, without relying on entities managed by third parties. We must acknowledge, though, that this identity rests on foundations we do not own, and therefore we could lose them at any moment.

Even if only a small percentage of businesses experience such disruptions, assuming it could never happen to us is a recipe for being completely unprepared.

Whenever possible, relying on national or at least European providers gives us a more consistent legal framework for dispute resolution. When we depend on global tech giants outside Europe, we must recognize that our leverage is minimal. Legal action is rarely a realistic option: the delays introduced by litigation are incompatible with the speed at which the digital world moves.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Can I keep my .eu domain name after the post-Brexit transition period?
  • Outlawed by Amazon DRM
  • You don't own your Kindle books, Amazon reminds customer
  • Google threatens to block Australia from search engine

docs.title: The dangers of unwitting sharing
docs.text: 20 January 2021

docs.title: The dangers of unwitting sharing
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner digital-self-defence privacy

Every time we use a technological tool (smartphone, computer and beyond), we disseminate, intentionally or not, an enormous amount of information. Very few people stop to consider the potential consequences of this behavior.

Many keep claiming "I have nothing to hide", an argument that always reminds me of an ostrich burying its head in the sand.

docs.title: Information Dissemination vs. Information Communication
docs.text:
For the purposes of this article, I use "information communication" to describe actions where the confidentiality of the channel is implied (e.g., a direct message). Conversely, "information dissemination" refers to actions where the public nature of the channel is implicit (e.g., a public feed or bulletin board). In both cases, the action is voluntary.

I often reflect with others on how the use of technology leads to misperceptions. Posting a status update on a social network clearly implies that others will see it, but few people are fully aware that anyone in the world can access this content, from now on and potentially forever.

This lack of awareness can be attributed to a persistent misperception: when I interact with a social network, I am probably sitting safely at home or in an office, perhaps even alone. In reality, I am standing before a vast, crowded audience of potentially billions of people, and not only people. I am also subject to automated systems (bots, crawlers, scrapers) eagerly collecting my data. These entities have no equivalent in the physical world, which makes it difficult for us to be cautious about something we cannot fully comprehend.

Another misperception involves communications assumed to be private: it is easy to turn "confidential" information into public information. Yet when we communicate digitally with someone, we rarely pause to consider this risk.

docs.title: Data Misappropriation
docs.text:
Everything we make public online becomes a potential target for automated tools designed to collect and archive data. These datasets are then monetized: sold or leased to customers.

In other words, anything we make accessible can be commodified. The best-known example is personalized advertising, which requires millions of categorized user profiles. Emerging products raise additional concerns, such as ClearView, which built a massive facial recognition database from publicly available images (including social media content) and leases it to federal agencies.

With high probability, most of us are already catalogued.

In the near future, such databases may become commercially accessible. Anyone with a photo of a person could retrieve correlated information: other images, blog posts, social profiles... and this data is likely stored indefinitely.

A stalker's paradise.

docs.title: Threat Modeling
docs.text:
This leads to the central issue: how can the information I communicate or disseminate become a threat to me, my family or my organization?

Someone with access to my history, comments or opinions could selectively weaponize messages to discredit me in any context.

Likewise, a data breach such as the one involving Ho Mobile enables identity theft by anyone with minimal technical knowledge.

The more data a potential attacker gathers, the more sophisticated the fraud attempts become. Thinking "why would anyone target me?" is, once again, burying one's head in the sand. Cyber fraud is, in most cases, a business model designed to maximize profit with minimal effort. The profit derives, once again, from what I can provide, often under coercion. That "provision" may be money, but also actions or omissions: exfiltrating corporate projects, installing a device within a company network, or overlooking an investigation.

docs.title: Defensive Measures
docs.text:
The solution lies in strengthening our awareness while reducing the trail of personal information we leave behind.

In Zanshin Tech training sessions, a practical exercise highlights the importance of personal data: each participant receives physical cards, each representing a specific type of information (nickname, profile photo, full name, address, religion, sexual orientation, health conditions, intimate images, etc.). The exercise simulates a digital conversation through the exchange of cards. The key insight is clear: once a card is handed over, the original owner loses control, and the recipient can do with it as they wish.

Personally, I recommend a simple rule of thumb before sharing any piece of information: if it could be posted publicly in a town square, then it may be communicated or published. Otherwise, it should not. I apply this principle universally, to private messages, emails and public posts alike.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
This article aims to establish a baseline of awareness around the actions modern technologies have made so effortless: writing, communicating, sharing, and expressing opinions, judgments and emotions.

Beyond reflecting on what to share, with whom, where and how, I encourage everyone to first ask "should I share this at all?". The resulting self-awareness helps us understand the impulse that drives us to share and to take part in a digital community that is vastly different from its physical counterpart. That impulse, which we reveal every time we post, is extremely valuable information, especially for those who read between the lines.

docs.title: Theft and recovery of a Facebook account
docs.text: 26 September 2023

docs.title: Theft and recovery of a Facebook account
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced digital-self-defence passwords

This is the story of Vittoria (a pseudonym, hereafter referred to as V). A few days ago, V called me urgently: her Facebook account had been stolen by Nhang (a pseudonym, hereafter referred to as N). Identity theft is a criminal offense, punishable under Article 494 of the Italian Penal Code. This will be useful later on.

For those who use Facebook for work, such an event is extremely traumatic and must be handled with care.

docs.title: The Facts
docs.text:
• On Wednesday, V received notifications on Facebook warning her of unusual activity on her account. She followed the instructions and reported the suspicious activity, but since she was on a mobile device, she could not change the password or enable multi-factor authentication.
  • Thursday, 7:37 PM: Verify your payment method to resume posting ads (Attachment 1).
  • Thursday, 7:39 PM: Have you just added an email address? (Attachment 2).
  • Friday, 12:38 AM: Have you just removed your phone number? (Attachment 3).
  • Friday, 12:39 AM: Have you just removed your email address? (Attachment 4).

From this point on, V could no longer access her account from either her computer or her phone. She also noticed that the account now displayed N's first and last name.

We can reconstruct what probably happened:

  • V's password was stolen. This can be done in several ways, from simple phishing portals to data breaches (more or less public) to so-called infostealers.
  • V's account was not protected by multi-factor authentication (MFA).
  • N accessed V's account and locked her out by changing the password, the email address and the phone number.

docs.title: Facebook's First Failure: No Detection
docs.text:
For those who work in cybersecurity, these events are a series of indicators that, given V's usual behavior, point to a compromise (commonly called Behavioral Indicators of Compromise, or BIoC). To describe the mechanism simply: each event receives a score, and the events are evaluated together, based on the total score, not individually.

Specifically:

  • If an Italian profile, accessed only from Italy until now, is accessed from Vietnam, the event is highly suspicious and we assign it a score of 9/10.
  • If a user changes their account password and has never done so before, the event may be suspicious and we assign it a score of 1/10.
  • If a user changes the email address, the event may be suspicious and we assign it a score of 6/10.
  • If a user removes or changes their phone number, the event may be suspicious and we assign it a score of 6/10.
  • If a user changes the name on their profile to a radically different one, the event is highly suspicious and we assign it a score of 9/10.

It doesn't take a security expert to see that these five events, taken together, conclusively indicate a compromised account.

docs.title: Facebook's Second Failure: The "Not Me" Link
docs.text:
For each event described in The Facts, Facebook sent V an email. Clicking the "Not me" link starts a procedure that should have let V undo the changes and regain control of her account.

But it didn't go that way.

V had to send Facebook a live webcam recording of her identity document, but Facebook's automatic system judged the information insufficient to recognize V and to restore her access, leaving the account with N.

Again, it doesn't take a security expert to understand that when a user reports fraud through an official Facebook email, the changes were very likely fraudulent and should be reversed.

docs.title: Account Recovery
docs.text:
V still had two more Facebook emails with recovery links. The second attempt failed too, but with some difficulty she managed to start the third recovery procedure. This time she used her passport instead of the identity card, which always came out blurred: she took the time to photograph it properly with her phone, and Facebook recognized her and sent two recovery emails:

  • New email address added to Facebook (Attachment 5).
  • You can now access your account again (Attachment 6).

These two emails must be used in the order shown above: first, the email address must be confirmed with the corresponding confirmation code, then access to the account can be regained with the temporary password and PIN provided in the email.

But it was not over yet.

V got into the account, but the email change procedure failed. She found herself with an account:

  • whose password she did not know (the one in the email was a temporary, single-use password);
  • associated with N's email address;
  • associated with N's phone number.

V soon realized that any attempt to change the password, the email address or the phone number required a password, but not the one she had: Facebook wanted the password N had used to lock her out.

There is a procedure that works without the password, but it requires a confirmation PIN, sent to N's email address or phone.

In a moment of desperation and inspiration, V tried once more to open the Facebook app on her phone. This time the app logged in automatically but asked for confirmation from an already open session. V could now authorize the phone from the session she had left open on her computer, and within minutes she changed the email address and the phone number and set up multi-factor authentication.

But V cannot change her name for two months: it is a Facebook security policy. For two months, her friends will see her as Nhang.

docs.title: Other Facebook Failures
docs.text:
In retrospect, V reacted well, despite saying she is not good with technology: she was autonomous, had excellent intuitions and did not get discouraged. And yes, given how poorly Facebook's security systems work, she was also very lucky.

These are the other failures of Facebook:

  • Facebook has an official procedure for recovering stolen accounts, but it requires the email address or phone number associated with the stolen account. N had changed both, so V did not know them.
  • The document is captured through Facebook's own interface, and for some reason the image of the identity card came out blurred, even though V has a latest-generation phone. Photographing the passport, which is much larger than the electronic identity card, was a brilliant idea by V.

docs.title: Criminal Offense
docs.text:
Identity theft is a criminal offense that should be reported. Not so much because the Italian authorities can realistically act against Facebook, but because the stolen profile could be used to commit crimes. One must be able to demonstrate that, from a specific date, the account was no longer under one's control.

V went to the authorities to report the incident, but she could not assert her rights.

docs.title: Lesson Learned
docs.text:
Lately, I have often dealt with what I call the technofascism of social platforms, where poorly written automated systems and a strong interest in surveillance erase people's rights arbitrarily or at random.

I understand, however, that some people choose to use these platforms for specific reasons. To them I make an appeal: take precautions against scams.

In my approach to digital security, there are two types of accounts:

  • accounts linked to my identity, which I protect with strong, unique passwords and, where possible, multi-factor authentication;
  • disposable accounts, not linked to my personal identity, which I protect with fictitious data, strong passwords and, where possible, multi-factor authentication.

They say prevention is better than cure, and here it is truer than ever: as this story shows, recovering a stolen account takes a mix of stubbornness and luck. To be completely transparent: few accounts are ever recovered.

In summary, if your account is stolen:

  • seek help;
  • do not act in a panic; take the time to act correctly (for us, it was essential to work from a computer, keeping the phone as support);
  • use the recovery emails sent by the platform;
  • once you regain access, lock out the attacker (ask for advice);
  • if possible, use the official procedure, and repeat it daily, if necessary for months.

docs.title: An Open Question
docs.text:
One question stayed open at first: what is the point of stealing a Facebook account and changing its name, without asking for a ransom? In other words, where is the economic benefit of this kind of operation?

The answer came a few days later: N had used the Facebook account to add a credit card, unknown to V and probably stolen, and to create and pay for advertising campaigns.

docs.title: Weak Passwords and Unauthorized Access
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese digital-self-defence intermediate passwords

A few months ago, a new "collection" of data breaches began circulating: someone took the time to aggregate cleaned-up data from multiple past breaches into a single consolidated database. The result was a well-organized archive that contained more than a billion email addresses and the corresponding passwords.

This was nothing new, but its compact size and structured format made the dataset particularly interesting to analyze.

docs.title: We Have a Problem
docs.text:
While reviewing the file, it became clear that we face a significant issue: many people still do not understand how to manage passwords, or why it matters.

The analysis of a small but statistically significant portion of the database showed that the chosen passwords were extremely weak.

The problem is serious because the same careless behavior that individuals have in their private lives often extends to the workplace. This means that individuals expose themselves to risks such as identity theft, and they also expose their companies to corporate security breaches.

It is time to go back to the basics.

docs.title: How Attackers Think About Passwords
docs.text:
From the perspective of the attacker, the reasoning is straightforward:

  1. Define an objective (often financial gain).
  2. Assess the possible targets that can help achieve that objective.
  3. Select the targets that optimize the effort: those that are most vulnerable or have the most available information.
  4. Execute the attack.

With public online tools, past data breaches and marketplaces on the Darknet, attackers can identify potential victims easily. Exposed passwords and personal information give them a significant advantage.

docs.title: The Risks of Weak Passwords
docs.text:
By obtaining one or more passwords of a target, an attacker can infer patterns in the way the target thinks. The attacker can then try to access services with known or predictable credentials.

The risks are clear:

  • For individuals: account takeover and identity theft.
  • For organizations: unauthorized access to IT and telecommunication systems (as defined in article 615-ter of the Italian penal code).

This may sound like a distant threat, but the hyper-digital nature of today's world has led to an exponential increase in account theft reports. For organizations, this often shows up as anomalous login activity.

docs.title: How Not to Choose a Password
docs.text:
When creating passwords, many people believe they are being clever, but they often:

  • Fail to realize how common their logic actually is.
  • Underestimate the likelihood of being targeted.
  • Overlook the consequences of a focused attack.
  • Use trivial passwords (e.g., margherita).
  • Use predictable keyboard sequences (e.g., 1q2w3e4r).
  • Apply "creative" formulas that they believe to be unbreakable (e.g., googleLaVita3Bella).
  • Reuse the same password across multiple sites.

We must face reality: every account that contains personal data has value. The real question is how much value, and for email or social media accounts the answer is generally a lot.

From a corporate perspective, requiring users to set alphanumeric passwords of at least 12 characters, with uppercase, lowercase and special symbols, often results in passwords like PizzaMargherita2012!.

docs.title: Attacks Against Passwords
docs.text:
Let's return to the perspective of the attacker. Given the available information:

  • If a target reuses the same password across services, a single data breach exposes all their accounts, including the corporate ones.
  • If a target uses an algorithmic pattern, once one or two passwords are leaked, an attacker can deduce the formula and generate future credentials.
  • If a password is simple, brute force attacks (with ordered probability dictionaries) can crack it quickly.

In nearly all cases, attackers can compromise at least some accounts.

docs.title: Choosing and Managing Passwords
docs.text:
Given the threat landscape, every account must be protected by a password that is:

  • Unique: otherwise, one breach compromises everything.
  • Complex: otherwise, brute force attacks succeed in minutes.
  • Non-mnemonic: otherwise, attackers can reverse-engineer personal patterns from leaked credentials.

This leads to a practical challenge: how do we manage unique, complex and non-memorable passwords? The answer is password managers. Users need to remember only two things:

  1. The master password of the manager's database.
  2. The login credentials of their computer.

docs.title: Awareness and Training
docs.text:
This brings us to the main point: corporate security.

After an anomaly or a compromise, users are often asked to change their passwords. If the old password was Cristina43!, however, the new one will likely be Cristina44!, a useless change that lets the attacker keep access.

This is why training is crucial. Employees should not follow arbitrary rules they do not understand. They need awareness: they should recognize the personal benefits first, which then extend naturally to the company.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
I, too, once assumed that people understood the risks of weak passwords and how to manage them properly. Through conversations, I realized that the reality was very different. More importantly, I began to understand the motivations behind their poor choices.

By sitting down with people, discussing digital security and real-world consequences and, most importantly, listening, I was able to design a different strategy. This approach proved far more effective than generic "information security awareness" video courses.

The people I had the honor to train not only understood the risks, but also adopted a mindset that lets them think critically about the digital world. The benefits extended far beyond password security, reaching areas we had not even addressed yet.

docs.title: Introduction to EVE-NG platform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner eve-ng fundamentals

Developing automations that interact with network devices requires a development environment to test, learn and experiment with frameworks, integrations and automations. Over the years, virtualization has given anyone realistic copies of network devices. Today, anyone can, and should, have their own development environment.

In the past, I developed a web-based application for creating and managing virtual network labs: UNetLab, now managed by third parties under the name EVE-NG. It lets us implement our testing environment.

The EVE-NG Workbook is the guide for the students of my network automation courses, so that they can build an independent lab where they can study and develop automations and integrations.

If you find these guides useful, you can support the work on Patreon to get more in-depth guides and tutorials.

docs.title: Prerequisites for EVE-NG
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner eve-ng fundamentals

To set up an EVE-NG environment, you need some prerequisites in terms of knowledge, hardware and software.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Diving into network automation generally requires a solid understanding of Linux system usage and management. Linux is the most flexible system, rich in languages, libraries and frameworks that simplify the development of automation and integrations. I designed this series of courses to be accessible to anyone in the IT field, but experience in managing Linux systems is undeniably helpful.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: You can install EVE-NG in both physical and virtualized environments. A virtual environment is undoubtedly the easiest route initially. Over time, however, you will likely need a more performant environment based on physical hardware. Installing EVE-NG directly on physical hardware avoids the overhead caused by excessive layers of virtualization: EVE-NG already adds a virtualization layer to run the various devices, and if EVE-NG itself is virtualized, the overall performance may degrade.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
To get a complete EVE-NG environment, you need:

  • Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS for EVE-NG 5, or Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04 LTS for EVE-NG 6.
  • One or more images supported by EVE-NG.

You can install EVE-NG Community Edition directly from the ISO or OVF, but I encountered some issues in the past, so we proceed with a manual installation. This approach also lets us see some customizations in detail.

docs.title: Installing Ubuntu Linux
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner eve-ng linux

Now let's see how to install Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS so that it can host EVE-NG.

docs.title: Virtual Environment
docs.text:
In a virtual environment, typically VMware vSphere, I suggest creating a virtual machine with the following specifications:

  • Guest OS family: Linux.
  • Guest OS version: Ubuntu Linux (64-bit).
  • CPU: 4.
  • Hardware virtualization: expose hardware-assisted virtualization to the guest OS.
  • Memory: 8 GB.
  • Hard disk: 50 GB.
  • CD/DVD drive: the ISO file of Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS, previously uploaded to the ESXi server.

Pay special attention to the advanced CPU features: the hardware virtualization option must be enabled.

docs.title: Physical Environment
docs.text: As in the virtual environment, in a physical environment we need to enable hardware-assisted virtualization. This feature is in the BIOS configuration, and the specific setting may vary from computer to computer.

docs.title: Ubuntu Linux
docs.text:
Next, we boot the system and start the installation. In order, we are prompted to configure:

  • Language: English.
  • Layout: the keyboard layout we use.
  • Installation: Ubuntu Server.
  • Network connection: configure the network card according to our environment.
  • Disk: use the entire disk with LVM.
  • Profile: set up a user with a password.
  • Hostname: eve-ng.
  • Install the OpenSSH server.

We confirm the defaults for all the other settings and wait for the system to finish the installation. Once done, we restart the system.

docs.title: Installing EVE-NG 5
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner eve-ng

EVE-NG is installed from packages downloaded via APT from the official repository. We run all the following commands as the root user via SSH.

First, we add the official repository and the GPG key used to verify the packages:

wget -qO - https://www.eve-ng.net/focal/eczema@ecze.com.gpg.key | sudo apt-key add -
cat << EOF > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/eve-ng.list
deb [arch=amd64] http://www.eve-ng.net/focal focal main
# deb-src [arch=amd64] http://www.eve-ng.net/focal focal main
EOF

Next, we reload the repositories, upgrade the system and install EVE-NG CE along with other packages we will use later:

apt-get update
apt-get -y upgrade
apt-get -y install build-essential dnsmasq eve-ng iptables-persistent libbz2-dev libffi-dev libgdbm-dev libncurses5-dev libnss3-dev libreadline-dev libsqlite3-dev libssl-dev python3-pip zlib1g-dev

If we are prompted on how to handle the existing configuration file versions, we answer:

install the package maintainer's version

Before rebooting the system, we set a password for the root user and enable root login:

passwd
sed -i 's/#PermitRootLogin./PermitRootLogin Yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Then we perform an initial reboot:

reboot

We connect again via SSH as root, keeping in mind that the IP address may have changed. Then we complete the configuration by:

  • Changing the password of the root user.
  • Setting the hostname to eve-ng.
  • Setting the domain to example.com.
  • Configuring the network according to our environment.
  • Adding an NTP server, for example, if we work on a physical server.
  • Selecting the appropriate option for how the system accesses the Internet.

The system reboots again. Once it is reachable, the EVE-NG web interface is available on port 80 via HTTP. By default, we can log in with the admin user and the password eve.

We log in as admin and change the password to a more secure one by clicking on admin at the top right:

The last step to get a functional installation is to copy some device images into the system. We start with the files for IOL (IOS on Linux):

scp i86bi_LinuxL2-AdvEnterpriseK9-M_152_May_2018.bin root@172.25.82.167:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/
scp i86bi_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.SSA.high_iron_20190423.bin root@172.25.82.167:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/
scp iourc root@172.25.82.167:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/

Then we SSH into the EVE-NG server as root and make sure the permissions are correct:

/opt/unetlab/wrappers/unl_wrapper -a fixpermissions

We also verify that hardware-assisted virtualization is available: the following command returns output only if it is enabled.

egrep "vmx|svm" /proc/cpuinfo

Finally, we verify that the image is usable by creating a small lab with a single IOL node. We start the node and wait a few seconds before connecting to its console.

docs.title: Installing EVE-NG 6
docs.text: 05 October 2024

docs.text:

We log in as admin and change the password to a more secure one by clicking on admin at the top right:

The last step to get a functional installation is to copy some device images into the system. We start with the files for IOL (IOS on Linux):

scp i86bi_LinuxL2-AdvEnterpriseK9-M_152_May_2018.bin root@172.25.82.167:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/

docs.title: Customizing EVE-NG
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

Let's delve into the most important part: customizing EVE-NG for DevNetOps. In particular, we will:

  • Configure an internal network dedicated to device management.
  • Import the labs from the GitHub repository dedicated to DevNetOps courses.
  • Compile and install Python 3.10 (not required in EVE-NG 6).
  • Create a user dedicated to development, with a dedicated Python environment.
  • Use Visual Studio Code for remote development on the EVE-NG server.

docs.title: Configure an Internal Management Network
docs.text:
In automation, each lab we create requires a seemingly trivial yet essential characteristic: the IP addresses of the devices must be reachable from the automation system. The EVE-NG PRO version has a native feature (NAT Cloud) that simplifies this. In EVE-NG CE, we need a strategy to achieve the same result.

The goal is to configure an additional network on EVE-NG that lets us connect the management interfaces of the devices we use in our labs, whether they are virtual (internal to EVE-NG) or physical (PLCs and other external physical devices). The diagram below summarizes the idea:

First, let's clarify the networking of EVE-NG and introduce some Linux concepts.

A Linux system represents its network interfaces with names that have a prefix (eth, ens...) followed by an identifier number. A network interface can represent either a physical or a virtual network card. In our environment, the physical network card is eth0, but there are other network cards named pnet.

We can view the network interfaces of the system with one of the following commands:

ifconfig -a
ip link

The pnet interfaces are actually virtual switches (bridges) configured by default during installation:

$ brctl show
