bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
pnet0           8000.2ac1c946eac3       no              eth0
pnet1           8000.000000000000       no
pnet2           8000.000000000000       no
pnet3           8000.000000000000       no
pnet4           8000.000000000000       no
pnet5           8000.000000000000       no
pnet6           8000.000000000000       no
pnet7           8000.000000000000       no
pnet8           8000.000000000000       no
pnet9           8000.000000000000       no

In particular, the bridge pnet0 is associated with the physical interface eth0. In other words, anything associated with the bridge pnet0 is also transmitted on the eth0 network. As we will see in the web interface, we can add Cloud networks, which are simply the pnet bridges. The pnet0 network is also used for web access: the management IP address is associated with the bridge pnet0, as we can see with one of the following commands:

ifconfig pnet0
ip address show pnet0

We can then configure an IP address on the pnet9 network and connect the management interfaces of the devices to the Cloud9 network.

EVE-NG is based on Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS and configures the network through the /etc/network/interfaces file. We configure the part related to the pnet9 bridge as follows:

# Cloud devices
auto pnet9
iface pnet9 inet static
    address 169.254.1.1
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    bridge_ports none
    bridge_stp off

We use the APIPA network, which is defined to be local. In an enterprise context, this gives us reasonable certainty of not overlapping with other networks. We can delete the remaining pnet2 to pnet9 interfaces.

We can now reload the modified network configuration:

/etc/init.d/networking restart

If we ever want to associate a physical interface with this bridge, we add the following line:

bridge_ports eth1

For convenience, we assign IP addresses automatically to the network interfaces connected to the Cloud9 network. To do so, we use DHCP via Dnsmasq.

We configure Dnsmasq in /etc/dnsmasq.conf. We want only the DHCP service active, and only for the network managed by the pnet9 interface. The configuration is:

port=0
interface=pnet9
bind-interfaces
dhcp-range=169.254.1.2,169.254.1.254,3650d
log-dhcp

When done, restart the service:

systemctl restart dnsmasq

As we will see later for the automation part, we need a stable association between the IP addresses and the devices. We cannot rely on the dynamic mapping provided by Dnsmasq, so we define it statically. We map the hostname that the device presents during the DHCP request to a fixed address in Dnsmasq:

dhcp-host=SW1,169.254.1.101
dhcp-host=SW2,169.254.1.102
dhcp-host=SW3,169.254.1.103
dhcp-host=SW4,169.254.1.104

The list must be completed with all the names we use in this and future labs.

To complete our environment, the Cloud9 network must have access to the Internet. In other words, outbound traffic must be masqueraded (via NAT) using the IP address configured on the pnet0 interface.

First, we enable routing by editing /etc/sysctl.conf:

net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

We activate the setting with:

sysctl -p

We configure NAT with iptables to masquerade outbound traffic with the address of pnet0:

iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o pnet0 -j MASQUERADE

To save the changes, we use:

iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4

Although not strictly necessary, I recommend rebooting the system to make sure everything is configured correctly.

docs.title: Import Labs
docs.text:
Now we download the labs and make them available directly on the EVE-NG server:

git clone https://github.com/dainok/courses /opt/courses
ln -s "/opt/courses/EVE-NG labs" "/opt/unetlab/labs/DevNetOps labs"

By accessing the web interface of EVE-NG, we should now see the available labs. For example, let's open Simple Network Lab.unl, power on R1, and verify the IP address and the connectivity to the Internet:

Now let's verify that we can access the node from the EVE-NG server (user dev) with the username admin and the password cisco:

$ ssh admin@169.254.1.21
Unable to negotiate with 169.254.1.21 port 22: no matching key exchange method found. Their offer: diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

When we access very old devices, outdated ciphers can cause access problems. We can re-enable them in the ~/.ssh/config file:

Ciphers +aes128-cbc
HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
KexAlgorithms +diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

Host *
  ServerAliveInterval 5
  ServerAliveCountMax 3

At this point, we should be able to SSH into R1.

For completeness, the repository contains the complete dnsmasq.conf file with all the reserved DHCP records used in future labs. If we have made no customizations, we can update the configuration of the system:

cp -a "/opt/courses/EVE-NG setup/files/dnsmasq.conf" /etc/dnsmasq.conf
systemctl restart dnsmasq

docs.title: Compile and Install Python 3.10
docs.text:
This step is not required on EVE-NG 6, because Python 3.11 is available on Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04.

Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS, on which EVE-NG is based, comes with Python 3.8, which is too old for recent versions of the frameworks typically used for automation. The latest versions of Ansible, for example, require a newer version.

Let's download Python 3.10:

cd /usr/src
wget -q https://www.python.org/ftp/python/3.10.14/Python-3.10.14.tgz

We unpack the file, compile the sources and install the new version:

tar xzf Python-3.10.14.tgz
cd Python-3.10.14
./configure --enable-optimizations
make
make install

When done, the new Python interpreter is available at /usr/local/bin/python3.10.

docs.title: Create a Development Environment
docs.text:
Now we can create a user dedicated to development:

useradd -m dev -s /bin/bash
passwd dev

We can also create a dedicated Python environment using the interpreter installed earlier:

su - dev
python3.10 -m venv venv

For convenience, we configure the shell to load the Python environment at every new login. We add the following line to the .profile file:

source ~/venv/bin/activate

Finally, we configure SSH authentication with keys. From our desktop, we copy our public key to the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub dev@172.25.82.167

Now we can connect to the EVE-NG server as dev without entering the password. While we are at it, we create a directory for development:

mkdir src

docs.title: Use Visual Studio Code for Remote Development
docs.text:
To complete the configuration, we set up Visual Studio Code to develop remotely on the EVE-NG server with the dev user created earlier.

We start Visual Studio Code on our desktop, go to Extensions and install the Remote - SSH plugin.

We add a new host by going to Remote Explorer → Remotes → SSH → ➕:

  • Specify the command to connect to the host: ssh dev@172.25.82.167 -A.
  • Specify where to save the new host, typically .ssh/config.

At this point, we should be able to connect to the EVE-NG server:

We can now enrich our development environment by installing the following plugins for remote use:

  • Ansible by Red Hat.
  • GitHub Actions by GitHub.
  • HashiCorp Terraform by HashiCorp.
  • Jinja by wholroyd.
  • Pylance by Microsoft.
  • Python by Microsoft.
  • Terraform by Anton Kulikov.
  • TextFSM Template Syntax by andytruett.
  • YAML by Red Hat.

docs.title: EVE-NG network interfaces explained
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

The network infrastructure that EVE-NG uses to interconnect lab nodes is somewhat obscure. Let's explore how to identify the Linux interfaces of each virtualized node for debugging or simple analysis.

Let's take the following lab as an example:

docs.title: Required Information
docs.text:
Before we begin, we need the following data:

  • The user identifier (POD).
  • The lab identifier.
  • The identifiers of the nodes to analyze.
  • The identifiers of the interfaces to analyze.
  • The identifiers of the networks to analyze.
  • The execution space identifier.

docs.title: User Identifier (POD)
docs.text:
An administrator can see the user identifier under Management → User Management.

In this example, the POD assigned to my user is 5.

docs.title: Lab Identifier
docs.text:
We can find the lab identifier by opening the lab and navigating to Lab Details.

For instance, my lab identifier is 3b327c21-1585-499d-9a0d-4281e05f4532.

If we open the lab file with a text editor, the identifier is the id attribute of the lab object.

docs.title: Node Identifiers
docs.text:
Each node is identified by a number that we can see by opening the lab and navigating to Nodes.

If we open the lab file with a text editor, the identifier is the id attribute of the node object.

docs.title: Interface Identifiers
docs.text:
Each interface is identified by a number, which we can see by opening the lab file with a text editor. The interface identifier is the id attribute of the interface object.

Each interface is associated with a network (network_id), which represents the network the interface is connected to.

There is a key difference between QEMU and IOL node interfaces:

  • QEMU node interfaces start from identifier 0 and increment sequentially.
  • IOL node interfaces follow the formula ID = X + Y × 16, where X and Y are the slot and interface identifiers present in the EthernetX/Y name.

docs.title: Network Identifiers
docs.text:
Each network segment is identified by a number that we can see by opening the lab and navigating to Networks.

A network can be either a point-to-point link or a network object. A network object is an L2 network implemented by a Linux bridge rather than by an EVE-NG node. This view displays only the explicitly created networks, while all the point-to-point networks remain hidden.

If we open the lab file with a text editor, the identifier is the id attribute of the network object.

The visibility flag determines whether a network is visible in the web interface. For example, four networks are present, but only two are visible in the web interface:

  • Network R2-R7 (id=3).
  • Network R5-R7 (id=2).
  • Shared Network (id=4).
  • Mgmt Network (id=1).

When we create a point-to-point link, the network name is set using the node name and the source interface.

docs.title: Execution Space Identifier
docs.text:
The execution space is represented by a number associated with an open lab. This number remains assigned until the lab is closed.

We can access the database with the following command and the password eve:

mysql -u root -p eve_ng_db

Knowing the lab ID, we can retrieve the execution space identifier with a database query:

mysql> SELECT * FROM lab WHERE uuid="3b327c21-1585-499d-9a0d-4281e05f4532";
+----+--------------------------------------+---------------+-----------------+-----+
| id | uuid                                 | path          | name            | pod |
+----+--------------------------------------+---------------+-----------------+-----+
|  3 | 3b327c21-1585-499d-9a0d-4281e05f4532 | /Users/Andrea | Ansible Cisco XR |   5 |
+----+--------------------------------------+---------------+-----------------+-----+

In our case, the execution space identifier is 3.

docs.title: Node Interfaces
docs.text:
At this point, we have all the values we need to identify the interfaces in our system. Each interface name is built as follows: vunAAABBBBCCCDD.

Where:

  • AAA: the decimal execution space identifier.
  • BBBB: the decimal POD identifier.
  • CCC: the decimal node identifier.
  • DD: the hexadecimal interface identifier.

The first interface of node R2 in our lab (execution space 3, POD 5) has the prefix vun0030005002:

$ ifconfig | grep vun0030005002
vun003000500200: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000
vun003000500210: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000
vun003000500220: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000
vun003000500230: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000

Since R2 is an IOL node, its interfaces are 0, 16 (0x10), 32 (0x20) and 48 (0x30).

Each interface can be part of a network implemented with a Linux bridge. The names of the Linux bridges are built as follows: vnetAAABBBBEEEE.

Where:

  • AAA: the decimal execution space identifier.
  • BBBB: the decimal POD identifier.
  • EEEE: the decimal network identifier.

The network in our lab (execution space 3, POD 5, ID 4) is named vnet00300050004:

$ brctl show vnet00300050004
bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
vnet00300050004         8000.de24a99b6dc2       no                      vun003000500103
                                                        vun003000500220
                                                        vun003000500520

This network contains three interfaces:

  • vun003000500103: execution space 3, POD 5, node 1 (R7, QEMU), interface 0x3 (Gi0/3).
  • vun003000500220: execution space 3, POD 5, node 2 (R2, IOL), interface 0x20 (32, Eth0/2).
  • vun003000500520: execution space 3, POD 5, node 5 (R5, IOL), interface 0x20 (32, Eth0/2).

docs.title: Troubleshooting EVE-NG nodes that fail to start
docs.text: 03 August 2025

docs.title: Troubleshooting EVE-NG nodes that fail to start
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng troubleshooting

In this article, we will explore how to troubleshoot EVE-NG nodes that fail to start properly. The symptom is simple yet frustrating: when you start a node, it appears to launch but shuts down after a few seconds without any explanation.

Some architectural decisions made early on make it hard to surface backend errors to the user. It was a deliberate choice: with correct usage, such failures should be extremely rare. That held true for the most part, but in the few cases where it does not, the user is left helpless.

Here, we will walk through the troubleshooting steps. We will connect to the EVE-NG system via SSH as root and replicate the backend process manually to find the point of failure.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Logs are located in /opt/unetlab/data/Logs (note that UNetLab was the predecessor of EVE-NG, and much of its original structure remains). The file we need is unl_wrapper.txt, which records all the operations performed by the wrapper, the program that mediates communication between the node and the backend. Specifically, the wrapper manages the start, stop and console operations of a node.

Follow the log with this command:

tail -f /opt/unetlab/data/Logs/unl_wrapper.txt

Start the failing node and watch the output. The key lines are:

Aug 01 10:07:03 INFO: CWD is /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/2
Aug 01 10:07:03 INFO: starting /opt/unetlab/wrappers/qemu_wrapper -C 54179 -T 5 -D 2 -t "vIOS" -F /opt/qemu-2.4.0/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 -d 0 -- -nographic -device e1000,netdev=net0,mac=50:05:00:02:00:00 -netdev tap,id=net0,ifname=vun003000500200,script=no ...

docs.title: The Wrapper
docs.text:
As mentioned, the wrapper handles the communication between the backend and the node. It launches the node and manages the console.

The lines above reveal:

  • The current working directory of the wrapper (/opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/2).
  • The wrapper executable (/opt/unetlab/wrappers/qemu_wrapper).
  • The command the wrapper runs to launch the node (/opt/qemu-2.4.0/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 and its parameters).

The wrapper hides the errors raised by the virtualization software (QEMU in this case). To see them, we launch the node directly, bypassing the wrapper. This involves two simplifications:

  • We run the node as root, which has fewer restrictions.
  • We launch the node directly, without the wrapper.

In all the cases I analyzed, these simplifications did not prevent the error from reproducing. If an error appears, it is likely the root cause. If not, the problem may lie in the user's permissions or in the wrapper itself.

The command the wrapper uses is visible in the log: the -F parameter specifies the binary, and all the arguments after -- are passed to it. The other flags set the tenant ID (-T), the node ID (-D), the console port (-C) and the terminal title (-t). The terminal title is the node name, which helps to find the right process or log lines on a busy EVE-NG server.

docs.title: Manually Starting the Node
docs.text:
Connect to the EVE-NG server via SSH as root and go to the working directory of the node:

cd /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/2

From there, launch the node binary directly: run the program specified after the -F flag with all the parameters that follow --. The -d debug flag of the wrapper is not passed. For example:

/opt/qemu-2.4.0/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 -nographic -device e1000,netdev=net0,mac=50:05:00:02:00:00 -netdev tap,id=net0,ifname=vun003000500200,script=no ... -cpu host

Without the -d flag, error messages are printed directly to the terminal. In my case, the error was:

qemu-system-x86_64: -drive file=virtioa.qcow2,if=virtio,bus=0,unit=0,cache=none: Could not open 'virtioa.qcow2': No such file or directory

This indicates that the disk image virtioa.qcow2 was probably deleted after the node first started. Wiping the node and starting it again usually fixes the problem, because the image is recreated.

docs.title: Example: Troubleshooting IOL Nodes
docs.text:
The procedure is the same for IOL nodes. For instance, the log might show:

Aug 01 10:29:58 INFO: CWD is /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/3
Aug 01 10:29:58 INFO: starting /opt/unetlab/wrappers/iol_wrapper -C 47265 -L 3 -T 5 -D 3 -t "R3" -k 0 -F /opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/x86_64_crb_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.bin -d 0 -e 1 -s 0 -- -n 1024 -q -m 1024

Change to the node directory:

cd /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/3

Run the node binary manually (note the instance number required at the end):

/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/x86_64_crb_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.bin -n 1024 -q -m 1024 1

The number 1 at the end is the IOL instance.

docs.title: Automating EVE-NG installation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner eve-ng

I install an EVE-NG server every time I prepare a new course. For this reason, I created an Ansible playbook that, starting from an Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04 LTS installation, installs EVE-NG as described in the previous chapters.

The playbook is available in the GitHub repository dedicated to the DevNetOps courses. Let's install Ansible and retrieve the playbook from the repository:

git clone https://github.com/dainok/courses
cd courses
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cd "EVE-NG setup"

At this point, we need to modify the inventory (inventory.yml). In particular, we verify:

  • The IP address of the EVE-NG server (ansible_host).
  • That we can log in with a key (without a password) and, optionally, escalate privileges with sudo without being prompted for a password.
  • Whether we want to create users and how many (dev_users).

To let the users in the sudo group run any command without a password prompt, we edit the /etc/sudoers file with the following configuration:

%sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL

Finally, we run the playbook with the user we can log in with:

./playbook-eveng6-install.yml -u ubuntu
./playbook-eveng6-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags upload
./playbook-eveng6-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags python

At the end, we reboot the EVE-NG server.

To install EVE-NG 5, we start from an Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS installation and use the following playbooks:

./playbook-eveng5-install.yml -u ubuntu
./playbook-eveng5-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags upload
./playbook-eveng5-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags python

docs.title: EVE-NG Linux VM SSH troubleshooting
docs.text: 20 September 2025

docs.title: EVE-NG Linux VM SSH troubleshooting
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced docker eve-ng linux troubleshooting

Special thanks to Carlo Cianfarani for providing this post.

In this post, we explore how to troubleshoot and fix an issue on EVE-NG involving Linux VMs connected through a virtual router instance (Cisco XRd) implemented as a Docker container. Some time ago, I managed to extend EVE-NG to support Docker containers.

docs.title: Lab Scenario
docs.text:
In the scenario depicted, the Ethernet interfaces of the Linux VMs (e.g., plain e1000 or paravirtualized virtio-net) are attached to two different IP subnets, each implemented by a Linux bridge. The Linux VMs run on the QEMU hypervisor, which starts a multithreaded process in userspace for each VM: a main thread plus additional threads, one for each vCPU assigned to the VM.

We can check how EVE-NG networking is implemented under the hood with:

In the output above, vnet0_1 and vnet0_2 are both Linux bridges that implement the Ethernet links connecting the VMs to the interfaces of the virtual router. vunl0_1_0 and vunl0_2_0 are Linux TAP network devices that implement the backend of the virtual Ethernet interfaces of the VMs.

vnet0_3_1 and vnet0_3_2, on the other hand, are Linux veth network devices whose paired veth lives inside the network namespace of the Docker container.

The following command enters the namespaces (PID, network and user) of the XRd container and confirms the associations between the veth pairs.

In this lab, we can ping both local and remote IP addresses successfully, but SSH to the remote VM fails. Let's troubleshoot it.

When we attempt SSH from Linux VM1 to VM2, we can check the TcpInSegs, TcpInErrs and TcpInCsumErrors counters on VM2: they keep incrementing by the same amount (4 packets for each run).

This means VM2 is receiving TCP SYN packets (segments) with an invalid TCP checksum. To confirm it, I used the Linux ftrace framework through the trace-cmd frontend.

The virtual router instance connected to the Linux bridges is a Cisco XRd Docker container running IOS-XR 7.10.2. From a networking perspective, each Docker container runs in a Linux network namespace other than the root (or default) network namespace. EVE-NG creates a veth pair for every Ethernet link connected to the container. In our scenario, one veth device is connected to a Linux bridge in the root network namespace, while its pair lives in the dedicated network namespace of the container. With ftrace, we can dig into the Linux sk_buff kernel structures involved, checking the value of the field we are interested in (skb → ip_summed).

From the viewpoint of the Linux host, ftrace reports that the TCP SYN packets handled by the TAP backend of the Ethernet interface of VM1 in the RX path have ip_summed set to 3, while the TCP packets handled in the RX path by the veth device connected to the remote bridge have ip_summed set to 0.

These values are defined in the Linux kernel C header /include/linux/skbuff.h:

They correspond to CHECKSUM_PARTIAL and CHECKSUM_NONE, respectively. To understand clearly what was really going on, I opened this discussion on Stack Exchange.

The Linux ftrace framework lets us enable static tracepoints built into the kernel. Here we enabled the tracepoints netif_receive_skb_entry and netif_rx_entry, which sit within the relevant kernel network functions implemented by the host Linux kernel and exposed to the low-level device driver code. Then, in the reporting step, we filtered the trace file (trace.dat) with the -F option (nonessential trace entries for ARP requests and replies were filtered out).

According to the trace above, the process qemu-system-x86-11472 with PID 11472 is the main thread (Linux lightweight process) running the QEMU instance of VM1. The RX path processing on the vunl0_1_0 TAP interface runs in the context of this process (EVE-NG assigned node ID 1 to the VM1 node, hence the name vunl0_1_0 for the backend of the virtual Ethernet interface of VM1).

Likewise, spp-17445 is the PID of the thread running within the XRd Docker container. This thread runs the driver code that handles the RX path processing for the vnet0_3_2 veth device, paired with the corresponding veth device within the network namespace of the XRd container (here too, EVE-NG assigned node ID 3 to the XRd node).

As we can see, when we try SSH from VM1 to VM2, VM1 sends out TCP SYN packets with the ip_summed field of the sk_buff set to 3 (CHECKSUM_PARTIAL). This means the network stack of the VM1 kernel sends out TCP packets with an incomplete TCP checksum.

After many hours of troubleshooting, I identified the issue: by default, the Ethernet interfaces exposed to the VMs (e.g., e1000 or virtio-net) have TCP/UDP checksum offloading enabled. The network stack of the Linux kernel assumes that the underlying "NIC hardware" computes and fills in the correct TCP/UDP checksum in outgoing packets.

The problem is that the virtual NIC does not perform that computation at all in its TX path. As a result, TCP/UDP packets are sent with zeroed or corrupted checksum fields. On the receiving side, in the RX path processing, they are delivered to the network stack of the VM Linux kernel, which discards these invalid packets.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
The solution is straightforward: disable TX checksum offloading at the virtual NIC level. We can do it from within the Linux VM as follows (note that disabling RX checksum offloading is not an option, since it is not configurable).

Of course, we need to do the same on the remote Linux VM:

And SSH to the remote VM works.

A different kind of fix is also available. According to the Cisco documentation, there is an optional flag (chksum) applicable to the XRd interfaces. We can set it per interface through the Linux environment variables passed to the container (XR_MGMT_INTERFACES for management interfaces and XR_INTERFACES for data-plane interfaces). It forces the virtual router to compute the relevant TCP/UDP checksum for the ingress packets coming from that interface.

Let's check the current setting of those environment variables:

In the XR_INTERFACES environment variable above, the chksum flag is not set for the first two XRd interfaces (Gi0/0/0/0 and Gi0/0/0/1) used in the lab. Let's try to set the chksum flag for the Gi0/0/0/0 interface only (the XRd ingress interface for the traffic coming from VM1 to VM2). To do so, we stop and wipe the XRd node, so that the XRd Docker container restarts from scratch.

SSH to VM2 still fails, but we can confirm that VM2 receives TCP packets with the correct TCP checksum (TcpInErrs and TcpInCsumErrors no longer keep incrementing on VM2).

In the next step, we fix the issue the other way around by setting the chksum flag for the Gi0/0/0/1 interface:

And this works as well.

docs.title: EVE-NG (SW architecture and docker support)
docs.text: 22 November 2025

docs.title: EVE-NG (SW architecture and docker support)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced docker eve-ng media

Special thanks to Carlo Cianfarani for providing this post.

This presentation provides an in-depth overview of the EVE-NG software architecture, with a particular focus on its backend components, virtualization mechanisms, and the integration of Docker-based nodes.

It walks through the main architectural layers, from the AngularJS/PHP frontend and REST API framework to the internal handling of QEMU/KVM, networking models, and wrapper functions.

The final section highlights the software modifications implemented to extend EVE-NG with Docker support, including changes in PHP modules, wrappers, and system configuration. Together, these slides aim to give a clear understanding of how EVE-NG operates internally and how its capabilities can be expanded to support advanced virtual lab scenarios.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: • EVE-NG (SW architecture and docker support)

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - Introduction
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

If you have used EVE-NG seriously, not just for a quick lab but for building complex topologies that you need to tear down and rebuild regularly, you have probably felt the friction. Every time you want to recreate a lab, you are back in the browser: create the lab, add nodes one by one, pick images from dropdowns, wire interfaces by hand, configure management access. It works, but it does not scale, it is not repeatable, and it is impossible to version-control.

I am a network engineer, and I am used to treating infrastructure as code. EVE-NG has a REST API, so I asked myself: how hard can it be to write a CLI that talks to it properly?

This project is the answer. It is still early (a proof of concept, really), but the core workflow is already useful enough that I am sharing it.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
EVE-NG CLI is an interactive shell that connects to your EVE-NG server and lets you manage it from the terminal. It offers tab completion, command history and color-coded output. Under the hood it is all async Python, so operations that can run in parallel do.

The most powerful feature is lab import from a YAML file I call an HLD (High-Level Design). You describe your topology (nodes, images, interfaces, links) and the CLI does the rest: it creates the lab, provisions every network and node, wires the interfaces, attaches the management network to NAT and pushes the startup configurations for IOL devices. A 10-node lab goes from YAML to fully wired in about five seconds.

docs.title: The Full Framework
docs.text:
EVE-NG CLI is one piece of a broader framework designed to make EVE-NG labs fully repeatable and code-driven. The framework has three components:

  • IaC-ready images: pre-configured node images that are accessible via SSH from the moment they boot, through a dedicated Out-of-Band management network. No console access and no manual first-boot configuration are required.
  • EVE-NG CLI: an interactive terminal interface that builds complete labs from YAML files describing the topology (nodes, images, interfaces, links). One command, and the lab is fully wired.
  • Node configuration: scripts that connect to each node over the OOB network and push the feature configuration described in the HLD. The topology comes up, and the configuration follows automatically. This component is optional, a work in progress and not public yet.

This post focuses on the first two components. Node configuration will get its own post when it is ready for public use.

docs.title: Why Share It Now, at POC Stage?
docs.text: Because the direction of the project should come from people who actually use EVE-NG. I have my own workflow and my own pain points, but I am one person. If you are an EVE-NG power user and there is a workflow you wish you could script or automate, I want to hear about it before I spend weeks building the wrong thing.

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - IaC-ready images
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng iac

In the first post, I described the three components of this framework. The EVE-NG CLI handles lab creation, and node configuration (coming later) handles feature deployment. Both depend on one thing being true: every node in the lab must be reachable via SSH from the moment it boots, before any topology-specific configuration has been applied.

That is what IaC-ready images are for.

docs.title: What Makes an Image IaC-Ready
docs.text:
An IaC-ready image is a standard EVE-NG node image pre-configured with three things:

  • A known administrative user with SSH access enabled.
  • A dedicated management VRF, which keeps the OOB traffic entirely separate from the lab topology.
  • A management interface bound to that VRF and configured to get an IPv4 address via DHCP.

When the CLI imports a lab, it attaches the OOB management network to nat0 on the EVE-NG host automatically. Every node gets a DHCP address over that network at boot, regardless of what happens on the data-plane interfaces. From that point on, the node is reachable over SSH and ready for automated configuration.

The design is intentionally minimal. The image makes no assumptions about the lab topology: it only guarantees reachability. Everything else is handled at the node configuration layer.

IOL images are a special case. IOL loads its startup configuration from an external file (not baked into the image), so the CLI can push the minimal OOB configuration at lab creation time without any pre-configuration step. For QEMU-based images, the configuration must be embedded in the image itself, which is what the build process below handles.

IaC-ready images cannot be shared publicly because of copyright. The person running the framework must build each image from a legally obtained source.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
We clone the repository on the EVE-NG server and install the dependencies:

ssh user@your-eveng-server
git clone https://github.com/dainok/eveng-cli
cd eveng-cli
pip install poetry
poetry install

Then we install the Ansible collections required by the build playbooks:

cd playbooks
poetry run ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml

docs.title: Building IaC-Ready Images
docs.text:
The playbooks directory contains one playbook per supported image type:

  • playbook-c8000v.yml.
  • playbook-csr1000vng.yml.
  • playbook-iol.yml.
  • playbook-nxosv9k.yml.
  • playbook-viosl2.yml.
  • playbook-vios.yml.
  • playbook-vyos.yml.

Each playbook follows the same three-step process:

  • It searches a source directory for matching image files and copies them into /opt/unetlab/addons.
  • It boots a temporary node with the copied image and applies the OOB configuration.
  • It boots the configured image again and verifies that it can reach both pnet0 (the EVE-NG host interface) and the Internet.

For Cisco images, we need the source files from a legally obtained distribution. In my case, I downloaded refplat-20241223-fcs-iso.zip from the Cisco software portal (CML) and extracted the contents into /opt/unetlab-downloads. Then:

cd playbooks
poetry run ./playbook-vios.yml -e search_dir=/opt/unetlab-downloads

When it completes, the configured images appear in /opt/unetlab/addons/qemu, each with the -iac suffix in its name, for example vios-adventerprisek9-m.spa.159-3.m9-iac. That suffix lets the CLI (and you) tell at a glance which images support IaC and which do not.

To build all the supported images at once, a convenience script used in CI before each release is available:

./rebuild_all_templates.sh

This wipes all the existing -iac images and rebuilds them from scratch, which is useful both for testing and for an initial full setup.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a playbook fails, we can run the three steps manually to isolate the problem.

Step 1, copy the image only (skip the configuration):

poetry run ./playbook-vios.yml -e search_dir=/opt/unetlab-downloads -e template_config=false

Step 2, apply the OOB configuration to an already copied image:

poetry run config_scripts/vios_config.py vios-adventerprisek9-m.spa.159-3.m9-iac

Step 3, verify the reachability of the configured image:

poetry run config_scripts/vios_test.py vios-adventerprisek9-m.spa.159-3.m9-iac

Running these steps in sequence lets us pinpoint whether the failure is in image discovery, in the configuration step or in the connectivity verification.

Once the IaC-ready images are in place, we can reference them through the -iac suffix in our HLD YAML files, and the EVE-NG CLI picks them automatically when importing a lab. The next post covers the HLD format in detail.

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - HLD files
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

The primary reason EVE-NG CLI exists is to let you build labs from code. Every other command in the shell (folder navigation, image listing, lab inspection) supports that core workflow. The real feature is this: describe your network topology in a text file, run one command, and get a fully wired lab on the server in seconds.

That text file is the HLD (High-Level Design).

docs.title: The HLD Format
docs.text:
An HLD file is a structured YAML document. At its core, it contains a groups key, which holds one or more node groups. Each group defines a set of nodes that share the same image and are wired together in a specific topology.

You can define as many groups as you need and connect them to each other in arbitrary ways. This makes it possible to describe anything from a simple linear chain to a complex multi-tier network in a single file.

groups:
  - template: "*linux-adv*-iac.bin"
    prefix: R
    count: 4
    topology: linear
    features:
      - loopback:name=Loopback0
interfaces:
  - match: Loopback0
    address: 192.168.0.0/16
    mask: 32
    features:
      - ospf:area=0
  - match: Ethernet
    address: 10.0.0.0/8
    mask: auto
    features:
      - ospf:area=0

Every node in every group is connected by default to the OOB management network (attached to nat0). To exclude a group from OOB, for example a group of devices with no management interface, set use_oob: false on that group.

Optional per-group parameters:

  • ram: the amount of RAM to allocate to each node (MB).
  • cpu: the number of vCPUs to assign to each node.

The features and interfaces keys are reserved for the upcoming node configuration layer, which will push advanced configuration (OSPF, BGP, MPLS, etc.) to the nodes after the first boot. That part of the framework is not released yet.

Example topology files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Topology: Linear
docs.text:
Nodes are connected in a chain, each node linked to the next. Use count to set the number of nodes.

This is useful for simulating a simple WAN backbone, a sequence of routers along a path, or any scenario where traffic flows in a single direction along a chain.

docs.title: Topology: Ring
docs.text:
Nodes are connected in a closed loop: the last node connects back to the first. Use count to set the number of nodes.

This is a natural fit for OSPF ring topologies, resilient metro networks, or anywhere you need a loop with no single point of failure.

docs.title: Topology: Full Mesh
docs.text:
Every node is connected directly to every other node. Use count to set the number of nodes.

This is ideal for iBGP full-mesh scenarios, or any topology where all nodes need a direct adjacency.

docs.title: Topology: Hub-Spoke, Spine-Leaf and Star
docs.text:
This topology type creates a two-tier structure. A set of nodes acts as hubs, and the rest are spokes, each connected to all the hubs. The required parameters are:

  • hubs: the number of hub nodes.
  • count: the number of spoke nodes.
  • connect_hubs: set to true to interconnect the hubs in a full mesh, or false to leave them isolated.

The same topology type covers three different patterns, depending on how you configure it:

Hub-spoke: multiple hubs, connected to each other, with each spoke connected to all the hubs. This is a classic WAN or DMVPN layout.

Spine-leaf: multiple hubs (spines) that are not interconnected (connect_hubs: false), with each leaf connected to all the spines. This is the standard data center fabric topology.

Star: a single hub (hubs: 1) with all the spokes connected to it. It is simple and effective for scenarios with a central aggregation point.

docs.title: Topology: Defined
docs.text:
For anything that does not fit a regular pattern, the defined topology lets you specify connectivity explicitly. You provide a list of links, each containing the names of the nodes to connect, separated by a comma.

Node names are built from the prefix of the group and a sequential number (R1, R2, SW1, etc.).

The defined topology is also the mechanism for connecting nodes across different groups:

This makes it possible to model multi-tier topologies (core, distribution, access) entirely within a single HLD file.

The HLD format is still evolving. If you have a topology that is hard to express with the current types, or a use case that would benefit from a new topology mode, open an issue on GitHub or leave a comment below.

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - Usage and HLD Import
EVE-NG CLI - Usage and HLD Import
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

EVE-NG CLI is still in its early stages. The core workflow, building a lab from an HLD file, is fully functional. For everything else (starting and stopping nodes, connecting to consoles, advanced lab management), the EVE-NG web interface remains the right tool for now. This post covers what the CLI supports today and how to use it.

docs.title: Starting the CLI
docs.text:
The CLI needs to reach an EVE-NG server. You can provide the credentials interactively at startup, but the cleanest approach is to set them as environment variables before launching:

export EVENG_ADDRESS='10.0.0.1'
export EVENG_USERNAME='admin'
export EVENG_PASSWORD='eve'

Then we launch the CLI with:

poetry run eveng_cli/main.py

Once connected, we see the CLI prompt. At any point, we can type help to get the full list of available commands with their arguments and descriptions.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
The image ls command lists every node image available on the EVE-NG server: the template name, the image type and whether it was built as an IaC-ready image (indicated by the -iac suffix):

This is useful to check which images are available before writing an HLD file, and to confirm that the IaC-ready builds completed successfully.

docs.title: Folders
docs.text:
The folder command lets us browse and manage the folder tree on the EVE-NG server.

The last folder we navigated to is saved in the session cache as the current path, so subsequent commands that need a path can use it as a default. Both absolute and relative paths are supported.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
The lab command covers lab creation, inspection and deletion.

Importing a lab from an HLD file is the primary workflow. We start by navigating to the folder where we want to create the lab:

folder ls /Users/Andrea

Then we import the lab by pointing to a local HLD file:

lab add eveng_cli/tests/hld/hld-1-linear-vios.yml

The lab name is taken directly from the filename (without the .yml extension). The CLI then runs through the full import pipeline (creating networks, provisioning nodes, wiring interfaces, attaching the OOB network to nat0 and pushing the startup configurations for IOL nodes), printing a progress line for each step.

Once the lab is created, we can inspect it to verify its metadata and the node status:

This shows the lab name, ID, filename, version and author, followed by a table of all the nodes with their current status, type, image and resource allocation.

docs.title: What Is Missing
docs.text: A few commands are present in the shell but not implemented yet, most notably lab rm. They will be added in upcoming releases. For operations the CLI does not cover yet, the EVE-NG web interface remains fully usable alongside it: the CLI and the browser use the same API and the same data, so we can mix both freely.

docs.title: Key steps for Real-World success
docs.text: 27 November 2024

docs.title: Key steps for Real-World success
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner fundamentals

Before launching any automation project, even before opening our editor, we need to define the essential steps that make it succeed. It is equally important to understand the most common reasons why automation projects fail.

There is often a large gap between expectations and reality in the field, and this gap led me to build a practical approach from my own experience.

In an ideal world, the devices we work with are modern, standardized and compatible with each other, which makes tools, frameworks and orchestrators the perfect fit for rapid operational improvements. In reality, we often find a mix of newer devices and devices that reached end-of-support years ago, each with its own configuration that demands a precise and nuanced approach.

Formal training cannot fully prepare us for these scenarios, because their specific nature defies standardization in traditional courses. Ignoring them is no longer an option, though: the shortage of qualified personnel has made traditional infrastructure management unsustainable. Targeted training projects can improve operations greatly in a short time, and automation is the key to bringing the infrastructure back under control gradually.

docs.title: Key Factors for Project Success
docs.text:
Certain factors contribute significantly to the success of an automation project:

  • Understand the scenario: process automation or task automation.
  • Engage decision-makers: operational improvements require the involvement of the key stakeholders. Without their engagement and support, lasting improvements are nearly impossible.
  • Standardize processes and define use cases: automation requires a clear process. We must be able to define and standardize each step we plan to automate.
  • Modeling: part of the design phase, this step is crucial and often underappreciated. We must map and visualize each process, because this groundwork shapes the entire project.
  • Configuration approach: the choice between a golden configuration and a differential approach has a deep impact on the project, and it is often a long-term commitment.
  • Inventory: the inventory is not just a device list, but a structured set of input data for specific configurations.
  • Maintain an up-to-date lab: each automation project should include a test environment for continuous development and validation.
  • Prepare for large-scale outages: at scale, unmanaged errors can have significant repercussions. Accounting for potential issues is crucial.
  • Document thoroughly: proper documentation keeps the automated processes maintainable.
  • Write reusable code: reusable code lets us broaden the scope of the project over time.
  • Standardize the development environment: standardized, certified environments ensure a reliable automation platform.

These factors are listed by importance and follow their typical order of occurrence in a project.

docs.title: Single Task Automation
docs.text:
I call single task automation an activity that arises from a purely personal need: automating a series of one's own activities (tasks). In most cases, automation in a company starts like this. There are repetitive tasks and, if the person who performs them is creative enough, they write a small piece of software to automate them. Its characteristics are:

  • One-shot.
  • Based on procedural scripts, written to solve a task and generally not reusable.
  • Aimed at personal use.
  • It does not involve the team and remains confined to the individual.
  • Not included in any procedure.
  • Closely tied to the person who developed it.

In short:

  • It is easy to implement (pro).
  • It does not scale, causes a proliferation of scripts and is limited to specific tasks (con).

What characterizes this type of automation the most is its short lifecycle. It is born from the need of an individual and almost never becomes a process, so when the author changes role or company, the automation ceases.

Despite the very high number of hours saved, 80% of my automation projects died as soon as I changed role or company.

docs.title: Process Automation
docs.text:
I call process automation the automation, possibly arising from single task automation, that is accepted at the company level and therefore becomes the way to perform one or more specific tasks. The scripts are documented, maintained and used by a team of people. Moreover, they are the only authorized way to perform the associated tasks. Its characteristics are:

  • The automation is based on frameworks approved by the company and monitored for vulnerabilities.
  • People cannot act except through the approved scripts, which can be a problem in an emergency.
  • Compared to total freedom, the scripts offer little or no freedom of movement, which can also be a problem in an emergency.
  • Changes to the scripts are allowed only with prior authorization and testing.
  • The automation is approved by the company and defined as a standard.

In short:

  • The process is defined, standardized, less subject to human error and, especially with some frameworks, self-documented (pro).
  • Development is generally slower, because of the number of people involved in defining the process, standardizing it and developing it. In the long run, automation also erodes expertise: people get used to running scripts and lose sight of what lies underneath (con).

docs.title: Engaging Decision-Makers
docs.text: In my experience, the push for operational improvements often comes from individual contributors. Automation projects fail, however, unless the process owners are involved from the beginning. Effective operations often involve multiple teams, and changing established workflows requires organizational buy-in. Once the automation is in place, those who resist the transition will need the guidance and support of decision-makers to adapt.

docs.title: Design First and Foremost
docs.text:
A "learning by doing" approach, where we start scripting while we explore the capabilities of a framework, can lead to working solutions but often falls short of reusability and optimization. At some point, we face two options: we scrap everything and rebuild with the knowledge we gained, or we continue with the current approach and accept technical debt, a concept well covered by Gene Kim's books. If left unchecked, that debt grows into a larger problem over time.

"Learning by doing" is invaluable, but more complex projects also need a structured approach. A thoughtful design lets us face automation challenges without bias. Asking the right questions leads to reusable, maintainable solutions:

  • Who will use this automation? People, programs?
  • How will they access it? Through the CLI, orchestrators, APIs?
  • What parameters will they need?
  • When will it be used? Daily, in emergencies, at high frequency?
  • Why is it needed? For provisioning, troubleshooting, compliance?

docs.title: Standardize Processes and Define Use Cases
docs.text: Building automation requires transforming manual processes into automatic ones. Before coding, we must analyze the current process thoroughly, but, like modeling, this phase is often overlooked. In practice, I often end up piecing together the operational processes from the client's habits. Without predefined, standardized procedures, automation risks turning into an endless list of new features.

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
Modeling defines the infrastructure (the target of the automation) as a data structure, much like defining a database schema in application development. The choices made here should be as general as possible, while accommodating the tools we plan to use. Consider an example: an ACL that restricts access to devices:

10.0.7.0/24
10.15.0/24
172.15.0/24

In our scenario, the ACLs manage the primary, secondary and decommissioned sites, and each ACL is "permit" only, with an implicit deny at the end. This ACL structure, however, does not work directly with the Ansible cisco.ios.ios_acls module, which requires specific network and wildcard inputs. We can either:

  • Simplify our data model to match the requirements of the Ansible module, which makes it less readable and limits its flexibility.
  • Use advanced techniques to bridge the data model and the framework of choice, such as Jinja filters in Ansible.

docs.title: Configuration Approach
docs.text:
The choice between a golden configuration and an incremental approach depends not only on the capabilities of the devices, but also on the operational workflow. The choice is pivotal: once made, changing it often requires extensive redevelopment.

A golden configuration gives total control over the configuration but is complex, while the incremental approach is more adaptable but cannot track all the unauthorized changes.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text: In Ansible, an inventory is more than a device list: it includes all the parameters required to configure each device. A well-designed inventory depends on several factors, such as the device list, the input variables and the configuration approach.

docs.title: Up-to-Date Lab
docs.text: Automation projects require a continuous test environment. Each update must be validated in a lab before it goes live in production.

docs.title: Prepare for Large-Scale Outages
docs.text: Automation is essential to manage infrastructure at scale, but any error can affect multiple devices. A robust testing framework reduces this risk without eliminating it, so we should establish procedures for large-scale recovery.

docs.title: Development Environment
docs.text:
The development environment should be standardized, fully documented and reproducible. For Ansible projects, I recommend defining the Python dependencies in a requirements.txt file and the Ansible collections in a requirements.yml file, which gives us an isolated Python environment dedicated to Ansible.

Tracking the changes of the environment is essential. I prefer Git for this, together with tools like:

  • .gitignore to keep the environment clean.
  • Linters to ensure consistent code syntax.
  • Pipelines to validate every change.

docs.title: Simplifying the Data Structure
docs.text: 19 October 2025

docs.title: Simplifying the Data Structure
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals

In all the automation projects I have worked on, the operations teams usually lack the skills needed to manage the automation framework itself.

In other words, the data structures behind Ansible, Terraform and NaC are often too complex for operations teams to handle directly. They are difficult to understand and they increase the risk of mistakes.

And let's not forget: an error introduced into an automation system propagates instantly at scale. The first priority of any automation system must be to prevent errors that could compromise the infrastructure.

docs.title: A Hybrid Approach
docs.text:
Before starting an automation project, I always try to identify a data structure that the operations team can manage, and to define what their day-to-day responsibilities should be.

In most cases, their tasks are limited to creating and deleting objects (networks, addresses). This information often lives in an IPAM system, or sometimes just in Excel spreadsheets. From an Infrastructure-as-Code perspective, I prefer text-based data structures that can be stored and versioned in systems like GitHub or GitLab. Very often, I rely on CSV or YAML files stored alongside the automation code.

Reading data from a CSV and converting it into a structure compatible with Ansible, Terraform or NaC can be quite challenging, though. My approach is therefore to build a parser that reads the data from one or more sources and generates the native data structures required by Ansible, Terraform, NaC or even a combination of them.

This approach, also adopted by other colleagues, has several advantages:

  • The parser can be modified freely, because the generated files make it easy to detect whether a change has introduced errors.
  • It generates data structures for multiple frameworks (and thus redundancy) from a single source of truth.
  • Compliance checks can be embedded in the parser, to validate the resulting data structures.
  • It is fully compatible with CI/CD workflows.

docs.title: Review of SNMP Fundamentals
docs.text: 04 December 2024

docs.title: Review of SNMP Fundamentals
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals snmp

SNMP is a protocol developed to manage network devices. It was designed to configure devices, monitor them and receive push alerts. It was first conceived in 1988 and has evolved over time.

SNMP aimed to be a standard interface to devices, regardless of the vendor. It partially succeeded by formalizing a set of interfaces, but it also failed, because each vendor was allowed to extend the data structure with the interfaces needed to characterize its own devices.

Its security was a problem for several years, to the point that the implementation of device configuration functionalities was significantly limited.

SNMP has been a vital protocol for network monitoring, but its complexity, its initial insecurity and its centralized architecture led to the development of alternative solutions.

In this post, we review the SNMP ecosystem and how to implement and use versions 2 and 3.

docs.title: MIB
docs.text:
MIB is the modeling language that defines the data structure used by SNMP. The MIB (Management Information Base) defines a tree-structured data format that includes all the objects manageable via SNMP. Each object has a unique OID (Object Identifier), which gives access to that specific object.

The tree consists of a standard part and a custom part. Each company can define its own objects by attaching them to the enterprises branch. Since each object must be unique, any company that needs to define its own objects should request a free Private Enterprise Number from IANA. To date, more than 6000 companies have customized the use of SNMP. This has two consequences:

  • It is difficult to find a repository that contains all the updated MIBs.
  • Some MIBs may be incompatible with others, because they are based on different versions.

To retrieve the hostname of a system via SNMP, we can use the sysName object defined in the SNMPv2-MIB. sysName has ID 5, starting from system, which has ID 1. system attaches to mib-2, which has ID 1 and is part of mgmt. Moving up the tree, we find that the OID of sysName is iso.org.dod.internet.mgmt.mib-2.system.5, translated to 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.

sysName is defined as a string that can be accessed in both read and write mode:

sysName OBJECT-TYPE
    SYNTAX DisplayString (SIZE (0..255))
    MAX-ACCESS read-write
    STATUS current

Read and write are the only two permissions possible in SNMP. Security in the first two versions of SNMP was quite weak, so the write operation was disabled on almost all devices. SNMPv3 corrected the security issues, but SNMP remained a monitoring protocol rather than a configuration one.

On Linux, we can download the MIBs with the download-mibs command, included in the snmp-mibs-downloader package:

apt-get -y install snmp snmp-mibs-downloader
download-mibs

At this point, we should be able to translate OIDs correctly between textual and numeric formats:

snmptranslate -m ALL -TB sysNa
snmptranslate -m ALL .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5
snmptranslate -m ALL -On SNMPv2-MIB::sysName
snmptranslate -m ALL -Os .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5
snmptranslate -m ALL -Of .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5

The snmptranslate command converts a numeric OID into a textual OID. The options used in the commands above are:

  • -m ALL: use all the available MIBs.
  • -TB: search for an OID using a keyword.
  • -On: print a textual OID in numeric form.
  • -Os: print only the last element of the OID in textual form.
  • -Of: print the full textual OID.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
A query lets us read the value of one or more objects. The device must be configured to allow us to read that specific value. Here are some examples for SNMPv2 and SNMPv3.

The configuration for SNMPv2 is quite simple: we set a community and the type of access. In the example below, we use the community public, knowing that in a production environment we should use a much more complex string:

snmp-server community public RO

We can enrich the configuration by setting the location and contact fields:

snmp-server location Calisota
snmp-server contact Andrea Dainese
snmp-server ifindex persist

The ifindex persist setting lets the interfaces keep their ID even after a reboot.

We can read the value of a specific OID:

$ snmpget -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 sysName
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName = No Such Instance currently exists at this OID

In this case, the device reports that the OID sysName does not exist. The reason is that the complete OID is sysName.0:

$ snmpget -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 sysName.0
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: R1.example.com

For this reason, I tend to use snmpwalk, which does not stop at the requested OID but traverses all the branches it finds:

$ snmpwalk -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 sysName
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: R1.example.com

We also notice that the downloaded MIBs contain an error, reported with each command. This shows how complex it is to maintain an intact, error-free MIB repository.

Traditional monitoring systems poll devices regularly via SNMP and check the parameters that help determine the behavior of the device. This has two consequences:

  • As the number of devices grows, continuous polling overloads the monitoring system.
  • Continuous polling consumes device resources even when nothing significant changes.

docs.title: Set
docs.text:
The set action lets us assign a value to one or more OIDs. The device must be set up to authenticate and accept this type of operation. In its simplest form (SNMPv2), it requires a community with read-write permissions.

snmp-server community private RW

In the example above, we configured a Cisco device to accept write operations using the community private. In a production environment, the community should of course be a sufficiently complex string. As mentioned, because of the inherent weaknesses of the protocol, this type of implementation is rarely seen.

Once we have configured a privileged community, we can, for example, set the new hostname via SNMP:

$ snmpset -m ALL -v 2c -c private 169.254.1.118 sysName.0 s R1NEW.example.com
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: R1NEW.example.com

The operation changes only the hostname value. If we connect to the device, we discover that the configuration has not been saved. Saving the configuration via SNMP requires specific actions that depend on the device in use.

In the following sections, we see how to save the configuration via SNMP.

docs.title: Finding and Using a MIB
docs.text:
First, we need to check whether the save operation is possible via SNMP. As mentioned, the operation is not standard: if an OID exists, it is likely located within the private.enterprises branch.

We start by searching Google for cisco mib locator, which leads us to the official Cisco page that manages the MIB archive for all the devices:

If we search for config, we find a CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB. We download it along with its dependencies, CISCO-SMI and CISCO-ST-TC, and copy the three files into the /usr/share/snmp/mibs directory.

If the repository is correct, we should be able to verify an OID:

snmptranslate -m ALL -TB ccCopyProtocol

The process was one of trial and error:

  • We hypothesized the existence of an OID to save the configuration.
  • We used Google to find the Cisco MIB archive.
  • We assumed that the string config would be present in the MIB we needed.
  • We downloaded the dependencies until we had a working command.

If we now analyze the CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB, we see that:

This MIB facilitates writing of configuration files of an SNMP Agent running Cisco's IOS in the following ways: to and from the net, copying running configurations to startup configurations and vice-versa, and copying a configuration (running or startup) to and from the local IOS file system.

The MIB is the right one; we only need to understand how to use it.

If we keep reading, we find the following OIDs:

  • ccCopyProtocol: sets the protocol used to transfer the configuration, which we can ignore in our case.
  • ccCopySourceFileType: contains the source file type. The values are described in the ConfigFileType OID, specifically runningConfig=4.
  • ccCopyDestFileType: contains the destination file type. The values are described in the ConfigFileType OID, specifically startupConfig=3.
  • ccCopyEntryRowStatus: lets us start the copy (createAndGo=4).
  • ccCopyState: contains the result of the copy operation. The values are described in the ConfigCopyState OID (waiting=1, running=2, successful=3, failed=4).
  • ConfigCopyFailCause: contains the reason for the failure of the copy operation.

To save the configuration (copy running-config startup-config), we must set the following OIDs using a random index:

  • ccCopySourceFileType.777 i 4
  • ccCopyDestFileType.777 i 3
  • ccCopyEntryRowStatus.777 i 4

We can use a single command:

snmpset -m ALL -v 2c -c private 169.254.1.118 ccCopySourceFileType.777 i 4 ccCopyDestFileType.777 i 3 ccCopyEntryRowStatus.777 i 4

We can then check the outcome of the operation:

snmpget -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 ccCopyState.777

docs.title: SNMP Table
docs.text:
In some cases, certain OIDs can be represented together as a table. When this is possible, there is usually a specific OID that refers to this concept.

In the case above, there is the ccCopyTable OID, which we can query with the snmptable utility:

snmptable -m ALL -v 2c -c public -Cf , 169.254.1.118 ccCopyTable

In the example above, we print the table using a comma as the separator.

A more familiar example is printing the interface table:

snmptable -m ALL -v 2c -c public -Cf , 169.254.1.118 ifTable

docs.title: Trap
docs.text:
In addition to giving access to device data, SNMP can notify an external server of events (traps). The external server must have the necessary MIBs to translate the event, so that people can interpret it.

We can install a simple daemon that receives the traps sent by the devices:

apt-get -y install snmptrapd

The device must be configured to send traps to a specific host:

snmp-server host 169.254.1.1 version 2c public

We can choose which traps to enable, or enable them all indiscriminately:

snmp-server enable traps

The daemon must be configured to accept traps with the community we set (public). We configure the snmptrapd daemon through the /etc/snmp/snmptrapd.conf file:

authCommunity log,execute,net public
traphandle default logger

This way, we accept the traps with the public community and send all the traps to syslog with the logger command.

We restart the daemon:

systemctl restart snmptrapd

At this point, the received traps are forwarded to the syslog daemon:

Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: <UNKNOWN>
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: UDP: [169.254.1.118]:54361->[169.254.1.1]:162
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 1:1:18:10.81
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.4.1.0 iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.2.0.1
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.1.1.6.1.3.16 1
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.1.1.6.1.4.16 2
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.1.1.6.1.5.16 3
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.18.1.3.0 169.254.1.118
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.18.1.4.0 "public"
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.4.3.0 iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.2

The OIDs are numeric and difficult to read.

In the real world, the daemon is associated with a series of handlers that trigger notifications or actions through workflows.

docs.title: SNMPv3
docs.text:
So far, we have focused on SNMPv2. Its simplicity is also its main weakness: most field implementations use very simple communities, and the protocol does not encrypt them.

SNMPv3 operates on two levels: authentication and encryption. There are three possible security levels:

  • noAuthNoPriv: the channel is neither authenticated nor encrypted.
  • authNoPriv: the channel is authenticated (via MD5 or SHA) but not encrypted.
  • authPriv: the channel is authenticated (via MD5 or SHA) and encrypted (using DES or AES).

It is also possible to restrict access to the OID tree, specifying which branches to include or exclude.

The configuration of the devices is therefore more complex and requires creating:

  • A view that includes or excludes the OIDs.
  • A group associated with a security level and the required privilege (read or write).
  • A user associated with the group that meets the requirements of the associated security level.
snmp-server view ROOT iso included
snmp-server group PUB v3 noauth read ROOT
snmp-server group MONITOR v3 auth read ROOT
snmp-server group SECRET v3 priv read ROOT write ROOT
snmp-server user APP1 PUB v3 auth sha password1
snmp-server user APP2 MONITOR v3 auth sha password2
snmp-server user APP3 SECRET v3 auth sha password3 priv aes 256 secretpass3

We can then use the three users to perform queries:

snmpwalk -m ALL -v 3 -l noAuthNoPriv -u APP1 169.254.1.118 sysName
snmpwalk -m ALL -v 3 -l authNoPriv -u APP2 -a SHA -A password2 169.254.1.118 sysName
snmpwalk -m ALL -v 3 -l authPriv -u APP3 -a SHA -A password3 -x AES-256-C -X secretpass3 169.254.1.118 sysName

docs.title: Parsing text with TextFSM
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals textfsm

TextFSM is a framework developed by Google that transforms (parses) human-readable text into structured, machine-readable output.

TextFSM is available as a Python module and is one of the essential tools to automate a network device that requires CLI interaction, because it lets us interpret the output and make decisions.

Let's look at an example: we want to analyze the interfaces of a switch and shut down the ones that are not connected.

The following output is human-readable, but we cannot use it directly in a script.

MGMTSWITCH1#show interfaces status

Port        Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1     to SRV1:eth1-1     connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/2     to SRV2:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/3                        disabled     1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/4     to SRV3:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/5                        notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/6     to ESXi2:vmnic0    connected    trunk      a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/7     to SRV4:CIMC       connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/8     to Router:Gi0/0    connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/9                        notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/10                       notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX

TextFSM converts the output above into a structured format:

[['Gi1/0/1',
  'to SRV1:eth1-1',
  'connected',
  '58',
  'a-full',
  'a-1000',
  '10/100/1000BaseTX'],
 ['Gi1/0/2',
  'to SRV2:mgmt0',
  'notconnect',
  '58',
  'auto',
  'auto',
  '10/100/1000BaseTX'],
 ['Gi1/0/3', ' ', 'disabled', '1', 'auto', 'auto', '10/100/1000BaseTX'],
 ['Gi1/0/4',
  'to SRV3:mgmt0',
  'notconnect',
  '58',
  'auto',
  'auto',
  '10/100/1000BaseTX'],

docs.title: Finite State Machine
docs.text:
TextFSM operates as a finite state machine (FSM). It starts from the Start state and implicitly ends at the EOF state, which is reached at the end of the file.

The process works as follows:

  • The FSM reads the first line of the input text.
  • It matches the line against a set of rules, starting from the top.
  • If a rule matches, the FSM executes the corresponding action and "consumes" the line.
  • It reads the next line of the input and matches it against the rule set again, starting from the top.
  • When the entire input has been processed, the FSM terminates and returns the structured output.

The actions, described below, can modify the default behavior of the FSM.

docs.title: Rule Actions
docs.text:
A simple template contains a set of rules within the Start state, which is mandatory. The Start state is the entry point of the FSM and processes the rules defined within it, starting from the first.

Each rule consists of a regular expression followed by one or more optional actions. The actions fall into these categories:

  • Line Action: controls the selection of the next input line and, consequently, which rule is applied next.
  • Record Action: controls how the extracted values are stored in a record.
  • State Transition: moves the FSM to a different state.

Consider the following example:

Gi1/0/1
Gi1/0/2
Gi1/0/3
Gi1/0/4
Gi1/0/5
Gi1/0/6
Gi1/0/7
Gi1/0/8
Gi1/0/9
Gi1/0/10

The corresponding template is:

Value SLOT (\S+)
Value MODULE (\S+)
Value PORT (\S+)

Start
  ^\s*Gi${SLOT}/${MODULE}/${PORT}\s*$$ -> Record
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error "unexpected line"

In this example, we have three rules within the Start state:

  • The first rule matches the text Gi1/0/1 and extracts the fields SLOT, MODULE and PORT. When this rule matches, the Record action is used.
  • The second rule matches any line that contains zero or more spaces. The default action is NoRecord.
  • The third rule raises an error if a line does not match any of the previous rules. This is a best practice, because it catches template errors as early as possible.

docs.title: TextFSM Line Actions
docs.text:
As discussed, each TextFSM rule can trigger three types of actions: Line Actions, Record Actions and State Transitions.

Line Actions define the behavior of the FSM after processing the current input line:

  • Next (default): finishes processing the current line, reads the next one and resumes matching from the first rule of the current state.
  • Continue: retains the current line and does not reset the matching to the first rule. Processing continues as if no match had occurred (although the variable assignments still take place).

The Continue action is often used together with Record (e.g., Continue.Record) when a line both starts a new record and contains values that must be captured into fields.

Consider the following example:

PING 10.0.0.1:
  size=64 icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.211 ms

PING 10.0.0.2:
  size=64 icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.011 ms

The associated template:

Value DESTINATION (\S+)
Value SIZE (\S+)
Value SEQ (\S+)
Value TTL (\S+)
Value RTT (\S+)

Start
  ^PING.*$$ -> Continue.Record
  ^PING ${DESTINATION}:\s*$$
  ^\s*size=${SIZE} icmp_seq=${SEQ} ttl=${TTL} time=${RTT} ms\s*$$
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

In this example:

  • The first rule detects the beginning of a new record (and implicitly closes the previous one).
  • The second rule is triggered on the same input line and saves the field values into the new record.
  • The first record contains only null fields and is therefore discarded by the FSM.

Continue is frequently used when a field consists of a list of values located on the same line.

Consider the following example:

vlan 1 Gi1/0/1
vlan 2
vlan 3 Gi1/0/2, Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/5
vlan 4 Gi1/0/6, Gi1/0/7

The corresponding template:

Value VLAN (\S+)
Value List INTERFACES ([^,]+)

Start
  ^vlan.* -> Continue.Record
  ^vlan ${VLAN} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){1} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){2} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){3} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){4} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan.*
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

This example uses a more comprehensive approach:

  • As in the previous example, the first rule closes the current record.
  • From the second rule onward, the line is evaluated by multiple rules thanks to the Continue action.
  • The second rule captures the VLAN.
  • The third rule saves the first interface associated with the VLAN.
  • The fourth to seventh rules save the subsequent interfaces.
  • The eighth rule consumes the entire line, whose values were already saved by the previous rules.
  • Since we cannot know the interface names in advance, the interface regular expression matches a substring up to the next comma, which acts as the delimiter.
  • The same regular expression, including the comma, is reused in rules 4 through 7 to shift the captured value progressively.

docs.title: TextFSM Record Actions
docs.text:
As discussed, each TextFSM rule can trigger three types of actions: Line Actions, Record Actions and State Transitions.

The available Record Actions are:

  • NoRecord (default): the FSM moves to the next line of input and re-evaluates the rules from the beginning of the current state, using the same record.
  • Record: the collected values are saved into a record. The field options (explained later) can affect whether the record is stored: for example, a record that lacks a Required field is not saved.
  • Clear: clears all the fields of the current, unsaved record that are not marked as Filldown.
  • Clearall: clears all the fields of the current, unsaved record, including those marked as Filldown.
  • Error: raises an error and stops the execution of the FSM. We can provide an optional error message.

When both a Line Action and a Record Action are present, we separate them with a dot: e.g., Continue.Record, Next.NoRecord. We can always omit the default actions when they are not needed.

docs.title: State Transition
docs.text:
The final action type lets the FSM transition between states. As noted, the initial state is always Start and must be defined explicitly. The final state is implicitly EOF, reached once the entire input has been processed. A special state called End can also be invoked to terminate the execution early.

We can define as many states as we need and create rules to move between them.

A state transition consumes the current input line, and we cannot use Continue together with a state transition. This restriction keeps the FSM loop-free.

Consider the following example:

vlan 1 Gi1/0/1
vlan 2
vlan 3 Gi1/0/2, Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/5
vlan 4 Gi1/0/6, Gi1/0/7

The corresponding template:

Value VLAN (\S+)
Value List INTERFACES ([^,]+)

Start
  ^CONFIGURED -> VLANTable
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

VLANTable
  ^vlan.* -> Continue.Record
  ^vlan ${VLAN} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){1} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){2} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){3} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){4} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan.*
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

This example is similar to the previous one, but in this case we identify the lines that separate sections. The header lets us use a dedicated state for the VLAN analysis.

docs.title: Value Definitions
docs.text:
Now that we have clarified how the FSM works, we can look more closely at how values (fields) are defined in templates. Values are declared in the first section of the template, and each field follows this structure:

Value [option[,option...]] name regex
  • Value: indicates that the line defines a field.
  • option: modifies the behavior of the field within the FSM.
  • name: specifies the name of the field.
  • regex: defines how TextFSM extracts the value, using a regular expression.

The available options are:

  • Required: the record is valid only if this field is populated. Otherwise, the record is discarded.
  • Filldown: the value of the field is retained for the subsequent records, unless it is redefined or cleared. It is useful when a field, once defined, applies to multiple following records.
  • Fillup: similar to Filldown, but it applies the value to the previously captured records that do not yet have a value for this field.
  • Key: declares that the field contributes to the unique identifier of a row.
  • List: specifies that the field contains a list. The matched values are appended to this list.

The most complex part is often crafting suitable regular expressions. Here are a few common examples:

  • \S+: a sequence of non-whitespace characters.
  • \s+: a sequence of whitespace characters.
  • [^,]+: any sequence of characters excluding commas.
  • \d+: a sequence of digits.
  • [A-Fa-f0-9]+: a hexadecimal string.
