  • ([0-9a-fA-F]{2}:){5}[0-9a-fA-F]{2}: a MAC address in the format 01:23:45:67:89:ab (five xx: groups followed by a final xx).
  • \d+(\.\d+){3}: an IP address in the format 10.23.45.167 (digits, followed by three .xxx occurrences).
  • up|down|administratively down: a string that matches exactly one of these states.

An online regex testing tool is very helpful to validate our expressions quickly.

docs.title: TextFSM parsing non-tabular text
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals textfsm

Many network devices provide two commands to retrieve specific information: the first returns a summarized output in tabular format, while the second provides a more detailed view, typically in a non-tabular format where each entry is separated into a specific section.

The tabular format is more human-readable, but non-tabular text is significantly easier for a machine to interpret.

Let's look at an example: the show interfaces command displays detailed information about the interfaces configured on a switch.

GigabitEthernet1/0/1 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
  Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is ecbd.1d38.a901 (bia ecbd.1d38.a901)
  Description: to SRV1:eth1-1
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
     reliability 255/255, txload 1/255, rxload 1/255
  Encapsulation ARPA, loopback not set
  Keepalive set (10 sec)
  Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  input flow-control is on, output flow-control is unsupported
  ARP type: ARPA, ARP Timeout 04:00:00
  Last input 27w3d, output 00:00:01, output hang never
  Last clearing of "show interface" counters never
  Input queue: 0/2000/0/0 (size/max/drops/flushes); Total output drops: 0
  Queueing strategy: fifo
  Output queue: 0/40 (size/max)
  30 second input rate 0 bits/sec, 0 packets/sec
  30 second output rate 1000 bits/sec, 1 packets/sec
     4416551 packets input, 760890620 bytes, 0 no buffer
     Received 254313 broadcasts (23 multicasts)
     0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
     0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     0 watchdog, 23 multicast, 0 pause input
     0 input packets with dribble condition detected
     35009046 packets output, 5719203205 bytes, 0 underruns
     Output 10138785 broadcasts (0 multicasts)

The first step is to identify the pieces of information we are interested in, each of which must be associated with a regular expression. Here are a few examples:

  • Interface: mandatory, it serves as the key: \w+/\d+/\d+.
  • Bandwidth: a string delimited by a comma: [^,]+.
  • Description: a generic string that ends at the end of the line: .+.
  • Line status: one of several possible strings: up|down|administratively down.
  • MAC address: three hexadecimal sequences separated by dots: ([0-9a-f.]{4}\.){2}[0-9a-f]{4}.
  • MTU: a number: \d+.
  • Protocol status: one of several possible strings: up|down.
  • Interface type: a string delimited by a comma: [^,]+.

The value definitions in the template look like this:

Value Key,Required INTERFACE (\w+/\d+/\d+)
Value BANDWIDTH ([^,]+)
Value DESCRIPTION (.+)
Value LINE_STATUS (up|down|administratively down)
Value MAC (([0-9a-f.]{4}\.){2}[0-9a-f]{4})
Value MTU (\d+)
Value PROTOCOL_STATUS (up|down)
Value TYPE ([^,]+)

Next, we analyze the structure of the input text to decide where to insert the Record action that stores the data of each interface.

The information of each interface is grouped in a paragraph that begins with the interface name. Since the output starts with an interface name, we must work within the Start state (note that we cannot use a state transition together with the Continue action).

The line that specifies the interface name also signals the end of the previous record. A first attempt might be the following rule:

^${INTERFACE} is .*$$ -> Record

This rule has a clear flaw: it closes the record, but the data that describes the interface appears afterwards.

The correct approach is this: when we read a new interface line, we close the previous record and use the same line to populate the fields of the new record:

^\w+/\d+/\d+ is -> Continue.Record
^${INTERFACE} is .*$$

The first rule uses the same pattern as the second, but it does not assign any field values. It only closes the previous record and passes the line to the next rule, which opens the new record.

We can now add the subsequent rules to parse the rest of the text:

Start
  ^\w+/\d+/\d+ is -> Continue.Record
  ^${INTERFACE} is ${LINE_STATUS}, line protocol is ${PROTOCOL_STATUS} .*$$
  ^\s+Hardware is ${TYPE}, address is ${MAC} .*$$
  ^\s+Description: ${DESCRIPTION}$$
  ^\s+MTU ${MTU} bytes, BW ${BANDWIDTH}, .*$$
  ^\s+reliability
  ^\s+Encapsulation
  ^\s+Keepalive

The last three rules consume lines we are not interested in. As a best practice, all lines should be consumed, and an error should be raised when unexpected text is found.

Start
  ^\w+/\d+/\d+ is -> Continue.Record
  ^${INTERFACE} is ${LINE_STATUS}, line protocol is ${PROTOCOL_STATUS} .*$$
  ^\s+Hardware is ${TYPE}, address is ${MAC} .*$$
  ^\s+Description: ${DESCRIPTION}$$
  ^\s+MTU ${MTU} bytes, BW ${BANDWIDTH}, .*$$
  ^\s+reliability
  ^\s+Encapsulation
  ^\s+Keepalive
  ^\s+\w+-duplex
  ^\s+input
  ^\s+ARP
  ^\s+Last
  ^\s+Input
  ^\s+Queueing
  ^\s+Output
  ^\s+\d+ \w+ input
  ^\s+\d+ \w+ output
  ^\s+Received
  ^\s+\d+ runts
  ^\s+\d+ input
  ^\s+\d+ watchdog
  ^\s+\d+ output
  ^\s+\d+ unknown
  ^\s+\d+ babbles
  ^\s+\d+ lost
  ^. -> Error

The input text and the associated template are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: TextFSM parsing tabular text
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals textfsm

In the previous post, we discussed how to structure the output of the show interfaces command. Now, for educational purposes, let's see how to structure the equivalent command that returns its output in tabular format: show interfaces status.

Port        Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1     to SRV1:eth1-1     connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/2     to SRV2:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/3                        disabled     1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/4     to SRV3:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX

The first step is to identify the relevant pieces of information, each of which must be associated with a regular expression:

  • Interface: mandatory, it is also the key: \w+/\d+/\d+.
  • Name (description): an optional, generic string that may include spaces: .+?.
  • Status: one of several possible strings: connected|notconnect|disabled.
  • VLAN: a number: \d+.
  • Duplex: a non-space string: \S+.
  • Speed: a non-space string: \S+.

The value definitions in the template look like this:

Value Key,Required INTERFACE (\w+/\d+/\d+)
Value DESCRIPTION (.+?)
Value DUPLEX (\S+)
Value SPEED (\S+)
Value STATUS (connected|notconnect|disabled)
Value VLAN (\d+)

The structure of the input text is simpler than in the previous example: each line is a record.

^${INTERFACE} -> Record

The table includes a header, which we can either consume or use to define a specific state.

Our template therefore includes only the Start and Interface states. Since each line is a record, we need only a minimal number of rules:

Start
  ^Port -> Interface
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

Interface
  ^${INTERFACE}\s+${DESCRIPTION}\s+${STATUS}\s+${VLAN}\s+${DUPLEX}\s+${SPEED}\s+.*$$ -> Record
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

The input text and the associated template are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Pexpect as a tool of last resort
docs.text: 15 February 2026

docs.title: Pexpect as a tool of last resort
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals pexpect

Twenty years ago, when I started automating tasks on the distributed network I was managing, practically no automation tools were available. I started with Expect, which is still my lifesaver today: when I have no other way to interact with a system, Expect is my last resort.

Since I have moved all my development to Python, I now use Pexpect, which lets me integrate automation into an ecosystem I already know well.

docs.title: Preconfiguring Templates for EVE-NG
docs.text:
The goal I set for myself, as part of a larger project, is to preconfigure templates for EVE-NG. Specifically, I need to:

  • Import new templates.
  • Preconfigure each template so that the first interface always belongs to a management VRF, receives an IP address via DHCP, has a privileged user preconfigured and has SSH enabled.
  • Verify that the generated images work as expected (ping, login).
  • Verify the entire process in CI/CD mode after every significant change.

I divided the problem into four parts:

  • Ansible searches for the required files and prepares the environments under /opt/unetlab/addons/qemu.
  • A script configures each image.
  • A script runs an instance and verifies network reachability (ping) and login.
  • Pytest creates temporary instances, configures them and verifies them.

In this article, we focus on the two scripts that handle the configuration and the testing of the images with Pexpect.

docs.title: Starting the Node
docs.text:
In our case, we need to start a command (QEMU) and make decisions based on the output displayed on the screen.

cmd = get_start_qemu_node_cmd(template, **kwargs)
child = pexpect.spawn(
    cmd,
    encoding=None,
    timeout=10,
    echo=False,
)
child.logfile = TeeLogger()

In particular, we treat the output as a stream of bytes. This is necessary because most nodes do not output plain text, but a byte stream that may include special characters (screen clears, colors, etc.).

We needed the TeeLogger class to handle the output correctly and, optionally, save it to a file:

class TeeLogger:
    """Print output in stdout and in file."""

    def __init__(self, log_file=None):
        self.raw = None
        if log_file:
            self.raw = open(log_file, 'wb')

    def write(self, data):
        if isinstance(data, bytes):
            if self.raw:
                self.raw.write(data)
                self.raw.flush()
            text = data.decode(errors='ignore')
        else:
            if self.raw:
                self.raw.write(data.encode(errors='ignore'))
                self.raw.flush()
            text = data

        sys.stdout.write(text)
        sys.stdout.flush()

All that remains is to execute the process:

# Starting node
child = start_qemu_node(template, boot_from_cd=False, **NODE_CONFIG)

# Close before exit
def cleanup():
    """Cleanup before exit."""
    child.kill(signal.SIGTERM)

atexit.register(cleanup)

The cleanup function is called every time the script completes, whether successfully or with errors. Since we do not want the QEMU process to outlive the script, cleanup terminates QEMU before the script exits.

docs.title: Managing the Interactive Session
docs.text:
We are now ready to manage the boot process of the image and configure it as desired. Pexpect lets us detect a string sent by QEMU and execute actions accordingly.

First, for example, we want to send ENTER as soon as the bootloader screen appears:

# Boot menu
child.expect(rb'GNU GRUB', timeout=300)
child.sendline('')

If we are configuring a vIOS image, the next step is to exit the interactive configuration:

# Skip initial configuration
expect_output(
    child,
    'Would you like to enter the initial configuration dialog',
    ERRORS,
    timeout=300,
)
send_cmd(child, 'no')

Here we used two helper functions that simplify the management of the workflow.

The expect_output function waits for a specific text and raises an exception in case of errors or timeouts:

def expect_output(child, expected, errors, timeout=10):
    if isinstance(expected, (bytes, str)):
        expected = [expected]

    patterns = list(expected) + list(errors)
    output = b''

    try:
        res = child.expect(patterns, timeout=timeout)
        output += child.before

        if res < len(expected):
            while True:
                # Consume the rest of the line
                try:
                    child.expect(rb'.+', timeout=0.1)
                    output += child.before
                except pexpect.TIMEOUT:
                    break
            return res, output

        err = errors[res - len(expected)]
        raise RuntimeError(f'Command error {err!r} (expected={expected})')
    except pexpect.TIMEOUT:
        raise pexpect.TIMEOUT(
            f'Timeout occurred (expected={expected}, timeout={timeout})'
        )
    except pexpect.EOF:
        raise RuntimeError(f'EOF reached (expected={expected})')

The send_cmd function displays the text sent to QEMU in green, which makes the process easier to read:

GREEN = '\033[92m'
RESET = '\033[0m'

def send_cmd(child, text, delay=1):
    """Send command using to pexpect process."""
    time.sleep(delay)
    print(f'{GREEN}{text}↵{RESET}')
    child.send(text.encode() + b'\r')

We can then configure the image:

for line in [
    'configure terminal',
    f'username {NODE_CREDENTIALS["username"]} privilege 15 password {NODE_CREDENTIALS["password"]}',
    'hostname vios',
    'ip domain name example.com',
    'crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048',
    'ip ssh version 2',
    'line vty 0 15',
    'login local',
    'transport input ssh',
    'vrf definition mgmt',
    'address-family ipv4',
    'interface GigabitEthernet0/0',
    'vrf forwarding mgmt',
    'ip address dhcp',
    'no shutdown',
]:
    send_cmd(child, line)
    expect_output(child, CONFIG_PROMPT, ERRORS)
send_cmd(child, 'end')

And save the configuration before exiting:

# Save configuration
expect_output(child, EXEC_PROMPT, ERRORS)
send_cmd(child, 'write memory')
expect_output(child, '[OK]', ERRORS)
time.sleep(5)

docs.text:

docs.title: Automated reachability tests for EVE-NG templates
docs.text: 22 February 2026

docs.title: Automated reachability tests for EVE-NG templates
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng fundamentals pexpect

As in the previous post, we now start a QEMU node and verify that:

  • The management interface receives an IP address via DHCP.
  • We can ping the Internet through the management interface.
  • We can log into the node via SSH with privileged access.

docs.title: Waiting for DHCP Configuration
docs.text:
If we did this manually, we would check the interface status until we find a configured IP address. After a few minutes, we would probably suspect a network issue and stop the test.

We need to do exactly the same with Pexpect:

# Wait for IP address
ip_address = None
expect_output(child, EXEC_PROMPT, ERRORS)
for _ in range(10):
    try:
        send_cmd(child, 'show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0')
        _, output = expect_output(child, EXEC_PROMPT, ERRORS)
        match = re.search(rb'Internet address is (\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})', output)
        if match:
            ip_address = match.group(1).decode()
            break
    except pexpect.TIMEOUT:
        pass

if not ip_address:
    raise RuntimeError('IP Address not found')

The script makes 10 attempts with a 10-second pause between them. If no IP address is configured after 10 attempts, the script fails.

docs.title: Reachability Test
docs.text:
At this point, we test connectivity with ping:

# Test reachability
send_cmd(child, 'ping vrf mgmt 8.8.8.8 repeat 5 source GigabitEthernet0/0')
expect_output(child, '!!', ERRORS)

Here too, we wait for a confirmation which, on Cisco IOS-XE devices, means receiving at least two ! characters in response.

docs.title: Login Test
docs.text:
For the login test, we use the IP address detected earlier and test the access from the current system to the QEMU node. The most suitable library for this task is Paramiko:

ssh_client = paramiko.SSHClient()
ssh_client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())
try:
    ssh_client.connect(
        hostname=ip_address,
        username=NODE_CREDENTIALS['username'],
        password=NODE_CREDENTIALS['password'],
        timeout=10,
        look_for_keys=False,
    )
except Exception:
    raise RuntimeError('Cannot connect via SSH')

In this specific case, we do not verify the host key, because the system is disposable.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: Running the script manually lets us observe the entire testing process:

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
At this point, we can optionally consolidate all these steps into a single CI/CD validation pipeline, which runs on every change or whenever a new image is introduced.

The scripts are available in the GitHub repository dedicated to the DevNetOps courses.

docs.title: Collecting information from a network infrastructure
Collecting information from a network infrastructure
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals

During an assessment, we need to gather information from network devices, structure the data, organize it and prepare reports according to the requirements of the stakeholders. If we do this manually, the operational cost is very high. Automating it is not complex, but we need to understand how all the pieces fit together.

This series of articles is inspired by a real project. These are the requirements:

  • Collect information from dozens of devices.
  • The data to collect is partially known, and more may be added later.
  • Data collection must be schedulable and recurring.
  • We must be able to compare the differences between two time intervals.
  • Some reports must be generated whose structure is not known in advance.
  • The time available to implement the automation is extremely limited.

Some products meet part of these requirements, but others are so loosely defined that they demand a level of flexibility rarely found in off-the-shelf solutions. We therefore need a fast, if not immediate, approach that gets us to the result.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
The problem is actually quite straightforward: for simplicity, we separate the discovery phase from the reporting phase.

For the discovery, we proceed as follows:

  • We start from an inventory of all the devices (Cisco IOS XE).
  • We log into each device and retrieve all the necessary information by running a set of commands from a predefined list.
  • We save the raw output of each command to a dedicated file.
  • We use ntc-templates to convert the raw output to JSON.
  • We save all the outputs of a single scan in a specific directory.
  • The scan runs in parallel across multiple devices.

For the reporting, we proceed as follows:

  • We analyze only the data needed for the report, reading the JSON files.
  • We insert the relevant data into a SQLite database.
  • We generate the reports based on the specifications defined during the project.

The following reports will definitely be included:

  • Connected endpoints: MAC address, vendor, IP address, device and port the endpoint is connected to, and VLAN.
  • Physical interfaces: device, interface, CDP and LLDP neighbors, and total number of connected MAC addresses.

docs.title: Gathering structured network data with Netmiko and NTC Templates
Gathering structured network data with Netmiko and NTC Templates
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals netmiko ntc-templates

In the previous post, we planned how to collect information automatically from a large number of devices. Let's now walk through how to address each requirement step by step. Keep in mind that, because of the tight timeline, the automation is spaghetti code that is not easily reusable.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Any automation requires a configuration file to store the global parameters, and a place to store the credentials needed to access the devices. In our case, we save the configuration in a config.yaml file.

The inventory is described by a list that contains the FQDN and the IP address of each device:

inventory:
  - fqdn: switch11.example.com
    ip: 172.25.80.11
  - fqdn: switch12.example.com
    ip: 172.25.80.12
  - fqdn: switch13.example.com
    ip: 172.25.80.13

In our case, using only the FQDN was not enough, because:

  • Not all the device FQDNs were resolvable via DNS.
  • Identifying the devices only by IP address was not practical.

docs.title: Data to Collect
docs.text:
As in the previous step, we use config.yaml to specify all the data to retrieve from the devices:

commands:
  - show authentication sessions
  - show cdp neighbors detail
  - show dot1x all
  - show interfaces
  - show interfaces status
  - show interfaces switchport
  - show interfaces trunk
  - show inventory
  - show ip arp
  - show ip interface
  - show lldp neighbors detail
  - show logging last 200
  - show mac address-table dynamic
  - show running-config
  - show spanning-tree
  - show standby
  - show version
  - show vlan
  - show vrf

All the data needed for the assessment can be retrieved with show commands, so specifying the full list of commands to run on each device is straightforward:

  • Adding or removing a command is within anyone's reach.
  • Commands not supported by a specific device simply produce an empty or error output, which we can ignore.

docs.title: Device Access
docs.text:
The automation must access the devices via SSH, execute a command, collect the output, convert it to JSON and save both the raw and the JSON output to file.

We achieve this as follows:

  • Netmiko handles the device access and the command execution.
  • TextFSM with NTC Templates converts the output to JSON.

We use Netmiko to connect to a device:

ip_address = device.get("ip")
hostname = device.get("fqdn").upper()
netmiko_cfg = {
    'device_type': "cisco_ios",
    'host': ip_address,
    'username': secrets.get("username"),
    'password': secrets.get("password"),
}
try:
    ssh = ConnectHandler(**netmiko_cfg)
except NetmikoTimeoutException:
    print(f"{hostname} ({ip_address}): CONNECTING (TIMEOUT)")
    return device, 'Timeout'

Once connected, and before running any command, we prepare the environment: we create the directory structure that holds the output files and we disable the terminal paging on the connected device:

device_dir = f"output/{timestamp}/{hostname}"
timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d-%H:%M:%S")
os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(f"output/{timestamp}", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(device_dir, exist_ok=True)
ssh.send_command("terminal length 0")

We then execute each command:

for command in config.get("commands"):
    try:
        output = ssh.send_command(command, read_timeout=read_timeout)
    except ReadTimeout:
        print(f"{hostname} ({ip_address}): GETTING {command} (READTIMEOUT)")
        return device, 'ReadTimeout'

We save the raw output to a dedicated TXT file:

filename = f"{device_dir}/{slugify(command)}"
with open(f"{filename}.txt", "w") as fh:
    fh.write(output)

parsed_output = None

We then convert the output to JSON and save it to a dedicated file, but only if the conversion was successful:

parsed_output = None
try:
    parsed_output = get_structured_data(output, platform=platform, command=command)
except TextFSMError:
    pass
if isinstance(parsed_output, dict) or isinstance(parsed_output, list):
    with open(f"{filename}.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(
            parsed_output,
            fh,
            indent=2,
        )

Remember to disconnect from the device after the last command has been executed:

ssh.disconnect()

docs.title: Building network reports from structured JSON data
Building network reports from structured JSON data
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco fundamentals

In the previous post, we saw how to collect information from dozens of devices and convert it, where possible, to JSON.

Now we need to read the necessary information, store it and generate the required reports. We do not know in advance exactly which reports will be requested, but we can reasonably expect that we will need:

  • MAC address, IP address and VLAN of each connected endpoint.
  • CDP and LLDP neighbors of all the physical interfaces across all the devices.
  • Number of MAC addresses connected to each physical interface.

All this information is collected by our discovery script: we only need to read it, save it to a database, update it after each scan and generate the reports.

docs.title: Standardization
docs.text:
To correlate the data, we must define a standard and apply it consistently. In our case, two fields need to be standardized: the MAC address format and the interface name.

Cisco uses a proprietary format to represent MAC addresses. We want to standardize it so we can cross-reference it with external data, in particular to look up the vendor in the IEEE database.

We create a function that converts a MAC address from the Cisco format to the standard format:

def cisco_to_standard_mac(mac: str) -> str:
    """Convert a MAC Address from Cisco to standard format."""
    hex_digits = re.sub(r'[^0-9a-fA-F]', '', mac).lower()
    if len(hex_digits) != 12:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid MAC address: {mac}")
    return ":".join(hex_digits[i:i+2] for i in range(0, 12, 2))

We can then look up the vendor using, for example, the database provided by MAC Lookup.

The second point of attention is the interface naming: Cisco uses both the full name and an abbreviated form. Going from the full name (e.g., GigabitEthernet0/1) to the abbreviated form (e.g., Gi0/1) is straightforward, but the reverse can be tricky. We therefore always use the abbreviated name, converting the full name when necessary:

def truncate_interface_name(iface: str) -> str:
    """Truncate an Interface name so we can match rows on tables."""
    if iface.startswith("FiveGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("FiveGigabitEthernet", "Fi")
    if iface.startswith("FortyGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("FortyGigabitEthernet", "Fo")
    if iface.startswith("GigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("GigabitEthernet", "Gi")
    if iface.startswith("TenGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("TenGigabitEthernet", "Te")
    if iface.startswith("TwentyFiveGigE"):
        iface = iface.replace("TwentyFiveGigE", "Twe")
    if iface.startswith("TwoGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("TwoGigabitEthernet", "Tw")
    return iface

This lets us correlate the data from verbose outputs (e.g., show interfaces) with the data from table outputs (e.g., show mac address-table).

docs.title: Vendor Lookup
docs.text:
During an assessment, it can be very useful to know how many devices belong to a specific vendor. We have already seen how to standardize the MAC address format. We now load the database provided by MAC Lookup into memory, so we can use it for each MAC address:

# Load MAC Address lookup table
with open("maclookup-20260204.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    vendor_list = json.load(f)
vendor_map = []
for entry in vendor_list:
    prefix = entry["macPrefix"].lower()
    vendor_map.append((prefix, entry["vendorName"]))
vendor_map.sort(key=lambda x: -len(x[0]))

docs.title: Loading Data
docs.text:
We now scan the directory that contains the JSON outputs and look for the following files:

  • show-mac-address-table-dynamic.json
  • show-ip-arp.json
  • show-cdp-neighbors-detail.json
  • show-lldp-neighbors-detail.json

For each file type, we load the data into the SQLite database:

for json_file in arp_table_json_files:
    # Get discovery data (timestamp, device)
    timestamp_str = str(json_file).split("/")[1]
    timestamp_dt = datetime.strptime(timestamp_str, "%Y-%m-%d-%H:%M:%S")
    device = str(json_file).split("/")[2]
    vrf = str(json_file).split("/")[3].split("-")[4]

    with json_file.open(encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        # Load output file
        arp_table_data = json.load(fh)
        for row in arp_table_data:
            # Load entry
            ip_address = row["ip_address"]
            mac_address = row["mac_address"]
            iface = row["interface"]
            if mac_address == "Incomplete":
                # Skip incomplete MAC address
                continue
            mac_address = cisco_to_standard_mac(mac_address)

            # Add to bulk database operation
            arp_table_rows.append((
                device,
                mac_address,
                ip_address,
                iface,
                vrf,
                timestamp_dt,
                timestamp_dt
            ))

On large infrastructures, working on one object at a time is not feasible: we must prepare a list of operations and execute them all at once (bulk operations):

cursor.executemany("""
INSERT INTO arp_table (
    device,
    mac_address,
    ip_address,
    interface,
    vrf,
    created_at,
    updated_at
) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT(device, mac_address, ip_address, interface, vrf)
DO UPDATE SET
    updated_at = excluded.updated_at
WHERE excluded.updated_at > arp_table.updated_at;
""", arp_table_rows)
conn.commit()

docs.title: Creating Reports
docs.text:
Once all the data is in the database, generating the reports is straightforward. We produce them in CSV format, which is flexible and easy to work with:

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT device, interface, vrf, mac_address, ip_address, vendor, " \
    "vendor_prefix, created_at, updated_at FROM arp_table")
rows = cursor.fetchall()
with open(ARP_TABLE_CSV_FILE, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as fh:
    writer = csv.writer(fh, delimiter=";", quotechar='"', quoting=csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL)
    writer.writerow(["Device", "Interface", "VRF", "MAC Address", "IP Address",
                     "Vendor", "Vendor Prefix", "First Seen", "Last Seen"])
    writer.writerows(rows)

docs.title: Optimizing a network assessment automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals

In the previous posts, we covered how to automate an infrastructure assessment and how to manage the data to generate meaningful reports. This post closes the series with some considerations on how to optimize the automation.

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
Netmiko generally operates sequentially: it connects to a device only after the previous one is complete. In the past I have used Nornir and I consider it a very efficient scheduler, but it has its own logic and is not immediately intuitive.

Again, because of the very tight timeline, I preferred a quick-and-dirty solution: concurrent.futures.

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
    futures = [executor.submit(worker, device)
               for device in config.get("inventory")]

    for future in as_completed(futures):
        device, result = future.result()

The worker function encapsulates all the steps to connect to a device, execute the commands and handle the output. We can set the number of parallel executions with the max_workers parameter.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
The access credentials can be read from a file or from an environment variable. An environment variable is generally the preferred choice, but the decision depends heavily on where the automation runs.

In principle, the system should be hardened and secure, but on a project with very tight deadlines it is easy to underestimate this step. We can still do our best by using a restricted account that can run only show commands.

docs.title: JSON Conversion
docs.text:
The conversion of the output of each command to JSON deserves a brief explanation.

Netmiko handles this conversion automatically with the use_textfsm parameter. In our example, however, we took a different approach and managed the conversion manually with the get_structured_data function.

The reason comes from experience: we always want the raw output of each command to be available. It is useful during troubleshooting, or when we need to verify the exact output of a command. Moreover, the JSON conversion performed by the ntc_templates library could introduce errors that we cannot anticipate at this stage. By saving the original output of the command, we can verify later whether any error occurred and correct it if needed.

docs.title: MAC Address Randomization
docs.text:
Endpoint devices increasingly use pseudo-random MAC addresses when they connect to wireless networks. We can identify these MAC addresses by analyzing their format.

In our assessment, we set the vendor of such addresses to Unknown. To do this, we create a function that detects whether a MAC address is randomized:

def mac_to_vendor(mac: str) -> str:
    parts = mac.split(":")
    first_byte = int(parts[0], 16)
    if first_byte & 0x02:
        return "Locally Administered", None

    for prefix, vendor in vendor_map:
        if mac.startswith(prefix):
            return vendor, prefix
    return "Unknown", None

docs.title: Preotecting Your Development Environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco digital-self-defence docker fundamentals

For quite some time, I have been following with growing concern the evolution of the attacks that target open-source libraries, designed to compromise the software supply chain. The concept is straightforward: some libraries, developed and maintained by individuals or small teams, are distributed across millions of systems worldwide. Compromising one of these libraries means gaining control over an enormous network of machines.

The most notorious attack of this kind involved the XZ Utils library (2024). Its specific characteristics strongly suggest that it was state-sponsored. Fortunately, it was intercepted in its early stages, because the potential impact would have been catastrophic.

Other notable attacks of the same nature targeted PyTorch (2022), Colors and Faker (2022) and Axios (2026).

The latest incident, the Axios compromise, finally convinced me to change my development workflow fundamentally. Today, there is no reliable way to know whether the libraries we use, directly or transitively, contain malicious code. By the time we find out, it will be too late.

In my work, I often develop software integrations for multiple clients in parallel. If I used a compromised library in any one project, my machine would be compromised, and with it every client integration I am working on.

Given the increasing frequency of these events, and what I believe lies ahead, I concluded that the risk was no longer acceptable. I needed to change my approach.

docs.title: Sandboxing (macOS)
docs.text:
Coming from the Linux world, I have a strong appreciation for Firejail: it is simple to configure, easy to use and a solid model to follow when looking for an equivalent on macOS, my current platform.

Few people know that macOS includes a native sandbox. It is poorly documented and its long-term support is uncertain, but it exists, and in my opinion it is here to stay. On first read, it reminded me a lot of Firejail, so it became my first candidate.

The appeal of a native sandbox was clear: it would let me stay on my existing operating system without introducing additional infrastructure layers (which we explore later).

To use the sandbox, we need to create a profile: a configuration file that defines what is and is not permitted. Here is a basic example:

(version 1)
(allow default)

(deny network*)

(allow file-read-metadata
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]")
)

(deny file-read*
    (regex "^/Users/")
)
(allow file-read*
    (regex "^/dev")
    (regex "^/private")
    (regex "^/usr/bin")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.cache/pre-commit")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.ansible")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.gitconfig")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.ssh/known_hosts")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.terraform.d")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/src/")
)

The profile starts by inheriting the sandbox defaults, then extends them as needed. In this example, I allow the sandbox to read the metadata of the entire Users directory, but I restrict access to the file contents to specific subdirectories.

One limitation becomes apparent immediately: to avoid creating a separate profile for every development environment, I would need a generalized profile, but that means broader permissions, which defeats the purpose.

We can configure the write permissions in a similar way:

(deny file-write*)
(allow file-write*
    (regex "^/dev")
    (regex "^/private")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.cache/pre-commit")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.terraform.d")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/src/")
)

All malware needs outbound network access to function. My profile therefore disables networking entirely.

This makes many essential tools unusable, including package managers like pip and poetry. To address this, I created a second profile, identical to the first with one addition:

(allow network*)

With the profiles in place, we can execute a command inside the sandbox with:

sandbox-exec -f .profile.sb bash

$ sandbox-exec -f /Users/dainese/src/personal/template/.profile.sb bash

The default interactive shell is now zsh.
To update your account to use zsh, please run `chsh -s /bin/zsh`.
For more details, please visit https://support.apple.com/kb/HT208050.
localhost:~ dainese$ ls /Users/dainese/
ls: /Users/dainese/: Operation not permitted

The shell runs inside the sandbox and cannot execute operations that the host system would otherwise permit.

For convenience, I defined two shell aliases:

  • sb launches a sandbox with the no-network profile.
  • sbn launches a sandbox with the network-enabled profile.
alias sb='sandbox-exec -f /Users/dainese/src/personal/template/.profile.sb'
alias sbn='sandbox-exec -f /Users/dainese/src/personal/template/.profile-w-network.sb'

The final piece is logging. To understand what the sandbox blocks, and refine the profile accordingly, we can stream the sandbox events in real time with the log utility:

log stream --style compact --predicate 'sender=="Sandbox" && eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "python"'

$ log stream --style compact --predicate 'sender=="Sandbox" && eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "python"'
Filtering the log data using "sender == "Sandbox" AND composedMessage CONTAINS[c] "python""
Timestamp               Ty Process[PID:TID]
2026-06-06 09:39:19.294 E  kernel[0:59ffbf] (Sandbox) Sandbox: python3.12(49222) deny(1) file-read-data /Users/dainese

In this case, the sandbox reports that the running process is trying to access /Users/dainese.

After several weeks of use, I concluded that the sandbox was not the right approach. I had to add too many exceptions to avoid impacting project timelines, and every exception was a potential vulnerability. I needed a more flexible solution, better aligned with my actual workflow.

docs.title: From Sandbox to Containers
docs.text:
My IDE of choice is Visual Studio Code. VS Code has native Docker integration, which lets us run the entire development and testing lifecycle inside containers. I spent several days evaluating this feature, but I discarded it: the setup felt unnecessarily complex and, critically, it required per-project customization.

To be more precise: in my day-to-day work, the scope of what I develop varies enormously. It can range from complex integrations involving multiple heterogeneous environments (Python, Terraform, external services) to simple throwaway scripts written in under an hour and never touched again.

Both scenarios require external libraries, and both must be handled without significant overhead. I cannot spend an hour configuring an environment for a task that takes thirty minutes.

So I returned to containers, via Docker. I had avoided this solution on macOS because execution is not native (due to the processor architecture) and it requires a virtual machine as the Docker host. As it turns out, this constraint is an advantage: compared to a native Linux environment, it adds an isolation layer between macOS and the container.

The question was how flexible Docker on macOS is in practice.

docs.title: Containers via Docker Desktop
docs.text:
The standard solution for running Docker on macOS is Docker Desktop: essentially a management interface for the virtual machine that acts as the Docker host, plus image and container management.

The first step is to define which local macOS directories the containers can see. We configure it under Settings → Resources → File Sharing → Virtual File Shares.

In my setup, all the source code lives under a single root directory (src), organized into subdirectories: personal, 3rd-party (external collaborative projects) and nts (company projects).

The next step is building a base image that includes everything needed for development. I wrote a simple Dockerfile that defines the build steps:

FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV POETRY_HOME="/opt/poetry"
ENV POETRY_NO_INTERACTION=1
ENV POETRY_VERSION=2.3.4
ENV POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_IN_PROJECT=true
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV PRE_COMMIT_HOME=/src/.cache/pre-commit

ENV PATH="$POETRY_HOME/bin:$PATH"

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl git libatomic1 make openssh-client tree && curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 - && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Non-root user for security
RUN useradd -m dev
USER dev

# Add relaxed SSH client config
RUN mkdir -p /home/dev/.ssh && chmod 700 /home/dev/.ssh
COPY --chown=dev:dev ssh_config /home/dev/.ssh/config
RUN chmod 600 /home/dev/.ssh/config

WORKDIR /src

The key decisions in the image are:

  • The base image is Python 3.12-slim.
  • The environment variables are common to all my projects.
  • It includes development utility packages.
  • It has a non-root user with a relaxed SSH configuration.

Some of my integrations target legacy devices, so I occasionally need a weakened SSH configuration to keep compatibility:

KexAlgorithms +diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1
HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
Ciphers +aes128-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes256-ctr
MACs hmac-sha1,hmac-sha1-96

Host *
  ServerAliveInterval 5
  ServerAliveCountMax 3
  ForwardAgent yes

We build the image with:

docker build --no-cache -t python-dev .

Once the build is complete, we start a container with:

docker run -ti --rm -u dev python-dev:latest bash

At this point, all the pieces are in place. Let's put them together.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
My four core use cases are:

  • Running a one-off command.
  • Getting an interactive shell inside a container for multi-step operations, optionally chaining the output.
  • Running a long-lived server process (e.g., Django) in the same way.
  • Opening additional shells inside an already running container for cross-validation.

In all four cases, I need:

  • Access to the macOS filesystem, where Visual Studio Code runs.
  • A persistent environment (Python venv, Poetry, pre-commit) that does not need to be rebuilt from scratch each time.

We can launch a container with a mapped local directory as follows:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev python-dev:latest bash

The flags are:

  • --rm removes the container immediately after exit, which guarantees a clean state every time.
  • -v .:/src mounts the current macOS directory as /src inside the container, and -w /src sets it as the working directory.
  • -u dev runs the container as the non-root dev user.
  • -t and -i allocate a TTY and keep stdin open, so the container shell feels local.

To expose a TCP port, we use the -p flag to map a local port to the container.

docs.title: Use Case 1: One-Off Command
docs.text:
We navigate to the project directory and run:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev python-dev:latest poetry run ./build.py

The build script runs through Poetry inside the container. The container is destroyed immediately afterward.

docs.title: Use Case 2: Interactive Shell
docs.text:
We navigate to the project directory and run:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev python-dev:latest bash

From here, we can work continuously inside the container:

docs.title: Use Case 3: Server Process
docs.text:
We navigate to the project directory and run:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev -p 8000:8000 python-dev:latest bash

Port 8000 of the container is now reachable on port 8000 of macOS:

docs.title: Use Case 4: Additional Shell in an Existing Container
docs.text:
We retrieve the container ID from docker ps and run:

docker exec -ti 172d5701bbc6 bash

Any environment that requires persistence must write to /src, the only persistent directory. The code written there is saved on the macOS filesystem, but macOS never executes it directly. Python virtual environments, pip and Poetry are installed and run by the Linux container: they are not macOS-executable binaries. All dependencies and packages are scoped entirely to the container.

This approach covers 100% of my current use cases. It isolates the development environment of each project and keeps my macOS system clean of packages whose origin I cannot verify or control.

docs.title: Extensions, Libraries and Plugins
docs.text:
Some residual attack surface remains. In my case: Visual Studio Code extensions, browser extensions and a small number of Homebrew packages.

I have been operating under a zero-trust philosophy for some time. I install only the strictly necessary extensions, sourced exclusively from verified, reputable vendors. I keep browser extensions to an absolute minimum and install them only in a dedicated browser that has no access to credentials. I use a separate browser for security-sensitive tasks, and another for general browsing and anonymous research.

I use third-party software sparingly, only when essential and when containerization is not viable.

We cannot eliminate the risk of running malicious software inadvertently. With this setup, however, the attack surface is dramatically reduced.

docs.title: Git fundamentals for developers and IT professionals
docs.text: 06 September 2024

docs.title: Git fundamentals for developers and IT professionals
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese fundamentals git intermediate media

Git is a distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds to manage the Linux kernel source code. I use Git, together with GitHub, to manage:

  • The source code of the software I develop.
  • The source code and compiled files of my website.
  • The source code of the books I wrote.
  • My notes, written with Obsidian.

Git lets me track every change and, overall, the evolution of a repository. It is well suited to any file that can be represented as text. This is why, for the past few years, I have been writing text in Markdown and following the Documentation as Code approach.

Git is a vital tool that anyone working in IT should master, and it is essential for developers.

Before we start, here are some important considerations:

  • Storage: Git saves every version of every file. For text files, a change can be represented by just the modified lines, but for binary files a revision often means saving a full copy of the file. A repository may therefore grow in size, and it may require maintenance to reduce the space it uses and improve its performance.
  • Clean structure: especially in a team, it is important to adopt a common workflow. The repository should contain only the files necessary to recreate the environment, and no cache, compiled or temporary files.
  • Security: since Git saves permanent copies of all the files added to the repository, be careful about including files with sensitive information such as passwords. We can remove the references to such files locally, but this process is not fully effective on third-party platforms like GitHub.

In this series of posts, we explore the fundamentals of Git. To learn more, I recommend the following resources:

  • Pro Git Book by Scott Chacon and Ben Straub.
  • GIT for Beginners by Anthony Baire.

docs.title: Working Locally
docs.text:
Let's start by creating a local repository. We can initialize any directory, empty or not, as a Git repository:

$ mkdir test
$ cd test
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/dainese/src/test/.git/
localhost:test dainese$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)

The commands above create a .git directory, which contains all the information of the repository. As long as this directory remains intact, the contents of the repository are safe.

When we add a file like README.md, Git marks it as untracked. To include the file in the repository, we add it to the staging area (also called the index) with the add command. Only then can we commit it:

$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        README.md

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
$ git add README.md
$ git commit -m "Add readme file"
[main (root-commit) 18ded90] Add readme file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md

We can think of a commit as a snapshot of the current environment. The snapshot receives a unique identifier (SHA-1 hash), which lets us track it:

$ git log
commit 18ded90e0116a6c228b6a61a9229ff119a1f77f1 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:24:05 2024 +0200

    Add readme file

The commit is associated with the main branch. HEAD indicates our current position: it is a pointer to the commit we are working on.

Using the first characters of the commit ID, we can view its details:

$ git show 18ded90
commit 18ded90e0116a6c228b6a61a9229ff119a1f77f1 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:24:05 2024 +0200

    Add readme file

diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..62c8d0b
--- /dev/null
+++ b/README.md
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+Readme file

docs.title: Staging Area (Index)
docs.text:
The staging area, called the index, reflects the changes that will be consolidated by a commit. We can work with it using the following commands:

  • git add: adds a file to the staging area.
  • git rm: removes a file from the staging area and deletes it.
  • git reset: removes a file from the staging area but does not delete it.
  • git checkout: restores a file from the staging area (the file must not have been added).
  • git diff: shows the differences between the file in the staging area and the current file.

docs.title: Local Branches
docs.text:
When my workspace contains a dataset that only grows, I tend to work with a single branch. For example, my notes, my source code and the compiled version of my website are all stored in repositories with a single branch.

More complex projects need multiple branches. Generally:

  • The main branch contains the latest version of the code I consider stable.
  • I keep branches for the major previous releases, for historical purposes.
  • When I need to make changes, I create a dedicated branch, which I merge into the main branch once all the tests pass.

Let's see how to create a new branch:

$ git checkout -b add_doc
Switched to a new branch 'add_doc'

As an example, we add a file to the branch and create additional branches:

$ echo "Doc file" > HOWTO.md
$ git add HOWTO.md
$ git commit -m "Add howto file"
[add_doc c12d12e] Add howto file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 HOWTO.md
$ git checkout main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git checkout -b add_examples
Switched to a new branch 'add_examples'
$ echo "Example file" > EXAMPLES.md
$ git add EXAMPLES.md
$ git commit -m "Add example file"
[add_examples 8645356] Add example file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 EXAMPLES.md

A branch is a pointer to a commit. When we create a branch, we can specify the pointer (ID, tag, branch) or use the one we are currently on, as we did in the examples above.

Each commit can have:

  • 0 parents, if it is the initial commit.
  • 1 parent, if it is an ordinary commit.
  • 2 or more parents, if it is the result of a merge.

Let's check the current state of our repository:

$ git log --all
commit 86453561ff929c6d6decf6c14b798df7072e59d7 (add_examples)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:28:08 2024 +0200

    Add example file

commit c12d12e8c24d89dfd81505562635e11166d6304d (add_doc)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:27:27 2024 +0200

    Add howto file

commit 18ded90e0116a6c228b6a61a9229ff119a1f77f1 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:24:05 2024 +0200

    Add readme file

We have three commits, one for each branch, and we are currently on the main branch. We can merge the add_doc branch into main:

$ git merge c12d12e8c24d89dfd81505562635e11166d6304d
Updating 18ded90..c12d12e
Fast-forward
 HOWTO.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 HOWTO.md

In this example, we used the ID, but we could have used the branch name.

We can view all the branches with the git branch command, or delete a specific branch with git branch -d add_doc.

docs.title: Merge Conflicts
docs.text:
In the previous example, the branches worked on separate files, so no conflicts occurred. It is common, however, to work on the same files at the same time, and in that case the merge command notifies us of the conflicts:

$ git merge fce3122f882e68f922a718dbdf6ba6a675bec2b7
Auto-merging import.py
CONFLICT (add/add): Merge conflict in import.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

We can check the status:

$ git status
On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Changes to be committed:
        new file:   file2.py

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
        both added:      import.py

In this case, the file file2.py has been added to the staging area, but import.py has been modified by both branches and requires manual intervention. If we examine import.py, we see a structure similar to the following:

<<<<<<< HEAD
import file1

o = file1.obj()
=======
import file2

o = file2.obj()
>>>>>>> fce3122f882e68f922a718dbdf6ba6a675bec2b7

We must correct the file manually, add it to the staging area and commit the changes.

docs.title: Understanding HEAD
docs.text:
We have seen that HEAD is a pointer to a commit. Generally, HEAD points to the latest commit of a branch, so we can say that it always points to a branch.

If we decide to work on a specific commit that is not the latest of a branch (i.e., it does not point to a branch), we are in a detached HEAD state.

We can end up in a detached state in the following cases:

  • Checking out a specific commit hash (SHA-1).
  • Checking out a remote branch without fetching it first.

To make changes from a detached state, we must create a new branch.
