docs.title: Collaborating with Git by working with remote repositories and forks
docs.text: 10 September 2024

docs.title: Collaborating with Git by working with remote repositories and forks
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese fundamentals git intermediate

In the previous post, we covered the basics of using Git locally. Now let's move to real-world scenarios and see how to collaborate with Git through remote repositories.

Working with remote repositories gives us some new functionalities:

  • clone: creates a local copy of a remote repository.
  • pull: updates our local branch with the changes from the remote.
  • push: updates the remote branch with our local changes.

Typically, pull and push are not allowed directly on the main branch. This forces us to always create a new branch for our changes, which we then merge into the main branch.

Moreover, we often do not have permission to create branches on repositories we do not own. In this case, we create a fork, which is a copy of the entire repository we want to work on. We can then create a branch on the new repository, make our changes and ask the original repository, through a Pull Request (PR), to merge them.

Let's take it step by step.

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
First, let's clone a repository of our choice:

$ git clone https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates
Cloning into 'ntc-templates'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 20633, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (3872/3872), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (1262/1262), done.
remote: Total 20633 (delta 3069), reused 2953 (delta 2607), pack-reused 16761 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (20633/20633), 5.68 MiB | 11.11 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (11629/11629), done.

Once inside the directory, we can check which remote repositories our local repository is linked to:

$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (push)

origin is the default name used when we clone a remote repository. We can specify a different name with the -o flag.

docs.title: Fork
docs.text:
In network automation, we often need to fix or improve the code of publicly available frameworks, which is the essence of open source. The repository I chose to guide you through Git includes 46 contributions of mine so far, and I am sure many of you will find opportunities to contribute to this project as well.

The NTC Templates repository is not mine, and I cannot write to it directly. What we can do is create a fork of the repository. On GitHub, we visit the repository in a web browser, expand the Fork menu and create a new fork:

This creates a copy of the repository under our user account. The copy is independent of the original repository, so any change we make stays separate.

Next, let's clone the repository associated with our user account:

$ git clone https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates
Cloning into 'ntc-templates'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 16045, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (3368/3368), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (322/322), done.
remote: Total 16045 (delta 3210), reused 3046 (delta 3046), pack-reused 12677 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (16045/16045), 3.95 MiB | 9.51 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (9387/9387), done.

In this repository, we can create a branch and make all the changes we discussed in the previous post. To update our remote repository, we push the changes and, at least the first time, we specify which remote our branch (test) is associated with:

$ git push --set-upstream origin test
Enumerating objects: 4, done.
Counting objects: 100% (4/4), done.
Delta compression using up to 12 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (2/2), done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 273 bytes | 273.00 KiB/s, done.
Total 3 (delta 1), reused 1 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (1/1), completed with 1 local object.
remote:
remote: Create a pull request for 'test' on GitHub by visiting:
remote:      https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates/pull/new/test
remote:
To https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates
 * [new branch]      test -> test
branch 'test' set up to track 'origin/test'.

We can check which remotes are associated with each branch:

$ git branch -vv
  master d0f4bff [origin/master] cisco_ios_show_interfaces_switchport: Edge case (#1665)
* test   7c5e49f [origin/test] Just a test

Finally, let's add a new remote that also links our local repository to the original repository:

$ git remote add upstream https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates (push)
upstream        https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (fetch)
upstream        https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (push)

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
The fetch command synchronizes our local repository with the metadata of a remote repository. It does not transfer files, but it lets us check whether there are any changes available.

For example, we can use fetch to sync our local repository with the original one (upstream):

$ git fetch upstream
remote: Enumerating objects: 5207, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (2208/2208), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (1037/1037), done.
remote: Total 5207 (delta 1490), reused 1514 (delta 1168), pack-reused 2999 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (5207/5207), 1.90 MiB | 8.76 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (2651/2651), completed with 176 local objects.
From https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates
 * [new branch]      asa-show-acl-brief         -> upstream/asa-show-acl-brief
 * [new branch]      asa_show_run_object_network -> upstream/asa_show_run_object_network
 * [new branch]      feature/cisco_xr_l2vpn_mac -> upstream/feature/cisco_xr_l2vpn_mac

The branches created in the original repository after the fork are now available locally.

docs.title: Branch
docs.text:
As we have seen, our local repository is connected to two remote repositories, and a branch can exist in one or more of them. After the fetch command, we can view the branches:

$ git branch -a
  all
  master
* test
  upstream
  remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/master
  remotes/origin/add_allied_telesis
  remotes/origin/allied_telesis_show_arp
  remotes/origin/allied_telesis_show_etherchannel_summary
  remotes/origin/allied_telesis_show_interface

Remote branches are prefixed with remotes. As mentioned in the previous post, we can use checkout to switch to a specific remote branch, but this puts us in a detached state, because the branch is not available locally.

If we need to modify a remote branch, we associate it with a local branch (by convention, with the same name):

localhost:ntc-templates dainese$ git branch add_allied_telesis remotes/origin/add_allied_telesis
branch 'add_allied_telesis' set up to track 'origin/add_allied_telesis'.

docs.title: Advanced Git commands
docs.text: 19 September 2024

docs.title: Advanced Git commands
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals git

In the last two posts, we covered most of the essential Git features. Let's now look at some additional functionalities that may come in handy.

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
The .gitignore file specifies which files or directories must never be included in a Git repository. It is tailored to each repository and typically excludes:

  • Cache files.
  • Compiled files.
  • Temporary files.
  • Password files.

We can start from GitHub's suggested templates or create our own using the correct format.

docs.title: Stashing Your Work
docs.text:
Sometimes we need to put aside our current work to focus on something more urgent. If we made changes but we are not ready to commit, switching branches does not work, because Git does not know how to handle the uncommitted changes:

$ git checkout master
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
        file1.py
        file2.py

This is where stash comes in. It saves all our changes, including those staged for commit, and lets us retrieve them later:

$ git stash
Saved working directory and index state WIP on test4: 47f10c2 update

Now we can switch branches safely. To retrieve the stashed changes later:

$ git stash pop
On branch test4
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   file5.py

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   file1.py
        modified:   file2.py

Dropped refs/stash@{0} (add5e575a2620fee2141b1c97ab4ba8bc5d245f9)

We can also list all the stashed changes:

$ git stash list
stash@{0}: WIP on test4: 47f10c2 update
stash@{1}: WIP on master: 25372f7 merge

docs.title: Deleting Remote Branches
docs.text:
We can delete local branches with the branch command, but deleting a remote branch requires a push:

$ git push origin --delete allied_telesis_show_arp
To https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates
 - [deleted]         allied_telesis_show_arp

docs.title: Rebase
docs.text:
Rebase integrates changes in a way similar to merge, but it reapplies a series of commits starting from a different base, effectively rewriting the history of the repository. Be careful: it can cause inconsistencies, especially in public repositories where multiple people collaborate.

For example, take a repository with main and the branches fix3 and fix4 waiting to be merged:

If we merge the fix3 branch, the commit IDs are preserved:

The rebase operation, instead, modifies the history of the repository by reapplying the commits of the fix3 branch:

The commit ID of "add readme" has changed, which creates inconsistencies for the users who have not performed the rebase operation.

docs.title: Squashing Commits
docs.text:
When we merge, all the commits of a branch are normally preserved. Over time, this can create unnecessary overhead. We can instead consolidate multiple commits into one:

$ git merge --squash fix3
Squash commit -- not updating HEAD
Automatic merge went well; stopped before committing as requested

This prepares the commit without applying it, so we can review it before finalizing. After the squash, the entire history of the branch is condensed into a single commit.

In the repository of the previous example, we can see that the fix3 branch is not connected to the main branch:

At the end of the merge, we can delete the fix3 branch, because we no longer need it.

docs.title: Reinitializing a Repository
docs.text:
Sometimes we want to reset a repository and wipe out its history, for example when we make a private repository public. Here is how:

mv .git/config config.git
rm -rf .git
git init -b master
mv config.git .git/config
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push -u --force origin master

The steps are:

  • Save the configuration of the repository.
  • Delete the repository structure.
  • Reinitialize the repository.
  • Add all the content to the staging area.
  • Make the first commit.
  • Push the changes, overwriting the remote state.

Note that, on services like GitHub, commits can still be recovered if their ID is known. To erase the history of a repository completely on GitHub, we must delete the repository and recreate it.

docs.title: Undoing the Last Commit
docs.text:
We can undo the last commit without losing our changes:

git reset --soft HEAD~1

This works only if we have not pushed the commit yet. Once pushed, the commit remains recoverable through its ID.

docs.title: Recovering a Deleted File
docs.text:
Git tracks everything, so even if we commit a file that should not have been added and then delete it, we can still retrieve it. To list the deleted files:

localhost:test dainese$ git log --diff-filter D --pretty="format:" --name-only
password.txt

Then we find the commit ID:

localhost:test dainese$ git rev-list HEAD -n 1 -- password.txt
a73306c8511fbedad06a687cc342c1d50c9035f3

And we recover the file:

$ git checkout a73306c8511fbedad06a687cc342c1d50c9035f3^ password.txt
Updated 1 path from 652f7ba

I created a simple script that automates this process, available in my GitHub repository.

docs.title: Permanently Removing Deleted Files
docs.text:
A Git repository always keeps references to deleted files. A handy tool removes the deleted files from the history:

If we use bfg on the repository, the files are also removed from the history:

bfg --delete-files password.txt

The commit IDs have changed:

The old commit ID still exists, however, and if we know it, we can still recover the file:

$ git checkout 2fb4ce83b0015c4a44b45be2f5339613ddabe71f
localhost:test dainese$ ls password.txt
password.txt

To fix this, we must clean the cache:

$ git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive
Enumerating objects: 5, done.
Counting objects: 100% (5/5), done.
Delta compression using up to 12 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Writing objects: 100% (5/5), done.
Total 5 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0

We cannot perform this last operation on remote repositories like GitHub.

docs.title: Updating a Fork
docs.text:
As we have seen, once we fork a repository, it is no longer updated. If we need to submit a patch after a long time, we must start from an updated repository. We can either delete the fork and fork it again, or update it. Here is how to update it:

git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/master master
git rebase upstream/master
git push origin

We are updating the master branch from the upstream remote. All the other branches, local or on other remotes (like origin), remain unchanged.

docs.title: Updating a Branch
docs.text:
When we work on a branch for a long time, it may diverge significantly from the main branch, whether local or remote:

git fetch origin
git merge origin/main

docs.title: Selective Merge
docs.text:
In some cases, we need a selective merge that picks specific commits. Let's take an example we have already seen:

Now we want to merge only one commit of the fix3 branch:

$ git cherry-pick d09ad27123063a6414de0b3de5c3d7a0c2afb2cb
[main 2c57f06] add file4
 Date: Fri Sep 13 14:47:10 2024 +0200
 1 file changed, 0 insertions(+), 0 deletions(-)
 create mode 100644 file4.py

After the merge, the situation looks like this:

docs.title: Tag
docs.text:
We can use tags to mark a commit, which is then associated with a release. Here is how to create a tag:

git tag 0.1
git tag
git push origin --tags

docs.title: Contributing to NTC Templates with Git and GitHub
docs.text: 25 September 2024

docs.title: Contributing to NTC Templates with Git and GitHub
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals git ntc-templates

Let's finally see how to contribute to an open-source project. We use the NTC Templates project as a practical example: I have already developed 46 patches for it.

Let's assume we have already made the necessary changes and we now want to propose them for official inclusion in the NTC Templates repository.

docs.title: Configure Git
docs.text:
We configure the mandatory Git options:

git config --global user.email "andrea.dainese@pm.me"
git config --global user.name "Andrea Dainese"

docs.title: Fork, Clone, Update and Merge the Latest Changes
docs.text:
We fork the NTC Templates GitHub repository via the web and clone the fork locally:

git clone https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates

We add the original upstream:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates

If the repository is already present, we can either update it or recreate it. We covered both options in the previous posts.

docs.title: Make Changes
docs.text:
Our changes must be contained in a specific branch:

git checkout -b fix_for_old_hp_procurve

The NTC Templates project requires each template to be accompanied by a series of validation tests, which prevent regression errors. A regression error is caused by a patch that breaks something that previously worked. To avoid this, each template must include the input files and the expected output.

Our patch therefore includes:

  • The template: ntc_templates/templates/hp_procurve_show_mac-address.textfsm.
  • The raw output: tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.raw.
  • The parsed output: tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.yml.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
I always prefer to run a series of tests locally: it is faster and avoids using unnecessary external resources.

We prepare a Python virtual environment:

sudo apt-get install python3-venv python3-pip
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install tox textfsm ntc_templates pyyaml

When I develop or modify a template, I always create a small script that performs a quick functionality test. The script takes the input file and returns the result after processing it with the TextFSM engine:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import textfsm
import pprint

template_file = "ntc_templates/templates/hp_procurve_show_mac-address.textfsm"
raw_output_file = "tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.raw"

with open(template_file) as fd_t, open(raw_output_file) as fd_o:
    re_table = textfsm.TextFSM(fd_t)
    parsed_header = re_table.header
    parsed_output = re_table.ParseText(fd_o.read())

pprint.pprint(parsed_header)
pprint.pprint(parsed_output)

Or we can use the NTC Templates libraries:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import pprint
from ntc_templates.parse import parse_output

platform = "hp_procurve"
command = "show mac-address"
raw_output_file = "tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.raw"

data = open(raw_output_file, "r").read()
parsed_output = parse_output(platform=platform, command=command, data=data)

pprint.pprint(parsed_output)

Both scripts are available in the GitHub repository.

NTC Templates currently uses poetry to run the tests in the CI/CD pipeline. To run the same tests, we install poetry and run them:

curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -
poetry install
poetry run pytest

All the tests must pass before we proceed.

docs.title: Commit and Pull Request
docs.text:
We add the files, commit and create the pull request to the original repository.

The CI/CD pipeline runs and, if all the tests complete successfully, the patch is soon included in the official repository.

You can see one of the PRs that have already been approved.

docs.title: GitLab as the backbone of IaC
docs.text: 25 January 2026

docs.title: GitLab as the backbone of IaC
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced ci-cd cisco fundamentals git gitlab iac

GitLab has become the de facto standard for managing the software lifecycle within enterprises. It offers a huge number of features and adapts to almost any requirement, which makes it a broad and complex piece of software. For automation, we use GitLab as the foundation to provision our infrastructure as code (IaC).

In the series of posts about Cisco NDO and Cisco ACI, we saw how NaC (Network as Code) lets us configure our fabric in an IaC model. We also saw how an additional parser implements input data validation and defines configurations starting from simplified data structures designed for our infrastructure.

The next step is to move the validation, build and configuration process into a CI/CD pipeline, where:

  • Continuous Integration (CI): change requests are validated before they become part of the infrastructure configuration.
  • Continuous Deployment (CD): after approval by an authorized operator, the configurations are pushed to the production devices.

The entire system is not limited to Cisco NDO and ACI environments. It can be extended to any ecosystem that can be configured programmatically, in particular with Terraform. In this specific case, I implemented a pipeline that configures Cisco NDO, Cisco ACI, Cisco Intersight and VMware vSphere environments.

docs.title: Installing GitLab
docs.text:
I installed GitLab Community Edition on an Ubuntu Linux 24.04 VM:

curl -s https://packages.gitlab.com/install/repositories/gitlab/gitlab-ce/script.deb.sh | bash

At the end of the installation, we can log in as the root user with the password contained in the file /etc/gitlab/initial_root_password.

Before using GitLab, we may need to set the URL in the /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb file:

external_url 'http://172.24.9.183:8060/'

At this point, we can validate and apply the configuration:

gitlab-ctl check-config
gitlab-ctl deploy-page
gitlab-ctl reconfigure

docs.title: Creating a Repository
docs.text:
We now need a repository that contains the source code and manages the CI/CD process. We can create a new repository through the Web UI and upload the code we have already developed via the CLI:

The CI/CD process we designed works only if a Merge Request (MR) is created for every change. In other words, users work on a copy of the code, which is integrated into the main branch (main) only after all the tests have completed successfully. It sounds more complicated than it actually is.

We must protect the repository so that direct changes to the main branch are not allowed. To do this, we go to Settings → Repository → Branch rules and protect the main branch:

We also need to make sure that only working code is merged into the main branch. In Settings → Merge requests, we require the related pipeline to complete successfully before a merge is allowed:

docs.title: Credential Management
docs.text:
The process we created earlier was designed to use a local directory, so we need to adapt it to run within a CI/CD pipeline.

In particular, credentials can no longer be stored in clear text: they must be loaded as environment variables.

In Settings → CI/CD → Variables, we can insert all the required variables. In this case, we have six credentials (Intersight, APIC, vCenter):

The variables are not marked as protected, because we want to use them even in the pipelines triggered by each commit. Assuming that only authorized users have access to this repository, the risk is acceptable.

The environment variables can then be read as follows:

provider "aci" {
  url      = var.url
  username = var.MI_USERNAME
  password = var.MI_PASSWORD
  insecure = var.insecure
}

docs.title: Terraform State File
docs.text:
The second important change to our build process concerns the Terraform state file. The tfstate files can no longer be stored inside the same repository: they must be stored independently, and only one pipeline at a time can run.

GitLab can store the tfstate files itself. We only need to configure Terraform to use the HTTP backend:

terraform {
  backend "http" {
    address        = "http://172.24.9.183:8060/api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/site-mi"
    lock_address   = "http://172.24.9.183:8060/api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/site-mi/lock"
    unlock_address = "http://172.24.9.183:8060/api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/site-mi/lock"
    lock_method    = "POST"
    unlock_method  = "DELETE"
  }
}

By default, Terraform would use the LOCK method, which GitLab does not support. This configuration instructs Terraform to use the POST method on a specific lock file.

To configure the backend correctly, we need the project ID. We go to Settings → General → Naming, description, topics and read the ID associated with our repository:

Once the backend is configured, we instruct Terraform to upload the local tfstate to the backend:

terraform init -reconfigure

docs.title: GitLab Runner
docs.text:
The final step is to add one or more runners. A GitLab runner lets GitLab execute the operations described in a CI/CD pipeline.

We go to Settings → CI/CD → Runners → Project runners → Show runner installation and registration instructions:

We copy the command used to register a runner.

Then we connect to the GitLab VM via SSH, install Docker and install the runner:

curl -L "https://packages.gitlab.com/install/repositories/runner/gitlab-runner/script.deb.sh" | sudo bash
sudo apt install gitlab-runner -y

Finally, we register the runner with the command we copied earlier:

sudo gitlab-runner register --url http://172.24.9.183:8060/ --registration-token <REGISTRATION_TOKEN>

When prompted, we enter the executor (docker) and the default Docker image (alpine:latest).

docs.title: Designing a GitLab CI/CD pipeline for IaC
docs.text: 01 February 2026

docs.title: Designing a GitLab CI/CD pipeline for IaC
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced ci-cd cisco fundamentals git gitlab iac

Our CI/CD process is defined in GitLab by the .gitlab-ci.yml file, located in the root of our repository.

As mentioned earlier, a pipeline is triggered on every commit to validate the code. Specifically, it performs the following checks:

  • Formatting of all the files (linting).
  • Syntax and consistency of our infrastructure files (CSV files).
  • Creation of the infrastructure change plan (build and Terraform plan).

At this point, the user can create a Merge Request (MR), which is approved after a manual review.

After the approval, a second pipeline is triggered to apply the changes to the infrastructure.

docs.title: Check Stage
docs.text:
In the check stage, we build the Python and Poetry environment required for the execution. Then we run the validation tests and build the infrastructure files:

validate-data:
  stage: check
  image: python:3.11
  before_script:
    - pip install --no-cache-dir poetry
    - poetry --version
    - poetry config virtualenvs.in-project true
    - poetry install --no-interaction --no-ansi --with dev
    - poetry env info --path
  script:
    - poetry run pre-commit run -a
    - poetry run ./build-nac-data.py
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - nac-data/
      - site-mi/
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

I usually use pre-commit to run the validation tests. This way, any developer can check the results before committing the code and waiting for the pipeline outcome.

The build phase generates files in the nac-data and site-mi directories. These two directories are treated as artifacts and made available to the subsequent stages.

docs.title: Plan Stage
docs.text:
In the plan stage, the pipeline uses the artifacts created previously and runs Terraform to show the changes that would be applied in production.

mi-apic-plan:
  stage: plan
  image:
    name: hashicorp/terraform:1.14.3
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    TF_HTTP_USERNAME: "gitlab-ci-token"
    TF_HTTP_PASSWORD: $CI_JOB_TOKEN
  dependencies:
    - validate-data
  script:
    - cd site-mi
    - terraform init
    - terraform plan -out=tfplan
    - terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - site-mi/.terraform.lock.hcl
      - site-mi/.terraform/
      - site-mi/plan.txt
      - site-mi/tfplan
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

The Terraform state file is stored in GitLab through the HTTP backend. Access is managed with a user and a token that are always available within the GitLab pipeline. We can see the result under Operate → Terraform states:

docs.title: Apply Stage
docs.text:
The final stage runs only on a merge request (a commit on the main branch). In this stage, Terraform applies the plan produced in the previous stage.

mi-apic-apply:
  stage: apply
  image:
    name: hashicorp/terraform:1.14.3
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    TF_HTTP_USERNAME: "gitlab-ci-token"
    TF_HTTP_PASSWORD: $CI_JOB_TOKEN
  dependencies:
    - mi-apic-plan
    - validate-data
  script:
    - cd site-mi
    - terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan
  # when: manual
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"

We cannot link the validation pipelines (executed on every commit) with the deployment pipelines (executed on every merge request). The two pipelines are therefore independent and, unfortunately, redundant:

  • On every commit, the CI pipeline runs (check and plan stages), so that the code can be integrated into the main branch via a merge request.
  • On every merge request, the CD pipeline runs (check, plan and apply stages) and applies the configuration to the infrastructure.

In this example, we use the merge as the boundary between validation and application. Other variations are possible, for example by using the when option to define additional control points.

docs.title: Multiple Infrastructures
docs.text:
In my case, the infrastructure consists of Cisco NDO, Cisco ACI, Cisco Intersight (UCS) and VMware vSphere. The complete pipeline defines plan and apply jobs for each site and for each environment:

stages:
  - check
  - plan
  - apply
validate-data:
  stage: check
mi-apic-plan:
  stage: plan
mi-apic-apply:
  stage: apply
mi-vcenter-plan:
  stage: plan
mi-vcenter-apply:
  stage: apply
intersight-plan:
  stage: plan
intersight-apply:
  stage: apply

Each commit and merge request executes all eight jobs. Here too, we can optimize by running only the jobs affected by the changes to the infrastructure files.

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD + IaC in action
docs.text: 08 February 2026

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD + IaC in action
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced ci-cd cisco fundamentals git gitlab iac

Let's see in practice how to change our infrastructure with GitLab and the pipeline we created.

We open our GitLab repository, select the file to modify and edit it with the Web IDE:

We modify the infrastructure files the same way we would in Visual Studio Code:

When we are done, we go to source control and use the Create a new branch and commit function, with add-vlan-1510 as the name of the new branch:

Remember that the main branch is protected and direct commits to main are disabled.

We then return to our repository and go to Build → Pipelines to monitor the progress of the jobs:

In this case, we made a mistake. The details show that the job stopped during the data validation:

280  16:46:56 ValueError: With network 1509, VLAN is duplicated on site MI
281  16:46:56 Cleaning up project directory and file based variables
282  16:46:57 ERROR: Job failed: exit code 1

We defined a duplicated VLAN. We modify our code again, fix the error and check the new execution:

All the jobs completed successfully: the data has been validated and a plan has been prepared for each environment. We can open the plan jobs to review the operations that Terraform will execute:

If we are satisfied, we go to Code → Merge requests and create a new MR:

Up to this point, no changes have been applied: the main branch is intact, all the modifications are contained in a dedicated branch and the infrastructure has not been reconfigured:

When we press Merge:

  • The changes are integrated into the main branch.
  • A new pipeline is triggered, which runs all the jobs again and applies the changes to the infrastructure, without any further confirmation.

We return to Build → Pipelines and wait for the jobs to complete:

If we now check the status of the three environments, we can verify that they have been reconfigured and include VLAN 1510.

On the APIC, the BD and the EPG have been created:

On Intersight, the VLAN range has been updated:

On vCenter, the port group has been created:

docs.title: Diving into OAuth 2.0
docs.text: 21 August 2024

docs.title: Diving into OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese api fundamentals intermediate oauth

In this post, we explore some key concepts of the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework. Understanding OAuth 2.0 is crucial to work with APIs protected by this mechanism. OAuth 2.0 defines four main roles:

  • Resource Owner: the entity (often a person) that grants access to a protected resource.
  • Resource Server: the server that hosts the protected resource.
  • Client: the application that needs to access a protected resource and is authorized by the resource owner.
  • Authorization Server: the server that issues an access token to the client after the resource owner has authenticated and authorized the access of the client to the protected resource.

From our perspective, the resource server and the authorization server can be a single entity and typically exist within the same security perimeter.

OAuth 2.0 supports various workflows, known as grant types. Four types are defined, but two are the most commonly used:

  • Authorization Code (3-legged): preferred when the client is a web application running on a server and the resource server is owned by a third party.
  • Client Credentials (2-legged): necessary for machine-to-machine interactions. In this scenario, the client is also the resource owner, so no user authorization is needed.

docs.title: Authorization Code (3-legged)
docs.text:
This is the most common scenario for web applications that need to access third-party data and ask us to authorize that access. Let's consider a practical example: logging into LinkedIn with a Google account.

We start by opening a clean browser and logging into Google, then we access LinkedIn via Google. Google asks us to authorize LinkedIn to access our Google data (name, email, profile picture):

This diagram shows what happens behind the scenes:

  • (1) The user (resource owner) wants to access LinkedIn (OAuth Client) via the browser.
  • (2) LinkedIn redirects the user to Google (Authorization Server) via the pop-up, passing the client_id parameter that identifies LinkedIn as an application registered with Google.
  • (3, 4, 5) The user opens the Google pop-up, authenticates and authorizes LinkedIn to access their Google data.
  • (6) Through the user, Google sends an authorization code to LinkedIn.
  • (7) LinkedIn uses the authorization code to request an access token from Google.
  • (8) Google verifies the authorization code and sends an access token to LinkedIn.
  • (9, 10) LinkedIn uses the access token to access the resources of Google.

Remember that, in real-world scenarios, the resource server and the authorization server are usually a single entity.

docs.title: Client Credentials (2-legged)
docs.text:
This approach is used for machine-to-machine communication via APIs. In this case, there is no resource owner: the client can act as the resource owner, or it can be considered trustworthy based on the credentials it uses. No user authorization is required.

This diagram shows how it works:

  • (1) The application (client) requests an access token from the authorization server.
  • (1) The server (authorization server) verifies the credentials of the application and issues an access token.
  • (2) The application uses the access token to access the resources.

Again, in real-world scenarios, the resource server and the authorization server are typically a single entity.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
For more technical details on the OAuth 2.0 Framework, see the following links:

  • The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: the official specification of the OAuth 2.0 Framework (RFC 6749).
  • Diagrams And Movies Of All The OAuth 2.0 Flows: Takahiko Kawasaki created excellent diagrams for all four workflows.
  • OAuth Flows: the documentation of IBM DataPower Gateway gives a great overview of the OAuth 2.0 Framework. It includes the two diagrams used above, which are very well done.

docs.title: OAuth Authorization Code flow with Patreon
docs.text: 24 August 2024

docs.title: OAuth Authorization Code flow with Patreon
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese api fundamentals intermediate oauth

In the previous post, we introduced the OAuth 2.0 Framework. Now let's look at a practical example of the Authorization Code flow (3-legged).

The term "authorization code" refers to the fact that, in this process, we exchange a temporary token (the authorization code) for an access token, which grants us access to the protected resources.

docs.title: Patreon Integration
docs.text: Our example focuses on Patreon, where we want to automate certain tasks using the Patreon API. According to the documentation, authentication must be done via OAuth, and the full procedure is described there.

docs.title: Registering a New Application
docs.text:
First, we register a new application on Patreon. We go to Clients & API Keys → Create Client:

  • Name: Test API.
  • Description: Testing API via OAuth.
  • App Category: Member Benefits.
  • Redirect URIs: http://localhost:5000/callback.
  • Client API Version: 2.

After we confirm, the client application looks like this:

docs.title: Developing the WebApp
docs.text:
Next, we create a simple WebApp that implements the workflow we discussed:

In this scenario:

  • We act as the Resource Owner.
  • The WebApp we develop is the OAuth Client.
  • Patreon is both the Authorization Server and the Resource Server.

The flow is as follows:

  • (1) The user (resource owner) accesses the WebApp (OAuth Client) via a browser.
  • (2) The WebApp redirects the user to Patreon (Authorization Server) via a pop-up.
  • (3, 4, 5) The user authenticates on Patreon and authorizes the WebApp to access their Patreon data.
  • (6) Patreon sends an authorization code to the WebApp through the user.
  • (7) The WebApp uses the authorization code to request an access token from Patreon.
  • (8) Patreon verifies the authorization code and sends an access token to the WebApp.
  • (9, 10) The WebApp uses the access token to access the resources of Patreon.

docs.title: Setting Up the WebApp with Flask
docs.text:
We build the WebApp with Flask. It saves all the necessary access data in a secrets.yml file. The functions that save and read the configuration look like this:

def save_config():
    config = {
        "client_id": app.config.get("client_id"),
        "client_secret": app.config.get("client_secret"),
        "access_token": app.config.get("access_token"),
    }
    with open("secrets.yml", "w") as fh:
        yaml.dump(config, fh, default_flow_style=False)


def read_config():
    try:
        with open("secrets.yml", "r") as fh:
            config = yaml.safe_load(fh)
    except FileNotFoundError as err:
        config = {}
    app.config.update(
        client_id=config.get("client_id"),
        client_secret=config.get("client_secret"),
        access_token=config.get("access_token"),
    )

To start the WebApp, we run:

flask run

We open the browser and go to http://localhost:5000 to configure the WebApp with the Client ID and the Client Secret obtained earlier. In a real application, these credentials are stored within the application and are not accessible to the user:

After the configuration, we see a link to access Patreon and authorize the WebApp. The documentation specifies that this link must include three parameters, plus two optional ones:

  • response_type: code (the application is starting the authorization code flow).
  • client_id: the Client ID obtained during the Patreon setup.
  • redirect_uri: the URL where Patreon sends the authorization code after the user authorizes our WebApp.
  • scope (optional): the permissions the application requests.
  • state (optional): a value used as protection against CSRF.

Once the application is authorized, Patreon redirects the user to the callback URL, passing the authorization code and the state (see above). Since Patreon does not interact directly with the WebApp, we can create internal applications that are not externally accessible.

When the WebApp receives the authorization code from the user, it sends the code to Patreon. Patreon verifies the code and returns an access token to the WebApp. The WebApp sends the following to the Authorization Server:

  • code: the authorization code received through the redirection of the user.
  • grant_type: authorization_code.
  • client_id: the Client ID obtained during the Patreon setup.
  • client_secret: the Client Secret obtained during the Patreon setup.

The WebApp uses the access token it received to access the data of Patreon:

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {app.config['access_token']}"}
uri = "https://www.patreon.com/api/oauth2/api/current_user"
req = requests.get(uri, headers=headers)

The source code of the WebApp is available in this GitHub repository.

docs.title: OAuth Client Credentials flow with Patreon
docs.text: 26 August 2024

docs.title: OAuth Client Credentials flow with Patreon
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese api beginner fundamentals oauth

In the previous post, we covered how to implement the Authorization Code flow (3-legged) with the OAuth 2.0 Framework. Now let's look at a practical example of the Client Credentials flow (2-legged).

docs.title: Patreon
docs.text:
We keep using Patreon as our platform, building on what we discussed earlier.

First, we register a new application on Patreon. We go to Clients & API Keys → Create Client:

  • Name: Test API.
  • Description: Testing API via OAuth.
  • App Category: Member Benefits.
  • Redirect URIs: http://localhost:5000/callback.
  • Client API Version: 2.

After we confirm, the client application looks like this:

According to the official documentation, when we work with the API we can use the Creator's Access Token.

Next, we create a simple script that implements the workflow described above:

In this scenario:

  • The script we develop is the OAuth Client.
  • Patreon is both the Authorization Server and the Resource Server.

The flow is as follows:

  • (1) The server (authorization server) authenticates the script (OAuth client).
  • (2) The script can then access the resources (Resource Server).

Authentication in this case is straightforward and relies entirely on a token (the Creator's Access Token) obtained during the initial setup. In a real application, these credentials are stored within the application and are not accessible to the user.

In real-world scenarios, the resource server and the authorization server are typically a single entity. If that were not the case, the script would need to send the Client ID and the Client Secret to the authorization server (as discussed in the previous post) to obtain the access token required to access the resources.

As in the previous example, we must include the access token in the HTTP header of every API request:

headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {config['access_token']}"}
uri = "https://www.patreon.com/api/oauth2/api/current_user"
req = requests.get(uri, headers=headers)

The source code of the script is available in this GitHub repository.

docs.title: Simplifying documentation with Markdown and CI CD
docs.text: 05 February 2025

docs.title: Simplifying documentation with Markdown and CI CD
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ci-cd documentation fundamentals markdown

Documentation is a recurring challenge in every company I have encountered. It is a complex topic: creating documentation is labor-intensive, but keeping it up to date is even more demanding. The result is often outdated or non-existent documentation.

For years, I have worked on improving documentation processes. My approach is to improve the tools so they become more efficient, and to add automation. In many cases, we can derive the documentation directly from the infrastructure, which minimizes manual data collection and lets people focus on analysis, commentary and summarization.

It may look like a small detail, but I believe a different approach to documentation can bring significant benefits to organizations.

docs.title: What Makes Great Documentation?
docs.text:
Whatever platform a company uses, it should support all types of documentation: process, technical and compliance. Choosing the right tool requires considering the needs of all the teams. I recommend the following key features:

  • Export to PDF.
  • Support for macros, even complex ones.
  • Integration with APIs.
  • Metadata for each document: author, date, confidentiality level.

docs.title: Why I Avoid Traditional Word Processors
docs.text:
The most commonly used tool to write documents is Microsoft Word. In some cases, I have also seen LibreOffice or Wiki-style collaborative systems.

Microsoft Word is undoubtedly powerful and offers countless features, but its complexity often means that these features are underused.

I avoid traditional word processors for several reasons:

  • Incompatible with version control: their binary data structure does not work well with tools like Git.
  • Layout mixed with content: formatting and content are intertwined, which complicates workflows.
  • Inconsistent layouts: achieving uniform formatting can be unnecessarily time-consuming.

I find the combination of content creation and formatting inefficient. Authors should focus on writing, not on how their text looks, and save valuable time.

docs.title: Not Everything Needs to Be Documented
docs.text:
Over-documentation often highlights deeper process issues. Organizations should consider these key points:

  • Base skills: employees should have fundamental skills. Documentation is not a substitute for basic training.
  • Documentation is not reporting: documentation should be concise and essential for the operations of the company, unlike extensive reports.
  • Readability: hundreds of unreadable pages are a waste of time. Keep it simple and practical.
  • Regular updates: allocate time to maintain and update the documentation.
  • Standardization over customization: if every product requires unique documentation, consider standardizing the products instead of creating endless variations.

docs.title: The Perfect Tool for My Documentation Workflow
docs.text:
If you read the previous section, you understand why my ideal tool is not Microsoft Word or similar platforms. My perfect tool lets me write in Markdown while integrating external content dynamically.

In a corporate setting, I have successfully adapted to XWiki in the past.

For my personal projects, which are our focus here, I rely on Markdown files stored in Git repositories. This setup lets me manage document revisions seamlessly. Recently, I have been using Obsidian, although the specific tool is not critical.

All the documentation I create for myself, whether for my website, books, notes or courses, is written in Markdown and saved on Git. This workflow lets me focus entirely on the content without being distracted by formatting.

Presentations and spreadsheets, of course, require a different approach.

docs.title: Markdown: The Ideal Language for Simple and Effective Documentation
docs.text:
Markdown is a lightweight markup language created in 2004. It is designed to format documents, and its simplicity makes it very effective. We can easily convert Markdown files into HTML and style them with CSS.

One of the key advantages of Markdown is its readability: even in its raw form, it is structured in a way that is easy to read.

Markdown files are plain text, which means they work seamlessly with any text-searching tool and can be versioned easily with Git or similar systems.

One of the downsides of Markdown is the lack of an official standard. This can create confusion and, at times, compatibility issues between tools. Specifically:

  • Inconsistent syntax: for example, headings can be defined with # or =.
  • Limited feature support: some tools do not support all the Markdown features, such as tables.
  • Proprietary extensions: certain tools introduce unique features that are not universally compatible.

Despite these drawbacks, Markdown remains my ideal tool for documentation. Here is why:

  • Focus on content: it lets writers prioritize the message over the layout.
  • Comprehensive formatting options: it supports essential elements such as headings, paragraphs, bullet and numbered lists, images, tables, bold, italic and underlined text, links, code blocks and quotes.
  • Custom functionality: it can be extended to meet specific needs, which gives flexibility to diverse projects.

Whether we are building documentation, writing a book or organizing notes, Markdown lets us focus on what matters most: the content.

docs.title: My Ideal Workflow for Publishing
docs.text:
After extensive testing, I developed an ideal workflow:

The same content generates both the printed book in PDF format and the electronic version in ePub format. After various tests, I decided to use Pandoc to generate the ePub version and WeasyPrint to generate the PDFs. The PDFs, styled differently, are used both to share digital documents and to create printed ones.

Both scripts are available in my GitHub repository, together with the style sheets and an example book in both ePub and PDF formats.

docs.title: Electronic Version (ePub)
docs.text:
The process to generate the electronic version is very straightforward: Pandoc takes a template, converts the text directly from Markdown and applies the style sheets designed specifically for the ePub format. Pandoc also adds the cover and generates the table of contents (ToC).

The command I use to create an ePub from Markdown looks like this:

pandoc --from markdown-smart --to epub3 --toc --toc-depth=1 --css=css/fonts.css --css=css/common.css --css=css/epub.css --css=css/style.css --template=default.epub3 --epub-cover-image=cover.jpg --output book.epub --metadata-file=metadata.yml

I split the style sheets into multiple files, because some of them are also used to produce the printed version. The epub.css file contains all the styles specific to the electronic version.

The metadata file includes all the information embedded in the ePub file. In my case, it also includes specific details (like toc-title) that Pandoc needs to generate the ePub.

belongs-to-collection: Sample Books
creator:
  - role: author
    text: Andrea Dainese
description: null
rights: © 2024 Andrea Dainese
title:
  - text: Sample Book
    type: main
toc-title: Table of contents

The toc-title parameter, in particular, is not documented.

Pandoc comes with a set of templates to generate files in the most common formats, with default settings that work well in most cases. For ePub, the default template works perfectly as it is.

docs.title: Printed Version (PDF)
docs.text:
The process to generate the printed version is more complex, because we must enrich the style manually with:

  • Page numbers.
  • Page breaks.
  • Headers and footers.
  • A table of contents (ToC).

So far, I have not found a way to generate a PDF with an acceptable style directly from Markdown. After various tests, I decided to use the WeasyPrint suite. Specifically:

  • With the Markdown library, I convert the content into HTML.
  • I create a single HTML file manually, adding the header, the footer, the ToC and the individual chapters converted previously.
  • From Python, I use WeasyPrint to generate the PDF from the HTML file and apply the necessary style sheets.
weasyprint.HTML(f"{book_folder}.html").write_pdf(
    f"../{book_folder}.pdf",
    stylesheets=[
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/common/css/fonts.css"),
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/common/css/common.css"),
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/book/css/paper_size.css"),
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/book/css/style.css"),
    ],
    font_config=font_config,
)

Compared to other libraries, WeasyPrint gave me satisfying results, even with very complex style sheets.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
Once the publishing process is automated, we can integrate it into a CI/CD pipeline where every change or commit triggers a series of checks, followed by the publication.

In a business context, the pipeline could, for example:

  • Require confirmation or validation from a third party.
  • Notify the stakeholders of a new version of a document.
  • Highlight the differences compared to the previous version automatically.

For my personal content, my pipeline includes:

  • Checking the structure, integrity and compliance of the YAML files I use to describe each book.
  • Checking the structure, integrity and compliance of the style sheets (CSS).
  • Checking the structure, integrity and compliance of each Markdown file.
  • Checking the spelling in each Markdown file.

These four steps are checked before every commit with pre-commit, and they are also verified server-side after the push, through the CI pipeline.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Writing presentations with Markdown
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ci-cd documentation fundamentals jinja2 markdown

Previously, we discussed how to improve documentation management by focusing on content rather than tools. Specifically, we explored how to generate high-quality documents with Markdown, CSS and WeasyPrint.

For documents, optimization is not only about streamlining the writing of content, but also about automating parts of the process. Many business reports, for instance, can be generated automatically, and analysts only need to provide the commentary on the data.

For my personal productivity, I faced a similar challenge: improving the creation of slides in the same way.

docs.title: Microsoft PowerPoint
docs.text:
My experience with PowerPoint has been largely negative, and I know that many share this sentiment. In theory it supports master templates and offers a wide range of features, but in practice it has significant issues. Transferring content between presentations with different formats is error-prone, and it is difficult to maintain a consistent style.

In enterprise environments, it is common to find presentations with mismatched and outdated styles. Centralizing templates at the organizational level is virtually impossible.

docs.title: Google Slides
docs.text:
Google Slides impressed me with its simplicity. Its essential feature set is enough for my needs and allows clean presentations with consistent styles. Moving content between different presentations is also relatively easy.

From a strategic perspective, however, I am moving towards a cloud exit approach. Google uses a proprietary format that is fully functional only within its ecosystem. I can export presentations to other formats, but this reintroduces the very issues I wanted to avoid.

docs.title: Slides as Code
docs.text:
Several tools let us create slides in Markdown, including:

  • Slidev.
  • Marp.
  • Reveal.js.

Many of them are built on Node.js, which I am not familiar with, and some lack features essential to my workflow. I also wanted to avoid relying on a framework that I cannot fully control.

I therefore went back to the approach I had already developed for document generation: Markdown, CSS and WeasyPrint.

docs.title: Styling Considerations
docs.text:
Documents typically follow a structured format (unless we design highly customized brochures). CSS, especially as implemented in WeasyPrint, offers a high degree of customization, though it is not a perfect solution: laying out a webpage on a screen differs significantly from typesetting a PDF document.

The compromises required for document formatting were largely acceptable. Designing a presentation is an entirely different challenge, because slides are inherently more artistic.

My presentations, however, are usually technical, with a simple layout of text and images. For my use case, efficiency in structuring slides outweighs the need for pixel-perfect positioning of the elements.

docs.title: Defining the Presentation Structure
docs.text:
As in my document generation workflow, I use YAML to define the core parameters of each presentation:

title: Sample Presentation
subtitle: Recipes and real world examples by the creator of UNetLab
version: 1
language: en
logo: main
logos:
  main: ../templates/slides/images/logo-ad.png
  small: ../templates/slides/images/logo-ad-small.png
footer: © Andrea Dainese - No AI were harmed during the making of these slides.

This structure lets me associate different logos with different layouts. A dictionary stores the logo options, with a primary logo set as the default.

Each slide includes metadata that specifies the layout and the associated logo:

---
layout: title
logo: main
---
# Sample Presentation

## Recipes and real world examples by the creator of UNetLab

The content of the slide is written in Markdown.

Markdown has limitations (many of which are actually its strengths), but I needed flexibility. To address this, I added HTML support:

---
layout: main
logo: small
---
# #WhoAmI

## Andrea Dainese

- Senior Network & Security Architect with 20+ years’ experience in securing complex IT and OT infrastructures
- Focused on cyber security strategies, GDPR/ISO 27001 compliance and Automation
- Cisco (CCIE), VMware, Red Hat... certified
- Father of [Unified Networking Lab (UNetLab)](https://www.adainese.it/blog/2019/01/01/unified-networking-lab-unetlab-the-story/)
- Privacy and digital security evangelist

[https://adainese.it](https://adainese.it)
{: .right}

In this example, I use the attr_list extension to assign a .right class, which aligns the link to my website to the right. I also display the key links with FontAwesome icons embedded directly in HTML.

This approach fully met my requirements: I store presentations as Markdown in a Git repository and render them to PDF with a simple script that I completely control.

Any style update is reflected instantly in all the presentations.

docs.title: Template Processing
docs.text:
The script reads the individual slides (one per file) and compiles them into a single HTML file using a Jinja template:

<body>
    {% for slide in slides %}
    <section id="{{ slide.id }}" class="slide {{ slide.meta.layout }}-slide">
        <div class="content">
            {% if slide.logo %}<div class="logo"><img src="{{ slide.logo }}" /></div>{% endif %}
            {{ slide.content | safe }}
        </div>
        {% if footer %}<div class="footer">{{ footer }}</div>{% endif %}
        <div class="page_counter">{{ loop.index }} / {{ slides | length }}</div>
    </section>
    {% endfor %}
</body>
</html>

Each slide is wrapped in a <section> element, with an optional footer and the slide number.

The CSS styles are linked based on the metadata defined in each slide file.

docs.title: Generating the PDF
docs.text:
To compile the final presentation, we combine the Markdown content, the Jinja template, the style sheets and the fonts into a single PDF.

We read each Markdown file and store the content:

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=[
        "markdown.extensions.meta",
        "markdown.extensions.fenced_code",
        "markdown.extensions.codehilite",
        "markdown.extensions.footnotes",
        "markdown.extensions.tables",
        "markdown.extensions.attr_list",
        "markdown.extensions.md_in_html",
        "markdown_captions",
        "pymdownx.tilde",
        "pymdownx.caret",
    ]
)
slide_body = md.convert(md_document)
slide_meta = md.Meta

We use Jinja to generate the HTML presentation:

html_document = template.render(
    language=language,
    title=title,
    subtitle=subtitle,
    slides=slides,
    stylesheets=stylesheets,
    footer=footer,
)
with open("presentation.html", "w") as fh:
    fh.write(html_document)

We render the final PDF with WeasyPrint:

weasyprint.HTML("presentation.html").write_pdf(
    "../Sample Presentation.pdf",
    stylesheets=stylesheets,
    font_config=font_config,
    presentational_hints=True,
)

The output is visually comparable to a PDF generated by PowerPoint, with the advantages of version control, automation and full control over the style. A simple, scriptable workflow has significantly streamlined my slide creation while keeping flexibility and consistency.
