docs.title: An introduction to workflow and process automation with n8n and Camunda
docs.text: 07 December 2025

docs.title: An introduction to workflow and process automation with n8n and Camunda
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner camunda fundamentals n8n

In a corporate environment, the natural evolution of network automation is to plug directly into the business processes, making them faster and more cost-effective.

Over the past few years, I have often come across Camunda. Camunda is an open-source platform for business process automation and orchestration that coordinates complex workflows involving people, systems and devices.

In other words, Camunda lets us design business processes, orchestrate them, automate them and monitor them:

Camunda is built to handle complex, long-running processes represented with the BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation) standard. Different processes can communicate with each other by passing variables across workflows.

It is a great product, but I find it quite complex. Between 2019 and 2020, n8n was released: a tool with similar goals but much simpler to use.

n8n is a low-code/no-code automation platform that lets us build workflows connecting different applications, thanks to its 1000+ ready-made integrations. Each workflow runs independently from the others.

Camunda and n8n may look similar at first glance, but they are very different tools. NTConsult provides a great overview of how they compare:

Use Camunda when:

  • The process involves human tasks, SLAs, escalations or manual approvals.
  • Execution spans hours, days or weeks (e.g., onboarding, credit approvals).
  • You need audit trails, versioning and strict governance (e.g., AML, KYC).
  • You expect high concurrency or thousands of parallel instances.
  • You are coordinating multiple systems, events and services with full traceability.

Use n8n when:

  • You need quick automations triggered by events, APIs or schedules.
  • Execution is short (seconds or minutes).
  • You are building internal tools, notifications or SaaS integrations.
  • You want low-code speed for non-developers or DevOps workflows.
  • You are automating infrastructure tasks such as provisioning or cleanup.

Our focus here is workflow automation, that is, automating a set of tasks that belong to a broader business process. For this reason, we start with n8n, because:

  • It is very easy to learn.
  • It comes with many ready-to-use integrations.
  • It is the right tool to automate sequences of operational tasks.

docs.title: Automating user management with n8n and AI Agents
docs.text: 14 December 2025

docs.title: Automating user management with n8n and AI Agents
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ai fundamentals intermediate n8n

Managing users, groups and roles is one of the most repetitive and resource-intensive operational tasks for IT teams. The process is almost always triggered by HR after an organizational change, and HR submits a service request ticket to IT for each individual operation.

If we analyze this workflow, it is clearly inefficient: it requires asynchronous coordination between two teams, HR and IT. Conceptually, HR could interact directly with Microsoft Active Directory, the most common platform to manage users, groups and roles. In practice, this rarely happens, for an obvious reason: Active Directory is the backbone of the company, it is complex, and nobody outside IT wants to deal with it.

The proposed solution is a natural language interface that lets HR interact with Active Directory in a simple and secure way to:

  • Create a new user when someone joins the company.
  • Assign and modify groups and roles of existing users.
  • Disable users when someone leaves the organization.
  • Search and retrieve information about users and groups.

docs.title: Installing n8n
docs.text:
We can install n8n either as a Docker container or via npx. In this example, we use:

npx n8n
[license SDK] Skipping renewal on init: license cert is not initialized
Version: 1.119.1

Editor is now accessible via:
http://localhost:5678

Press "o" to open in Browser.

This gives access to the n8n web interface at http://localhost:5678/. The first step is to register the initial account:

During registration, we can optionally provide a valid email address to receive a free license that unlocks some premium features.

At this point, n8n is installed and operational. This setup is suitable for development, not for production environments.

docs.title: Workflow Overview
docs.text:
We want to create a workflow that lets an operator, through a natural language agent (bot):

  • Retrieve a list of users.
  • Get the details of a specific user.
  • Search for a user.
  • Create a user and assign a role (standard, staff, admin).
  • Disable a user.
  • Activate a user.

Before executing any modification, the bot must request explicit confirmation.

We use n8n, Django and Django REST Framework to create this simple workflow. The workflow requires two main components:

  • Chat Trigger: provides the chat interface and triggers the workflow.
  • AI Agent: interacts with the user in natural language and performs actions.

The AI Agent requires access to:

  • An LLM engine (we use Google Gemini).
  • A storage system for the history of the interactions (we use Simple Memory).
  • Tools to execute operations (we use the HTTP Request Tool to interact with Django via API).

docs.title: Chat Trigger Configuration
docs.text:
For this prototype:

  • We use Hosted Mode.
  • We make the chat publicly accessible.
  • No authentication is required.

docs.title: AI Agent (IAM Bot) Setup
docs.text:
To configure the agent, we need to:

  • Configure a prompt.
  • Associate an LLM engine.
  • Define the storage for the history of the interactions.
  • Associate the operational tools.

Associating an LLM engine: n8n provides a list of supported models. We select Google Gemini, add the credentials and the engine is ready.

Configuring storage: we add a storage module so the agent can use past interactions. The main setting is the number of previous interactions to keep:

Associating tools (HTTP Request Tool): the agent needs "hands" to act in our context. It is best to create minimalist tools, to keep the agent simple and reduce potential risks.

We interact with the Django user database via REST API. The tools we create are:

  • GetUserList: GET http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/
  • GetUserDetail: GET http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/{{ $fromAI('id') }}
  • SearchUser: GET http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/?search={{ $fromAI('search') }}
  • CreateUser: POST http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/ first_name={{ $fromAI('first_name') }}, last_name={{ $fromAI('last_name') }}, username={{ $fromAI('username') }}, is_active=True, is_staff={{ $fromAI('is_staff') }}, is_superuser={{ $fromAI('is_superuser') }}
  • DisableUser: PATCH http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/{{ $fromAI('id') }}/ is_active=False
  • ActivateUser: PATCH http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/{{ $fromAI('id') }}/ is_active=True

The $fromAI() syntax passes data from the conversation of the agent to the API calls seamlessly.

docs.title: Building the AI Agent
docs.text:
The final step is to assemble the agent with the user, the LLM engine and the tools. The key task is prompt design, which instructs the agent to act correctly.

For this MVP, we focus on a functional setup:

  • Use an LLM to draft an initial prompt.
  • Define clearly the capabilities and the permissions of the agent.
  • Define the user data structure.
  • List all the available tools with their parameters and formats.
  • Set the operational rules.
  • Define the style and the behavior of the AI.
  • Provide example scenarios.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
We can now test the platform through the chat window of the workflow, to validate the functionality in real time:

After fixing the issues, we can inspect the data structure exchanged between the nodes:

Finally, we can run the workflow in a more professional chat environment:

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
I chose n8n for its simplicity, which allows rapid prototyping. However:

  • The same workflow could be implemented with a web form, which is less interactive but faster and more efficient.
  • A full Python-based solution with an on-prem LLM is possible, but significantly more complex.

Important note: this prototype does not log the user who starts the request or the action performed. In production, non-repudiation is critical: each workflow execution must record the requester, the chat interaction and the resulting modification.

The final prompt and the code are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Approaching OT/ICS Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance intermediate ot-ics

A few days ago, together with Rocco Sicilia and FESTO Academy, I presented a webinar on the approach to OT/ICS cybersecurity. We often spend time raising cybersecurity awareness, and this webinar focused on giving cybersecurity fundamentals to OT managers.

docs.title: Understanding the Attacker's Point of View
docs.text:
The main discussion was about the threat actors, in other words the attackers. Understanding the attackers gives us the big picture of their different business models (the "why", using a definition by Simon Sinek). We focused on:

  • The evolving cybercrime phenomenon.
  • The value the attacker is looking for.
  • The types of attackers, their goals and their budgets.

Then we discussed some popular cyberattacks. WannaCry and NotPetya (2017) are, in my opinion, IT attacks. The OT/ICS-specific attacks include Stuxnet (Iran, 2010), BlackEnergy (Ukraine, 2015), Triton (Saudi Arabia, 2017), the water supply of a Florida city (2021), Colonial Pipeline (2021) and the recent Viasat attack (2022).

IT and OT attacks have different targets, but we reviewed how attackers usually breach enterprises: three out of four threat vectors are based on human behavior, and only one is based on technology.

docs.title: Why Do We Interconnect Critical Devices to the Internet?
docs.text:
Given the previous section, the question is legitimate and the answer is obvious: the Industry 4.0 era is based on fast and automatic interactions (data exchanges). Data can be transmitted automatically between components, plants, systems, suppliers and customers. The faster and more automatic the process, the more profitable the business.

Cyberspace provides tools, methods, and interactions to get more opportunities.

But at the same time:

It is considered the fifth theater of warfare.

Staying out of cyberspace, or interconnecting everything without considering the consequences, are both extreme solutions. We need to find the right balance between them.

Find the correct proportion between freedom, even unconscious, and security

docs.title: Peculiarities of OT/ICS Devices
docs.text:
The next chapter was about the peculiarities of OT/ICS. The audience was already aware of them, but we presented them from an IT perspective:

  • They are designed for "availability": the same term is used in the IT world with a different meaning.
  • They are extremely sensitive to Ethernet disruptions and overloads. Remember that Ethernet networks can fail by design (STP convergence).
  • Their communications do not guarantee confidentiality, integrity and availability, which are fundamental attributes in IT security.
  • They have a long life: compared to the IT world, we can find 20-year-old plants.
  • They are not subject to the same life cycle as IT components: production OT/ICS components (including HMIs) are usually "untouchable".

Based on our experience, we presented seven common issues:

  • Shadow OT: nobody knows exactly what is installed in the plant networks and why (e.g., WiFi networks, cloud-based telemetry, vulnerable devices, default passwords, remote access devices). This leads to unmanaged risk.
  • Weak and sensitive protocols: OT/ICS protocols do not follow the CIA triad used in IT, but they run on Ethernet networks. This leads to unexpected behaviors.
  • Long-lived devices: plants installed 5 years ago and never maintained are vulnerable to well-known attacks. OT/ICS plants tend to be legacy, weak and harmful.
  • Remote maintenance: third-party operators can connect to critical plants at any time and act locally, and they can watch sensitive production processes and information (espionage and sabotage).
  • Removable storage: third-party operators are used to upgrading software with untrusted USB keys. It is not uncommon for malware to spread via USB even today.

The list is not meant to be complete: these are the main issues that industries report to us.

docs.title: How Should We Approach Cybersecurity in OT/ICS Environments?
docs.text:
There is no need to reinvent the wheel: many standards and frameworks are available. The webinar discussed the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (NIST), the CIS Controls, UNI ISO 31000:2018 Risk management - Guidelines, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations (800-171 and 800-172) and the Secure Architecture for Industrial Control Systems (Purdue Model).

The IEC 62443 standard deserves a special mention: both integrators and customers should take it into account. We do not yet have regulations for the medical and industrial sectors, so IEC 62443 can serve as a guideline.

The purpose of this phase is to plan a strategy that takes the standards above into account.

docs.title: What Should We Do in Practice?
docs.text:
Cybersecurity is a process, implemented with organizational and technical measures. In practice, we want to build a continuous improvement process that starts from the first major issue: Shadow OT.

We cannot protect what we don't know.

The first step is to assess the OT/ICS infrastructure and find out what is installed, its purpose, its business impact and its weaknesses or robustness. Then we can move on to the suppliers, partners, third parties and employees, and evaluate the cybersecurity risk.

We can assume a 4-phase improvement process:

  • Check: measure the cybersecurity posture (get qualitative or quantitative values for the many cybersecurity aspects).
  • Act: analyze the associated risk and highlight the unacceptable risks.
  • Plan: define a strategy to mitigate the unacceptable risks, taking into account standards and regulations.
  • Do: govern and supervise the implementation.

It is a PDCA cycle, but I start from the third phase because I assume that the first two were already completed during the first iteration. The next CHECK phase is expected to produce better KPIs (Key Performance Indicators).

docs.title: IT-OT Convergence
docs.text:
An interesting discussion was about IT and OT convergence: should we go for it?

I consider IT and OT two different worlds with different values and rules. In my opinion, they cannot converge and they should not. IT follows the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad, while OT follows a sort of Safety, Reliability and Productivity triad. Moreover, uniqueness is something to avoid in IT (we do not want to reinvent the wheel), while customization is expected in OT/ICS.

IT and OT cybersecurity, however, must converge. Cybersecurity must be a common overlay for all the departments of an organization. The convergence point of IT and OT cybersecurity is defined by:

  • Safety first.
  • A risk-based approach.
  • An open mindset and dialogue with stakeholders.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Preparing a webinar or a training path is a good way to review concepts and organize them in a coherent flow. I hope that auditors can get a different point of view on OT/ICS security. Slides are available, and we will deliver an additional session in the future.

docs.title: Assume breach design
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced design governance

There is much discussion around Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), but the concept of Assume Breach Design seems not to have been formalized yet. At least, a Google search does not return results. The term Assume Breach Paradigm is used, and I want to apply it to infrastructure design. So I am appropriating the term, in a manner of speaking, and explaining why changing the mindset could be beneficial.

As always, the idea comes from field experience: I realize that infrastructure design, from a cybersecurity perspective, follows a traditional approach. In the 1990s and 2000s, it was common to implement a DMZ network, a server network and sometimes a client network. Policies were designed based on application needs and were never formalized. This approach, still frequently used today, relies on the classic 3-tier architecture of web applications (clients, servers and databases), which had to be implemented separately. From a security standpoint, this led to separating these components logically with a firewall.

What I see today is precisely the consequence of this: systems are separated based on application logic, not security logic. The result is that companies have security zones that separate application components (Internet, DMZ, client, server, OT, Guest), and policies derive from application needs, not from security requirements.

A case in point: server networks typically contain the backend and the databases of the entire company. If one is compromised, the whole network is at risk.

A second, equally telling example: I imagine that anyone who has implemented firewall policies has done so based on an application request. The vast majority of firewall policies originate from application needs, and their impact is rarely evaluated because rejecting the request is not an option.

docs.title: Policy Design
docs.text:
The first attempt at a mindset shift was almost ten years ago. I was in a position to influence the network and security architecture of the company I worked for and, following the advice of an ISO 27001 auditor, I formalized the interactions between the different security zones.

The idea was to publish a manifesto so that everyone in the company would know the rules that govern the firewalls.

Here are some examples:

  • The server network cannot receive connections from the Internet.
  • The DMZ network can access the server network only through the HTTP/HTTPS protocols.
  • The server and DMZ networks can access the Internet only on a specific list of addresses and protocols.

All the rules were designed to reduce the risk of compromise or lateral movement, but there were some fundamental errors.

The first error (mine) was that I conducted the evaluation myself, and at the time my experience was primarily in defensive security. A few years later, when I began working on offensive security as well, I realized that the approach was correct but the assumptions were incomplete.

The second error (company-wide) was failing to give this work the importance it deserved. It was seen as an obstacle created by a paranoid technician, rather than as a document meant to design secure applications within the company.

Specifically, the 3-tier paradigm was converted to Client (Internet) - Reverse Proxy (DMZ) - Server. A reverse proxy with no functionality other than forwarding connections from the Internet to the internal network has only one consequence: it exposes the internal network directly to the Internet. This should be obvious, but even today I find several configurations like this.

The last consequence was that, when I left that company, the manifesto was shelved and forgotten.

docs.title: A Technical Matter
docs.text:
The experience helped me over the years to offer an approach to the technical teams that need to organize firewall policies. Shifting the focus from the policy to the needs of the systems, before deciding where to place them, helps prevent problems instead of chasing them.

The formalization of the policies never worked because companies saw it as a technical issue, unrelated to the business.

In particular, the words a CEO said to me a few years ago were illuminating: cybersecurity is a technical problem, and thus it is entrusted to the CIO.

docs.title: The Purpose of the DMZ
docs.text:
Another factor that drove me to rethink the approach to defending companies is my frequent task of analyzing firewall policies to bring order and logic. Almost always, I find NAT rules that allow direct access from the Internet to internal systems. Often these are needs related to specific applications, IoT systems, cameras or building automation in general.

In all these cases there is a DMZ, which makes me ask what the purpose of having a DMZ is if internal systems are still directly exposed.

What I discovered is that the DMZ is often created without a clear understanding of the concept behind it.

Originally, the DMZ network was meant to be the segment of the infrastructure most at risk: the policies that govern the traffic to and from the DMZ were meant to be particularly stringent. Some might call this the Zero Trust approach today.

Many years ago, the systems in the DMZ network did not have Internet access. If a system was compromised, it could not communicate outward.

Over the years, this paradigm has crumbled (like many others) because many application frameworks require external resources (XML schemas, telemetry, licenses).

The concept of "containment" in the DMZ has gradually eroded, and today a DMZ network risks becoming just another network. Quite frequently, I find:

  • Databases residing in the DMZ.
  • DMZ networks that can access the Internet indiscriminately.
  • Internal systems that can access the DMZ indiscriminately.
  • Unrestricted Internet access from the DMZ and the internal networks.
  • Weak systems exposed on the Internet, residing in the DMZ or even in internal networks.
  • Reverse proxies that map internal systems to the Internet without any security mechanism.

I could go on, but I believe the point is clear.

docs.title: Defense in Depth
docs.text:
The idea behind the Defense in Depth paradigm is to protect a system from cyberattacks with a multi-layered approach. In other words, we should not rely on a single protection (the firewall), but provide multiple layers that can act together if one or more protections fail.

To be clear, a defense layer could consist of:

  • Firewall.
  • VPN.
  • Anti-malware.
  • MFA.
  • Monitoring.
  • Vulnerability scanner.
  • IDS/IPS.
  • Physical security.

Defense in Depth is promoted by the NSA, which advises associating each layer with one or more of the five cybersecurity functions defined in the cybersecurity framework formalized by NIST.

I find the Defense in Depth approach absolutely correct but, in my opinion, it risks being too technical and thus disconnected from the business. In a way, it was the mistake I made: unable to speak to the business side, I could not secure the space I needed.

docs.title: Zero Trust Architecture
docs.text:
ZTA, unfortunately, is becoming a mantra. NIST defines ZTA in the document SP 800-207, which should be studied before discussing ZTA. I summarize some points that are useful for my reflections, quoting directly from the original document.

That is, authorized and approved subjects (combination of user, application (or service), and device) can access the data to the exclusion of all other subjects (i.e., attackers). To take this one step further, the word "resource" can be substituted for "data" so that ZT and ZTA are about resource access (e.g., printers, compute resources, Internet of Things IoT actuators) and not just data access.

ZTA pertains to data access, where the data can reside on any system, including printers, IoT systems and, of course, servers, databases and so on. The subject is digital data in any form.

Access to resources is determined by dynamic policy—including the observable state of client identity, application/service, and the requesting asset—and may include other behavioral and environmental attributes.

Data access is determined by dynamic policies built on who requests the data and who holds it. Policies may consider other environmental or behavioral attributes.

Requesting asset state can include device characteristics such as software versions installed, network location, time/date of request, previously observed behavior, and installed credentials. Behavioral attributes include, but not limited to, automated subject analytics, device analytics, and measured deviations from observed usage patterns.

Today we build policies based on the identity of the source and the destination. The identity of the destination typically consists of an IP address and a port. The identity of the source is slightly more complex, because it considers not only the IP address but also the associated user. In more complex infrastructures, the source is also validated against specific requirements on patch status and the presence of anti-malware.

We rarely use attributes related to location and time. Even less frequently, we use behavioral attributes (e.g., whether the client behaves differently than expected).

The ZTA approach requires allowing access to data only when strictly necessary. To achieve this, we would need to:

  • Identify the source in terms of device, user, application that requests the data, location of the client, time of the request, behavior of the source and compliance status.
  • Identify the means by which the request arrives (Internet, VPN, private network, encryption, etc.).
  • Identify the requested data and the requested operation.

Technologies that implement almost all (but not all) the features required by ZTA exist, but it is still not a paradigm that is widely implemented today.

The reason, in my opinion, is always the same: ZTA is seen as a technical approach, detached from the business.

docs.title: Assume Breach Design
docs.text:
Let's move on to the assume breach paradigm applied to design. The core idea is quite simple: my architectural choices are guided by the assessment of the risk of a potential breach. We could call it risk-based design, but in my opinion the term would be less effective.

There are two important premises:

  • We must be able to assess thoroughly the possible attack paths against the infrastructure.
  • We must be able to evaluate the impact of potential breaches on the business.

The first point requires specific offensive skills that differ from those of someone who designs and defends an infrastructure. Those who do not use these skills will make substantial mistakes in designing the defenses.

The second point requires the ability to conduct a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) for each attack scenario.

Only after these assessments can we determine which defenses to implement. In this sense, Defense in Depth and ZTA are consequences of Assume Breach Design, not its premises.

Let's return to the example of particularly large server networks that contain the backends and databases of all the company applications. The consequence of this design is that, if one is compromised, the attacker can move relatively easily to all the critical business systems. If we assess this scenario correctly, we realize that it is unacceptable. At this point, we can implement a microsegmentation technology and try to reduce the traffic flows between these hosts. We can also consider monitoring technologies that identify traffic anomalies. Both approaches have pros and cons, and there is no one-size-fits-all solution. The assessment of the business risk helps us determine the available budget and, consequently, select the solution that best fits our context.

I can, therefore, break down ZTA into parts and decide where it is important. The decision is based on a risk analysis of the attack scenarios: in other words, Assume Breach Design.

docs.title: Post Breach
docs.text:
All the infrastructures I know have grown gradually and without structure. In other words, there is never any documentation that describes how the infrastructure, in terms of servers and applications, was created. On the one hand, the task would be impossible with traditional tools. On the other, the assume breach paradigm forces us to think about how we would respond to an attack.

In almost all cases (and I am being optimistic), if we notice an ongoing attack in our infrastructure, we cannot say for sure how far it has spread. In other words, we do not know how to eradicate the attack from the infrastructure unless we rebuild it completely.

The Infrastructure as Code paradigm can help us build our infrastructure (or part of it) from text files. Microservices and containers allow us to do the same in the application domain. If we embrace this mindset, we realize that we can rebuild the entire infrastructure at any moment, and the build process can serve as documentation.

The advantages are immediate: documentation, standardization, compliance, and so on. The complexity of the tools, however, remains a barrier to adoption for many organizations. The rigidity of the infrastructure is an apparent problem that reveals the underlying operational chaos.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The Assume Breach Design approach aims to bring the business back to the center of decision-making. The infrastructure exists to serve one purpose: the business of the company. The protections that the technical teams decide on today are implemented to safeguard that business.

Putting the business back at the center means shifting cybersecurity from a technical matter to a business necessity.

For too many years, I have seen IT departments treated as a black hole that absorbs budget. The effects of this mindset are clear to everyone. Maybe it is time for a change.

docs.title: Crisis management
docs.text: 10 February 2021

docs.title: Crisis management
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance incident-management intermediate

Note: I wrote this article a few months ago but never published it. I have now revisited it, adding some updated reflections.

This period has taught us many lessons at different levels. Today I want to focus on one in particular: the importance of having a plan for emergencies.

According to an investigative report by Report, "Virus and State Secrets", one of the main weaknesses that severely impacted the ability to respond was the absence of an emergency plan that was:

  • Shared with all the people involved.
  • Clear and complete, down to the details.
  • Comprehensive, covering a wide range of scenarios.

In recent weeks, an additional factor has emerged: the reliability of the supply chain during global crises.

docs.title: Shared
docs.text:
When an emergency occurs, people need to know that a plan exists and that it specifies exactly what actions to take.

In Incident Response engagements, I have often found emergency plans tucked away in drawers, never communicated, let alone practiced.

Awareness alone is not enough, though: people must internalize the plan so they can act as a team, not as individuals driven by panic or anxiety. One of the most important and fascinating aspects of my job is training staff through simulated scenarios with increasing levels of stress.

The concept of Kata comes from martial arts and was later adopted by Toyota in organizational management. It teaches us that only by practicing behaviors repeatedly can we internalize them and apply them effectively when it really matters.

docs.title: Clarity and Completeness
docs.text:
An emergency plan must be clear and complete. In high-stress situations, people cannot be expected to think calmly and rationally. They must follow a predefined plan that includes every necessary detail.

Examples of seemingly obvious yet essential information include:

  • Roles and responsibilities of team members.
  • Internal and external communication procedures.
  • How to file a report with law enforcement.
  • How to assess and, if needed, notify a data breach to the Data Protection Authority.

Some of these steps may look "obvious" and easy to look up online, but under stress people forget, misjudge or waste time. In real crises, confusion and disorganization are common: people even forget basics such as the network topology, the location of the devices or how to access them.

This is not about "experience". It is about the ability to work under stress.

Here again, training is key: if the plan defines roles and procedures clearly, and people are trained accordingly, the team is much more likely to perform effectively.

Realistic training also tests how individuals react under pressure. The goal is not that everyone stays calm, but that leadership at all levels (board, line managers, team leaders) can guide and reassure the team in a moment of crisis.

As Report highlighted, chains of command must function, because people need structured points of reference.

docs.title: Comprehensive Scenarios
docs.text:
We cannot anticipate every possible crisis, but a good risk assessment helps identify the most critical scenarios. That assessment is the foundation for building targeted emergency plans.

Today, most cyber threats revolve around ransomware: attackers exfiltrate sensitive data and then try to render the infrastructure unusable.

An attack on a telecom network is very different from an attack on an ICS/OT system, a database or a file-sharing platform hosting next season's product catalog. Just as the attacks differ, the response plans must differ too. Reacting to an attempt to poison a water treatment plant requires entirely different actions than handling the outage of a call center's phone system.

docs.title: Equipment Availability
docs.text:
Preparedness also depends on the scenarios considered in the crisis plan. If scenarios are missing or unrealistic, you end up improvising under pressure.

As COVID-19 showed, effective operations require tested and ready-to-use equipment. In a health emergency, that might mean stockpiled medical gear and medicines. In a cyber crisis, it means having "clean" workstations available: functional, charged, with all the necessary accessories (network cables, serial adapters, Wi-Fi/4G connectivity, etc.).

Without planning, we get what we saw: governments rushing to procure medical equipment mid-crisis, and companies scrambling to buy laptops to enable remote work in a hurry.

docs.title: Supply Chain Reliability
docs.text:
One lesson that Report did not highlight, but that has since become clear, is the fragility of the supply chain during global crises.

The slow and uneven distribution of vaccines showed how suppliers may struggle to meet expectations or, in some cases, prioritize certain entities over others.

When selecting suppliers, organizations must now consider not only technical and contractual factors but also geopolitical ones: in times of crisis, political decisions may override contractual obligations, favoring some regions or countries over others for commercial, economic or strategic interests.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Observation is essential for understanding the world around us, but to be useful it must be detached and objective. It lets us see the many parallels between the physical and digital worlds.

COVID-19 has shown that real-world crises can teach us valuable lessons for cyber crisis management and make companies more resilient to the inevitable challenges ahead.

The ultimate goal is not just to make organizations safer, but also more competitive. Reliability is now a differentiator in the marketplace, and in these times it can make all the difference.

Successfully surviving a cyber attack is one of the best credentials an organization can show, arguably stronger than simply claiming never to have faced one.

docs.title: Cybersecurity: fashion or strategy
docs.text: 12 October 2024

docs.title: Cybersecurity: fashion or strategy
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance

I could not find a suitable title for this post, in which I gather various insights from the past few days. Sooner or later I plan to discuss them with Rocco Sicilia.

I start with a provocation: cybersecurity has been under the spotlight for some years now, and I would call it "trendy" (we will see why). Various hypes follow one another, creating needs and fears with the aim of selling solutions and services. There is nothing wrong with this, but we need to distinguish acting out of "trendiness" from strategic action.

Acting out of "trendiness" is an impulse, aesthetic and sometimes very personal, often done out of emulation. It is difficult to trace the motivation behind such choices, precisely because they are impulses. For the purpose of this post, security measures chosen on impulse are not guided by a strategy and, as we have discussed several times, they are often ineffective. This mode is extremely widespread and easy to identify: if I ask "why" a security measure (NAC, firewall, security awareness training software...) was implemented, the answer tends to be (I exaggerate and simplify) "because". Almost always, these measures are not integrated into a process and are not monitored, which we have also discussed.

Strategic action starts with an analysis and inserts security measures into a higher-level design. Each measure is chosen and placed with a specific purpose and measured accordingly. There may be exceptions, but they are well documented and temporary (with an end date), because an exception weakens the protections we have implemented.

A real example that touches on the fundamentals is the firewall. All companies have one, whether perimeter or dual bastion. Almost no company defines policies, though: they are written by technicians and are often hated because they limit other people's work. Strategic action starts from the purpose of the infrastructure, which is to support the business. The infrastructure must provide services, which are implemented through servers. To function, these servers have connectivity needs and therefore risks. We mitigate the risks by dividing servers into areas, and these areas can communicate with each other only under certain rules, which are translated into firewall policies. In an ideal world, I should NEVER find publicly exposed systems placed in networks considered secure. I do find them, and they are often historical relics, abandoned and unchecked, exposed precisely for "historical reasons".

Because security in companies is done by technicians, nobody has the strength to bring cybersecurity to the corporate level.

And then the CISO arrives.

The responsibility for cybersecurity is dumped onto the CISO. I mean "dumped": the problem, once relegated to technicians, is now relegated to a manager so that the company can keep forgetting about it. Let's start with the basics:

  • A CISO who does not report to the board cannot do the job.
  • A CISO who does not have a budget cannot do the job.
  • A CISO who does not have veto power cannot do the job.
  • A CISO who is not consulted before any technological choice cannot do the job.

It has been said many times: cybersecurity is a corporate problem, but everyone keeps pretending otherwise. A couple of years ago, I had the opportunity to interview some CEOs of enterprises close to me. Their answers were enlightening because they let me enter their mindset and understand their needs. In short, cybersecurity is not a topic of interest to them, because it is delegated to the CIO or CISO (depending on the company).

There are many exceptions, of course, but the dominant behavior I notice is the one I described.

docs.title: Discontinued IoT products
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced digital-self-defence governance iot

I had an interesting chat with a friend: he told me that the app that manages his photovoltaic system had stopped working. The vendor had upgraded the cloud API and broken compatibility with older products. I expect to see this more and more in the future.

docs.title: How Firms Develop APIs
docs.text:
I worked with developers for many years. In my experience, once a project starts, the developers analyze, choose the proper framework, build the software and test it, maybe with a CI/CD approach, and everything is fine. Sooner or later, though, the framework becomes obsolete, and so do the libraries and the operating systems. Sooner or later, a new OS will not be compatible with the old versions of the frameworks, and the code will probably not be compatible with the new versions of the framework either.

To me, this is a small form of "lock-in": the software we develop is bound to a specific version of a specific framework, installable on a specific operating system. Sooner or later, upgrading the whole ecosystem requires a deep review and update of the code.

And that is the problem.

docs.title: Product Lifecycle
docs.text:
What is missing from the beginning is the product lifecycle. This is not about developers, it is about product management and business strategy. If we develop a new cloud-based game, we can assume that it will stand for a few years:

The cloud infrastructure, the API and the software must be maintained, or the business is affected: a data breach or an outage damages the reputation of the app, the customers and the revenues.

At some point, the app is retired, simply because revenues no longer cover major upgrades and infrastructure.

As I said, a game stands for a few years, I guess no more than 3.

Sometimes a new product replaces the old one. In that case, customers are usually migrated to the new product with some sort of special offer.

docs.title: The IoT Problem
docs.text:
With IoT, ICS/OT, medical devices, automotive and building automation products, the playground changes: customers buy products that can be expensive, and those products are expected to last for many years. Consumer products are expected to last 10 years, and industrial and medical products and cars 20 years.

How can we manage a 20-year product lifecycle based on a 5-year OS lifecycle?

Short story: we can't.

Long story: the problem must be decoupled. We have the device and the cloud services. We could maintain the cloud services, with expensive major upgrades, and maintain API compatibility with legacy devices. That means we must design our API and its security carefully from the beginning. We could maintain the firmware of legacy devices, fixing security bugs even for 15-year-old products. But we cannot stop the world: for example, security protocols are replaced and we cannot influence that. If a security protocol (TLS 1.0) is deprecated, secure communications are no longer permitted unless we upgrade both the devices and the API services. Legacy devices, however, probably cannot support a larger firmware.

Standard Released in Deprecated in Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) 1997 2004 Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) 2003 2006 Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2) 2004 - Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) 2018 - SSL 2.0 1995 2011 SSL 3.0 1999 2015 TLS 1.0 1999 2021 TLS 1.1 2006 2021 TLS 1.2 2008 - TLS 1.3 2018 - Bluetooth 1.0B 1999 2006 Bluetooth 1.1 2001 2006 Bluetooth 1.2 2003 2009 Bluetooth 2.0 2004 2019 Bluetooth 2.1 2007 2019 Bluetooth 3.0 2009 2019 Bluetooth 4.0 2010 2019 Bluetooth 4.1 2013 2019 Bluetooth 4.2 2014 2025 Bluetooth 5 2016 2027 Bluetooth 5.1 2019 2029 Bluetooth 5.2 2019 2030 Bluetooth 5.3 2021 2031

If you wonder how many SSL 3.0 enabled web servers are currently running on the Internet:

In the industrial sector, we know that we face unsupported systems and applications, and we can secure them by working on the perimeter. With consumer IoT and building automation, the story is different.

docs.title: The Revenues and the Ponzi Method
docs.text:
Let's focus again on consumer IoT devices. My friend made an interesting assumption:

It's like a Ponzi scheme, in which the last users are paying for the whole infrastructure.

The consumer IoT business model is usually based on selling products. Nobody is willing to pay monthly for, for example, the remote management of an air conditioner. But air conditioners are expected to work for 10 years. So the later users, who buy the products, pay for the whole infrastructure.

The vendors also acquire data (telemetry), but I am not sure that the value of that data pays for the whole infrastructure (servers, development, licenses, software, security assessments, audits, compliance, etc.).

docs.title: A Possible Solution?
docs.text:
We know that:

  • No software can stand for 10 years. This is an assumption, but feel free to bring your own experience.
  • At some point, infrastructure and development require major, uneconomic upgrades.
  • The collected data (telemetry) is interesting but does not pay for the whole infrastructure.
  • The infrastructure costs and the Ponzi scheme do not work.
  • We face the same issue in ICS/OT.

My solution involves an approach similar to the one I use in ICS/OT: protect the perimeter. There is currently no reason why some consumer devices need to be cloud-connected. We should open and document the API so that home automation hubs can include and manage these devices. The hubs would be responsible for protecting the home perimeter, without needing the cloud.

This does not cover all device types, but at least home devices can be managed and maintained without invasive cloud services.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: I am convinced that any cloud-based IoT device can die within a few years. I am also worried about my data: I prefer to limit my home security perimeter by avoiding cloud services. Moreover, I suspect that we are addicted to data: do we really need to see our energy consumption anywhere and at any time?

docs.title: ICS/OT/IoT Security: challenges and protection strategies
docs.text: 05 September 2024

docs.title: ICS/OT/IoT Security: challenges and protection strategies
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iot ot-ics

It is time to revisit the ICS/OT world, as it has unique characteristics that influence its processes and tools.

First, I categorize this broad field into three groups:

  • Systems localized within a confined area (e.g., a building or campus).
  • Systems geographically distributed but accessible through protected or dedicated networks (SCADA systems often fall into this category).
  • Systems geographically distributed and connected to the Internet without additional controls (IoT systems often fall into this category).

I chose this classification because, as we will see in the following posts, it dictates our ability to mitigate risks with additional security measures. Other categorizations are useful too (for example, one based on risk), but this is the one I use as a starting point.

In my experience, most ICS/OT/IoT systems have a longer lifespan than the support period of their individual components. This is crucial when planning a realistic strategy. Even though some regulations require components to be upgradable, we will inevitably face situations where we need to protect components that are no longer sold, supported or maintained.

docs.title: Lifespan vs. Support Duration
docs.text:
ICS/OT/IoT systems often stay operational for longer than the manufacturers of their components anticipated. In other words, the components (particularly the software, but not only) are no longer supported, yet the integrated system is still in use.

Anyone familiar with the industrial, medical, maritime or oil & gas sectors (and I would add banking) sees this daily: systems are built on components such as Windows and remain active well beyond the end of their support period. This is unavoidable for three reasons:

  1. These systems are generally untouchable: no changes or updates are permitted because their effects are unknown. In some cases, vendors strongly advised me against updating IEC 62443-certified products, even though the standard allows it.
  2. Many of these systems have a very high acquisition cost, in the millions or tens of millions. Decommissioning or even a simple refit is an unjustifiable cost for a system that still does the work it was bought for.
  3. I have often encountered operational systems supplied by defunct companies, with no support available. Here too, the cost of a new system is unjustifiable.

The three points above mainly stem from the approach of the companies and people who design such systems. They are built to perform their tasks safely, even under stress. When we started talking about Industry 4.0 and connecting systems designed to work in isolation to an IP network, however, we introduced a new risk: cyber risk.

In conversations with suppliers and customers of ICS/OT/IoT systems, I realize that cyber risk is often not even considered. As a professional, I find some topological choices rather peculiar.

Manufacturers and integrators still need to grasp the implications of putting fragile technologies (from a cyber perspective) on IP and connecting them to the Internet.

The regulatory world is moving in a certain direction (see NIS, the machinery regulation, IMO). Will we finally see concrete results? Personally, I am not so optimistic.

docs.title: Component Lifespan
docs.text: Regulations and reality are one thing. Now let's look at some examples showing that the lifespan of a component is inevitably shorter than the lifespan of the system. Systems keep being used until they fail and repairs become more expensive than buying a new system.

docs.title: Bluetooth
docs.text: In recent years, I have noticed a preference for Bluetooth in the ICS world, because it simplifies reconfiguration activities. Specifically, Bluetooth is used to send some non-emergency control commands remotely. We should consider the risks introduced by a wireless protocol, but for now let's focus on the protocol releases. A new Bluetooth standard is released every 2-3 years. In an industrial system with a lifespan of 15 years, we can therefore find very old and potentially vulnerable protocol releases.

docs.title: WiFi
docs.text:
A similar discussion applies to WiFi, which has been used in ICS for years to manage mobile parts. In just under 20 years, four security standards (WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3) were introduced one after the other to address security issues.

Today, it is quite common to find ICS systems based on WEP, where the WiFi network is an extension of the wired field network.

docs.title: HMI
docs.text:
Even today, almost all the HMI systems I encounter are based on Microsoft Windows. Starting from Windows XP, we have seen 6 different versions in 23 years, roughly one every 4 years. It is just as easy to find ICS/OT systems still running Windows XP.

As recent history has shown, some systems run even older versions, released more than 30 years ago, and being old does not necessarily mean they need to be replaced.

Ubuntu is fairly widespread too, and an LTS release has a lifespan of about 5 years. Since no development is aligned with the latest release, a system that is around 3 years old is already out of support. This affects not only ICS but typically OT and IoT systems as well.

docs.title: Vulnerability Management
docs.text:
Managing vulnerabilities does not necessarily mean updating. It means managing risk, which we can do by implementing additional security measures.

I generally advise against running vulnerability assessments on ICS/OT components. Here is why:

  1. ICS/OT systems are extremely fragile, and it is highly likely (I would say certain) that a VA activity will negatively impact them.
  2. ICS/OT systems are generally untouchable. Even if we find vulnerabilities, we cannot mitigate them with updates or EDR.
  3. As mentioned, ICS/OT systems have a long lifespan, so we will almost certainly find vulnerabilities due to obsolete systems.

The point is that in ICS/OT environments there will almost certainly be severe, unpatchable vulnerabilities. In my experience this assumption has always held, and we can build our strategy on it.

In the IoT world we can draw similar conclusions, with one complication: IoT systems are generally connected directly to the Internet, with all the consequences that follow.

docs.title: Defense Strategies
docs.text:
We have established that ICS/OT systems are vulnerable and unpatchable. Our vulnerability management plan cannot rely on patching. Instead, we need to build a series of layers that reduce risk adequately.

I start from the so-called Purdue model, which gives us a foundation for approaching the problem correctly. In general, there should be no direct traffic from OT networks to IT/Internet networks and vice versa. I say "should" because, in my experience, the Purdue model is often not applicable today. I often find ICS/OT systems with contractual (not technical) requirements for direct Internet access.

My approach today is to create a particularly stringent security perimeter around the ICS/OT environment, inspired by the concept of ZTA (Zero Trust Architecture). A combination of firewalls and IDS lets me control access to ICS/OT systems and monitor anomalies within the networks. It may sound simple, but consider that:

  • Many ICS/OT systems reside together on large networks (I have seen thousands of IPs on a single 10.0.0.0/8 network).
  • What we see is not necessarily what is there: numerous 3G/4G/5G gateways implement an independent, invisible Internet access point directly into the ICS/OT network.
  • In many environments, VPN terminators are installed by contract to enable remote assistance (and, once identified, these might be the lesser evil).

ICS/OT security, therefore, starts with an assessment to understand how chaotic the situation is and which paths exist.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
We have seen some critical aspects of a proper security strategy. One of them deserves further discussion, even though in most cases it is not feasible.

ICS/OT systems within a company often reside on a single, large network. Compromising one component exposes all systems to the same risk. We also know that ICS/OT systems are untouchable, so changing the addressing scheme is not an option. In this case, technologies that segment L2 networks transparently can help. Personally, I have experience with the VLAN Insertion feature offered by Palo Alto Networks. Other vendors have similar implementations with the same goal: segmenting or micro-segmenting an L2 network transparently.

I consider this measure impractical in most cases because the production world is often the responsibility of an OT Manager who comes from the OT world, not from IT. I notice a certain skepticism, if not fear, when "IT technologies" are proposed in OT. The OT Manager opposes the change and shifts the responsibility for any production downtime onto whoever alters the topology.

In some cases, I have seen people sit down and look for a compromise that satisfies everyone. In many cases, however, nobody wants to take the risk of changing the status quo, and everything stays the same.

docs.title: Network Access
docs.text:
We discussed how to segment ICS networks to reduce the impact of a breach. Now let's touch on a topic that is both trendy and delicate. The idea behind NAC solutions is to enable network access for permitted devices while keeping out all the others. There are some important considerations to keep in mind:

  • A device that is allowed access can still be compromised.
  • Today's NAC solutions rely on the 802.1x protocol, plus a series of compromises when this protocol cannot be used.

In the ICS world, most devices (if not all) do not support 802.1x, which requires compromises such as MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass). We must also consider the risk posed by "silent" devices, those that receive traffic more than they send it, which might require further compromises.

I am not demonizing NAC solutions, but I want to stress that security is built in layers, and NAC is just one layer. Like any security measure, it has its own impacts. You can find more reflections on this topic in the "802.1x bypass" episode of the podcast I host with Rocco Sicilia.

docs.title: Code Security
docs.text: Finally, I want to address a topic that is still very niche, unfortunately: the security of code in the context of PLCs. Some PLC vulnerabilities are caused by how the PLCs are programmed. We can prevent them by writing correct code. This is not my area of expertise, so I leave you with the Top 20 Secure PLC Coding Practices and encourage you to follow Sarah Fluchs on LinkedIn.

docs.title: Improvised vulnerability management
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance intermediate vulnerability-management

On March 3rd, the Italian CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) published a bulletin reporting the active exploitation of critical Microsoft Exchange vulnerabilities.

That was the moment when companies should have triggered a risk assessment immediately, followed by a business impact analysis and an actionable response plan.

docs.title: Assessing the Vulnerability
docs.text:
The assessment in this case is straightforward: four severe Microsoft Exchange vulnerabilities (with CVSSv3 scores up to 9.1) that, when chained together, can lead to full server compromise. Specifically, attackers can:

  • Access and exfiltrate user emails.
  • Install malware on the server, turning it into a foothold for further attacks.

The impact should therefore be considered "high".

The Italian CSIRT also warned that these vulnerabilities were already being exploited. That makes the likelihood of attack against unprotected, Internet-exposed Microsoft Exchange servers "high" as well.

Given this risk level, many organizations should have treated patching as an urgent priority.

docs.title: Problem Solved?
docs.text:
Here is the real issue: the grey zone between the discovery of a vulnerability and the moment when systems are fully patched.

Even if you deploy the Microsoft Exchange patches quickly, can you really say you acted in time?

docs.title: Threat Hunting
docs.text:
Vulnerability management should also address this grey zone. Actively analyzing systems to determine whether they have already been compromised, and how, reduces the chance of unpleasant surprises later.

In this specific case, between March 5th and 7th, most Microsoft Exchange servers worldwide were already targeted with malware designed for remote control.

Some of these servers received the second phase of the attack in the following two days.

docs.title: A Silent Threat
docs.text: Given the speed of the attack's evolution, we can easily predict what happens next: lateral movement across the network, data exfiltration, destruction of archives through ransomware, and extortion via data leak threats.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The purpose of this article was not to detail vulnerability management procedures, but to highlight the importance of embedding threat hunting into the process itself.

Patch management is not "install and forget", nor can it be relegated to "quarterly activities". In cases like the one described, action must be fast and fully aware of today's threat landscape.

docs.title: Log management is more than a log collector
Log management is more than a log collector
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance log-management

Many companies (hopefully) collect logs in a central system, for compliance and sometimes for root cause analysis. In this post, I want to recap that log management is not just about log collection, and why and how the process should be designed.

docs.title: Why Do We Collect Logs?
docs.text:
In short, log management is about collecting logs and storing them for analysis. By design, any system logs locally, so we need to clarify why we want a formal process for log management.

Let's start with the compliance part: ISO 27001 mentions log management in Annex A 12.4.

Event logs should be produced, retained, and regularly reviewed to record user activities, exceptions, defects, and information security events.

The GDPR does not mention log collection specifically, but Art. 5 refers to the ability to demonstrate compliance:

The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1 ('accountability').

In Italy, we also have a specific mention of logging (Amministratori di Sistema or AdS, and the AGID minimal requirements):

Caratteristiche di mantenimento dell´integrità dei dati raccolti dai sistemi di log sono in genere disponibili nei più diffusi sistemi operativi, o possono esservi agevolmente integrate con apposito software. Il requisito può essere ragionevolmente soddisfatto con la strumentazione software in dotazione, nei casi più semplici, e con l´eventuale esportazione periodica dei dati di log su supporti di memorizzazione non riscrivibili. In casi più complessi i titolari potranno ritenere di adottare sistemi più sofisticati, quali i log server centralizzati e "certificati". Tuttavia il provvedimento del Garante non affronta questi aspetti, prevedendo soltanto, come forma minima di documentazione dell´uso di un sistema informativo, la generazione del log degli "accessi" (login) e la loro archiviazione per almeno sei mesi in condizioni di ragionevole sicurezza e con strumenti adatti, in base al contesto in cui avviene il trattamento, senza alcuna pretesa di instaurare in modo generalizzato, e solo con le prescrizioni del provvedimento, un regime rigoroso di registrazione degli usage data dei sistemi informativi. Le misure minime sono un importante supporto metodologico, oltre che un mezzo attraverso il quale le Amministrazioni, soprattutto quelle più piccole e che hanno meno possibilità di avvalersi di professionalità specifiche, possono verificare autonomamente la propria situazione e avviare un percorso di monitoraggio e miglioramento.

The mention is specific to Italian companies, but it makes sense: we should all be able to review the activity of systems and users regularly, or during an incident analysis. Being able to demonstrate what happened in an incident means that we have our infrastructures (and data) under control. That is the GDPR accountability principle.

docs.title: How Do We Collect Logs?
docs.text:
Any well-designed system and application implements local logging by default. With dozens, hundreds or thousands of log sources, we must collect logs in a central location. Otherwise, we spend days just correlating events between different systems. Moreover, if a system is compromised, its logs are probably compromised too.

So we need to:

  • Collect logs from multiple sources in a central storage.
  • Keep timestamps coherent.
  • Categorize logs based on their content (debug logs, administrative events, errors...).
  • Set the retention based on the log category (we probably want to discard debug logs after a few days, whereas we want to keep administrative logs for months).
  • Preserve the CIA attributes (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability).
  • Normalize and correlate logs based on usernames, IP addresses, timestamps, sources...

We probably want to collect logs from:

  • Security appliances and applications (firewall, EDR, WAF, NAC, IDS/IPS...).
  • Ingress and egress web gateways (load balancer, web proxy...).
  • Authentication systems (LDAP, Active Directory, remote access, servers, endpoints, appliances...).
  • Network services (DHCP, DNS...).
  • Applications.
  • ...

docs.title: What Do We Do with Logs?
docs.text:
We collect logs not for compliance, but because they have value. We can use them to:

  • Analyze application errors (new bugs after a software release).
  • Highlight anomalies (potential attacks, data exfiltration).
  • Review activities (verify administrator logs for permission abuse).
  • Analyze root causes (problem management).
  • Hunt threats (find ongoing attacks).
  • Activate automatic alerting and reporting.

We may realize that we do not need a simple log collector but a SIEM, because most of the tasks we expect are about security management (threat hunting, finding users who abuse permissions...). The answer is yes: we analyze logs for security purposes. We also collect application logs for debugging, but they serve security too.

We should still evaluate log collectors because:

  • We have to review user activities (a GDPR requirement).
  • We want to debug application and network issues (they are security incidents too, but rarely managed by the SOC).
  • SIEM solutions are usually more expensive, and many companies have to decide which logs to discard.

Ideally, the log management process should be almost fully automated:

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
I am convinced that there is no distinction between incidents and security incidents. Because of the GDPR, any event impacting the CIA attributes of personal data is a data violation (or data breach). Based on that, most events are potentially security events (we can discard debug and maybe informational events). With this idea, any SOC should be able to identify cyber threats as well as network and application issues.

The real world works differently, and I know I am an idealist.

Besides that, we need to collect logs and improve alerting and reporting to obtain a resilient infrastructure. This is part of the log management process.
