docs.text:
• Art. 5 GDPR Principles relating to processing of personal data
  • System Administrator FAQ (Italian)
  • Log Management Workflow (draw.io format)
  • Guide to Computer Security Log Management (NIST 800-92)
  • Minimal security requirements for public administrations (Italian)

docs.title: Secure critical infrastructure "by design" and "by default"
Secure critical infrastructure "by design" and "by default"
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance ot-ics

I was reflecting with friends and clients on a topic that concerns all of us: the security of connected devices. Whether we are producers or users, in private or corporate environments, no one is excluded.

Often, when I raise these points, people label me as "paranoid". That is true, but for good reasons.

In today's cloud hype, many people buy "smart" devices like connected thermostats without asking what will happen when they become obsolete, no longer updatable or even unusable. Or without wondering whether the real business of certain manufacturers is not the device itself, but the collection and resale of data.

This article is not about privacy, though. It is about device security and the risks of a hyper-connected world, where technological enthusiasm often runs faster than awareness.

docs.title: Managing Critical Systems from a Tablet
docs.text:
At the beginning of my career, fixing a fault required dedicated Windows clients and stable connections: mobile access was a rare luxury.

Today, I see water distribution and treatment plants monitored from a tablet, anywhere. With a few clicks, a technician can check gates and levels. "No changes can be made, it's read-only," I am told.

Anyone in cybersecurity knows how thin the line is between "read-only" and "full control": sometimes it is just a bit on the server side, or worse, on the client side.

That is why incidents like the Florida water plant attack should not surprise us.

docs.title: IoT and the Lightness of Industry 4.0
docs.text:
The real mistake behind Industry 4.0 is assuming that those who design industrial devices, always focused on physical safety, are automatically able to handle cybersecurity.

I have seen critical networks designed as if they were just "cables carrying information", with no regard for network best practices. Consumer-grade switches bought in supermarkets were used instead of industrial-grade hardware designed for extreme conditions.

It is no surprise, then, that devices like those from General Electric revealed serious design flaws that can be exploited easily.

At the root, there is always the same issue: lack of awareness. If we have never looked at systems from the perspective of an attacker, we cannot imagine the consequences of poor design choices.

docs.title: The Consumer Side
docs.text:
The consumer IoT market is no better.

On one side, some vendors are finally integrating security into their development process. On the other, the race to the lowest price floods the market with cheap, poorly designed devices, often with hardcoded backdoors that make them impossible to secure.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
We are at the beginning of a new era, where security can no longer be ignored.

Early signals from both Europe and the U.S. already point in this direction: cybersecurity as a mandatory requirement for product commercialization. Those who move early will gain a significant competitive advantage.

The rest, as often happens, will come running, and unprepared.

docs.title: Securing user authentication under IEC 62443
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance ot-ics

I am discussing the IEC 62443 certification with an organization that builds and sells ICS plants which are risky from a safety perspective. The organization currently complies with the Machinery Directive (Directive 2006/42/EC of the European Parliament), but it does not consider cyber risk. Compliance is not mandatory today, but more and more customers ask for some "security" compliance.

Without reinventing the wheel, I chose the IEC 62443 framework as a guideline to evaluate the AS-IS situation and define the next steps.

IEC 62443 is very complete, but in this post I focus on AAA: Authentication, Authorization and Accounting.

docs.title: User Authentication in OT (and Medical Devices)
docs.text:
AAA functions are described in many parts of IEC 62443, at both system and component levels. Let's look at some requirements from IEC 62443-3-3 (I quote a few of them only as examples):

Security measures shall not adversely affect essential functions of a high availability IACS unless supported by a risk assessment. (Support of essential functions)

The control system shall provide the capability to identify and authenticate all human users. This capability shall enforce such identification and authentication on all interfaces which provide human user access to the control system to support segregation of duties and least privilege in accordance with applicable security policies and procedures. (SR 1.1 – Human user identification and authentication)

The control system shall provide the capability to employ multifactor authentication for human user access to the control system via an untrusted network (SR 1.1 RE 2 – Multifactor authentication for untrusted networks)

Automatic denial of access for control system operator workstations or nodes should not be used when immediate operator responses are required in emergency situations. (SR 1.11 – Unsuccessful login attempts)

The control system shall provide the capability to limit the number of concurrent sessions per interface for any given user (human, software process or device) to a configurable number of sessions. (SR 2.7 – Concurrent session control)

The control system shall provide the capability to centrally manage audit events and to compile audit records from multiple components throughout the control system into a system-wide (logical or physical), time-correlated audit trail [...] (SR 2.8 RE 1 – Centrally managed, system-wide audit trail, IEC 62443)

Medical devices have similar requirements.

In short:

  • AAA must be implemented properly: user and non-user access must be authenticated, authorized and logged.
  • In some cases, additional security measures may be required (MFA).
  • Emergency access (firecall) must be provided.
  • Security measures cannot affect essential functions.

These statements may sound contradictory, but we are missing an important piece: the context.

docs.title: The Context
docs.text:
In the real world, plants and medical devices are installed in specific contexts. Most of them are installed in a restricted area where only authorized personnel can enter and operate. In an emergency, they must operate as fast as possible. We should also differentiate the security measures for reading, writing and administrative operations.

I often see remote access to plants and medical devices for service assistance.

Finally, we need to evaluate the risk of the information available on the HMI, for both local and remote access. Medical devices are more critical, but ICS HMIs can also store confidential information (recipes, production details, etc.).

docs.title: A Hypothetical Approach
docs.text:
I do not have a magic recipe that fits any organization, but we can make some assumptions:

  1. Setting the same PIN or password for every HMI and user is useless and does not comply with IEC 62443 (users must be identified).
  2. In a restricted area, a read-only view may not require authentication.
  3. Some remote connections may not require a username and password. For example, remote control rooms can be authenticated by IP or VPN, and require stronger authentication only for write or administrative operations.
  4. Fast emergency access must be guaranteed.
  5. Any remote user must be identified with a strong authentication method (user, password, MFA).
  6. Security measures cannot affect essential functions, so we can offload AAA to external devices (firewalls, captive portals, NACs, etc.).

docs.title: Post-Incident Analysis Involving Casualties
docs.text:
The most critical situation a plant can face is one that involves casualties or physical damage. In these cases, we need to find the root cause and collect evidence that can help the investigation.

This is where logging and its security features, integrity and availability, come in. Every event should be logged and made permanent. The events I would log include:

  • Access (unauthenticated).
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Event logging and accounting.
  • Chat (especially during service assistance).
  • Software and configuration changes.
  • Output of integrity tests (systems and components).
  • State of each component (especially during service assistance).

The manufacturer should consider WORM media for accounting:

The control system shall provide the capability to determine whether a given human user took a particular action. (SR 2.12 – Non-repudiation)

In a specific event, a good logging platform with WORM media helped to prove that the customer, and not the manufacturer, caused the casualties.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: I often see OT and medical devices protected by simple PINs. Every time, I ask why they use the same 5-digit PIN, shared among all the authorized users and probably known by many more people. Blind compliance is useless: if we do not evaluate the context, we are not protecting a device, we are just scrolling a checklist.

docs.title: The Darwin's Law of Evolution for computers
docs.text: 09 October 2017

docs.title: The Darwin's Law of Evolution for computers
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance

We are living in the "hype" era, where everything is sold as the Holy Grail for a non-existent problem. Let's analyze things with a critical eye.

Prompted by a friend, who is writing a couple of very good posts that I recommend, I am sharing my thoughts about automation, the future of network engineers, AI and so on. This is my own point of view, the result of 20 years in the IT world, at work and at home.

It seems to me that vendors push more and more cool words, at a higher rate than in the past. A few years ago the "IT outsourcing" mantra lasted for a while, and everyone had to "outsource" something to become a good manager. Then came the "cloud" era, but it was too early, so it was a false start. In the last two years, many "mantras" have arrived together: big data, cloud (again, but with a different awareness), cybersecurity, automation and machine learning. They are too many! Not so many years ago, the idea of the cloud could be compared to a startup selling something that was not ready for the enterprise market. In the last few years, thanks to Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Salesforce and others, enterprises and IT managers can approach a valid cloud strategy with more awareness.

Lesson learned: it is better to wait for the second generation to get a mature technology.

I would add another one:

Lesson learned: a successful startup aims to be bought by a big company. Buying cloud services from small companies can lead to unexpected changes in services and licenses.

Now let's apply the thesis above to the current mantras, especially automation, machine learning and cybersecurity.

I think I can say that networking vendors include automation in every product. We have REST APIs to program every device, and UIs (user interfaces) that should help us manage the whole infrastructure with a few clicks and without knowing what is below. The real world is different from what marketing tells us, though: there are a lot of bugs that make the software unusable or dangerous.

Moreover, asking vendors for support gives fewer results than a walk to Santiago de Compostela or Lourdes.

docs.title: Vendor Software and Support
docs.text:
It seems to me that vendors are not interested in selling good software: everything must be developed and sold "agile" (no matter that the agile methodology is a completely different thing). The most critical aspect is that the quality of the support teams is terrible: a lot of FTE time is spent debugging what the vendor should analyze, there are a lot of embarrassing "it's by design" limits and, really, too many untrained people unable to support anything or anyone.

Lesson learned: vendors cannot write good software, and apparently they do not care much about it. They are only interested in selling ideas, not real and working features.

Let's move on to machine learning, the "hype" that will make humans useless. Computers can learn and detect things better than humans, and they can analyze a lot of data in a relatively short time, so big data is not a problem anymore. But, because there is always a "but", the real world is a little different. If someone uses Facebook to guess sexual orientation, we should ask ourselves how much of that research is "marketing" and how much is "real". The answer is that machine learning, used to detect whether a photographed man is gay, is slightly more efficient than an untrained human. So current machine learning algorithms perform better than thousands of untrained people. That is still a good thing, but we should remember that machine learning algorithms do not (currently) perform like experts.

Lesson learned: (current) machine learning algorithms perform slightly better than untrained humans, but they can manage a lot of data much faster than humans.

But machine learning applied to automation and cybersecurity will save the world! (Maybe.)

The security of our infrastructures, software, IoT and electronic devices is embarrassing. We have a lot of non-upgradeable devices (mobile phones, IoT devices, set-top boxes...) and a lot of devices with a vulnerable design. We also have infrastructures managed by untrained (cheap) people all around the world, and critical services exposed to the Internet with default or blank passwords. Meanwhile, a lot of vendors sell the Holy Grail of security.

The Holy Grail is apparently not enough, because thousands of computers are still infected by the WannaCry ransomware, and sooner or later someone will pay the price.

Lesson learned: cybersecurity is the current mantra, but it will not help much.

So we have mature cloud services, but automation, machine learning and security are still too young. The last year showed that connecting everything to the Internet is not always a good idea, especially if we connect hospitals, 911 emergency numbers, pacemakers, airplanes or IoT devices.

Should we live like the Amish? That is indeed a possibility, and when I retire I will certainly think about it.

docs.title: What Will the Future Look Like?
docs.text:
To conclude my train of thought:

  • Will the cloud kill IT experts? No, because infrastructures must be managed, platforms must be well deployed, and services must be well designed and well implemented.
  • Will automation kill network experts? No, because network experts started to automate things 10 years ago, and the current "hype" is not changing things much. You have to know what is below if you want to implement a good and effective solution.

docs.title: Is Cybersecurity Only a New "Hype"?
docs.text:
The network has always been asked to fix poorly designed software. I could write a lot about why the "stretched data center" is a bad choice, but this is not the right post. I see more and more good tools used to fix the wrong thing (containers used as VMs, snapshots used as backups...). The network layer cannot fix every single mistake of the layers above, and sooner or later those layers will pay a price.

I think that Darwin's Law of Evolution by Natural Selection is valid for computers and electronic devices too. It could also have a dramatic impact on human life.

docs.title: The importance of the CISO
docs.text: 19 February 2021

docs.title: The importance of the CISO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance

In this particularly challenging period for companies, many long-ignored or underestimated information security issues are coming to light. Several accelerating factors have put corporate security under pressure. The most relevant are:

  • The need to expose services globally has allowed us to reach international customers easily, but it has also made us equally accessible to potential attackers worldwide.
  • The availability of electronic money (cryptocurrencies) has made it easy to move capital across the globe without intermediaries such as banks.
  • Low awareness of information security has led to short-sighted decisions, whether due to budget constraints or a lack of skills to assess risks properly.
  • Reliance on third-party cloud resources has expanded the infrastructure, often increasing the attack surface unknowingly.
  • The lack of security assessment during rapid application development has resulted in the release of immature applications: functional but insecure.
  • The pandemic has forced many companies to improvise business continuity plans under tight deadlines.

The result of these six factors is an explosive mix, whose effects we are starting to see today, though many remain hidden from mainstream news. I would argue that we are just at the beginning: cybercrime is not only a huge business, it has also become the "fifth dimension" of conflict.

We can also admit that we have willingly ignored some tools, choosing the short path rather than the long-term one:

  • We often pursued international certifications such as ISO/IEC 27001 or PCI-DSS merely to obtain the "seal", rather than to add real value to the company.
  • GDPR compliance has often focused on the legal aspects, rather than on the complexity of IT processes, except in rare cases.

docs.title: A Predictable Failure
docs.text: Recent data breaches have triggered an "arms race" within companies, which hire security leaders (CISOs) and expect them to solve these challenges without strategy, budget, technical staff or the necessary commitment. I still see job offers where the future CISO reports to the CIO, an evident conflict of interest.

docs.title: Starting from the Beginning
docs.text:
Management must understand the risk posed by cyberattacks, but it often lacks the objective data even to consider the possibility. From this awareness, management must decide whether and how to act, delegating responsibility and authority accordingly.

What is needed is awareness, commitment and a leader with a cross-functional vision, covering company processes, risks and infrastructure, who can guide employees toward greater information security awareness.

Companies often look for a CISO as an internal hire, but this approach has drawbacks:

  • Experienced people who can guide the information security strategy come at a high cost.
  • CISOs reporting to the CIO often have limited independence and reduced operational capabilities.
  • Internal people may focus too narrowly on their immediate context, lose sight of the global threat landscape over time and risk becoming overly political.

docs.title: A Growth Path
docs.text:
In my work, I often meet companies that recognize the need to address information security but struggle to develop an effective strategy. Many want to begin a structured growth path, starting with management and training the existing staff. The goal is not to outsource the CISO function (which is rarely effective), but to give the tools to the people in the company who are in a position to act.

Through this gradual path, clients gain:

  • An understanding of the risks related to their infrastructure.
  • Awareness of how technological choices directly impact the business.
  • Improved processes over time, and higher overall security.

Most importantly, training the staff gives them the skills to manage security independently within the company going forward.

docs.title: The value of a Risk Based VA
The value of a Risk Based VA
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance risk-assessment vulnerability-management

In this article, I explain why we run a VA, why the traditional approach is dangerous and how we should manage the risk bound to vulnerabilities.

I also discuss a few false myths about VA.

I hope this article helps you approach the vulnerability management process in a way that reduces the unmanaged risk bound to vulnerabilities.

docs.title: The Purpose of a VA
docs.text:
Almost every company should request a yearly VA. In practice, they often request a VAPT (whatever that means). When I try to understand the reason behind this legitimate request, I realize it is not so clear: we do a VAPT every year because everybody does.

So let's start from the beginning. A Vulnerability Assessment (VA) is a measure. Specifically, a VA counts the known vulnerabilities present in systems and applications. VA scanners are signature-based: if they find application X, they estimate vulnerability Y.

Yes, VA scanners estimate vulnerabilities: they do not verify them. Most modern VA scanners include DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): they try to break web applications and report estimated web vulnerabilities.

Finally, VA scanners exclude custom applications and often exclude popular web frameworks (WordPress, Drupal...) too. The reason is simple: VA scanners rarely include signatures for a specific web application framework. Other specialized scanners exist: WordPress users, for example, should use specific scanners such as WPScan.

The outcome of a VA is a list of detected vulnerabilities:

  • An estimated risk value is usually included for each vulnerability (VAs are not context-aware).
  • Custom systems and applications are not evaluated (VA scanners do not include specific signatures).
  • Risk mitigations are not evaluated (VAs are not context-aware).

docs.title: Legacy Approach
docs.text:
In a legacy VA approach, the outcome is the input of a patch management process: we know what is vulnerable, and we need to patch.

This approach has some issues:

  • Blind patching: patching everything is not sustainable. In practice, IT teams start patching from the easiest systems with a best-effort approach. The result is that critical, mission-critical systems (SAP, Oracle, CRM...) are rarely patched.
  • Context-less: VA outcomes do not consider the security controls in place. Systems and applications in a high-security zone are patched with the same urgency as exposed services, just because they are affected by the same critical vulnerability.
  • Time-to-patch: with a yearly VA, in the worst case, a critical patch could be considered 1 year after its release.

docs.title: Risk-Based VA
docs.text:
In a risk-based approach, we add the context. The outcome of a VA must be enriched with:

  • Inherent risk: the risk bound to each specific vulnerability, excluding the mitigations in place.
  • Mitigation factor: how much the security controls in place (firewalls, IPSs, WAFs...) mitigate the risk.
  • Residual risk: the risk bound to each specific vulnerability, considering all the mitigation factors.

We can calculate the inherent risk as impact x likelihood.

All values depend on the application, but we can simplify and assume that:

  • Impact depends on the vulnerable networks, because once a network is compromised, all the systems it includes can be compromised too.
  • Likelihood depends on the vulnerability (available exploits, difficulty of exploitation...).
  • The mitigation factor depends on the security zone, because we can assume that security controls are deployed equally to secure a specific set of networks.
  • Residual risk is inherent risk x mitigation factor.

We need to define another value, the risk appetite: the risk value that the organization is willing to accept.

With a risk-based approach, the VA report is enriched (as discussed above) and ordered by residual risk:

  1. Vulnerabilities with a residual risk lower than or equal to the risk appetite are discarded.
  2. Vulnerabilities with a medium risk must be managed within, for example, 10 working days.
  3. Vulnerabilities with a critical risk must be managed within, for example, 3 working days.

A risk-based approach is deterministic and does not leave the risk unmanaged.

docs.title: False Myth: Provider Rotation
docs.text:
The first false myth I want to discuss is provider rotation. Many organizations I know change the provider (the company that executes the VA) every year, because they believe a different partner will detect different vulnerabilities. This is wrong, because:

  • VA providers use commercial software from Tenable, Rapid7 and others. I am not saying they are all equal, I am saying that changing the partner does not mean the tool is different.
  • Even if I change the VA scanner every year, it is unacceptable to discover vulnerabilities one year later just because I changed the tool (unmanaged risk).
  • Changing the tool means a different VA report format: to evaluate the process, I need to correlate KPIs between different tools, which is not easy.

docs.title: False Myth: VAPT
docs.text:
Organizations focus on VAPT only, often meaning a legacy VA. As discussed before, VA scanners are not designed to detect all the vulnerabilities that can affect organizations. VA scanners are a precious way to scan a large infrastructure quickly, within an acceptable time, but they are not designed to go deep.

DAST can help, but it is still bound to a specific context.

PT should be considered after the previous steps (VA and DAST) to evaluate critical custom services (HR portals, CRM...).

Organizations that limit themselves to VA do not manage the risk bound to custom applications.

docs.title: False Myth: VA as a Patch Management Tool
docs.text:
As mentioned, with a yearly VA we can have unmanaged vulnerabilities for one year (in the worst case). We can reduce the interval, but unless we execute a complete VA every week, we need a different approach.

A working vulnerability management process requires discovering, prioritizing and remediating vulnerabilities.

We can use a VA in the discovery phase, but the right input comes from vendor security feeds (Microsoft, Cisco, Red Hat...). We should:

  • Obtain new vulnerabilities on a daily basis.
  • Evaluate the associated risk.
  • Define how to mitigate it (patching, additional security controls...).

With this approach, VAs are used to verify the vulnerability management process, not to start it. Of course, this approach depends on other processes such as asset management, software management and change management.

docs.title: DIY and Automate
docs.text:
I am an automation addict, and I automate every boring process I can. In my view, large organizations should be able to execute VAs by themselves, and automate them from the scan phase to the report phase, including most of the risk assessment considerations.

Let's try to design the process:

  • The asset and software inventories contain what is running within the organization. The inventories also contain the impact score (the business value of the asset).
  • We can estimate a mitigation factor for each security zone, calculated by taking into account the security controls in place (firewalls, IPSs, WAFs...). This is not accurate, but it can work initially.
  • Based on the asset and software inventories, we can get the relevant vulnerabilities from vendor feeds.
  • Based on the estimated risk score (usually provided by vendors), we can calculate the inherent risk and report the medium and critical vulnerabilities.
  • An analyst analyzes the report and defines the next steps.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: We learned how to move from the legacy VAPT approach to a risk-based vulnerability management process. It is not easy, but the legacy approach leaves the risk unmanaged. VA scanners are valuable tools if used in the right way. They are dangerous if we use them as the single input of the vulnerability management process.

docs.title: Top management security
docs.text: 25 January 2021

docs.title: Top management security
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner digital-self-defence governance

The recent MyFreeCams case is a perfect example to explain to top management why the digital security of individuals should be addressed across all levels of an organization. Their data breach had both reputational and digital security impacts. I use MyFreeCams here only as an example.

docs.title: The Case
docs.text:
MyFreeCams, an adult chat service, suffered a data breach: 2 million accounts were exfiltrated. The stolen data included usernames, email addresses and plain-text passwords.

Once again, we see how often online services lack even the most basic security measures, and how these failures directly threaten users.

docs.title: Threat Modeling
docs.text:
When I deliver training on personal digital security, I hope that threat modeling becomes second nature: before signing up for a new service, people should pause and reflect on how it might become a risk. With time, users start to see the many facets of each platform.

Let's analyze how the MyFreeCams breach could directly impact individuals.

docs.title: Identity Theft
docs.text:
Many people still reuse the same password across multiple accounts. With username, email and password exposed, attackers can try to log in to other services: email, social media, e-commerce and more.

They can even lock users out of their accounts by resetting the credentials (identity theft).

Larger providers (like Google) often detect suspicious activity and block unusual access attempts. Smaller platforms usually lack such safeguards.

docs.title: Blackmail
docs.text:
MyFreeCams provides adult video chat services, so exposing user data could damage reputations. It is highly likely that some users will receive blackmail emails: pay up, or your use of the service will be revealed.

This is not new. In 2015, the dating service Ashley Madison suffered a breach that exposed 32 million users, including 15,000 government and military employees, who then received extortion attempts.

Blackmail does not always mean money. Sometimes the demand is for a certain action, or inaction.

docs.title: How to Respond After the Fact
docs.text:
Defenses should be planned in advance, but we also need to know how to react when the damage is done. Let's take two likely threats from the MyFreeCams breach:

  • Identity theft due to password reuse.
  • Blackmail aimed at harming reputation.

The first is easier to fix: change every account that used the same password, replacing it with a secure, unique, unpredictable one.

The second is more complex and sensitive. If you face blackmail, the first step is to contact law enforcement. Never negotiate with criminals whose only goal is to make money.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Personal digital security is one of my main concerns, whether I am speaking to young people or adults, and it is critical in business too. If the infrastructure is strong, it is far easier for attackers to target people than to break hardened defenses. Attacks on the reputation of individuals can spill over into the company, especially when the targets are key figures.

That is why awareness must start at the top. I believe digital security culture should be a central part of everyone's life, both private and professional. If people learn to navigate technology responsibly at home, they bring that awareness into the workplace, with huge benefits.

Simply delivering corporate video courses on cybersecurity, GDPR, spam or phishing is not enough. Without context and real-life relevance, those concepts remain sterile, with little value, usefulness or impact.

docs.title: Training in managing cyber attacks
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance

A cyber attack against a company can feel very similar to a terrorist attack. Shock, disbelief, fear and confusion are common emotions in the first hours after the incident is discovered.

Those first hours are also the most critical: this is when we must define the recovery strategies, and the ability to stay focused on the objective makes the difference.

docs.title: Acting on Instinct
docs.text:
In any traumatic event, panic reflexes often emerge. They are survival mechanisms deeply rooted in our biology:

  • Flee from predators stronger than us.
  • Freeze if there is no time to escape.
  • Fight to protect our children or buy them time to run.

A cyber attack, however, is not a physical threat in the same room, and we cannot fight it with instinct. Recognizing panic signals and regaining clarity is essential to focus on the real goal: restoring services and minimizing damage.

Strong leadership plays a key role here. Leaders must reassure people, channel their energy and guide them toward the shared objective. Wasting energy fighting colleagues (fight) does not help: the threat is elsewhere and, in fact, it has already passed.

This is why many emergency plans, even well designed on paper, fail in reality: under pressure, rationality often gives way to instinct.

docs.title: Training as a Discipline
docs.text:
In my work, I emphasize training as a way to build habits: habits that help us react to attacks in a structured, fast and effective manner.

Training prepares people not only by defining procedures but also by training the mind to stay clear-headed when chaos takes over. Repetition conditions the brain to follow precise patterns, especially under stress.

This is not a new invention. I simply borrow from practices already used in the military and from the wisdom of martial arts.

docs.title: Training vs. Education
docs.text:
In cybersecurity, the difference between education and training is substantial:

  • Education provides the theoretical and practical foundations to build and manage security.
  • Training develops the mindset needed to react effectively when danger strikes.

Limiting training to technical staff is a mistake. True resilience involves the entire organization. Some examples:

  • Training non-technical staff to recognize suspicious behavior and stop phishing attacks before they spread.
  • Training security guards to spot weaknesses in their daily routines.
  • Training top management to avoid exposing digital information that could compromise their reputation or physical safety.
  • Training team leaders to manage crises with calm authority, guiding their people with confidence.

docs.title: Final Thoughts
docs.text:
The real outcome of training is not only handling a crisis effectively. It is building a team that is cohesive, aware and resilient, able to work together more effectively while contributing to the overall security posture of the company.

In the end, cybersecurity is not just about technology. It is about people, and how prepared they are when the unexpected happens.

docs.title: VA scanners for patch management: good or bad?
VA scanners for patch management: good or bad?
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance risk-assessment vulnerability-management

Nowadays (hopefully) all companies run regular vulnerability assessments. They often use different partners or tools each year, and they often limit themselves to vulnerability assessments.

A VA is not the end of a security strategy, it is just a small step at the beginning. And changing providers every year is not as useful as you think: in my opinion, there are more cons than pros.

A VA does what its name says: a vulnerability assessment. VA scanners just find and count network vulnerabilities. Once you have a VA report, you are doing vulnerability management, not patch management or application life cycle management: those are different, concatenated processes.

Let me say it again:

VA scanners are used in vulnerability management, not patch management.

And:

VA scanners are used in vulnerability management, not in application life cycle management.

We mentioned three different processes:

  • Patch management: updating software to the currently supported versions.
  • Application life cycle management: disposing of or migrating legacy end-of-life applications.
  • Vulnerability management: reducing the risk of known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Patch Management
docs.text:
Patch management is the process of distributing and applying software updates. Patches correct errors (bugs), and sometimes bugs lead to security issues (vulnerabilities). In this post, we focus on vulnerabilities: the bugs that can affect confidentiality, integrity and/or availability (CIA). The GDPR uses the same attributes (Art. 32.1.b):

the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of processing systems and services;

The patch management process should describe:

  • How to be notified of a new software update.
  • How to evaluate the risk of installing or not installing the software update.
  • The SLA associated with the risk from the previous step.
  • How to request the installation of the software update.

Examples:

  1. CVE-2019-0708 (BlueKeep): a remote code execution vulnerability with a CVSSv3 score of 9.8 in Microsoft Windows RDP.
  2. CVE-2020-2021: an authentication bypass vulnerability with a CVSSv3 score of 10 in Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect.

The first vulnerability affects Microsoft Windows systems with RDP enabled, the second one affects Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect with SAML authentication enabled.

What is the associated risk?

Of course, it depends. It depends on the vulnerable assets: where they are (network location), how they are protected (security measures), the "value" they have for the organization... This information is stored in the asset inventory and governed by the asset management process.

Examples:

  1. We have a vulnerable, exposed Palo Alto Networks firewall with GlobalProtect. The impact is high, the likelihood is high (a public exploit is available) and there is no mitigation: the risk is severe.
  2. We have several vulnerable Microsoft Windows systems in the industrial network. The network is restricted and protected by a firewall with an IPS feature. We cannot upgrade those endpoints, the impact is high and the likelihood is high (a public exploit is available): the risk is maximum, but the firewall mitigates it by 80% (the risk is low).

Most organizations implement time-based patch management. In other words, they declare that they patch everything every 6 months. In many cases, this is wrong because:

  • Every organization has something that cannot be patched or disposed of.
  • There is always some urgency that delays the update process.

Moreover, in the example above, there is no patch for the Palo Alto Networks vulnerability, so the patch management process cannot mitigate it.

Acting this way leads to unmanaged risk (see the conclusions).

docs.title: Application Life Cycle Management
docs.text:
Application Life Cycle Management (ALM) covers several aspects of an application, from its initial planning through its retirement. In this post, we focus on the update and retirement phases.

To simplify, applications and their components must be updated. When (not if) components become obsolete, we must update the application to support newer or different components. In the real world, when components are retired, nobody updates the application anymore: after years, nobody knows how to change the code.

Finally, at the end of their life, applications must be retired. In the real world, applications are retired when nobody uses them anymore, and that can take years.

docs.title: Vulnerability Management
docs.text:
Vulnerability management is the process of evaluating the risk of known vulnerabilities and deciding how to mitigate them. Security assessments (including vulnerability assessments, penetration tests, attack simulations...) are the tools used to discover unknown vulnerabilities. Another important input of the vulnerability management process is the security feeds.

The output of any security assessment is a list of prioritized actions required to manage the risks of the discovered vulnerabilities.

Many companies use the VA as the basis of patch management: once the VA has detected the vulnerabilities, they are analyzed, evaluated and patched.

This is a pretty common approach in enterprises, and it is the fastest way to understand what is in place and plan the remediation. If you use the VA in the patch management process, however, consider that:

  • You discover vulnerabilities only after the VA.
  • In the worst-case scenario, you are vulnerable from the day after the previous VA until the next one (unmanaged risk).

Without a vulnerability management process, organizations that run the VA yearly can have unmanaged risk for 12 months (see the conclusions).

docs.title: VA Scanner Limits
docs.text:
Please be aware that:

  • Network vulnerabilities are just a minor part: we should also look for local vulnerabilities. Attackers use local vulnerabilities for privilege escalation after they gain local access, maybe through malware or a custom vulnerable application (e.g., Log4j).
  • VA scanners look for known, signature-based vulnerabilities. Sometimes they try to analyze web applications (DAST), but they never recognize uncommon or custom applications. For example, VA scanners do not detect all the vulnerabilities in WordPress, Joomla and similar applications. We need specialized scanners (e.g., wpscan).

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
VA scanners are great tools to find out quickly what is running within the organization and the associated vulnerabilities. Even if we run the VA every month, a critical vulnerability can put the organization at risk for one month (worst case). Sometimes this is acceptable, sometimes not. If we cannot define it clearly, we are not managing the risk properly.

VA scanners are still a fundamental tool for organizations, and they are the fast path to assess unknown environments. After a while, however, organizations should introduce vulnerability management together with patch management: monitoring security feeds reduces the risk of newly released vulnerabilities in days, not months.

For severe vulnerabilities, we can assume that patches must be installed within 24 hours. In the example above, the change request for the Palo Alto Networks patch has high priority. We can skip the Microsoft Windows patch because the risk is lower than the risk appetite (and also because updating an HMI is a mess).

If everything is going fine, VA scanners do not find severe vulnerabilities. In practice, if the processes above are in place, the vulnerability assessment verifies that the critical patches are installed and the obsolete applications are retired.

Moreover, if you change the VA provider every year, ask yourself whether it makes sense, considering that:

  • Most partners use VA scanners from two or three vendors.
  • It is not easy to compare KPIs automatically between different software.
  • The value is not in the automatic VA report, but after it (risk analysis, remediation plan).

And finally, if you run the n-th yearly VA and nothing more, you are not managing cyber risk at all. You are just following some odd guidelines. Sad but true.

docs.title: Vulnerability Management
docs.text: 02 December 2024

docs.title: Vulnerability Management
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance vulnerability-management

A lot has already been said about Vulnerability Management (VM), and I have touched on this topic several times before. Yet managing vulnerabilities remains a significant challenge for most organizations.

Our offensive activities consistently show that, when an attack succeeds, the attack path often hinges on software or logical vulnerabilities. More often than not, the IT department already knew about these vulnerabilities but, for one reason or another, could not mitigate them.

In other words, the success of the offensive action stems from widely known vulnerabilities.

And this is not a rare scenario.

docs.title: What Is a Vulnerability?
docs.text:
In the most common (and technical) sense, a vulnerability is a software flaw that can compromise confidentiality, integrity and/or availability. This definition covers only a specific category, though. If we broaden the concept, the term "vulnerability" can also apply to:

  • Processes.
  • People.
  • Configurations.

docs.title: Process Vulnerabilities
docs.text: A process vulnerability arises when workflows fail to ensure confidentiality, potentially exposing sensitive information to unauthorized individuals. For example, I once came across a box of employee pay slips left unattended. The employee handling the box was following the correct procedure, but the procedure itself did not account for such risks.

docs.title: Psychological Vulnerabilities
docs.text: These occur when attackers exploit human weaknesses through social engineering techniques. Phishing, tailgating and piggybacking are classic examples that target psychological vulnerabilities to extract sensitive information.

docs.title: Configuration Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Also known as logical vulnerabilities, these arise when, for instance, a network share allows unauthorized access. Often such issues result from oversight, but in some cases they happen because the person responsible for the setup lacked the necessary security knowledge.

We could also mention physical vulnerabilities (e.g., locks, doors, gates), but focusing too much on these technical aspects might detract from the broader applicability of this discussion.

docs.title: Managing Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Many people immediately associate "vulnerability management" with patching. Managing a vulnerability, however, does not mean simply eliminating it with a software patch. It means assessing the associated risk and mitigating it. Mitigation strategies can include:

  • Patching or reconfiguring the system.
  • Shutting down the vulnerable system.
  • Training employees.
  • Adding security controls.
  • ...

In extreme cases, we can transfer the risk through insurance (although insurers typically exclude companies they deem too high-risk after their evaluations).

docs.title: Evaluating a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Not all vulnerabilities are created equal. Each vulnerability has unique characteristics regarding type, impact, exploitability and mitigability. This means we cannot rely solely on standard reports: we need to complement them with public information, which changes over time, and with data specific to our organization.

In other words, we need a risk-based mindset when we address vulnerabilities.

One critical aspect to emphasize: the risk associated with a vulnerability changes over time. Typically (though not always), someone discovers a vulnerability, it is eventually exploited and then it becomes dangerous. Furthermore, 2024 alone has shown us several examples of patches that failed to fully resolve issues. This highlights the need to monitor each vulnerability continuously.

To assess vulnerabilities better, we should evaluate the likelihood that someone exploits them maliciously. This evaluation can consider:

  • Whether the vulnerability is practically exploitable.
  • Whether public exploits exist.
  • Evidence, on a global scale, of exploitation by threat actors.
  • Which assets are affected, particularly regarding the data they contain.
  • The potential for lateral movement, i.e., spreading from a compromised asset to adjacent assets.
  • Existing security measures designed to block threats targeting the vulnerable assets.

A simplified approach might distill this into three primary factors:

  • Likelihood of exploitation, based on the global threat landscape.
  • Impact on the organization if someone exploits the vulnerability.
  • Mitigation effectiveness due to existing security controls.

docs.title: CVSS Score ≠ Risk
docs.text:
Before discussing how to assess a vulnerability, we need to clarify a common misconception: the CVSS value cannot be the foundation of our vulnerability assessment process.

The first reason is that a vulnerability may not have an associated CVE. There are various reasons why this might happen:

  • The person who discovered the vulnerability may not have the time or inclination to obtain a CVE designation.
  • The vulnerability might not pertain to software, which makes it impossible to associate a CVE.

The second reason, as noted on the FIRST website, is that the CVSS value is calculated under the assumption that all the prerequisites for exploiting the vulnerability are met:

if a specific configuration is required for an attack to succeed, the vulnerable system should be assessed assuming it is in that configuration.

CVSS measures the severity of a vulnerability, not the risk associated with it. With appropriate caution, we can use it to calculate risk, but we must fill the gap for vulnerabilities without an associated CVE.

docs.title: Practically Assessing a Vulnerability
docs.text:
My approach emphasizes practical and sustainable actions that let companies achieve swift and effective improvements in corporate security. Even at the cost of oversimplifying the theory, my focus is always on the objective.

We have seen that CVSS cannot be the sole metric, both because it requires contextualization and because not all vulnerabilities have an associated CVE.

Many tools for detecting vulnerabilities simplify the process by assuming a risk factor. This makes the tool easier to use, but we must supplement the resulting data with contextual information.

In practice, the simplest (but, as we will see, incorrect) approach is to use vulnerability scanning tools that identify latent vulnerabilities and associate a risk factor with each.

Unfortunately, it is quite common for vulnerability scans to reveal thousands, or even tens of thousands, of vulnerabilities of varying severity in an organization. It is equally common that the managers who review such reports despair, as the task ahead seems insurmountable.

The issue is that, in any organization, certain activities take precedence over everything else. In other words, vulnerabilities keep accumulating because:

  • Some systems cannot be shut down.
  • Some systems are untouchable.
  • Some systems are critical but no longer supported.
  • Nobody wants to risk deploying a flawed patch and compromising a critical business service.

I have previously discussed the Assume breach design concept, which I revisit here: we should design every system with the understanding that it could eventually be compromised. Specifically, if an organization has untouchable systems, we must place them in a high-security area. This is always the case in the ICS/OT domain, which I addressed in a dedicated post.

In this context, vulnerability management should begin at the design phase, incorporating security measures to reduce the risk of compromise. After the design phase, we can still make efforts to rethink the architecture, although they are labor-intensive.

My approach to evaluating a vulnerability, appropriately simplified (and incomplete), involves:

  • Using the risk factor suggested by the vulnerability scanning tool.
  • Adjusting this factor if the context requires it.
  • Applying a corrective value that reflects the impact on the organization.
  • Applying a corrective value that reflects the security measures implemented within the organization.

In practice:

  • The risk factor is rarely customized.
  • The risk factor considers the vulnerability net of any existing security measures, meaning it represents a publicly exposed asset.
  • The impact on the organization is a pre-calculated factor for each security zone (I assume that a compromise can propagate freely within the same zone).
  • The corrective value is pre-calculated for the security measures present in the organization (firewalls, IPS, EDR, SIEM, etc.).

Obviously, the approach is imprecise, incomplete and partly incorrect (we will see why later). Its contribution to organizations is significant, though:

  • Thousands of vulnerabilities are now weighted based on the security measures in place, which makes it possible to define priorities.
  • Security measures are considered, which allows us to discuss whether we should move untouchable assets to separate zones.
  • The impact of a complete attack is considered, not just that of the vulnerable asset.
  • It allows us to define justifications for why certain assets might remain unpatched.

This approach, sometimes referred to as risk-based vulnerability assessment, is gaining increasing traction. In particular, I see the compliance and insurance sectors welcoming a risk-based approach and evaluating it positively.

In other words, it is justified for critical vulnerabilities to exist, provided that we manage them with a risk-based approach.

docs.title: Predicting the Future
docs.text:
In a pragmatic approach, we consider something a vulnerability if it can be exploited. Many vulnerabilities require such specific conditions that exploitation becomes unfeasible in practice. The CVSS value takes into account the complexity of the attack, but with only two possibilities: low and high.

FIRST has defined a parameter that represents the probability that someone exploits a vulnerability in the next 30 days:

EPSS is a measure of exploitability. Specifically, EPSS is estimating the probability of observing any exploitation attempts against a vulnerability in the next 30 days.

The value of EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), which is variable over time, helps us define the SLA to mitigate each vulnerability associated with a CVE.

docs.title: Mitigating a Vulnerability
docs.text:
At this point, we should have a list of vulnerabilities with the associated risk, net of security measures (inherent risk), and a mitigation factor that represents the security measures in place (EDR, firewall, awareness, etc.). The combination of these two factors tells us the risk that someone exploits a vulnerability, considering the security measures (residual risk).

Before we sort this list in descending order of risk and start compiling the remediation plan, we are missing one last factor: the risk appetite. This factor indicates the level of risk that our organization considers acceptable. Once we define it, we automatically ignore all the vulnerabilities with a residual risk below this factor. If we have any doubts, it means our risk model has some flaws.

We now have a list of real, exploitable vulnerabilities for which the risk is not acceptable. We must therefore define actions to reduce the risk of each vulnerability.

We can:

  • Resolve the risk, for example by updating the vulnerable software or shutting it down.
  • Mitigate the risk by implementing a new security measure (e.g., moving the vulnerable system to a higher security zone).
  • Transfer the risk, for example through insurance or third parties.

docs.title: Patching
docs.text:
Often we can resolve a vulnerability by installing an update. We must ask ourselves when to do it, though. I have seen organizations with monthly patching policies, at best. In the worst cases, systems are updated once a year or even less frequently.

First, each system and application should have a well-defined maintenance window.

Second, we must associate a specific SLA with each risk category: the higher the risk, the faster we must install the updates and, consequently, the shorter the intervals between maintenance windows. Paradoxically, the more critical a system is from a business perspective, the more frequently we must take it offline for maintenance.

For this reason, organizations tend to perform what I call "blind patching", which focuses not on risk but on the systems that are easiest to update. This is exactly why hundreds or thousands of vulnerabilities accumulate in many companies.

Another consideration is that patching activities often lack proper "dignity". The people responsible for patching do it at their own risk:

  • If everything goes well, they receive no recognition.
  • If something goes wrong, they are blamed for the disruption and are responsible for restoring the service.

In this environment, people avoid taking on patching tasks, which causes further delays. If we think that the lack of patching is a resource problem, we soon discover that the real issue is that nobody wants to press the button and take on the associated responsibility.

From an organizational perspective, it is unrealistic to have a cross-functional team responsible for software updates. Each system serves an application necessary for the business. In this sense, applications and systems have an assigned owner who guarantees the service. If we want the process to work, we cannot decouple the responsibility for the application from the responsibility for its updates.

The final consideration concerns the maximum time to mitigate a vulnerability. This time depends on conditions that change over time (as we discussed with EPSS). It is worth citing a Cloudflare report:

CVEs exploited as fast as 22 minutes after proof-of-concept published

22 minutes is an impossible time frame to manage these vulnerabilities manually. In 22 minutes, we might not even notice the new vulnerability. We need a different approach.

docs.title: Mitigating Risk
docs.text:
We have already stated that patching is one of the possibilities for managing software vulnerabilities. In many cases, however, we cannot patch. The typical reasons are:

  • The application cannot be stopped frequently enough to allow continuous patching.
  • The application is no longer supported, and updates are no longer available.
  • The application is no longer sold and/or the vendor no longer exists.

There are also more operational reasons, such as:

  • Nobody wants to take responsibility for updating a mission-critical application.
  • There is no proper rollback system.
  • The risk of encountering issues is higher than the risk of leaving the application as it is.

This situation is common in ICS/OT environments, especially in manufacturing, medical, naval, utilities, oil and gas... On closer inspection, though, every company has applications that cannot be updated.

We must also consider that business processes are very often tied to a specific application. The evolution of this application is often faster than the speed at which business processes can evolve. A prime example: the company relies on a specific CRM with customizations that are key to its business processes. Subsequent major releases of that CRM do not guarantee full portability of the customizations, which forces the company to spend time and resources chasing each successive release.

It becomes clear that if we use patching as the only method to resolve software vulnerabilities, we will always have a set of unmanageable objects.

If we return to a risk-based approach, things change.

If we know the risk associated with each application (and thus each asset), we can isolate it in a specific security zone protected by adequate security measures. For example, if we have industrial systems that are both particularly vulnerable and important, we can isolate them in a secure zone. We can limit and control the communications to and from this zone to reduce the risk of compromise.

We have just described the Purdue model (SANS Secure Architecture for Industrial Control Systems), which suggests creating a containment zone between the IT and OT worlds.

We may not be able to implement the Purdue model in your company (and probably we cannot), but we can use the idea to separate critical, non-upgradable applications from manageable ones. By optimizing security measures, we can create a barrier strong enough to protect even the most fragile devices.

Security measures can include:

  • Firewalls with particularly stringent rules.
  • Web Application Firewalls (WAF).
  • EDR / XDR.
  • Behavioral analysis.
  • Active monitoring services.
  • NAC (Network Access Control).
  • Microsegmentation.
  • Network probes.
  • Honeypots.
  • ...

In practice, my advice is to start with a well-structured asset inventory. We should characterize each asset based on its impact on business operations (see NIS2) and on personal data (GDPR). Each asset should also have a defined maintenance window: this value is key to understanding how much we can operate on an asset without impacting the business.

Where the maintenance window is not enough to ensure proper maintenance, we need to mitigate the potential risk of compromise by enhancing the security measures.

We can then define the necessary security zones, protected by additional security measures. Ideally, we can represent these security measures with a numerical factor, which we use to calculate the residual risk. This way, each security zone has a mitigation factor associated with the assets it contains.

This approach lets us extend traditional vulnerability scanning tools by including the context, i.e., the protection derived from the security zone in which the assets reside.

docs.title: VA Scanner
docs.text:
The most common system today for identifying software vulnerabilities within an organization is the Vulnerability Assessment (VA). Specifically, we are talking about vulnerability scanner applications that scan the network for known vulnerabilities. They detect vulnerabilities through signatures: if a service announces its version and that version is vulnerable, the scanner reports the service as vulnerable.

It is clear that these tools are often overrated.

docs.title: Generic Risk
docs.text:
Vulnerability scanners provide a report of the detected vulnerabilities and associate a risk with each one. This risk factor is obviously incomplete: it lacks context.

We have already seen how to assess risk by associating specific information about the asset and the available security measures.

docs.title: Limited Coverage
docs.text:
The effectiveness of a scanner, or its ability to find all the vulnerabilities in the infrastructure, is tied to the signature database it uses. No scanner can have 100% coverage, for two reasons:

  • The software landscape is highly diverse, and there are products (like WordPress) that a vast ecosystem of plugins can extend.
  • Almost every organization has custom applications.

The utility of a vulnerability scanner is undeniable, because it lets us analyze thousands of devices in a very short time. We must also plan deeper analyses of well-known applications that the scanner may not cover.

It is also worth mentioning that many companies turn to different vendors to perform the VA, hoping to gain better coverage over time. If all the companies use the same scanner, the result is obviously the same. At most, the interpretation may vary.

docs.title: Local Vulnerabilities
docs.text: In almost all cases, vulnerability assessments are limited to network scanning. This means that they completely overlook all the local vulnerabilities, such as those that attackers could exploit to escalate privileges after gaining local access.

docs.title: Annual Scanning
docs.text:
If we conduct vulnerability assessments to detect vulnerabilities, we must consider the maximum time that may pass between the moment a vulnerability becomes public (and starts being exploited) and the moment we become aware of it.

We have seen that active exploitation of a vulnerability can occur within minutes of its disclosure. Conducting annual, semi-annual, quarterly or even monthly scans therefore makes little sense.

docs.title: Detection vs. Verification
docs.text:
Vulnerability scanning systems are not meant to discover vulnerabilities. They are meant to check the vulnerability management process.

In other words, if the vulnerability management process works correctly, the report of the scanner is almost always (if not always) redundant.

docs.title: Vulnerability Management Process
docs.text:
The vulnerability management process brings together all the considerations we have made so far and formalizes the operational procedures. The process begins when someone detects a new vulnerability, which can happen through various sources:

  • Reports.
  • Automated tools.
  • Individuals.

We analyze and evaluate each report to understand the associated risk. If the inherent risk, reassessed based on the existing security measures, exceeds the activation threshold, we must trigger the change management process to mitigate the vulnerability further.

To summarize:

  • Patch management involves updating software to supported versions. Updates that resolve functional bugs are part of this process.
  • Application life cycle management involves removing or migrating obsolete applications that have reached the end of their life cycle.
  • Vulnerability management involves reducing the risk associated with known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
We have seen that the time interval between the discovery of a technical vulnerability and its exploitation "in the wild" is very small. On the other hand, technical vulnerabilities are constant, and managing the updates that address them requires significant effort. We have also seen that the most critical systems are the hardest to update, both because they are hard to halt and because nobody wants to modify critical systems that are working.

Today we cannot think of addressing the vulnerability management process without automatic or semi-automatic systems. The most basic form of automation, usually applied to end-user devices, is a weekly update. More complex workflows, upon confirmation, update the systems first on test groups, then on groups of increasing criticality.

My experience tells me that the more a process is defined and automated within the organization, the less likely people are to question it. In other words, if a system stops working because someone updated it manually, the responsibility falls on that person. If an automated organizational process updates a system, the organization accepts and manages any malfunction.

docs.title: Immutable OS and Containers
docs.text:
"Immutable" systems do not allow modifications. In other words, we create and configure an immutable system, typically through an automated process, and then destroy it without anyone modifying it. Containers behave the same way in this regard.

Likewise, we do not update immutable systems and containers: we destroy and recreate them from an updated base template.

This approach, used by organizations with a strong DevOps culture, is ideal for:

  • Managing system changes, including updates.
  • Creating test groups of increasing criticality.
  • Applying updates on a daily or hourly basis.
  • Rolling back to the previous version in a matter of seconds.

docs.title: SBOM and Vulnerabilities in Templates
docs.text:
Those who develop software, and even those who only use open-source software, should monitor the vulnerabilities of the libraries their main application depends on. This may seem, and indeed is, a monumental task. We can tackle it by structuring an automated process to perform these checks.

The goal is to prevent situations like the one we saw with Log4Shell.

One potential approach uses the CycloneDX utility to get a list of the libraries used by a specific piece of software in a standard format (SBOM, or Software Bill of Materials). A second utility can then use this list to analyze any vulnerabilities:

cyclonedx-npm package.json > sbom.json
bomber scan sbom.json

The mechanism can certainly be improved, but it is a first step in structuring a process that monitors, as much as possible, the applications installed within the organization.

docs.title: Post Patching (Threat Hunting)
docs.text:
We reach the end of this long post by considering the vulnerability life cycle:

Once we resolve a vulnerability, we must ask ourselves a key question: is it possible that someone has already exploited it? How should we proceed?

The answer is not simple and depends heavily on the vulnerability. In some cases, Indicators of Compromise (IoC) associated with the vulnerability help us determine whether it has already been exploited, but in many cases these indicators are not available.

Ideally, organizations regularly perform an activity (threat hunting) aimed at detecting the silent threats already inside the organization that, for some reason, other security systems did not detect or block.

Our vulnerability management process could therefore trigger specific threat hunting activities for the vulnerability we are managing. For example, we might want to start in-depth analyses for particularly critical vulnerabilities with an EPSS score above 70%.

docs.title: What does it take to secure any SME organization
What does it take to secure any SME organization
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance intermediate

Managing cybersecurity is expensive, we all know that. Not managing it is even more expensive. In my experience, an SME recovers from a critical cyberattack in 5-10 days, if it can recover at all (I know companies that lost everything because of a cyberattack).

So how can an SME adopt a minimal but effective cybersecurity strategy?

To plan a strategy, we need to understand common cyberattacks and threat actors.

docs.title: SMEs, Threat Actors and Cyberattacks
docs.text:
First, let's describe an SME:

  • Privately owned (I often find a single owner).
  • Manufacturing sector.
  • A maximum of 150 employees, most of them working in production.
  • A maximum of $50 million in annual receipts.
  • A very small or outsourced IT department.
  • A low IT budget.
  • Low cybersecurity awareness: management often does not want to be bothered with security topics.
  • Increasing security compliance requirements.

SMEs need to protect:

  • Production.
  • CRM.
  • Intellectual property.

Threat actors targeting SMEs probably want to:

  • Compromise the company and ask for a ransom (usually).
  • Steal intellectual property (seldom).
  • Sabotage the company (rarely).

Based on the above, the most frequent cyberattack is ransomware.

docs.title: Lifecycle of a Ransomware Attack
docs.text:
The New Zealand CERT describes the lifecycle of a ransomware attack.

In short, there are 4 ways for an attacker to get inside an organization:

  • Phishing.
  • Password guessing.
  • Vulnerability exploitation.
  • Email.

Three out of four are people-based attacks. Using social engineering techniques, attackers try to:

  • Steal valid credentials by persuading people to enter them in malicious web portals.
  • Guess passwords using public data breaches, assuming people reuse passwords.
  • Persuade people to download and execute malware to take control of computers inside the organization.

docs.title: Designing an Effective Cybersecurity Strategy
docs.text:
Based on the most probable attack, we can design a cybersecurity strategy that reduces the risk. We must always remember that we are talking about SMEs, so the budget is limited.

We can mitigate the risk of an attacker getting inside the organization as follows:

  • Technical measures:
  • Multi-Factor Authentication: MFA for email access and remote access VPNs (mitigates phishing and password guessing).
  • Antispam: filter out malicious emails (mitigates phishing and email).
  • Logging: detect invalid login attempts (mitigates password guessing).
  • Security Assessment: detect vulnerabilities via VA, DAST and PT (mitigates vulnerability exploitation).
  • Patching: keep applications up to date. Because the IT department is very small, patching must happen automatically (mitigates vulnerability exploitation).
  • Endpoint Detection and Response: a good EDR to stop malware (mitigates email).
  • Segregation: well-configured network and host-based firewalls that drop malicious incoming and outgoing connections (mitigate the last attack phases).
  • Data Protection: in the worst-case scenario, we must be able to get our data back (mitigates the last attack phase).
  • Organizational measures:
  • Policies and Procedures: enforce password security (mitigates password guessing).
  • Training: test how good employees are at detecting social engineering attacks (mitigates phishing and email).

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: I think this is the minimal set of technical and organizational measures that any organization should implement to reduce the risk of cyberattacks. Even very small organizations should evaluate the security controls described above.

docs.title: Leveraging Nautobot as a SSOT
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner nautobot ssot

Every company should move away from Excel sheets as databases for managing the infrastructure and adopt a structured system as the foundation of its operational workflows.

The goal is a single repository that contains all the infrastructure data, including:

  • VLANs, IP networks, IP addresses and VRFs (IPAM).
  • Sites, physical and virtual devices.
  • Rack configuration and cabling.

This type of data structure is often called SSOT, or Single Source of Truth, which implies that the database:

  • Reflects what is configured in the infrastructure.
  • Serves as the source for various workflows.

In reality, things are a bit different: a SSOT, as defined here, is not truly a "source" but more of a destination. For instance:

  • VLANs, IP networks, IP addresses and VRFs are configured within the devices. We can always create a new VLAN inside a device without updating the SSOT.
  • VMs are configured within the virtual environments (e.g., ESXi). We can always add a VM locally to a host (e.g., ESXi) in a way that the orchestrator (e.g., vCenter) or the SSOT cannot see.

That is why I prefer the term Single Pane Of Glass (SPOG). A SPOG is a dashboard that collects data from external sources and presents it in an integrated and coherent way. From a SPOG, we can run workflows that change the state of the systems.

To summarize:

  • A unified data structure that shows the state of the infrastructure is essential to reduce operational costs.
  • It is not accurate to call it strictly a SSOT (Single Source Of Truth).
  • We should approach the problem by developing a SPOG (Single Pane Of Glass).
  • A SPOG should be fed, or at least verified, with real data from the infrastructure (often from the individual devices).
  • We can associate workflows with the SPOG to make changes to the infrastructure.

From here on, we use the terms SSOT and SPOG interchangeably for simplicity, now that we have clarified the differences.

Here is an example:

  • We use Nautobot (or NetBox) as the SSOT.
  • We feed it with data from the devices of the infrastructure.
  • We define profiles to associate with the switch interfaces.
  • When we change the profile associated with an interface in Nautobot, the configuration of the switch is updated automatically.

In the next posts, we implement this workflow from scratch in a development environment. We do not cover how to move the development environment to production.

docs.title: Choosing the foundation for our SSOT
Choosing the foundation for our SSOT
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner nautobot ssot

The first topic is the choice of the software that serves as the foundation for our SSOT (Single Source of Truth). Our goal is a data structure that consolidates the critical information about our infrastructure, such as:

  • VLANs, IP networks, IP addresses and VRFs (IPAM).
  • Sites, physical and virtual devices.
  • Rack configuration and cabling.

In essence, we are looking for an IPAM (IP Address Management) tool that can also store other types of data. This data structure is the base for automated workflows, so it needs to be:

  • Well documented.
  • Designed with an API-first approach.
  • Open source.
  • Extensible via plugins.
  • Written in a widely used automation language (Python).

We have two main candidates: Nautobot and NetBox. Nautobot is a fork of NetBox created in 2021. The main reason for its development was to evolve the product into a platform that automates the processes of an organization.

Both products are undergoing significant restructuring, often with substantial breaking changes. This affects the future of our integration:

  • Our implementation must keep up with the updates of the product: our integration must not prevent future updates of the SSOT.
  • The closer we stay to the official features of the product, the fewer customizations we need, which simplifies future updates.
  • Fewer customizations mean fewer problems, so we use standard constructs.
  • The product must support interface roles.

Demo versions of both products are available:

  • demo.netbox.dev: registration required.
  • demo.nautobot.com: username demo, password nautobot.
  • next.demo.nautobot.com: username demo, password nautobot.

The demos show that the next version of Nautobot can assign roles to interfaces, a feature that is not available in the current versions of NetBox or Nautobot. The demo had a bug, which should now be resolved and integrated in the demo.

The decision is therefore clear: we use the upcoming version of Nautobot to implement our SSOT.

docs.title: Installing Nautobot in your lab environment
Installing Nautobot in your lab environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner lab nautobot

In this post, we install Nautobot in a lab environment. For a production installation, refer to the official documentation. Nautobot requires a Python version between 3.8 and 3.11, so we first check that we have the correct one:

$ python3 -V
Python 3.11.9

Next, we create a dedicated Python environment:

mkdir /opt/nautobot
python3.11 -m venv /opt/nautobot/venv
source /opt/nautobot/venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip wheel setuptools
pip install --no-binary=pyuwsgi nautobot

We use PostgreSQL as the database. After installing PostgreSQL, we create a dedicated database and user for Nautobot:

$ psql postgres
create user nautobot with password '<DB_PASSWORD>';
create database nautobot;
grant all privileges on database nautobot to nautobot;

We configure Nautobot with the following environment variables:

export NAUTOBOT_ROOT=/opt/nautobot
export NAUTOBOT_DB_HOST=localhost
export NAUTOBOT_DB_NAME=nautobot
export NAUTOBOT_DB_USER=nautobot
export NAUTOBOT_DB_PASSWORD=<DB_PASSWORD>
export NAUTOBOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=*
export NAUTOBOT_DEBUG=True

We initialize the basic configuration, which is saved to /opt/nautobot/nautobot_config.py:

nautobot-server init

We update the database:

nautobot-server migrate

We create the first administrative user:

nautobot-server createsuperuser

Finally, we start the Nautobot server:

nautobot-server runserver

We can now access Nautobot at http://localhost:8000/ with the credentials of the admin user created earlier.

docs.title: Installing a Development Version of Nautobot
docs.text:
As discussed, the feature we need (interface roles) is available in the next version of Nautobot. We follow the official guide to install it.

First, we activate the Python environment created before:

cd /opt/nautobot
source venv/bin/activate

We uninstall the current version of Nautobot:

pip uninstall -y nautobot

We download the next version from GitHub:

git clone --depth 1 --branch next https://github.com/nautobot/nautobot

We install the version we just downloaded:

cd nautobot
poetry install

We update the database:

nautobot-server migrate

We start Nautobot:

nautobot-server runserver

docs.title: Populating our SSOT with Automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate nautobot ssot
