Now we need to populate our Single Source of Truth (SSOT). Adding the interfaces of each device manually is impractical, so we automate the process: we read the configuration of the devices and create the corresponding SSOT objects.

There is currently no official system for automatic device discovery. This is why I developed NetDoc years ago, although it works only with NetBox.

Let's create a simple automation for this task.

We use the following tools:

  • Netmiko to connect to the devices and retrieve information.
  • NTC Templates to parse the information into structured data.
  • The REST API of Nautobot to create the SSOT objects.

We assume that the device is created manually in our SSOT for convenience, so our automation only populates the interfaces.

Let's develop the automation step by step.

docs.title: Parameters Needed for Our Automation
docs.text:
Our automation requires the following parameters:

  • nautobot_base_url: the URL to access Nautobot.
  • nautobot_apikey: the API key to make REST API requests to Nautobot.
  • host: the IP address of the physical device to read.
  • username: the username to access the physical device.
  • password: the password to access the physical device.

We create the API key in Nautobot under User → Profile → API Tokens → Add a token.

In the example script, some parameters are read interactively while others are defined statically in the code. The script is a simple example and must not be used as it is in production environments.

docs.title: Connecting to the Device and Retrieving Information
docs.text:
Next, we connect to the device and retrieve the information we need. In this example, the device is a Cisco IOS XE switch, and two commands provide the data we need:

  • show version: to retrieve the hostname of the device.
  • show interfaces: to retrieve all the configured interfaces and their additional parameters.
with ConnectHandler(**data) as net_connect:
    show_version = net_connect.send_command("show version", use_textfsm=True)
    show_interfaces = net_connect.send_command("show interfaces", use_textfsm=True)

The use_textfsm parameter transforms the human-readable output into structured data immediately. The transformation (parsing) is performed with the TextFSM library by Google and NTC Templates.

docs.title: Processing the Retrieved Data
docs.text:
Now that we have the data in a structured format, we clean it up and extract only the following parameters:

  • Hostname (standardized to uppercase).
  • Interface name, description and link status.
device_name = show_version[0]["hostname"].upper()
device_interfaces = {
    item["interface"]: {
        "description": item["description"],
        "status": "Active" if item["link_status"] == "up" else "Decommissioning",
    }
    for item in show_interfaces
}

docs.title: Updating Data on Nautobot
docs.text:
We are now ready to update the data on Nautobot. To do this, we need to:

  • Retrieve the device ID by its name. We assume that the device already exists in Nautobot.
  • Add the interfaces associated with the device only if they do not already exist.

First, we retrieve the devices by filtering on their name:

# Ingesting data to Nautobot
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Token {nautobot_apikey}",
    "Accept": "application/json",
}

# Get device ID
url = f"{nautobot_base_url}/api/dcim/devices/?name={device_name}"
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30).json()
if req["count"] < 1:
    raise ValueError(f"{device_name} not found")
device_id = req["results"][0]["id"]

If the device exists, we use device_id to retrieve the interfaces associated with it. If an interface does not exist, we create it:

# Ingesting data to Nautobot
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Token {nautobot_apikey}",
    "Accept": "application/json",
}

# Get device ID
url = f"{nautobot_base_url}/api/dcim/devices/?name={device_name}"
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30).json()
if req["count"] < 1:
    raise ValueError(f"{device_name} not found")
device_id = req["results"][0]["id"]

In both cases, we assume that the structure of Nautobot does not allow multiple devices with the same name, or multiple interfaces with the same name within the same device.

docs.title: Preparing to Run the Script
docs.text:
Before running the script, we must create the device in Nautobot. Here are the steps.

Create a Device Role: we navigate to Organization → Roles → Add, with Content Type = dcim|device:

Create a Manufacturer: we go to Devices → Manufacturers → Add:

Create a Device Type: in Devices → Device Type → Add, we associate it with the Manufacturer created before:

Create a Location Type: we set up a Location Type in Organization → Location Type → Add, with Content Type = dcim|device:

Create a Location: we add a Location in Organization → Locations → Add, and associate it with the Location Type created before:

Create the Device: finally, in Devices → Devices → Add, we associate the Device Role, the Device Type and the Location, and we use the hostname in uppercase:

docs.title: Running the Script
docs.text:
Now we can run the script. If everything works, the device in Nautobot is populated with all its interfaces:

This process ensures that the device is set up correctly in Nautobot before the automation script populates its interfaces.

We can download the script from GitHub.

docs.title: Integrating Ansible with Nautobot
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate nautobot

Integrating Ansible with Nautobot involves two main aspects:

  • Reading information from Nautobot with Ansible.
  • Running Ansible playbooks to update device configurations.

Let's focus on the first point. To make the information in Nautobot available to Ansible, we need a dynamic inventory. Network to Code provides a specific Ansible collection for Nautobot that includes an inventory plugin. We can install the collection with:

ansible-galaxy collection install networktocode.nautobot

Before configuring the inventory, we make sure the following information is complete in Nautobot for the device:

  • The IP address for device access.
  • The username and password for device access.
  • The connection method Ansible uses to access the device.
  • The device interfaces with the associated profiles.

docs.title: Configure the Primary IP Address
docs.text:
To configure the management IP address, we follow these steps:

Create a network prefix: navigate to IPAM → Prefixes → Add:

Create an IP address: go to IPAM → IP Addresses → Add:

Associate the IP address with a device interface: go to Devices → Devices, select the device, then Interfaces, edit the management interface, open IP Addresses and select the newly created IP address:

Set the IP address of the interface as the primary address: go to Devices → Devices, select the device, then Primary IPv4 and select the correct IP address:

docs.title: Device Custom Attributes
docs.text:
Next, we create two custom attributes to define the parameters Ansible uses to connect to the devices.

We go to Extensibility → Custom Fields and add the connection and network_os attributes, both associated with the dcim|device type:

Now we populate the attributes for each device:

  • connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli.
  • network_os: cisco.ios.ios.

docs.title: Interface Profiles
docs.text:
We define the profiles to associate with the interfaces. Let's assume we have three profiles initially:

  • access: for interfaces connecting PCs.
  • isl: for inter-switch link interfaces.
  • trunk: for interfaces connecting servers or firewalls.

We go to Organization → Roles → Add and add the three profiles of type dcim|interface:

Finally, we associate some interfaces with the newly defined roles by going to Devices → Devices, selecting the device and opening Interfaces:

docs.title: Ansible Inventory
docs.text:
We define the Ansible inventory file that reads the configuration from Nautobot. Following the official documentation, we create an inventory.yml file that returns the necessary information:

plugin: networktocode.nautobot.inventory
api_endpoint: http://localhost:8000
token: <NAUTOBOT_API_TOKEN>
validate_certs: false
config_context: false
interfaces: true
compose:
  ansible_connection: custom_fields.connection
  ansible_network_os: custom_fields.network_os
keyed_groups:
  - key: device_types
    prefix: type
  - key: manufacturers
    prefix: manufacturers
  - key: location
    prefix: location
  - key: device_roles
    prefix: role

This simple configuration is not suitable for a production environment, but it allows us to:

  • Retrieve a list of devices with the parameters Ansible needs.
  • Retrieve the list of interfaces for each device with the associated profile.
  • Group devices into groups.

We verify that the inventory works with the following command:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list

The output should include:

  • For each device, the variables ansible_connection, ansible_host and ansible_network_os.
  • For each device, the interfaces list containing all the interfaces.
  • For each interface, the variables description, enabled, role and status.

The Ansible inventory can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: The Ansible role breakdown
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible nautobot

Now we need to translate the interface roles defined in Nautobot into specific configurations for the switches. We create an Ansible role that uses the inventory described in the previous post to configure the interfaces of each device.

docs.title: Fetch Running Configuration
docs.text:
First, we retrieve the current running configuration from the switch:

- name: GETTING RUNNING CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - show running-config
  register: show_running_config

Retrieving the running configuration once, and reusing it in the following tasks, improves overall performance.

docs.title: Create Data Structures
docs.text:
Next, we generate the data structures with the details we need from Nautobot:

- name: SETTING INTERFACE PROFILES
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    interface_profiles: >-
      {
        {% for interface in interfaces %}
          {% if interface.role %}
            "{{ interface.name }}": "{{ interface.role.name }}",
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      }
    interface_cfgs: >-
      [
        {% for interface in interfaces %}
          {% if interface.role %}
            {
              "name": "{{ interface.name }}",
              {% if interface.enabled %}
                "description": "{{ interface.description }} ({{ interface.role.name }})",
                "enabled": true,
              {% else %}
                "enabled": false,
              {% endif %}
            },
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      ]
  • interface_profiles links each interface to its profile.
  • interface_cfgs holds the configurations for the ios_interfaces module.

We process only the interfaces that have an associated profile.

docs.title: Limit the Data Structure (Optional)
docs.text:
Optionally, we can limit the data structure to a single interface from the command line:

- name: FILTERING INTERFACES
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    interface_profiles: >-
      {
        {% for interface_name, profile in interface_profiles.items() %}
          {% if interface_name == interface_limit %}
            "{{ interface_name }}": "{{ profile }}",
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      }
    interface_cfgs: >-
      [
        {% for interface in interface_cfgs %}
          {% if interface.name == interface_limit %}
            {{ interface }},
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      ]
  when: interface_limit is defined

docs.title: Apply the Interface Profile Configuration
docs.text:
For each interface, we include an external configuration file:

- name: ATTACHING PROFILE TO INTERFACE
  ansible.builtin.include_tasks: "profile_{{ interface.value }}.yml"
  with_dict: "{{ interface_profiles }}"
  loop_control:
    loop_var: interface

The profile file uses the ios_config module to apply the configuration commands:

- name: "APPLYING PROFILE ISL TO INTERFACE {{ interface.key }}"
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    config: "{{ show_running_config.stdout.0 }}"
    lines:
      - switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
      - switchport mode trunk
      - switchport nonegotiate
      - udld port aggressive
    parents: "interface {{ interface.key }}"
    before: "default interface {{ interface.key }}"

This step is the slowest, so optimizations are crucial.

docs.title: Set Interface Description and State
docs.text:
Finally, we apply the configuration data we prepared:

- name: "SETTING INTERFACE STATUS"
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config: "{{ interface_cfgs }}"
    state: merged

This task manages the state of the interface (shutdown and no shutdown) with the native module.

docs.title: Running the Playbook
docs.text:
We run the playbook on all the devices, or we limit it to a specific interface:

./playbook-interface-configuration.yml
./playbook-interface-configuration.yml --extra-vars interface_limit=GigabitEthernet1/0/47 --limit MGMTSWITCH1

With these steps, we automate the configuration of the network interfaces with Ansible and Nautobot.

We can download the Ansible role from GitHub.

docs.title: Orchestrating Ansible playbooks for Nautobot integration
Orchestrating Ansible playbooks for Nautobot integration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner nautobot

It is currently not possible to run Ansible playbooks directly from Nautobot. There are some proposals, but nothing concrete has been implemented yet.

The only option is an external orchestrator that runs the playbook regularly or when an operator requests it. Here are some options:

  • Crontab: schedules playbook runs at regular intervals.
  • Ansible Tower: a web-based solution to manage and schedule Ansible playbooks.
  • AWX: the open-source version of Ansible Tower.
  • Spacelift: a flexible CI/CD platform for infrastructure as code.

Each of these tools has its own features and capabilities, so we choose the one that best fits our environment and requirements.

docs.title: Key insights from developing Nautobot and Ansible integrations
Key insights from developing Nautobot and Ansible integrations
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible behind-the-scene nautobot

Beyond the topics of the previous posts, my work on this project focused on four key areas:

  • The data structure of Nautobot.
  • The REST API of Nautobot.
  • Integrating Ansible with Nautobot.
  • Running Ansible playbooks from Nautobot.

Let's look at the challenges I encountered and the solutions that I left out of the previous posts.

docs.title: Nautobot's Data Structure
docs.text:
To use Nautobot effectively, we need to plan the data structure carefully to avoid costly changes later. Understanding the structure also lets us simplify the automation scripts.

Each object in Nautobot is identified by a UUID, such as 2170a207-43b2-422a-a90d-51a4908b85fb. This choice allows us to change any attribute without issues. Since the identifier of a device is a UUID and not a name, we must consider:

  • Can two devices have the same name?
  • Can two interfaces on the same device have the same name?

Quick tests show that the answer is no to both questions, so we can simplify the automation scripts safely.

docs.title: Django Shell
docs.text:
Nautobot is built on Django, a Python-based web application framework. Django provides a shell that allows easy interaction with the data structure.

I had to decide whether to develop the automations with the shell or with the REST API.

We invoke the shell with the command:

nautobot-server shell

For example, to retrieve the list of the interfaces associated with a device, we can use this simple script:

from nautobot.dcim import models

models.Interface.objects.filter(device__name="MGMTSWITCH1")

This option is appealing, but the shell is available only locally on the instance that runs Nautobot. When Nautobot runs in containers, accessing the shell can be complex or impossible.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
REST APIs are useful when they are well documented, which is not the case with Nautobot. The documentation includes examples, and local installations provide the documentation of the API calls at http://localhost:8000/api/docs/. Some features, such as filtering, are poorly documented and require trial and error.

The device_id filter worked, but device_name returned an error:

{"device_name": ["Unknown filter field"]}

After numerous attempts, I found a bug from 2023. Eventually, I realized that the API filters are actually FilterSets, so device can filter by name or label.

The equivalent code is:

url = "http://localhost:8000/api/dcim/interfaces/?device=MGMTSWITCH1"

req = requests.get(url, headers=headers).json()

Remember to handle pagination.

docs.title: Django Shell or REST API
docs.text: I chose the REST API for its broader compatibility, despite the difficulties.

docs.title: Integrating Ansible with Nautobot
docs.text:
network.toCode() provides a specific Ansible collection for Nautobot. I needed a way to use Nautobot as an Ansible inventory without building one from scratch.

The plugin documentation is a good starting point and includes examples.

The challenge is defining a data structure that includes:

  • The Ansible-specific parameters (ansible_connection, ansible_network_os, ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_ssh_pass).
  • A group that identifies the devices.
  • A list of interfaces, with a profile for each device.

There are three options:

  • The inventory contains all the necessary information from Nautobot.
  • The playbook defines the information, except for the group with the correct variables.
  • A mix of both.

I chose to move the information to Nautobot, to experiment with custom fields. In practice, usernames and passwords are stored in a vault; for simplicity, I hardcoded them in the playbook.

After testing, I found the correct combination. Two custom fields map to variables:

compose:
  ansible_connection: custom_fields.connection
  ansible_network_os: custom_fields.network_os

Each device is associated with three groups, based on its attributes:

keyed_groups:
- key: device_types
  prefix: type
- key: manufacturers
  prefix: manufacturers
- key: location
  prefix: location

compose and keyed_groups are standard Ansible features, and they required some trial and error. I used the following command to test:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list

docs.title: The Ansible Playbook
docs.text:
Creating an optimized Ansible playbook requires experience. I reused a role I had developed previously with slight modifications.

First, I read the configuration from Nautobot and created two data structures:

  • interface_profiles: maps the interfaces to the profiles.
  • interface_cfgs: contains the data structure for the ios_interfaces module.

This approach was necessary because the ios_l2_interfaces module does not support all the parameters we need. The solution was to use the ios_config module for the configuration of the interface and ios_interfaces for the specific parameters (description and status).

The result is a simple list of CLI commands that any network engineer can read and modify:

lines:
- switchport access vlan 53
- switchport voice vlan 54
- no cdp enable
- no lldp receive
- no lldp transmit
- spanning-tree bpduguard enable
- spanning-tree portfast edge
- switchport mode access
- switchport nonegotiate

I used Jinja to create the data structure, for better performance:

ansible.builtin.set_fact:
  interface_profiles: >-
    {
      {% for interface_name, profile in interface_profiles.items() %}
        {% if interface_name == interface_limit %}
          "{{ interface_name }}": "{{ profile }}",
        {% endif %}
      {% endfor %}
    }

We verify the data structure as JSON with the debug module, to avoid issues such as missing commas:

ok: [MGMTSWITCH1] => {
"msg": "{\n\"GigabitEthernet1/0/44\": \"interface_access\"\n\"GigabitEthernet1/0/45\": \"
interface_isl\"\n\"GigabitEthernet1/0/47\": \"interface_trunk\"\n}"

}

Once corrected:

ok: [MGMTSWITCH1] => {
    "msg": {
        "GigabitEthernet1/0/44": "interface_access",
        "GigabitEthernet1/0/45": "interface_isl",
        "GigabitEthernet1/0/47": "interface_trunk"
    }
}

The next step is to enable the execution of the playbook for a specific interface:

./playbook-interface-configuration.yml --extra-vars interface_limit=GigabitEthernet1/0/47

I cleaned the data structures to keep only the filtered element. The association of the profile is done with include_tasks, which is optimal for network engineers who deal with a profile for each interface.

Finally, description and the status of the interface are configured with the ios_interfaces module, which simplifies the management of the shutdown and no shutdown commands.

docs.title: Introduction to OT/ICS
docs.text: 12 February 2025

docs.title: Introduction to OT/ICS
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals ot-ics

Operational Technology (OT) encompasses the systems that monitor and control industrial operations. Within OT, Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are the technologies that automate and manage industrial processes.

IT professionals have decades of experience securing networks, systems and applications, but cybersecurity in OT/ICS is a relatively new concern. In industrial environments, availability takes priority over integrity and confidentiality: ICS software is often designed for speed and efficiency rather than security. This difference makes OT/ICS systems uniquely vulnerable to cyber threats.

docs.title: OT (Operational Technology)
docs.text:
OT is the hardware and software used to monitor, control and automate industrial processes, critical infrastructure and manufacturing plants. It differs from IT (Information Technology) because its primary focus is operational continuity and physical safety, whereas IT is concerned with data management and cybersecurity.

Key OT components:

  • Industrial Control Systems (ICS).
  • Sensors and actuators.
  • Supervisory and control systems (SCADA, DCS).
  • Embedded devices (PLC, RTU).
  • Industrial networks (Industrial Ethernet, Modbus, Profibus, etc.).

docs.title: ICS (Industrial Control Systems)
docs.text:
ICS are a subset of OT that includes all the technologies used to monitor and control automated industrial processes. They are deployed in manufacturing, energy, transportation, utilities and other critical industries to ensure safe and efficient operations.

Types of ICS:

  • SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition).
  • DCS (Distributed Control System).
  • PLC (Programmable Logic Controller).
  • RTU (Remote Terminal Unit).

docs.title: SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition)
docs.text:
SCADA is a supervisory system used to monitor and control industrial processes distributed over large geographical areas, such as power grids, pipelines and water treatment plants. It collects data from remote sensors and devices, so that operators can make decisions in real time.

Key SCADA components:

  • Supervisory computers: centralized servers that collect and process data from field devices (PLCs, RTUs) and provide visualization tools for operators.
  • Human-Machine Interface (HMI): the graphical interface that operators use to monitor and control industrial processes.
  • Communication networks: the infrastructure that connects the SCADA components (Ethernet, serial, radio, cellular, satellite).
  • Remote Terminal Units (RTU): remote field devices that collect data from sensors and transmit it to the SCADA system.
  • Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC): controllers that execute real-time logic and automation tasks.

docs.title: DCS (Distributed Control System)
docs.text:
A DCS is an automation system designed for real-time process control in large, localized industrial facilities, such as oil refineries, chemical plants and power plants. Unlike SCADA, which is optimized for wide-area monitoring, a DCS is designed for tightly integrated process control within a single site.

Key DCS components:

  • Process Control Units (PCU): localized control units that manage industrial processes in real time.
  • Field devices (sensors, actuators, valves, etc.): interface directly with the physical processes.
  • Engineering workstations: used to configure and optimize the control logic.
  • Operator consoles (HMI): interfaces to monitor and manage plant operations.
  • Industrial communication networks: connect the different DCS components (e.g., Fieldbus, Profibus, OPC-UA).

docs.title: PLC (Programmable Logic Controller)
docs.text:
A PLC is a specialized industrial computer used to control machinery and processes in manufacturing and automation environments. PLCs are essential components of both SCADA and DCS systems, because they provide real-time monitoring and decision-making.

Key PLC features:

  • Real-time operation: executes logic based on the inputs from sensors and generates outputs to control machinery.
  • Modular architecture: allows customization with input/output (I/O) modules.
  • Industrial protocol support: communicates via Modbus, PROFINET, EtherCAT and other protocols.
  • High reliability: designed for continuous operation in harsh environments.

docs.title: Summary of Key Differences
docs.text: System Primary Function Best for Geographical Scope Control Approach OT Industrial operations and automation Manufacturing, utilities, energy Local and global Ensures uptime and safety ICS Monitoring and controlling industrial processes Industrial environments Local and global Integrates SCADA, DCS, PLC, RTU SCADA Supervisory control and data acquisition Remote monitoring (e.g., power grids, pipelines) Large-scale, geographically distributed Centralized monitoring DCS Real-time process automation and control Complex, high-precision manufacturing (e.g., chemical plants, oil refineries) Localized within a facility Distributed control with redundancy PLC Logic execution and machine control Automated processes (e.g., assembly lines, robotic systems) Localized control Executes predefined automation logic

docs.title: IT vs. OT: Key Differences
docs.text:
IT and OT are increasingly interconnected, but they differ in priorities, lifecycle management and security approach:

  • System lifecycle: IT systems typically have a 3-5 year lifecycle, with frequent upgrades and replacements. OT systems are built for longevity and often operate for 10-30 years without major changes.
  • Patching and updates: in IT, regular updates and patches are standard practice to mitigate vulnerabilities. In OT, patching is infrequent or even impossible, because downtime can disrupt critical industrial processes.
  • Priorities: IT security protects data (confidentiality, integrity, availability), in that order of concern. OT prioritizes safety, availability and uptime: an industrial system must run without interruption, even at the expense of data protection.
  • Risk approach: IT deals with cybersecurity risks, such as data breaches and malware. OT must consider both cyber and physical risks, because failures can lead to equipment damage, environmental hazards or even loss of life.

These differences make OT environments harder to secure and require specialized cybersecurity strategies that balance safety, reliability and risk management.

docs.title: Final Thoughts
docs.text:
Understanding the differences between OT, ICS, SCADA, DCS and PLCs is essential for anyone working in industrial automation, cybersecurity or operational technology. As IT and OT converge, securing these systems against cyber threats becomes increasingly important.

In simple terms:

  • Industrial operations rely on sophisticated, mission-critical computer systems (SCADA).
  • In OT/ICS environments, security is not the top priority: availability and uptime come first.
  • Operators can manually override plant operations with a mouse, keyboard or touchscreen, both locally and remotely.
  • Malicious software can manipulate plant behavior in the same way an authorized operator would through the HMI.

For a deeper understanding, refer to the Guide to Industrial Control Systems (ICS) Security (NIST 800-82).

docs.title: Introduction to Modbus protocol
docs.text: 19 February 2025

docs.title: Introduction to Modbus protocol
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner modbus ot-ics

Modbus is a widely used industrial communication protocol, originally developed by Modicon (now part of Schneider Electric) in 1979. It is open, royalty-free and simple to implement, which makes it one of the most popular protocols for connecting Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), Remote Terminal Units (RTUs), sensors and other industrial devices.

Modbus is primarily used for data exchange in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems and distributed control systems (DCS). The protocol is designed for reliable and deterministic communication, which is essential in industrial automation environments.

docs.title: Modbus Protocol Overview
docs.text:
Modbus uses a client-server architecture (historically called master-slave):

  • The client (master) initiates the requests, reading from or writing to the devices.
  • The servers (slaves) respond to the requests but never initiate communication on their own.

A client (such as an HMI or a SCADA system) communicates with one or more servers (such as PLCs, RTUs or field devices) over a network. In RTU mode, each server is assigned a unique 8-bit address, from 1 to 247. Modbus RTU (Remote Terminal Unit) usually runs over RS-485 (serial network).

Modbus TCP (Modbus over TCP/IP):

  • Encapsulates Modbus messages inside TCP/IP packets, for transmission over Ethernet networks.
  • Uses port 502 as the standard communication port.
  • Does not need the timing-based message separation of RTU, which makes it easier to integrate with modern IT networks.
  • Allows multiple clients to communicate with a single server, unlike Modbus RTU, which supports only one master.

Modbus data is organized in "registers", which store information in predefined formats. Each register type serves a specific purpose:

Register Numbers Type Address Name Data Type Value Range 1-9999 Read-Write %IX Status/Coil (State controls) bool 0 or 1 10001-19999 Read-Only %QX Input Contact (State information) bool 0 or 1 30001-39999 Read-Only %QW Input Registers (Numerical values) uint, word 0 to 32767 40001-49999 Read-Write %IW Holding Registers (Numerical values) uint, word 0 to 32767

Holding registers and input registers handle analog values, while coils and discrete inputs handle binary (on/off) signals.

docs.title: Modbus Function Codes
docs.text:
Modbus uses function codes to perform operations on registers and coils. The function code specifies whether data is read or written and which type of data is accessed.

Function Code Description Register Type 1 Read Coil Coil (Discrete Output) 2 Read Discrete Input Discrete Input 3 Read Holding Registers Holding Register (16-bit) 4 Read Input Registers Input Register (16-bit) 5 Write Single Coil Coil (Discrete Output) 6 Write Single Holding Register Holding Register (16-bit) 15 Write Multiple Coils Coil (Discrete Output) 16 Write Multiple Holding Registers Holding Register (16-bit)

Each request consists of:

  • Function code (e.g., 03 for reading holding registers).
  • Start address (the register or coil address).
  • Number of registers or coils.
  • Data (for write operations).
  • Error checking (CRC for RTU, checksum for ASCII, or TCP checksum for Modbus TCP).

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Modbus remains one of the most widely used industrial communication protocols, thanks to its simplicity, reliability and interoperability. As IT and OT networks converge, however, securing Modbus communication is critical to prevent cyber threats and operational disruptions.

Despite its widespread use, Modbus has no built-in security mechanisms, which exposes it to threats such as:

  • Eavesdropping: Modbus traffic can be intercepted and read.
  • Unauthorized commands: there is no authentication, so any device can issue commands.
  • Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks: an attacker can modify Modbus traffic.

For more information, see Modbus 101 - Introduction to Modbus.

docs.title: Why build an OT/ICS Cybersecurity lab?
docs.text: 29 January 2025

docs.title: Why build an OT/ICS Cybersecurity lab?
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals lab ot-ics

For several years now, I have been deeply interested in the security challenges of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Operational Technology (OT). I live in a region renowned for its manufacturing excellence, and many of my clients operate in this domain. This proximity has let me witness firsthand how ICS/OT security is evolving.

When I first started talking about applying cybersecurity to ICS/OT systems, I quickly realized I was ahead of the curve. At the time, the primary focus in ICS/OT environments was operational continuity. OT managers cared more about uptime, process efficiency and reliability than about the risks posed by cyber threats.

The landscape has been shifting gradually. Traditionally isolated ICS/OT systems have started to interact more closely with IT environments. The trend accelerated significantly around 2020, when connecting ICS/OT systems to the Internet for real-time remote support and monitoring became common practice.

This convergence of IT and OT brings both opportunities and challenges. On the one hand, connectivity improves efficiency and reduces the response time of troubleshooting. On the other hand, it exposes previously isolated systems to cyber threats they were not designed to handle.

To deepen my understanding, experiment with ICS/OT-specific security solutions and give meaningful demonstrations to clients and stakeholders, I needed dedicated environments, part physical and part virtual. These labs are controlled spaces where I can test vulnerabilities, evaluate defensive mechanisms and simulate real-world attack scenarios.

In this series of posts, I explore the different approaches to building ICS/OT labs: from hardware configurations to virtualized environments, and from affordable setups to more advanced scenarios. My aim is to provide a practical guide for anyone interested in this field.

docs.title: An ICS lab with VirtuaPlant
docs.text: 26 February 2025

docs.title: An ICS lab with VirtuaPlant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner lab ot-ics

VirtuaPlant is an Industrial Control Systems (ICS) simulator developed by Jan Seidl in 2015. Most PLC simulators only let you read and write tags, while VirtuaPlant adds real-world-like control logic, which makes it a more advanced and interactive learning tool.

It uses a game library and a 2D physics engine to provide a graphical user interface (GUI) that simulates the physical world behind the control system. This helps users visualize industrial processes and understand how control systems interact with real-world mechanics.

Originally, VirtuaPlant included only one scenario. Later, an external contributor (GitHub user prjpet) added a second one.

The biggest issue with VirtuaPlant today is that it has been stagnant since 2015. Installing it on modern systems is extremely difficult, because of outdated OS requirements, dependencies and libraries, many of which are now deprecated.

To overcome these problems, I modified the project and converted it into a Docker container, which makes installation and deployment much easier on modern systems.

The Dockerfiles for this setup are available in my GitHub repository. They are the foundation of our ICS/OT security lab.

docs.title: Installing VirtuaPlant Bottle Filling plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

The first scenario available in VirtuaPlant simulates a basic bottle-filling plant. It includes a graphical Human-Machine Interface (HMI) that lets users interact with the simulated industrial process.

The simulation and the HMI communicate using the Modbus protocol. The simulation acts as a basic PLC, handling both the control logic and the visualization of the plant.

Both the simulation and the HMI are graphical applications developed in Python 2.7 with the Pygame library. Since they rely on Linux-based systems, both components must run on Linux machines.

docs.title: Installing the Simulation (PLC) Container
docs.text:
Before installing the scenario, we need two Linux systems with Docker installed. I used the latest Ubuntu LTS and followed the official Docker installation guide. Once the systems are ready, we install the PLC simulation container on the first machine:

docker run --name plc --rm -d -p 443:6901 -p 502:5020 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-bottle-filling-plc:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest PLC simulation container for the Bottle Filling Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container when it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 443 (web interface) and port 502 (Modbus communication with the PLC).
  • Sets a password for VNC access.

After a few moments, we can access the PLC simulation by entering the IP address of the host in a web browser, on port 443:

We log in with the username kasm_user and the password set in the Docker command.

Once logged in, the simulation environment is ready to start:

We can press ESC at any time to restart the simulation.

docs.title: Installing the HMI Container
docs.text:
Next, we install the HMI container on the second Linux machine:

docker run --name hmi --rm -d -p 443:6901 -e PLC=172.26.104.12 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-bottle-filling-hmi:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest HMI container for the Bottle Filling Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container when it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 443 for web-based interaction.
  • Defines the IP address of the PLC (-e PLC=<PLC_IP>) to establish the communication.
  • Sets a password for access.

We open the HMI web interface using the IP address of the second machine and port 443, and log in with kasm_user and the password set when the container was started:

We press "Run" to start the plant simulation. If everything is configured correctly, the bottle-filling plant begins operating.

docs.title: Attacking the Bottle Filling plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese attack intermediate modbus ot-ics

This scenario is an introduction to attacking a Modbus-based PLC. The goal is to understand the behavior of the system gradually, by monitoring the PLC registers before launching the attack.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Phase
docs.text:
Before attacking, we must analyze the behavior of the plant. This means monitoring the PLC registers to identify the active ones and understand how they are used.

For this purpose, I developed a small tool that continuously monitors the Modbus registers to determine which ones are in use. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

To monitor the PLC for 15 seconds, we run:

./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -t holding -k 15

From our observations, only holding registers are used, specifically registers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 16. Register 16 holds the value 1, which deserves further investigation.

We also see that these registers store binary information (0 or 1), even though Modbus offers dedicated boolean registers for this purpose.

The system operates in three phases:

  • Initialization: the conveyor moves the first bottle under the nozzle.
  • Filling: the nozzle opens and fills the bottle.
  • Moving: the conveyor moves the next bottle into position.

This cycle repeats indefinitely. In a real attack, the adversary would probably have no physical view of how the system operates, but for this lab we simplify the analysis.

From the three phases above, we can identify:

  • Sensors: used to read the state of the plant. There are two sensors: bottle presence and full bottle.
  • Actuators: used to change the state of the plant. There are three actuators: plant (on/off), roller and nozzle.

After observing the behavior of the plant and the associated states for some time, we can state that:

  • The only registers in use are holding registers.
  • Five holding registers are used.
  • The holding registers store binary information, using 0 and 1.
  • Registers 1, 3 and 16 are set when the roller is moving the bottle and the nozzle is closed.
  • Registers 2, 4 and 16 are set when the roller is stopped and the nozzle is filling a bottle.
  • In a newly started plant, only registers 3 and 16 are set.

From this, we can deduce that:

  • Register 16 (actuator) defines the state of the plant (on/off).
  • Register 3 (actuator) defines the state of the conveyor (on/off).
  • Register 1 (red sensor) defines whether the bottle is full.
  • Registers 2 and 4 change value together.

They are associated with the nozzle actuator and the green bottle presence sensor, but we need further analysis to tell them apart.

docs.title: Attack Phase
docs.text:
An attack on a PLC assumes that we can overwrite the values of the registers and that the PLC reacts accordingly. This may seem paradoxical to those coming from IT: does the PLC act on external values written by the attacker, instead of executing its programmed logic? The answer is yes. PLCs often rely on external inputs without strict validation, so they are susceptible to register manipulation. The attacker writes directly into the memory registers of the PLC, and the control logic treats those values as valid.

In the previous phase, we observed that only holding registers with the values 0 and 1 are used, specifically:

  • Register 1: red sensor, defines whether the bottle is full.
  • Register 2: to be verified.
  • Register 3: actuator, defines the state of the conveyor (on/off).
  • Register 4: to be verified.
  • Register 16: actuator, defines the state of the plant (on/off).

Now let's try to force the register values by overwriting them continuously. For this purpose, I developed a small tool that continuously writes a specific value to one or more Modbus registers of a PLC. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

First, let's check register 4:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 4 1

The nozzle remains permanently open:

We can now complete our analysis:

  • Register 1: red sensor, defines whether the bottle is full.
  • Register 2: green sensor, defines whether the bottle is in position.
  • Register 3: actuator, defines the state of the conveyor (on/off).
  • Register 4: actuator, defines the state of the nozzle (open/closed).
  • Register 16: actuator, defines the state of the plant (on/off).

Now we can plan different attack scenarios by manipulating the actuators.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Plant Permanently Off
docs.text:
Regardless of the state of the sensors, the plant remains off, even if an operator intervenes manually via the HMI.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 16 0

Effect: the production line remains halted.

docs.title: Scenario 2: Nozzle Open and Conveyor Stopped
docs.text:
In this attack, the plant is active and the nozzle remains open, but the conveyor does not operate.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 3 0 -s h 4 1 -s h 16 1

Effect: water waste and potential flooding of the facility.

In this scenario, the attack script competes with the PLC: the script tries to stop the motor, while the PLC tries to start it as soon as the sensor detects a full bottle.

A more advanced version of the attack also manipulates the two sensors:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 1 0 -s h 2 1 -s h 3 0 -s h 4 1 -s h 16 1

The effect is more stable:

If the operator tries to turn off the plant via the HMI, the action has no effect.

docs.title: Scenario 3: Conveyor Active and Nozzle Closed
docs.text:
In this attack, the plant is active, the nozzle remains closed and the conveyor runs continuously:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 1 0 -s h 2 0 -s h 3 1 -s h 4 0 -s h 16 1

Effect: the production line produces empty bottles.

Here too, if the operator tries to shut down the plant via the HMI, the action has no effect.

docs.title: Installing VirtuaPlant Oil Refinery plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

The second VirtuaPlant scenario simulates an oil refinery. It was added by an external contributor (GitHub user prjpet) and, like the first one, it includes a graphical HMI.

The simulation and the HMI communicate using the Modbus protocol. The simulation acts as a basic PLC, handling both the control logic and the visualization of the plant.

Both the simulation and the HMI are graphical applications developed in Python 2.7 with the Pygame library. Since they rely on Linux-based systems, both components must run on Linux machines.

docs.title: Installing the Simulation (PLC) Container
docs.text:
Before installing the scenario, we need two Linux systems with Docker installed. I used the latest Ubuntu LTS and followed the official Docker installation guide. Once the systems are ready, we install the PLC simulation container on the first machine:

docker run --name plc --rm -d -p 443:6901 -p 502:5020 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-oil-refinery-plc:22

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the PLC simulation container for the Oil Refinery Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container when it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 443 (web interface) and port 502 (Modbus communication with the PLC).
  • Sets a password for VNC access.

After a few moments, we can access the PLC simulation by entering the IP address of the host in a web browser, on port 443:

We log in with the username kasm_user and the password set in the Docker command.

Once logged in, the simulation environment is ready to start:

We can press ESC at any time to restart the simulation.

docs.title: Installing the HMI Container
docs.text:
Next, we install the HMI container on the second Linux machine:

docker run --name hmi --rm -d -p 443:6901 -e PLC=172.26.104.22 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-oil-refinery-hmi:22

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the HMI container for the Oil Refinery Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container when it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 443 for web-based interaction.
  • Defines the IP address of the PLC (-e PLC=<PLC_IP>) to establish the communication.
  • Sets a password for access.

We open the HMI web interface using the IP address of the second machine and port 443, and log in with kasm_user and the password set when the container was started:

We press "Run" to start the plant simulation. If everything is configured correctly, the oil refinery plant begins operating.

docs.title: Attacking the Oil Refinery plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced attack ot-ics

We have already seen how to attack the Bottle Filling system. This article follows up on that analysis, in a significantly more complex scenario.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Phase
docs.text:
The Bottle Filling system operated automatically. The Oil Refinery, instead, requires the supervision of an operator who interacts with it via an HMI: in particular, the operator decides when to move from one processing phase to the next.

We analyze how the PLC registers change while we interact with the HMI.

For this purpose, I developed a small tool that continuously monitors the Modbus registers to determine which ones are in use. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

A real attack would be much more complex, because the attacker has no visual feedback from the HMI or from the system itself.

To monitor the behavior of the PLC continuously, we run:

./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -t holding

System idle: all registers report the value 0.

Filling the tank: as soon as the feed pump is activated, register 1 is set to 1. When the crude oil reaches the level sensor, register 1 returns to 0 and register 2 is set to 1.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 1: actuator, defines the state of the feed pump (open/closed).
  • Register 2: sensor, detects whether the tank is full (tank level sensor).

Draining the tank: when the discharge valve is opened, register 2 remains unchanged, register 3 is set to 1, and registers 6 and 7 increment.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 3: actuator, controls the tank discharge valve (open/closed).
  • Register 6: sensor, requires further investigation.
  • Register 7: sensor, requires further investigation.

Water discharge: when the water discharge valve is opened, registers 2 and 3 remain unchanged, register 8 is set to 1 and register 6 increments.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 6: sensor, measures the amount of discharged water.
  • Register 8: actuator, controls the water discharge valve (open/closed).

Oil discharge: when the oil discharge valve is opened, registers 2, 3 and 8 remain unchanged, register 4 is set to 1 and register 7 increments rapidly.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 4: actuator, controls the oil discharge valve (open/closed).
  • Register 7: sensor, measures the amount of produced oil.

docs.title: Attack Phase
docs.text:
Before planning the attacks, let's summarize the findings of the reconnaissance:

  • Register 1: actuator, controls the feed pump (open/closed).
  • Register 2: sensor, detects whether the tank is full (tank level sensor).
  • Register 3: actuator, controls the tank discharge valve (open/closed).
  • Register 4: actuator, controls the oil discharge valve (open/closed).
  • Register 6: sensor, measures the amount of discharged water.
  • Register 7: sensor, measures the amount of produced oil.
  • Register 8: actuator, controls the water discharge valve (open/closed).

Registers 6 and 7 are the only ones with incremental values.

Now let's try to force the register values by overwriting them continuously. For this purpose, I developed a small tool that continuously writes a specific value to one or more Modbus registers of a PLC. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Feed Pump Forced Closed
docs.text:
Regardless of the state of the sensors, the feed pump remains closed, even if an operator intervenes manually via the HMI.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 0

Effect: the production line remains halted.

docs.title: Scenario 2: Feed Pump Open and Tank Level Sensor Disabled
docs.text:
Regardless of the level of crude oil in the tank, the pump remains open.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 1 -s h 2 0

Effect: the crude oil overflows from the tank and floods the facility.

docs.title: Scenario 3: Oil Discharge Valve Forced Closed
docs.text:
The feed pump and the water discharge valve are forced open, while the oil discharge valve is forced closed.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 1 -s h 3 1 -s h 4 0 -s h 8 1

Effect: all the oil is discharged through the water pipeline, contaminating it.

docs.title: Scenario 4: Altered Product
docs.text:
The feed pump is forced open, the water discharge valve is forced closed, and the oil discharge valve is forced open.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 1 -s h 3 1 -s h 4 1 -s h 8 0

Effect: the oil is not properly refined.

docs.title: Scenario 5: Unknown Production Data
docs.text:
The values of the two sensors are overwritten with arbitrary values.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 6 999 -s h 7 111

Effect: it becomes impossible to determine accurately the amount of refined oil. Operators and all the processes that rely on this data are compromised.

docs.title: An ICS lab with GRFICSv2
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner lab ot-ics

GRFICSv2 (Graphical Realism Framework for Industrial Control Simulations) is an Industrial Control Systems (ICS) simulator developed by Fortiphyd and released in 2020. Unlike VirtuaPlant, GRFICSv2 integrates an HMI, a PLC and a simulation environment. The simulation emulates a chemical plant, which is controlled and monitored by simulated remote I/O devices through a simple JSON API.

docs.title: Officially Released Components
docs.text:
The following components are distributed as OVA (Open Virtual Appliance) files, compatible with VirtualBox:

  • Simulation: the ChemicalPlant VM runs a detailed simulation of the chemical process. The simulated remote I/O devices interact with the system through a JSON API and are controlled by the PLC VM using the Modbus protocol.
  • PLC: the plc_2 VM is a customized version of OpenPLC (GitHub). It relies on an outdated version of the libmodbus library, which contains known buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
  • HMI: the ScadaBR VM hosts an operator interface (HMI) built with ScadaBR, an open-source SCADA software. The HMI lets operators monitor the process data collected by the PLC and send control commands.
  • pfSense firewall/router: the pfSense VM works as a firewall and router, managing network security and routing between the DMZ and the ICS network.
  • Engineering Workstation (EWS): the Ubuntu 16.04 VM acts as the engineering workstation, with the tools to program OpenPLC, and sits in the ICS network.

docs.title: Network Configuration
docs.text:
GRFICSv2 requires two VirtualBox networks:

Adapter Name Type Gateway Address vboxnet0 DMZ VirtualBox Host-Only Ethernet Adapter 192.168.90.100/24 vboxnet1 ICS VirtualBox Host-Only Ethernet Adapter 192.168.95.1/24

Each of the five VMs must be assigned to these networks as follows:

VM Adapter Network Address Credentials Simulation 2 ICS 192.168.95.10 simulation/Fortiphyd PLC 1 ICS 192.168.95.2 user/password HMI 1 DMZ 192.168.90.5 scadabr/scadabradmin/admin EWS 1 ICS 192.168.95.5 workstation/password FW 1 DMZ 192.168.90.100 admin/pfsense FW 2 ICS 192.168.95.1 admin/pfsense

docs.title: Limitations and Enhancements
docs.text:
The main limitation of GRFICSv2 is its dependency on VirtualBox, which restricts the integration of third-party appliances and services. To make it more flexible and easier to deploy, I converted GRFICSv2 into a Docker-based system, which simplifies the installation and makes it more compatible with modern environments.

The Docker implementation is not flawless yet, but GRFICSv2 remains a valuable tool to gain hands-on experience with PLC, HMI and engineering workstation environments.

The Dockerfiles for this setup are available in my GitHub repository. They are the foundation for building an ICS/OT security lab.

docs.title: Installing the GRFICSv2 Chemical plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate ot-ics

As we have seen, the GRFICSv2 simulator consists of four main components: HMI, PLC, simulator and EWS.

In a real ICS environment, the HMI, the PLC and the simulator are connected to the field network, where a gateway handles the communication between the OT network and the field devices. The EWS (Engineering Workstation) is instead located in the OT network and communicates with the HMI and the PLC through the router/gateway.

We can organize these components as best suits our needs. The following instructions configure all the components in the same OT network, as we did previously with VirtuaPlant.

The HMI, the PLC and the simulator communicate using the Modbus protocol. Unlike real systems, the HMI is a web-based interface. The EWS, which is typically Windows-based, is represented here by a Linux system with the OpenPLC SDK.

The complete scenario consists of four distinct components, each running in its own container. They can also all run on the same Docker host.

docs.title: Installing the Chemical Plant Container
docs.text:
Before setting up the environment, we need four Linux systems with Docker installed (or a single one, if we run everything on the same host). I used the latest Ubuntu LTS and followed the official Docker installation guide.

Once the systems are ready, we install the simulation container on the first machine:

docker run --name simulation --rm -d -p 80:80 -p 5020:5020 -p 5021:5021 -p 5022:5022 -p 5023:5023 -p 5024:5024 -p 5025:5025 dainok/grficsv2-simulation:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest Chemical Plant simulation container.
  • Automatically removes the container when it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 80 (web interface) and ports 502X (Modbus communication with the PLC).

After a few moments, we can access the simulator web interface by entering the IP address of the host in a web browser, on port 80.

docs.title: Installing the PLC Container
docs.text:
The PLC is implemented with OpenPLCv2. A newer version of OpenPLC exists, but the differences are too significant, so the only way to ensure compatibility was to keep this outdated version.

We install the PLC container on the second machine:

docker run --name plc -d -p 502:502 -p 80:8080 -e SIM=172.26.104.33 dainok/grficsv2-plc:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest PLC container for the Chemical Plant.
  • Does not remove the container automatically when it is stopped (--rm is omitted).
  • Exposes port 80 (web interface) and port 502 (Modbus communication with the simulator).
  • Configures OpenPLC to connect to the simulator at the IP address 172.26.104.33.

After a few moments, we can access the PLC web interface using the IP address of the host in a web browser, on port 80.

docs.title: Installing the HMI Container
docs.text:
Next, we install the HMI container on the third Linux machine:

docker run --name hmi --rm -d -p 80:8080 dainok/grficsv2-hmi:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest HMI container for the Chemical Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container when it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 80 for web-based interaction.

After a few moments, we open the HMI web interface using the IP address of the host and port 80, and log in with:

  • Username: admin.
  • Password: admin.

docs.title: Configuring the PLC Connection in the HMI
docs.text:
We navigate to Data Sources and edit the PLC source.

We change the host address, setting it to the IP address of the Docker host where OpenPLC is running.

We save the configuration and return to the main screen. The HMI should now display real-time values from the PLC.

Finally, we press the Start button to activate the plant. If everything is configured correctly, the production process begins.

The quantity of product should increase over time. If nothing changes, or if the pressure slowly decreases, something is wrong. In that case, we restart both the PLC and the simulation containers:

  • Stop both containers.
  • Restart the simulation first.
  • Wait a few seconds, then restart the PLC.

docs.title: Installing the EWS Container
docs.text:
Finally, we install the Engineering Workstation (EWS) container on the fourth Linux machine:

docker run --name ews -d -p 443:6901 --privileged --shm-size=512m -e VNC_PW=password dainok/ews:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest EWS container for the Chemical Plant.
  • Does not remove the container automatically when it is stopped (--rm is omitted).
  • Exposes port 443 for web-based access.
  • Sets a password for login.

We open the EWS web interface using the IP address of the machine and port 443, and log in with kasm_user and the password set when the container was started.

The EWS is an Ubuntu Linux 22.04 system with the following pre-installed software:

  • OpenPLC Editor: to develop and modify PLC programs.
  • Web browser: to upload software to OpenPLC.

docs.title: Uploading a PLC Program
docs.text:
In Applications → Development, we find the OpenPLC Editor application. In the Documents folder, the project grficsv2-simplified_te is already available and preloaded on the PLC.

If needed, we can load the project and generate the program for OpenPLC:

We open a web browser, connect to the PLC and upload the program by clicking Upload Program:

OpenPLC uploads, compiles and runs the program.

This is an older version of OpenPLC, so issues may occur. If we run into problems, we try restarting the PLC container.

docs.title: Attacking the Chemical plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate ot-ics

Compared to VirtuaPlant, this scenario is more complex and lets us explore attacks on a PLC in greater detail.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Phase
docs.text:
As before, we analyze the holding registers and the coils:

./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.32 -t holding


./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.32 -t coil

Among the coils, only register 0 is set.

docs.title: Attack Phase
docs.text:
Coils store binary values, which makes them ideal for controlling the operational state of the entire plant.

We can modify coil 0 and verify that it stops the plant:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.32 -s c 0 1

From this point on, the HMI can no longer start the plant, because every interaction is immediately overridden by the attack.

docs.title: Uploading a Malicious Program
docs.text:
In VirtuaPlant the PLC was simulated by the same application as the plant. Here, instead, we have a PLC that runs its own control program (OpenPLC), together with its Engineering Workstation (EWS). The EWS is typically used to develop, test and deploy PLC programs.

An attacker who gains access to the EWS can analyze the existing program, modify it and upload a malicious version to the PLC.

In real environments, PLCs often have a hardware switch that must be in the correct position to allow software overwrites. In every facility I have visited, however, these switches were left in "Program Mode", which nullifies this security measure.

Let's assume that the attacker gains control of the EWS and can upload the grficsv2-simplified_te program.

  • Among the Function Blocks, there is a function called pressure_control.
  • At the top, we can see all the defined variables, including pressure_sp (setpoint).
  • The variable is initialized to 58981.
  • The attacker changes it to 65535, so that the pressure rises uncontrollably.

Once the program is compiled and uploaded to the PLC, the pressure slowly increases and stresses the plant:

Eventually, the pressure reaches a critical point and the plant explodes:

The original training videos, Fortiphyd ICS Training - GRFICS, are available on their YouTube channel.

docs.title: Industrial network segmentation with VLAN Insertion
Industrial network segmentation with VLAN Insertion
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced media ot-ics palo-alto-networks

In real industrial environments, it is common to find all the OT/ICS devices configured with IP addresses of a single large network. Different production lines or plants can then communicate with each other without any filtering.

User PCs are often part of the same network, for various reasons. Unfortunately, these PCs are more exposed to malware, because corporate policies are not applied consistently. A malware infection inside an OT/ICS network can spread easily, because the defenses are weak.

Our lab implements two plants: the Bottle Filling Plant and the Oil Refinery Plant. In our setup, the two plants must not communicate with each other, even though they reside in the same IP network.

The goal is to segment the OT/ICS network transparently, with minimal disruption.

Benefits of VLAN Insertion:

  • No IP address changes are required.
  • Downtime is minimal.
  • Network visibility increases.
  • IT and OT resources are clearly separated.
  • Customized policies can be applied to the different zones.
  • Deep packet inspection is possible on a per-zone basis.
  • Potential issues are identified and isolated faster.
  • The solution scales up or down as needed.

docs.title: Grouping OT/ICS Devices Without Reconfiguration
docs.text:
Our lab includes the following devices:

Plant Role Address VLAN Bottle Filling Plant HMI 172.26.104.11/24 104 Bottle Filling Plant PLC 172.26.104.12/24 104 Oil Refinery Plant HMI 172.26.104.21/24 104 Oil Refinery Plant PLC 172.26.104.22/24 104

To segment the network transparently, we deploy Palo Alto Networks firewalls configured with VLAN Insertion. This feature groups devices into specific VLANs and enforces communication policies between them.

After the segmentation, the devices are organized into two groups, each containing all the components of its plant:

Plant Role Address Group (VLAN) Bottle Filling Plant HMI 172.26.104.11/24 102 Bottle Filling Plant PLC 172.26.104.12/24 102 Oil Refinery Plant HMI 172.26.104.21/24 103 Oil Refinery Plant PLC 172.26.104.22/24 103

It is technically possible to separate HMI and PLC into different groups and let the firewall control their communication. In a real setting, however, this may not be feasible: OT managers typically prefer to keep HMI and PLC units in the same physical location, with no additional security layers in between.

docs.title: Switch Configuration
docs.text:
Currently, all the ICS/OT devices reside in VLAN 104. We keep this VLAN for routing while the devices are moved to their final VLANs, without changing their IP addresses.

We create the necessary VLANs on the switch:

  • VLAN 102: LAB_SEC_OT_L2_1.
  • VLAN 103: LAB_SEC_OT_L2_2.

Additional requirements:

  • Configure a loop prevention algorithm on the switches.
  • Make sure the firewall is connected via a trunk port that carries VLANs 102 and 103.

Once all the ICS/OT devices have been migrated and connectivity has been verified, VLAN 104 can be removed.

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text: We now enable VLAN Insertion on the firewall.

docs.title: Step 1: Create Security Zones
docs.text:
Navigate to Network → Zones → Add and create the following zones:

  • LAB_SEC_OT_L2_1 (Layer 2).
  • LAB_SEC_OT_L2_2 (Layer 2).

docs.title: Step 2: Create Subinterfaces
docs.text:
Each ICS/OT group is assigned a subinterface with:

  • The correct VLAN tag.
  • The appropriate security zone.

Navigate to Network → Interfaces → Add and create the subinterfaces.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the VLAN Interface
docs.text: Navigate to Network → Interfaces → VLAN → Add and create a VLAN interface.

docs.title: Step 4: Create the VLAN Mapping
docs.text:
Navigate to Network → VLANs → Add and associate the VLAN interface with the subinterfaces.

This configuration maps the network 172.24.106.0/24 onto VLANs 102 and 103 and enforces the security policies accordingly.

Once all the configurations are applied, the policy rules are committed and the devices are moved to the correct VLANs, the segmentation is complete.

docs.title: Policy Considerations
docs.text:
Policies use L2 or L3 zones as follows:

  • Inter-VLAN communication: source and destination are the Layer 3 zone assigned to the VLAN interface.
  • Intra-VLAN communication: source and destination are the Layer 2 zones assigned to the subinterfaces.

docs.title: Virtual Firewall Considerations
docs.text:
If we use a virtual device, we must remember that the firewall behaves like a switch and manipulates incoming and outgoing frames. The virtual network must therefore allow:

  • Promiscuous mode: to receive frames that are not addressed to the network interface of the firewall.
  • Forged transmit: to forward (transmit) frames that originate from other devices.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: • Applying VLAN Insertion in ICS/SCADA

docs.title: Industrial network segmentation with Private VLANs
Industrial network segmentation with Private VLANs
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco ot-ics

We have seen how to segment an OT/ICS network transparently into groups using VLAN Insertion from Palo Alto Networks. This feature let us divide our lab environments into groups without reconfiguring any IP address, and it lets us define policies that allow specific communications between groups when necessary.

Since the early 2000s, a standard feature has been available to achieve a similar result: Private VLAN, also known as port isolation, which segments devices into groups of ports.

docs.title: Private VLAN
docs.text:
Private VLANs are defined in RFC5517 as VLAN-based "forced forwarding". In other words, the forwarding of frames is determined at the VLAN level.

Two types of VLANs are defined:

  • Primary VLAN: handles the traffic common to all the groups.
  • Secondary VLAN: is associated with groups of ports and can be either Isolated or Community. In an Isolated VLAN, each port can communicate only with the primary VLAN. In a Community VLAN, each port can communicate with the primary VLAN and with all the ports of the same Community VLAN.

There are three types of ports:

  • Promiscuous Access Port (P-Port): can communicate with any other port, regardless of the VLAN assignment.
  • Host Isolated Access Port (I-Port): is associated with an Isolated VLAN and can communicate only with P-Ports.
  • Host Community Access Port (C-Port): is associated with a Community VLAN and can communicate with P-Ports and with all the other C-Ports of the same VLAN.

In a real environment, there are likely several interconnected switches. Moreover, the network gateway is often a firewall that may not be VLAN-aware.

From an operational standpoint, I strongly recommend using switches of the same model and automating the PVLAN configuration, to minimize human error.

docs.title: Broadcast Traffic
docs.text:
A switch configured with PVLAN must handle broadcast traffic in a particular way. Consider ARP requests: a single request must be propagated across ports, even those in different secondary VLANs.

  • Broadcast traffic from a promiscuous port is forwarded to all the ports of the primary VLAN, including those in isolated and community VLANs.
  • Broadcast traffic from an isolated port is forwarded only to the promiscuous ports of the primary VLAN associated with the isolated port.
  • Broadcast traffic from community ports is forwarded to all the ports of the same community and to all the associated promiscuous ports. It is not forwarded to other communities in the primary VLAN or to isolated ports.

docs.title: PVLAN Trunks
docs.text:
In a distributed network, inter-switch links (ISL) configured as trunks are necessary. Trunking carries multiple VLANs and is essential for the secondary PVLANs (Community and Isolated VLANs).

  • Regular PVLAN trunk: when both switches support PVLAN, regular trunks can be used. Each switch recognizes and handles the PVLANs correctly.
  • Promiscuous PVLAN trunk: used to connect a device that must communicate with all the ports, such as a firewall or a router. When it sends a frame, the switch replaces the secondary PVLAN ID with the primary PVLAN ID.
  • Isolated PVLAN trunk: used when the connected device handles only isolated ports. When it sends a frame, the switch replaces the primary PVLAN ID with the isolated secondary PVLAN ID.

For isolated PVLAN trunks, the switch is responsible for isolating the ports within the isolated PVLAN, which can be enforced with the switchport protected command.

docs.title: Segregating a Plant with PVLAN
docs.text:
Compared to VLAN Insertion, Private VLANs are less flexible: groups can either communicate fully or not at all. We cannot selectively allow or block specific communications. Before deploying PVLANs in OT/ICS environments, it is therefore crucial to identify the required communications.

To segment our ICS/OT devices transparently, we configured them in separate Community VLANs:

Plant Role Address VLAN Bottle Filling Plant HMI 172.26.104.11/24 110 Bottle Filling Plant PLC 172.26.104.12/24 110 Oil Refinery Plant HMI 172.26.104.21/24 110 Oil Refinery Plant PLC 172.26.104.22/24 110

docs.title: Switch Configuration
docs.text:
All the ICS/OT devices reside in VLAN 110, which we keep for routing and for the promiscuous ports. The devices are moved to their final VLAN without changing their IP addressing.

First, we configure the secondary Community VLANs:

vlan 111
  name LAB_SEC_OT_SEC_1
  private-vlan community
vlan 112
  name LAB_SEC_OT_SEC_2
  private-vlan community

Next, we define the primary VLAN and associate it with the secondary VLANs:

vlan 110
  name LAB_SEC_OT_L3
  private-vlan primary
  private-vlan association 111-112

docs.title: Host Access Ports (C-Port and I-Port)
docs.text:
We use a host port when an endpoint device is connected directly to an access port of the switch. In private VLANs, host ports are part of the secondary VLANs, which can be either community or isolated. Configuring a private VLAN host port takes two steps: first, we define the port as a private VLAN host port, then we configure the host association between the primary and secondary VLANs.

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 switchport private-vlan host-association 110 111
 switchport mode private-vlan host

This configuration places the port in primary VLAN 110 and secondary VLAN 111 (Community), which makes it a C-Port.

docs.title: Promiscuous Access Ports (P-Port)
docs.text:
We use a promiscuous port when a device is connected directly to an access port of the switch. This device, typically a gateway, needs to communicate with all the host ports, both community and isolated. In a private VLAN domain, promiscuous ports are part of the primary VLAN. Configuring a promiscuous port takes two steps: first, we define the port as promiscuous, then we configure the mapping between the secondary VLANs and the primary VLAN.

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport private-vlan mapping 110 111-112
 switchport mode private-vlan promiscuous

docs.title: Promiscuous Trunk Port
docs.text:
We use a promiscuous trunk port when a device that does not support PVLAN, typically a gateway, is connected directly to a trunk port of the switch. In a private VLAN domain, promiscuous trunk ports are part of the primary VLAN. They can carry multiple primary VLANs, and multiple secondary VLANs of a given primary VLAN can be mapped to a promiscuous trunk port.

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport private-vlan trunk allowed vlan 102-104,110
 switchport private-vlan mapping 110 111-112
 switchport mode private-vlan trunk promiscuous

Here we configured a trunk to the gateway. VLANs 102, 103 and 104 are regular VLANs. VLANs 111 and 112 are secondary PVLANs associated with the primary VLAN 110. VLAN 110 is allowed on the trunk because, on a promiscuous trunk port, the traffic destined for a secondary VLAN is mapped using the tag of the associated primary VLAN.

docs.title: Isolated Trunk Port
docs.text:
This is not our case, but if we need to configure a trunk port connected to a device that does not support PVLAN and manages devices in an isolated VLAN, we must use a different syntax:

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport private-vlan trunk allowed vlan 102-104,110
 switchport private-vlan association 110 113
 switchport mode private-vlan trunk secondary

The upstream devices must know that VLAN 113 is isolated, to handle broadcast and unicast traffic correctly.

With uniform switch models and promiscuous PVLAN trunks used only for gateways, we keep the network complexity low and still segment the OT/ICS environment properly.

docs.title: Why OT security is not IT security (and why it matters)
docs.text: 29 August 2026

docs.title: Why OT security is not IT security (and why it matters)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance iec62443 ot-ics

I recently finished the ISA IC32 course, the first module of the IEC 62443 certification path. I liked it. Some modules were explained really well, but overall it was not enough to understand the standard thoroughly and to face the exam. So I decided to write a short series of articles: to fix the concepts in my own head first, and hopefully to help you do the same.

docs.title: IT and OT Are Different. But Why?
docs.text: We all know that IT and OT must be treated differently. I am not sure it is always clear why. So let's start from there, because everything else in the standard builds on it.

docs.title: Different Priorities: AIC, Not CIA
docs.text:
In IT we think in terms of CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, in this order. In an IACS (Industrial Automation and Control System) the order flips and becomes AIC: Availability comes first.

Why? Because in some sectors a stopped plant is a physical safety problem for people long before it is an economic one. A chemical process that cannot be controlled is not a "service outage".

Here is an example I like. In IT, three failed logins lock the account, which is textbook good practice. Now imagine a plant operator who mistypes the password in the middle of an emergency. If the system locks him out, the lockout can be more dangerous than the typo. The control that protects confidentiality ends up hurting availability, and in OT availability wins.

docs.title: Different Time Scales
docs.text:
A server in IT is replaced every 3-5 years. A control system can stay in service for 15-20 years, often longer than its designers ever imagined. The maintenance windows we take for granted in IT often do not exist in OT. Think of a pharmaceutical plant: updating a production system can mean re-validating the entire process. You do not "just apply the patch on Tuesday".

This is why, later in the series, we will spend a whole article on patch management. It is not a detail, it is one of the hardest parts of the job.

docs.title: Don't Throw Away What You Know
docs.text:
The course makes one point clear right away, and I think it is an important one: this is not about throwing away what we know from IT and starting from scratch.

Today's IACS run on Windows, TCP/IP and Ethernet. Most IT practices are still valid: hardening, segmentation, access control, backup and monitoring. The real work is spotting early the 10% that is different, and treating it accordingly, before it turns into an incident.

If you come from IT, I suggest looking for that 10% in three places:

  • Anything that automatically blocks, locks or reboots, because it may collide with availability.
  • Anything that assumes you can patch or restart at will.
  • Anything that assumes a short equipment life cycle.

docs.title: How IEC 62443 is organized
docs.text: 05 September 2026

docs.title: How IEC 62443 is organized
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance iec62443 ot-ics

In the previous article I explained why industrial control system security needs an approach different from IT. Now let's look at the structure of the standard from above.

The first time you open the table of contents of IEC 62443 it looks confusing. There are many parts, with cryptic numbering, and it is not obvious who each of them is for or what it is for.

The trick is to stop thinking of it as a book. The standard is organized in six groups, each with a different audience. They are not six chapters to read in sequence: they are six different tools, and you will rarely need all of them.

docs.title: The six groups
docs.text:
General (62443-1-x). Terminology, concepts and the security life cycle. Anyone approaching the subject for the first time should start here: before talking about zones and conduits you need to know what the words mean.

Policy & Procedures (62443-2-x). For people who have to build a security program inside an organization: asset owners, IT and security managers. Among other things, this is where you find 62443-2-1 (the security management system, the CSMS) and 62443-2-3 on patch management. We will come back to both. Part 2-4 is also here: it contains the requirements for service providers.

System (62443-3-x). For people who design: system integrators, architects. This is where the risk assessment lives (3-2) and where you decide which security level is needed in which zone. Part 3-3 contains the system requirements, organized by the seven foundational requirements.
