Component (62443-4-x). For people who build components: vendors of PLCs, HMIs, network devices. Part 4-1 is about the secure development process, part 4-2 about the technical requirements of the single component.

Then there are two more recent groups, with their own numbering:

Profiles (62443-5-x). Adapt the standard to a specific sector (pharma, energy...).

Evaluation (62443-6-x). How conformity is verified and certified, with the target on parts 2-x and 4-2.

For the IC32 course and exam, these last two are barely mentioned. Know that they exist and what they are for, and that is enough.

docs.title: Why the structure is not just bureaucracy
docs.text:
The structure mirrors exactly how a real project moves:

  1. The asset owner defines the acceptable risk (Policy & Procedures).
  2. The system integrator translates that risk into an architecture (System).
  3. The supplier builds components that satisfy the requirements (Component).

If in a project someone skips one of these steps, everything that follows is built on a risk nobody actually defined. This is, in my experience, the most common failure mode: not a missing firewall, but a missing decision.

docs.title: The IEC 62443 roles
docs.text: 12 September 2026

docs.title: The IEC 62443 roles
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance iec62443 ot-ics

Who guarantees the security of a plant?

It looks like a trivial question, and the naive answer is usually: the integrator. But, and there is always a "but", if you open the contract, there is no mention of it. No responsibility at all.

IEC 62443 assigns the roles more precisely than it seems at first sight. And the accountability, the ultimate responsibility, the one you cannot delegate, always stays with the asset owner. Always, even when most of the technical work is handed over to an integrator. The asset owner can delegate activities. Not the risk.

docs.title: The four roles
docs.text:
Asset owner. The one who owns and operates the plant, and who is accountable. There is a task that is theirs and nobody else can do it for them: defining the tolerable residual risk, meaning how much risk the organization accepts to live with after the countermeasures. If this step is skipped, everything that follows is built on an implicit assumption instead of a decision. In the standard the asset owner is mainly in parts 2-1, 2-4, 3-2 and 3-3.

Integration service provider. Designs and implements the solution according to the asset owner's requirements (when there are any): technical specifications, installation, configuration, testing, up to handover.

Maintenance service provider. Comes in after handover and stays as long as needed: patching, updates, change management, up to the decommissioning of systems at end of life.

Product supplier. Builds the product (PLC, HMI, network component...) designed to be independent from the specific plant. Provides the hardening guidelines and handles vulnerability management on its own product. Here the reference parts are 4-1 and 4-2, plus 3-3 for the system requirements the product has to support.

Around them there are the support roles: regulators, insurers, certification bodies. They do not execute anything on the plant, but they shape what is required, how it is verified and what happens when something goes wrong.

docs.title: A detail that creates a lot of confusion
docs.text:
These are roles, not companies. One organization can play several roles at the same time, and one role can be shared among several organizations. A plant that does its own maintenance is asset owner and maintenance service provider at once. A big vendor can be product supplier and integrator.

What the standard asks you to hold firm is not "who is who" on paper, but who answers for what. A good exercise: take your last project and write next to every activity the name of the person who is accountable and the one who is responsible. If you find activities with no name next to them, you found your first finding.

docs.title: Why this comes before the technical terms
docs.text: With this map in mind, the technical vocabulary of the next articles (zones, conduits, security levels) makes much more sense: every concept exists to answer the responsibility of one of these roles.

docs.title: Zones and conduits
docs.text: 19 September 2026

docs.title: Zones and conduits
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance iec62443 ot-ics security

Our network is segmented.

I hear this sentence often, and have for years, and it means nothing. So much that I ended up introducing another word: segregation. Different word, maybe clearer meaning.

IEC 62443 speaks about security zones: an area that groups assets with the same acceptable risk level, with a clear boundary between inside and outside. Note what the definition is built on: not the technology, not the IP addresses, but the risk.

docs.title: The printers example
docs.text:
The simplest example I found in the course is also the most effective: the printers.

Industrial printers (for labels, reports, alarms) do not control the process, but they are very easy to compromise: old firmware, default passwords, nobody ever updates them.

Putting them in a separate area is not an excess of zeal. It is acknowledging that in there the acceptable risk is different from the one of the control room, and acting on it. PLCs and printers have different criticalities and different needs. If they are treated the same, you have to protect the printers like PLCs (expensive and often impossible) or the PLCs like printers (dangerous).

docs.title: Sub-zones: inherit from the parent, add your own
docs.text:
In the first version of this article I left sub-zones out, because I found it hard to explain them in a way that was both clear and short. A comment made me realize that, without them, the printers example is incomplete. So let me try.

In the very common case, the printers already sit together with the production systems. They live in the production zone, so they inherit a set of its characteristics: the policies, the rules, the way they are managed. That is the "parent" relationship. On top of that, they have their own characteristics, stricter in some aspects (isolation, restrictions on who can talk to them), and that is the sub-zone: the dashed box inside the production zone in the picture.

The mental model I use: the sub-zone is not a separate world. It is a part of the parent zone that has additional rules.

Two more examples that I find useful:

  • The historian. It lives in the production zone, but it needs wider policies than the rest, because it has to talk with the enterprise side to deliver its data. Here the sub-zone is the opposite of the printers: not more restricted, but more open, and for that reason it is better to have it as an explicit exception than to open up the whole production zone for it.
  • External vendors. Suppliers who access remotely are a good candidate for a dedicated zone, not a sub-zone. Their risk profile is different, they are not under your control, and their access has to go through well-defined conduits.

The question to ask is always the same: is the acceptable risk of these assets the same as their neighbours'? If yes, they stay together. If it differs a little and the rest is shared, think sub-zone. If it differs a lot, think a dedicated zone.

docs.title: A zone with no network: the laptop and the USB stick
docs.text:
If you come from network security, a zone looks like a VLAN or a subnet. Something with an IP range and a firewall in front. So a zone made of a USB stick sounds strange. It is not, and the standard asks for it (ZCR 3.4, in 3-2): devices that make temporary connections to the system should be grouped into a separate zone.

Think of the engineering laptop of a maintenance technician. In one week it is on the office network to read email, in the vendor's lab to download a firmware, on the hotel Wi-Fi during a business trip. Then it goes into the plant and gets plugged into the control network to modify a PLC program. With a USB stick carrying the project files, going back and forth.

The risk of that laptop is not the risk of the control network. It is the sum of every place it has been. And that risk travels with the device. This is the reason it gets its own zone: not because of where it sits, but because of what it brings with it. The standard says the same thing in its own words: because of the temporary nature of the connection, these devices may also connect to other networks outside the zone.

So how do you draw a zone that has no IP range? The boundary is the device and the media, plus the physical place where they live and where they are checked. The logical boundary says "these laptops and these USB sticks". The physical boundary says "the maintenance cabinet and the check-in station".

And the conduit? Same lesson as the next section, with a very concrete case. The conduit between this zone and the control zone is not a cable. It is a check-in station: a malware scan, a list of approved media, a log of who plugged what and when. The measures are the conduit.

The standard also gives an exception worth knowing: a handheld device that is used inside a single zone and never leaves its physical boundary may be included in that zone. The risk comes from the travelling, not from the device itself.

docs.title: Conduits are not cables
docs.text:
Between one zone and another you need conduits: the controlled communication channels that let data through without compromising it.

A very common mistake is to think that a conduit is a cable. It is not. A conduit is the set of measures that govern that connection: a firewall, a VPN, an authentication system, the protocols you allow and the ones you block. The cable is only part of it. A conduit has its own security level, just like a zone.

docs.title: Who draws it, and greenfield vs brownfield
docs.text:
The architecture is typically designed by the integration service provider (see the previous article). But the designer always starts from a decision that cannot be taken alone: how much risk the asset owner is willing to accept. A zone model drawn without that input is a drawing, not a security architecture.

The examples above are the brownfield case: the plant exists, the printers are already there next to the production systems, and you work with what you have. If instead you are designing a new plant, you can make different evaluations and start from a cleaner sheet. But be careful: in the end every zone, sub-zone and conduit has to be translated into technical configurations (VLANs, firewall rules, access lists). That is where the discussion opens on microsegmentation and similar approaches, which is a topic for another day.

docs.title: Practical rules I take away
docs.text:
• Every boundary must exist for a precise reason that you can write in one sentence. If you cannot, remove it or justify it.
  • Group by risk and function, not by "what is physically close".
  • Remember that the only way into a zone is a conduit, and every conduit has an owner.
  • Before creating a new zone, ask whether a sub-zone is enough. It is easier to keep and to explain.

A well segmented network is not the one with the most firewalls. It is the one where every boundary exists for a precise reason.

docs.title: Security Levels
docs.text: 26 September 2026

docs.title: Security Levels
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance iec62443 ot-ics security

What is the security level (SL) of your plant?

This question opens a mini-series inside the series. Squeezing the whole topic into one article would have made it unclear, so I split it in three: this one on the levels, the next on the three types of SL, and then SL as a vector.

docs.title: What an SL is
docs.text:
The security level is a number from 0 to 4 that says how much a boundary, a zone or a conduit resists a category of attacker. Mind the words: it is applied to zones and conduits (previous article), not to "the plant".

It is not a generic "more secure / less secure" scale. The standard ties each level to a precise attacker profile:

  • SL1: protection against casual or coincidental violation. Someone stumbles where he should not, with no intention at all.
  • SL2: protection against intentional violation using simple means: low resources, generic skills, low motivation.
  • SL3: protection against intentional violation using sophisticated means: moderate resources, skills specific to industrial systems, moderate motivation.
  • SL4: protection against intentional violation using sophisticated means with extended resources: IACS-specific skills and high motivation. The nation-state (sponsored) attacker profile.

SL0 also exists, but only as a value: it means no specific requirement or protection. You will see it later in the vector.

docs.title: Two consequences
docs.text:
First: going up one level means designing countermeasures built to resist an adversary with more resources and more competence. It is not "the same plus a bit more". The cost and the effort do not grow linearly, and some measures that are fine at SL2 are simply not enough at SL3.

Second, and it is a prerequisite of the first: it is not that easy to define an attacker with "simple means", "sophisticated" or "extended". Who is that, in practice? A bored teenager, a competitor, a criminal group with ransomware, a state? And if we are not able to define these categories, we are not able to define the measures needed either.

That is why, in my opinion, SL is more useful as a common language than as a precise measure. It forces a conversation between asset owner, integrator and vendors about who we are afraid of, which is usually a conversation nobody has had. Rocco Sicilia and I already talked about this problem in the past on the Info Sec. Unplugged podcast.

SL alone still does not mean anything, because there are three different ways to measure it.

docs.title: Security level: target, capability, achieved
docs.text: 03 October 2026

docs.title: Security level: target, capability, achieved
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance iec62443 ot-ics security

In the previous article I covered the four security levels, from 1 to 4. But the topic is still incomplete: there are three types of SL, and they are used at different moments.

docs.title: The three types
docs.text:
Target (SL-T) is what you want to achieve. You decide it after a risk assessment, before designing anything: it is a goal, not yet a reality. It is assigned to a zone or to a conduit.

Capability (SL-C) is what a component can deliver. It is a characteristic of the product, independent of where it will be installed. For a component, SL-C is defined (and declared) by the vendor and says what you can obtain if the component is configured correctly. A component with SL-C 2 does not give you SL 2 by itself: it gives you the possibility to get there.

Achieved (SL-A) is what you really have, measured on the real system once implemented. It is the number that tells you whether you are meeting the goal or just declaring it.

docs.title: The natural flow
docs.text:
The flow, in theory, is:

  1. start from a target (SL-T);
  2. choose components with an adequate capability (SL-C);
  3. measure the achieved (SL-A) to verify the goal has really been reached.

The arrows in the picture say it: you choose the components against the target, you measure the result.

docs.title: The real world
docs.text:
We know the real world is a bit different: the plant arrives, it gets installed, switched on, and then somebody thinks about security. This makes everything more complicated, but not impossible. We start from an SL-A (the starting point) that has to get closer to an SL-T, often with no idea of what the SL-C of the components is.

In this case the work is reconstructive: you inventory the components, you look for vendor documentation (or you ask for it), you compare with the target and you find the gaps. Where the component is not enough, you compensate with something around it, a topic for a later article (common component security constraints, the CCSC).

docs.title: SL-A is not static
docs.text:
There is a detail that ties this topic to the life cycle: SL-A decays over time. Countermeasures age, configurations drift, new vulnerabilities appear. The line in the chart goes down while the target stays where it is.

The goal of the standard is that, at any moment, SL-A ≥ SL-T. Which means the work does not end when the system goes into production. Compared with the IT world, it is the continuous process of patch management, extended to everything that keeps your SL alive: reviews, audits, access rights, backups, monitoring.

docs.title: Security Level as a Vector
docs.text: 10 October 2026

docs.title: Security Level as a Vector
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance iec62443 intermediate ot-ics security

In the last two articles I talked about the four security levels and the three ways to measure them. But the security level can also be represented as a vector.

docs.title: Seven values, seven questions
docs.text:
SL can be written as a vector of seven values, one per foundational requirement (FR). Moving from an SL number to an SL vector lets you differentiate the fundamental requirements. Here they are, with the question I use to remember each one:

  • FR1, IAC (Identification and Authentication Control). Who are you? Do you really know who is accessing the system?
  • FR2, UC (Use Control). What can you do? Once inside, what are you allowed to do, and what not?
  • FR3, SI (System Integrity). Has it been modified? Did somebody alter code, configuration or data without authorization?
  • FR4, DC (Data Confidentiality). Who can read? Who has access to the information that circulates?
  • FR5, RDF (Restricted Data Flow). Where can data go? Does data stay where it should, or can it end up where it shouldn't?
  • FR6, TRE (Timely Response to Events). How do I react? What happens when something goes wrong, and how fast?
  • FR7, RA (Resource Availability). Does it stay available? Does the system hold, even under attack?

The order above is the official one and it is worth learning by heart: in the exam, "FR5" has to immediately mean "restricted data flow". Each value goes from 0 to 4, where 0 means no specific requirement.

Why is it useful? Because "SL3" says very little. A zone with the vector {2 2 1 1 3 1 3} is not "SL3": it needs strong protection on data flow and availability (a typical choice for a control zone), and much less on confidentiality (the data of a PLC loop is rarely a secret). Same SL3, different protection on each requirement.

docs.title: Closing the theory
docs.text:
Let me wrap up this theoretical part:

  • SL is a value from 1 to 4: every level is associated with a threat actor profile.
  • SL has three types: SL-T (the goal), SL-C (the potential), SL-A (the current state). The aim is SL-A ≥ SL-T. Before building a plant I must have clear ideas and select components with an adequate SL-C.
  • For clarity, SL can be written as a vector of seven components, each answering a specific question.

A formal remark: saying "the plant has SL3" is formally incorrect, because SL applies to zones and conduits, not to the whole plant. In informal use, "the plant is SL3" usually means that the highest value is 3.

docs.title: In practice: twin matrices
docs.text: What follows is my own suggestion, not something from the standard, but it works well for me.

docs.title: SL-T and SL-A as twin matrices
docs.text:
For every zone and conduit you have an SL-T and an SL-A. Put them side by side: FR per row, zone or conduit per column. Where SL-A < SL-T, color the cell. You see the gaps in one glance.

In the example, the gaps are Z2 on FR3 (integrity), Z1 on FR6 (response), and the conduit C2 on FR5 (data flow). Notice that the Z3 printers zone has SL-T 0 on FR6: it is a choice, not a mistake, and it should be written down and approved by the asset owner.

docs.title: SL-C of components against SL-T of the zone
docs.text:
Once SL-T is defined, I must make sure that the components have a compatible SL-C. The same trick works: one column per component, one row per FR.

A gap in a component does not automatically block the zone: another component or a countermeasure around it can compensate. But the compensation has to be a conscious, documented decision.

docs.title: The IEC 62443 map
docs.text: 17 October 2026

docs.title: The IEC 62443 map
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics security

IEC 62443 does not have one diagram. It has about ten, with similar names, and during the course I needed a map not to get lost.

This article is that map. Bookmark it, because the next articles come back to it one piece at a time.

docs.title: 1. The Common Thread
docs.text: There is only one thread (diagram 1). You start from the CSMS (Cyber Security Management System), you assess the risk, you draw zones and conduits, you assign an SL-T, you break it down into the seven FR (foundational requirements), you derive the requirements, you choose the countermeasures, then you monitor and improve. Everything else, models and life cycles included, is just a different view of this chain.

docs.title: 2. The Four Models
docs.text:
There are four models, and each one derives from the previous one (diagram 2).

Reference Model (diagram 3). The one everybody calls "Purdue". It gives the conceptual base with its levels from 0 to 4. Levels 0 to 3 are the industrial (OT) side, level 4 is the enterprise (IT) side. A note: the industrial DMZ between levels 3 and 4 that you see in many drawings is a widely recommended best practice, not a layer of the official model. In the picture I show it to make the point that IT and OT should not talk directly.

Asset Model (diagram 4). It says what I have: physical and logical components, with their attributes and relations. It is the inventory that everything else depends on.

Reference Architecture (diagram 5). It says how it is built, and it is unique for every company.

Zone and Conduit Model (diagram 6). It says where I draw the boundaries. Policies are born here, and are applied to the assets.

docs.title: 3. The Life Cycles
docs.text:
There are two independent life cycles: the one of the product, on the vendor side, and the one of the automation solution, on the plant side.

The second one can be read in three phases (Assess, Develop & Implement, Maintain), in eight phases (diagram 7), or from the services point of view, who does what and when (diagram 8). In the eight-phase view, the ISA courses are mapped on the phases: IC32 covers the fundamentals of all of them, IC33 risk assessment, IC34 design, IC37 maintenance.

There is also a third cycle, the one of the security level (diagram 9): same scheme, but referred to a zone and not to a physical asset. The two cycles have different phase gates, but they influence each other: a change to an asset can trigger work on the security level, and a new vulnerability can force you to act on the asset.

docs.title: 4. Two Processes to Keep at Hand
docs.text:
The seven ZCR steps of 62443-3-2 (diagram 10): identify the SUC (system under consideration), initial risk assessment (worst case), partition into zones and conduits, compare the initial risk with the tolerable one, detailed risk assessment (which gives the SL-T), document the CRS (cybersecurity requirement specification), approval by the asset owner. If the initial risk is already tolerable, you skip straight to documentation.

The five phases of patching of 62443-2-3 (diagram 11): information gathering, monitoring and evaluation, patch testing, patch deployment, verification and reporting. And then it starts over. The installation times in the picture, one week for high priority, three months for medium, two years or the next outage for low, are indicative values from the course material, and in the real world they are agreed per plant.

docs.title: 5. The CCSC
docs.text: Finally, the CCSC (Common Component Security Constraints, diagram 12): four constraints that hold for all the component requirements of 62443-4-2. Do not compromise the essential functions, provide compensating countermeasures outside the component where it is not enough, apply least privilege, develop with a secure process.

docs.title: Mandate, perimeter (SUC) and inventory (ZCR1)
docs.text: 17 November 2026

docs.title: Mandate, perimeter (SUC) and inventory (ZCR1)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics security

Where do you actually start?

The first mistake in an OT security project is usually not a technical one. It is starting without knowing why you are doing it, and without knowing what you are protecting.

So step zero asks three questions: why, who, what.

docs.title: Why: The Mandate on One Page
docs.text:
ISA/IEC 62443-2-1 lists a typical mistake: starting a security program without a rationale tied to the mission of the organization. You don't need a fifty-page document. You need one page that says which business risk you want to reduce, in words understood by whoever signs the budget.

A possible starting point is revenue, and how much of it depends on the systems you want to protect.

  • If they become unavailable, how much do we lose for every day of downtime?
  • What is the maximum downtime we can sustain?
  • How much can a cyber incident affect the safety of people?

If you need a hook, look at what happened in the last few weeks. Coordinated attacks hit the refrigeration controllers of supermarkets across Europe, starting in France in October and spreading to Belgium, Ireland, Sweden and others. According to press reports, attackers abused the defrost mode to push temperatures up to 50 °C, and stores had to throw away stock. Many of the controllers were running outdated software. That is not a story about exotic malware. It is a story about a business that depended on a system nobody had put in the right place on the risk register.

A one-page mandate can be as simple as this:

  • Why: which business risk we want to reduce (production stop, quality, safety of people, legal obligations).
  • Goal: what must be different in one or two years.
  • Scope: which plants or systems are involved.
  • Responsibilities: who is the sponsor, who coordinates.
  • Resources: time, people and an indicative budget.

This outline is a practical suggestion, inspired by the program charter in NIST SP 800-82. It is not a list from IEC 62443.

docs.title: Who: Sponsor, Coordinator, Working Group
docs.text:
You need two clear roles. A sponsor, who has the authority to decide and to release resources. A coordinator, who keeps the thread. Around them, a small group with the right skills: OT, IT, production and, where it exists, safety.

Without this, the risk assessment becomes an exercise of the security department alone, and the people who know how the plant really runs are not in the room.

Remember the stakeholders from the earlier post: the asset owner is the accountable role. The sponsor comes from that side.

docs.title: What: The SUC
docs.text:
Here the standard has a precise name: SUC, System Under Consideration. ISA/IEC 62443-3-2 opens its process with the first requirement, ZCR 1: identify the SUC, define its security perimeter and identify all access points (clause 4.2.1).

A few useful details:

  • The SUC includes all the IACS assets necessary to provide a complete automation solution.
  • It can contain several subsystems: BPCS, DCS, SIS, SCADA, vendor packages, and also technologies like IIoT or cloud services.
  • External services and support to the IACS are part of the picture too.

One practical tip, mine and not the standard's: if you have more than one system, start from one only. A SUC that is too big makes the risk assessment slow and vague. A small one can be closed, you learn from the first round, and you repeat it on the others.

docs.title: The Inventory
docs.text:
You start from what exists on paper: network diagrams, architecture, data flows. Then you go to the field and verify.

The second step is the one that counts. It often happens that something shows up that was not on the drawing: an undocumented connection, a vendor with remote access, a forgotten PC in a cabinet. This is why "the plant is isolated" is a sentence to be verified, not believed. And the access points that emerge here, logical and physical, are exactly the ones ZCR 1 asks you to identify.

As a starting point for the inventory (again a practical suggestion): an identifier, asset type and function, location, vendor and model, firmware or OS version, network interfaces and protocols, connections to the outside, owner, and whether the vendor still supports it.

docs.title: Typical Mistakes
docs.text:
• Starting without a rationale tied to the mission: the program stays a technical initiative that nobody defends.
  • No management support, and therefore no resources when you need them.
  • Building the inventory from drawings only, without a field check.
  • Defining a SUC that is too big for a first round.

docs.title: What You Have in Hand at the End
docs.text:
Three things:

  • A one-page mandate.
  • A written definition of the SUC.
  • An inventory with the network diagram.

It is not the most exciting part of the journey, but everything else rests on it.

To follow this post, it helps to review the ZCR diagram we already covered in The IEC 62443 map.

docs.title: The initial risk assessment (ZCR2)
docs.text: 18 November 2026

docs.title: The initial risk assessment (ZCR2)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics risk-assessment security

You have a mandate, a defined SUC and an inventory. Before talking about firewalls, security measures and security levels, there is one question to ask: what is the worst that can happen if this system is unavailable or tampered with?

ISA/IEC 62443-3-2 calls this the initial cyber security risk assessment (ZCR 2, clause 4.3). It is not the detailed analysis. It is a first, rough picture of the worst case, and it comes before you split the system into zones and conduits.

docs.title: What the Standard Asks
docs.text:
ZCR 2.1 says the organization shall perform a cyber security risk assessment of the SUC, or confirm that a previous one still applies, to identify the worst-case unmitigated risk that could result from interference with, breach of, or disruption of mission-critical IACS operations.

Three words matter here:

  • Worst case: you are not estimating what is likely, you are estimating what hurts most.
  • Unmitigated: you reason as if firewalls, passwords and procedures did not exist.
  • SUC: you assess the system as a whole, not each component.

The standard lists the areas to look at: health, safety, environmental impact, business interruption, production loss, product quality, financial, legal, regulatory and reputation.

docs.title: The Table
docs.text:
In practice it is a table. The rows are the worst-case scenarios and the columns are the impact areas. In each cell: high, medium or low.

Example rows: loss of control of the process, safety system disabled or altered, plant stopped for days because ransomware reached the OT network, theft of recipe data. The last column asks whether the result exceeds the tolerable risk.

The scenarios in the figure are illustrative. Yours will depend on the plant.

docs.title: You Don't Start from Zero
docs.text:
• If the process is hazardous, a process hazard analysis (PHA) almost certainly exists. The standard says to reference the results of the PHA and of the functional safety assessment (IEC 61511) to identify the worst-case impacts.
  • The standard also suggests taking into account threat intelligence from governments and sector ISACs.
  • The answers from your one-page mandate (maximum sustainable downtime, loss per day of stop) are the natural input for the business columns.

The assessment of the initial risk is often done with a risk matrix that relates likelihood, impact and risk, such as a corporate risk matrix. Examples are in Annex B of the standard.

docs.title: The Comparison: ZCR 4
docs.text:
ZCR 4.1 is a single requirement. The initial risk is compared with the tolerable risk of the organization. If it exceeds it, a detailed risk assessment (ZCR 5) is mandatory. If it does not, you document the result and you stop there.

Who defines what is tolerable? The asset owner. It is the same point I made in the post about stakeholders: if nobody has formalized the tolerable risk, this comparison has nothing to compare against.

The standard also says that the initial assessment helps in two other ways: it prioritizes the detailed assessments, and it helps group assets into zones and conduits, which is the next step.

docs.title: Two Practical Notes
docs.text:
• Use one method. The standard says initial and detailed assessments should come from the same framework and use a consistent risk ranking scale, otherwise the results are not comparable. Use your corporate risk matrix if you have one.
  • Don't chase precision. This is a first pass. If another hour of discussion doesn't change the color of a cell, the cell is fine. (This one is my opinion, not the standard's.)

docs.title: Typical Mistakes
docs.text:
• Counting the existing countermeasures, and so ending up with a table that says everything is fine.
  • Mixing up impact and likelihood. Here we only ask how bad it can get.
  • Running it inside the security department only, without production and safety.
  • Using a different scale from the one used later in the detailed assessment.

docs.title: What You Have in Hand at the End
docs.text:
Three things:

  • The worst-case table for the SUC.
  • The comparison with the tolerable risk.
  • A priority list for the detailed risk assessment.

To follow this post, it helps to review the ZCR diagram we already covered in The IEC 62443 map.

docs.title: Partitioning the SUC into zones and conduits (ZCR3)
docs.text: 24 November 2026

docs.title: Partitioning the SUC into zones and conduits (ZCR3)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics risk-assessment security

We have the SUC and the worst case. Now the system has to be divided into zones and conduits. This is ZCR 3 in ISA/IEC 62443-3-2 (clause 4.4), and it is where you see whether security is designed or improvised.

docs.title: The base requirement: ZCR 3.1
docs.text:
The organization shall group IACS and related assets into zones or conduits as determined by risk. The grouping shall be based on the results of the initial cyber security risk assessment, or on other criteria:

  • criticality of assets
  • operational function
  • physical or logical location
  • required access (for example, least privilege)
  • responsible organization

The intention, as the standard puts it, is to identify the assets that share common security requirements, so that common security measures can be defined for them.

docs.title: How you start
docs.text: The standard gives an example. First divide the facility into operational areas, such as materials storage, processing, finishing. Then divide each area into functional layers: manufacturing execution systems (MES), supervisory systems (HMIs), primary control (BPCS, DCS, RTUs, PLCs) and safety systems. Models such as the Purdue reference model are often used as a basis. Product supplier reference architectures can help too. If you read the post on the map of the models, this is the Reference Model at work.

docs.title: The cases the standard spells out
docs.text:
ZCR 3.2 to 3.6 give guidance based on best practice. The standard says explicitly that this is not an exhaustive list.

  • ZCR 3.2, business vs IACS: IACS assets shall be in zones logically or physically separated from business or enterprise assets. They are different systems, with different functions, owners, locations and impact on health, safety and environment.
  • ZCR 3.3, safety: safety related assets shall be separated from non-safety assets. If they cannot be separated, the entire zone shall be identified as safety related. Safety zones typically need higher protection.
  • ZCR 3.4, temporary devices: maintenance laptops, portable equipment, USB devices should be in a separate zone. They face a wider variety of threats and may connect to other networks. An exception: a handheld that never leaves a single zone may be included in it.
  • ZCR 3.5, wireless: wireless devices should be in zones separated from wired ones. A wireless access point is typically modelled as the conduit between the two, and may need extra controls such as a firewall.
  • ZCR 3.6, external networks: remote access is outside the physical boundary of the SUC, so it should be modelled as separate zones with its own security requirements. Think of employees, suppliers and partners connecting for maintenance, optimization or reporting.

Note the verbs. ZCR 3.2 and 3.3 say "shall". ZCR 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6 say "should". It is the kind of detail that shows up in exam questions.

ZCR 3.1 also asks for special attention to safety instrumented systems, wireless systems, systems directly connected to Internet endpoints, systems that interface to the IACS but are managed by other entities, and mobile devices.

docs.title: How many zones?
docs.text:
This is my opinion, not the standard's: don't make fifty. Every extra zone is a boundary to design, a conduit to defend, a record to maintain. Start with few zones, each with a written reason. If two zones have the same requirements, they are one zone.

And it is not a one-shot decision. The standard says the assignment of assets to zones and conduits may be adjusted based on the results of the detailed risk assessment.

If you wonder where the printers go, or when to use a sub-zone, I covered that in the post on zones and conduits. The short version: it depends on whether they need different security requirements.

If you come from network security, a zone with no IP range may sound strange. The maintenance laptop and the USB stick are the best example: the risk travels with the device, so the device gets its own zone. I added a section on this to the zones and conduits article.

docs.title: The card of each zone
docs.text:
Later (ZCR 6.4, clause 4.7.5) the standard asks to document, for each zone and conduit: a name or identifier, accountable organization, logical boundary, physical boundary if applicable, safety designation, logical and physical access points, data flows for each access point, connected zones or conduits, list of assets with classification, criticality and business value, SL-T, applicable security requirements and policies, assumptions and external dependencies.

Right now the SL-T field stays empty. It is filled in after the detailed risk assessment. But it is worth opening a card per zone now, and filling what you already know.

docs.title: Typical mistakes
docs.text:
• One big zone for "the plant". It is easy to draw and it protects nothing.
  • A zone for every device. It cannot be maintained.
  • Forgetting remote access, the maintenance laptop or the wireless network because they are "not part of the system".
  • Mixing safety and non-safety assets without declaring the whole zone as safety related.
  • Drawing a conduit as a cable. A conduit is a logical grouping of the communication channels and the measures that protect them.

docs.title: How to build the three outputs
docs.text: The standard asks for two things in the cyber security requirements specification (CRS): a drawing, or a set of drawings, that illustrates the zone and conduit partitioning of the entire SUC, with each asset assigned to a zone or a conduit (ZCR 6.3); and the characteristics of every zone and conduit (ZCR 6.4). It does not say how they must look. What follows is my practical way, not the standard's.

docs.title: The zone and conduit drawing
docs.text:
Don't start from a blank page. Take the network diagram from step zero and draw the zones on top of it.

  • Draw the SUC perimeter first, dashed, with all the access points you identified.
  • One box per zone, with an identifier (Z-01, Z-02) and a name that says what is inside, not where it is.
  • One line per conduit, with an identifier (C-01, C-02) and the measures written on it: "firewall", "VPN with MFA", "check-in station". If you cannot write a measure on it, you have drawn a cable, not a conduit.
  • Mark the safety related zones in a different colour, so nobody has to look for them.
  • Show the zones outside the perimeter too: remote access, temporary devices, wireless.
  • Keep one overview page that a non-specialist can read. Detail goes on separate pages, one per zone if needed.
  • Put a date, a version and an owner on it. A drawing that nobody maintains is wrong within a year.

The figure is an overview drawing in this spirit.

docs.title: Every asset assigned to a zone or conduit
docs.text:
This is the inventory from step zero with one more column: the zone. A small example:

Asset ID Asset Type Location Zone or conduit PLC-01 Packaging line PLC Controller Line 2 cabinet Z-03 Control SW-01 Control switch Network Line 2 cabinet Z-03 Control HMI-01 Operator panel HMI Line 2 Z-02 Supervisory SCADA-01 SCADA server Server Control room Z-02 Supervisory HIST-01 Historian Server Control room Z-02 Supervisory (talks to business: candidate sub-zone) SIS-01 Safety controller Safety Line 2 cabinet Z-04 Safety FW-01 Firewall to office network Network Server room C-01 Business to supervisory LAPTOP-01 Engineering laptop Laptop Maintenance Z-05 Temporary devices USB-01..06 Maintenance USB sticks Media Maintenance Z-05 Temporary devices

Three checks that take ten minutes and find real problems:

  • The number of assets in this table is the same as in the inventory. If not, someone is missing.
  • Every asset is in exactly one zone or conduit. None in zero, none in two.
  • Every conduit connects exactly two zones, and every zone has at least one conduit.

Most of the arguments in a workshop happen on the rows with a note in the last column. That is fine: write the note and the decision.

docs.title: A card for each zone
docs.text:
One page per zone and per conduit, with the items listed in ZCR 6.4. The next figure shows the card of the temporary devices zone, filled in. Two things to notice. The fields SL-T and security requirements stay open for now, and that is correct: they are filled in after the detailed risk assessment (the standard notes that the security requirements cannot be finalized until then). And the logical boundary of this zone is not an IP range: it is "these laptops and this media".

If a field cannot be filled, don't leave it blank. Write what is missing and who will find out. That list of open points is the first to-do list of the next steps.

docs.title: What you have in hand at the end
docs.text:
Three things: the zone and conduit drawing, every asset assigned to a zone or conduit, and a card for each zone.

To follow this post, it helps to review the ZCR diagram we already covered in The IEC 62443 map.

docs.title: Threats and vulnerabilities (ZCR4-5)
docs.text: 26 November 2026

docs.title: Threats and vulnerabilities (ZCR4-5)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics risk-assessment security

We have zones and conduits. The comparison with the tolerable risk (ZCR 4) was made on the worst case, without looking at who attacks: we assumed the incident happens. If that risk exceeds the threshold, the detailed risk assessment starts: ZCR 5 in ISA/IEC 62443-3-2, clause 4.6. It applies to every zone and conduit. Here threats are needed, because now we estimate how likely they are. It begins with two questions: who can hurt us, and where are we weak.

docs.title: Why We Are Here: ZCR 4
docs.text:
Before the threats, a quick look at the door we came through. ZCR 4.1 is the comparison I described in the initial risk assessment: the worst-case risk of the SUC is compared with the tolerable risk of the organization. If it exceeds it, the detailed assessment (ZCR 5) is mandatory. If it does not, you document the result and you stop.

So ZCR 5 is not optional "extra work" that the security team decides to do. It is the consequence of a comparison, and the asset owner owns the other side of that comparison, the tolerable risk.

The two assessments look similar, but they are different:

Initial (ZCR 2, then ZCR 4) Detailed (ZCR 5) Scope the SUC as a whole each zone and conduit Question how bad can it get? what can go wrong, and how likely is it? Input worst-case consequences threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood Result go / no go for the detailed assessment the target security level (SL-T)

The scale must be the same in both, otherwise the results cannot be compared. We will meet the second comparison with the tolerable risk in the next post (ZCR 5.7), this time per threat.

docs.title: The vocabulary
docs.text:
These terms are asked in the exam, and they are easy to confuse. The definitions are in 3-2, clause 3.1.

  • Threat: a circumstance or event with the potential to adversely impact operations or assets, including the IACS.
  • Threat source: the intent and method targeted at the intentional exploitation of a vulnerability, or a situation and method that may accidentally exploit a vulnerability.
  • Threat vector: the path or means by which a threat source can gain access to an asset.
  • Threat environment: a summary of information about threats (sources, vectors, trends) that can affect a defined target, such as a company, a facility or a SUC.
  • Vulnerability: the weakness. For a threat to succeed, it has to exploit at least one.

Note that the threat source includes accidents. We will come back to this.

docs.title: ZCR 5.1: Identify the Threats
docs.text:
The requirement is a list of the threats that could affect the assets in the zone or conduit. Each threat description should include:

  • the threat source
  • its capability or skill level
  • the possible threat vectors
  • the assets potentially affected

The examples in the standard are deliberately unspectacular:

  • a non-malicious employee physically accesses the process control zone and plugs a USB memory stick into one of the computers;
  • an authorized support person logically accesses the process control zone using an infected laptop;
  • a non-malicious employee opens a phishing email, compromising their access credentials.

If you read the section on the maintenance laptop and the USB stick in Zones and conduits, you already know the first two: it is the scenario behind the temporary devices zone.

Notice that in all three nobody wants to cause damage. The threat source is not only the attacker. ISA/IEC 62443-1-1 lists accidental threats and non-validated changes among the common forms of threat, and describes the insider as a trusted person (employee, contractor or supplier) who can be a threat even without intent, for example by bypassing a security control "to get the job done".

You don't need a hundred rows. The standard says it is acceptable to summarize by grouping sources, assets and entry points into classes. Ten realistic scenarios are better than eighty invented ones.

docs.title: ZCR 5.2: Identify the Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
The requirement: analyze the zone or conduit to identify and document the known vulnerabilities of the assets it contains, including the access points.

The standard explains why: a threat is successful only if it exploits one or more vulnerabilities in an asset, so knowing the vulnerabilities helps to understand the threat vectors.

A generally accepted approach is a vulnerability assessment (the standard refers to ISA-TR84.00.09). Known vulnerabilities can also be found through ICS-CERT and the IACS product suppliers. The technical report on patching (ISA-TR62443-2-3) adds national CERTs and other situational awareness organizations, and strongly recommends checking these sites throughout the week, or better, subscribing to their email notifications.

This is where the inventory pays back. Without vendor, model and firmware or software version, you cannot know whether a known vulnerability applies to you.

docs.title: An Aid That Is Not in the Standard
docs.text: To understand how real attackers target industrial systems, MITRE ATT&CK for ICS catalogs tactics and techniques observed in real events. NIST SP 800-82 suggests it for characterizing threats. NIST also groups threat sources into four categories: adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental. This is not part of IEC 62443, but it is a useful checklist so you don't forget the accidents.

docs.title: The Table
docs.text:
In practice, you write a table per zone. The columns: threat source, skill, vector, affected assets. The figure shows four rows. The first three are the standard's examples. The fourth, a criminal group using vendor remote access, is my own example, and the skill levels are illustrative.

A second list, per asset, holds the known vulnerabilities: asset ID, vendor, model, version, the reference of the vulnerability, and where you found it.

docs.title: Typical mistakes
docs.text:
• A threat list made only of hackers. Many real incidents start with a mistake or a change nobody validated.
  • Copying a generic list from the internet, with nothing about your zones and your access points.
  • Looking for vulnerabilities without an inventory that has versions.
  • Forgetting the access points: ZCR 5.2 asks for them explicitly.
  • Starting with a hundred scenarios and never finishing.

docs.title: What You Have in Hand at the End
docs.text:
Two things:

  • The list of threats for each zone and conduit.
  • The list of known vulnerabilities for each asset.

To follow this post, it helps to review the ZCR diagram we already covered in The IEC 62443 map.

docs.title: From threats to the target SL (ZCR5)
docs.text: 01 December 2026

docs.title: From threats to the target SL (ZCR5)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics risk-assessment security

Fine, so which security level do we choose?

If the answer comes in ten seconds, it is usually a number picked out of thin air. The target is built, threat by threat, and the standard tells you how, at least up to a point. This is the part of the detailed risk assessment that goes from the list of threats to the SL-T of each zone and conduit.

docs.title: Where we are
docs.text: We have the SUC, the worst case, the zones and conduits, and the list of threats and vulnerabilities (ZCR 5.1 and 5.2). Now, for each threat on each zone or conduit, the standard asks us to work out how much it hurts, how likely it is, and what that means for the security level.

docs.title: ZCR 5.3: consequence and impact
docs.text:
Each threat scenario has to be evaluated for the consequence if it materializes. The standard asks to document the worst case in terms of risk areas such as personnel safety, financial loss, business interruption and environment.

Two practical points that come straight from the text:

  • Do not start from zero. Existing PHAs and other risk assessments (IT, functional safety, business, physical security) should be reviewed to help determine the consequences.
  • If the worst-case impact is low, the team may decide to move on to the next threat. Not every scenario deserves a full analysis.

The measure can be qualitative or quantitative. Typically the organization uses a consequence scale defined in its own risk management system. Annex B of the standard gives an example, with categories A (high), B (medium) and C (low) across operational, financial and health, safety and environment aspects.

Category Operational: outage at one site Operational: outage at multiple sites Operational: national infrastructure and services Financial: cost (million USD) Financial: legal Financial: public confidence HSE: people onsite HSE: people offsite HSE: environment A (High) >7 days >1 day Impacts multiple sectors or disrupts community services in a major way >500 Felony criminal offense Loss of brand image Fatality Fatality or major community incident Citation by regional agency or long-term significant damage over large area B (Medium) <2 days >1 hour Potential to impact sector at a level beyond the company >5 Misdemeanor criminal offense Loss of customer confidence Loss of work day or major injury Complaints or local community impact Citation by local agency C (Low) <1 day <1 hour Little to no impact to sectors beyond the individual company. Little to no impact on community. <5 None None First aid or recordable injury No complaints Small, contained release below reportable limits

docs.title: ZCR 5.4: unmitigated likelihood
docs.text:
Then, for each threat: how likely is it that it materializes? Here the standard has a rule that is easy to get wrong and easy to find in an exam: the likelihood is unmitigated. Existing cybersecurity countermeasures of the zone should not be considered. They are "hypothetically eliminated".

There is one exception that deserves attention. The determination does recognize:

  • countermeasures that are inherent to the IACS components;
  • non-cyber independent protection layers, such as physical security, mechanical safeguards (a pressure safety valve, for example) or emergency procedures that are in place.

Factors to consider include the motivation and capability of the threat source, the history of similar threats, known vulnerabilities (from ZCR 5.2, so the inventory pays off again) and the attractiveness of the target.

Likelihood is evaluated twice in the detailed assessment: now without countermeasures, to establish the unmitigated risk, and later (ZCR 5.9) with them, to establish the residual risk. That is the topic of the next post.

One more detail: consequence-only methodologies are allowed. They do not factor likelihood in and implicitly assume it is constant, for example always present, a value of 1.

docs.title: ZCR 5.5: unmitigated risk
docs.text: Easy one: impact and unmitigated likelihood combined. It is usually done with a risk matrix, which establishes the relationship between likelihood, impact and risk. Annex B shows several: 3 x 3, 3 x 5, 5 x 5 and others. And it says something I like, and that you should take seriously: matrices vary in size, scales and colors, and it is critical that the team uses the one approved by the asset owner for the facility being assessed.

docs.title: ZCR 5.6: determine SL-T
docs.text:
Here is the requirement, in one line: an SL-T shall be established for each security zone or conduit. It can be a single value or a vector (see Security Level as a Vector, and Annex A of 62443-3-3).

And here is the surprise: there is no prescribed method. The standard's guidance lists some approaches that organizations use:

  1. establish the SL-T from the difference between the unmitigated risk and the tolerable risk;
  2. establish it from the SL definitions in Annex A (the attacker profiles of Security Levels: casual, simple means, sophisticated means with moderate resources, sophisticated means with extended resources);
  3. if a risk matrix is used, start from a reasonable estimate of SL (it can also be none), evaluate the risk taking into account the countermeasures that this SL implies, and if the risk is not acceptable, raise the SL, meaning add countermeasures, until it is. The SL that comes out becomes the SL-T.

Why does it matter? Because the purpose of the SL-T is to communicate the desired level of security for a zone or conduit to the people who design, implement, operate and maintain it. It is a communication tool before being a calculation.

docs.title: ZCR 5.7: compare with the tolerable risk
docs.text:
The unmitigated risk of each threat is compared with the organization's tolerable risk. It is the same yardstick used in ZCR 4, but now the comparison is made threat by threat and zone by zone, not once for the whole SUC. If it exceeds it, the organization has to decide whether to accept, transfer or mitigate it. To mitigate, we continue with the next steps (existing countermeasures, residual risk, additional countermeasures). Otherwise, the result is documented and we proceed with the next threat.

Who decides what is tolerable? Not the integrator, not the consultant. The asset owner, as we saw in the post about the roles. It is also the reason why tolerable risk ends up written in the CRS (ZCR 6.8).

docs.title: A worked example (invented, but realistic)
docs.text:
Let me make it concrete. Take the control zone of a plant. Three scenarios, using the same kind of examples the standard uses for threats: an authorized support person connects an infected laptop, an employee falls for a phishing email and loses credentials, a non-malicious employee plugs a USB stick into a computer.

I use the 3 x 5 matrix of Annex B (likelihood 1 to 5, severity A to C). The scale and the values below are mine, not the standard's. The asset owner has declared that "Medium or lower" is tolerable.

# Threat Impact Unmitigated likelihood Risk Versus tolerable 1 Infected laptop of a support person A 3 Med-high Above: mitigate 2 Phishing, credentials stolen B 4 Med-high Above: mitigate 3 Non-malicious USB stick B 2 Med-low Tolerable: document

Threat 3 stops here, documented. Threats 1 and 2 move on. For them, we apply the third approach of ZCR 5.6: start from an estimate, say SL 1, check the matrix again with the countermeasures that this level implies, find the risk still above the tolerable, raise to SL 2, and check again.

docs.title: From the risk to the vector (my suggestion)
docs.text:
A vector needs seven values. The standard does not tell you how to get them, so here is what I would do, and I mark it as my method, not the standard's: for each threat that must be mitigated, note which foundational requirements its countermeasures live in, and give those FRs the level that the iteration gave you.

  • Threat 1 (infected laptop): integrity of the system (FR3, SI), restriction of data flow (FR5, RDF), response to events (FR6, TRE).
  • Threat 2 (stolen credentials): identification and authentication (FR1, IAC), use control (FR2, UC).
  • Nobody in this tiny example worries about confidentiality (FR4, DC) or availability (FR7, RA): they stay at 1.

Result: {2 2 2 1 2 2 1}. In a real assessment you will have dozens of scenarios, and each FR takes the highest level that any threat requires. A 0 is allowed if you really need no protection on that FR, but it should be a conscious, written decision approved by the asset owner.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Counting existing firewalls and antivirus in the unmitigated likelihood. They come later, in ZCR 5.8 and 5.9.
  • Throwing away the non-cyber protections (the pressure valve, the guard, the procedure) as if they did not exist. They are recognized.
  • Using a risk matrix that nobody in the organization has approved.
  • Writing "SL3" for the whole plant. The SL-T is per zone and conduit, and ideally a vector.
  • Letting the integrator decide the tolerable risk.

docs.title: What You Have in Hand at the End
docs.text:
For each zone and conduit: the impact, the unmitigated likelihood and the unmitigated risk of every threat; the comparison with the tolerable risk; and the SL-T, as a value or a vector. This is the first time in the series that the target of Security level target, capability, achieved gets a real number.

To follow this post, it helps to review the ZCR diagram we already covered in The IEC 62443 map.

docs.title: Patch or compensate OT/ICS vulnerabilities?
docs.text: 04 December 2026

docs.title: Patch or compensate OT/ICS vulnerabilities?
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced governance iec62443 ot-ics security vulnnerability-management

Patch or compensate? A risk decision, not a rule.

We have the list of vulnerabilities. The textbook answer is: patch them. In OT, most of the time, that does not work.

docs.title: Why patching is slow in OT
docs.text:
• Equipment lives fifteen or twenty years, and the vendor stops releasing patches long before that. When no patch exists, there is nothing to apply.
  • When a patch exists, it has to be validated with the integrator, tested, and installed in an outage window that may be a year away.
  • HMIs are often Windows PCs, but in my experience they are usually left alone, because the vendor does not guarantee the system will keep working if you change something. Sometimes you cannot even install an antimalware.
  • A PLC that works is left as it is.

So the update cycle is slow. The risk management cycle has to be faster.

docs.title: What the standard says
docs.text:
IEC 62443 is less far from this than it may look. ISA-TR62443-2-3, the patch management report, says that when a vulnerability is announced the asset owner should assess whether it applies to their systems. If the patch is not available, or the system cannot be patched right away because of its criticality, the appropriate action may be to take countermeasures. It also says that patching should be scheduled in an outage window when feasible, and tested in a non-production environment ahead of the window when possible.

There is a second mechanism, from the security level part of the series. If a component cannot reach the SL-T required by its zone (its SL-C is lower), the gap is closed with compensating countermeasures around the component. This is the idea behind the common component security constraints, which we saw in the map post. The standard does not ask you to update the PLC. It asks you to know that you cannot, to write it down, and to compensate.

docs.title: A decision, not a rule
docs.text: For each vulnerability there are three options: patch, compensate, or accept. The figure shows the flow. The question that matters first is whether a patch exists and the integrator has validated it on your system. If yes, plan it in a window and test first. If no, compensate.

docs.title: Where to act
docs.text:
These are my practical suggestions, not the standard's.

  1. The entry points you control: firewalls, VPNs, remote access gateways → patch them fast. These are what stands between the outside and the PLC you cannot patch. Here lies your main compensation: segregation, filters and IPS can reduce the exposure and prevent attacks.
  2. Ports and media on the HMIs: USB disabled or blocked, and removable media passed through a check-in station, as in the temporary devices zone. It does not touch the vendor's software.
  3. Passive network monitoring: if you cannot install anything on the device, monitoring has to sit on the network. There are OT products designed for this, which observe traffic without agents (Cisco Cyber Vision is one example). I mention it as a category, not as a recommendation: it has a cost, and its value depends on how well your zones are already defined. It's a technical shift, not a solution: technologies must be managed and maintained. But at least here we can act.
  4. The residual risk, in writing: what is left after the controls is accepted by the asset owner, as we said in the post on roles. Without that signature, "we compensated" is just a hope.

docs.title: Compensating controls are not free
docs.text: They have to be maintained, tested, and they fail too. Moving everything there moves the debt, it does not remove it. A vulnerability that is not fixed behind a single firewall is a risk that depends on that firewall. That is why the inventory, the zones and the vulnerability list matter: a fast risk cycle is only possible if the work was done before.

docs.title: What about buying better equipment?
docs.text: On new purchases you can ask for products developed under ISA/IEC 62443-4-1 and components certified to 4-2. But that does not change the installed base, and a vendor's commitment is worth what the vendor is worth if it disappears or discontinues the line. I would not make it a pillar of the strategy.

docs.title: My opinion, in one sentence
docs.text: In OT, the patch is the exception you plan. The controls are the rule.

docs.title: Introducing Cortex XSOAR
docs.text: 12 August 2024

docs.title: Introducing Cortex XSOAR
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cortex-xsoar palo-alto-networks

Cortex XSOAR is an orchestration and automation system that unifies the components of a security infrastructure. It integrates with third-party security and incident management vendors, so that the events they raise automatically become incidents within Cortex XSOAR.

Once the incidents are created, Cortex XSOAR runs playbooks that enrich them with information from other connected products. The enriched data helps us build a complete picture of the situation, so that nothing is overlooked.

We can apply automation and rules to these incidents to decide whether they require further investigation or can be closed safely. This filtering lets security analysts focus on the minority of incidents that genuinely need attention, which improves the efficiency of security operations.

This learning path follows the Cortex XSOAR Customer Success Engineering Training course and provides details on how to create a lab and tackle each lesson.

docs.title: Incident Lifecycle
docs.text:
This learning path follows the incident lifecycle:

The lifecycle begins with strategic planning. During this phase, we assess the security needs of the organization, define the objectives and determine the integrations and workflows that Cortex XSOAR must manage.

This phase lets us design the workflow for incident management. The planning phase typically comes first, but my perspective is different: before designing a workflow, we need to understand the capabilities of the product. The lesson dedicated to planning is therefore postponed to the end. First we learn how the product works and what its features are, and then we approach the design phase with that knowledge.

docs.title: Setting Up Your Cortex XSOAR Lab Environment
docs.text: 12 August 2024

docs.title: Setting Up Your Cortex XSOAR Lab Environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cortex-xsoar lab palo-alto-networks

In this post, we set up a lab environment to experiment with Cortex XSOAR by Palo Alto Networks. This tutorial follows the content of the video XSOAR Engineer Training - Part 2: Incident Types & Fields.

docs.title: Download and Install Cortex XSOAR
docs.text:
We start by downloading the trial version of XSOAR. We receive a file of approximately 1 GB, named something like demistoserver-6.12-857430.sh, and we copy it to a Linux system. I am using Ubuntu Linux 22.04 for this setup.

We run the installation as the root user:

bash /tmp/demistoserver-6.12-857430.sh

The installation process is straightforward and prompts us to set the credentials to access XSOAR via the web interface.

When the installation is complete, we can access XSOAR via the web with the credentials we set. A pop-up notifies us that the license is missing:

The Community Edition provides a 30-day full-featured license, which gives us a complete experience of the capabilities of Cortex XSOAR. We simply press Cancel and continue with the setup.

docs.title: Update Installed Content Packs
docs.text: We navigate to Marketplace → Installed Content Packs, select all the content packs that need updating and click Update. We may receive a warning that the updates could introduce breaking changes. Since this is a new installation, we proceed with the updates.

docs.title: Install the Sample Event Generator Plugin
docs.text:
We need a plugin to generate some sample events. Normally the events are collected from a SIEM, but for our lab we use a simpler alternative.

We go to Marketplace → Browse and search for JSON Sample Incident Generator. We install the JSON Sample Incident Generator package, which includes an integration that generates custom events within XSOAR.

Next, we navigate to Settings → Integrations → Sample Incident Generator → Add Instance and configure the instance as follows:

  • Name: JSONSampleIncidentGenerator_url_events.
  • Do not fetch.
  • The raw JSON string to use as the sample data: paste the content from this GitHub repository.

We click Test, then Save & Exit.

If we do not see the integration, we refresh the browser.

docs.title: Configuring Incident Classification in Cortex XSOAR
docs.text: 19 August 2024

docs.title: Configuring Incident Classification in Cortex XSOAR
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cortex-xsoar incident-management palo-alto-networks

In this post, we set up the classification feature, which transforms events into specific incident types. This guide expands on the content of the videos XSOAR Engineer Training - Part 2: Incident Types & Fields and XSOAR Engineer Training - Part 3: Classification and Mapping.

docs.title: Set Up Incident Classifier
docs.text:
We navigate to Settings → Objects Setup → Classification & Mapping → New Incident Classifier. At the top, we select the JSONSampleIncidentGenerator_url_events instance we created in the previous post, so we can work with the sample events.

On the right, we see a list of the existing incident types in XSOAR:

A PAN-OS URL Log Incident type already exists, but our events do not originate from PAN-OS, so we create a new incident type specific to the data we are analyzing.

We go to Settings → Objects Setup → Incidents → Types and select PAN-OS URL Log Incident. With the Detach button, we can modify the object and explore its structure. After making our changes, we click Reattach to restore the original state.

docs.title: Create a New Incident Type
docs.text:
We create a new incident type with the following settings:

  • Name: URL Alerts.
  • Run playbook automatically: set (best practice).
  • Post process using: unset (script executed before closing the incident).

Now we define the fields that need to be populated. We go to Indicators Extraction Rules and check whether a field for URL categories exists. If it does not, we save and exit.

docs.title: Create Custom Fields
docs.text:
We go to Settings → Objects Setup → Incidents → Incidents Fields and create two new custom fields:

  • URL Category: Short text.
  • Suspicious URL: Short text.

We chose not to use the URL type because it would make the field clickable, which is not desirable for suspicious URLs: they should be treated as plain text.

docs.title: Define Indicator Extraction Rules
docs.text:
We return to Settings → Objects Setup → Incidents → Types → URL Alerts → Edit → Indicators Extraction Rules. These rules define how indicators are extracted from each event and used to populate the incident. Indicator extraction can be:

  • Inline: playbooks run after the indicator extraction is complete (blocking).
  • Out of Band: indicator extraction and playbook execution run in parallel (non-blocking).
  • None: no indicator extraction.

Best practices suggest using None when possible, and Inline when the playbook depends on the indicators.

We add the following fields:

  • Suspicious URL: add URL and Domain.
  • Source IP: add IP.
  • Source Username: add Email.

This way, the three fields generate the associated indicators: URL, Domain, IP and Email.

docs.title: Finalize the Classifier
docs.text:
We go back to Settings → Objects Setup → Classification & Mapping → New Incident Classifier and select the JSONSampleIncidentGenerator_url_events instance.

When we select a sample event in the type field, we see options like url allowed and url blocked. We drag these two values to the right column, under the URL Alerts incident type. This categorizes all the url allowed and url blocked incidents as URL Alerts.

At the bottom, we can choose how to classify the events that do not fall into these categories. In our case it is unnecessary, but we select URL Alerts anyway.

We save the classifier as URLAlertClassifier.

docs.title: Configure the Sample Incident Generator
docs.text:
We go to Settings → Integrations → Sample Incident Generator → ⚙️ and configure:

  • Fetches incidents.
  • Classifier: URLAlertClassifier.
  • Incidents Fetch Interval: 00:01 (the events from the JSON are generated every minute).

After a few minutes, we stop the fetching (Do not fetch) and go to Incidents:

The events are categorized as URL Alerts, but the indicators are not extracted correctly.

We delete all the incidents and move on to the next step.

docs.title: Introduction to Palo Alto firewall automation
Introduction to Palo Alto firewall automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner firewall fundamentals palo-alto-networks

Firewall automation is still a relatively under-discussed topic compared to the automation of network devices. This is likely due to complexity: firewall policies tend to be a long list of rules, created by different people for different (application) purposes and aggregated together. The order of the rules is often crucial and has a direct impact on performance, so creating a model to describe them is far from simple. Other tasks can be automated, but in my experience they are of relatively minor importance.

Let's take a step back and identify the activities a security engineer performs throughout the lifecycle of a firewall:

  • Provisioning: one-time or occasional tasks that configure the foundation of a firewall (IP addressing, routing, VLANs, DNS, NTP, licenses, etc.).
  • Rules: tasks that add, modify or delete rules in response to changes in the services that pass through one or more firewalls.
  • Maintenance: tasks that monitor the status of a firewall or troubleshoot anomalies and unexpected behaviors.

On Palo Alto Networks firewalls, we can interact with the device in the following ways:

  • Web User Interface.
  • Command Line Interface (CLI) via SSH.
  • XML API.
  • External Dynamic Lists.
  • SDKs (Python, PHP).
  • Frameworks (Ansible, Terraform).
  • Direct configuration changes.

In complex environments, Panorama is often used to manage all the firewalls centrally. We can interact with Panorama in all the same ways described for individual firewalls.

Except for the Web User Interface, all the other interfaces enable the creation of automations and integrations.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via CLI
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via CLI
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner firewall netmiko palo-alto-networks

The first method we discuss is screen scraping, a topic already covered in previous posts. We use screen scraping to automate devices that are designed to be managed via CLI and have no APIs that cover all the scenarios we are interested in. It is commonly used with network devices.

As we will see, Palo Alto Networks firewalls offer XML-based APIs that make screen scraping less attractive, except in very specific cases.

On Palo Alto Networks firewalls, screen scraping can be useful to perform specific monitoring and troubleshooting actions.

Let's look at a couple of examples.

The first example is a request from a client several years ago. The client wanted a device locator that identifies the location of a device based on its MAC address or IP address. We needed to gather the MAC address table and the ARP table from all the devices. For the ARP table, we retrieved the output of the show arp all command and converted it into a machine-readable format (parsing): this is screen scraping.

We use two tools:

  • netmiko to connect to the devices, execute the command and collect the output.
  • NTC Templates to transform the output into JSON.

The sample script is quite simple:

  • It defines the data needed to connect to the device.
  • It defines the command to execute.
  • It connects to the device, sends the command and uses NTC Templates to structure the output.
device = {
    "device_type": "paloalto_panos",
    "ip": "172.25.10.4",
    "username": "admin",
    "password": getpass(),
    "fast_cli": False,
}
net_connect = ConnectHandler(**device)
result = net_connect.send_command("show arp all", use_textfsm=True)

Netmiko offers a wide range of connectors to manage different devices. The device must specify a type that combines the vendor and the operating system. The full list is available in the GitHub source. In our case, we selected paloalto_panos.

Generally, we do not need to specify additional options, but there still seems to be a bug in prompt recognition. With screen scraping, it is normal to run into anomalies caused by the interpretation of the output.

Finally, we use NTC Templates to transform the text into JSON. We can use NTC Templates by installing the Python package:

pip install ntc-templates

Or by using a local repository and setting the NET_TEXTFSM environment variable:

export NET_TEXTFSM=/Users/dainese/src/ntc-templates/ntc_templates/templates

The output of the script is as follows:

In this specific case, the output was added to a database, which, through a web interface, let the user find the location of a specific MAC address.

The script is available on GitHub.

docs.title: Configuration Commands with Netmiko
docs.text:
We can use Netmiko for some basic configurations. For example, we can remove the default configuration or add basic settings (NTP, DNS, etc.). Netmiko may be simpler to implement and maintain than a full Python script.

Let's look at a simple script that deletes the default configuration:

commands = [
    'delete rulebase security rules "rule1"',
    "delete network virtual-wire default-vwire",
    "delete zone trust network virtual-wire",
    "delete zone untrust network virtual-wire",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 virtual-wire",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 virtual-wire",
    "delete zone trust",
    "delete zone untrust",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/1",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/2",
    "commit",
]
net_connect = ConnectHandler(**device)
net_connect.send_config_set(commands)
net_connect.disconnect()

The script is available on GitHub.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via XML API
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via XML API
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced api firewall palo-alto-networks

Palo Alto Networks firewalls provide XML-based APIs to interact with the system. To use the API, the first step is to generate an API key that authenticates our requests:

curl -k -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -X POST https://firewall/api/?type=keygen -d 'user=admin&password=password'

Alternatively, we can use a simple Python script:

headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
}
data = {
    "user": "admin",
    "password": getpass(),
}
url = "https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=keygen"
req = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=data, verify=False)

At this point, we can use the XML API to perform any operation normally executed via the web interface or the CLI. We must pass the token as a GET parameter in every API request. The documentation is available directly on the firewall at https://172.25.10.4/php/rest/browse.php.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Operational Commands via XML API
docs.text:
Let's revisit the example of the previous post and retrieve the ARP table. The documentation provides the XML call to execute: https://172.25.10.4/php/rest/browse.php/op::show::arp.

The script is straightforward:

headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
}
url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=op&cmd=<show><arp><entry name = 'all'/></arp></show>&key="
url = url + getpass()
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
req.raise_for_status()

The output is the ARP table in XML format:

<response status="success"><result>
  <dp>dp0</dp>
  <timeout>1800</timeout>
  <total>13</total>
