  <entries>
    <entry>
      <interface>ethernet1/1.581</interface>
      <ip>172.25.81.254</ip>
      <mac>fc:10:1a:ce:e3:12</mac>
      <port>ethernet1/1</port>
      <status>  c  </status>
      <ttl>916</ttl>
    </entry>
    <entry>
      <interface>ethernet1/1.100</interface>
      <ip>172.26.100.11</ip>
      <mac>00:50:56:9d:4b:0b</mac>
      <port>ethernet1/1</port>
      <status>  c  </status>
      <ttl>877</ttl>
    </entry>

XML is not the most Python-friendly format. The official documentation warns about various risks:

We can, however, treat the XML output of the firewall as trusted and proceed with the ElementTree library.

Compared to JSON, navigating XML requires more experience. The example below shows how to extract data from the XML response returned by the firewall:

root = ET.fromstring(req.text)
for entry in root.iterfind(".//result/entries/"):
    interface = entry.find('interface').text
    ip = entry.find('ip').text
    mac = entry.find('mac').text
    print(f"{interface},{ip},{mac}")

The output of the script is similar to the following:

ethernet1/1.581,172.25.81.254,fc:10:1a:ce:e3:12
ethernet1/1.100,172.26.100.11,00:50:56:9d:4b:0b
ethernet1/1.101,172.26.101.11,00:50:56:9d:1e:d1
vlan.104,172.26.104.11,00:50:56:9d:fb:39
vlan.104,172.26.104.12,00:50:56:9d:e3:96
vlan.104,172.26.104.21,00:50:56:9d:90:e2
vlan.104,172.26.104.22,00:50:56:9d:8a:13
vlan.104,172.26.104.31,00:50:56:9d:d6:b7
vlan.104,172.26.104.32,00:50:56:9d:a3:60
vlan.104,172.26.104.33,00:50:56:9d:1c:ea
vlan.104,172.26.104.34,00:50:56:9d:cd:11
vlan.104,172.26.104.41,00:50:56:9d:8f:7e
vlan.104,172.26.104.42,00:50:56:9d:47:26

Following the documentation, we can also explore the show interface command:

The payload to retrieve all the interfaces is:

<show><interface>all</interface></show>

Note the syntax difference compared to the show arp command.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via XML API
docs.text:
Palo Alto Networks firewalls can be configured via either the XML API or the REST API. The documentation is available directly on the firewall at https://172.25.10.4/php/rest/browse.php/config.

As an example, let's configure the two DNS servers of Google on the firewall. The documentation is somewhat limited:

If we expand our research, we find working examples that guide the creation of the script:

# xpath = "/config/shared/address/entry" # Shared (Panorama)
xpath = "/config/devices/entry[@name='localhost.localdomain']/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address/entry"

# Create elements
for name, ip in addresses.items():
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=config&action=set&xpath={xpath}"
    url = url + f"[@name='{name}']&element=<ip-netmask>{ip}</ip-netmask>"
    url = url + f"&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()

Key points:

  • The URL must include the path that specifies whether the object is created under shared or within vsys1.
  • The payload is sent via GET together with the required parameters: attributes are marked with @, and the XML content is passed in the element variable.
  • The token is provided via the key parameter.
  • In case of malformed payloads or attributes, the HTTP status is always 200 and the error is contained in the response body:
<response status="error" code="13"><msg><line>set failed, may need to override template object first</line></msg></response>

Similarly, we can retrieve the configured objects:

xpaths = [
    "/config/shared/address/entry", # Shared (Panorama)
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address", # VSYS
]
for xpath in xpaths:
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=config&action=get&xpath={xpath}&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()
    root = ET.fromstring(req.text)
    for entry in root.iterfind(find_path):
        name = entry.attrib["name"]
        address = entry.find("ip-netmask").text
        print(f"{name},{address}")

Note that the paths for shared and vsys differ from those used to create the objects.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Commit via XML API
docs.text:
After modifying the configuration of the firewall, we need a commit operation, which consists of:

  • Executing the commit.
  • Retrieving the job ID.
  • Waiting for the job to complete.
  • Verifying the result of the job.

We use the XML API to automate the entire process. Note that the REST APIs currently do not support this operation:

url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=commit&cmd=<commit></commit>&key={token}"
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
req.raise_for_status()

The response includes the job ID:

job = root.find("./result/job")
job_id = None
if job is not None:
    # msg = root.find("./result/msg")
    job_id = job.text
else:
    msg = root.find("./msg")

We then wait for the job to complete:

while progress < 100:
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=op&cmd=<show><jobs><id>{job_id}</id></jobs></show>&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()
    root = ET.fromstring(req.text)
    result_el = root.find("./result/job/result")
    if result_el is not None:
        result = result_el.text
    progress = int(root.find("./result/job/progress").text)
    print(f"Job ID {job_id}: {progress}%")
    time.sleep(5)

The final result should be OK.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via XML API
docs.text:
Let's now see how to delete the default configuration with the XML API. As a reminder, the documentation is hosted locally on the firewall at https://172.24.1.34/php/rest/browse.php.

As noted before, the documentation is minimal:

Further searches do not help much, because the task is quite specific. Before scripting, we must understand the structure of the XML-based API better.

Let's export and analyze the configuration of the firewall:

      <vsys>
        <entry name="vsys1">
          <application/>
          <application-group/>
          <zone>
            <entry name="trust">
              <network>
                <virtual-wire>
                  <member>ethernet1/1</member>
                </virtual-wire>
              </network>
            </entry>
            <entry name="untrust">
              <network>
                <virtual-wire>
                  <member>ethernet1/2</member>
                </virtual-wire>
              </network>
            </entry>
          </zone>

XML represents a hierarchical structure. In this example, vsys contains child elements such as application, application-group and zone. zone, in turn, contains two child elements that represent the security zones. In an XML document, we can reference elements with XPath. For the specifics, see the official Palo Alto Networks documentation.

Two concepts are important:

  • Attributes: defined within the element as parameters. For example, vsys/entry includes the attribute name=vsys1. We reference attributes with the @ symbol.
  • Values: the text content of the elements. For example, the member element in the first zone has the value ethernet1/1.

We must define the full paths of the elements to delete. By analyzing the configuration, we can extract the complete list:

xpaths = [
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='rule1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/virtual-wire/entry[@name='default-vwire']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='trust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='untrust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/2']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/2']",
]

Unlike the CLI method, we need two operations for the import path: we must remove the interfaces from the import section before deleting them.

Finally, when we select the devices/entry path, we do not specify localhost.localdomain explicitly. Our environment contains only one entry, so this is acceptable: the element is unique.

The complete script is as follows:

# Defining paths
xpaths = [
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='rule1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/virtual-wire/entry[@name='default-vwire']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='trust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='untrust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/2']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/2']",
]
# Deleting objects
for xpath in xpaths:
    url = f"https://172.24.1.34/api/?type=config&action=delete&xpath={xpath}&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    # req.raise_for_status()

Note that, for XML API calls, the HTTP status code is always 200. The actual result is contained in the response payload. If the call succeeds, the response is:

<response status="success" code="20"><msg>command succeeded</msg></response>

If the element does not exist:

<response status="success" code="7"><msg>Object doesn't exist</msg></response>

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Finding the Correct Command
docs.text:
As we have seen, the XML API documentation is not very comprehensive. A recurring issue is identifying the correct syntax to execute a command. A very simple method converts a CLI command into its XML equivalent. Let's see how to do it with the command that displays the ARP table:

We used the following commands:

  • debug cli on: enables the translation of each CLI command into its XML equivalent.
  • set cli op-command-xml-output on: shows the output of operational commands in XML format.

There is also a third command:

  • set cli config-output-format xml: shows the configuration in XML format instead of the traditional set format.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via REST API
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via REST API
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced api firewall palo-alto-networks

Palo Alto Networks firewalls were originally designed around XML APIs. The JSON-based REST APIs were introduced later, so their implementation is currently incomplete and, as we will see, prone to certain errors. As noted earlier, the API documentation is available directly on the firewall at https://172.25.10.4/restapi-doc.

My recommendation is to use the REST API only for specific, well-tested tasks. In all other cases, it is preferable to rely on the XML API.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via REST API
docs.text:
Currently, we can use the REST APIs only for configuration tasks. All the other operations, including the commit, must still be performed with the XML API.

Let's take the same example of the previous section and create the two DNS servers of Google on the firewall. The REST API documentation is more comprehensive, but it is sometimes incomplete and not always easy to interpret:

If we use the API without reading the documentation carefully, we receive the following error:

{"code":3,"message":"Missing Query Parameter: name","details":[{"@type":"CauseInfo","causes":[{"code":7,"module":"pan_api","description":"Missing Query Parameter: name"}]}]}

Here is a working example:

# Create elements
for name, ip in addresses.items():
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/restapi/v10.2/Objects/Addresses?name={name}&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1"
    data = {
        "entry": {
            "@name": name,
            "ip-netmask": ip,
        },
    }
    req = requests.post(url, json=data, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()

The documentation lists the query parameters, but the examples often omit them. In particular:

  • The URL must include both the name and location parameters. If the location is vsys, we must also specify the vsys name.
  • The payload is sent via a POST request together with the required parameters. Its structure is similar to the XML example shown earlier.
  • The token is passed in the X-PAN-KEY header.
  • If the payload or the parameters are incorrect, the HTTP status code is 400.

We also note a redundancy: the name parameter is used in both the URL and the request body.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via REST API
docs.text:
Let's now remove the default configuration with the REST API. The script is relatively simple, but we first need to identify the appropriate API endpoints. The documentation is available locally on the firewall at https://172.24.1.34/restapi-doc/.

These are the APIs to call with the DELETE method:

urls = [
    f"{base_url}/Policies/SecurityRules?name=rule1&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/VirtualWires?name=default-vwire",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=trust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=untrust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/1", # Validation error
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/2", # Validation error
]

Finding the correct API for the zone deletion took some time, because it is not documented. The last two API calls generate an error that does not occur in the web interface:

{"code":9,"message":"Reference Not Zero","details":[{"@type":"CauseInfo","causes":[{"code":10,"module":"panui_mgmt","description":"Reference Not Zero: ethernet1\/1 cannot be deleted because of references from:. import -> network -> interface. import -> network -> interface. import -> network -> interface. import -> network -> interface."}]}]}

As a result, the script lacks part of the logic compared to what we do via CLI or the web interface. This happens because the REST APIs are effectively a wrapper over the XML API, and this layer still has limitations and bugs. The final script remains simple nonetheless:

# Defining API
base_url = "https://172.24.1.34/restapi/v10.2"
urls = [
    f"{base_url}/Policies/SecurityRules?name=rule1&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/VirtualWires?name=default-vwire",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=trust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=untrust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/1", # Validation error
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/2", # Validation error
]
# Deleting objects
for url in urls:
    req = requests.delete(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    # req.raise_for_status()

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN-OS SDK
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN-OS SDK
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced firewall palo-alto-networks

In previous posts, we explored how to automate some operations on Palo Alto Networks firewalls by using the XML API and the REST API directly. According to the official documentation, ready-to-use libraries are available for several programming languages (PHP, Go, Python).

I believe Python is the most suitable language to write automations and integrations, so we focus on the Python SDKs. Two libraries are available:

  • pan-python: developed and maintained personally by Kevin Steves. It allows low-level operations on PAN-OS systems.
  • pan-os-python: developed and maintained officially by Palo Alto Networks. It enables high-level interaction with firewalls and Panorama, similar to the CLI or the Web interface. It depends on specific versions of pan-python and is not compatible with the latest one.

The documentation is available online, and the relationships between the APIs are described through diagrams.

On some systems, we may encounter the following error:

from distutils.version import LooseVersion # Used by PanOSVersion class ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'distutils'

In this case, we need to install a specific version of setuptools:

pip install 'setuptools>=75.1.0'

The library organizes its methods into the following modules:

  • base
  • device
  • errors
  • firewall
  • ha
  • network
  • objects
  • panorama
  • plugins
  • policies
  • predefined
  • updater
  • userid

docs.title: Operational Commands via pan-os-python
docs.text:
Let's revisit the previous example and print the ARP table. According to the documentation, we can use the same syntax as the CLI:

Doing so, however, results in the following error:

panos.errors.PanDeviceXapiError: show -> arp -> all has unexpected text. show -> arp is unexpected show is unexpected

On closer inspection, we learn that the library translates the CLI syntax into XML. This translation is not available for all the commands, and in such cases we must use the XML format:

As shown earlier, we can translate commands from the CLI format to the XML format with debug cli on.

At this point, the script becomes almost identical to the one shown earlier:

token = getpass("Token: ")
fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Getting elements
root = fw.op("<show><arp><entry name='all'/></arp></show>", cmd_xml=False)
for entry in root.iterfind(".//result/entries/"):
    interface = entry.find("interface").text
    ip = entry.find("ip").text
    mac = entry.find("mac").text
    print(f"{interface},{ip},{mac}")

The library returns an ElementTree object, which we can handle as discussed before.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via pan-os-python
docs.text:
Modifying the configuration of the firewall via SDK becomes simpler once we understand how the library works. Here is an example:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Create elements
for name, ip in addresses.items():
    fw.add(AddressObject(name=name, value=ip, type="ip-netmask")).create()

First, the Firewall class defines the access parameters. It does not perform any action itself: it only defines the configuration to access the firewall.

Then the AddressObject class manages the objects of type Address. In the example, we create two ip-netmask objects that contain the addresses of the DNS servers of Google. The script updates the configuration but does not commit the changes.

Similarly, we can read the configured objects:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Getting configured elements
for entry in AddressObject.refreshall(fw):
    name = entry.name
    address = entry.value
    location = entry.vsys
    print(f"{name},{address},{location}")

In this case, the refreshall method retrieves the configuration from the firewall and returns the Address objects section.

The scripts are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Commit via pan-os-python
docs.text:
The Firewall class includes a convenient method to commit the changes. As discussed before, the commit is an asynchronous job: we must wait for its completion and verify the exit code:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Commit
job_id = fw.commit()
if job_id:
    result = fw.syncjob(job_id)
    if not result["success"]:
        print("ERROR: failed to commit.")

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via pan-os-python
docs.text:
Finally, let's see how to delete the default configuration with the pan-os-python library. With the previous examples, we now understand how the library works. The challenge is identifying the appropriate classes for the different object types:

  • SecurityRule (child of Rulebase).
  • VirtualWire.
  • Zone.
  • EthernetInterface.

Once we identify the correct classes, the script becomes straightforward:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Delete default rule
rulebase = Rulebase.refreshall(fw)
for rule in SecurityRule.refreshall(rulebase):
    if rule.name == "rule1":
        rule.delete()

# Delete default vwire
for vwire in VirtualWire.refreshall(fw):
    if vwire.name == "default-vwire":
        vwire.delete()

# Delete default zones
for zone in Zone.refreshall(fw):
    if zone.name in ["trust", "untrust"]:
        zone.delete()

# Delete default interfaces
for intf in EthernetInterface.refreshall(fw):
    if intf.name in ["ethernet1/1", "ethernet1/2"]:
        intf.delete()

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN SDK
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN SDK
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced firewall palo-alto-networks

In the previous post, we explored the official pan-os-python library maintained by Palo Alto Networks. We also noted that this library builds on the personal work of Kevin Steves, who developed the pan-python library for low-level operations on PAN-OS systems. Kevin also included several command-line tools to perform operations via CLI instead of Python.

The documentation is available online in reStructuredText format. The following modules are supported:

  • pan.afapi: provides CLI access to AutoFocus via panafapi.
  • pan.licapi: manages PAN-OS licenses via CLI with panlicapi.
  • pan.wfapi: interfaces with WildFire via CLI with panwfapi.
  • pan.xapi: enables operations via the XML API, accessible via CLI with panconf and panxapi.

As the examples show, the PAN SDK is essentially an interface to the XML API, with some added conveniences. The examples that follow resemble those of the XML API post.

The PAN SDK relies on the ElementTree module of Python, whose documentation reminds us:

A large number of log entries can cause a memory exception which may not be possible to catch.

docs.title: Operational Commands via pan-python
docs.text:
Let's revisit a previous example and print the ARP table. The documentation is minimal and has no examples. First, we create an api object with the connection details of the firewall:

ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
ctx.check_hostname = False
ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
fw = xapi.PanXapi(hostname="172.24.1.34", api_key=token, ssl_context=ctx)

We can now issue a command to print the ARP table:

fw.op(cmd="<show><arp><entry name='all'/></arp></show>", cmd_xml=False)
root = fw.element_root
for entry in root.iterfind(".//result/entries/"):
    interface = entry.find("interface").text
    ip = entry.find("ip").text
    mac = entry.find("mac").text
    print(f"{interface},{ip},{mac}")

The command syntax is identical to the one covered in the XML API post.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via pan-python
docs.text:
Let's now see how to add objects to the configuration of the firewall. According to the documentation, the supported methods include set(), get(), edit(), delete(), move(), rename() and clone().

As discussed before, this example also follows the XML API syntax:

for name, ip in addresses.items():
    # xpath = "/config/shared/address/entry" # Shared (Panorama)
    xpath = "/config/devices/entry[@name='localhost.localdomain']/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address/entry" # VSYS
    xpath = xpath + f"[@name='{name}']"
    element = f"<ip-netmask>{ip}</ip-netmask>"
    fw.set(xpath=xpath, element=element)

We can print the configured addresses in a similar way:

xpaths = [
    "/config/shared/address/entry", # Shared (Panorama)
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address", # VSYS
]
for xpath in xpaths:
    if "/shared/" in xpath:
        location = "Shared"
        find_path = ".//result/"
    else:
        location = "VSYS"
        find_path = ".//result/address/"

    fw.get(xpath=xpath)
    root = fw.element_root
    for entry in root.iterfind(find_path):
        name = entry.attrib["name"]
        address = entry.find("ip-netmask").text
        print(f"{name},{address},{location}")

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Commit via pan-python
docs.text:
The xapi class includes the commit() method, which manages the commit operation and the associated job:

cmd = "<commit></commit>"
fw.commit(cmd=cmd, sync=True)
if "no changes to commit" in fw.status_detail:
    pass
elif fw.status != "success" or "successfully" not in fw.status_detail:
    print("ERROR: failed to commit.")

The code is not particularly clean, because it checks both the status of the job and its textual description. As an alternative, we can use an asynchronous commit together with the job() method to verify the status manually:

cmd = "<commit></commit>"
fw.commit(cmd=cmd, sync=False)
root = fw.element_root
job = root.find("./result/job")
job_id = None
if job is not None:
    # msg = root.find("./result/msg")
    job_id = job.text
else:
    msg = root.find("./msg")

# Wait for job
if job_id:
    progress = 0
    result = None
    while progress < 100:
        fw.op(cmd=f"<show><jobs><id>{job_id}</id></jobs></show>", cmd_xml=False)
        root = fw.element_root
        result_el = root.find("./result/job/result")
        if result_el is not None:
            result = result_el.text
        progress = int(root.find("./result/job/progress").text)
        print(f"Job ID {job_id}: {progress}%")
        time.sleep(5)

    if result != "OK":
        print("ERROR: failed to commit.")

This example is similar to the one covered with the XML API.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via pan-python
docs.text:
Finally, let's see how to remove the default configuration with the pan-python library. The previous examples showed the similarities between the XML API and pan-python:

token = getpass("Token: ")
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
ctx.check_hostname = False
ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
fw = xapi.PanXapi(hostname="172.24.1.34", api_key=token, ssl_context=ctx)

# Defining paths
xpaths = [
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='rule1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/virtual-wire/entry[@name='default-vwire']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='trust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='untrust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/2']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/2']",
]
for xpath in xpaths:
    fw.delete(xpath=xpath)

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating operations with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 31 August 2025

docs.title: Automating operations with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner palo-alto-networks scm

The management of Palo Alto Networks firewalls is gradually shifting from traditional on-premises administration, either directly or via Panorama, to a cloud-based model. The product that enables centralized, cloud-based management of Palo Alto Networks firewall infrastructures is Strata Cloud Manager (SCM).

This management paradigm introduces several fundamental changes:

  • Data format: Panorama is XML-based, while SCM uses JSON.
  • Configuration model: Panorama relies on Device Groups, Templates and Template Stacks. SCM uses configuration scopes, where snippets are reusable scopes that we can apply to folders or devices.
  • Variables: variables exist in Panorama but with a limited scope. SCM extends them and allows their use even within security policies.

The approach to structuring complex infrastructures changes significantly. Our focus here is not the design of the architecture, but the creation of automation that makes migrations and ongoing operations more efficient.

We do not cover how to work manually within SCM. We explore how to interact with SCM through its API.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
There is no official CLI for SCM. Calvin Remsburg, however, developed a personal CLI module and an accompanying SDK that enable command-line management.

The project is worth reviewing, but several caveats apply:

  • It is a personal project, not an official tool.
  • It does not cover all the operational scenarios.
  • It can be complex to use.
  • It was developed with Claude by Anthropic.

In my view, SCM-CLI can help to automate some tasks. I prefer, however, to use official tools or build my own, so that I can maintain them freely. The reason is simple: when we work with APIs or SDKs, bugs are common, and we need either vendor support or full control to implement workarounds.

docs.title: Ansible
docs.text: Calvin Remsburg also developed an Ansible module, built on pan-scm-sdk. The same considerations as for the CLI apply here.

docs.title: Terraform
docs.text:
Palo Alto Networks released an official Terraform provider, but it comes with no guarantees: the software is provided as is. The current version (0.11.0) indicates that the provider is still considered unstable.

The associated GitHub repository shows active development, but many features are still missing.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Before writing any code, we need to understand the ecosystem and its complexity.

SCM is a web-based application that builds its interface through multiple API calls:

Inspecting the application with the browser developer tools shows that the web interface does not always use the same APIs exposed to developers. For instance, the network activity of the interface shows no calls to /config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces.

In some cases, such as the view of the interface details, we can identify the specific API calls that populate the page. As we will see, however, the web UI uses a different backend API system, which makes it largely irrelevant for automation.

When we automate SCM, we must therefore rely entirely on the official API documentation. From experience, this increases complexity and development time significantly because:

  • The documentation is never fully complete.
  • The documentation is rarely up to date.
  • Examples for specific use cases are often missing.
  • We need iterative testing to develop reliable automations.

docs.title: Recommended Approach
docs.text:
Ideally, web applications follow an API-first design, where the UI consumes the same APIs available to developers. This ensures consistency and reduces the complexity of automation.

With SCM, a hybrid approach is often necessary:

  • Rely on the official documentation despite its limitations.
  • Use the web UI and the APIs in parallel, to understand the exact impact of each operation and the structure of the objects involved.

docs.title: Authenticating to the Strata Cloud Manager API
docs.text: 07 September 2025

docs.title: Authenticating to the Strata Cloud Manager API
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese api beginner palo-alto-networks scm

According to the official documentation, before making any API call we must obtain an access token with our username, password and tenant service group.

We can then use the token to authorize the subsequent API requests.

http_username = f"{username}@{tenant_id}.iam.panserviceaccount.com"
basic_auth = HTTPBasicAuth(http_username, password)
data = {
    "grant_type": "client_credentials",
    "scope": f"tsg_id:{tenant_id}",
}
url = "https://auth.apps.paloaltonetworks.com/oauth2/access_token"
req = requests.post(url, auth=basic_auth, headers=headers, data=data)
req.raise_for_status()
token = req.json()["access_token"]

Together with the token, the API returns its validity period, 900 seconds (15 minutes), which we must take into account when designing automations.

The token is a JSON Web Token (JWT), a standardized, encoded JSON object. By decoding it, we can inspect the claims and the metadata it contains:

docs.title: Example: Retrieving the List of Registered Devices
docs.text:
As a first example, let's retrieve the list of the devices registered in SCM.

From the API documentation homepage, we use the search bar to locate the relevant endpoint:

As shown earlier, the first step is to authenticate and generate a token valid for 15 minutes:

# Get token
headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
}
http_username = f"{username}@{tenant_id}.iam.panserviceaccount.com"
basic_auth = HTTPBasicAuth(http_username, password)
data = {
    "grant_type": "client_credentials",
    "scope": f"tsg_id:{tenant_id}",
}
url = "https://auth.apps.paloaltonetworks.com/oauth2/access_token"
req = requests.post(url, auth=basic_auth, headers=headers, data=data)
req.raise_for_status()
token = req.json()["access_token"]

Next, we use the list-devices API endpoint to retrieve the inventory:

# Get devices
headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"
}
req = requests.get("https://api.strata.paloaltonetworks.com/config/setup/v1/devices", headers=headers)
req.raise_for_status()
pprint(req.json())

The response contains the list of devices in JSON format:

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Optimizing Strata Cloud Manager API usage
docs.text: 14 September 2025

docs.title: Optimizing Strata Cloud Manager API usage
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced api palo-alto-networks scm

Before moving forward, let's review our current approach to invoking the API:

  • We use the requests library.
  • We must first generate an authentication token.
  • Many parameters are passed repeatedly in multiple calls.
  • We must verify whether the token has expired.

We can improve this workflow by creating a lightweight extension of the requests library.

The extension should handle the token management automatically, including the renewal when needed.

It is also useful to centralize the handling of headers and URLs, to keep the code clean and concise.

docs.title: Implementing a Custom API Client
docs.text:
To achieve this, we create a new class called APIClient:

class APIClient(requests.Session):
    """APIClient is a specialized HTTP client for interacting with the Palo Alto Networks API."""

    def __init__(self, tenant_id: int, username: str, password: str) -> None:
        """Initialize the APIClient and perform the first authentication."""

        # Initialize the parent requests.Session
        super().__init__()

        # Authentication endpoint for Palo Alto Networks
        self.auth_url = "https://auth.apps.paloaltonetworks.com/oauth2/access_token"

        # Store credentials and tenant information
        self.tenant_id = tenant_id
        self.username = username
        self.__password = password

        # Will hold the Bearer token once authenticated
        self.__token = None

        # Perform the initial authentication right away
        self.__authenticate()

The class must handle the following:

  • TSG ID (also called tenant ID).
  • Username.
  • Password.
  • Token, including the generation and renewal logic.

The authentication URL is always the same, so we can define it directly in the code.

When an APIClient object is initialized, the authentication process starts:

    def __authenticate(self) -> None:
        """Authenticate with the Palo Alto endpoint and store the Bearer token."""

        # Build HTTP Basic Auth
        basic_auth = HTTPBasicAuth(
            f"{self.username}@{self.tenant_id}.iam.panserviceaccount.com",
            self.__password,
        )

        # Headers for the token request
        headers = {
            "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
        }

        # Body parameters for client credentials grant
        data = {
            "grant_type": "client_credentials",
            "scope": f"tsg_id:{self.tenant_id}",
        }

        # Send the POST request to the auth server
        req = requests.post(self.auth_url, auth=basic_auth, headers=headers, data=data)
        req.raise_for_status()

        # Save the access token for later requests
        self.__token = req.json()["access_token"]

As seen earlier, the authentication method calls a specific API to obtain a token and stores it for later use.

docs.title: Overriding Requests for SCM
docs.text:
To integrate with SCM, we override the request method of our client and add the required logic:

    def request(self, method: str, url: str, **kwargs) -> Response:
        """Send an HTTP request with automatic Bearer token handling."""

        # Ensure the headers dictionary exists
        if "headers" not in kwargs:
            kwargs["headers"] = {}

        # Add Authorization header with the current Bearer token
        kwargs["headers"]["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self.__token}"

        # Accept JSON responses by default
        kwargs["headers"]["Accept"] = "application/json"

        # For POST/PUT requests, set Content-Type to application/json
        if method.lower() in ["post", "put"]:
            kwargs["headers"]["Content-Type"] = "application/json"

        # If the given URL is just a path, prefix it with the API base URL
        if url.startswith("/"):
            url = f"https://api.strata.paloaltonetworks.com{url}"

        # Execute the request
        req = super().request(method, url, **kwargs)

        # Retry once if token expired
        if req.status_code == 401 and req.json()["message"] == "Invalid Request Token.":
            # Token expired
            self.__authenticate()
            # Retry once
            kwargs["headers"]["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self.__token}"
            req = super().request(method, url, **kwargs)

        return req

The key logic is at the end:

  • The request is executed.
  • If the token has expired, the client authenticates again and retries the request.

docs.title: Additional Optimizations
docs.text:
This approach streamlines our work because it:

  • Injects the token into every request automatically.
  • Generates the headers dynamically and adapts them when we send payload data.
  • Builds the request URL with the FQDN if it is not already included.

With this improvement, we can rewrite the previous device-listing example with the new client:

client = APIClient(
    tenant_id=tenant_id,
    username=username,
    password=password,
)
req = client.get("/config/setup/v1/devices")
req.raise_for_status()
pprint(req.json())

The result: we cut the code roughly in half, which makes it cleaner and easier to maintain.

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Retrieving firewall interfaces with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 21 September 2025

docs.title: Retrieving firewall interfaces with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner firewall palo-alto-networks scm

Let's look at a second example that illustrates both the functionality and the complexity of the SCM APIs.

In this scenario, we want to retrieve the Ethernet interfaces of the firewalls. A quick search in the documentation leads us to the correct API endpoint.

With the custom class we created earlier, the code is straightforward:

# Get interfaces
req = client.get(f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces")
req.raise_for_status()
interfaces = req.json()
pprint(interfaces)

This, however, returns no results.

docs.title: Understanding API Parameters
docs.text:
The documentation shows that we can specify certain parameters, although they are not mandatory.

Logically, requesting a list of interfaces without specifying the target firewall is incomplete. It also makes sense to identify the firewall by its ID rather than its hostname, because hostnames can change.

If we adapt the code to request the interfaces of each device ID, we get:

# Get devices
req = client.get("/config/setup/v1/devices")
req.raise_for_status()
devices = req.json()

# For each device, get interfaces
for device in devices["data"]:
    device_id = device["id"]
    device_hostname = device["hostname"]

    req = client.get(f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces?device={device_id}")
    req.raise_for_status()
    interfaces = req.json()

docs.title: Final Output
docs.text:
With this change, the script works as expected and produces the following output:

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Modifying an object in Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 28 September 2025

docs.title: Modifying an object in Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate palo-alto-networks scm

This example is particularly relevant because it directly affects operational workflows.

Before diving into it, let's review the HTTP methods used in REST APIs. HTTP defines five default methods that map to the CRUD operations: Create, Read, Update, Delete:

  • GET: retrieve a resource.
  • POST: create a new resource.
  • DELETE: remove a resource.
  • PUT and PATCH: update an existing resource.

The difference between PUT and PATCH is crucial:

  • PATCH updates only the specified fields.
  • PUT replaces the entire resource with the provided fields.

docs.title: Example: Updating Interface Comments
docs.text:
As an example, let's modify the comment of the interfaces associated with a firewall.

Note that the SCM APIs implement only the PUT method: PATCH is not supported.

This means we cannot update a single attribute, such as the comment, on its own.

# Edit comment (WRONG)
interface_details = {
    "comment": f"{interface_name} managed via API ({api_timestamp})"
}
req = client.put(interface_url, json=interface_details)
req.raise_for_status()

If we set only the comment field with PUT, the interface is reset to its default settings and only the comment is preserved. This happens because PUT overwrites the resource entirely with the supplied data.

docs.title: Workaround for the Missing PATCH Method
docs.text:
Since PATCH is unavailable, the correct approach is to:

  • Retrieve the full interface structure with GET.
  • Modify the desired attribute (in this case, the comment).
  • Apply the updated structure back with PUT.
# Get interface details
interface_url = f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces/{interface_id}"
req = client.get(interface_url)
req.raise_for_status()
interface_details = req.json()

# Edit comment
interface_name = interface_details["name"]
interface_details["comment"] = f"{interface_name} managed via API ({api_timestamp})"
req = client.put(interface_url, json=interface_details)
req.raise_for_status()

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Creating an interface in Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 05 October 2025

docs.title: Creating an interface in Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner palo-alto-networks scm

Let's look at the last relevant example: creating a new interface.

To create an interface, we use the POST method and provide the correct data structure. The challenge is determining what that structure should look like.

Earlier, we decided to adopt a hybrid approach and use both the documentation and the web interface to develop our automations.

Following this method, we create an interface in the browser, retrieve its data structure via API and use it as a template.

{
    "comment": "$int-2 managed via API (8b7d5262)",
    "device": "023009004281",
    "id": "52ccaad7-ada5-42d4-b8e1-bd7305ba2abb",
    "layer3": {
        "adjust_tcp_mss": {
            "enable": false
        },
        "interface_management_profile": "mgmt-full",
        "ip": [
            {
                "name": "192.168.1.1/24"
            }
        ],
        "lldp": {
            "enable": false
        }
    },
    "link-duplex": "auto",
    "link-speed": "auto",
    "link-state": "auto",
    "name": "ethernet1/2"
}

Once we have the correct payload format, the code is straightforward:

data = {
    "name": interface_name,
    "comment": "Created via API",
    "link-speed": "auto",
    "link-duplex": "auto",
    "link-state": "auto",
    "layer3": {
        "interface_management_profile": interface["mgmt_profile"],
        "ip": [{"name": interface["address"]}],
        "lldp": {"enable": False},
    },
}
req = client.post(
    f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces?device={device_id}", json=data
)
req.raise_for_status()

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Networks firewalls
docs.text: 02 February 2022

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Networks firewalls
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible firewall palo-alto-networks

I spent a few Twitch sessions talking about the automation of Palo Alto Networks firewalls. We used approaches different from the ones we used with Cisco devices. At first, we developed a few simple Ansible playbooks. In the last sessions, we developed a very small Django web application to enable and disable network flows programmatically.

docs.title: Ansible with Palo Alto Networks Firewalls
docs.text:
The Palo Alto Networks module for Ansible has some prerequisites:

pip install pan-os-python pan-python pandevice xmltodict requests requests_toolbelt

Then we install the PAN-OS Ansible collection:

ansible-galaxy collection install paloaltonetworks.panos

The interpreter_python option in the ansible.cfg file must point to the interpreter that has the PAN-OS libraries installed. This is important when we use a virtual environment.

The firewall credentials are not passed in the standard way: we must pass a specific dictionary to each task. We populated the dictionary from the Ansible parameters as follows:

- set_fact:
    provider:
        ip_address: "{{ ansible_host }}"
        password: "{{ ansible_password }}"
        username: "{{ ansible_user }}"

docs.title: Getting Facts
docs.text:
The Palo Alto Networks module does not use the gather_facts parameter. It defines a custom task to retrieve the facts:

- paloaltonetworks.panos.panos_facts:
    provider: "{{ provider }}"

docs.title: Sending Operational Commands
docs.text:
The panos_op module sends commands to the firewall. The module translates the given command into XML and uses the XML API. Some commands can fail, so the best way is to specify the commands with the XML syntax. The following command fails:

cmd: 'show arp management' # Fails with "show -> arp has unexpected text."

The following command works:

cmd: "<show><arp><entry name='management'/></arp></show>"
cmd_is_xml: true

The API browser, available on the firewall at the /api URL, helps to find the right request. The API above is available at /php/rest/browse.php/op::show::arp.

We used panos_op to get the system info and the ARP table.

Because the operational commands are sent in XML format, the Ansible module converts the output to JSON automatically. Remember that XML can be converted to JSON/YAML and back, but XML attributes are usually lost in the process.

docs.title: Sending Configuration Commands
docs.text:
We wrote the fourth playbook to test the configuration commands. The Ansible module offers many configuration commands, but we limited ourselves to configuring some parameters of the management interface.

We also discussed how to "zero-touch provision" a Palo Alto Networks firewall. We did not test the scenario, but we agreed that we could write a working playbook.

docs.title: Configuration Templating
docs.text:
Configuration commands can manage many features of a firewall, but we tested a different approach: configuration templating. Because Palo Alto Networks firewalls have the commit feature, in my opinion this is the best approach.

The idea is:

  • Prepare a configuration template (Jinja2).
  • Build the firewall configuration from the template, using an external configuration file (the model).
  • Upload the firewall configuration file and enable it.

The fifth playbook implements this approach.

Pros and cons of this approach:

  • The entire firewall configuration can be stored in a CMDB file (pro).
  • The firewall configuration is always consistent (pro).
  • We can configure almost everything (pro).
  • We do not need to run checks before inserting a specific configuration in a running firewall (pro).
  • We need to spend a lot of time designing the firewall model (con).

docs.title: Programming the Firewall Using External Feeds
docs.text:
Many firewalls can read external feeds: we can use their content as a source or destination in access lists. This approach is perfect to allow temporary access. In the last session we created a small web application with Django.

The application provides feeds that contain IP addresses. Each IP address has an expiration date, and once it expires it is removed from the feed.

docs.title: Installing Django
docs.text:
We install Django in a Python environment (see S01E01):

pip install Django==4.0.1

docs.title: Creating the Django Application
docs.text:
We create the first Django project and an application within it:

django-admin startproject feedapp
cd feedapp
django-admin startapp edlprovider
./manage.py migrate

By default, the database is an SQLite file stored under the Django root folder. We must load the app in the settings.py file stored in the feedapp folder:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    "edlprovider",
]

We create the admin user:

./manage.py createsuperuser

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
In the simplest version of our application, we expect that:

  • An admin user adds one or more EDL objects (lists of IP addresses).
  • An admin user adds one or more IP addresses to an EDL object.
  • An expiration time can optionally be set on each IP address.
  • Unexpired IP addresses are available in a text list under a specific, non-guessable URL.

In other words, we have two objects:

  • EDL with ID, name and URL.
  • IP with name, expiration date (optional) and associated EDL.

When the model is complete, we update the migration scripts and upgrade the database schema:

./manage.py makemigrations
./manage.py migrate

docs.title: Admin Page
docs.text:
By default, Django provides an admin page for each model. We enable it by adding the following lines to the admin.py file:

admin.site.register(models.EDL)
admin.site.register(models.IPAddress)

We open the Django application at the /admin URL and add one EDL with at least one IP address.

docs.title: Printing EDLs
docs.text:
The view.py file serves custom HTTP requests. We need to print the content of each EDL when a GET request asks for the EDL ID (slug). The URL is defined in the rrapp/urls.py file.

All the IP addresses linked to a specific EDL are printed in text format if their expiration date is in the future.

docs.title: Starting the Server
docs.text:
In the settings.py file, we can configure Django to serve any client. This is an insecure configuration. We add * to ALLOWED_HOSTS:

ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']

We start the application:

./manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000

The Django application is now reachable. We use the /admin URL and log in with the superuser credentials created before.

docs.title: Using the EDL from a PANW Firewall
docs.text:
Once an EDL is populated, we can use it as a source or destination in ACLs.

We can debug an EDL with the following commands:

admin@fw> request system external-list stats type ip name EDL1
admin@fw> request system external-list show type ip name EDL1
admin@fw> request system external-list refresh type ip name EDL1

One last note: when an IP address is removed from an EDL, the session is not cleared. In other words, the established sessions are maintained and the new sessions are dropped.

A script should clear the sessions related to the expired IP addresses:

admin@fw> clear session all filter rule TestEDL1 destination 192.168.28.152

Also note that the firewall usually probes the URLs every 5 minutes, so the clear command should run 5 minutes after the expiration date. We should extend the web application to track the requests and whether the sessions have been cleared.
