docs.title: Introduction to MISP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner misp threat-intelligence

MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform) is an open-source software solution to collect, store, distribute and share cybersecurity indicators and threat intelligence related to incident analysis and malware analysis. It is designed for incident analysts, security professionals, ICT specialists and malware reverse engineers, to support their daily operations and share structured information efficiently.

MISP was launched in 2011 to manage Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in a structured way. It has since evolved and is now used by national CERTs and NATO, which gave the platform its name. Today, MISP is also used by organizations like ACN and by various entities that need structured IoC management.

MISP has also been used by the European Payments Council (EPC) to share timely information that helps prevent and intercept fraudulent activities in payment transactions. For further details, see the CIPA note.

docs.title: A Threat Intelligence Tool
docs.text:
Threat intelligence, or "threat intel", is actionable insight into current or emerging cybersecurity threats. It helps individuals and organizations understand past, present and future risks better.

Threat intelligence is more than IoC management. It can also provide insight into the motivations behind emerging threats, such as geopolitical tensions between nations. At a more granular level, it can involve specific data, such as the IP addresses associated with suspicious activities.

MISP supports threat intelligence activities with:

  • Complete management of IoCs (Indicators of Compromise).
  • A flexible and precise taxonomy system based on tags, which defines each piece of stored data (GitHub).
  • A variety of feeds available by default in any MISP installation.
  • Third-party tools and integrations that extend its functionality.
  • Open protocols and data structures.

docs.title: Automation-Oriented
docs.text:
MISP is designed to be integrated into automated or semi-supervised processes.

It provides complete APIs for custom integrations with third-party solutions, and PyMISP integrates MISP natively into Python projects.

We can export IoCs in multiple formats, including various native IDS formats, OpenIOC, plain text, CSV, MISP JSON, STIX (XML and JSON, versions 1 and 2), NIDS exports (Suricata, Snort and Bro/Zeek), RPZ zones and cache formats for forensic tools. We can add other formats, such as PDF, through misp-modules or custom built-in export modules.

docs.title: Installing MISP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner misp threat-intelligence

Installing MISP is relatively straightforward and well documented in the user guide. The user guide does not yet mention Ubuntu 24.04, although the installation script is available in the repository.

apt-get update
apt-get upgrade -y
wget -O /tmp/INSTALL.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MISP/MISP/refs/heads/2.5/INSTALL/INSTALL.ubuntu2404.sh
bash /tmp/INSTALL.sh

The installation starts and displays each step as it proceeds:

At the end, it shows the credentials to access the platform:

By default, the platform is accessible at https://misp.local. If the system is reachable through a different FQDN, we update the /var/www/MISP/app/Config/config.php file:

<?php
$config = array (
  'debug' => 0,
  'MISP' =>
  array (
    # 'baseurl' => 'https://misp.local',
    'baseurl' => 'https://172.24.1.18',

We also modify the /etc/apache2/sites-available/misp-ssl.conf file, which handles the HTTPS redirection:

<VirtualHost _default_:80>
    ServerAdmin admin@misp.local
    ServerName misp.local

    # Redirect permanent / https://misp.local
    Redirect permanent / https://172.24.1.18

    LogLevel warn
    ErrorLog /var/log/apache2/misp.local_error.log
    CustomLog /var/log/apache2/misp.local_access.log combined
    ServerSignature Off
</VirtualHost>

We reload the configuration:

apachectl graceful

Then we log in with the credentials displayed during the installation.

docs.title: Enabling Feeds
docs.text:
We can now enable one or more default feeds in MISP. We go to Sync Actions → Feeds:

We edit the feeds and enable them. When we return to the event list, we see the events imported from the feeds:

docs.title: Creating an Event
docs.text:
Next, let's create an event. We navigate to Event Actions → Add Event, using a spam email as the base:

When we create an event, the following parameters are required:

  • Distribution: the sharing level of the event. Your organization only (0), This community only (1), Connected communities (2), All communities (3), Sharing group (4), Inherit Event (5).
  • Analysis: the status of the threat analysis. Initial (0), Ongoing (1), Complete (2).
  • Threat level: High (1), Medium (2), Low (3), Undefined (4).

Once the event is created, we associate the attributes that best describe the threat. Since we are analyzing an email, we include:

  • The subject.
  • The IP address of the sending server.
  • The destination email address.
  • The source email address.
  • Any links contained in the email.
  • Any attachments found in the email.

When we create an attribute, the following parameters are required:

  • Category: the category of the attribute, which in this case is Payload delivery.
  • Type: the type of the attribute, chosen from a predefined list based on the best match.
  • Distribution: the sharing level of the attribute.

The final step is to tag the event and its attributes properly. Best practice is to tag the event itself, and to tag individual attributes only when strictly necessary. If an appropriate cluster exists, we can also use MISP Galaxy (GitHub).

We can also assign the appropriate TLP level. The TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) was created to support the proper sharing of sensitive information. TLP uses a series of labels that define who may share the information:

  • TLP:CLEAR: the information can be shared freely without restriction, subject to copyright or proprietary considerations.
  • TLP:GREEN: the information can be shared with peers and partner organizations, but not publicly.
  • TLP:AMBER: the information carries potential privacy, reputational or operational risk, and can be shared only within the organization of the recipient and its clients.
  • TLP:AMBER+STRICT: same as TLP:AMBER, but sharing is restricted to the organization of the recipient only.
  • TLP:RED: the information is highly sensitive and must not be shared beyond the original recipients.

When we complete these steps, the event looks like this:

docs.title: Integrating and automating MISP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner misp threat-intelligence

MISP is a platform for threat intelligence, not for incident management. It helps to manage Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in a structured way, so it must be integrated into an existing ecosystem.

TheHive is very often used as the incident management platform, but integration requests commonly involve also Splunk, Elastic, Maltego and detection and prevention systems (antispam, honeypot, firewall, etc.).

A MISP event does not represent a security incident: it represents a threat that we analyze and evaluate from a threat intelligence perspective. Much of the work (defining IoCs and artifacts) has likely already been done on other platforms. We evaluate the event and its IoCs to determine whether they add value for us and for the communities we belong to.

docs.title: Automating MISP Tasks
docs.text:
We can identify the following activities to automate:

  • Creating events by ingesting data from external sources (TheHive, honeypot, etc.).
  • Making the IoCs available to external platforms (firewalls, EDR, antispam, SIEMs, etc.).
  • Facilitating incident analysis by providing IoCs to external platforms (Maltego, TheHive, etc.).
  • Sending and receiving feedback on events (thumbs up = observed and malicious, thumbs down = observed but not malicious).

docs.title: API
docs.text:
MISP offers APIs in OpenAPI 3.0.0 format that allow programmatic interaction with the platform.

To use the API, we need an authentication key. We generate it under My Profile → Auth keys → Add authentication key:

We include the key in the Authorization header.

docs.title: PyMISP
docs.text:
Alternatively, we can use the Python library PyMISP, which allows native interaction with MISP in Python.

In my experience, PyMISP is more challenging to use than the native APIs. The documentation is not always clear, and for some tasks I had to reverse engineer the code.

docs.title: CIRCL
docs.text: CIRCL is the CERT for the private sector, municipalities and non-governmental organizations in Luxembourg. CIRCL is a very active contributor to MISP, and its website offers excellent MISP documentation.

docs.title: Consuming MISP IoCs from a Firewall
Consuming MISP IoCs from a Firewall
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese firewall intermediate misp threat-intelligence

Once our MISP instance is configured, it contains threat intelligence data that prevention tools such as firewalls and email gateways can use.

Let's see how to extract IoCs from MISP. Specifically, we create a list of IP addresses that perimeter systems block proactively.

Modern firewalls can ingest External Dynamic Lists (EDLs), which are text files, hosted on web servers, that contain lists of IP addresses. We can reference these lists in security policies to take specific actions.

The number of IP addresses that EDLs can manage might seem substantial, but the limits are relatively low compared to the global volume of IP-based IoCs.

This shows why we must manage IoCs in a structured way, with particular attention to their lifecycle.

docs.title: Native Export
docs.text:
MISP natively supports exporting attributes in multiple formats. Under Event Actions → Export, we can generate IoC lists in various formats:

Further down the page, we can immediately retrieve the lists of IoCs for a specific attribute type in plain text:

For instance, clicking ip-dst returns a file with all the ip-dst attributes marked as exportable for IDS purposes.

As discussed, however, the list might exceed the limits of our firewall. We therefore need more control over the export process.

docs.title: Export via API
docs.text:
By building our own IoC export mechanism, we gain control over the number, type, date and format of the indicators.

We want a list of all the IP-type IoCs, with a limited number of entries, and we want the most recent ones first. The request looks simple, but fulfilling it requires a robust lifecycle management of the IoCs, which is a non-trivial task. Consider, for example, an IP address related to a C2 server:

  • When can we consider it obsolete?
  • How do we define it as obsolete?
  • Can an obsolete IP become relevant again? How do we handle this case?

In this post, we assume that the lifecycle of the IoCs is already managed properly, and we focus only on the automation process.

Our goal is to generate a list of IP addresses (both ip-src and ip-dst), limit the total number and prioritize the most recent entries.

We use the restSearch API, which provides paginated lists of attributes based on the specified parameters.

The request is a POST with the following parameters:

data = {
    "controller": "attributes",
    "type": ["ip-src", "ip-dst"],
    "to_ids": True,
    "deleted": False,
    "timestamp": last_days_unix,
    "order": "timestamp desc",
    "limit": config["export"]["last_ioc"],
}
url = f"{config['misp']['url']}/attributes/restSearch"
req = requests.post(url, json=data, **params_post)
req.raise_for_status()

We then parse the output into a plain-text list of unique IP addresses:

for item in req.json()["response"]["Attribute"]:
    if item["value"] not in ip_list:
        ip_list.append(item["value"])
ioc_page = "\n".join(ip_list).encode("utf-8")

The full script is available in the GitHub repository. When we run it, it provides the IoC list in plain text via HTTP:

./get_ioc_to_edl_api.py

Most recent IoC:  Wed May 14 15:38:15 2025
Most old IoC:     Wed Nov 27 09:37:03 2024
Exporting 2549 IP addresses
Webserver started on port 8080
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:31:50] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:31:50] "GET /favicon.ico HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:32:01] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:32:01] "GET /favicon.ico HTTP/1.1" 200 -

Generating the list consumes time and computing resources of the MISP server. In production environments, it is advisable to update the list on an event-driven or scheduled basis and to populate a cache file that we then serve to the security tools.

docs.title: Export via SDK
docs.text:
We can generate the same list with PyMISP. The code is very similar to the API-based approach:

res = misp.search(
    controller="attributes",
    type_attribute=["ip-src", "ip-dst"],
    # to_ids=True, # Filter not working
    deleted=False,
    timestamp=last_days_unix,
    order="timestamp desc", # Filter not working asc/desc
    limit=config["export"]["last_ioc"],
    pythonify=False,
)

In my tests, however, I ran into some issues: the to_ids filter does not seem to work correctly, and neither does the sorting. The sorting issue directly affects the ability to retrieve the most recent IoCs.

At the moment, I prefer the API-based approach.

Both scripts are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Network simulators are a must
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner lab unetlab

For anyone working in IT, theory alone is not enough. Practical experience is crucial to grasp concepts and develop the skills needed to design, configure and manage complex environments. In the early 2000s, network administrators often bought second-hand hardware to build labs where they could study and experiment with configurations before deploying them in production.

Then virtualization arrived. It simplified the process and made labs accessible to many people without expensive hardware. Network administrators used simulators first, but they have since become foundational for the training of all IT professionals.

Today, it is unimaginable to work without simulated environments. Both professionals and students need them to experiment, study and stay up to date. Simulators were once mainly for network administrators, but now they include ready-made scenarios for both defensive and offensive security.

docs.title: The Benefits of Using Network Simulators
docs.text:
• Accessibility: from students to professionals, anyone can access complex network environments without expensive equipment.
  • Safety: we can run tests in a secure environment, without the risk of compromising real networks.
  • Flexibility: we can experiment with configurations that would be impractical or too risky on a real network.
  • Certification preparation: for those preparing for certifications like CCNA, CCNP and others, these tools provide a practical environment to practice.
  • Demos and PoCs: a simulated environment is ideal for showing technological solutions realistically.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Network simulators and emulators are now indispensable in IT training and research. They offer a safe, accessible and flexible way to experiment and learn, so we can acquire practical skills without the constraints of physical hardware. Whether you are a student aiming for a certification or a professional who wants to test new configurations, these tools are an essential part of your toolkit.

docs.title: iou-web the beginning
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

I have been working with network simulators since around 2011, when I decided to pursue my CCIE R&S certification. Around that time, another pivotal event set me on the path of development: Cisco released a binary called IOL (IOS on Linux), which essentially simulated a Cisco IOS router. Unlike other solutions, it required significantly fewer resources to simulate this router.

Back then, GNS3 was the only available option. It used Dynamips to emulate the hardware needed to run official IOS images. The emulated platforms were limited, though, and we had to optimize them manually to minimize resource usage. I faced two major issues that were deal-breakers for me:

  • I was working with two different computers, and synchronizing the environment between them with GNS3 was complicated.
  • The combination of GNS3 and Dynamips was unstable.

I decided to create my own interface to manage simulators based on IOL. After a few months, iou-web was born: a PHP-based web interface that orchestrated the creation and management of labs for IOL. My requirements were:

  • Portability: labs must be exportable and importable.
  • Stability: running labs must be stable and avoid crashes.
  • Performance: labs must run on a cheap laptop or VM.

Meanwhile, I discovered that Cisco had developed similar software internally, called WebIOL. WebIOL was developed in Perl and released exclusively to Cisco employees, with basic labs from the Cisco 360 program.

After a couple of alpha versions, I released iou-web publicly on January 23rd, 2012.

Unlike GNS3, which supported real IOS images via Dynamips, iou-web supported only IOL. IOL was faster than Dynamips, though, so many users preferred iou-web.

Basically, iou-web, often referred to as webiou, was a web interface for IOU. It allowed users to:

  • Create network topologies: build topologies for IOU easily through a user-friendly web interface.
  • Manage devices: start and stop devices with simple web-based controls.
  • Visualize topologies: view a graphical L2 diagram of the network topology for better understanding and management.

The old historical iou-web repository is available to the public on GitHub.

docs.title: UNetLab the evolution of iou-web
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

In 2013, I realized that iou-web was too limited. I needed a "unified" approach to emulate a network, including firewalls, load balancers and more. Multicasting with IOL was also problematic. I had several new prerequisites:

  • Include vendor virtual appliances in labs.
  • Integrate real IOS images in labs.
  • Possibly include emulators from different vendors.
  • Support multi-user environments.

I rewrote iou-web completely to create an extensible network emulator. The core idea was:

  • Each node (emulated device) must be attached to a common layer.
  • A suitable common layer is an Ethernet Linux bridge (with OVS support).

On October 6th, 2014, UNetLab, also known as UNL, was released to the public. It was developed in PHP with a REST API framework and a single-page application (jQuery), and within a few months it gained five to six hundred daily users. I wanted to name it UNL, but the website URL was not available.

Initially, I considered including Huawei eNSP, but eNSP nodes required a specific string, so nobody was able to run eNSP nodes outside of eNSP.

Thousands of people around the world used UNetLab every month. It gave me immense satisfaction and hands-on experience in managing widely distributed production software.

In 2015, because I had limited spare time, a group of enthusiasts forked UNetLab, and EVE-NG was released on January 5th, 2017. I am not part of the EVE-NG team.

In 2014, I had an interesting chat with a member of the Cisco VIRL team during CLEUR 2014 in Milan.

The old historical UNetLab repository is available to the public on GitHub.

Other resources that mention UNetLab:

  • Packet Pushers PQ Show 61: The UNetLab Project.
  • Approaches and algorithms of virtual telecommunication networks analysis in UNetLab environment (IEEE conference).

docs.title: UNetLab v2 addressing limitations
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner docker unetlab

In recent years, my focus has shifted towards network automation. I still need a unified network emulator platform, but the prerequisites have evolved. Before diving into the new requirements, let's highlight the limitations of UNetLab:

  • Per-host pod limit: each host can run up to 256 independent pods because of the console port limit.
  • Per-lab node limit: each pod or lab can run up to 127 nodes because of the console port limit.
  • Per-user pod limit: each user can run only one pod or lab at a time because of the console port limit.
  • Single host: there is no support for distributed installations of UNetLab (we can use OVS, but many frame types are filtered by default).
  • Config management: using expect scripts to get and put startup configurations is slow, unpredictable and cannot cover all node types.
  • No support for Dynamips serial interfaces.
  • No topology changes: by design, we cannot change the topology while the lab is running.

The console port limit exists because each node console has a fixed port, calculated as follows:

ts_port = 32768 + 128 * tenant_id + device_id

Moreover, no more than 512 IOL nodes can run in the same lab, because the device_id must be unique for each tenant.

UNetLab v2 must address these issues and meet new requirements:

  • Run a distributed lab (across local or geographically distributed nodes).
  • Support an unlimited number of nodes in a lab.
  • Allow each user to customize a lab without affecting the original copy.
  • Link the serial interfaces between IOL and Dynamips.
  • Configure the nodes via Ansible, NAPALM or other tools.

I knew how to create a distributed network emulator, but I needed an easy way to run nodes within a dedicated namespace. The answer came from vrnetlab: using Docker.

Because of the limitations of UNetLab, I decided to rewrite it from scratch. EVE-NG, a fork of UNetLab, works to overcome these limitations, but I pursued a new path.

docs.title: UNetLab v2 Architecture
docs.text:
The architecture may seem complex, but it was straightforward to implement.

UNetLab v2 was based on:

  • Docker: controllers, routers and lab nodes run inside Docker containers.
  • Python: replaces C, PHP and Bash with Python 3.
  • Python-Flask + NGINX: implements and exposes the APIs.
  • Memcached: caches authentication for a better user experience.
  • Celery + Redis: manages long asynchronous tasks in the background.
  • MariaDB: stores all the data, user information and running labs.
  • Git: manages version control for the original labs.
  • jQuery + Bootstrap: implements the UI as a single-page application.
  • iptables + Linux bridge: allows SSH connections to just-started lab nodes.
  • IOL, QEMU and Dynamips: run the lab nodes.

A UNetLab v2 cluster must have at least one node, which can be physical or virtual. The first node is the master and contains a controller and a router, while the additional nodes contain only routers. Each node also runs multiple lab nodes. Controllers, routers and lab nodes are Docker instances.

The controller container:

  • Exposes the web UI and the APIs to user clients, routers and lab nodes.
  • Receives registration requests from routers and lab nodes.
  • Manages lab nodes via routers.
  • Contacts lab nodes via Ansible, NAPALM, etc.
  • Provides routing tables to routers.
  • Is accessible via SSH on port 2222.

The router containers:

  • Register with the controller.
  • Expose the Docker Remote API and the lab node API.
  • Obtain routing tables from the controller.
  • Route lab packets between nodes and routers.
  • Ensure connectivity between the controller and the remote lab nodes via OpenVPN.

The node containers:

  • Register with the controller.
  • Run emulated nodes (IOL, Dynamips or QEMU).
  • Bind a management interface of the emulated nodes to a local bridge.
  • Route packets between the local router and the emulated node for the non-management interfaces.
  • Manage emulated links (up/down).

Since the controller and the routers know both the inside and the outside IP addresses, users can deploy UNetLab v2 nodes anywhere (in the same LAN, AWS, Google Compute Engine, Azure, behind a firewall). Each UNetLab v2 cluster requires the following ports:

  • TCP 2222: SSH connection to the controller.
  • TCP 80/443: HTTP/HTTPS requests to the controller.
  • TCP 5443: HTTPS requests to the router.
  • UDP 5005: routed packets between different UNetLab v2 nodes.
  • UDP 1194: network reachability between the controller and the remote lab nodes.

UNetLab v2 was never completed, but the source code is available on GitHub.

docs.title: UNetLab v3 wishing list
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

UNetLab v2 was a partly good idea, but some choices complicated the implementation and hurt performance. In particular, managing UNetLab's network in user space would have caused serious problems, even though it would have made horizontal scalability easier.

I also had a serious doubt: does it make sense to build my own virtualization system today, when several already exist and are maintained by companies that can do it far better than I can? I first considered ESXi, but after the Broadcom acquisition I leaned towards Proxmox. ESXi would have forced me to give up physical link simulation, while Proxmox lets me use the same strategy as in UNetLab.

Using an existing hypervisor greatly simplifies development, at the cost of a substantial sacrifice: systems such as IOL and Dynamips would no longer be supported. Dynamips is not a big loss, but IOL has always been my favorite system for building lightweight labs.

docs.title: UNetLab v3 Wishlist
docs.text:
I should split the list into functional and non-functional requirements, but for now let's simply build a wishlist together.

My hypothetical UNetLab v3 wishlist includes:

  • Free, open source and community-driven.
  • The ability to share labs, template repositories and playbooks easily.
  • Support for Ansible, Nornir, NAPALM and Netmiko playbooks.
  • A unified platform, focused on network and security labs.
  • Multi-user, multi-tenant and multi-role (e.g., student and teacher).
  • Easy scalability.
  • An API-first approach, with a CLI and a web interface.

Lab features:

  • Each lab is isolated by default.
  • Labs can be interconnected.
  • Labs can be shared between users.
  • A management network is deployed per lab.
  • The management network is hidden in the topology.
  • The management network is reachable by all nodes.
  • A DHCP server is deployed per lab.
  • An Internet gateway can be deployed per lab.
  • A fake Internet gateway can be deployed.
  • Labs are described by a human-readable YAML file.
  • Labs could contain an inventory compatible with Ansible.
  • Imported labs should allow selecting alternative templates if the original ones are not available.
  • Labs could be signed by users.
  • Live changes (jitter, delay, interface up/down) should be reflected immediately in the running lab.
  • Marketplace: a place where users and teachers can share labs and learning paths.
  • Automation: all relevant nodes in a lab should be reachable by automation software by default.
  • Packet capture: users should be able to capture packets from any interface.
  • Scale-out: labs could be run on multiple compute nodes.

Template features:

  • Templates are described by a YAML file.
  • The descriptor specifies the vendor, OS, version, management interface and credentials.
  • The vendor and OS fields should be defined to make templates compatible with external labs.
  • Plugins should be provided for node configuration.
  • Playbooks could be provided to configure specific node features (interfaces, OSPF, etc.).
  • Templates are preconfigured with DHCP, a user and a password.
  • Templates could be signed by users.

Link features:

  • Links can be L1 or L2.
  • L1 links are transparent bridges that forward any frame.
  • Bridges can connect a physical port to a lab to include physical devices (e.g., PLCs).

Node features:

  • Nodes could be configured automatically via playbooks (e.g., IP addresses, loopbacks, OSPF, CDP, LLDP).
  • Users can send commands to multiple nodes.
  • Users can send commands through a Jinja template.

Scalability:

  • L1 links are intra-host.
  • L2 links can be inter-host and used to span a lab across multiple hosts.

Teaching features:

  • Multi-tenancy: each teacher can manage an independent environment.
  • Classes: users are divided into classes within each tenant (class-level visibility).
  • Users should be able to start and possibly modify their lab (user-level visibility).
  • Shared access: users could access the same running lab.
  • Design mode: changing a lab should not affect running copies; any lab could be converted into a "template".
  • Solo mode: non-teachers should be able to write and run labs without worrying about classes or students.
  • Content writer: labs should include additional content, such as slides and videos.
  • Auto-evaluation: teachers could include scripts to evaluate users automatically.

Definitions:

  • Host: a system that runs nodes.
  • Lab: a topology that interconnects multiple nodes.
  • Node: a virtualized system, part of a lab, running on a host.
  • Link: a virtual network connection between nodes.
  • Template: the base image from which a node can be executed.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Developing UNetLab has been one of the most rewarding hobbies I have ever had. I have met many interesting people, most of whom I am still in touch with. It also taught me how critical it is to maintain software used worldwide without letting bugs disappoint its users. Sometimes, I still dream about developing UNetLab again.

docs.title: Proxmox optimizing virtualization
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner proxmox unetlab

During the development of the first version of UNetLab, I dedicated significant time to creating a flexible QEMU/KVM orchestrator. At that time, virtualization-ready images were rare. Choosing a specific QEMU version or parameter could determine the success or failure of virtualizing a particular device.

Years later, the landscape has changed completely: virtualization is almost always an option, because vendors use virtualized environments to build labs. Most vendors now release images for both VMware and QEMU/KVM.

IOU remains a topic of interest, though: it is a lightweight image that simulates a Cisco IOS XE environment. We can think of IOU as a container that does not use standard networking. It could be transformed into a container, but that is another story.

By forgoing IOU (and Dynamips), we can simplify virtualization management. Specifically, we can rely on an existing hypervisor. For years, I considered ESXi, but after the Broadcom acquisition, I explored other options. After analyzing various environments, including libvirt, I chose Proxmox for several reasons:

  • It runs on top of a standard Linux OS, which we can modify if needed.
  • It provides REST APIs, which we still need to verify.
  • It allows kernel modifications to simulate physical links.
  • It is well supported and under active development.
  • It is open source.
  • It scales horizontally and supports VXLAN.
  • It supports LXC natively (but not Docker).

On paper, Proxmox looks like the perfect base for UNetLab v3. During development, however, we want to abstract the interaction between UNetLab and Proxmox, so that we can substitute the hypervisor without rewriting code.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
Scalability is a key factor for UNetLab v3. UNetLab v1 was designed to scale up, i.e., by increasing the resources of the host, which is costly and limited.

For UNetLab v2, I considered implementing an MPLS-like network to simulate the physical links between nodes on different hosts. This had two issues:

  • Slow performance, because packets were handled in user space, not kernel space.
  • Complexity, because it required writing a new network protocol.

For UNetLab v3, I plan to use VXLAN to extend the networks between hosts. It has both advantages and disadvantages:

  • Hypervisors and operating systems support VXLAN natively.
  • VXLAN does not allow the simulation of physical links (some frames are filtered).

The solution is to divide the problem:

  • L1 links, implemented as in UNetLab v1, are intra-host only.
  • L2 links, implemented via VXLAN, extend labs across multiple hosts.
  • At lab startup, an algorithm defines groups of nodes on the same host and distributes them across the hosts, allowing user modifications.

The complexity lies in the last point, but it is theoretically feasible. The open question is whether we can move nodes between servers, and how to manage it.

By following these principles and leveraging modern tools, UNetLab v3 aims to be a powerful, flexible and scalable network emulator for the next generation of network professionals.

docs.title: Patching the Proxmox kernel
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced proxmox unetlab

Proxmox offers various constructs for building virtual networks. We focus on bridges to emulate physical links, as we did in UNetLab v1.

Linux bridges handle frames differently:

  • Broadcast frames are forwarded to all ports.
  • Multicast frames are forwarded to a subset of ports.
  • Peer-to-peer frames are not forwarded.
  • All other frames are forwarded to all ports.

The key files in the Linux kernel sources are br_input.c and br_sysfs_br.c.

In br_input.c, the br_handle_frame function decides whether to forward or discard a frame based on the destination MAC address. Frames with destination 0x01 are always discarded. A mask called fwd_mask affects the outcome of the function in some cases.

We want to introduce the mask concept for the 0x01 case as well.

In br_sysfs_br.c, the set_group_fwd_mask function sometimes prevents the evaluation of group_fwd_mask. We modify it to always evaluate the mask.

With the modified kernel, we can control the /sys/class/net/vmbr1/bridge/group_fwd_mask mask to enable or disable the forwarding of any packet. Our modified kernel accepts values up to 65535, which forwards any frame and achieves our goal.

docs.title: Compiling the Kernel
docs.text:
To compile a kernel for Proxmox, we need a system with Proxmox VE installed.

We install the dependencies:

apt-get install -y git build-essential dh-make dh-python sphinx-common asciidoc-base bison dwarves flex libdw-dev libelf-dev libiberty-dev libnuma-dev libslang2-dev libssl-dev lintian lz4 python3-dev xmlto zlib1g-dev

We remove the conflicting packages:

apt-get purge -y proxmox-headers\*

We check the installed kernel version:

uname -r

In the Proxmox kernel sources, we find the commit titled "update ABI file for 6.8.4-2-pve". The corresponding commit is 4cab886f26f9c8638593b8c553996c97ca9acc21.

We clone the repository:

git clone git://git.proxmox.com/git/pve-kernel.git /usr/src/pve-kernel
cd /usr/src/pve-kernel

We check out the specific version:

git checkout 4cab886f26f9c8638593b8c553996c97ca9acc21
make clean
make build-dir-fresh

We modify /usr/src/pve-kernel/Makefile, adding -unl to the EXTRAVERSION variable. Then we edit br_input.c and br_sysfs_br.c in /usr/src/pve-kernel/submodules/ubuntu-kernel/net/bridge.

We compile the kernel:

make

We install the newly compiled packages on each Proxmox host:

dpkg -i /usr/src/pve-kernel/unl.deb

docs.title: Enabling the Transparent Bridge
docs.text:
We activate the patch by modifying the mask of each bridge:

echo 65535 > /sys/class/net/br1/bridge/group_fwd_mask

docs.title: Updating the Patch
docs.text:
The unetlab-kernel repository contains updated scripts and precompiled packages. To update the patch:

  • Save the original br_input.c and br_sysfs_br.c files in a safe location.
  • Modify the files according to the latest patch.
  • Create a new patch with diff -Naur.
  • Update the patch.

The precompiled patches and packages are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Creating templates for Proxmox
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate proxmox unetlab

Let's prepare the templates that generate the nodes of our labs. We start with VyOS, an open-source router and firewall. VyOS is available as a rolling release and can be downloaded in ISO format from GitHub. In this example, we use the vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso image, downloaded to /usr/src on a Proxmox host.

The official documentation guides us through creating a VyOS node on Proxmox. We go through the steps to create a VyOS template and a basic lab with two interconnected VyOS nodes.

On my Proxmox host, I added an external disk named unetlab to store the ISO images:

pvesh get /nodes/proxmox1/storage

pvesh is the CLI for the Proxmox REST APIs. Learning it now simplifies our future interactions with Proxmox hosts via API.

The Proxmox documentation tells us the required location for the ISO file. We copy the downloaded file and import it:

cp /usr/src/vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso /var/tmp/pveupload-0001
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/storage/unetlab/upload -content iso -filename vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso -tmpfilename /var/tmp/pveupload-0001

We verify that the ISO file is available:

pvesh get /nodes/proxmox1/storage/unetlab/content

Next, we create and configure the virtual machine so that it:

  • Boots from the ISO image.
  • Has a dedicated management network interface.

We use the parameters from the Proxmox documentation and the VyOS documentation:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu -tags unl,template -name template-vyos-vyos-202407171706 -vmid 9001 -cpu host -socket 1 -cores 1 -memory 2048 -scsihw virtio-scsi-single -scsi0 unetlab:2 -net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0 -serial0 socket -ostype other -cdrom unetlab:iso/vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso

We established a naming and tagging standard for our Proxmox templates: each template has a prefix, and every object is tagged with unl and a specific tag relevant to the object.

We start the node and configure it via CLI:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/status/start

We access the console via the web interface or the CLI:

qm terminal 9001

If the console is occupied, we free it with:

killall socat

The default credentials are:

  • Username: vyos.
  • Password: vyos.

We install the OS on the disk and reboot:

install image
reboot

We configure the device with a management VRF and an interface configured via DHCP:

configure
set vrf name mgmt
set vrf name mgmt table 100
set interfaces ethernet eth0 vrf mgmt
set interfaces ethernet eth0 address dhcp
delete interfaces ethernet eth0 hw-id
commit
save

We configure only one network interface for now: additional interfaces are added when we create nodes from the template. In VyOS, each interface is initially assigned a specific MAC address. To use a node as a template, we remove this association with hw-id.

We exit the console and shut down the node:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/status/stop

We remove the CD-ROM drive, which is no longer needed, and convert the node to a template:

pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/config -delete cdrom
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/config -boot legacy=c
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/template

With these steps, we created a reusable VyOS template for Proxmox.

docs.title: Simulating an L1 link in Proxmox
Simulating an L1 link in Proxmox
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced lab proxmox unetlab

We now have all the elements needed to simulate an L1 link. Let's create a simple lab with two interconnected VyOS nodes.

docs.title: Create an L1 Network Bridge
docs.text:
First, we create a network bridge that simulates the L1 link. We start by defining a naming convention for our network components:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/network -iface unlbr1 -type bridge -autostart 1
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/network

docs.title: Clone VyOS Nodes from the Template
docs.text:
Next, we clone two VyOS nodes from the template and connect a second network interface to the newly created bridge:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/clone -newid 10001 -full 0 -name node-vyos1
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/clone -newid 10002 -full 0 -name node-vyos2
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/config -tags unl,root
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10002/config -tags unl,root
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/config -net1 virtio,bridge=unlbr1
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10002/config -net1 virtio,bridge=unlbr1

docs.title: Start the VyOS Nodes
docs.text:
We start the two VyOS nodes:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/status/start
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10002/status/start

We wait a few minutes for the nodes to boot, then we configure the new network interfaces.

docs.title: Configure the Network Interfaces and Enable LLDP
docs.text:
On each node, we configure the new network interface and enable the LLDP protocol to validate the patch:

configure
set service lldp
set service lldp interface all
set interfaces ethernet eth1 address '192.168.0.1/24'
commit
save

docs.title: Enable the Forwarding of All Frames
docs.text:
To enable the forwarding of all frames, we run the following commands:

echo 65535 > /sys/class/net/unlbr1/bridge/group_fwd_mask
echo 0 > /sys/devices/virtual/net/unlbr1/bridge/multicast_snooping

Each L1 link requires a manual command to enable the forwarding of all frames. Currently, we cannot perform this operation through the API, but we will revisit it in the future.

docs.title: Verify Connectivity
docs.text:
If everything is configured correctly, we should see the adjacent router via the LLDP protocol:

show lldp neighbors

Capability Codes: R - Router, B - Bridge, W - Wlan r - Repeater, S - Station
                  D - Docsis, T - Telephone, O - Other

Device    Local Port    Protocol    Capability    Platform                          Remote
Port
--------  ------------  ----------  ------------  --------------------------------  ------
--------------
vyos      eth1          LLDP        R             VyOS 1.5-rolling-202407171706     eth1

We can confirm that the two nodes see each other via the LLDP protocol, which bridges typically filter.

docs.title: Testing stretched networks with Proxmox
docs.text: 04 August 2024

docs.title: Testing stretched networks with Proxmox
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced proxmox unetlab

Let's explore how the SDN functionality of Proxmox works. We use the SDN structure to implement extended L2 networks, so that we can run labs across multiple hosts.

docs.title: Create an SDN Zone
docs.text:
First, we create a zone:

pvesh create /cluster/sdn/zones -type=vxlan -zone=unlzone1 -peers=172.25.82.157,172.25.82.158 -ipam=pve
pvesh set /cluster/sdn/zones

In the peers list, we add the IP addresses of all the Proxmox hosts.

docs.title: Create a Bridge Associated with the Zone
docs.text:
Next, we create a bridge linked to the zone to connect the nodes:

pvesh create /cluster/sdn/vnets -vnet=unlnet1 -tag=1000004 -zone=unlzone1
pvesh set /cluster/sdn/zones

Then we associate the network with the nodes as shown in the previous steps.

If everything is configured correctly, nodes running on different hosts can ping each other, using both the native VLAN and a tagged VLAN.

docs.title: Design Considerations
docs.text:
From a design perspective, we need to decide how to manage zones and networks within UNetLab: should we create a single zone with all the Vnets, or a zone for each Vnet?

According to the official documentation, a zone defines a virtually separated network. The documentation lacks detail, so we need to understand the constructs created at the OS level.

When we created the zone, we specified the IP addresses of the Proxmox hosts that share it. Proxmox writes this configuration to /etc/pve/sdn/zones.cfg and generates the /etc/network/interfaces.d/sdn file. There are no network namespace configurations (ip netns).

We can deduce that the zone is a Proxmox-defined structure that translates into VXLAN interfaces. Since UNetLab does not use L3 networks, we can use a single zone for the entire UNetLab cluster.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
During my first test, the two VyOS nodes could not communicate. By connecting to the two Proxmox servers via SSH, we can see how the SDN configuration translates at the OS level.

The network interfaces of the nodes are associated with a bridge:

brctl show unlnet3

bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
unlnet3         8000.6659fe6b9723       no              tap10001i1
                                                        vxlan_unlnet3

The TAP interface belongs to the node, while the VXLAN interface allows communication with the nodes on other hosts.

We check the forwarding table for frames with:

bridge fdb show | grep vxlan

66:59:fe:6b:97:23 dev vxlan_unlnet3 vlan 1 master unlnet3 permanent
66:59:fe:6b:97:23 dev vxlan_unlnet3 master unlnet3 permanent
00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan_unlnet3 dst 172.25.82.158 self permanent
ba:2f:72:71:47:0a dev vxlan_unlnet4 vlan 1 master unlnet4 permanent
ba:2f:72:71:47:0a dev vxlan_unlnet4 master unlnet4 permanent
00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan_unlnet4 dst 172.25.82.158 self permanent

The MAC addresses on the left should match the network interfaces of the nodes running on the remote host. In my case, the remote VyOS node had its network interfaces reversed, which resulted in an incorrect connection.

We can verify further by analyzing the traffic between the hosts:

tcpdump -i vmbr0 -nn udp and port 4789

IP 192.168.0.1 > 192.168.0.3: ICMP echo request, id 35144, seq 2, length 64
13:02:10.899649 IP 172.25.82.158.46121 > 172.25.82.157.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000
IP 192.168.0.3 > 192.168.0.1: ICMP echo reply, id 35144, seq 2, length 64
13:02:11.900765 IP 172.25.82.157.35416 > 172.25.82.158.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000
IP 192.168.0.1 > 192.168.0.3: ICMP echo request, id 35144, seq 3, length 64
13:02:11.901642 IP 172.25.82.158.46121 > 172.25.82.157.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000
IP 192.168.0.3 > 192.168.0.1: ICMP echo reply, id 35144, seq 3, length 64
13:02:12.902939 IP 172.25.82.157.35416 > 172.25.82.158.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000

docs.title: Lab modeling for UNetLab v3
docs.text: 13 September 2024

docs.title: Lab modeling for UNetLab v3
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner lab unetlab

We ran a series of field tests to check whether the idea we are working on is feasible and functional. The results are positive: the APIs support most of the key features (but not all).

Our next step is to define and model the data structure of the lab environment.

One of the main issues of UNetLab was that users had to build a lab manually, node by node, setting up interfaces, addresses and routing before getting a functional environment. We address this by introducing two states:

  • HLL (High Level Lab): a rough outline of the lab in terms of nodes, links and features.
  • LLL (Low Level Lab): a detailed lab generated from the HLL.

Below, we describe the data structure. Full examples are available in the UNetLab repository.

docs.title: Nodes and Features
docs.text:
Here is an example with 4 VyOS nodes configured with a loopback and OSPF on all interfaces:

nodes:
  - template: vyos-vyos
    prefix: R
    count: 4
    features:
      - loopback
      - ospf:area=0

Features reference specific Ansible playbooks that configure each node. Variables can be passed with :. The nodes are named R1, R2, R3 and R4.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
The 4 nodes can be connected in a full mesh:

topologies:
  - type: full-mesh
    match:
      - R

Or in a custom topology:

topologies:
  - type: defined
    links:
      - R1, R2, R3
      - R1, R4
      - R3, R4

You can also mix and match topologies:

topologies:
  - type: full-mesh
    match:
      - Site1R
  - type: full-mesh
    match:
      - Site2R
  - type: defined
    links:
      - Site1R1, Site2R1
      - Site1R2, Site2R2

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
Addressing is defined like this:

ipv4_addresses:
  - match: Loopback
    address: 192.168.0.1/16
    mask: 32
  - match: Ethernet
    address: 10.0.0.0/8
    mask: auto

Addressing is configured interface by interface, using the first match. The subnet mask can be set manually or automatically. In the latter case, the interfaces are assigned as follows:

  • Loopback interfaces get a /32 subnet.
  • Tunnel interfaces get a /31 subnet.
  • Ethernet interfaces get the smallest subnet needed to cover all the connected hosts.

To keep it simple, network allocation follows a sequential order based on the first available segment.

In the example above:

  • Loopback interfaces get an address starting from the 192.168.0.1/32 network.
  • Ethernet interfaces get an address starting from the 10.0.0.0 network, with the smallest mask required for all the expected addresses.

Interfaces not involved in the topology are disabled.

docs.title: From HLL to LLL
docs.text:
Once the user has defined the HLL, they can confirm it and generate the detailed topology (the LLL). Any change made to the HLL regenerates the LLL, overwriting any customizations. It will be possible to modify the LLL, which from that point on becomes the only relevant version.

Here is an example of what the LLL might look like:

lll:
  groups:
    - name: Nodes R (vyos-vyos)
      template: vyos-vyos
      match: R
      features:
        - loopback
        - ospf:area=0
  nodes:
    - id: 6964F62C-0376-4ECF-8F03-E1FEADB94194
      name: R1
      interfaces:
        Loopback0:
          ipv4_address: 192.168.0.1/32
        Ethernet1:
          ipv4_address: 10.0.0.0/31
        Ethernet2:
          ipv4_address: 10.0.0.2/31
        Ethernet3:
          ipv4_address: 10.0.0.4/31

Links can be generated like this:

links:
  - id: 9E510FC0-B9D6-459E-9EF0-9113607D2502
    name: R1:Ethernet1 - R2:Ethernet1
    interfaces:
      - node_id: 6964F62C-0376-4ECF-8F03-E1FEADB94194
        interface: Ethernet1
      - node_id: 210827C6-9E59-4CCE-80AC-FD294DDC205E
        interface: Ethernet1

docs.title: Customizations
docs.text:
Once the LLL has been generated, the user can customize it without altering the HLL, which is preserved for historical reasons.

Each node can be modified individually or through a group, with node-specific settings taking priority over group settings.

Links can be customized in terms of bandwidth, delay and packet drop.

docs.title: Management Network
docs.text: The management network is mandatory: management interfaces are reserved and therefore not considered by the LLL.

docs.title: Internet Connectivity
docs.text: In this initial approach, we did not include Internet connectivity. We can imagine a special node that, once connected to the topology, enables Internet access.

docs.title: Lab Interconnection
docs.text:
In this first version, we did not consider linking labs together. We can envision special shared links that allow multiple labs to interconnect.

Since each link references a virtual network, once a virtual network is defined it can be attached to all labs using its UUID.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Any metadata describing the lab is grouped under a specific key:

meta:
  author: Andrea Dainese
  name: Test Lab 1
  description: First test lab

docs.title: Working on a Lab
docs.text:
When a user wants to work on a specific lab (run it or modify it), a copy with a unique UUID is created. Depending on the permissions, this copy can be read, modified or executed. The user always works on the instance copy and never on the original.

Based on the permissions, the user can save the copy by overwriting the original or by saving it as a new copy. Users running a copy do not see any changes unless they reload it from the original.

Closing a lab means deleting the instance copy and all the associated files.

To make node names editable, each node is assigned a UUID. Interface names are static and depend on the node type (template).

docs.title: UNetLab v3 architecture
docs.text: 23 October 2024

docs.title: UNetLab v3 architecture
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

The architecture of UNetLab involves several components that must interact with each other and report the progress of tasks to the user. We can identify the following components:

  • The web interface lets users interact with UNetLab and manage users and labs.
  • The Proxmox hosts manage the nodes and networks of the labs according to the instructions received from the users, and notify the status of the nodes.
  • The orchestrator is the engine that manages the tasks and the input received from the user through the web interface and from the hosts through a specific agent.

docs.title: The Orchestrator
docs.text:
At first glance, we can imagine a Redis server that collects the input from the users (via the web interface) and from the hosts. The orchestrator receives the messages from Redis, transforms them and forwards them to the web interface or to the agents running on the hosts.

In this sense, the orchestrator is a background daemon.

We can imagine two types of data stored in Redis:

  • Actions: for example, starting a specific node.
  • Messages: for example, a notification that a node started successfully.

docs.title: The Web Interface
docs.text: The web interface is served through Django. It receives the user input and transforms it into tasks sent to the orchestrator via Redis. Similarly, it receives the messages used to notify users via Redis.

docs.title: The Agent
docs.text:
On the Proxmox hosts, we can envision an agent that:

  • Executes the requested actions, such as starting a node.
  • Notifies the outcome of the requested actions.
  • Regularly reports the status of the system (host, nodes, templates, networks...).
  • Executes actions that Proxmox does not support natively (see the L1 links mentioned before).

Regarding the status notifications, we can imagine that the agent reports only the actual changes, to reduce the workload of the orchestrator and the web interface. If you recall, the old version of UNetLab polled continuously to check the status of the nodes. This put a significant burden on both the client-side web interface and the server-side resources.

We can also imagine that, at regular intervals, the agent sends a complete set of information to avoid any discrepancy that might grow over time.

The system status should include:

  • Host status: reachability and resources used.
  • Data store status: available space and user quota usage.
  • Network status: which networks are available and their type (L1, L2).
  • Node status: which nodes are available, whether they are on or off, resource consumption, associated users and associated images.
  • Image status: which images are available and their characteristics.

docs.title: Preparing a Proxmox cluster for UNetLab v3
docs.text: 30 September 2024

docs.title: Preparing a Proxmox cluster for UNetLab v3
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate proxmox unetlab

UNetLab requires a cluster with one or more correctly configured PVE hosts. This page contains all the commands needed to configure a PVE host.

docs.title: Install the Custom Kernel for UNetLab
docs.text:
To enable L1 links, UNetLab needs a kernel with a specific patch. The kernel and the patch are released in the unetlab-kernel repository. You can either download the correct release or compile your own with the provided script.

To download the custom kernel, run the following commands:

cd /usr/src
export TAG=6.8.8-3
wget https://github.com/dainok/unetlab-kernel/releases/download/${TAG}/proxmox-headers-${TAG}-pve-unl_${TAG}_amd64.deb
wget https://github.com/dainok/unetlab-kernel/releases/download/${TAG}/proxmox-kernel-${TAG}-pve-unl_${TAG}_amd64.deb

Now install the custom kernel:

apt-get update
apt-get install -y build-essential
dpkg -i proxmox-*-${TAG}-pve-unl_${TAG}_amd64.deb

When it is done, reboot the host:

reboot

docs.title: Add Nodes to the Cluster
docs.text:
Create a cluster and add the current node:

pvesh create /cluster/config -clustername unetlab -nodeid 1

Retrieve the fingerprint value with the following command:

pvesh get /cluster/config/join -output-format json-pretty | grep pve_fp

Next, add the remaining hosts to the cluster by running the following command on each host:

pvesh create /cluster/config/join -fingerprint <pve_fp> -hostname <primary_ip> -password <root_password>

Finally, verify that all nodes have been added:

pvesh get /cluster/config/nodes

docs.title: Configure a Dedicated Datastore
docs.text:
In this specific case, a separate disk is dedicated to UNetLab. Let's partition, format and mount it:

echo "start=2048, type=83" | sfdisk /dev/sdb
mkfs -t ext4 /dev/sdb1
mkdir /unetlab
echo "/dev/sdb1 /unetlab ext4 defaults 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
mount /unetlab

Before proceeding, repeat the same operation on any other Proxmox host.

Next, add the directory so that it can be used as a datastore:

pvesh create /storage -storage unetlab -type dir -path /unetlab -shared 0 -nodes proxmox1,proxmox2 -content images,rootdir,iso,vztmpl

docs.title: Preparing VyOS image for UNetLab v3
docs.text: 30 October 2024

docs.title: Preparing VyOS image for UNetLab v3
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate proxmox unetlab

As our first image, we choose VyOS, which is publicly available on GitHub. We work from a single host, and later we can distribute our image. Let's download the image to the host:

wget -O- https://github.com/vyos/vyos-nightly-build/releases/download/1.5-rolling-202409220007/vyos-1.5-rolling-202409220007-generic-amd64.iso > /var/tmp/pveupload-0000

The file name must strictly follow the regex /var/tmp/pveupload-[0-9a-f]+.

We upload the image to the unetlab datastore with the correct name:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/storage/unetlab/upload -content iso -filename vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.iso -tmpfilename /var/tmp/pveupload-0000

We delete the image from the temporary directory:

rm -f /var/tmp/pveupload*

docs.title: Preparing the Template
docs.text:
Next, we create a temporary VM to install and configure VyOS:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu -cores 1 -cpu host -cdrom unetlab:iso/vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.iso,media=cdrom -memory 2048 -name template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007 -net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0 -ostype other -scsihw virtio-scsi-single -sockets 1 -tags "unl;template" -virtio0 unetlab:2,format=qcow2,backup=1,iothread=on -vmid 1000 -serial0 socket -vga none

In this case, we disabled the graphics card and added a serial interface to use as a terminal.

We start the virtual machine:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/status/start

At this point, we open the console of the VM from the web interface of the Proxmox host. We log in with the user vyos and the password vyos, then install the operating system on the disk with the command:

install image

The installation guides us through a few questions:

[...]
Would you like to continue? [y/N] y
What would you like to name this image? (Default: 1.5-rolling-202409220007)
Please enter a password for the "vyos" user:
Please confirm password for the "vyos" user:
What console should be used by default? (K: KVM, S: Serial)? (Default: S)
[...]
Which one should be used for installation? (Default: /dev/vda)
Installation will delete all data on the drive. Continue? [y/N] y
[...]
Would you like to use all the free space on the drive? [Y/n]
[...]
Which file would you like as boot config? (Default: 1)
[...]

Once the installation is complete, we reboot the node with the reboot command.

As soon as the node is back online, we configure it for UNetLab. Specifically, we set up a management interface, ideally in a dedicated VRF:

configure
set vrf name mgmt
set vrf name mgmt table 100
set interfaces ethernet eth0 vrf mgmt
set interfaces ethernet eth0 address dhcp
set service ssh vrf mgmt
delete interfaces ethernet eth0 hw-id
commit
save

We shut down the node:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/status/shutdown

We remove the CD-ROM and set the boot order:

pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/config -delete cdrom
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/config -boot legacy=c

Now we convert the node into a template:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/template

docs.title: Verifying the Template
docs.text:
Before continuing, let's verify that the template works correctly. We create a node from the template and check that the first interface gets an IP address via DHCP, and that SSH access works with the username and password:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/clone -newid 10001 -full 0 -name node-vyos1
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/config -tags "unl;node;user_root" -net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/status/start

Once finished, we shut down the node and delete it:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/status/stop
pvesh delete /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001

If the template has issues, we can convert it back to a VM and reconfigure it:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/config -template 0

docs.title: Backup and Export
docs.text:
Finally, we create a backup:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/vzdump -storage local -vmid 1000 -mode stop

We can retrieve the file /var/lib/vz/dump/vzdump-qemu-1000-*.vma*, which is the image of our template. We can use this file to recreate the template on other nodes. For simplicity, we rename it to vzdump-qemu-template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.vma.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
If the unetlab datastore is not shared among all the hosts in the cluster, we copy the backup to the other hosts:

scp /var/lib/vz/dump/template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.vma root@172.25.82.158:/var/lib/vz/dump

Then we import the backup, assigning a new ID to the template:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox2/qemu -vmid 1001 -archive local:backup/vzdump-qemu-template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.vma

docs.title: Developing UNetLab v3 with AI (LLM)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ai beginner unetlab

UNetLab v3 is built on Django along with various other frameworks. I am not a professional developer, nor do I consider myself one, yet I am often told that my prototypes are extremely useful, especially because I can build them in very short timeframes.

Since software development is not my main job, however, my coding activity is irregular, and long breaks between projects make me lose familiarity with the syntax. In the past, Google was my primary tool: I constantly searched for code snippets and constructs just to recall the correct syntax. Using the official documentation, Googling for suggestions and searching for examples to solve specific problems was very time-consuming.

With the advent of "artificial intelligence", I experimented with different approaches until I found a more efficient workflow that I now use successfully.

docs.title: ChatGPT for Code Generation
docs.text:
A couple of years ago, I started using ChatGPT to generate the code I needed directly. My prompts were along these lines:

Create a Python function using Netmiko to connect to a Cisco device, elevate privileges, retrieve the MAC address table, parse it with TextFSM, and return a dictionary where the keys are interface names and the values are lists of MAC addresses.

At the time, the results were almost always subpar: the generated code often included fictional functions and generally did not work.

Adapting the generated code took longer than writing it from scratch.

Moreover, describing in detail what I want takes significant time for my needs: converting my ideas into descriptive text always leads to incomplete or oversimplified instructions.

docs.title: Copilot in Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
About a year ago, I tried a second approach. Following a colleague's suggestion, I enabled GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code and started using it as a coding assistant. The experience was insightful because it made me reflect on my own workflow.

At first there was a "WOW" effect: Copilot seemed to understand what I needed and proactively suggested code snippets. I no longer had to write prompts, and the interaction felt more natural.

I soon realized, however, that the constant suggestions of Copilot were disrupting my mental flow.

When I code, I enter a focused mental state where I translate my ideas into code, following a "red thread" of logic as I go. The suggestions of Copilot interrupted this state and triggered my critical-thinking mode, since each suggestion needs to be evaluated in context.

Switching back and forth between these two mental modes was exhausting. At some point, I began to trust the suggestions of Copilot subconsciously, losing control over my own code.

There was a specific incident where I had to debug a faulty function. Copilot suggested a fix that looked perfect, and I trusted it. I adapted the rest of the code to that function, only to discover an hour later that the suggestion contained a structural flaw, which invalidated all the subsequent modifications.

I lost an hour and had to spend another hour dismantling and rewriting everything correctly.

That was when I understood what was happening. I disabled Copilot and returned to my usual workflow.

I wrote a LinkedIn post about it, expecting a flame war, but I received valuable feedback instead, mostly about the way I approach coding.

Still, as mentioned, programming is only a side activity for me, needed to build prototypes that others will industrialize later. It does not make sense for me to formalize a "proper" development workflow: others will always do it better than I can.

docs.title: Building Complete Apps with Replit
docs.text:
More recently, new generative tools have emerged that promise to build entire applications. Many testimonials claim they created fully functional prototypes in just a few hours. Curious but skeptical, I decided to try Replit.

I asked it to generate a Django app for managing firewall rules. As I said, describing a software project fully is challenging, especially during the prototyping phase, when requirements are incomplete and feasibility is still uncertain.

I was not looking for a finished product, but for a starting structure: a skeleton with models, views and templates already set up.

Initially, Replit generated a Flask app. I appreciate Flask, but I prefer Django for larger, more complex projects. I asked Replit to convert the app to Django. It replaced some code and showed me a preview of the requested app, suggesting that it was working correctly in the Replit backend.

The reality was different: the code was a hybrid of Flask, Django and non-existent functions, completely non-functional.

There is also the infamous case of a similar service, Builder.ai, which turned out to be powered by a team of human developers behind the scenes: essentially a scam to attract millions in funding.

docs.title: ChatGPT as a Tutor
docs.text:
Recently, I received an important piece of advice: use LLMs as mentors, asking for guidance, not code. I greatly respect the person who suggested this, so I gave it a try.

Using an LLM as a tutor means asking how to do something, not to do it. Specifically, I started asking:

  • How to achieve a specific feature in Django.
  • Where a specific function is used in Django.
  • Which approaches exist to solve a particular problem.

This approach has proven effective because:

  • I stay focused until I hit a specific issue that requires further analysis.
  • I can ask targeted questions without worrying about edge cases (I handle them myself).
  • I can take only what I need, adapt the code and style, and integrate it coherently.
  • Most importantly, I get a single interface for documentation, examples and community knowledge.

Over the last two months, this method let me resume work on UNetLab v3, stalled for over a year, and make significant progress. I implemented WebSockets, replaced RQ with Celery, and built robust APIs with comprehensive error handling.

docs.title: How LLMs Work
docs.text:
It is important to understand how an LLM works. I am not the best person to provide a full technical explanation, but I can share my perspective.

In simple terms, LLMs are statistical models that generate outputs based on input patterns and probabilistic associations. They do not think or understand. The concept of "thinking" is arguably philosophical, and I believe computers will never truly possess it, as thought is not purely mechanical.

LLMs also do not "hallucinate": they simply produce text without any concept of reality. Reality cannot be derived from statistical affinity.

Using LLMs (even as tutors) requires keeping this in mind:

  • The output must always be verified.
  • The output style can vary (lack of consistency).

I noticed that LLM-generated code may alternate between single and double quotes, may or may not include comments, may mix snake_case with camelCase, and sometimes uses outdated or imaginary functions.

docs.title: Reverse Engineering
docs.text:
On rare occasions, I had to read the source code of a framework to understand its behavior or fix specific bugs. Reverse engineering is extremely time-consuming, especially when the code is highly optimized.

Sometimes I used LLMs to explain the purpose of a particular function. Occasionally I found useful insights, but often I did not.
